meta.publicPolicy: Only Karnataka/Kannada-connected candidates are projected into the public generated module. BharatRajya is never used as the final citation; underlying sources require item-level verification.

kingdoms.name: Adi
kingdoms.description: The Adi (formerly called 'Abor'), among the largest peoples of Arunachal, governed by the powerful 'kebang' village council and long resistant to outside control.

kingdoms.name: Ahmadnagar Sultanate
kingdoms.description: The Nizam Shahi sultanate, one of the five states the Bahmani kingdom broke into. It joined the alliance that won at Talikota in 1565 and annexed Berar in 1574. Chand Bibi held the fort against Akbar's army through a siege of four months.

kingdoms.name: Ahom Kingdom
kingdoms.description: Tai-Ahom kingdom that ruled the Brahmaputra valley for 600 years; ceded to the British in 1826 after the Burmese invasion.
kingdoms.spanNote: Extended 23 Sept 2026: Purandar Singh's Upper Assam, 1833-38 (HCIP IX pp. 134-135).

kingdoms.name: Alwar
kingdoms.description: A Rajput state of eastern Rajputana.

kingdoms.name: Anuradhapura Kingdom
kingdoms.description: The first Sinhalese kingdom, and one of the longest-lived states in Asian history. Rajaraja Chola I sacked Anuradhapura in 993, and Rajendra I ended the kingdom in 1017 by capturing Mahinda V, who died in exile in India.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Sena II; Mahinda IV; Mahinda V

kingdoms.name: Apatani
kingdoms.description: The Apatani of the Ziro valley, renowned worldwide for sustainable wet-rice and fish cultivation and their self-governing 'bulyang' councils.

kingdoms.name: Awadh
kingdoms.description: Wealthy Nawabi kingdom of Awadh (Oudh); annexed by the British in 1856, a key grievance of 1857.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Asaf-ud-Daula, Ghazi-ud-Din Haidar, Saadat Ali Khan II, Saadat Khan, Safdar Jang, Shuja-ud-Daula, Wajid Ali Shah.

kingdoms.name: Ay kingdom
kingdoms.description: The oldest ruling line of south Kerala, holding the ports and hills around Vizhinjam. The Pandyas sacked Vizhinjam c. 765 and the Velvikkudi plates record the Ay-Vel suppressed c. 788, but the house outlasted its conquerors — its Sangam-era roots are far older than this atlas.

kingdoms.name: Ayudha dynasty of Kannauj
kingdoms.description: The short line that held Kannauj between Yashovarman and the Pratihara conquest — and became the prize everyone else fought over: Vatsaraja defeated Indrayudha, Dharmapala deposed him for Chakrayudha, and Nagabhata II swept Chakrayudha aside. The tripartite struggle in miniature.

kingdoms.name: Bahawalpur State
kingdoms.description: A princely state along the Sutlej/Indus; acceded to Pakistan and merged in 1955.

kingdoms.name: Bahmani Sultanate
kingdoms.description: The first Muslim kingdom of the Deccan, proclaimed at Gulbarga in 1347 by Hasan Gangu as Alauddin Bahman Shah when the Deccan nobles threw off Delhi. It broke into five sultanates — Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar and Berar.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Ahmad Shah Wali, Alauddin Bahman Shah, Firuz Shah, Humayun Shah, Mahmud Gawan as minister, Mahmud Shah Bahmani II, Muhammad Shah I-II, later puppet sultans.

kingdoms.name: Baloch
kingdoms.description: Not a single state but the Baloch country of the eastern Balochistan hills — Sibi, Kachhi, Zhob and Loralai — held by tribal chiefs rather than a dynasty while Arab, Ghaznavid and Mughal power claimed overlordship over it in turn. Mapped here after Schwartzberg.

kingdoms.name: Baltistan & Gilgit (local rulers)
kingdoms.description: Baltistan (Maqpon of Skardu) and the Gilgit/Hunza/Nagar principalities; absorbed into Dogra J&K in the 1840s.
kingdoms.spanNote: Hunza, Nagar, Chilas and Ghizer stayed with their own rulers past 1848 (HCIP IX).

kingdoms.name: Bangladesh
kingdoms.description: The People's Republic of Bangladesh — independent from Pakistan after the 1971 Liberation War.

kingdoms.name: Banswara State
kingdoms.description: A southern Rajputana state of the Bagar country, parted from Dungarpur in 1527 under a junior Sisodia line; Rawal Pratap submitted to Akbar in 1576 (Bakshi vol. 2 p. 26). Merged into Rajasthan in 1948.

kingdoms.name: Baroda (Gaekwad)
kingdoms.description: A leading Maratha-origin princely state in Gujarat, held by the Gaekwads from the 1720s and one of the five entitled to a salute of twenty-one guns.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Gaekwad dynasty; reformer Sayajirao Gaekwad III

kingdoms.name: Chindaka Naga (Chakrakota)
kingdoms.description: The Chindaka Nagas of Chakrakota - the old name of Bastar - ruled the Dandakaranya interior from Barsur, appearing about 1023 in the train of Rajendra Chola's army. Intermittently feudatory to the Cholas and Chalukyas and raided by the Kalachuris, the line is traced in inscriptions to Harischandra in 1324, when Annamadeva's Bastar state succeeds it.

kingdoms.name: Bastar State
kingdoms.description: A large forested state of the Chhattisgarh plateau, among the biggest princely states of India by area and among the smallest by revenue.
kingdoms.spanNote: One state from c. 1324 under Annamadeva. The Kakatiya descent is a dynastic CLAIM resting on a 1703 text, not established fact, and rule passed through the female line to the Bhanj Deo house in 1936 — so the state is continuous even where the dynasty label is not. Merged into India 1 January 1948.

kingdoms.name: Benares State
kingdoms.description: The Kashi Naresh’s state around Varanasi. The family’s power dates from Mansa Ram in 1737 and the Raja held a wide zamindari under Awadh and then the Company; after 1794 he kept only a family domain, and a princely state was re-created for him in 1911 with a 13-gun salute.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Balwant Singh and Chait Singh in the 18th century; Vibhuti Narayan Singh at the merger

kingdoms.name: Bengal (Nawab)
kingdoms.description: Semi-independent Mughal province; passed to British control after Plassey (1757) and the grant of Diwani (1765).

kingdoms.name: Bengal Sultanate
kingdoms.description: Bengal as an independent sultanate, from Ilyas Shah's seizure of Lakhnauti and Sonargaon in 1342. He pushed the frontier west to Banaras, bringing Firuz Tughluq's army down on him. Delhi never recovered it; the Mughals took it after breaking the Karranis.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Alauddin Husain Shah, Ghiyasuddin Azam, Ilyas Shah, Karrani rulers, Nusrat Shah, Raja Ganesha/Jalaluddin, Sikandar Shah.

kingdoms.name: Bharatpur
kingdoms.description: The leading Jat kingdom, raised by Badan Singh and Suraj Mal in the eighteenth century around the mud fortress of Bharatpur, which held out against the Company in 1805.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Jat dynasty; founded by Badan Singh / Suraj Mal

kingdoms.name: Bhati kingdom of Lodhruva
kingdoms.description: The Bhati Rajput state of the deep Thar, seated at Tanot from the early ninth century and then at Lodhruva, which Deoraj took from the Lodra Rajputs. Lodhruva was sacked by Mahmud of Ghazni in 1025 and by the Ghurids in 1152; Rawal Jaisal moved the capital to his new fort of Jaisalmer in 1156. The chronology is bardic and tentative.

kingdoms.name: Bhauma-Kara dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Buddhist house of Tosali, ruling coastal Odisha from Guheshvarapataka near modern Jajpur, and notable for six reigning queens — the last four one after another. The map holds them in Tosali from the atlas's start and gives them Kongoda about 736, when they drove out the Shailodbhavas; 736 is also year one of their own era and the accession of the first king anyone can name. That epoch is disputed — 736 and 831 are both argued — so every Bhauma-Kara date here could be a century out. Their last dated inscription falls in 949.

kingdoms.name: Bhavnagar
kingdoms.description: A leading Kathiawar (Saurashtra) port state under the Gohils.

kingdoms.name: Bhopal
kingdoms.description: A central Indian Muslim-ruled state founded by the Afghan Dost Mohammad Khan in 1707 and governed for a century by its Begums.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Founded by Dost Mohammad Khan; ruled by Begums 1819–1926

kingdoms.name: Bijapur (Adil Shahi)
kingdoms.description: One of the five Deccan sultanates that succeeded the Bahmanis; a major power across Karnataka and the southern Deccan until Aurangzeb annexed it in 1686.

kingdoms.name: Bikaner
kingdoms.description: A Rajput desert state founded by a Rathore prince of Jodhpur.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rathore dynasty; founded by Rao Bika
kingdoms.spanNote: Rathore state begun by Rao Bika in 1465; city founded 1488. No capital move, no rename — the two records are the same word. Merged into Greater Rajasthan 30 March 1949.

kingdoms.name: Bilaspur (Kahlur)
kingdoms.description: A western-Himalayan hill state (Kahlur).

kingdoms.name: Brahmin dynasty of Sindh
kingdoms.description: The line founded by Chach of Aror, which ruled Sindh for eighty years until Raja Dahir fell to Muhammad ibn Qasim at the Battle of Aror in 712 — the campaign that brought the Islamic world to the Indus.

kingdoms.name: British Ceylon
kingdoms.description: The British crown colony of Ceylon; the Kandyan kingdom fell in 1815, and the whole island was governed as one colony until independence in 1948.

kingdoms.name: British Raj
kingdoms.description: Direct rule of India by the British Crown, established in 1858 after the Revolt of 1857 dissolved Company rule. Lasted until independence and Partition in 1947.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Queen Victoria, Empress of India (1876); the Viceroys

kingdoms.name: Bundi
kingdoms.description: The parent Hadoti Rajput state of the Hada Chauhans, from which Kota was separated in the seventeenth century.

kingdoms.name: Bushahr
kingdoms.description: A high-Himalayan hill state on the upper Sutlej.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Founded by the Bushahr royal house

kingdoms.name: Calicut (Zamorin)
kingdoms.description: The Zamorin's kingdom of Calicut on the Malabar coast of north Kerala; overrun by Hyder Ali of Mysore in 1766 and annexed by the British in 1792.
kingdoms.spanNote: Extended 23 Sept 2026: restored as a Mysore tributary 1769-1773 (Kareem scan pp. 63-70; Menon p. 245).

kingdoms.name: Caliphal Sindh (Umayyad–Abbasid)
kingdoms.description: Sindh and Multan as a governed frontier province of the Umayyad and then Abbasid caliphates — the easternmost province Damascus and Baghdad ever held. Caliphal authority dissolved in the Anarchy at Samarra, leaving the Habbarids at Mansura and the Banu Munabbih at Multan.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Muhammad ibn Qasim; the governors of Sindh

kingdoms.name: Carnatic (Arcot Nawab)
kingdoms.description: The Carnatic under its own nawabs, ruling from Arcot. Aurangzeb appointed the first subahdar of the Carnatic in 1692, but the state dates properly from 1710, when Saadatullah Khan I made the nawabship hereditary and moved the court from Gingee to Arcot. Ceded to the British in 1801.

kingdoms.name: Central Kerala principalities
kingdoms.description: The independent Nair kingdoms of central Kerala between Cochin and Venad — Thekkumkur, Vadakkumkur, Kayamkulam, Ambalapuzha (Chembakassery) and Purakkad. They were annexed by Marthanda Varma's Travancore between 1742 and 1753.

kingdoms.name: Chahamana (Chauhan)
kingdoms.description: The Chauhan houses of Rajputana, first at Shakambhari near Sambhar, then Ajmer and Delhi. Prithviraja III won the first battle of Tarain and fell in the second in 1192; cadet branches held on at Ranthambore, where Hammira ruled from 1283, and at Jalor.

kingdoms.name: Chalukya (Badami)
kingdoms.description: The first Chalukya empire, rulers of the Deccan for two centuries from Vatapi: Pulakeshin II halted Harsha at the Narmada and took Vengi; Vikramaditya II stormed Kanchi. Dantidurga’s revolt ended the line in 753 — but its cadet branches at Vengi and later Kalyani carried the name for five more centuries. The flag shown here is a modern reconstruction, not a surviving banner. It is drawn from the insignia the records name: the Boar or Varaha — "The Early Chalukyas had the Boar as their family emblem, said to have been received through the grace of Narayana" (The Classical Age, HCIP III, printed p. 423) — and the palidhvaja, the banner of paramount sovereignty (same volume, printed p. 130). That sentence is about this Badami line specifically; the Kalyani branch inherited the device.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Pulakeshin II; Vikramaditya II; Kirtivarman II

kingdoms.name: Chamba
kingdoms.description: One of the oldest hill states of the western Himalaya, ruled from Chamba on the Ravi until it acceded in 1948.

kingdoms.name: Chandela dynasty
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Dhanga, Hammiravarman, Nannuka, Paramardi, Trailokyavarman, Vidyadhara, Viravarman, Yashovarman.

kingdoms.name: Chandra dynasty
kingdoms.description: Rulers of south-eastern Bengal from Vikramapura, rising out of feudatory rank in Harikela. Srichandra’s long reign left the richest copperplate record of the period; Govindachandra, the last of the line, faced the Chola raid into Bengal.

kingdoms.name: Chaulukya (Solanki)
kingdoms.description: The Gujarat house of Anhilwara, from Mularaja's wars for Saurashtra and Kutch to the Vaghela succession. Under Jayasimha Siddharaja and Kumarapala the court became a centre of Jain learning around Hemachandra, and the Rudra Mahalaya at Siddhapur was built.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Bhima I, Bhima II, Chamundaraja, Jayasimha Siddharaja, Karna, Kumarapala, Mularaja.

kingdoms.name: Chavda dynasty of Gujarat
kingdoms.description: The house that founded Anahilavada Patan and ruled northern Gujarat before the Chaulukyas. Samantasimha was supplanted by his adopted nephew Mularaja I, who founded the Solanki line.

kingdoms.name: Chera Perumal kingdom
kingdoms.description: The second Chera kingdom, ruling Kerala from Mahodayapuram near modern Kodungallur. It broke up around 1124 under internal fragmentation and Chola pressure, leaving the Venad, Kolathunad, Perumpadappu and Eranad chiefdoms as its successors.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara; Bhaskara Ravi; Rama Kulasekhara

kingdoms.name: Chhattisgarh Princely States
kingdoms.description: A cluster of forested feudatory states of the Chhattisgarh plateau — Bastar, Kanker, Raigarh, Surguja and their neighbours — administered through the Central Provinces.

kingdoms.name: Chitral State
kingdoms.description: A mountain principality of the Hindu Kush under its Mehtars, tributary first to Kashmir and then to the British agency at Gilgit.

kingdoms.name: Chola dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Tamil empire that grew from Vijayalaya's capture of Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyar into the strongest power in the peninsula. Its fleets took Ceylon and raided Kadaram, and its inscriptions record village assemblies electing their own committees.

kingdoms.name: Chutia (Sadiya) Kingdom
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Birpal, Dharmanarayan, Gauradhwajpal, Jayadhwajpal, Karmadhwajpal, Laksminarayan, Mayuradhwajpal, Nitypal, Ratnadhwajpal, Sankhadhwajpal, Satyanarayan, Vijayadhwajpal, Vikramadhwajpal.

kingdoms.name: Cochin
kingdoms.description: A small Kerala princely state of the Malabar coast, in turn a Portuguese, Dutch and British protectorate, and among the earliest in India to take up representative government.

kingdoms.name: Cooch Behar
kingdoms.description: A princely state of northern Bengal under the Koch kings.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Bir Narayan, Biswa Singha, Jagaddipendra Narayan, Lakshmi Narayan, Nara Narayan, Pran Narayan, Rup Narayan.

kingdoms.name: Dandakaranya forest chiefs
kingdoms.description: The forest centuries of the Dandakaranya: between the last Nala records and the first dated Chhindaka Naga inscription (c. 1023), the Bastar country names no dynasty at all. An editorial label in the manner of Jangaldesh — the silence of the record, named rather than painted over.

kingdoms.name: Dang States
kingdoms.description: Five Bhil chieftaincies of the Dangs; their forests were leased to the British under paramountcy, never directly administered; merged 1948.

kingdoms.name: Datia
kingdoms.description: A Bundela Rajput state of Bundelkhand.

kingdoms.name: Delhi Sultanate
kingdoms.description: The sultanate of Delhi under five successive houses — Mamluk, Khalji, Tughluq, Sayyid and Lodi. Qutb al-Din Aibak's break with Ghazni left it free to grow as an Indian power, and its armies reached Madurai under Muhammad bin Tughluq.

kingdoms.name: Deva dynasty of Samatata
kingdoms.description: The Buddhist Devas of Devaparvata near modern Comilla, patrons of the Mainamati monasteries. Their attested floruit is the late 8th and early 9th century, before Harikela’s rise under Kantideva.

kingdoms.name: Dewas
kingdoms.description: Maratha Puar princely state in Malwa, famously split into Dewas Senior and Dewas Junior branches.

kingdoms.name: Dholpur
kingdoms.description: A small Jat state on the Chambal: the Ranas of Gohad, moved here by the British when Gohad went back to Sindia in 1805. The same house before 1806 is painted on this map as 'Gohad (Jat Ranas)'.

kingdoms.name: Dir State
kingdoms.description: A frontier princely state of the Pashtun north-west.

kingdoms.name: Dogra J&K
kingdoms.description: The princely state of Jammu & Kashmir under the Dogra dynasty, bought from the Company by Gulab Singh at Amritsar in 1846 and held until 1947.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Founded by Gulab Singh; last ruler Hari Singh acceded to India in 1947
kingdoms.spanNote: From 1818 as Gulab Singh's fief under Lahore (Gupta V p. 65); independent from March 1846.

kingdoms.name: Dungarpur State
kingdoms.description: The Guhilot principality of Vagad, set up in the twelfth century by Samant Singh of the Mewar house (Bakshi vol. 1 p. 97); a Mughal vassal from Rawal Askaran's submission to Akbar in 1576.

kingdoms.name: Durrani (Afghan) Empire
kingdoms.description: Afghan empire that controlled the northwest — Kashmir, Multan, Peshawar and the Punjab — in the later 18th century.
kingdoms.spanNote: Extended 23 Sept 2026: Dera Ghazi Khan to 1819 and the Mankera Nawabs to 1820 (Gupta V pp. 60, 64, 75). Bannu stayed Afghan until Ranjit Singh took it in 1825 (Gupta V p. 59).

kingdoms.name: East India Company
kingdoms.description: The English East India Company, a chartered trading corporation that became a territorial power after Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764), ruling much of India until the Crown took direct control in 1858. Its rule is dated from 1757; the three settlement towns it governed earlier — Madras from 1639, Bombay from 1661, Calcutta from 1690 — are shown from those years, but a fortified factory is not a state.

kingdoms.name: East Pakistan
kingdoms.description: The eastern wing of Pakistan (1947–1971) before it became independent Bangladesh.

kingdoms.name: Eastern Chalukya dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Vengi branch of the Chalukyas, ruling the Andhra country for four and a half centuries. Independent rule effectively ended around the turn of the millennium under Chola dominance; the line merged into the Cholas when the Eastern Chalukya prince Kulottunga I took the Chola throne in 1070.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Kubja Vishnuvardhana; Vijayaditya III; Rajaraja Narendra

kingdoms.name: Eastern Ganga dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 140 heads its chapter 'The Eastern Gangas (c. A.D. 750-1000)' and traces the Early Eastern Gangas of Kalinganagara well before it; the dynasty reckoned by its own Ganga era, whose epoch falls c. A.D. 498.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: the Kalinganagara line of Devendravarman and Rajendravarman; Vajrahasta III; Anantavarman Chodaganga; Narasimhadeva I, builder of Konark; Kapilendra Deva.

kingdoms.name: Emirate of Multan
kingdoms.description: The autonomous emirate of southern Punjab, independent of the Abbasids from about 861 and taken over by Ismaili rulers around 959. Mahmud of Ghazni defeated Fateh Daud and ended it in 1010.

kingdoms.name: Faridkot
kingdoms.description: A small Sikh state of the Punjab.

kingdoms.name: French India
kingdoms.description: French coastal enclaves — Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahé, Yanam and Chandernagore — held from the seventeenth century until their transfer to India in the 1950s.

kingdoms.name: Gahadavala (Kannauj)
kingdoms.description: The last great house of Kannauj, ruling the Ganga country from Kannauj and Varanasi. Govindachandra threw back Ramapala's elephants; Jayachandra fell to an arrow facing Mu'izz al-Din at Chandawar in 1194, but his son Harishchandra held Kannauj again by 1197.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Adakkamalla, Chandradeva, Govindachandra, Harishchandra, Jayachandra, Madanapala, Vijayachandra.

kingdoms.name: Gajapati Empire
kingdoms.description: The Odishan empire that followed the Gangas, its kings styled Gajapati, lord of elephants. Kapilendra pushed south into Telangana and the Tamil country. The war between his sons after his death let Bahmani and Vijayanagara armies into the Godavari districts.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Kakharua Deva, Kalua Deva, Kapilendra Deva, Prataparudra Deva, Purushottama Deva.

kingdoms.name: Galo
kingdoms.description: The Galo people of the Siang valleys, organised by clan and village 'kebang' council.

kingdoms.name: Garhwal Kingdom
kingdoms.description: The Panwar (Parmar) kingdom of the Garhwal Himalaya, which unified the fifty-two garhs and held them until the Gorkha conquest of 1803-04.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Ajay Pal; Fateh Shah; Lalit Shah; Pradyumna Shah

kingdoms.name: Gauda chiefs (matsyanyaya)
kingdoms.description: Not a dynasty but the atlas’s name for a condition: the century of matsyanyaya — ‘the law of fishes, big eating small’ — that followed Shashanka’s fall, when Bengal had no paramount power and armies from Kannauj and Kashmir passed through. It ended when the chiefs elected Gopala.

kingdoms.name: Ghaznavid Empire
kingdoms.description: The Turkic empire of Ghazni whose raids and annexations brought the Punjab under Muslim rule for the first time. Multan fell in 1010 and the Punjab was annexed in 1021–22; after losing the west to the Seljuks the dynasty ruled from Lahore until Mu’izz al-Din Ghuri took the city in 1186.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Mahmud of Ghazni; Mas’ud I; Khusrau Malik

kingdoms.name: Ghurid Empire
kingdoms.description: The empire of Ghur in the Afghan highlands, once vassals of Ghazni, which turned east after the Khwarizm Shahs blocked its path west. Mu'izz al-Din won Tarain in 1192, and his commanders Aibak and Bakhtiyar Khalji carried Ghurid rule to Delhi and Bengal. The flag shown here is a modern reconstruction, not a surviving banner. No emblem for the Ghurids is named anywhere in this project’s library; their coinage is epigraphic, and the bull-and-horseman jital they struck was an inherited Hindu Shahi and Chahamana coin type kept for circulation rather than a Ghurid device. Treat the design as illustrative until a numismatic catalogue can support it.

kingdoms.name: Golconda (Qutb Shahi)
kingdoms.description: Deccan sultanate of the eastern plateau (Telangana and coastal Andhra), famed for its diamonds; annexed by Aurangzeb in 1687.

kingdoms.name: Gondwana (Gond kingdoms)
kingdoms.description: The Gond kingdoms of central India — Garha-Mandla, Deogarh, Chanda and Ratanpur — that ruled the forested Gondwana belt until the Marathas (Bhonsle) absorbed them in the mid-18th century.
kingdoms.spanNote: Extended 23 Sept 2026: the Garha-Mandla Gond crown survived as a Maratha tributary to the Bhonsle transfer of 1786 (Sardesai II p. 213; HCIP VIII p. 429).

kingdoms.name: Gurjara-Pratihara Empire
kingdoms.description: The northern empire that held Kannauj through the tripartite struggle with the Palas and Rashtrakutas, and whose resistance is credited with checking Arab expansion beyond Sindh for two centuries. Mahmud of Ghazni drove Rajyapala from Kannauj in 1018; the line ended in 1036.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Nagabhata I; Nagabhata II; Mihira Bhoja; Mahendrapala I

kingdoms.name: Gurjaras of Bhillamala
kingdoms.description: The Gurjara kingdom of Bhillamala in the Rajasthan–Gujarat borderland, home of the astronomer Brahmagupta, battered by the Arab campaigns of the 720s and 730s and absorbed into the rising Pratihara power.

kingdoms.name: Gwalior (Scindia)
kingdoms.description: A major Maratha-origin princely state of central India under the Scindias.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Scindia dynasty; founded by Ranoji Scindia
kingdoms.spanNote: Mahadji held the Gwalior fort for the Peshwa from 1766 (HCIP VIII p. 255); the house is drawn as a Maratha vassal from 1771.

kingdoms.name: Habbarid Emirate
kingdoms.description: The Arab dynasty that ruled Sindh from Mansura as an autonomous emirate from about 861, after the province ceased to be governed directly from Baghdad. Mahmud of Ghazni destroyed Mansura in 1026.

kingdoms.name: Hada Chauhan
kingdoms.description: The Hada branch of the Chauhans, who took Haroti from the Minas and made Bundi their capital in 1241 (Bakshi vol. 1 p. 101); Mughal vassals from Rao Surjan's alliance of 1569.

kingdoms.name: Harikela
kingdoms.description: The one house the library names for the country of Harikela - eastern Bengal, and at its widest a synonym for Vanga. Known from a Chittagong copper-plate of the Buddhist Maharajadhiraja Kantideva, who reigned in the century after Devapala's death; kings with names ending in -chandra follow him. Harikela itself is a country, named by the seventh-century Chinese pilgrims and on silver coin, not a dynasty of a thousand years.

kingdoms.name: Hill Rajas (Himachal)
kingdoms.description: The patchwork of Himalayan Rajput hill states (Kangra/Katoch and others) before Sikh and then British control.
kingdoms.spanNote: The protected Simla hill states after 1815.

kingdoms.name: Hindu Shahi kingdom
kingdoms.description: The dynasty of Kabul, Gandhara and the Punjab that met the first Ghaznavid invasions. Jayapala’s defeats and Trilochanapala’s death in 1021 opened the Punjab to Mahmud of Ghazni; the founding date is genuinely uncertain, with 822, 843, 850 and 870 all argued.

kingdoms.name: Holkar (Indore State)
kingdoms.description: A Maratha-origin princely state of Malwa under the Holkars.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Holkar dynasty; founded by Malhar Rao Holkar; regent Ahilyabai Holkar

kingdoms.name: Hoysala Kingdom
kingdoms.description: The Karnataka house of Dwarasamudra. Vishnuvardhana is called the maker of the kingdom, and his grandson Ballala II took the title of an independent king. Ballala III fought Delhi's armies for decades and died at Madurai; Vijayanagara absorbed the rest.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Ballala II, Ballala III, Narasimha I, Narasimha II, Narasimha III, Nripa Kama, Someshvara, Vinayaditya, Vishnuvardhana.

kingdoms.name: Hyderabad
kingdoms.description: The Nizam's dominions — the largest and richest princely state, founded by Asaf Jah I in 1724 and acceded to India in 1948.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rose under Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I; fell under the last Nizam Osman Ali Khan (Operation Polo 1948)

kingdoms.name: Idu Mishmi
kingdoms.description: The Idu Mishmi of the Dibang valley, accomplished weavers and shamanic priests of the eastern Himalaya.

kingdoms.name: Ikkeri (Keladi) Nayak
kingdoms.description: Coastal-Karnataka kingdom of the Keladi Nayakas, absorbed by Hyder Ali of Mysore in 1763.

kingdoms.name: India
kingdoms.description: The Republic of India — independent from British rule in 1947 and a sovereign republic from 1950.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rose under Jawaharlal Nehru as first PM

kingdoms.name: Jaintia Kingdom
kingdoms.description: Hill kingdom of the Jaintia (Pnar); annexed by the British in 1835.

kingdoms.name: Jaipur
kingdoms.description: The largest Rajputana state: the Kachhwaha kingdom of Amber, whose chiefs served as Mughal generals from Akbar's reign, and which moved to the new city of Jaipur in 1727.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Kachwaha dynasty; founded by Sawai Jai Singh II
kingdoms.spanNote: One Kachhwaha state. Founded by Dulha Rai (sources give 1028 or c. 1128); capital moved from Amber to the new city of Jaipur in 1727 by Sawai Jai Singh II — the sole reason for two names. Merged into Greater Rajasthan 30 March 1949.

kingdoms.name: Jaisalmer State
kingdoms.spanNote: One Bhati (Yaduvanshi) state, founded 1156 when Rawal Jaisal moved from Lodhruva to the new fort. The first record was named for the clan and the second for the state. Merged into Greater Rajasthan 30 March 1949 — the atlas had 1947, out of step with Jaipur, Jodhpur and Bikaner, which joined the same union the same day.

kingdoms.name: Jammu hill states
kingdoms.spanNote: Extended 23 Sept 2026: Ranjit Dev's Jammu, tributary to the Durranis and then the Bhangis, to Ranjit Singh's conquest of 1809 (Gupta IV pp. 329-337; Gupta V p. 65). Kishtwar stayed a separate hill state until Gulab Singh annexed it in May 1821 (Gupta V p. 73).

kingdoms.name: Jaunpur Sultanate
kingdoms.description: The Sharqi kingdom of the eastern Ganga plain, begun when Malik Sarwar, titled Malik-us-Sharq or Lord of the East, was sent to govern Jaunpur as Delhi's authority collapsed. It ran from Aligarh to Darbhanga, and its court made Jaunpur the Shiraz of the East.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Hussain Shah Sharqi, Ibrahim Shah Sharqi, Mahmud Shah, Malik Sarwar/Khwaja-i-Jahan, Mubarak Shah.

kingdoms.name: Jhalawar State
kingdoms.description: A Rajputana state carved out of Kota in 1838.

kingdoms.name: Jhansi
kingdoms.description: Maratha principality of Jhansi; lapsed in 1853; its Rani became an icon of the 1857 revolt.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Shiv Rao Bhau, Raghunath Rao Newalkar, Gangadhar Rao, Rani Lakshmibai.

kingdoms.name: Jind
kingdoms.description: A Sikh Phulkian state of the Punjab.

kingdoms.name: Jodhpur (Marwar)
kingdoms.description: The Rathore kingdom of Marwar in western Rajasthan.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Ajit Singh, Chandrasen, Hanwant Singh, Jaswant Singh, Maldeo, Man Singh, Rao Chunda, Rao Jodha, Rao Siha, Takht Singh, Umaid Singh.
kingdoms.spanNote: Rathore Marwar from Rao Siha at Pali in 1243; capital Pali → Mandore (1395) → Jodhpur (1459). "Marwar" is the region and "Jodhpur" the capital, not two states. Merged into Greater Rajasthan 30 March 1949.

kingdoms.name: Junagadh
kingdoms.description: A Kathiawar state whose ruler acceded to Pakistan in 1947; integrated into India after a plebiscite in 1948.

kingdoms.name: Kachari Kingdom
kingdoms.description: Dimasa-Kachari kingdom of the Barak valley; annexed by the British in 1832.

kingdoms.name: Kachchhapaghata dynasty
kingdoms.description: Rulers of the Gwalior country, first as Chandela and Pratihara feudatories, from Vajradaman’s capture of the Gopadri fort. Inscriptions carry their rule to at least 1155 and records to 1194; Gwalior fort fell to Qutb al-Din Aibak in 1196.

kingdoms.name: Kadathanadu
kingdoms.description: A kingdom of North Malabar ruled by the Porlathiri dynasty (dispossessed rulers of Polanad), centred near Vatakara. Its coast is where the French established Mahé in 1725; absorbed by Mysore in Hyder Ali's 1766 conquest of Malabar.

kingdoms.name: Kakatiya dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Telugu house of Warangal, Chalukya feudatories who rose as Kalyani fell — Prola took Taila III prisoner and Rudra I finished the Chalukya claim. Ganapati reached Kanchi about 1250 and made his daughter Rudramba his heir; Warangal fell to Delhi's armies in 1323. The flag shown here is a modern reconstruction, not a surviving banner. No Kakatiya emblem is named anywhere in this project’s library; settling it would need an epigraphic corpus of their inscriptions. Treat the design as illustrative until one can support it.

kingdoms.name: Kalachuri of Tripuri (Chedi)
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Gangeyadeva, Gayakarna, Jayasimha, Karna, Kokalla I, Vamaraja, Vijayasimha, Yashahkarna.

kingdoms.name: Kalahandi State
kingdoms.description: A princely state of western Odisha.

kingdoms.name: Kalat (Khanate)
kingdoms.description: The largest Baloch state, ruled by the Ahmadzai Khans from the seventeenth century and in treaty with the British from 1876.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Khanate of Kalat under the Ahmadzai khans

kingdoms.name: Kalhora (Sindh)
kingdoms.description: The Kalhora dynasty of Sindh, displaced by the Talpur Amirs in 1783.

kingdoms.name: Kamarupa
kingdoms.description: The old kingdom of Pragjyotisha-Kamarupa in the Brahmaputra valley, under the Varman, Mlechchha and Pala lines and their successors. Its later kings - Timgyadeva, Vaidyadeva, Rayarideva and Vallabhadeva, whose grant of 1185 is the last of them - ruled on until the Kamata kingdom followed in the thirteenth century.

kingdoms.name: Kampili Kingdom
kingdoms.capital: Kampili / Kummata (Anegundi), on the Tungabhadra near Hampi

kingdoms.name: Kannauj (Yashovarman)
kingdoms.description: Yashovarman raised Kannauj from its post-Harsha obscurity into a power that campaigned to Bengal, patronised the poet Vakpati (whose Gaudavaho celebrates the campaign) and Bhavabhuti, and fell when Lalitaditya of Kashmir turned on his former ally, c. 740–752. Yashovarman himself died c. 740 (HCIP III, p. 131: reign "between A.D. 700 and 740"); the label covers his house, whose obscure successors held Kannauj under Karkota shadow until the Ayudhas emerge (753). The flag shown here is a modern reconstruction, not a surviving banner. No emblem for Yashovarman’s house is named anywhere in this project’s library. Treat the design as illustrative until a source can support it.

kingdoms.name: Rashtrakutas of Kannauj
kingdoms.description: The Rashtrakuta house that took Kanauj out of the wreck Mahmud of Ghazni left in 1018. HCIP gives them a chapter of their own: Chandra "established his supremacy over Kanauj during the period of disorder", and his descendants held Gadhipura until Chandradeva the Gahadavala seized the throne from Gopala about 1090, after which the family moved east to Budaun.

kingdoms.name: Kapurthala
kingdoms.description: A Sikh princely state known for its Francophile architecture.

kingdoms.name: Karauli State
kingdoms.description: A Rajput state of eastern Rajputana claiming descent from Krishna.

kingdoms.name: Karkota dynasty of Kashmir
kingdoms.description: The Kashmiri dynasty whose greatest ruler, Lalitaditya Muktapida, campaigned across northern India and built the Martand Sun Temple. The line was in collapse from about 840 and ended when Avantivarman deposed Utpalapida in 855.

kingdoms.name: Kathiawar Minor States
kingdoms.description: The dense patchwork of small Saurashtra (Kathiawar) princely states and estates.

kingdoms.name: Katyuri kingdom
kingdoms.notableRulers: Vasu Dev; Brahma Dev; Subhiksharaja Dev
kingdoms.description: The dynasty of Kartikeyapura in the Kumaon Himalaya, whose reach extended into the far west of modern Nepal — Brahmadev Mandi in Kanchanpur is their foundation, and the Doti Raika chiefs descend from a Katyuri branch. The line fragmented in the mid-eleventh century.

kingdoms.name: Katyuri successor chiefs
kingdoms.notableRulers: (the Raikas of Doti and other branches)
kingdoms.description: The branch houses left by the Katyuri kingdom’s fragmentation c. 1065 — the Raikas of Doti among them — holding the far west of Nepal until the Khasa Malla expansion.

kingdoms.name: Kerala chiefdoms (pre-Chera)
kingdoms.description: Kerala before the Chera Perumal state: the country of the Vel chiefs and temple corporations, with no paramount polity until Sthanu Ravi, the first attested Chera Perumal, c. 844. An editorial label — the silence of the record, named honestly.

kingdoms.name: Khadga dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Buddhist house of eastern Bengal attested by copperplates and the account of the Chinese pilgrim Sheng-che; conventionally c. 625 to the early 8th century.

kingdoms.name: Khairpur State
kingdoms.description: A Talpur-ruled princely state of Sindh.

kingdoms.name: Khampti
kingdoms.description: The Tai-Khampti, Theravada Buddhists who migrated from the Irrawaddy in the 18th century — the only Arunachal people with their own script — forming a chiefdom around Namsai.

kingdoms.name: Khasa chiefs (pre-Malla)
kingdoms.description: The Khasa people of the Karnali highlands under their own chiefs, the highest valleys within the Tibetan imperial sphere until 842. Nagaraja’s kingdom of Sinja united them c. 1100 into the Khasa Malla state. An ethnonym label in the manner of Limbuwan.

kingdoms.name: Khasi States
kingdoms.description: Group of ~25 Khasi native states under British paramountcy, never directly ruled; acceded to India in 1947.

kingdoms.name: Khurda (Bhoi)
kingdoms.description: Hindu kingdom of Khurda (Bhoi dynasty), guardians of the Jagannath temple at Puri, 1568–1804.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Ramachandra Deva I; Purushottama Deva; Divyasingha Deva

kingdoms.name: Kingdom of Coorg
kingdoms.description: Haleri kingdom of Coorg (Kodagu); annexed by the British in 1834.

kingdoms.name: Kingdom of Maryul
kingdoms.description: The first Ladakhi kingdom, founded by Lhachen Palgyigon of the Tibetan royal line after the empire’s collapse; Petech dates it to about 950. It ruled until Lhachen Bhagan deposed the last of the line in 1460 and founded the Namgyal dynasty.

kingdoms.name: Kingdom of Sikkim (Namgyal)
kingdoms.description: The Himalayan kingdom of Sikkim, ruled by the Namgyal dynasty of Chogyals from 1642. A British protectorate from 1861 and an Indian protectorate from 1950, it remained a monarchy until it merged with India in 1975.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Chakdor, Gyurmed, Palden Thondup Namgyal, Phuntsog Namgyal, Sidkeong, Tashi, Tensung, Tenzing, Tsugphud.
kingdoms.spanNote: 1642 is the consecration of Phuntsog Namgyal at Yuksom, the conventional date. HCIP IX p. 1065 says 1641. The Gorkhas held West and South Sikkim from 1793 until the treaty of 1817; Britain's protectorate was recognised by the Anglo-Chinese convention of 17 March 1890 (HCIP IX p. 1061) and, like every other British paramountcy on this map, is not painted as an overlord line.

kingdoms.name: Kolathunad
kingdoms.spanNote: Extended 23 Sept 2026: restored as a Mysore tributary 1776-1788 (Kareem scan p. 68).

kingdoms.name: Kolhapur
kingdoms.description: The senior Maratha principality of the Kolhapur Bhonsles (junior line of Shivaji's house); a princely state under British paramountcy from 1812 until 1949.

kingdoms.name: Konbaung (Burmese) Empire
kingdoms.spanNote: From 1812 as Manipur's overlord (HCIP IX p. 131).

kingdoms.name: Kota
kingdoms.description: A Hadoti Rajput state carved out of Bundi.

kingdoms.name: Kumaon Chand
kingdoms.description: The Chand kingdom of Kumaon, a polity entirely separate from Garhwal, ruling from Champawat and later Almora until the Gorkhas took it in 1790.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Som Chand; Baz Bahadur Chand; Udyot Chand; Mohan Chand

kingdoms.name: Kutch
kingdoms.description: The large desert-and-coast kingdom of Kutch under the Jadejas.
kingdoms.spanNote: One Jadeja state; "Cutch" is the British-era romanisation. Jadeja rule from c. 1147 (traditional), unified under Rao Khengarji I with the capital fixed at Bhuj in 1548–49. Became a Chief Commissioner’s Province 1 June 1948.

kingdoms.name: Ladakh (Namgyal)
kingdoms.description: Buddhist kingdom of Ladakh under the Namgyal dynasty; conquered by the Dogras (Zorawar Singh) 1834-42.

kingdoms.name: Later Gupta dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Magadha house — unrelated to the imperial Guptas whose name they carried — that outlived Harsha and held Bihar until the rising Pala power absorbed them around 750.

kingdoms.name: Licchavi dynasty of Nepal
kingdoms.description: The dynasty of the Kathmandu Valley that left Nepal’s earliest inscriptions. Its end is genuinely contested: mainstream scholarship closes the Licchavi era around 750, while Nepali tradition runs it to the founding of the Nepal Sambat era in 879, the convention followed here.

kingdoms.name: Lohara dynasty of Kashmir
kingdoms.description: The two Lohara dynasties on the throne of Kashmir, from Samgramaraja (1003) to Vantideva - the same family as the Kingdom of Lohara painted beside it in the hills, but a different state: Srinagar and the valley, not the Lohrin fief, and the two were often at odds. HCIP V p. 103: Vantideva (1165-72) died childless and was the last of the line; the people of Kashmir then elected Vuppadeva, who began a new house.

kingdoms.name: Madurai Nayak
kingdoms.description: Telugu warrior-governors who became independent kings of the Tamil south after the decline of Vijayanagara.

kingdoms.name: Magar and Gurung chiefdoms (Magarat)
kingdoms.description: The Magar and Gurung country of the Gandaki basin — the Magarat of Nepali tradition, remembered as twelve chiefdoms — under its own chiefs until the Khasa Malla expansion of the 12th century. An ethnonym label in the manner of Limbuwan.

kingdoms.name: Maitraka of Valabhi
kingdoms.description: The rulers of Saurashtra for three centuries, whose capital Valabhi was a famed seat of Buddhist learning ranked with Nalanda. The dynasty ends c. 776; tradition blames Arab sea-raids, though no source records the fall.

kingdoms.name: Malwa Sultanate
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Baz Bahadur, Dilawar Khan, Ghiyasuddin, Hoshang Shah, Mahmud II, Mahmud Khalji.

kingdoms.name: Mandi
kingdoms.description: A western-Himalayan hill state of the Beas valley.

kingdoms.name: Manipur
kingdoms.description: An ancient kingdom in the eastern hills; it briefly fought the British in 1891 and acceded to India in 1949.

kingdoms.name: Maratha Empire
kingdoms.description: Confederacy of Maratha chiefs led by the Peshwa; the dominant power in 18th-century India before British paramountcy.
kingdoms.spanNote: 1653 is the swarajya complete in Poona and Satara (HCIP VII p. 289); the coronation of 6 June 1674 gave it a crown, not a beginning.

kingdoms.name: Mauryas of Chittorgarh
kingdoms.description: The Mori (Maurya) chiefs of Chittor, attested by the Manmori inscription of 713, whom tradition credits with building the great fort — and losing it to Bappa Rawal in 728.

kingdoms.name: Mayurbhanj State
kingdoms.description: The largest Odisha princely state, held by the Bhanj line, and the last of the Odisha states to merge with the union, in 1949.

kingdoms.name: Mishmi
kingdoms.description: The Digaru and Miju Mishmi of the Lohit and Anjaw hills, traders and weavers of the far eastern frontier.

kingdoms.name: Monpa & Sherdukpen
kingdoms.description: Mahayana-Buddhist Monpa and Sherdukpen peoples of the western Kameng hills, self-governed through village and clan councils.

kingdoms.name: Monpa (Tawang Monastery)
kingdoms.description: Tibetan-Buddhist Monpa people of the Tawang region, administered through the Tawang Monastery (founded 1681) under a parliamentary 'Kato' council linked to Lhasa, until India's integration in 1951.

kingdoms.name: Mrauk U
kingdoms.spanNote: Chittagong was Arakanese until the Mughal capture of 26 January 1666 (HCIP VII pp. 229-230).

kingdoms.name: Mughal Empire
kingdoms.description: The once-great empire, by the later 18th century reduced to titular authority around Delhi under Maratha then British protection.

kingdoms.name: Mukunda Deva
kingdoms.description: The last independent Hindu king of Odisha (of the Bhoi–Chalukya line). He overthrew the Bhoi rulers in 1560 and ruled until the Karrani Sultans of Bengal conquered Odisha in 1568.

kingdoms.name: Mysore
kingdoms.description: The Kingdom of Mysore under the Wadiyars — a model princely state in southern Karnataka.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Wadiyar dynasty; interrupted by Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan (1761–99); revived under the Crown

kingdoms.name: Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu)
kingdoms.description: The Sultanat-i-Khudadad ('God-given state'). Hyder Ali seized power from the Wadiyars in 1761; his son Tipu Sultan, the Tiger of Mysore, ruled until he fell defending Seringapatam in 1799. A militarised, Persianate-Islamic state with its own flag, calendar, coinage and famous war-rockets, it fought four Anglo-Mysore Wars against the East India Company. After Tipu's death the British restored the Hindu Wadiyars as a princely state.

kingdoms.name: Nagpur (Bhonsle)
kingdoms.description: Bhonsle Maratha kingdom of Nagpur and Chhattisgarh; lapsed to the British in 1854.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Appa Sahib, Janoji, Mudhoji, Raghoji I, Raghoji II, Raghoji III.

kingdoms.name: Najib-ud-Daula (Rohilla)
kingdoms.description: Rohilla Afghan chief who, after the Third Battle of Panipat (1761), became regent (Mir Bakhshi) of the titular Mughal court and the effective ruler of Delhi until c.1771, when the Marathas under Mahadji Scindia retook the capital. The Mughal emperor remained on the throne in name throughout.
kingdoms.spanNote: Najib's regency at Delhi and his jagirs in Hariana and the upper Doab, 1761-70; his heirs' country is drawn as the imperial jagir it nominally was.

kingdoms.name: Nala dynasty
kingdoms.description: The old house of the Bastar–Koraput country, attested from the 5th–6th centuries at Pushkari and by the Podagada inscription; a later branch — Prithviraja, Viruparaja and Vilasatunga, builder of the Rajivalochana temple at Rajim — carried the name into the 8th century. Their dates are coarse, their fall unrecorded.

kingdoms.name: Nawanagar (Jamnagar)
kingdoms.description: A Kathiawar coastal state of the Jadeja Rajputs, founded in August 1540 by Jam Rawal on the Jethwa port of Nagnath after he was driven out of Kutch, and known for its pearl fisheries and for the cricketers of its ruling house.

kingdoms.name: Nepal
kingdoms.description: The Shah kingdom of Nepal — never colonised; effective power lay with the hereditary Rana prime ministers from 1846 to 1951.
kingdoms.notableRulers: United by Prithvi Narayan Shah; ruled in practice by Rana premiers

kingdoms.name: Nocte
kingdoms.description: The Nocte of the Patkai hills (Tirap), organised in powerful hereditary village chieftaincies.

kingdoms.name: Nyishi
kingdoms.description: The Nyishi, the largest people of Arunachal, living in clan-based village communities across the central hills.

kingdoms.name: Oiniwar
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Bhogishvara, Ganeshvara, Kameshvara Thakur, Kirti Singh, Lakhima Devi regency, Shiva Singh, later Oiniwars.

kingdoms.name: Oman (Gwadar exclave)
kingdoms.description: The port of Gwadar — a coastal exclave of the Sultanate of Oman until sold to Pakistan in 1958.

kingdoms.name: Orchha
kingdoms.description: The senior Bundela Rajput state of Bundelkhand.

kingdoms.name: Orissa Princely States
kingdoms.description: The many feudatory states of Odisha — Mayurbhanj, Keonjhar, Patna, Kalahandi and their neighbours — merged with the province in 1948 and 1949.

kingdoms.name: Pakistan
kingdoms.description: The Islamic Republic of Pakistan — created at Partition in 1947 from the Muslim-majority north-west and east.

kingdoms.name: Pala Empire
kingdoms.description: The Buddhist dynasty that ruled Bengal and Bihar for four centuries, founded when Gopala was raised to the throne by an assembly of chiefs to end a long anarchy. Under Dharmapala and Devapala it contested Kannauj with the Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas, and its patronage carried Vikramashila and Nalanda to their height.

kingdoms.name: Pallava dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Tamil dynasty whose rock-cut architecture at Mahabalipuram and Kanchipuram founded the Dravidian temple tradition. The last Pallava, Aparajita Varman, was defeated and killed by Aditya I Chola around 897, when Tondaimandalam passed to the Cholas.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Mahendravarman I; Narasimhavarman I; Aparajita Varman

kingdoms.name: Panduvamshi dynasty
kingdoms.description: The rulers of Dakshina Kosala from Sirpur, whose last known king, Balarjuna, reigned over fifty-seven years to c. 790. The Somavamshis who later ruled Odisha were probably their offshoot — the atlas hands one to the other.

kingdoms.name: Pandya dynasty
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Arikesari, Jatavarman Sundara, Kadungon, Maravarman Sundara, Varagunavarman, later Tenkasi Pandyas.

kingdoms.name: Panna
kingdoms.description: A Bundela state known for its diamond mines.

kingdoms.name: Paramara (Malwa)
kingdoms.description: The Paramaras of Malwa, installed at Dhara and Ujjayini by the Rashtrakuta Govinda III about 812 and his vassals for a century and a half. Their kings rode north with Rashtrakuta armies - Vakpati I probably went with Indra III to Kannauj in 916 - and Malwa was the launchpad from which the Deccan contested the imperial city. Siyaka II threw off the yoke and sacked Manyakheta itself in 972; under Bhoja, Dhara became one of the great courts of India.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Arjunavarman, Bhoja, Mahalakadeva, Munja/Vakpati II, Naravarman, Siyaka, Udayaditya, Upendra.

kingdoms.name: Pashtun tribal areas
kingdoms.description: Autonomous Pashtun tribal territory of the northwest frontier; never directly ruled, loosely under British influence after 1849.

kingdoms.name: Patiala
kingdoms.description: The premier Sikh princely state of the Punjab (a Phulkian state).
kingdoms.notableRulers: Phulkian (Sidhu) dynasty; founded by Ala Singh
kingdoms.spanNote: From Abdali's 1761 rescript to Ala Singh (Sarkar II p. 482).

kingdoms.name: Patna State (Balangir)
kingdoms.description: A western Odisha princely state of the Chauhan line, ruled from Patnagarh and later from Balangir.

kingdoms.name: Patola Shahis of Gilgit
kingdoms.description: The Buddhist kings of Gilgit on the road between India and Central Asia, patrons of the bronze workshops and the Gilgit manuscripts. Tibet took Little Palola in 737–38, the Tang restored the line in 747, and after the Tang withdrawal the valleys passed into the Tibetan sphere.

kingdoms.name: Porbandar
kingdoms.description: The Jethwa Rajput state of the Barda coast, dated from the seventh century. Rana Vikmatji Khimoji took Porbandar from the Mughals in 1671 and built its fort; his son Sartanji moved the capital there from Chhaya in 1685, which is why some sources date the state from then. A thirteen-gun-salute state, in treaty with the East India Company from 1809, acceded on 15 August 1947 — and the birthplace of Mohandas Gandhi.

kingdoms.name: Portuguese India
kingdoms.description: Portuguese coastal enclaves — Goa, Damão, Diu and their dependencies — held from 1510 until the Indian action of 1961.

kingdoms.name: Pudukkottai (Tondaiman)
kingdoms.description: The only princely state in the Tamil country, ruled by the Tondaiman line from 1686 and merged in 1948.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Martanda Bhairava, Raghunatha Raya Tondaiman, Rajagopala Tondaiman, Ramachandra Tondaiman, Vijaya Raghunatha.

kingdoms.name: Rajpipla
kingdoms.description: A forested princely state of eastern Gujarat.

kingdoms.name: Rajputana Minor States
kingdoms.description: Smaller Rajputana princely states beyond the major houses.

kingdoms.name: Ramnad (Setupati)
kingdoms.description: The Marava kingdom of Ramnad under the Sethupathis ('guardians of the bridge' to Rameswaram); a turbulent semi-independent power in the Tamil far south.

kingdoms.name: Rampur State
kingdoms.description: A Rohilla Pathan princely state of the upper Gangetic plain.

kingdoms.name: Rashtrakuta Empire
kingdoms.description: The Deccan empire that at its height reached from the Ganga to Kanyakumari and was described by Arab travellers as one of the four great empires of the world. Krishna I commissioned the Kailasa temple at Ellora. The feudatory Tailapa II overthrew the line in 973.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Dantidurga; Krishna I; Govinda III; Amoghavarsha I

kingdoms.name: Ratanpur Kalachuri kingdom
kingdoms.spanNote: Extended 23 Sept 2026: Ratanpur's Haihaya house held Chhattisgarh to the Maratha conquest (CPG pp. 8-9).

kingdoms.name: Reddy kingdom
kingdoms.notableRulers: Prolaya Vema Reddy; Anavota Reddy; Anavema Reddy; Kumaragiri Reddy
kingdoms.description: The Reddi kingdom of coastal Andhra, founded at Addanki and ruled from Kondavidu and Rajahmundry; its armies campaigned as far as Cuttack and Kanchi, and it patronised Srinatha and classical Telugu letters.

kingdoms.name: Rewa
kingdoms.description: The premier princely state of Baghelkhand in central India.

kingdoms.name: Rohilkhand (Rohillas)
kingdoms.description: Principality of Afghan (Rohilla) settlers in the upper Ganga plain; conquered by Awadh with British help in the Rohilla War of 1774.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Ali Mohammed Khan; Hafiz Rahmat Khan

kingdoms.name: Saindhava dynasty
kingdoms.description: The ‘lords of the western sea’ who held west Saurashtra from Ghumli after the Maitraka collapse, while the rest of the peninsula fell to petty chiefs.

kingdoms.name: Sambalpur
kingdoms.spanNote: Extended 23 Sept 2026: the Chauhan Rajas of Sambalpur to the 1849 lapse (CPG p. 12; HCIP IX pp. 90, 444).

kingdoms.name: Satara
kingdoms.description: The Maratha Chhatrapati's restored state of Satara; lapsed to the British in 1848.

kingdoms.name: Sawantwadi
kingdoms.description: Konkan coastal kingdom of the Sawant-Bhonsles; a princely state under the British until 1948.

kingdoms.name: Sena dynasty
kingdoms.description: The house that replaced the Palas in Bengal: Vijayasena took Varendra from Madanapala and overran east Bengal. Ballalasena and Lakshmanasena were authors themselves and made the court a centre of Sanskrit letters; the line later ruled on from Vikrampura.

kingdoms.name: Seraikela-Kharsawan
kingdoms.description: Two small adjoining princely states of the Chota Nagpur plateau.

kingdoms.name: Seuna (Yadava)
kingdoms.description: The Deccan house of Devagiri, Chalukya feudatories until Bhillama V made himself an independent king in 1185. Singhana II carried Yadava arms to the Kaveri; Malik Kafur took Ramachandra prisoner to Delhi in 1307 and the line ended a decade later. The flag shown here is a modern reconstruction, not a surviving banner. The records are unusually clear about the device: "They carried the Suvarna-Garuda-dhvaja (banner of a golden Garuda), which also appears as the device on the seals of their charters, sometimes alone, and sometimes along with the figure of Hanuman. In at least one case, the monkey-god alone appears as lanchhana or crest" (The Struggle for Empire, HCIP V, printed p. 197).
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Bhillama V, Dridhaprahara, Harapaladeva, Jaitugi, Krishna, Mahadeva, Ramachandra, Shankaradeva, Singhana II.

kingdoms.name: Shailodbhava dynasty
kingdoms.description: The house of Kongoda — roughly the undivided Ganjam and Puri districts, south of the Mahanadi — self-described as 'born of a rock'. The Bhauma-Karas of Tosali drove them out of Kongoda about 736; a surviving branch held Tekkali as a feudatory of the Kalinga Gangas.

kingdoms.name: Shilahara of North Konkan
kingdoms.description: The senior Shilahara house, ruling the Thana, Alibag and Ratnagiri country from Kapardin I under the Rashtrakutas to Aparaditya II - the branch that stayed outside the Chalukya empire when the south fell to Taila II, and whose king Mallikarjuna was killed by Kumarapala's minister in the Konkan war of 1162.

kingdoms.name: Sikh Empire
kingdoms.description: Sikh Empire founded by Ranjit Singh; spanned Punjab, Kashmir and the northwest; annexed by the British in 1849.

kingdoms.name: Sikh misls
kingdoms.description: The Sikh confederacy of independent warbands that ruled the Punjab before Ranjit Singh unified them into the Sikh Empire (1799).
kingdoms.spanNote: Gujrat's Bhangis held to December 1810 (Gupta V p. 60).

kingdoms.name: Sindh (Talpur Amirs)
kingdoms.description: Talpur Amirs of Sindh; conquered by Sir Charles Napier for the British in 1843.

kingdoms.name: Sirmaur
kingdoms.description: A Himalayan hill state of present-day Himachal Pradesh.

kingdoms.name: Sirohi State
kingdoms.description: The Deora Chauhan state at the foot of Mount Abu, from Lumbha's occupation of the Arbuda country c. 1311 (Bakshi vol. 5 p. 35); the capital at Sirohi town from 1425. Rao Surthan fought Akbar and Jahangir and never acknowledged Mughal supremacy.

kingdoms.name: Sivaganga (Marava)
kingdoms.description: Marava chieftaincy that split from Ramnad; famed for early resistance to the British under the Maruthu brothers.

kingdoms.name: Somavamshi dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Somavamshis rose in the Sambalpur tract of western Odisha - the eastern part of old South Kosala - about 915, took the Bhauma-Kara realm of coastal Utkala in the mid-10th century, and under Yayati II held Kosala and Utkala together. Yayati I founded Yayatinagara on the Mahanadi. An older chronology begins the line with Janamejaya in 882; this atlas follows HCIP (c. 915). The Eastern Gangas took the coast by 1112 and the west fell to the Telugu-Chodas and Kalachuris. The flag shown here is a modern reconstruction, not a surviving banner. It follows the device on their own charters: "The seal of their early records bears not the Garuda or the bull emblem but the Gaja-lakshmi symbol (although they were Saivas), like that of the Sarabhapuriyas and the Kalachuris" (The Age of Imperial Kanauj, HCIP IV, printed p. 146).

kingdoms.name: Sri Lanka
kingdoms.description: Independent Ceylon from 1948, a republic and renamed Sri Lanka in 1972.

kingdoms.name: Sur Empire
kingdoms.description: The Afghan empire that interrupted the Mughals — Sher Shah beat Humayun at Chausa and Kanauj and held Hindustan for five years. He surveyed the land for revenue, and struck a silver rupee that the Mughals, and the Company down to 1835, went on using. The flag shown here is a modern reconstruction, not a surviving banner. No emblem for the Surs is named anywhere in this project’s library; Sher Shah’s coinage is epigraphic — the kalima and his titles, not a figure. Treat the design as illustrative until a numismatic catalogue can support it.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Firuz Shah, Ibrahim Suri, Islam Shah, Muhammad Adil Shah, Sher Shah Suri, Sikandar Suri.

kingdoms.name: Surguja State
kingdoms.description: A forested princely state of northern Chhattisgarh.

kingdoms.name: Tagin
kingdoms.description: The Tagin of the Upper Subansiri highlands.

kingdoms.name: Tangsa
kingdoms.description: The Tangsa (and Singpho) peoples of the Patkai foothills around Changlang.

kingdoms.name: Tanjore (Thanjavur) Nayak
kingdoms.description: Nayak kingdom of the Kaveri delta; a centre of Tamil and Telugu culture, later taken by the Marathas of Tanjore.

kingdoms.name: Tehri Garhwal State
kingdoms.description: The Garhwal kingdom of the Himalayas, left to the Panwar rajas at Tehri after the Company took the eastern half of Garhwal in 1815.

kingdoms.name: Thakuri dynasty of Nepal
kingdoms.description: The line traditionally dated from Raghavadeva and the inauguration of the Nepal era in October 879, holding the Kathmandu Valley until the Malla period opens around 1200. Some historians dispute whether it was a single coherent dynasty at all, and its king-list chronology is unreliable.

kingdoms.name: Thanjavur (Maratha)
kingdoms.description: The Maratha kingdom of Thanjavur, founded by Shivaji's half-brother Venkoji (Ekoji); a great patron of Tamil and Carnatic culture, it became a British protectorate in 1799 and was annexed in 1856.

kingdoms.name: Tibetan Empire
kingdoms.description: The empire that dominated Inner Asia and reached into the western Himalaya, and under which Buddhism was established in Tibet. It fractured after the assassination of Langdarma in 842, beginning the Era of Fragmentation.

kingdoms.name: Tibetan successor chiefs
kingdoms.description: Ladakh in the Era of Fragmentation: local lords of the old Tibetan imperial aristocracy, until Nyima-Gon’s westward migration founded the kingdom his son Palgyigon would rule as Maryul, c. 930.

kingdoms.name: Karnata dynasty of Mithila
kingdoms.description: The house Nanyadeva founded at Simraungadh on 10 July 1097, ruling Mithila - the country the records call Tirhut - from the Nepal terai down to the Ganga, until the Oiniwars followed them in the fourteenth century.

kingdoms.name: Tomara dynasty of Delhi
kingdoms.description: The house that held Dhillika and the upper Doab before the Chahamanas. Tradition carries the line back to Anangapala I in 736, but the early names are legendary and the family is a Pratihara feudatory until the ninth century, so the map begins them in 850.

kingdoms.name: Tomara dynasty of Gwalior
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Dungarendra Singh, Kalyanmal, Kirti Singh, Man Singh Tomar, Vikramaditya, Vir Singh Dev.

kingdoms.name: Tonk
kingdoms.description: Muslim-ruled princely state in Rajputana, founded by the Pindari leader Amir Khan.

kingdoms.name: Travancore
kingdoms.description: A prosperous princely state of the Kerala coast, consolidated by Marthanda Varma in the 1740s and noted for its schooling and its public works.

kingdoms.name: Tripura
kingdoms.description: A long-lived hill kingdom of the north-east under the Manikya kings.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rulers included: Bir Bikram Kishore, Bir Chandra, Dhanya Manikya, Govinda Manikya, Krishna Manikya, Ratna Manikya, Vijaya Manikya II.

kingdoms.name: Turk Shahi kingdom
kingdoms.description: The Turkic dynasty of Kabul and Gandhara that held the mountain gate of India against the Umayyad and Abbasid push for a century and a half. Its last king, Lagaturman, was deposed by his Brahmin minister Kallar c. 822 — the beginning of the Hindu Shahis.

kingdoms.name: Udaipur (Mewar)
kingdoms.description: The senior-most Rajput house — Mewar under the Sisodias, which alone refused a marriage alliance with the Mughals, and which ruled from Chittorgarh and then from Udaipur.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Sisodia dynasty of Mewar; Maharana Pratap
kingdoms.spanNote: Sisodia Mewar. Rana Hammir retook Chittor in 1326; capital moved to Udaipur in 1568 after Akbar sacked Chittorgarh. Acceded 1947, merged into the Rajasthan Union 18 April 1948.

kingdoms.name: Udaiyarpalayam
kingdoms.description: A Tamil palayam (poligar chiefdom) in the Ariyalur country, founded by Chinna Nalla Kalatkal Tola Udaiyar and shielded by dense forest and broken terrain. It kept its own court at Udaiyarpalayam, a lion flag and a Varaha ensign, and struck its own coin, the Udaiyarpalayam pudhupanam, ruling as a quasi-independent vassal under Vijayanagara, the Gingee Nayaks and later the Nawab of Arcot, who annexed it in January 1765; the family continued as zamindars until 1956.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Chinna Nalla Kalatkal Tola Udaiyar (founder); the Udaiyar poligars

kingdoms.name: Utpala dynasty of Kashmir
kingdoms.description: The Kashmiri house founded by Avantivarman, remembered for Suyya’s great flood-control and irrigation works on the Jhelum. The strict dynastic line ended in 939; the succession of Yashaskara, Parvagupta and finally Queen Didda carried it to the Lohara accession in 1003.

kingdoms.name: Varman dynasty of Bengal
kingdoms.description: A short-lived house that took south-eastern Bengal from the Chandras and held it until Vijayasena absorbed it into the Sena realm. Its beginnings are genuinely uncertain — sources place Jatavarman’s rise anywhere between 1035 and 1075.

kingdoms.name: Vijayanagara Empire
kingdoms.description: The empire founded by the Sangama brothers Harihara and Bukka on the Tungabhadra, which held the far south for two centuries against the Deccan sultanates. Their allied armies broke it at Talikota in 1565; later kings ruled from Penukonda and Vellore.
kingdoms.capital: Hampi (Vijayanagara) to 1565; then Penukonda, Chandragiri (1592) & Vellore (1604)

kingdoms.name: Wancho
kingdoms.description: The Wancho of the Longding hills, known for their wood-carving and strong chiefly village democracies.

kingdoms.name: Western Chalukya Empire
kingdoms.description: The Kalyani Chalukyas, who overthrew the Rashtrakutas in 973 and fought the Cholas for the Deccan for two centuries. Vikramaditya VI’s fifty-year reign was the high point; the Kalachuris usurped Kalyani between 1157 and 1183, and the Seunas drove Someshvara IV into exile in 1189. The flag shown here is a modern reconstruction, not a surviving banner: no picture of a Chalukya standard has come down to us. It is drawn from the insignia the records do name — the Varaha or boar, "their family emblem, said to have been received through the grace of Narayana", and the palidhvaja, the banner of paramount sovereignty (The Classical Age, HCIP III, printed pp. 423 and 130).
kingdoms.notableRulers: Tailapa II; Someshvara I; Vikramaditya VI

kingdoms.name: Western Ganga dynasty
kingdoms.description: The long-lived house of southern Karnataka, patrons of Jainism and of Kannada letters; the colossal Gommateshvara at Shravanabelagola was raised by their minister Chavundaraya. Rajaraja Chola I ended their rule in Gangavadi around the year 1000.

kingdoms.name: Vanga–Samatata chiefs (matsyanyaya)
kingdoms.description: Editorial label. After the last attested Khadga king (c. 690s), east Bengal fell to obscure petty kings amid the anarchy a contemporary record calls matsyanyaya (HCIP III, pp. 79-80).

kingdoms.name: Magadha chiefs (matsyanyaya)
kingdoms.description: Editorial label. The Later Guptas end in or shortly before the second quarter of the 8th century (HCIP III, pp. 63-64); Magadha is obscure until Gopala.

kingdoms.name: Nepal (post-Licchavi kings)
kingdoms.description: Editorial label. After Jayadeva II (last date 737) Nepal's history is 'very obscure' for two centuries, under Tibetan and at times Pala supremacy (HCIP III, pp. 73-74; HCIP IV, pp. 10-11).

kingdoms.name: Terai chiefs
kingdoms.description: Editorial label. No source places the Gauda anarchy in the Nepal Terai; the tract between the hill kingdoms and the plains powers is unrecorded.

kingdoms.name: Dimasa (Hidamba) kingdom
kingdoms.description: The Barak valley and North Cachar hills, mapped by Schwartzberg (plate IV.1) as Hidamba, distinct from Kamarupa — the forerunners of the Dimasa/Kachari kingdom.

kingdoms.name: Kongu chiefdoms
kingdoms.description: The Kongu country had its own rulers — Pallavamalla allied 'with the rulers of Kongu' (Sastri, block 139) — contested by the Pandyas from c. 700 and annexed by Varaguna I in the 770s.

kingdoms.name: Jalandhara–Trigarta kingdom
kingdoms.description: The hill kingdom of Jalandhara-Trigarta, attested from Hiuen Tsang's day (HCIP III, p. 111) through the 12th century (HCIP IV, p. 118, 170); taken for Ghazni only under Ibrahim, c. 1090 (HCIP V, p. 30).

kingdoms.name: Chamba kingdom
kingdoms.description: The Varman line of Chamba, established in the 6th century; Ajita-varman flourished in the mid-8th (HCIP IV, p. 122). One of the longest-lived hill states of the Himalaya.

kingdoms.name: Kuluta kingdom
kingdoms.description: The Kuluta kingdom of the upper Beas, a named kingdom in the 7th century (HCIP III, p. 111) with chiefs still recorded in the 10th (HCIP IV, p. 122).

kingdoms.name: Uddiyana kingdom
kingdoms.description: The Swat valley kingdom of Uddiyana, whose king received Tang investiture in 720; dependent on Kashmir in the mid-8th century (HCIP III, p. 622).

kingdoms.name: Pratiharas of Avanti
kingdoms.description: 'Early in the eighth century A.D. a Pratihara chief Nagabhata was ruling in this region... capital at Ujjayini' (HCIP III, p. 154) — the seed of the Gurjara-Pratihara empire.

kingdoms.name: Pratihara of Mandavyapura (Mandore)
kingdoms.description: The elder Pratihara branch of Harichandra's line at Mandore, ruling Marwar from the 6th century (HCIP III, p. 65), absorbed as the imperial line rose.

kingdoms.name: Gurjaras of Nandipuri (Lata)
kingdoms.description: The Gurjara principality of Lata between the Mahi and the Kim (HCIP III, p. 66); last king Jayabhata IV, last date A.D. 735 (p. 221).

kingdoms.name: Chahamanas of Broach
kingdoms.description: Chahamana Bhartrivaddha II ruled Broach in A.D. 756 as feudatory of Nagavaloka (HCIP III, p. 157, 226).

kingdoms.name: Caliphal Makran (Umayyad–Abbasid)
kingdoms.description: Coastal Makran was an Arab province and the springboard of the 711 conquest of Sindh (HCIP III, p. 29); Caliphal control lapsed to local Maliks around the Saffarid takeover c. 870.

kingdoms.name: Alupa dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Alupas of Tulu-nadu, acknowledging Chalukya, Rashtrakuta and later Hoysala overlords but ruling the South Kanara coast in their own name for centuries (Sastri, block 133). Schwartzberg maps them at Udayavara through 1200 and an Alupa queen still ruled South Canara in 1279-92.

kingdoms.name: Adigaiman of Tagadur
kingdoms.description: The Adigaiman line of Tagadur, in the Pallava orbit; an Adigaiman fought in the confederacy of the 770s (Sastri, block 139).

kingdoms.name: Bana kingdom (Perumbanappadi)
kingdoms.description: The Banas of Perumbanappadi, feudatories of the Pallavas — Jayanandivarman held territory of Nandivarman c. 775 (Sastri, block 139; HCIP IV, pp. 151-152).

kingdoms.name: Telugu Chodas of Renadu
kingdoms.description: The Telugu-Choda chiefs of Renadu, in Rayalaseema from the 7th century (Sastri, block 130), under Chalukya and then Rashtrakuta suzerainty.

kingdoms.name: Chalukya of Lata (Navsari)
kingdoms.description: The Chalukya viceroyalty of Lata, a cadet house with its own succession at Navsari. Its viceroy Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin destroyed an Arab army near Navsari c. 738 and was titled Anivartaka-nivartayitri, 'repeller of the unrepellable'. Dantidurga extirpated the house c. 750, years before the Rashtrakutas overthrew Badami itself (HCIP III, p. 184).

kingdoms.name: Kamboja-Pala dynasty (Gauda)
kingdoms.description: The Kamboja usurpers of Gauda and Radha, attested by the Irda copper-plate of Nayapala and the Dinajpur pillar - a 10th-century house that took west Bengal from the weakened Palas until Mahipala I recovered his fatherland c. 988 (Schwartzberg plate IV.1; The Struggle for Empire, pp. 25, 805).

kingdoms.name: Parvagupta dynasty (Queen Didda)
kingdoms.description: Parvagupta seized the throne of Kashmir in 949, a year after the poisoning of the elected Brahman king Yasaskara. His son Kshemagupta married Didda of Lohara, who ruled first as regent and then, from 980, in her own name - the queen who dominated Kashmir for half a century and bequeathed it to her Lohara kin.

kingdoms.name: Velanandu Choda dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Chodas of Velanadu, Chola viceroys of Vengi who declared their independence at the end of Rajaraja II's reign, c. 1173, and held the Krishna-Godavari coast until the Kakatiya absorption under Ganapati (Sastri, A History of South India, block 174).

kingdoms.name: Bana dynasty (Dakshina Kosala)
kingdoms.description: The Banas of Dakshina Kosala, whom Schwartzberg places across Chhattisgarh from the mid-8th century. Their one firmly dated king, Vikramaditya I (c. 870-95), built the temple at Pali near Ratnapur. A different house from the southern Banas of the Kolar country.

kingdoms.name: Gurjaras of the Punjab (Alakhana)
kingdoms.description: The Gurjara house of the Punjab doabs, subordinate allies of the Gurjara-Pratiharas from the mid-9th century. Its attested king Alakhana lost the Takka-land east of the Chenab to Sankaravarman of Kashmir c. 888 and passed under Hindu Shahi protection; the house fades from record after 902.

kingdoms.name: Lahore kings (Bharat's line)
kingdoms.description: The local kings of Lahore remembered in the Adab-ul-Muluk: Hah son of Bhadra, who founded Lohur and "ruled there for seventy-five years", then Bharat and Handrat, until Jayapala the Shahi annexed the kingdom in 999.

kingdoms.name: Kikan (Jat chiefs of the Bolan)
kingdoms.description: The Jat state of the Bolan hill country, which the Arab governors of Sindh raided again and again and never held: "though often defeated, never yielded, and that Pass remained sealed to the invaders." Conquered at last by the Saffarids c. 870.

kingdoms.name: Madra kingdom
kingdoms.description: The old Madra country of the central Punjab, whose ruler appears among the vassal chiefs at Dharmapala's imperial durbar at Kannauj - the Pala empire's farthest-flung courtier. Painted for the Chenab-Ravi country from 761, after Lalitaditya of Kashmir, to the Pratihara conquest of the Punjab in 822; a Pala vassal 790-805.

kingdoms.name: Chalukyas of Saurashtra (Una)
kingdoms.description: A Chalukya house ruling southern Saurashtra around Una and Junagadh from the latter eighth century, feudatory to the Gurjara-Pratiharas after Valabhi's fall.

kingdoms.name: Sauryas (Varaha dynasty)
kingdoms.description: The Varaha kings of central Saurashtra: Mahavaraha fought Krishna I's Rashtrakutas, and Jayavaraha was ruling west of Wadhwan in 783.

kingdoms.name: Chapas of Vardhamana (Wadhwan)
kingdoms.description: The Chapa (Chavda) house the Pratiharas set over eastern Saurashtra after destroying Valabhi; Dharanivaraha of this line was Mahipala's feudatory in 914.

kingdoms.name: Guhila (Chatsu branch)
kingdoms.description: The southern Guhila line at Chatsu, attested from Dhanika's inscription of 684 - first under the Mauryas of Chittorgarh, then feudatories of the imperial Pratiharas, ruling the Jaipur-Tonk country.

kingdoms.name: Rashtrakutas of Berar (Achalapura)
kingdoms.description: The Rashtrakuta feudatory line of Berar under the Chalukyas of Badami, attested from the Multai grant of 709. Dantidurga rose from this country to overthrow his overlords and found the empire in 753.

kingdoms.name: Early Bhanja dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Bhanja houses of the Keonjhar-Mayurbhanj uplands, ruling "almost continuously" since Disabhanja of Sitabhinji; their dated Khinjali line emerges in the tenth century.

kingdoms.name: Khasa chiefs of Darvabhisara
kingdoms.description: The Khasa house founded by the merchant Nara, who "established his authority over Darvabhisara" while puppet kings sat on the Karkota throne; his son Naravahana still held the Rajouri-Punch hills under Sankaravarman of Kashmir.

kingdoms.name: Arab governors of Sindh (house of Musa)
kingdoms.description: From 836, when Musa named his own son Imran his successor, "the governors of Sindh ruled practically as independent chiefs" - a hereditary house in all but name, the bridge from the Caliphal province to the Habbarid emirate of 854.

kingdoms.name: Kalachuri of Sarayupara
kingdoms.description: The collateral Kalachuri branch on the Sarayu, founded by Rajaputra in the late eighth century; Sankaragana of this line served the Pratihara Bhoja as feudatory. A named royal house where the map once showed only imperial wash.

kingdoms.name: Malayaketu dynasty (Vijayapura)
kingdoms.description: The Maharajadhirajas of Vijayapura at the Himalayan foot - Jayaditya I, Dharmaditya, Jayaditya II (ruling A.D. 870) - bearing full imperial titles in their own small kingdom between the Pratihara and Pala empires.

kingdoms.name: Rashtrakutas of Lata
kingdoms.description: The Gujarat branch of the imperial Rashtrakutas, founded when Govinda III set his brother Indra over Lata; Karka Suvarnavarsha restored Amoghavarsha to the throne, and Dhruva I fought the empire itself for a generation. The line lasted "till the first half of the tenth century".

kingdoms.name: Paramara (Vagada branch)
kingdoms.description: Dambarasimha's line of the Paramaras, ruling Vagada - modern Banswara and Dungarpur - as vassals of the main branch at Dhara until the early twelfth century.

kingdoms.name: Bhanja of Khinjali
kingdoms.description: The Khinjali Bhanjas - Silabhanja I, Satrubhanja, and Ranabhanja of the fifty-eight-year reign - whose kingdom "corresponded to the old feudatory states of Baud and Sonpur" on the middle Mahanadi.

kingdoms.name: Bhanja of Khijjinga
kingdoms.description: The Bhanja house of Khiching in Mayurbhanj, ruling Bhanjabhumi roughly 850-1000 - heirs of a family "ruling in Orissa almost continuously since the fourth or fifth century".

kingdoms.name: Vaidumba dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Vaidumbas, "in possession of the Renandu seven-thousand country in the ninth century" from Irigaya onward, holding the Cuddapah uplands between the great powers from the ninth to the thirteenth century.

kingdoms.name: Chahamanas of Pratapgarh
kingdoms.description: The local Chahamana house of Partabgarh in southern Rajputana, "a source of great pleasure to king Bhojadeva" - loyal vassals on the Pratihara empire's southern rim.

kingdoms.name: Nolamba dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Nolamba-Pallavas of Nolambavadi 32,000 - the Chitaldrug country - fighting their neighbours "with the support of the Western Gangas" from Mangi to Mahendra I, until Butuga II earned the name Nolambakulantaka, "death to the Nolamba race".

kingdoms.name: Yasaskara dynasty of Kashmir
kingdoms.description: When the Utpala line guttered out in 939, an assembly of Brahmans elected one of their own, Yasaskara, king of Kashmir. He ruled nine years and was poisoned; within a year Parvagupta had murdered his boy successor and taken the throne.

kingdoms.name: Thakkiya family chiefs
kingdoms.description: The officer of the Thakkiya family to whom Sankaravarman of Kashmir handed the Punjab territories he stripped from the Pratihara Mahendrapala - a paper principality that evaporated with Kashmir's own collapse after 902.

kingdoms.name: Chudasama
kingdoms.description: The Yaduvanshi house of Saurashtra, from Vamanasthali (Vanthali) and, from Navaghana, from inside the fort of Junagadh - a branch of the Sammas of Sindh by their own reckoning. They held the peninsula until the Chaulukyas broke them in 1125, came back under Mandalika I in 1294, bent to Delhi after Muhammad bin Tughluq took Junagadh in 1350, and ended when Mandalika III gave up the fort to Mahmud Begada in 1470; the state was annexed in 1472. THIS ATLAS USED TO CALL THEM "Abhira (Chudasama) of Vanthali", after HCIP V pp. 75-76 - but HCIP is there repeating Hemachandra, court poet to the Chaulukya kings who invaded them, whose Dvyashraya-Kavya calls Graharipu an Abhira and a tyrannical shepherd preying on pilgrims to Somnath. Their own epigraphs - Dhandusar 1389, Neminath on Girnar c. 1454 - call them Yaduvanshi. (Correction, 18 September 2026.)
kingdoms.notableRulers: Graharipu; Navaghana; Khengara; Mandalika I; Mandalika III

kingdoms.name: Vemulavada Chalukya dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Chalukya feudatories of Vemulavada in the Karimnagar country, loyal swords of the Rashtrakutas: Narasimha II rode with Indra III to the Ganga, and Arikesari II sheltered a fugitive Vengi king - and patronised Pampa, the first great poet of Kannada, who made his patron the Arjuna of his Bharata.

kingdoms.name: Chaulukya of Lata (Barappa's line)
kingdoms.description: The Chaulukya line Taila II planted in Lata after Manyakheta fell - his general Barappa, who beat the old Rashtrakuta feudatories, was killed by Mularaja's son Chamundaraja, and Barappa's son Gongiraja won the country back. A Deccan garrison kingdom wedged between Gujarat and the Chalukya empire.

kingdoms.name: Chahamana of Naddula (Nadol)
kingdoms.description: The Chahamana branch founded at Nadol by Lakshmana, youngest son of Vakpatiraja I of Shakambhari. Sobhita annexed Mount Abu; his successor Baliraja lost Abu, Jalor and Bhinmal to the Paramara Munja.

kingdoms.name: Paramara of Abu (Chandravati)
kingdoms.description: The Paramara branch Munja set over Mount Abu about 980 under his son Aranyaraja, ruling the Sirohi hills from Chandravati - the house that would raise the Dilwara temples' patrons.

kingdoms.name: Paramara of Jabalipura (Jalor)
