kingdoms.description: Munja gave Jalor to his son Chandana and Bhinmal to his nephew Dusala, detaching both from the Chahamanas of Nadol - a Paramara wedge across southern Marwar.

kingdoms.name: Telugu Choda dynasty (Jata Choda Bhima)
kingdoms.description: For twenty-seven years the throne of Vengi was held by Jata Choda Bhima, a Telugu Choda who killed Danarnava and took the kingdom - the interval later Eastern Chalukya inscriptions call simply the interregnum. Rajaraja Chola ended it by restoring Saktivarman in 999.

kingdoms.name: Shilahara of Kolhapur
kingdoms.description: The third Shilahara house, founded by Jatiga in the South Maratha country of Kolhapur, Miraj and Karhad, ruling as independent or semi-independent sovereigns after the Rashtrakuta empire fell, until the Yadavas ended them.

kingdoms.name: Satrughnadeva of Tribhandapura
kingdoms.description: A raja named Satrughnadeva, known from a single stone inscription of his reign at Bhatinda - the one named ruler the sources give for the cis-Sutlej plains between the fall of Pratihara power and the coming of the Ghaznavids.

kingdoms.name: Kingdom of Lohara
kingdoms.description: The hill kingdom of the Lohrin valley behind Punch - one district on this map, and NOT the same polity as the Lohara dynasty of Kashmir beside it. This is the family’s home: its princess Didda married Kshemagupta of Kashmir and ruled the valley for half a century, and in 1003 her adopted heir Samgramaraja took the Kashmir throne. Lohara itself kept its own lords through all of it, and in 1101 it was from here that Uchchala and Sussala marched on Harsha and took Kashmir a second time. HCIP IV p. 113: "Simharaja, king of Lohara, identified with the valley of Lohrin".

kingdoms.name: Kingdom of Rajapuri
kingdoms.description: The hill kingdom of Rajapuri, modern Rajauri, on the road from the Punjab into Kashmir - conquered by Didda's general Phalguna, and subdued again by Tunga when its king Prithvipala turned hostile.

kingdoms.name: Chamundaraja of Jhalawar
kingdoms.description: The Maharajadhiraja Chamundaraja, ruling the Jhalawar country in 971 - the independent king whose realm formed the northern boundary of Siyaka II's Malwa until Munja pushed the Paramara frontier past him.

kingdoms.name: Kachchha kingdom of Lakha
kingdoms.description: The kingdom of Kachchha under Lakha son of Phula, who rode to the aid of Graharipu of Vanthali against Mularaja and died in the battle; Kachchha-desa passed to the Chaulukyas after him.

kingdoms.name: Shilahara of South Konkan
kingdoms.description: The southern Shilahara house, set over the Konkan coast by the Rashtrakuta Krishna I under its founder Sanaphulla. Taila II brought it under Chalukya suzerainty, as the Kharepatan grant of Rattaraja in 1008 records - the reason this coast wears an overlord where the Shilaharas to the north do not.

kingdoms.name: Western Ganga (Kolar branch)
kingdoms.description: The Ganga branch of Kolar and the north-eastern Gangavadi, whose Prithvipati I fell fighting for the Pallavas at Sripurambiyam and whose Prithvipati II held the Bana country as Parantaka Chola's feudatory - a house whose overlord was the Tamil south while the main Ganga kingdom at Talakad served the Rashtrakutas. Absorbed into Butuga II's kingdom in 941.

kingdoms.name: Rashtrakutas of Badaun
kingdoms.description: The Kanauj Rashtrakutas after Kanauj: driven from Gadhipura about 1090, the family settled at Budaun - "one of the mothers of cities, and one of the chiefest of the country of Hind" - and held the Panchala country under Tribhuvana, Madanapala, who repulsed Sultan Mas'ud III, and their successors until Qutb-ud-din took the kingdom in 1202.

kingdoms.name: Dandabhukti kingdom
kingdoms.description: The independent kingdom of Dandabhukti in the Midnapore country, whose king Dharmapala was the first ruler Rajendra Chola defeated on his march to the Ganga - one of the three states the Chola records show standing free of the Palas in the lower delta.

kingdoms.name: Southern Radha (Sura kings)
kingdoms.description: Ranasura's kingdom of Southern Radha, west of the Bhagirathi, which the Chola records show independent of the Palas when Rajendra came north; the Kalachuri Karna occupied it later "probably by defeating king Ranasura or his successor".

kingdoms.name: Kaivarta kingdom of Varendra
kingdoms.description: The kingdom the Kaivartas made out of the Pala collapse. Divya took Varendri about 1075 and was followed by his brother Rudoka and his nephew Bhima - three kings in succession, which is why the books treat them as a dynasty and not a rising. Ramapala won the homeland back only after assembling every feudatory he could buy.

kingdoms.name: Urasa (Hazara hill kingdom)
kingdoms.description: The hill kingdom of Urasa in the Hazara country, which beat off Ananta of Kashmir and was later conquered by Kalasa's general; its ruler sat among the eight hill kings who assembled at Kalasa's court in 1087.

kingdoms.name: Kalachuris of Kalyani
kingdoms.description: The house that took the Deccan throne from the Chalukyas and held it for a quarter of a century. Bijjala was a Chalukya feudatory of Tardavadi who seized real power in 1156 while Taila III was a prisoner of the Kakatiyas, ruled outright from 1162, and was followed by Sovideva, Mallugi, Sankama, Ahavamalla and Singhana. Somesvara IV won Kalyana back in 1181. Their reign is also the setting of Basava and the Virashaiva movement. The flag shown here is a modern reconstruction, not a surviving banner. No device is recorded for the Kalyani branch itself; the Kalachuris at large are credited with the Gaja-Lakshmi seal — "like that of the Sarabhapuriyas and the Kalachuris" (The Age of Imperial Kanauj, HCIP IV, printed p. 146) — so this reconstruction carries the parent house's device, which is an inference rather than an attestation for Kalyani.

kingdoms.name: Kingdom of Srihatta
kingdoms.description: A line of its own in the Surma valley - Kharavana, Gokuladeva, Narayana, Kesavadeva, Isanadeva - neither Varman nor Sena. HCIP V p. 35 is explicit that the Varmans "are not known to have asserted their supremacy on any country beyond East Bengal". Srihatta kept its own kings until Sikandar Khan Ghazi conquered it in 1303.

kingdoms.name: Yaduvamshi kings of Bayana-Sripatha
kingdoms.description: The Yadu house that held the Bharatpur tract and the Mathura country through the twelfth century, between the Chahamanas and the Gahadavalas, until the Ghurids besieged Bayana in 1195-96 and Kunwarpal submitted.

kingdoms.name: Vuppadeva dynasty of Kashmir
kingdoms.description: The line that followed the Loharas. Vantideva (1165-72) was the last king of the second Lohara dynasty; on his death the people of Kashmir elected Vuppadeva, and his line and its successors held the valley until Suhadeva lost it in 1320 and the Sultanate began.

kingdoms.name: Principality of Rohana
kingdoms.description: The southern Sinhalese realm. After Vijayabahu I died in 1110 Ceylon broke into rival kingdoms, and Rohana - the country south and east of the Mahaweli - went its own way until Parakramabahu I reunited the island in 1153.

kingdoms.name: Paramara of Vidarbha (Chanda)
kingdoms.description: The southern branch of the Paramaras, ruling the Vidarbha country round Nagpur and Chanda. Naravarman held the Nagpur region and Chanda before 1104, and a minor branch of the house was still ruling there when the Seuna Singhana defeated the Paramara Bhoja at Chahanda in the thirteenth century. Vidarbha lies north of the Godavari, the stated northern limit of the restored Chalukya realm, and no ruler of this branch between those two points is named in the sources this atlas is built on.

kingdoms.name: Saffarid dynasty
kingdoms.description: Ya'qub ibn Layth's line of Sistan, which displaced the Tahirids in Khurasan in 872 and ruled from a seat outside the subcontinent. Sindh, Multan included, was reckoned part of its dominions until the Samanids took Khurasan in 903, after which Mansura and Multan went their own ways. It holds no ground on this map because its own capital lay beyond it.

kingdoms.name: Dhar
kingdoms.description: The Puar (Pawar) Maratha house of Dhar, a state of the Central India Agency and one of the two Puar states of Malwa, the other being Dewas. Central India Agency states drawn from Schwartzberg, A Historical Atlas of South Asia, plate VIII (The Indian Empire, administrative divisions 1947), which shows each of these as a state and not as British territory. The atlas had them as East India Company and then British Raj from 1818, which was wrong: the Central Provinces around them were British India, but these were not. Painted from the settlement of 1818, when they passed from Maratha domination to British protection. The houses themselves are older than that; the atlas dates the years each held ground under its own name, as it does elsewhere.

kingdoms.name: Ratlam
kingdoms.description: A Rathore Rajput state of Malwa in the Central India Agency, and the largest of the Malwa Agency salute states. Central India Agency states drawn from Schwartzberg, A Historical Atlas of South Asia, plate VIII (The Indian Empire, administrative divisions 1947), which shows each of these as a state and not as British territory. The atlas had them as East India Company and then British Raj from 1818, which was wrong: the Central Provinces around them were British India, but these were not. Painted from the settlement of 1818, when they passed from Maratha domination to British protection. The houses themselves are older than that; the atlas dates the years each held ground under its own name, as it does elsewhere.
kingdoms.spanNote: Painted from 1653 as a Mughal, then Maratha, tributary (HCIP VIII pp. 24, 145).

kingdoms.name: Jhabua
kingdoms.description: A Rathore Rajput state in the Bhil country of western Malwa, under the Bhopawar Agency of Central India. Central India Agency states drawn from Schwartzberg, A Historical Atlas of South Asia, plate VIII (The Indian Empire, administrative divisions 1947), which shows each of these as a state and not as British territory. The atlas had them as East India Company and then British Raj from 1818, which was wrong: the Central Provinces around them were British India, but these were not. Painted from the settlement of 1818, when they passed from Maratha domination to British protection. The houses themselves are older than that; the atlas dates the years each held ground under its own name, as it does elsewhere.
kingdoms.spanNote: Painted from 1653 as a Mughal, then Maratha, tributary (HCIP VIII pp. 24, 145).

kingdoms.name: Barwani
kingdoms.description: A Sisodia Rajput state on the Narmada, in the Bhopawar Agency of Central India. Central India Agency states drawn from Schwartzberg, A Historical Atlas of South Asia, plate VIII (The Indian Empire, administrative divisions 1947), which shows each of these as a state and not as British territory. The atlas had them as East India Company and then British Raj from 1818, which was wrong: the Central Provinces around them were British India, but these were not. Painted from the settlement of 1818, when they passed from Maratha domination to British protection. The houses themselves are older than that; the atlas dates the years each held ground under its own name, as it does elsewhere.
kingdoms.spanNote: Painted from 1653 as a Mughal, then Maratha, tributary (HCIP VIII pp. 24, 145).

kingdoms.name: Alirajpur
kingdoms.description: A Rathore state of the Bhil country west of the Narmada, in the Bhopawar Agency of Central India. Central India Agency states drawn from Schwartzberg, A Historical Atlas of South Asia, plate VIII (The Indian Empire, administrative divisions 1947), which shows each of these as a state and not as British territory. The atlas had them as East India Company and then British Raj from 1818, which was wrong: the Central Provinces around them were British India, but these were not. Painted from the settlement of 1818, when they passed from Maratha domination to British protection. The houses themselves are older than that; the atlas dates the years each held ground under its own name, as it does elsewhere.
kingdoms.spanNote: Painted from 1653 as a Mughal, then Maratha, tributary (HCIP VIII pp. 24, 145).

kingdoms.name: Rajgarh State
kingdoms.description: An Umat Rajput state of eastern Malwa, in the Central India Agency. Central India Agency states drawn from Schwartzberg, A Historical Atlas of South Asia, plate VIII (The Indian Empire, administrative divisions 1947), which shows each of these as a state and not as British territory. The atlas had them as East India Company and then British Raj from 1818, which was wrong: the Central Provinces around them were British India, but these were not. Painted from the settlement of 1818, when they passed from Maratha domination to British protection. The houses themselves are older than that; the atlas dates the years each held ground under its own name, as it does elsewhere.
kingdoms.spanNote: Painted from 1653 as a Mughal, then Maratha, tributary (HCIP VIII pp. 24, 145).

kingdoms.name: Chhatarpur
kingdoms.description: A Bundela state of Bundelkhand, in the Central India Agency, neighbouring Panna and Orchha. Central India Agency states drawn from Schwartzberg, A Historical Atlas of South Asia, plate VIII (The Indian Empire, administrative divisions 1947), which shows each of these as a state and not as British territory. The atlas had them as East India Company and then British Raj from 1818, which was wrong: the Central Provinces around them were British India, but these were not. Painted from the settlement of 1818, when they passed from Maratha domination to British protection. The houses themselves are older than that; the atlas dates the years each held ground under its own name, as it does elsewhere.

kingdoms.name: Gupta Empire
kingdoms.description: The empire of India's Classical Age. Chandragupta I took the imperial title in 320; Samudragupta's Allahabad pillar lists the nine kings of the north he uprooted and the twelve of the south he defeated and released (HCIP III, The Classical Age, pp. 7-9); Chandragupta II destroyed the Western Kshatrapas and brought the Arabian Sea ports under Pataliputra. Skandagupta threw back the Huns c. 455, but the line wore out under them: after Budhagupta the emperors held little beyond Magadha and Bengal, and the last dated imperial record is the Damodarpur plate of 543. The atlas paints the house from 300 in Magadha alone, as the pre-imperial home of Srigupta and Ghatotkacha.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Chandragupta I; Samudragupta; Chandragupta II Vikramaditya; Kumaragupta I; Skandagupta

kingdoms.name: Vakataka dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Deccan power of the Gupta age. Vindhyasakti's line ruled Vidarbha from the mid-third century; Pravarasena I performed four horse-sacrifices and pushed into Malwa and Bundelkhand; his great-grandson Rudrasena II married Chandragupta II's daughter Prabhavatigupta, who ruled as regent for her sons. The Vatsagulma branch under Harishena cut the later Ajanta caves. The house fades from the record c. 510-520 (HCIP III, ch. VIII).
kingdoms.capital: Nandivardhana / Pravarapura; Vatsagulma (Washim) for the cadet line
kingdoms.notableRulers: Pravarasena I; Rudrasena II; Prabhavatigupta (regent); Pravarasena II; Harishena

kingdoms.name: Western Kshatrapas
kingdoms.description: The Saka satraps of Malwa, Gujarat and Saurashtra, a line that lasted almost four centuries and dated its silver coins so carefully that its fall can be read to the year: Rudrasimha III's last issues are of c. 397-415, when Chandragupta II 'destroyed' the Sakas and took Ujjain and the western ports (HCIP II; HCIP III p. 17).
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rudradaman I; Rudrasena II; Rudrasimha III

kingdoms.name: Kushan Empire (late)
kingdoms.description: The last Kushans. After Vasudeva I the great empire of Kanishka shrank to Gandhara and the Punjab, its later kings known almost only from coins and from the Sasanian governors ('Kushanshahs') who took the north-west from them. Samudragupta's Allahabad pillar still names 'Daivaputra Shahi Shahanushahi' among the foreign rulers who sent embassies. Painted here for 300-350, with the frontier approximate.

kingdoms.name: Naga dynasty of Padmavati
kingdoms.description: The Bharasiva Nagas who ruled the Gwalior-Mathura country between the Kushans and the Guptas, performing ten horse-sacrifices on the Ganga according to Vakataka records. Samudragupta 'violently uprooted' Ganapatinaga and Nagasena among the kings of Aryavarta (HCIP III p. 7); their coins come from Pawaya, Mathura and Vidisha.

kingdoms.name: Ahichchhatra kingdom
kingdoms.description: The kingdom of Panchala's old capital in the fourth century, ruled by Achyuta, whose coins bearing the legend 'Achyu' were found at Ahichchhatra and who is the 'Achyuta' uprooted by Samudragupta with the Naga kings (HCIP III p. 7). An editorial name for a polity the sources give only a king.

kingdoms.name: Magha dynasty of Kaushambi
kingdoms.description: The Maghas of Kausambi and Bandhogarh, a local line of the second and third centuries known from dated inscriptions and coins. Painted for 300-334 on the doubtful assumption that a Magha remnant outlived the Kushans until Samudragupta's conquest of the Ganga-Yamuna country (HCIP II).

kingdoms.name: Yaudheya republic
kingdoms.description: The warrior republic of the Sutlej-Yamuna country, whose coins with the legend 'Yaudheya-ganasya jayah' come from Rohtak, Sunet near Ludhiana and Bhatner. They fought Rudradaman in the second century and paid tribute to Samudragupta in the fourth (HCIP III p. 8); they vanish from the record by c. 400.

kingdoms.name: Madra (Madraka) republic
kingdoms.description: The Madrakas of the upper Punjab, one of the frontier peoples who 'gratified the imperious commands' of Samudragupta with tribute and homage (HCIP III p. 8). Their old capital Sakala became the seat of the Huns in the sixth century.

kingdoms.name: Malava republic
kingdoms.description: The Malavas of eastern Rajasthan, who gave their name to Malwa and their era of 58 BCE to half of India. Their coins come by the thousand from Nagar near Tonk, and their sacrificial pillars from Nandsa (226). Samudragupta lists them among his tributaries; by the fifth century their country was the Guptas'.

kingdoms.name: Abhira dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Abhiras who took the Nasik country from the Satavahanas: Isvarasena's inscription at Nasik is dated in his ninth regnal year, and the Puranas allow the line ten kings. The Allahabad pillar counts the Abhiras among Samudragupta's tributary peoples (HCIP III p. 8). Their later history is dark.

kingdoms.name: Chutu dynasty (Banavasi)
kingdoms.description: The Chutu Satakarnis of Banavasi, heirs of the Satavahanas in the western Deccan, known from the Banavasi and Malavalli inscriptions. Mayurasarman's Kadambas replaced them at Banavasi c. 345 (HCIP II; HCIP III ch. XI).

kingdoms.name: Kadamba dynasty (Banavasi)
kingdoms.description: Founded by Mayurasarman, the Brahmana student who, insulted by a Pallava guard at Kanchi, 'took to the sword' and carved a kingdom in the forests of the Western Ghats (Talagunda pillar; HCIP III ch. XI). Kakusthavarman married his daughters to the Guptas and the Vakatakas; Ravivarman fought the Pallavas and the Gangas. The Chalukyas of Vatapi, once their feudatories, absorbed the kingdom in the sixth century.

kingdoms.name: Kalabhra dynasty
kingdoms.description: The 'Kalabhra interregnum': 'some time about A.D. 300 or a little later the whole country was upset by the predatory activities of the Kalabhras', who eclipsed the three Tamil crowns for nearly three centuries (Sastri, A History of South India, pp. 130 ff.). The Buddhist king Achchutavikkanta patronised monasteries in the Chola country. The Velvikudi grant records how the Pandya Kadungon 'recovered' the land from them c. 575-600.
kingdoms.capital: the Kaveri delta and Madurai country

kingdoms.name: Ikshvaku dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Ikshvakus of the Krishna valley, successors of the Satavahanas in Andhra, whose capital Vijayapuri at Nagarjunakonda was one of the great Buddhist centres of the third century. The Pallavas took their country c. 325 (HCIP II).

kingdoms.name: Salankayana dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Salankayanas of Vengi, whose king Hastivarman is one of the twelve southern rulers Samudragupta 'captured and then liberated' (HCIP III p. 7). Their copper plates from the Godavari delta run to the early fifth century, when the Vishnukundins replaced them.

kingdoms.name: Ananda dynasty (Kandarapura)
kingdoms.description: The Ananda-gotra kings of Kandarapura, in the Guntur country south of the Krishna, known from the Gorantla and Mattepad plates. Kandara founded the line early in the sixth century, married a daughter to a Pallava prince and took the title Lord of Trikutaparvata from the Vishnukundins; his kingdom was never more than the Guntur and Tenali taluks, wedged between the Vishnukundins to the north and the Pallavas to the south (Sastri, A History of South India, pp. 102-103).

kingdoms.name: Vishnukundin dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Telugu dynasty that held the Krishna-Godavari country for two centuries. Madhavavarman I, 'the real founder of the greatness of the family', claimed eleven horse-sacrifices and a marriage into the Vakatakas; Pulakesin II overthrew the last king c. 616-624 and installed his brother at Vengi as the first Eastern Chalukya (HCIP III ch. X).
kingdoms.notableRulers: Madhavavarman I; Vikramendravarman II; Manchana Bhattaraka

kingdoms.name: Mathara dynasty of Kalinga
kingdoms.description: The Matharas (or Pitribhaktas) of Kalinga, whose kings styled themselves 'lord of all Kalinga' and ruled from the Mahendra hills to Pishtapura in the fourth and fifth centuries. They are painted from 300 up the Orissa coast, where no other dynasty is known before the Guptas (HCIP III ch. X; p. 92). The Eastern Gangas succeeded them at Kalinganagara in 498.

kingdoms.name: Mahakantara kingdom (Vyaghraraja)
kingdoms.description: 'Vyaghraraja of Mahakantara' — the Great Forest, 'probably forest regions in Jeypore State, Orissa' — is the second of the twelve southern kings named on Samudragupta's Allahabad pillar (HCIP III p. 7). A kingdom known from that one line, carried back to 300 in Bastar and Koraput before the Nalas.

kingdoms.name: Dakshina Kosala kingdom (pre-Sharabhapuriya)
kingdoms.description: 'Mahendra of Kosala' heads Samudragupta's list of the southern kings (HCIP III p. 7): the Chhattisgarh plain, the old Dakshina Kosala, had its own kings through the fourth and fifth centuries, though their names beyond Mahendra are lost. An editorial umbrella until the Sarabhapuriyas appear c. 475.

kingdoms.name: Sharabhapuriya dynasty
kingdoms.description: The kings of Sarabhapura in Dakshina Kosala, known from a long series of copper plates and from Prasannamatra's gold coins struck on the Gupta model. They held the Mahanadi plain for a century and a quarter until the Panduvamsis of Mekala moved down to Sripura (HCIP III ch. XI).

kingdoms.name: Parivrajaka and Uchchakalpa chiefs
kingdoms.description: Two families of feudatory maharajas who ruled the Vindhyan forest tract in the last century of the Guptas and dated their grants in the Gupta era 'while the Guptas ruled the earth'. Hastin's Parivrajakas and Sarvanatha's Uchchakalpas are the clearest picture we have of how the empire's marches were governed (HCIP III chs. II-III).
kingdoms.capital: Uchchakalpa (Unchehra); the Parivrajaka seat in Bundelkhand-Baghelkhand

kingdoms.name: Traikutaka dynasty
kingdoms.description: The Traikutakas of the Konkan coast, who took over from the Abhiras and used their era of 248. Dahrasena performed a horse-sacrifice; Vyaghrasena's grants come from Surat and Pardi. The house held the western seaboard from the Kshatrapas' fall to the rise of the Kalachuris (HCIP III ch. VIII).

kingdoms.name: Sura dynasty (Surat)
kingdoms.description: A line known from a single Banaras copper plate 'of the first half of the sixth century': 'the Sura kings may be regarded as ruling in the Surat region after the fall of the Traikutakas' and were 'probably subdued by the Kalachuris in the second half of the sixth century' (HCIP III pp. 190-191).
kingdoms.notableRulers: the Sura kings of the Banaras grant

kingdoms.name: Bharukachchha kingdom (Samgamasimha)
kingdoms.description: 'Samgamasimha, ruler of Bharukachchha (Broach)', is named in the Sunaokala grant of the year 292 (540 CE) as an independent king of the Narmada mouth; Nirihullaka of the Sankheda grant, later a feudatory of the Kalachuri Sankaragana, may be his descendant (HCIP III p. 192).

kingdoms.name: Mauryas of Konkan
kingdoms.description: The Mauryas of the Konkan, who held the coast from their island fortress of Puri. Chandravarman's Vada inscription belongs to this line. Pulakesin II 'besieged Puri, the goddess of fortune of the western sea', with hundreds of ships and ended the kingdom c. 620 (Aihole prasasti; HCIP III ch. VIII).
kingdoms.capital: Puri (the island of Elephanta or Gharapuri)

kingdoms.name: Bhoja dynasty of Goa (Chandrapura)
kingdoms.description: The Bhojas of Goa, whose copper plates from Siroda and Shiroda show a small kingdom around Chandrapura on the Zuari from the fourth to the sixth century, under the shadow first of the Kadambas and then of the Chalukyas (HCIP III).

kingdoms.name: Samatata kingdom
kingdoms.description: The kingdom of the Meghna delta, 'Samatata' — a frontier state that 'gratified the imperious commands' of Samudragupta with tribute (HCIP III p. 8). Vainyagupta's Gunaighar grant of 507 was issued from here; the Khadgas took the country in the seventh century.

kingdoms.name: Pushkarana kingdom (Chandravarman)
kingdoms.description: Chandravarman, 'lord of Pushkarana', cut his record on the Susunia rock in Bankura in the early fourth century (Sircar, Select Inscriptions I, no. 40) and is the Chandravarman whom Samudragupta uprooted among the nine kings of Aryavarta (HCIP III p. 8). His kingdom in Radha is painted until that conquest.

kingdoms.name: Vanga kingdom (Gopachandra line)
kingdoms.description: Three independent kings of Bengal — Gopachandra, Dharmaditya and Samacharadeva — known from the Faridpur copper plates and the Mallasarul plate of Burdwan, who used imperial titles as Gupta authority dissolved in the delta in the mid-sixth century (HCIP III ch. on Bengal).

kingdoms.name: Gauda kingdom (Shashanka)
kingdoms.description: The first great king of Bengal. Sasanka, once perhaps a Gupta feudatory, ruled Gauda from Karnasuvarna, held Magadha, Dandabhukti, Utkala and Kongoda, and in 606 killed Rajyavardhana of Thanesar — the act that made Harsha's career. Xuanzang, no friend, still found his kingdom intact in the 630s; it collapsed after his death c. 637 (HCIP III ch. V).

kingdoms.name: Davaka kingdom
kingdoms.description: 'Davaka' is named beside Samatata and Kamarupa among the frontier kingdoms that paid Samudragupta tribute (HCIP III p. 8) — the Kapili valley in central Assam. It was absorbed by Kamarupa by the sixth century, probably under Bhutivarman.

kingdoms.name: Kartripura kingdom
kingdoms.description: 'Kartripura', the fourth frontier kingdom of the Allahabad pillar, is placed in Kumaon and Garhwal; Xuanzang's Brahmapura (c. 630) is the same country (HCIP III p. 8, where the Katuria-Raj identification is noted as uncertain). The atlas continues the same hill kingdom as the Katyuri from 700.

kingdoms.name: Gonanda dynasty (Kashmir)
kingdoms.description: Kalhana's kings of Kashmir before the Karkotas — Meghavahana the Buddhist, Pravarasena II who founded Pravarapura (Srinagar) — a chronology the Rajatarangini gives at lengths no one credits. 'The last king of the Gonanda dynasty named Baladitya' left no son, and Durlabhavardhana founded the Karkota line c. 625 (HCIP III p. 132). The Hun Mihirakula's spell in the valley is painted inside it.

kingdoms.name: Kidarite kingdom
kingdoms.description: The 'Kidara Kushanas': Kidara's Huns took Gandhara from the Sasanians in the mid-fourth century and ruled the Punjab and Kashmir with a coinage that copied the Kushan and Gupta types (HCIP III ch. II). The Hephthalite Alchon Huns destroyed them c. 460-470.

kingdoms.name: Alchon Huns
kingdoms.description: The Hunas of Indian record. Toramana overran Malwa c. 500-510 (his Eran boar inscription); his son Mihirakula, 'the tyrant', ruled from Sakala over the Punjab, Kashmir and Malwa until Yasodharman broke him at Sondani in 528 and Baladitya of Magadha refused him tribute. He died in Kashmir c. 540; the Hun hold on the plains went with him (HCIP III chs. II-III; Sung Yun; Xuanzang).

kingdoms.name: Nezak Huns
kingdoms.description: The Nezak kings of Kapisa and the Kabul valley, known from their bull-headed-crown coinage. Xuanzang in 630 found Gandhara and Bannu subject to Kapisa. The Turk Shahis replaced them c. 665, as the first Arab raids reached Kabul. District assignment is low-confidence.

kingdoms.name: Sasanian Empire
kingdoms.description: Persia's last pre-Islamic empire. Shapur I's inscription at the Ka'ba-i Zardusht claims Turan, Makuran, Paradan and 'Hind' to the borders of Peshawar; Sasanian governors held Makran and the Kushan north-west, and Sasanian trade ran the Persian Gulf. The Arabs ended the dynasty in 651; their armies were in Makran by 644. Painted here for the Makran and Turan marches only.
kingdoms.notableRulers: Shapur I; Shapur II; Khusrau I

kingdoms.name: Rai dynasty of Sindh
kingdoms.description: The Hindu kings of Sindh before Chach, known from the Chach-nama: five Rais in 137 years, whose kingdom stretched from Kashmir to Makran and from the sea to Kannauj's marches, with Multan and Brahmanabad as its provinces. Chach, the Brahmin minister, took the throne from the last Rai's widow c. 632 (HCIP III ch. X).
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rai Diwaji; Rai Sahiras; Rai Sahasi II

kingdoms.name: Aulikara dynasty (Dasapura)
kingdoms.description: The Aulikaras of Mandsaur, Gupta feudatories who became the deliverers of northern India. Yasodharman's victory pillar records how Mihirakula, 'whose head had never been brought low before any but Siva', bowed before him at Sondani (528); his Mandsaur inscription of 532 claims dominion from the Brahmaputra to the western ocean. The meteor passed within a decade (HCIP III ch. II).

kingdoms.name: Maukhari dynasty
kingdoms.description: The house that made Kannauj a capital. Isanavarman took the imperial title after his Haraha victories of 554 over 'the Andhras, the Sulikas and the Gaudas'; Sarvavarman killed the Later Gupta Damodaragupta; Grahavarman married Harsha's sister and was murdered in 606 by the Malava king — after which the Maukhari realm passed to Harsha (HCIP III ch. IV).

kingdoms.name: Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) dynasty
kingdoms.description: Harsha's house. Prabhakaravardhana of Thanesar fought the Huns and the Gurjaras; his son Rajyavardhana was murdered by Sasanka in 606, and the sixteen-year-old Harsha took the throne and 'waged incessant warfare' until the north from the Punjab to Bengal acknowledged him. Xuanzang and Bana describe his court; Pulakesin II stopped him on the Narmada. The empire died with him in 647 (HCIP III ch. V).

kingdoms.name: Kannauj (post-Harsha)
kingdoms.description: The kingdom of Kannauj between Harsha and Yasovarman. Harsha's minister Arjuna seized the throne in 648, plundered the Chinese embassy and was carried off to China by Wang Xuance's Tibetan-Nepalese force (HCIP III pp. 124-125); 'for more than half a century thereafter the history of Kanauj is wrapt in obscurity' (HCIP IV, foreword). Painted until Yasovarman appears c. 725.

kingdoms.name: Kalachuri of Mahishmati
kingdoms.description: The early Kalachuris, who rose on the Narmada as the Guptas fell and ruled Malwa, Gujarat, the Konkan and Vidarbha from Mahishmati; Sankaragana held Ujjain by 595. Mangalesa 'put to flight' Buddharaja c. 602, and Pulakesin II finished the kingdom; its Chedi cousins at Tripuri carried the name on (HCIP III ch. IX).

kingdoms.name: Takka kingdom (Punjab)
kingdoms.description: Xuanzang's 'Cheh-ka': the kingdom of the Takkas, stretching 'from the Beas to the Indus' with Multan and Parvata as its dependencies, which he crossed in 630 (Beal, Si-yu-ki, i). An editorial label for the post-Hun Punjab kingdom whose rulers' names are lost. Painted again for the Ravi-Sutlej plains from 761, after Lalitaditya of Kashmir, until the Pratiharas take the Punjab in 822.

kingdoms.name: Pariyatra kingdom (Bairat)
kingdoms.description: Xuanzang's 'Po-li-ye-ta-lo', the kingdom of Pariyatra in the Aravalli country of eastern Rajasthan, with its capital at ancient Vairata (Beal, Si-yu-ki, i). An editorial label for the country between the Aulikaras and the Pratiharas, whose kings are unnamed.

kingdoms.name: Vigraha–Mudgala chiefs of Tosali
kingdoms.description: The Vigraha and Mudgala families who held North and South Tosali — the Orissa coast from Balasore to Puri — in the last century of Gupta suzerainty. Prithivivigraha 'was ruling over Kalinga, in the dominion of the Guptas', in 569-70 (Sumandala plates; HCIP III pp. 92-93). Painted as tributaries of the Guptas to 550 and independent after.

kingdoms.name: Mana dynasty (Tosali)
kingdoms.description: 'In the last quarter of the sixth century A.D. a Mana dynasty ... was ruling over the greater part of Orissa': Sambhuyasas ruled 'Northern and Southern Tosali, which comprised nearly the whole of Orissa from Balasore to Puri District', between 580 and 603 (Soro plates; HCIP III p. 93). Painted in Kendujhar and Mayurbhanj.

kingdoms.name: Zhangzhung kingdom
kingdoms.description: The old kingdom of western Tibet, the Bon country around Kailash, which held Ladakh and the trans-Himalayan valleys until Srong-btsan-sgam-po conquered it c. 644 and folded it into the Tibetan Empire. The district assignment is low-confidence.

kingdoms.name: Marudesa (desert chiefs)
kingdoms.description: Editorial label for Marwar and the Thar between the Kshatrapa and Gupta centuries. The Guptas never held Western Rajputana (HCIP III, p. 12), and no dynasty is recorded in the desert until the Huns and then the Pratiharas of Mandor; the silence of the record, named rather than painted over, in the manner of Jangaldesh.

kingdoms.name: Khanzadas of Nagaur
kingdoms.notableRulers: Shams Khan Dandani; Firuz Khan; Mujahid Khan
kingdoms.description: The Muslim Khans of Nagor, a branch of the Gujarat sultans' family: Firuz Khan son of Shams Khan Dandani did homage to his nephew Ahmad Shah in 1433, and after his death in 1451-2 his brother Mujahid Khan and his son Shams Khan fought over the fort, drawing Rana Kumbha and Qutbuddin of Gujarat into the Nagor war (Bakshi vol. 5 pp. 12-21). Maldeo of Marwar took Nagaur in 1536; under Akbar it was a sarkar administered directly by the empire.

kingdoms.name: Jethwa
kingdoms.capital: Ghumli, then Shrinagar, then Ghumli again, then Ranpur, then Chhaya
kingdoms.notableRulers: Rana Sangaji; Rana Shiyaji; Rana Bhanji
kingdoms.description: The Jethwa Rajputs of the Barda coast, the oldest ruling house of the Saurashtra peninsula, who followed the Saindhavas at Ghumli and held the western horn for a thousand years. Their country was Jyeshthukadesh, the land of the Jethwas. Ghumli was the capital until 1313, when Barmaniyaji Jadeja stormed it and Rana Bhanji fled to Ranpur; Jam Rawal took the port of Nagnath in 1540 and made it Nawanagar; the seat moved on to Chhaya, and in 1671 Rana Vikmatji Khimoji took Porbandar from the Mughals. The house held the title Rana from Sangaji, who won it from the Vaghelas, until the last Rana died in 1979. Vassals of whoever held Gujarat, and never conquered outright by any of them.

kingdoms.name: Pattikera
kingdoms.description: The kingdom east of the old Brahmaputra whose capital, from the eleventh century, was Pattikera on the Mainamati hills near Comilla - named in a Nepalese manuscript of 1015 and, as Patikkara, in the Burmese chronicles as the western limit of Anoratha's Burma. Its one dated king, Harikaladeva Ranavankamalla, took the throne in 1202-03; his line was overthrown by the Devas.

kingdoms.name: Deva dynasty of Samatata and Vanga
kingdoms.description: The thirteenth-century Devas - no kin of the eighth-century house of Devaparvata - who rose from a village headman under Pattikera to the lordship of Samatata and Vanga. Damodara ended Harikaladeva's line; his son Danujamadhava Dasarathadeva, the Danuj Rai of the chronicles, met Balban at Sonargaon in 1283. The country beyond the Meghna held out until 1326-27.

kingdoms.name: Gohad (Jat Ranas)
kingdoms.notableRulers: Bhim Singh Rana; Chhatra Singh Rana; Kirat Singh Rana
kingdoms.description: The Jat Ranas of Gohad, between the Chambal and Gwalior: 'a Jat power distinct from the Bharatpur family' that 'raised its head but was crushed by the Maratha advance from Malwa' (Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 419). Bhim Singh Rana took Gwalior fort in 1740; the Marathas took it from Gohad in 1754-55, the Rana had it back before Mahadji Sindhia took it in 1766 (HCIP VIII p. 255), Warren Hastings gave it back to Rana Chhatra Singh after Popham's escalade of 1780, and Mahadji stormed it for good on 31 July 1783 and seized Gohad and the Rana on 25 February 1784 (Sarkar III p. 273). Restored by the British in 1804, exchanged for Dholpur when Gohad went back to Sindia in 1805 (HCIP VIII p. 499): the same house continues on this map as Dholpur, 'the sole remnant of that large principality of Gohad'.
kingdoms.spanNote: 1740 is the Jat seizure of Gwalior fort and 1805 the treaty of Mustafapur that returned Gohad to Sindia; the Rana's line continues as Dholpur from 1806. The fort years and the roll's dates are web-sourced (Wikipedia: Gohad State; Battle of Gwalior (1754)); the possession of Gwalior in 1757-62, 1766-80 and from 1783, and the sieges of 1766, 1783 and 1784, are Sarkar's and HCIP VIII's.

kingdoms.name: Farrukhabad (Bangash)
kingdoms.notableRulers: Muhammad Khan Bangash; Qaim Khan; Ahmad Khan Bangash
kingdoms.description: The Bangash Nawabs of Farrukhabad, an Afghan house of the middle Doab. Muhammad Khan Bangash, a Kaghazai Karlai soldier of fortune who rose with Farrukhsiyar, founded the city in 1714 and held at his greatest 'the whole district of Farrukhabad, the western half of Cawnpur, nearly the whole of Mainpuri and Etah' as the Emperor's jagirdar and viceroy of Allahabad and Malwa (Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 29). Qaim Khan fell to the Rohillas in 1749 and Safdar Jang seized the country; Ahmad Khan's rising swept the wazir out and beat him at Ram Chatauni (1750), and the peace of 1752 left the house Farrukhabad and its mahals. Its Nawab ceded the state to the Company in 1802 (Sarkar IV p. 266).
kingdoms.spanNote: 1714 is the founding of Farrukhabad city (Sarkar I p. 29); 1802 the cession to the Company, a year after Awadh's of November 1801 (Sarkar IV p. 266). Sarkar gives Muhammad Khan's death as 1743 on p. 39 and 1748 on p. 29; the roll follows p. 39. The Awadh tribute of the later Nawabs is not drawn.

kingdoms.name: Sonda (Swadi Rajas)
kingdoms.description: The Swadi (Sonda) Rajas of the Kanara uplands, feudatories first of Vijayanagara and then of Bijapur. Shivaji took Ponda, Karwar and Sonda in 1675 (Sardesai I, chronology); in 1756 'Sondha agreed to pay 8 lacs' to the Peshwa (Sardesai II p. 329); in 1763 Haidar Ali 'conquered Sonda, the king of Sonda, Savai Immadi Sadasiv, flying to the Portuguese for protection and surrendering to them his territory below the Ghats' (HCIP VIII p. 455).
kingdoms.spanNote: Painted only for Uttara Kannada, 1653-1762; its tributary ties to Bijapur and the Mughals are undated in the library and not drawn.

kingdoms.name: Chitradurga (Nayaka)
kingdoms.description: The Beda Nayakas of Chitradurga, a palegar house of the Vijayanagara successor world that held the Chitradurga-Davanagere country through the Bijapur, Mughal (Sira) and Nizam years. Hayavadana Rao I p. 313 names 'the Beda chiefs of Chintanakal (Chitaldrug)'; Haidar made them pay tribute in 1762 (HR II pp. 425-426) and took the fort in March 1779 (HR III block 244).
kingdoms.spanNote: Before 1762 the Nayakas were 'long held to be subject to [Sira's] jurisdiction' (HR II p. 425); the library gives no tribute dates, so no Mughal or Nizam vassal line is drawn.

kingdoms.name: Palghat (Palakkad Rajas)
kingdoms.description: The Palakkad Achans, a Malabar house distinct from the Zamorin, who called in Mysore against him - Kareem (scan pp. 30, 286) from 1732, Menon p. 243 in 1756-57 ('Komu Achan, the Raja of Palghat, sought the help of the king of Mysore'). Haidar built the Palghat fort in 1766 and kept Palghat in every settlement.
kingdoms.spanNote: Painted for Palakkad district to Haidar's 1766 occupation.

kingdoms.name: Bhutan (Deb Raja)
kingdoms.description: The Drukpa state of Bhutan, whose Deb Raja held the Duars along the foot of the hills. HCIP IX p. 1020: the tribute 'paid by Bhutan to the Cooch Behar Raja for the province of Falakata' passed to the Company in 1774; p. 1021: the claims of the Deb Raja to 'Falakata and Julpaish' were decided 'in favour of the Deb Raja's rights'; p. 1022: the Bengal Duars were still Bhutanese in 1864.
kingdoms.spanNote: Painted only for Alipurduar from 1774. Kokrajhar, Chirang and Kalimpong were probably Bhutanese too, but the library does not name them.

kingdoms.name: Matak (Bar Senapati)
kingdoms.description: The Moamaria country of Matak under its Bar Senapati, left to its own chief after the Burmese war. HCIP IX p. 133: 'Moamarias of Matak (Lakhimpur) under Bar Senapati ... handed over to their chiefs who acknowledged British suzerainty ... treaties executed in May, 1826'; p. 142: 'annexed Matak to the Lakhimpur district in November, 1839'.

kingdoms.name: North Cachar (Tularam)
kingdoms.description: Tularam Senapati's hill country, the eastern part of the old Kachari kingdom. HCIP IX pp. 137-138: Tularam held 'the hill portions ... by virtue of the treaty of 1829', retained 'the hilly eastern part' in 1834, and his country was 'formally annexed ... in 1854'.

kingdoms.name: Afsharid Persia
kingdoms.description: Nadir Shah's Persia. Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 121: 'After his conquest of Delhi, Nadir Shah annexed the subah of Kabul and all the portions of the Panjab and Sindh lying west of the Indus river down to the sea, as well as the province of Tatta or lower Sindh and the ports situated in it.' Nasir Khan governed Kabul and Peshawar for him (Sarkar I p. 127); the Khan of Kalat submitted (Aitchison XI block 390).
kingdoms.spanNote: On this map only its Indian conquests, 1739 to Nadir's murder in 1747.

kingdoms.name: Peshawar Sardars (Barakzai)
kingdoms.description: The Barakzai brothers of Peshawar - Yar Muhammad, then Sultan Muhammad, with Kohat under Pir Muhammad. Gupta V pp. 171-172: Ranjit Singh occupied Peshawar in November 1818 but 'left no troops'; after Naushahra (March 1823) Yar Muhammad 'continued as a tributary Governor of the Lahore Durbar'; 'From 1823 to 1834 it was administered by Barakzai brothers ... In 1834 ... brought directly under the control of the Lahore Durbar' (block 315).

kingdoms.name: Kaithal (Bhais)
kingdoms.description: The Bhais of Kaithal. Gupta IV block 76: 'In 1767 he [Desu Singh] seized the principality of Kaithal from two Afghan chiefs'; block 80: 'Kaithal was the second largest state after Patiala ... Bhai Udai Singh ... died without a male issue on 15 March, 1843' and it lapsed. Protected from 1809 (Gupta IV p. 136).

kingdoms.name: Cis-Sutlej Sikh chiefs
kingdoms.description: The Sikh chiefs between the Sutlej and the Jamuna taken under British protection in 1809 - Ladwa, Thanesar, Buriya, Kalsia, Radaur, Shahabad, Manimajra, Malerkotla, Malodh and others. Gupta IV p. 134, Ochterlony's proclamation: 'The territories of the Sikh chiefs lying between the rivers Satluj and the Jamuna have been taken under British protection ... The British Government will not charge any tribute'; p. 138: they 'were allowed to exercise full authority in all civil, criminal and fiscal matters'. Only lapsed estates became British (p. 139).
kingdoms.spanNote: A collective label, like Rajputana Minor States: the atlas cannot paint thirty chiefships separately at district scale.

events.text: Battle of the Ten Kings: King Sudas and the Bharatas defeated a large tribal confederation beside the Parushni, the modern Ravi River.
events.belligerents: Bharata–Trtsu (Sudas) vs a ten-tribe confederation (Puru, Yadu, Anu, Druhyu and others)
events.outcome: Bharata–Trtsu victory; linked to Bharata expansion and the later Kuru polity
events.source: Krishna (manual fill)

events.text: Battle of the Hydaspes: Alexander defeats Porus on the Jhelum, the first major recorded battle in Indian history
events.source: Jadunath Sarkar

events.text: Chandragupta Maurya overthrows the Nandas and founds the Maurya Empire
events.source: Upinder Singh

events.text: Kalinga War: Its carnage leads Ashoka to embrace Buddhism and non-violence
events.source: Upinder Singh

events.text: Battle of Venni: Karikala Chola defeated a Chera–Pandya-led confederacy of eleven rulers at Venni.
events.belligerents: Chola kingdom vs a Pandya–Chera-led confederacy with minor Velir chiefs
events.outcome: Chola victory under Karikala; the eleven-ruler confederacy defeated
events.source: Krishna (manual fill)

events.text: Battle of Talaiyalanganam: Pandyan king Nedunjeliyan II defeated a coalition of the Cholas, Cheras and five Velir chiefs at Talaiyalanganam.
events.belligerents: Pandya kingdom vs Chola–Chera coalition with five Velir chiefs
events.outcome: Pandyan victory; the seven-ruler coalition defeated, Chera ruler captured
events.source: Krishna (manual fill)

events.text: The Kalabhra interregnum begins: "Some time about A.D. 300 or a little later the whole country was upset by the predatory activities of the Kalabhras" — the three Tamil crowns eclipsed for nearly three centuries; a Buddhist Kalabhra king Achchutavikkanta patronises monasteries in the Chola country.
events.source: Sastri, A History of South India scan 12, 130; HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 265-266

events.text: Rudrasimha II seizes the Western Kshatrapa throne: A usurper from a collateral line ousts the legitimate heir at Ujjain; the Saka satrapy limps on for another century under his line.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 46 (chronology p. 707)

events.text: Sridharavarman sets up an independent kingdom: A Saka chief, once a Kshatrapa officer, rules independently in the Sanchi–Eran country of eastern Malwa — a sign of the Kshatrapa break-up before the Guptas arrive.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 47 (Kanakhera and Eran inscriptions)

events.text: Chandragupta I founds the Gupta Empire, opening India's Classical Age
events.source: R. C. Majumdar

events.text: The Gupta era begins: Chandragupta I is crowned Maharajadhiraja: On 26 February 320 the reckoning later used from Bengal to Kathiawad commences — most probably the coronation of Chandragupta I, whose marriage to the Licchavi Kumaradevi united two principalities of Bihar into the kingdom his son would make an empire.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 4-5

events.text: Pravarasena I dies — Vakataka emperor; "about the end of the first quarter of the fourth century".
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 177

events.text: Chandragupta I dies — Succeeded by Samudragupta, chosen over other claimants.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 5-6

events.text: Samudragupta succeeds to the Gupta throne: Chosen by his father over other claimants, the "hero of a hundred battles" begins the reign that gives the Allahabad prasasti its subject.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 6-7

events.text: Samudragupta's conquest of Aryavarta: nine named kings of the north — the Nagas of Padmavati, Vidisa and Mathura (Nagasena, Ganapatinaga), Achyuta of Ahichchhatra, Chandravarman of Pushkarana (Bankura) and others — were 'violently uprooted' and their kingdoms annexed.
events.belligerents: Gupta Empire (Samudragupta) vs the Naga kingdoms, Ahichchhatra, Pushkarana and others
events.commanders: Samudragupta
events.outcome: Gupta victory; the kingdoms are annexed and directly administered
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 8 (Allahabad prasasti, the nine Aryavarta kings); Sircar, Select Inscriptions no. 2

events.text: Kumarajiva is born — Born at Kucha of an Indian father; trained in Kashmir; to China 401; died 413. Off the map.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 608

events.text: Mayurasarman founds the Kadamba kingdom at Banavasi: The first Kannada royal house — a Brahmana who "took to the sword" against the Pallavas and was crowned by them.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 270-272 (Talagunda pillar); chronology p. 707 (c. 340-70)

events.text: Mayurasarman founds the Kadamba kingdom: the Brahmana student insulted at Kanchi 'took to the sword', defeated the Pallava frontier guards and the Banas, and forced the Pallavas to crown him — the Talagunda pillar tells the story. He also fought the Abhiras and Traikutakas.
events.belligerents: Kadamba dynasty (Mayurasarman) vs Pallava dynasty; vs the Banas, Abhiras and Traikutakas
events.commanders: Mayurasarman
events.outcome: Kadamba kingdom established at Banavasi with Pallava recognition
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 192, 270-272 (Talagunda pillar; Chandravalli inscription)

events.text: Samudragupta subdues the forest kingdoms: 'all the Atavika-rajyas' of the Vindhyan tract east of Jabalpur are reduced to servitude on the way south.
events.belligerents: Gupta Empire vs the Atavika (forest) kings
events.commanders: Samudragupta
events.outcome: Gupta victory
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 9

events.text: Samudragupta's Dakshinapatha campaign: twelve southern kings — Mahendra of Kosala, Vyaghraraja of Mahakantara, Mahendragiri of Pishtapura, Hastivarman of Vengi, Vishnugopa of Kanchi, Ugrasena of Palakka and others — were 'captured and then released' to rule as tributaries.
events.belligerents: Gupta Empire (Samudragupta) vs Kosala, Mahakantara, Pishtapura, Vengi (Salankayana), Kanchi (Pallava) and others
events.commanders: Samudragupta; Vishnugopa (Pallava); Hastivarman (Salankayana)
events.outcome: Gupta victory; the southern kings reinstated as tributaries — grahana-moksha
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 7, 9-10; p. 258 (the Pallava Vishnugopa)

events.text: Konganivarman Madhava founds the Western Ganga line: The Gangas of Kuvalala (Kolar) and later Talakad, who will hold southern Karnataka for six centuries, begin "about the middle of the fourth century", perhaps in the confusion left by Samudragupta's southern march.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 268-269; Sastri, A History of South India scan 104

events.text: Pushyavarman founds the Varman dynasty of Kamarupa: The first historical king of Assam, whose kingdom the Allahabad prasasti lists among the frontier states paying tribute to Samudragupta; thirteen generations follow to Bhaskaravarman.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 89 (Nidhanpur and Doobi plates); chronology p. 707

events.text: The Allahabad prasasti is composed: Harishena's eulogy of Samudragupta, engraved on the Asokan pillar at Prayaga — the single most important political document of the age, naming the kings of Aryavarta and Dakshinapatha, the frontier kingdoms and the tribal republics.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 7-12; Sircar, Select Inscriptions no. 2

events.text: The Silappadikaram and Manimekalai: The twin Tamil epics of the merchant's daughter Kannaki and the Buddhist nun Manimekalai are generally placed in the post-Sangam centuries, c. 300-500 — the last flowering before the Kalabhra dark age.
events.source: Sastri, A History of South India ch. on literature (date debated); HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 327

events.text: Meghavarna of Ceylon sends a mission to Samudragupta: The Sinhalese king asks leave to build a monastery for Ceylonese pilgrims at Bodh Gaya; the Mahabodhi sangharama Hiuen Tsang later saw was the result.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 11; chronology p. 707 (352-79)

events.text: Mahasena of Ceylon dies — Builder of the Jetavana; last king of the Mahavamsa proper.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 407; chronology p. 708

events.text: Samudragupta dies — c. 375-380.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 15

events.text: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya becomes emperor: After the shadowy Ramagupta episode, the son of Samudragupta takes the throne he will hold to c. 414 — the reign of the Saka conquest, Fa-hien's visit and Kalidasa's tradition.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 15-18; chronology p. 708

events.text: Prabhavatigupta rules the Vakataka kingdom as regent: The daughter of Chandragupta II, widowed by Rudrasena II, governs Vidarbha for her minor sons for some twenty years — Gupta influence reaches the Deccan through her.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 179-181

events.text: Rudrasena II (Vakataka) dies — Died young; his widow Prabhavatigupta became regent. HCIP chronology: c. 400.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 180; chronology p. 708

events.text: Gupta–Saka War: Chandragupta II destroys the Western Kshatrapas — the Saka ruler Rudrasimha III is defeated and his kingdom of Malwa, Gujarat and Kathiawad annexed — the end of three centuries of Saka rule in the west.
events.belligerents: Gupta Empire (Chandragupta II) vs Western Kshatrapas (Rudrasimha III)
events.commanders: Chandragupta II; Amrakardava (general)
events.outcome: Gupta victory; Malwa and Saurashtra annexed; Gupta silver coinage begins in the west
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 18-20 (Udayagiri and Sanchi records of 401 and 412; Rudrasimha III defeated and his kingdom annexed)

events.text: Fa-hien's pilgrimage through India: The Chinese monk travels the Gupta empire 400-411 — Mathura, Kanauj, Pataliputra, Tamralipti — and Ceylon 411-12, and leaves the earliest outsider's picture of the Classical Age: mild government, no death penalty, prosperous cities.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 22, 613-614; chronology p. 708

events.text: Chandragupta II's Vanga and Vahlika campaigns: the Mehrauli iron-pillar record of 'Chandra' claims the defeat of a confederacy of hostile chiefs in Vanga and a crossing of the seven mouths of the Sindhu to conquer the Vahlikas.
events.belligerents: Gupta Empire (Chandragupta II) vs the Vanga chiefs; vs the Vahlikas
events.commanders: Chandragupta II
events.outcome: Gupta victory claimed
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 20 (Mehrauli iron pillar, CII III no. 32)

events.text: Rudrasimha III dies — Last Western Kshatrapa, defeated by Chandragupta II; the line ends c. 400-410.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 19

events.text: The Mehrauli iron pillar: The rustless pillar of "king Chandra", raised as a standard of Vishnu on a hill called Vishnupada and later moved to Delhi — the record of Chandragupta II's Vanga and Vahlika wars.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 20; CII III no. 32

events.text: The Udayagiri caves are cut under Chandragupta II: The Varaha and Vishnu cave-temples at Udayagiri near Vidisa, with an inscription of the emperor's minister Virasena dated 401 — the earliest datable monuments of Gupta art.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 19-20 (Udayagiri inscription, Gupta year 82)

events.text: Kumarajiva dies — Died at Chang-an. Off the map.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 608

events.text: Chandragupta II dies — c. 414-415.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 22; chronology p. 708 (376-414)

events.text: Kumaragupta I Mahendraditya succeeds: Forty years of peace and asvamedha — the reign in which Nalanda is founded and the Gupta silver coinage spreads through the west; it ends with the Pushyamitra and Hun wars.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 23-25; chronology p. 708 (415-55)

events.text: Skandagupta is born — Approximate; crown prince fighting the Pushyamitras before 455.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 25 (inferred)

events.text: Nalanda is founded: Hiuen Tsang attributes the first monastery at Nalanda to "Sakraditya" — identified with Kumaragupta I — on which five kings built in turn; the university of the Classical Age.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) ch. XX; Hiuen Tsang (Beal II, 167-170). Year conventional.

events.text: The king of Ka-pi-li sends an embassy to China: A ruler of Kapilavastu — or Davaka — writes to the Sung court; the first Indian embassy to China of the period, followed by Mahanaman of Ceylon's letter the same year.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 90; chronology p. 709

events.text: Mahanaman of Ceylon dies — Murdered by his son Svastisena; Buddhaghosa's patron.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 285

events.text: Mitrasena of Ceylon dies — Killed by the Damila Pandya.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 285

events.text: The Damila conquest of Anuradhapura: Mitrasena, newly crowned, 'was killed by a Damila named Pandya who came from the coast of South India' — six Tamil kings rule the north for twenty-seven years while the Sinhalese nobles hold out in Rohana.
events.belligerents: Pandya (Tamil adventurer) vs Anuradhapura Kingdom (Mitrasena)
events.commanders: Pandya; Mitrasena (killed)
events.outcome: Tamil occupation of northern Ceylon, 433-460
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 285 (Mahavamsa / Culavamsa)

events.text: The silk-weavers of Dasapura build a sun temple: A guild of weavers migrated from Lata raises a temple of the Sun at Mandasor under Kumaragupta and the Aulikara Bandhuvarman; restored by the same guild in 473 — the classic record of Gupta-age guild life.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 442; chronology p. 709 (437-38, 473)

events.text: Vakataka–Kadamba war: the Vatsagulma Vakataka Vindhyasakti II (Vindhyasena) is 'represented as having defeated the king of Kuntala' — the Kadamba Kakusthavarman, who nonetheless married his daughters to the Vakataka and Gupta houses.
events.belligerents: Vakataka dynasty (Vatsagulma branch) vs Kadamba dynasty (Kakusthavarman)
events.commanders: Vindhyasakti II; Kakusthavarman
events.outcome: Vakataka victory claimed; alliance by marriage follows
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 183, 185 (Ajanta cave XVI inscription; Talagunda pillar)

events.text: Kakusthavarman dies — c. 450.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 272; chronology p. 709

events.text: The Talagunda pillar records the Kadamba origins: Kakusthavarman's prasasti at Talagunda tells how Mayurasarman won a kingdom and how the Kadamba princesses married Guptas and Vakatakas — the foundation text of Karnataka's dynastic history.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 270-272

events.text: Dhatusena's liberation: the Moriya prince from Rohana defeats the six Damila kings one after another and restores Sinhalese rule at Anuradhapura; he builds the Kalawewa and the great Avukana Buddha.
events.belligerents: Anuradhapura Kingdom (Dhatusena) vs the Damila kings
events.commanders: Dhatusena
events.outcome: Sinhalese restoration, 460
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 285

events.text: Kumaragupta I dies — Died during the Pushyamitra and Hun crises.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 25

events.text: Skandagupta and the Pushyamitras: the Bhitari record shows the Guptas' 'fortunes tottering' in a war with the Pushyamitras, whom Skandagupta defeated as crown prince before his accession.
events.belligerents: Gupta Empire (Skandagupta) vs the Pushyamitras
events.commanders: Skandagupta
events.outcome: Gupta victory
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 25

events.text: Skandagupta repels the Huns: the Bhitari pillar records the crown prince's 'complete victory' over the Hunas who had broken into Gandhara — the struggle 'was severe' and the empire was saved for a generation.
events.belligerents: Gupta Empire (Skandagupta) vs Hephthalite (White) Huns
events.commanders: Skandagupta
events.outcome: Gupta victory; Hun advance halted c. 460
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 25-27, 35 (Bhitari inscription; Junagadh inscription; the Kathasaritsagara echo)

events.text: The Bhitari pillar of Skandagupta: Skandagupta's own account of the tottering fortunes of his house, the Pushyamitra war and the Hun victory, set up at Bhitari in Ghazipur.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 25-27

events.text: The Sudarsana lake bursts at Girnar: The Mauryan reservoir, repaired by Rudradaman in 150, breaks its embankment "in a night"; Skandagupta's governor Parnadatta and his son Chakrapalita rebuild it in 456-58 and record it beside Asoka's edicts.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 61 (Junagadh inscription of Skandagupta, Gupta years 136-138)

events.text: The White Huns take Gandhara: crossing the Hindu Kush, the Hephthalites set up an independent kingdom in Gandhara 'and set up a king who was cruel and vindictive' — the base for Toramana's later invasion.
events.belligerents: Alchon Huns (the Hephthalite advance) vs Kidarite kingdom and the Gupta frontier
events.outcome: Hun kingdom established at Gandhara c. 460
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 26, 35 (Sung Yun's account)

events.text: Manadeva raises the Changu Narayan pillar: The earliest dated inscription of Nepal (Saka 386): the Licchavi king Manadeva records his father's death and his own campaigns east and west of the valley.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 83-84

events.text: Skandagupta dies — c. 467; the last great Gupta.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 28

events.text: Bhatarka founds the Maitraka state of Valabhi: The Gupta senapati of Saurashtra makes himself master of the peninsula as the empire loosens; his descendants rule from Valabhi for three centuries.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 61-62; chronology p. 709 (c. 465-75)

events.text: The Ajanta caves of the Vakataka age: Under Harishena of Vatsagulma and his minister Varahadeva the great painted viharas — caves XVI, XVII, I and II — are excavated: the Bodhisattva Padmapani, the Jatakas, the "Persian embassy" scene.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 184-186 (Ajanta cave XVI inscription); art chapter

events.text: Aryabhata is born — Self-dated: aged 23 in Kali 3600 = 499. Born, by tradition, at Kusumapura or in Asmaka.
events.source: Aryabhatiya, Kalakriya 10; HCIP III ch. XX

events.text: Dhatusena dies — Murdered — walled up alive — by his son Kasyapa.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 285

events.text: Kasyapa's patricide: the Mahavamsa's king Kasyapa I walls his father Dhatusena into a wall and seizes the throne; his brother Moggallana flees to India — the crime for which Kasyapa builds his fortress-palace at Sigiriya.
events.belligerents: Anuradhapura Kingdom: Kasyapa I vs Dhatusena and Moggallana
events.commanders: Kasyapa I; Dhatusena (killed)
events.outcome: Kasyapa I usurps the throne; Sigiriya built
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 285-286

events.text: Sigiriya: Kasyapa builds his rock fortress: The patricide king of Ceylon raises palace, gardens and the Lion-gate on the rock of Sigiriya, with the painted "cloud maidens"; abandoned after his death in battle.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 285-286

events.text: Budhagupta's Eran pillar: Maharaja Matrivishnu's pillar at Eran, dated Gupta year 165, shows Budhagupta still sovereign in Malwa "between the Kalindi and the Narmada" — the last firm date of imperial Gupta rule in the west.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 30-31

events.text: Moggallana's return: Kasyapa I, coming down from Sigiriya to meet his brother's Indian-recruited army, is deserted by his own troops and cuts his throat on the field; Moggallana I restores the capital to Anuradhapura.
events.belligerents: Anuradhapura Kingdom (Moggallana I with Tamil mercenaries) vs Kasyapa I
events.commanders: Moggallana I; Kasyapa I (killed)
events.outcome: Moggallana I king, 496
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 286

events.text: Kasyapa I of Ceylon dies — Cut his own throat on the battlefield when his army deserted him.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 286

events.text: The Ganga era begins in Kalinga: Indravarman I of the Eastern Gangas founds the reckoning used by the dynasty for five centuries; Kalinganagara becomes their seat.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 215; chronology p. 710

events.text: Paramartha is born — Born at Ujjain; the translator who took Yogachara to China.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 611 (Chinese biographies)

events.text: Budhagupta dies — c. 500; the empire begins to break up after him.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 32

events.text: Harishena (Vakataka) dies — c. 500-510; the Vakataka kingdom collapses under his sons.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 186

events.text: Ravivarman's succession war: the Kadamba Ravivarman 'secured the throne by defeating a combination of his enemies, including Vishnuvarman of the younger branch', whom he killed; Vishnuvarman's overlord, the Pallava Chandadanda (Santivarman), was also fought.
events.belligerents: Kadamba dynasty (Ravivarman) vs the younger Kadambas (Vishnuvarman) and Pallava dynasty (Santivarman/Chandadanda)
events.commanders: Ravivarman; Vishnuvarman (killed)
events.outcome: Ravivarman sole Kadamba king; later triumphs over the Western Gangas
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 273, 278 Re-dated from 497 to 500: the row names the Pallava Santivarman (Chandadanda), whom this atlas dates 500-525, so 497 put him in the field three years before his accession. HCIP gives no year for the war; both dates are approximate and 500 is the first that holds all the parties at once.

events.text: The Dasavatara temple at Deogarh: The finest surviving Gupta structural temple, with its Anantasayana, Gajendramoksha and Nara-Narayana panels, c. 500. The Bhitargaon brick temple in Kanpur is of the same generation.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) art chapter (ch. XVIII); date conventional

events.text: Toramana overruns Malwa: advancing from the Punjab, the Hun chief conquers 'a large part of Western India'; his boar-inscription at Eran shows Malwa in his first regnal year.
events.belligerents: Alchon Huns (Toramana) vs Gupta Empire
events.commanders: Toramana
events.outcome: Hun victory; Malwa, Rajasthan and the Doab under Hun rule
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 35 (Eran boar inscription, Toramana's year 1)

events.text: The earliest Maitraka land-grant: Maharaja Dronasimha of Valabhi, "anointed by the paramount sovereign in person", issues the first of the great series of Valabhi copper plates.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 61; chronology p. 710

events.text: Vainyagupta rules in East Bengal: The Gunaighar plate of Maharaja Vainyagupta (Gupta year 188) shows a Gupta prince holding Samatata with the imperial titles — the seed of Bengal's separate kingdom.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 33, 40; chronology p. 710

events.text: Battle of Eran: Bhanugupta 'the bravest man on the earth' fights 'a famous battle' with the Hun Toramana; his feudatory Goparaja falls and his wife mounts the pyre — the earliest dated sati record in India (Gupta year 191).
events.belligerents: Gupta Empire (Bhanugupta) vs Alchon Huns (Toramana)
events.commanders: Bhanugupta; Goparaja (killed); Toramana
events.outcome: Indecisive / Hun advantage — Eran remains in Hun hands
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 33-34 (Eran pillar of Goparaja, Gupta year 191 = 510)

events.text: Goparaja dies — Killed at Eran fighting beside Bhanugupta; his wife became sati — the first dated sati record.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 33

events.text: Mihirakula's conquests: the son of Toramana rules from Sakala over the Punjab, Kashmir and Malwa and is styled 'lord of the earth' — Cosmas calls the Hun chief 'the Lord of India'; his Gwalior inscription is of his 15th year.
events.belligerents: Alchon Huns (Mihirakula) vs the Gupta and regional kings
events.commanders: Mihirakula
events.outcome: Hun supremacy in the north-west and Malwa, c. 515-528
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 35-37 (Gwalior inscription; Cosmas; Hiuen Tsang)

events.text: Toramana dies — c. 515; succeeded by Mihirakula.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 35

events.text: Sung Yun visits the Hun court in Gandhara: The Wei envoy sent for Buddhist books finds the Hephthalite king ruling Gandhara "in the third generation" of conquest, cruel and hostile to the Law — the eyewitness account of Hun India.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 35-36, 615; chronology p. 710

events.text: Bodhidharma sails for China: The monk "third son of an Indian king, probably the Pallava king of Kanchi", received by Emperor Wu of Liang, brings the meditative school to China — Chan, and later Zen. Date and person semi-legendary.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 612, 616

events.text: Kumaradasa of Ceylon dies — The poet-king.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 286

events.text: Gopachandra founds an independent kingdom of Vanga: South and east Bengal "shook off the suzerainty of the Guptas" under Gopachandra, Dharmaditya and Samacharadeva, who "assumed the title Maharajadhiraja and issued gold coins like the Gupta emperors".
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 40-41, 77; chronology p. 711 (c. 525-75)

events.text: Baladitya defeats Mihirakula: Narasimhagupta Baladitya of Magadha, first refusing tribute, takes refuge 'in an island', then captures the Hun in battle and spares him at his mother's plea — Mihirakula retires to Kashmir.
events.belligerents: Gupta Empire (Narasimhagupta Baladitya) vs Alchon Huns (Mihirakula)
events.commanders: Narasimhagupta Baladitya; Mihirakula
events.outcome: Gupta victory; Mihirakula released, withdraws to Kashmir
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 37-38 (Hiuen Tsang's account)

events.text: Battle of Sondani: Yasodharman of Dasapura shatters Mihirakula — the Hun king 'whose head had never been brought to obeisance to any other save Sthanu' pays respect to the Aulikara's feet. Two victory pillars stand at Sondani near Mandasor.
events.belligerents: Aulikara dynasty (Yasodharman) vs Alchon Huns (Mihirakula)
events.commanders: Yasodharman; Mihirakula
events.outcome: Decisive Aulikara victory; Hun power in Malwa broken
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 37, 40 (Mandasor pillars of Yasodharman, c. 532)

events.text: Silabhadra is born — Born a prince of Samatata; abbot of Nalanda at 106 when Hiuen Tsang met him.
events.source: Hiuen Tsang (Beal); HCIP III ch. XX — date web-attested, verify

events.text: Mihirakula seizes Kashmir and sacks Gandhara: the fugitive Hun 'stirred up a rebellion, killed the king and placed himself on the throne of Kashmir', then 'killed the king of Gandhara, exterminated the royal family, destroyed the stupas and sangharamas'.
events.belligerents: Alchon Huns (Mihirakula) vs Kashmir; vs Gandhara
events.commanders: Mihirakula
events.outcome: Hun conquest of Kashmir and Gandhara; Mihirakula dies soon after
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 38; Kalhana, Rajatarangini I

events.text: Yasodharman's war of conquest: after Sondani the Aulikara claims dominion 'from the Lauhitya to the western ocean, from the Himalaya to Mahendra' and defeats Gupta feudatories — 'he rose and fell like a meteor between 530 and 540'.
events.belligerents: Aulikara dynasty (Yasodharman) vs Gupta Empire and its feudatories
events.commanders: Yasodharman
events.outcome: Short-lived Aulikara supremacy in Malwa and the north
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 39-42 (Mandasor pillars; Sumandala plate contra)

events.text: The Mandasor pillars of Yasodharman: Two pillars at Sondani proclaim the Aulikara "who rules from the Lauhitya to the western ocean" and to whose feet Mihirakula bowed — the record of the Hun defeat.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 39-40 (Mandasor inscription, Malava year 589 = 532)

events.text: The contest for Malwa: in 533 Malwa is 'being ruled by the governor of Isanavarman, the Maukhari'; two years later Kumaragupta III re-establishes Gupta sway and styles himself 'Lord of the three seas'.
events.belligerents: Maukhari dynasty (Isanavarman) vs Gupta Empire (Kumaragupta III)
events.commanders: Isanavarman; Kumaragupta III
events.outcome: Gupta recovery of Malwa, 535
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. xvi (introduction)

events.text: Cosmas Indicopleustes describes India and Ceylon: The Alexandrian merchant-monk who had sailed the Indian Ocean writes his Christian Topography: the Hun "Lord of India", the pepper ports of Male (Malabar), the Persian Christians and the king of Taprobane.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 36; chronology p. 711

events.text: Ravivarman (Kadamba) dies — c. 537.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 273

events.text: Durvinita's wars: the Western Ganga Durvinita fights the Pallavas and the Kadambas for Kongu and the Punnata country — victories at Andari, Alattur, Porulare and Pelnagara are recorded, and his daughter married the Chalukya Pulakesin II.
events.belligerents: Western Ganga dynasty (Durvinita) vs Pallava dynasty; vs Kadamba
events.commanders: Durvinita
events.outcome: Ganga expansion into Kongu and the Tamil borderland
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 269-270

events.text: Mihirakula dies — Died in Kashmir "soon after" seizing it; c. 540-542.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 38

events.text: Yasodharman dies — "Vanished into darkness" — his empire perished with him, c. 540.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 40-41

events.text: Pulakesin I fortifies Badami and founds the Chalukya kingdom: The Chalukya makes the hill-fort of Vatapi his capital and performs the asvamedha — the dynasty that will rule the Deccan for two centuries steps out of Kadamba vassalage.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 231 (Badami cliff inscription, Saka 465 = 543)

events.text: Pulakesin I fortifies Vatapi: the Chalukya makes 'the hill-fort of Vatapi' his capital in 543 and performs the asvamedha — the Kadamba feudatory becomes a sovereign, and Kadamba power ends under Harivarman (c. 547).
events.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Pulakesin I) vs Kadamba dynasty (Harivarman)
events.commanders: Pulakesin I
events.outcome: Chalukya independence; Badami fortified; Kadamba dynasty ends
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 231, 273 (Badami cliff inscription of 543)

events.text: Paramartha sails from India to China: The scholar-monk of Ujjain and Pataliputra reaches China in 546 and translates the Yogachara texts of Asanga and Vasubandhu; he dies there in 569.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 611; chronology p. 711

events.text: Harivarman (Kadamba) dies — The last Kadamba of Banavasi; c. 547.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 273

events.text: Elephanta: the great cave of Siva: The Mahesamurti and the Siva cave on the island of Gharapuri are cut in the sixth century, under the Kalachuris of Mahishmati or the Konkan Mauryas.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) art chapter; attribution debated

events.text: Isanavarman's victories: the Haraha inscription of 554 has the Maukhari defeat 'the Andhras with their thousands of elephants, the Sulikas and the Gaudas' and take the imperial title; either he or his son also 'fought with the Hunas and defeated them'.
events.belligerents: Maukhari dynasty (Isanavarman) vs Vishnukundin Andhras, the Sulikas and the Gaudas
events.commanders: Isanavarman
events.outcome: Maukhari ascendancy in Madhyadesa; Isanavarman crowned Maharajadhiraja
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 68-69 (Haraha inscription, Vikrama 611 = 554); p. 209 (the Vishnukundin Madhavavarman I as the Andhra)

events.text: Madhavavarman I's eleven asvamedhas: the Vishnukundin 'real founder of the greatness of the family' claims eleven horse-sacrifices and a thousand other rites — conquests toward the west (Trikuta-Malaya) that brought him against the Maukhari Isanavarman's Andhra campaign.
events.belligerents: Vishnukundin dynasty (Madhavavarman I) vs neighbours (Vakataka successors; Maukhari)
events.commanders: Madhavavarman I
events.outcome: Vishnukundin ascendancy over the eastern Deccan
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 207-209 (Ipur, Polamuru and Chikkulla plates)

events.text: Tirumular and Karaikkal Ammaiyar: the first Saiva saints: A sixth-century Saiva yogi, Tirumular, composes the Tirumantiram; the poetess of Karaikkal is remembered as the earliest of the sixty-three Nayanars — the Bhakti movement stirs in the Tamil south.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 328; Sastri, A History of South India ch. on religion

events.text: Isanavarman takes the imperial title: The Haraha inscription of Vikrama 611 proclaims the Maukhari Maharajadhiraja after his victories over the Andhras, Sulikas and Gaudas — a new imperial house at Kanauj.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 68-69

events.text: Kumaragupta III dies — Died at Prayaga after his victory over Isanavarman (Aphsad inscription); HCIP's chronology extends the reign to c. 570.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 43, 75

events.text: Maukhari–Later Gupta war: Isanavarman is 'defeated by Kumaragupta and probably also by Damodaragupta' in the struggle for the remnants of the Gupta empire; Kumaragupta III dies at Prayaga after his victory.
events.belligerents: Later Gupta dynasty (Kumaragupta III, Damodaragupta) vs Maukhari dynasty (Isanavarman)
events.commanders: Kumaragupta III; Damodaragupta; Isanavarman
