events.outcome: Later Gupta victories; Kumaragupta III dies at Prayaga
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 68, 75-76 (Aphsad inscription)

events.text: Guhadatta founds the Guhila principality of Mewar: A chief "established a small principality in the western part of the old State of Udaipur" after the Gupta collapse — the ancestor of the Ranas of Mewar. Date traditional.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 157-159 (Atpur inscription of 977)

events.text: Pulakesin I dies — c. 566.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 231; chronology p. 711

events.text: Paramartha dies — Died in China.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 611

events.text: The Sumandala plate: Gupta suzerainty still acknowledged in Orissa: King Prithivivigraha rules Kalinga "in the dominion of the Guptas" in Gupta year 250 — the last echo of the empire, half a century after Yasodharman claimed to have swept it away.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 42, 92

events.text: Kirtivarman I's conquests: the Chalukya 'was the night of doom to the Nalas, the Mauryas and the Kadambas' — Vanavasi and the Kadamba domain absorbed, the Konkan Mauryas and the Nalas of Bastar defeated.
events.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Kirtivarman I) vs Kadamba, Mauryas of Konkan and Nala dynasty
events.commanders: Kirtivarman I
events.outcome: Chalukya expansion over Kuntala, Konkan and the Nala country
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 232-233 (Aihole prasasti; Mahakuta pillar)

events.text: Simhavishnu conquers the Chola country: the Pallava 'not only suppressed the Kalabhras but conquered the whole country up to the Kaveri and even came into conflict with the Pandyas and the ruler of Ceylon' — the beginning of the Greater Pallavas.
events.belligerents: Pallava dynasty (Simhavishnu) vs Kalabhra dynasty; vs Pandya and Ceylon
events.commanders: Simhavishnu
events.outcome: Pallava rule extended to the Kaveri; Kalabhra power in Tondaimandalam and the Chola country ended
events.source: Sastri, A History of South India scan 134; HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 258, 266

events.text: Damodaragupta dies — Killed in battle against the Maukhari Sarvavarman.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 76

events.text: Isanavarman dies — c. 576; succeeded by Sarvavarman.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 70; chronology p. 711

events.text: Sarvavarman avenges his father: the Maukhari Sarvavarman defeats and kills Damodaragupta in battle — the Aphsad record says the Later Gupta 'fell asleep' on the field after breaking the Maukhari elephant line.
events.belligerents: Maukhari dynasty (Sarvavarman) vs Later Gupta dynasty (Damodaragupta)
events.commanders: Sarvavarman; Damodaragupta (killed)
events.outcome: Maukhari victory; Damodaragupta killed
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 70, 76 (Aphsad inscription of Adityasena)

events.text: Mangalesa dedicates Cave III at Badami: The great Vishnu cave, "the earliest dated Hindu cave temple in India" (Saka 500), with its Varaha, Trivikrama and Narasimha reliefs — the Chalukya style is born.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 233-234 (Badami cave inscription of Mangalesa, Saka 500)

events.text: Mahasenagupta on the Lauhitya: the Later Gupta king 'advanced up to the Brahmaputra and won a great victory' over Susthitavarman of Kamarupa; the Kamarupa princes Supratishthita and Bhaskara are later captured by 'the king of Gauda'.
events.belligerents: Later Gupta dynasty (Mahasenagupta) vs Kamarupa (Susthitavarman)
events.commanders: Mahasenagupta; Susthitavarman
events.outcome: Later Gupta victory on the Brahmaputra; no permanent result
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 76, 92 (Aphsad inscription; Harshacharita; Doobi plates)

events.text: Prabhakaravardhana makes Thanesar a power: The first Pushyabhuti to take the title Maharajadhiraja — "a lion to the Huna deer, a burning fever to the king of Sindhu, a troubler of the sleep of the Gurjara king" (Bana).
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 96-98; chronology p. 712

events.text: Tivaradeva 'obtained mastery of the entire Kosala country': the Panduvamsi of Sripura conquers South Kosala and claims Utkala — the Sarabhapuriyas are displaced.
events.belligerents: Panduvamshi dynasty (Tivaradeva) vs Sharabhapuriya dynasty; Utkala
events.commanders: Tivaradeva
events.outcome: Panduvamsi rule over Dakshina Kosala
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 220 (Rajim and Baloda grants)

events.text: Varahamihira dies — c. 587.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 317; chronology p. 712

events.text: Harshavardhana is born — Sixteen at his accession in 606 (Hiuen Tsang); born at Sthanvisvara.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 100-101

events.text: Kadungon ends the Kalabhra interregnum: the Pandya 'recovered the territory under the Kalabhra occupation' — the Velvikudi grant remembers the Kali king Kalabhran driven from the Pandya country.
events.belligerents: Pandya dynasty (Kadungon) vs Kalabhra dynasty
events.commanders: Kadungon
events.outcome: Pandya restoration at Madurai
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 265-267 (Velvikudi grant)

events.text: Aggabodhi I of Ceylon dies — Thirty-three years of building and irrigation.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 287

events.text: The Kalachuris hold Ujjain: Sankaragana's Abhona plates (Kalachuri year 347) are issued from Ujjayini — northern Maharashtra, Gujarat and western Malwa under one Kalachuri king.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 74, 195

events.text: The Kalachuris take Ujjain: Sankaragana, son of Krishnaraja, is 'in possession of Ujjayini' by 595 — the Later Guptas of Malwa are pushed out and the Kalachuris hold northern Maharashtra, Gujarat and parts of Malwa.
events.belligerents: Kalachuri of Mahishmati (Sankaragana) vs Later Gupta dynasty (Mahasenagupta)
events.commanders: Sankaragana
events.outcome: Kalachuri occupation of Malwa
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 74, 191, 195 (Abhona plates, Kalachuri year 347 = 595)

events.text: Kirtivarman I dies — Leaving minor sons; his brother Mangalesa took the throne.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 233; chronology p. 712

events.text: Mangalesa takes Revatidvipa: the Chalukya regent conquers the island fortress of Revatidvipa (Redi, south of Vengurla) from the Konkan Mauryas and installs a governor of the Bappura family.
events.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Mangalesa) vs Mauryas of Konkan
events.commanders: Mangalesa
events.outcome: Chalukya victory; the Konkan coast under Chalukya control
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 234 (Goa grant of 610-11)

events.text: Brahmagupta is born — Thirty years old when he completed the Brahmasphutasiddhanta in Saka 550 (628), by his own statement.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 323

events.text: Bhaskara I is born — Approximate; wrote in 629.
events.source: HCIP III ch. XX; date conventional

events.text: Dharmakirti is born — Approximate — "beginning of the seventh century".
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 391

events.text: Durvinita dies — c. 600.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 269

events.text: Hiuen Tsang is born — Born at Lo-yang; the pilgrim of India 630-644. Foreign-born — include for the atlas's "Birth" layer only if non-Indian figures are wanted.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 618; chronology p. 712

events.text: Jinagupta dies — Gandharan monk-translator, died in China.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 611

events.text: Simhavishnu dies — c. 600.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 258

events.text: Sirpur: the Lakshmana temple of the Panduvamsis: Queen Vasata's brick temple to Vishnu at Sripura, the Panduvamsi capital on the Mahanadi — the finest brick shrine of the age. Date approximate.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 220-221 (Sirpur inscriptions of Vasata and Balarjuna)

events.text: The Mahabodhi temple at Bodh Gaya: The tall brick temple over the seat of enlightenment, described by Hiuen Tsang, takes its present form in the Gupta and post-Gupta centuries.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) art chapter; Hiuen Tsang (Beal II)

events.text: Chach conquers Sindh: the Brahmin minister who seized the Rai throne 'conquered a portion of Makran and forced the people of Kandabil (east of Kalat) to pay tribute', fixing his frontier at the Kirman border.
events.belligerents: Brahmin dynasty of Sindh (Chach) vs Rai dynasty of Sindh; vs Makran and Kandabil
events.commanders: Chach
events.outcome: Brahmin dynasty established; Makran border secured
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 166 (Chach-nama; accession 602 by its chronology)

events.text: Chach seizes the throne of Sindh: The Brahmin minister marries the widow of Rai Sahasi II and founds the dynasty that Muhammad ibn Qasim will destroy — 602 by the Chach-nama's own reckoning, which modern scholars place a generation later.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 166 (Chach-nama; chronology uncertain)

events.text: Mangalesa defeats Buddharaja: the Chalukya 'put to flight' the Kalachuri Buddharaja, son of Sankaragana, and 'appropriated the royal fortunes of the Katachchuris' — recorded in the Mahakuta pillar of 602.
events.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Mangalesa) vs Kalachuri of Mahishmati (Buddharaja)
events.commanders: Mangalesa; Buddharaja
events.outcome: Chalukya victory; Kalachuri power south of the Narmada broken
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 192, 196, 233 (Mahakuta pillar inscription, 602)

events.text: Prabhakaravardhana dies — Died of fever at Thanesar; his queen Yasomati followed him on the pyre (Bana).
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 98-99

events.text: The Malava–Gauda strike: on the news of Prabhakaravardhana's death 'the king of Malava' Devagupta kills the Maukhari Grahavarman at Kanauj and imprisons his queen Rajyasri; Rajyavardhana 'routed the Malava army with ridiculous ease'.
events.belligerents: Later Gupta dynasty (Devagupta of Malava) vs Maukhari dynasty (Grahavarman); then Pushyabhuti (Rajyavardhana) vs Devagupta
events.commanders: Devagupta; Grahavarman (killed); Rajyavardhana; Bhandi
events.outcome: Grahavarman killed; Devagupta then routed by Rajyavardhana
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 99-100, 121 (Harshacharita; Madhuban and Banskhera plates: "Devagupta and other kings defeated by Rajyavardhana")

events.text: Devagupta of Malava dies — Routed by Rajyavardhana; presumed killed or deposed.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 99, 121

events.text: Grahavarman dies — The last Maukhari, killed by Devagupta of Malava.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 99

events.text: Harsha and Bhaskaravarman make alliance: The envoy Hamsavega brings the Kamarupa king's offer of "perpetual friendship" to Harsha's camp — the eastern alliance that outflanks Sasanka.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 91, 100 (Harshacharita)

events.text: Harsha ascends the throne of Thanesar: At sixteen, after the murders of his brother-in-law and brother, Harshavardhana takes the crown "without any hesitation" and vows vengeance on Gauda; the Harsha era begins.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 100-102

events.text: Harsha's war of vengeance: with 5,000 elephants, 2,000 horse and 50,000 foot Harsha 'waged incessant warfare, until in six years he had fought the five Indias' — the Gauda enemy driven from Kanauj, the Malava power broken, Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa won as ally.
events.belligerents: Pushyabhuti (Harsha) vs Gauda (Sasanka), Malava (Devagupta) and others
events.commanders: Harsha; Bhandi; Bhaskaravarman (ally)
events.outcome: Harsha master of Madhyadesa; Kanauj becomes his capital
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 100-108 (Hiuen Tsang; Bana)

events.text: Rajyavardhana dies — Murdered by Sasanka.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 99, 122

events.text: The murder of Rajyavardhana: 'allured to confidence by false civilities on the part of the king of Gauda', the victorious Pushyabhuti is killed unarmed at Sasanka's table — the crime that brings Harsha to the throne and to his vow of vengeance.
events.belligerents: Gauda kingdom (Sasanka) vs Pushyabhuti (Rajyavardhana)
events.commanders: Sasanka; Rajyavardhana (killed)
events.outcome: Rajyavardhana murdered; Harsha succeeds at Thanesar
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 99, 122 (Bana; Hiuen Tsang; the Madhuban plate's "Gauda")

events.text: The Silameghavanna wars: the usurper Silameghavanna kills Moggallana III (608); the general Srinaga 'fled to South India and came back with a large army of Damilas' to seize the Northern Province, but the king 'succeeded in crushing the invading army completely'.
events.belligerents: Anuradhapura Kingdom (Silameghavanna) vs Srinaga with Damila (Tamil) troops
events.commanders: Silameghavanna; Srinaga
events.outcome: Sinhalese victory
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 287-288

events.text: Mahendravarman I cuts the first Pallava rock temples: The Mandagapattu cave records the "curious-minded" king's boast of a temple without brick, timber, metal or mortar — the beginning of Tamil stone architecture, continued at Tiruchirappalli and Mamallapuram.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 259-260; Sastri, A History of South India scan 134

events.text: Mangalesa dies — Killed in the civil war with Pulakesin II.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 234

events.text: Narasimhavarman I is born — Approximate; king at c. 630.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 260 (inferred)

events.text: Pulakesin II becomes Chalukya king: After the civil war that killed his uncle Mangalesa, the greatest of the Badami Chalukyas begins the reign that will face Harsha, take Vengi and end at Vatapi.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 234; chronology p. 713 (610-11 to 642)

events.text: The Chalukya civil war: Mangalesa, trying to secure the throne for his own son, is defeated and killed by his nephew Pulakesin II, who 'saved his homeland from enemies' and took the crown in 610-11.
events.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami): Pulakesin II vs Mangalesa
events.commanders: Pulakesin II; Mangalesa (killed)
events.outcome: Pulakesin II king; Mangalesa dead
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 234, 237 (Aihole prasasti; Hyderabad plates of 612)

events.text: Pulakesin II restores the kingdom: Appayika and Govinda, who came 'with elephant troops' from north of the Bhima, are broken by bheda — Govinda won over, Appayika 'defeated and expelled'; then Vanavasi, the Kadamba capital, is besieged and reduced, and the Gangas and Alupas submit.
events.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Pulakesin II) vs Appayika and Govinda; vs Kadamba (Banavasi); Ganga and Alupa
events.commanders: Pulakesin II; Durvinita (Ganga, submits and gives a daughter)
events.outcome: Chalukya victory; Kadambas, Gangas, Alupas subdued
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 235 (Aihole prasasti)

events.text: Pulakesin's fleet takes Puri: the Mauryas of the Konkan are attacked at their island capital 'Puri' (Elephanta or Rajpuri), 'invaded by Pulakesin's battleships and captured' — 'a hundred ships' in the Aihole verse.
events.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Pulakesin II) vs Mauryas of Konkan
events.commanders: Pulakesin II
events.outcome: Chalukya victory; the Konkan submits
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 236 (Aihole prasasti)

events.text: Battle of Narmada: Harsha against Pulakesin — Harsha 'gathered troops from the five Indies' and went south in person; on the Narmada line his elephants 'fell in the battle and he was seized with fear' — the Chalukya took the title Paramesvara for 'defeating the war-like lord of all the region of the north'. Hiuen Tsang: Harsha 'has not yet conquered their troops'.
events.belligerents: Pushyabhuti (Harsha) vs Chalukya (Badami) (Pulakesin II); the Latas, Malavas and Gurjaras (Dadda II) on the Chalukya side
events.commanders: Harsha; Pulakesin II; Dadda II
events.outcome: Harsha checked; the Narmada (or a line further north) becomes the frontier
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 105-106, 109-110, 115, 236-237 (Aihole prasasti; Hiuen Tsang; the Paramesvara title)

events.text: Battle of Pullalur: Pulakesin II, having taken Vengi, drives south into Tondaimandalam; Mahendravarman I 'claims a victory at Pullalur' (Pallur, near Kanchi) but 'the Chalukya penetrated far into the heart of the Pallava kingdom'.
events.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Pulakesin II) vs Pallava dynasty (Mahendravarman I)
events.commanders: Pulakesin II; Mahendravarman I
events.outcome: Chalukya advance halted short of Kanchi; both sides claim the day
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 238, 259 (Aihole prasasti; Kasakudi plates); Sastri, A History of South India scan 134

events.text: Harsha and Valabhi: Dhruvasena II of Valabhi is defeated by Harsha and 'saved by the support of the Gurjara king Dadda II' of Broach; the war ends in a marriage — Harsha's daughter given to the Maitraka king.
events.belligerents: Pushyabhuti (Harsha) vs Maitraka of Valabhi (Dhruvasena II) and Gurjaras of Nandipuri (Dadda II)
events.commanders: Harsha; Dhruvasena II; Dadda II
events.outcome: Valabhi defeated but preserved; matrimonial alliance
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 104-105, 109-110 (Navsari grant of the Gurjaras; Hiuen Tsang)

events.text: Sasanka's last known date: The Ganjam grant of Madhavaraja II of Kongoda acknowledges the Gauda king's suzerainty in Gupta year 300 — Sasanka's power then reached the Orissa coast; he is dead by the mid-620s.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 107; chronology p. 713

events.text: Pulakesin II conquers the east coast: Pishtapura's ruling house is overthrown and the Vishnukundin Vikramendravarman III defeated; Pulakesin's brother Vishnuvardhana is left as viceroy at Vengi and completes the conquest by about 631 — the Andhra country is a province of Badami, and only from 634 does the viceroy's line drift into the independent Eastern Chalukya house.
events.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Pulakesin II) vs Vishnukundin dynasty (Vikramendravarman III) and the Pishtapura kings
events.commanders: Pulakesin II; Kubja Vishnuvardhana; Vikramendravarman III
events.outcome: Chalukya victory; the Eastern Chalukya kingdom of Vengi founded (624)
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 209-210, 238, 252 (Aihole prasasti; Kopparam plates); HCIP III pp. 250-252 (viceroyalty c. 615-633, conquest completed c. 630-31); Sastri p. 134

events.text: Amsuvarman dies — c. 621 (modern dating; HCIP gives 651).
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 85

events.text: The Eastern Chalukya kingdom of Vengi is founded: Pulakesin II installs his younger brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana as ruler of the conquered Andhra country — a line that will last five centuries.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 238, 252

events.text: Pulakesin II and Khusrau II exchange embassies: Tabari records an embassy from "the king of India" to the Sasanian court in 625-26; tradition sees the Persian embassy in return painted on the walls of Ajanta cave I.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 240 (Tabari); chronology p. 713

events.text: Sasanka dies — Last dated 619; dead before Harsha's eastern campaign of 641. Hiuen Tsang has him die of a foul disease as divine punishment.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 107

events.text: Durlabhavardhana founds the Karkota dynasty of Kashmir: The son-in-law of the last Gonanda king takes the throne; Hiuen Tsang will find the dynasty ruling "five other countries" from the valley.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 132

events.text: Brahmagupta completes the Brahmasphutasiddhanta: At Bhillamala under the Chapa king Vyaghramukha, the thirty-year-old astronomer writes the treatise that first treats zero as a number and gives rules for negative quantities — carried to Baghdad a century later as the Sindhind.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 161, 323; chronology p. 713

events.text: Appar and Sambandar lead the Saiva revival: Tirunavukkarasar (Appar), who turned Mahendravarman I from Jainism, and the boy-saint Tirujnanasambandar, who reconverted the Pandya court, sing the Tevaram hymns through the Tamil country — the Bhakti movement in full voice.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 328; Sastri, A History of South India scan 134, 370

events.text: Battle of Manimangalam and the sack of Vatapi: Pulakesin's second Pallava war — Narasimhavarman I 'repeatedly defeated king Vallabha' at Pariyala, Manimangala and Suramara, and his general Siruttondar took Badami in 642 — Pulakesin II 'was defeated and probably killed'. Narasimhavarman styled himself Vatapikonda.
events.belligerents: Pallava dynasty (Narasimhavarman I) vs Chalukya (Badami) (Pulakesin II)
events.commanders: Narasimhavarman I; Paranjoti (Siruttondar); Pulakesin II (killed)
events.outcome: Decisive Pallava victory; Badami taken and burnt; thirteen years of Chalukya eclipse
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 240-241, 260 (Kuram plates; Badami rock inscription of Narasimhavarman; Periyapuranam on Siruttondar)

events.text: Hiuen Tsang's travels in India: The Chinese Master of the Law crosses the Hindu Kush in 630 and spends fourteen years in India — Kashmir, Kanauj, Nalanda, Kamarupa, Kanchi, Badami — leaving the fullest description of the subcontinent before the Mughals.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 100, 618; chronology pp. 712-714

events.text: Mahendravarman I dies — c. 630.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 259

events.text: The rathas and reliefs of Mamallapuram: Narasimhavarman I Mamalla gives his name to the port where the monolithic rathas, the Arjuna's Penance relief and the cave-temples are cut — the seaboard workshop of Pallava art.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 260-261; art chapter

events.text: Jetthatissa and Aggabodhi III: the throne changes hands by battle four times — Jetthatissa III defeats Aggabodhi III, who returns 'with a contingent of Damila troops' and kills him; Dathopatissa 'came with a great South Indian force' and was killed by Kasyapa II.
events.belligerents: Anuradhapura factions with South Indian (Pallava/Pandya) mercenaries
events.commanders: Aggabodhi III; Jetthatissa III (killed); Dathopatissa I (killed); Kasyapa II
events.outcome: Kasyapa II king by 641
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 288

events.text: Hiuen Tsang at Kashmir and Taxila: The pilgrim spends two years (631-33) in Kashmir, where the Karkota king lends him twenty scribes, and finds Taxila a dependency of Kashmir and Gandhara desolate.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 132-133

events.text: Prabhakaramitra dies — Nalanda monk, died in China.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 621

events.text: The Aihole prasasti of Pulakesin II: Ravikirti's Sanskrit eulogy on the Meguti Jain temple (Saka 556) records the Chalukya's conquests from the Konkan to Kanchi and his check of Harsha — and dates itself by the Mahabharata war.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 235-237

events.text: Arab raid on Thana: The first Arab raid on India — a naval expedition from Oman strikes Thana near Bombay under the Caliphate of 'Umar — repulsed, and the Caliph forbids further sea ventures; raids on Broach and Debal follow.
events.belligerents: Rashidun Caliphate vs the Konkan (Mauryas / Chalukya sphere)
events.commanders: 'Uthman al-Thaqafi (governor of Bahrain) — expedition of his brother Hakam
events.outcome: Arab raid repulsed
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 167 (Baladhuri)

events.text: Tirujnanasambandar is born — Born at Sirkali; approximate — a contemporary of Appar and Narasimhavarman I.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 328; Sastri, A History of South India

events.text: Harsha exchanges embassies with the Tang court: Harsha's envoy reaches Chang-an and Tai-tsung sends Liang Huai-ching in return — the first of four Chinese missions to Kanauj in seven years.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 120; chronology p. 714

events.text: Harsha's eastern conquest: after Sasanka's death Harsha 'conquered Magadha' — styled king of Magadha in 641 — and carried his raids through West Bengal and Orissa 'up to Kongoda', subjugating the old dominions of the Gauda king.
events.belligerents: Pushyabhuti (Harsha) vs the Gauda successors and Sailodbhavas of Kongoda
events.commanders: Harsha; Bhaskaravarman (ally)
events.outcome: Harsha holds Magadha, Odra and Kongoda; Bhaskaravarman takes Karnasuvarna
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 107, 110 (Ma-twan-lin; Hiuen Tsang; the Ganjam grant of 619 as Sasanka's last date)

events.text: Tibet takes Nepal: with the marriage of Bhrikuti and the Chinese embassies of 643, Srong-btsan-sgam-po's suzerainty is acknowledged in the valley; the Nepalese army marches for the Tibetans against Kanauj in 648.
events.belligerents: Tibetan Empire (Srong-btsan-sgam-po) vs Licchavi dynasty of Nepal (Narendradeva)
events.commanders: Srong-btsan-sgam-po; Narendradeva
events.outcome: Nepal a Tibetan dependency to 702
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 85-86, 137-138 (T'ang annals; Levi)

events.text: Hiuen Tsang at Kanchi: The pilgrim finds the Pallava capital "the birthplace of Dharmapala", with a hundred monasteries, and hears of Ceylon from the monks who fled its civil war.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 260

events.text: Pulakesin II dies — "Defeated and probably killed" when Narasimhavarman I took Badami.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 240

events.text: Arab conquest of Makran: The Arabs reach Makran and Sindh — after Cadesia the Muslim armies enter Makran; a force sent against Debal (the port of Sindh) is 'defeated and their leader killed by the governor of Chach' according to the Chach-nama, though Arab historians record a victory.
events.belligerents: Rashidun Caliphate vs Brahmin dynasty of Sindh (Chach)
events.commanders: Hakam ibn Amr; Chach's governor at Debal
events.outcome: Arab repulse at Debal per the Chach-nama; Makran annexed
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 166-169

events.text: Bhaskaravarman takes Karnasuvarna: with Sasanka gone, the Kamarupa king occupies the Gauda capital — his Nidhanpur grant is issued 'from the camp of victory at Karnasuvarna' while Harsha reduces Magadha and Kongoda.
events.belligerents: Kamarupa (Bhaskaravarman) vs Gauda kingdom (Sasanka's successors)
events.commanders: Bhaskaravarman
events.outcome: Kamarupa occupation of Karnasuvarna
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 91, 107 (Nidhanpur plates)

events.text: Chinese envoys find Narendradeva on the throne of Nepal: The Licchavi restored with Tibetan help receives the Tang mission bound for Magadha; Nepal is now within the Tibetan orbit.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 85, 137

events.text: Harsha's assembly at Kanauj: Twenty kings, three thousand monks and the Chinese pilgrim attend the great religious assembly in honour of Mahayana; a fire in the tower and an attempt on the king's life mar it.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 116-119

events.text: Hiuen Tsang at the court of Bhaskaravarman: The Kamarupa king, "a devout Brahmana", entertains the pilgrim for a month and then escorts him to Harsha's assembly with twenty thousand elephants and thirty thousand boats.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 91-92, 116

events.text: The quinquennial distribution at Prayaga: At the confluence Harsha gives away the accumulated wealth of five years to Buddhists, Brahmanas and the poor, ending with the clothes on his back — the sixth such Mahamoksha-parishad of his reign.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 119-120

events.text: Dhruvasena II dies — c. 644; succeeded by Dharasena IV.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 147

events.text: Harsha dies; his empire dissolves: The last great emperor of the north dies without an heir; his minister Arjuna usurps the throne and "the history of Kanauj is wrapt in obscurity" for half a century.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 121, 124; HCIP IV p. xii

events.text: Harshavardhana dies — c. 646-647; "left no able successor".
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 121

events.text: Valabhi conquers the Gurjara kingdom of Nandipuri: Dharasena IV Chakravartin of Valabhi issues grants from Broach in 648 — the Maitrakas briefly master the Gurjaras of Lata.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 147; chronology p. 714

events.text: Wang Xuance's revenge: the usurper Arjuna of Tirabhukti, who seized Harsha's throne and plundered the Chinese embassy, is crushed by 1,200 Tibetan and 7,000 Nepalese troops — the capital 'captured after a siege of three days', Arjuna taken prisoner to China.
events.belligerents: Kannauj (post-Harsha) (Arjuna / Arunasva) vs the Tang embassy of Wang Xuance with Tibetan Empire and Licchavi dynasty of Nepal troops
events.commanders: Wang Xuance; Arjuna (captured); troops of Srong-btsan-sgam-po and Narendradeva
events.outcome: Arjuna defeated and carried to China; 580 towns submit
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 124-125 (T'ang annals)

events.text: Bhaskaravarman dies — c. 650; "the century following his death may be regarded as a dark period in the history of Kamarupa".
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 141

events.text: Srong-btsan-sgam-po dies — The founder of the Tibetan empire; off the map.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 635

events.text: The Kasika-vritti is written: Jayaditya and Vamana's commentary on Panini's grammar — the standard gloss for thirteen centuries — is composed about the middle of the seventh century.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 311, 319; chronology p. 715

events.text: Bhartrihari dies — Forty years before I-tsing wrote (691).
events.source: I-tsing, Record (Takakusu); HCIP III ch. XIX

events.text: Narendradeva of Nepal sends a mission to China: The Licchavi king's embassy reaches the Tang court; Nepal is described as a country of merchants and copper coinage.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 137; chronology p. 715

events.text: Vikramaditya I restores the Chalukyas: thirteen years after the fall of Badami the son of Pulakesin II 'rehabilitated the fortunes of his dynasty', defeating the confederacy of three kings that had overrun the kingdom and recovering his ancestral lands.
events.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Vikramaditya I) vs Pallava dynasty (Narasimhavarman I / Mahendravarman II) and their allies
events.commanders: Vikramaditya I
events.outcome: Chalukya restoration
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 241, 261

events.text: Adityasena of Magadha performs the horse-sacrifice: The Later Gupta king assumes the imperial titles and celebrates the asvamedha; his Aphsad inscription rehearses his line back to Krishnagupta. "Magadha rose to a position of imperial greatness."
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 126-127, 358 (Aphsad inscription)

events.text: Sendan's Chera war: the third Pandya, Sendan (645-670), takes the title Vanavan — 'suggests his victory over the Cheras' — the first Pandya thrust into Kerala since the Sangam age.
events.belligerents: Pandya dynasty (Sendan) vs the Chera / Kerala chiefs
events.commanders: Sendan
events.outcome: Pandya victory
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 267

events.text: The Kikan disaster: a 'great Arab expedition' sent into Sindh under the Caliphate of Ali is destroyed — 'the people of Kikan rout the Muslim army and kill most of the Muslim host, including their leader' (663); the Bolan hill tribes hold the passes.
events.belligerents: Kikan (Jat chiefs of the Bolan) vs Rashidun / Umayyad Caliphate
events.commanders: Harith ibn Murrah al-Abdi (killed)
events.outcome: Arab army destroyed; the land route into Sindh closed for a generation
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 169

events.text: The Turk Shahi and the Arabs at Kabul and Zabul: the Arabs 'proceeded to Zabulistan and defeated the people', but 'the kings of Zabul and Kabul combined and inflicted a severe defeat upon the Muslim army' — frontier wars that run to 699.
events.belligerents: Turk Shahi kingdom (Kabul, Zabul) vs Umayyad Caliphate
events.commanders: Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura; Ubaidullah (died of grief)
events.outcome: Arab advance beyond Kabul checked
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 167-168

events.text: The first Pallava expedition to Ceylon: Narasimhavarman I gives the exiled Sinhalese prince Manavamma an army; 'in spite of a victory over the forces of Dathopatissa II, the expedition was a failure' and Manavamma returns to Kanchi.
events.belligerents: Pallava dynasty for Manavamma vs Anuradhapura Kingdom (Dathopatissa II)
events.commanders: Manavamma; Narasimhavarman I (sponsor)
events.outcome: Pallava-backed invasion fails
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 261, 289 Re-dated from 668 to 663. Both Ceylon expeditions sat on 668, twenty years apart. The first is Narasimhavarman I’s (r. 630-668) against Dathopatissa II (r. 659-667), so 663 is inside both reigns.

events.text: Hiuen Tsang dies — Died at Chang-an. Off the map.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 620

events.text: Narasimhavarman I dies — c. 668.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 261

events.text: Sendan dies — c. 670.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 267

events.text: Vikramaditya I takes Kanchi: the Chalukya 'captured Kanchi and destroyed the family of Mahamalla'; by the Gadval plates of 674 his camp lay at Uragapura (Uraiyur) on the Kaveri — 'undertaken to efface the disgrace' of 642.
events.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Vikramaditya I) vs Pallava dynasty (Mahendravarman II, Paramesvaravarman I)
events.commanders: Vikramaditya I; Paramesvaravarman I
events.outcome: Chalukya occupation of Kanchi; camp at Uraiyur 674
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 241-242, 261-262 (Gadval plates, 674) Re-dated from 668 to 670: the row names Paramesvaravarman I, who acceded in 670, and rests on the Gadval plates of 674; 668 put the capture before the king it names.

events.text: Chach dies — After a forty-year reign by the Chach-nama; succeeded by his brother Chandar.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 166

events.text: I-tsing's years in India: The Chinese pilgrim comes by sea in 671, studies ten years at Nalanda and writes the Record of the Buddhist Religion — the picture of Indian monastic life after Harsha.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 2, 620; chronology p. 715

events.text: Battle of Peruvalanallur: Paramesvaravarman I turns the tide — Vikramaditya I, 'although his army consisted of several lakhs, was obliged to flee covered only by a rag' at Peruvalanallur near Lalgudi; the Chalukya withdraws from the Pallava country.
events.belligerents: Pallava dynasty (Paramesvaravarman I) vs Chalukya (Badami) (Vikramaditya I)
events.commanders: Paramesvaravarman I; Vikramaditya I
events.outcome: Pallava victory; Chalukya army withdraws
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 261-262 (Kuram plates)

events.text: The Chalukya camp at Uraiyur: Vikramaditya I's Gadval plates, issued from Uragapura on the Kaveri, show the Chalukya army in the heart of the Chola country after the capture of Kanchi.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 241, 261

events.text: Battle of Nelveli: Arikesari Maravarman Parankusa 'won a great victory at Nelveli' (Tirunelveli), and 'extirpated the Paravas of the coast'; further victories over the Cheras are recorded in the Velvikudi grant.
events.belligerents: Pandya dynasty (Arikesari Maravarman) vs the Cheras and the Paravas
events.commanders: Arikesari Maravarman
events.outcome: Pandya victory
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 267 (Velvikudi and Larger Sinnamanur plates)

events.text: Manavamma takes Ceylon: the second Pallava expedition, 'which sailed from Mahabalipuram', lands Manavamma with a great army; he 'succeeded in defeating totally the titular king Hastadamshtra II and the administrator Pustakushtha' and seizes the throne he holds for thirty-five years.
events.belligerents: Pallava dynasty (Narasimhavarman I / Paramesvaravarman I) for Manavamma vs Anuradhapura Kingdom (Hatthadatha II)
events.commanders: Manavamma; Hatthadatha II
events.outcome: Manavamma king of Ceylon c. 668/676-703
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 261, 289 (Culavamsa; Geiger dates 676) Re-dated from 668 to 676, the date this row’s own source already gives (Geiger). The revised Sinhalese chronology puts Manavamma’s accession at 684; on either reckoning 668 is too early, and the second expedition cannot share a year with the first.

events.text: Narendradeva dies — c. 679; succeeded by Sivadeva II.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 137

events.text: Adityasena dies — c. 680.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 127

events.text: Vikramaditya I dies — 681.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 245; chronology p. 716

events.text: The Chatsu inscription of Dhanika: The earliest dated Guhilot record: a chief of the Chatsu branch in eastern Rajasthan, Vikrama 741.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 160; chronology p. 716

events.text: Valabhi conquers Nandipuri again: Siladitya III of Valabhi issues grants from the Gurjara capital in 685 — the second Maitraka occupation of Lata.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 149; chronology p. 716

events.text: Nanna Rashtrakuta rules at Achalapura: The Rashtrakutas of Berar — Durgaraja, Govindaraja, Svamikaraja, Nannaraja Yuddhasura — hold Elichpur under the Chalukyas; the Multai grant of 709 is Nanna's. The kin, perhaps, of Dantidurga's line.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 201-202; chronology p. 716

events.text: Paramesvaravarman I dies — c. 695.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 262

events.text: Rajasimha begins the Kailasanatha of Kanchi: Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha (695-722) raises the first great structural temple of the Pallavas at Kanchi and the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 262, 281

events.text: Vinayaditya and the 'Lord of the North': the Chalukya Vinayaditya claims to have overcome 'the lord of all the north' and seized his banners — HCIP suggests Yasovarman of Kanauj — the first Deccan blow struck at the Gangetic power.
events.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Vinayaditya) vs an unnamed northern king (? Yasovarman)
events.commanders: Vinayaditya; Vijayaditya (crown prince)
events.outcome: Chalukya claim of victory in the north
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 130, 245

events.text: Vinayaditya dies — 696.
events.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 245; chronology p. 716

events.text: Umayyad campaigns in India: During the first half of the 8th century, a series of battles took place in the Indian subcontinent between the Umayyad Caliphate and Indian kingdoms.
events.belligerents: Caliphal Sindh (Umayyad–Abbasid) vs Karkota dynasty of Kashmir, Gurjara-Pratihara Empire and the Mauryas of Chittorgarh
events.outcome: Victory of Indian kingdoms
events.commanders: Chavotaka king, Lalitaditya Muktapida, Yashovarman — Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, Junayd ibn Abd ar-Rahman al-Murri, Tamim ibn Zayd al-Utbi
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Battle of Aror: Muhammad ibn Qasim defeated and killed Raja Dahir of Sindh; Aror, Multan and the lower Indus passed to the Umayyad caliphate — the Islamic world’s first province in India.
events.belligerents: Umayyad Caliphate (Muhammad ibn Qasim) vs Brahmin dynasty of Sindh (Raja Dahir)
events.outcome: Umayyad victory; Sindh becomes a Caliphal province
events.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

events.text: Raja Dahir dies — Killed at the battle on the Indus near Aror, fighting Muhammad ibn Qasim; the last Brahmin king of Sindh.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Junaid's raids into Western India: Junaid, the Umayyad governor of Sindh, crushed Jaisimha, who had renounced the treaty submission his family had made to the caliphate and then pushed far beyond Sindh, his columns overrunning Marumada (Jaisalmer-Jodhpur), Vallamandala, Broach and Malwa as far as Ujjain, and defeating the Saindhava, Kachchhella, Saurashtra, Chavotaka, Maurya and Gurjara kings. The gains proved short-lived and were lost under his successor Tamim.
events.belligerents: Caliphal Sindh (Umayyad–Abbasid) (Junaid) vs the kingdoms of Rajasthan, Gujarat and Malwa - Gurjaras of Bhillamala, Pratiharas of Avanti, Chalukya (Badami) viceroys of Lata
events.outcome: Arab victories, soon reversed
events.commanders: Junaid, governor of Sindh — Jaisimha of Sindh and the kings of western India
events.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), pp. 172-173; raids dated A.D. 724-738 in chronology p. 717. date approximate: raids spread over c. 724-738

events.text: Martand: Lalitaditya builds the sun temple: The great Karkota temple of the sun on the Martand plateau above Anantnag, the largest of its age in Kashmir.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Yashovarman's Gauda campaign: the king of Kanauj marched east, conquered West and East Bengal, and defeated and killed the lord of Gauda who also ruled Magadha — the exploit that gave Vakpati's poem Gaudavaho its name.
events.belligerents: Kannauj (Yashovarman) vs Gauda chiefs (matsyanyaya)
events.outcome: Kanauj victory; the Gauda king slain
events.commanders: Yashovarman — the lord of Gauda
events.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), pp. 127-128, 143. date approximate: conquest placed between A.D. 725 and 735

events.text: Lalitaditya defeats the Tibetans: the Karkota emperor of Kashmir, in alliance with Yashovarman of Kanauj, beat back the Tibetans and the mountain tribes of the north-west frontier; his appeal of 733 for a Chinese alliance against Tibet won recognition but no troops, and he prevailed unaided.
events.belligerents: Karkota dynasty of Kashmir (Lalitaditya) vs Tibetan Empire
events.outcome: Kashmiri victory
events.commanders: Lalitaditya Muktapida — Tibetan and Dard chiefs
events.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), p. 133. date approximate: early in Lalitaditya's reign (acc. c. 724)

events.text: Siege of Nandipura: shortly after the boy-king Nandivarman II Pallavamalla was chosen by the people (730), a hostile combination organised by the Pandyas championed the pretender Chitramaya and besieged Nandivarman at Nandipura near Kumbakonam; his general Udayachandra raised the siege, beheaded Chitramaya and won several victories in the Tanjore country.
events.belligerents: Nandivarman II Pallavamalla vs Chitramaya and the Pandyas
events.outcome: Pallava (Nandivarman II) victory
events.commanders: Udayachandra (for Nandivarman II) — Chitramaya, backed by Rajasimha I Pandya
events.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), pp. 262-263; also Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India (siege of Nandipuram). date approximate: war fought in the years after Nandivarman's accession in 730

events.text: Battle of Rajasthan: The repulse of the Arab campaigns — the Umayyad push beyond Sindh into Rajasthan and Gujarat was broken by Nagabhata I of the Pratiharas, the Chalukya viceroy Pulakeshin, and the Mewar chiefs — the caliphate’s Indian frontier fixed at the desert for three centuries.
events.belligerents: Caliphal Sindh (Umayyad–Abbasid) vs Gurjara-Pratihara Empire (Nagabhata I), Chalukya (Badami) (Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin) and allied Indian powers
events.outcome: Indian victory; Arab expansion beyond Sindh halted
events.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

events.text: Arab invasion of the Saindhava kingdom: in or before 739 the Arabs of Sindh invaded the realm of the Saindhavas of western Saurashtra, ruled from Bhutambilika (Ghumli) in a gorge of the Barda hills, during the reign of Pushyadeva.
events.belligerents: Caliphal Sindh (Umayyad–Abbasid) vs Saindhava dynasty (Saurashtra)
events.outcome: Indecisive; Saindhava power survived
events.commanders: unknown Arab commander — Pushyadeva
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 99; chronology p. 506 (c. 739). date approximate: 'in or before A.D. 739'

events.text: Bappa Rawal seizes Chittorgarh: the Guhila chief Bappa, who resisted the Arab raiders more successfully than his neighbours, took the fortress of Chitrakuta (Chittor) from the Mori (Maurya) king Manuraja, whose kingdom had been battered by the Arab incursions of 725-738.
events.belligerents: Guhilas of Mewar vs Moris (Mauryas) of Chittor
events.outcome: Guhila victory
events.commanders: Bappa Rawal — Manuraja
events.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), p. 162: Maurya Dhavala still honoured in a Kota-region record of 738-39, so Bappa "can hardly" have taken Chitor before 738; Tod gives 728, Ojha 734 - the atlas paints c. 740 and records the dispute. Chittorgarh, Rajasthan - not Chittoor, Andhra.

events.text: Lalitaditya turns on Yashovarman: the Karkota emperor of Kashmir, once his ally against the Tibetans, defeated the lord of Kannauj and made the Ganga plain acknowledge Kashmiri power for a generation.
events.belligerents: Karkota empire (Lalitaditya Muktapida) vs Kannauj (Yashovarman)
events.outcome: Kashmiri victory; Yashovarman reduced to tribute
events.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

events.text: Vikramaditya II captures Kanchi: the Chalukya emperor invaded the Pallava kingdom to efface his predecessors' disgrace, defeated his 'natural foe' and took Kanchi — but instead of sacking the city restored to its temples the valuables taken from them. Nandivarman II soon recovered his capital.
events.belligerents: Chalukyas of Badami vs Pallavas
events.outcome: Chalukya victory; Kanchi occupied and later recovered
events.commanders: Vikramaditya II — Nandivarman II Pallavamalla
events.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), p. 263; chronology p. 717 (c. 740)

events.text: Dantidurga's Malwa expedition: after the death of his Chalukya overlord in 747 the Rashtrakuta Dantidurga marched north, extinguished the Gurjara kingdom of Nandipuri in southern Gujarat, and proclaimed the conquest of Malwa by performing the Hiranyagarbha-dana ceremony at its capital Ujjayini, where the defeated Gurjara king is said to have served him as door-keeper. The victory was not followed by annexation: Nagabhata I was still acknowledged as suzerain at Broach in 756 and left a kingdom in Malwa and Rajputana to his successors.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakuta Empire vs Gurjara-Pratihara Empire
events.outcome: Rashtrakuta victory and the submission of the Gurjara king, but no lasting conquest north of the Kim
events.commanders: Dantidurga — Nagabhata I
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 20: "The Rashtrakuta king Dantidurga, who reigned between c. A.D. 733 and 758, is said to have defeated the Gurjara king and made him serve as a door-keeper (pratihara) when he performed the Hiranyagarbha-dana ceremony at Ujjain"; same page, "it is more or less certain that his Gurjara adversary could not have been anybody else but Nagabhata I" and "it does not appear that Dantidurga's military victory was followed by any permanent conquest". Printed p. 2 places the expedition after A.D. 747: "Then he led an expedition into Malwa; and proclaimed its conquest by performing Hiranyagarbha-dana ceremony at its capital Ujjayini." Date approximate (c. 748-750). DISAGREEMENT ON THE RECORD: Wikipedia states flatly that Dantidurga defeated and subdued Nagabhata I in Gujarat and Malwa; HCIP IV reports the door-keeper episode only as a claim ("is said to have"), notes that the identification with the Pratihara rests on a pun on pratihara that "is not accepted by all" (printed p. 20), and holds at printed p. 21 that "in spite of initial discomfiture Nagabhata was able to leave to his successors a powerful principality comprising Malwa and parts of Rajputana and Gujarat".

events.text: Battle of Venbai: The Battle of Venbai was a military engagement fought in the 8th century CE between the Pandya kingdom under Maravarman Rajasimha I and the Chalukya ruler Kirtivarman II.
events.belligerents: Pandya Kingdom vs Chalukya Empire, Western Ganga Dynasty
events.outcome: Decisive Pandya victory
events.commanders: Maravarman Rajasimha I, Marangari — Kirtivarman II, Sripurusha
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Dantidurga overthrows the Chalukyas: the Rashtrakuta feudatory defeated Kirtivarman II and took Vatapi, ending two centuries of Badami Chalukya rule over the Deccan.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakuta (Dantidurga) vs Chalukya of Badami (Kirtivarman II)
events.outcome: Rashtrakuta empire founded
events.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

events.text: Dantidurga dies — c. 756; the founder of Rashtrakuta power, who overthrew the Chalukyas of Badami.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Arab fleet repulsed off the Barda hills: Hisham, governor of Sindh for Caliph al-Mansur, sent Amru bin Jamal with a fleet of barks against the Barada coast of Saurashtra; the Saindhavas, self-styled 'masters of the western sea', routed the invaders under the leadership of Krishnaraja.
events.belligerents: Caliphal Sindh (Umayyad–Abbasid) vs Saindhava dynasty (Saurashtra)
events.outcome: Saindhava naval victory
events.commanders: Amru bin Jamal — Krishnaraja
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 99; The Classical Age (HCIP III), chronology p. 718 (758). date approximate: Hisham appointed c. 756, expedition 758

events.text: Krishna I extinguishes the Chalukya empire: Kirtivarman II, defeated but not destroyed by Dantidurga, retired to Karnataka and reorganised his forces for a further trial of strength; the new Rashtrakuta king Krishna I met the challenge so successfully that the Badami Chalukya empire was wiped out of existence by about 760.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakutas vs Chalukyas of Badami
events.outcome: Rashtrakuta victory; end of the Badami Chalukya empire
events.commanders: Krishna I — Kirtivarman II
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 3. date approximate: Krishna I's accession by 758; Chalukya power finally extinguished by c. 760

events.text: The Kailasa is cut at Ellora: Krishna I’s monolithic temple to Siva, carved from the top of the basalt down; the largest single rock-cut structure in the world.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Sack of Vizhinjam: The Pandyas sack Vizhinjam — Jatila Parantaka stormed the Ay port below the hills of Thiruvananthapuram, opening a generation of Pandya pressure on the Ay country.
events.belligerents: Pandya dynasty (Jatila Parantaka) vs Ay kingdom
events.outcome: Pandya victory; Ay chiefs reduced
events.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

events.text: Krishna I occupies Gangavadi: the Rashtrakuta emperor invaded the Western Ganga kingdom of Sripurusha, was encamped at Manne in 768, and effected a military occupation of the country, having earlier held the Ganga capital Manyapuram for a time.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakutas vs Western Gangas
events.outcome: Rashtrakuta victory; military occupation of Gangavadi
events.commanders: Krishna I — Sripurusha Muttarasa
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 3, 160; chronology p. 507 (768)

events.text: Battle of Pennagadam: the Pandya king Nedunjadaiyan (Varaguna I) won a great victory over the Kadava (Pallava) at Pennagadam near Tanjore, on the southern bank of the Kaveri, and went on to crush a rising of petty chieftains headed by Ay-vel, ruler of the hill country between Tirunelveli and Travancore.
events.belligerents: Pandyas vs Pallavas (Kadava)
events.outcome: Pandya victory
events.commanders: Nedunjadaiyan (Varaguna I) — the Kadava (Pallava) king
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 158. date approximate: early in Nedunjadaiyan's reign (acc. c. 765); recorded in the Velvikudi grant of his 3rd regnal year

events.text: Gopala dies — c. 770; the elected founder of the Pala line, chosen "to end the anarchy" (matsyanyaya).
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Rashtrakuta conquest of Vengi: Krishna I sent his crown-prince Govinda against Vishnuvardhana IV, the Eastern Chalukya king of Vengi; the expedition succeeded, the whole of the later Hyderabad territory was incorporated into the Rashtrakuta empire by c. 772, and peace was sealed by the marriage of Vishnuvardhana's daughter Silabhattarika to prince Dhruva.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakutas vs Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi
events.outcome: Rashtrakuta victory
events.commanders: Govinda (crown-prince, for Krishna I) — Vishnuvardhana IV
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 3. date approximate: campaign c. 769-772; annexation completed c. 772 Date: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 3: "incorporated in the Rashtrakuta empire in c. 772".

events.text: Krishna I dies — The Rashtrakuta who cut the Kailasa out of the rock at Ellora.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Second Arab naval expedition against Barada: about 776 the Arabs again sent a fleet against the Saindhava coast and captured a town (probably Ghumli), but were forced to withdraw — officially by an epidemic, in reality by the Saindhava king Agguka I, who 'rescued his country drowning in an ocean of naval force'; Caliph al-Mahdi thereupon gave up all designs on India.
events.belligerents: Caliphal Sindh (Umayyad–Abbasid) vs Saindhava dynasty (Saurashtra)
events.outcome: Saindhava victory; Arab withdrawal
events.commanders: unknown Arab commander — Agguka I
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 99-100; chronology p. 507 (c. 776)

events.text: Dhruva deposes Govinda II: when the pleasure-loving Govinda II tried to remove his brother Dhruva from the administration, Dhruva rose in revolt; Govinda sought help from the rulers of Kanchi, Gangavadi, Vengi and Malwa, but Dhruva defeated and dethroned him before their armies could arrive, ascending the Rashtrakuta throne before the end of 780.
events.belligerents: Dhruva vs Govinda II (Rashtrakuta civil war)
events.outcome: Dhruva's victory and usurpation
events.commanders: Dhruva Dharavarsha — Govinda II
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 4; chronology p. 507 (c. 780)

events.text: Pandya conquest of Kongu: Nedunjadaiyan (Varaguna I) conquered the Adigaimans of Tagadur (Dharmapuri) and brought the Kongu country under his control in spite of the aid they obtained from the Chera and Pallava rulers, making him master of the Tanjore, Tiruchirapalli, Salem and Coimbatore regions.
events.belligerents: Pandyas vs Adigaimans of Tagadur, with Chera and Pallava aid
events.outcome: Pandya victory; Kongu annexed
events.commanders: Nedunjadaiyan (Varaguna I) — the Adigaiman of Tagadur
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 158. date approximate: recorded in the Madras Museum plates of his 17th regnal year (c. 782)

events.text: Dhruva annexes Gangavadi: punishing the allies of his deposed brother, Dhruva defeated the Ganga king Sripurusha, took the crown-prince Shivamara prisoner, and annexed the whole of Gangavadi, pushing the Rashtrakuta frontier to the Kaveri; the Pallava Dantivarman bought him off with an indemnity of elephants and Vengi sued for peace.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakutas vs Western Gangas
events.outcome: Rashtrakuta victory; Gangavadi annexed
events.commanders: Dhruva Dharavarsha — Sripurusha and Shivamara II
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 4, 160. date approximate: shortly after Dhruva's accession in 780

events.text: The struggle for Kannauj opens: with Yashovarman gone and the Ayudhas holding Kanyakubja on sufferance, the Pratiharas from Avanti, the Palas from Bengal and the Rashtrakutas from the Deccan all turned on the imperial city. The contest ran for a century and a half; the engagements themselves are recorded year by year from 786.
events.outcome: The contest opens; no single engagement
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 22-28. This row FRAMES the contest and is not an engagement: the Wikipedia overview article was being carried as a single battle, pinned at Indore, with an outcome covering thirty years. The engagements are recorded individually from 786.
events.commanders: Vatsaraja Durlabharaja I Nagabhata II Kakka Vahukadhavala Sankaragana — Dhruva, Govinda III

events.text: Vatsaraja defeats the lord of Gauda: the first encounter of the tripartite war, fought as the Pratihara and the Pala closed on Kannauj from opposite directions. Vatsaraja, aided by his Chahamana feudatory Durlabharaja of Sakambhari, won completely and carried away the Gauda king's umbrellas of state, but was beaten by the Rashtrakuta Dhruva before he could gather the spoils.
events.belligerents: Gurjara-Pratihara Empire vs Pala Empire
events.outcome: Pratihara victory; Dharmapala's state umbrellas taken, though the advantage was lost within a few years to the Rashtrakuta invasion
events.commanders: Vatsaraja, with Durlabharaja I of Sakambhari — Dharmapala
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 45: "The first encounter took place between the Pratihara ruler Vatsaraja and Dharmapala, probably somewhere in the Gangetic Doab, in which the former gained a complete victory. He is said to have 'appropriated with ease the fortune of royalty of the Gauda' and 'carried away Gauda's umbrellas of state.'" Feudatory aid at printed p. 22: "Vatsaraja was aided in this expedition by his feudatory chiefs, one of whom, the Chahamana Durlabharaja of Sakambhari". Date approximate: HCIP gives no year, placing the encounter before Dhruva's northern expedition of c. 786-790. DISAGREEMENT ON THE RECORD: Wikipedia calls this an invasion of Bengal in which Durlabharaja I pursued and defeated Dharmapala in Gauda; HCIP IV, printed p. 23, holds that the claim that Durlabharaja "overran the whole of Bengal up to the confluence of the Ganga and the sea" comes from "a poetical work composed about four centuries after the event described" and is "difficult to take it as literally true", and that "it cannot be said definitely whether Vatsaraja actually invaded Bengal, or met and defeated the lord of Gauda somewhere in the Doab".

events.text: Adi Shankara is born — By tradition at Kalady on the Periyar, in 788.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Dhruva's northern expedition: entering the contest for Kanauj as a third claimant in c. 786, the Rashtrakuta emperor crossed the Narmada, occupied Malwa, and crushed Vatsaraja near Jhansi, driving him into the deserts of Rajputana; he then routed Dharmapala on the outskirts of the Doab, capturing the Pala king's white imperial umbrellas, before returning south c. 790 laden with booty.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakuta Empire vs Gurjara-Pratihara Empire and Pala Empire
events.outcome: Rashtrakuta victory over both Vatsaraja and Dharmapala
events.commanders: Dhruva Dharavarsha — Vatsaraja; Dharmapala
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 5. date approximate: campaign c. 786-790 (midpoint given)

events.text: Dharmapala's durbar at Kannauj: with the Rashtrakutas withdrawn to the Deccan and Vatsaraja's power broken, the Pala king convoked a great assembly at Kannauj to proclaim himself suzerain and to seat Chakrayudha on the throne in place of the defeated Indrayudha. The rulers of Bhoja, Matsya, Madra, Kuru, Yadu, Yavana, Avanti, Gandhara and Kira attended and gave their assent, the high-water mark of Pala paramountcy in northern India.
events.outcome: Chakrayudha installed at Kannauj as a Pala nominee; Dharmapala acknowledged as paramount lord of northern India
events.commanders: Dharmapala; Chakrayudha
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 46: "His main object in convoking the great assembly was to proclaim himself as the suzerain and install Chakrayudha on the throne of Kanauj in place of Indrayudha whom he had defeated. The durbar was attended by a number of vassal chiefs among whom are mentioned the rulers of Bhoja, Matsya, Madra, Kuru, Yadu, Yavana, Avanti, Gandhara and Kira, who uttered acclamations of approval, 'bowing down respectfully with their diadems trembling.'" Same page: "we must hold that Dharmapala must have enjoyed, at least for some time, the unique position of a paramount lord in Northern India", and "These states were not annexed by Dharmapala, but their rulers acknowledged his suzerainty". Date approximate: HCIP gives no year, placing the durbar after Dhruva's return to the south of c. 790 (chronology, printed p. 508) and within Dharmapala's reign of c. 770-810 (printed p. 45). Not a battle: this is an assembly and an investiture, filed as Political. NOT IN WIKIPEDIA's Tripartite Struggle article, which mentions the imperial court only in passing under Dharmapala's conquest of Kannauj.

events.text: Govinda III crushes the revolt of Stambha: the accession of Govinda III in 793 was challenged by his elder brother Stambha, viceroy of Gangavadi, at the head of 'twelve kings' joined by the released Ganga prince Shivamara; Govinda quelled the rebellion, took his brother prisoner and magnanimously reinstated him, while Shivamara was returned to prison.
events.belligerents: Govinda III vs Stambha and twelve confederate kings
events.outcome: Govinda III's victory; undisputed overlord of the Deccan by c. 795
events.commanders: Govinda III — Stambha (Ranavaloka) and Shivamara II
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 6, 160. date approximate: rebellion quelled A.D. 793-795

events.text: Indra of Lata checks Nagabhata II: Nagabhata's advance into north Gujarat and Malwa brought the Pratiharas up against the Rashtrakuta viceroyalty of the north while Govinda III was held in the Deccan by his brother's revolt and the war with the Gangas. The viceroy Indra met the attack, and each side claimed the victory — Indra's records say he alone defeated the lord of the Gurjaras, the Pratiharas that they kept the forts they had taken in Malwa.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakuta Empire vs Gurjara-Pratihara Empire
events.outcome: Indecisive; neither side gained a decisive victory, the Rashtrakuta northern frontier held and Nagabhata II probably kept some hill-forts in Malwa
events.commanders: Indra, Rashtrakuta viceroy of the north (Lata), and his son Karkka — Nagabhata II, with his feudatory Vahukadhavala
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 26: "This took place probably about A.D. 794-95, early in the reign of Govinda III, when the new king was engaged in the south in putting down the rebellion of his brother and fighting with the Ganga ruler. The brunt of the attack fell upon his viceroy of the north, Indra, who 'alone' is said to have defeated the Gurjara lord. But, as noted above, the Pratiharas also claimed victory, and probably gained some hill forts in Malwa. The northern frontier was, however, guarded effectively by Indra and his son Karkka, who says in one of his records that the Rashtrakuta king had 'caused his arm to become an excellent door-bar of the country of the lord of Gurjaras.'" Printed p. 25: "It may be concluded, therefore, that no party gained a decisive victory, though Nagabhata probably retained some of the captured hill-forts." Dated 794-795 in HCIP's own chronology, printed p. 508: "794-795 Conflict between Nagabhata and the Rashtrakutas (p. 26)". Coordinate approximate: a point on the Lata-Malwa frontier in the Narmada valley; the sources locate no battlefield. Distinct from Govinda III's own northern expedition of c. 800, already recorded. NOT IN WIKIPEDIA's Tripartite Struggle article, which mentions Indra only as securing the Vindhya passes for his brother. The year is placed in the first years of Nagabhata II as this atlas dates them (795-833, Wikipedia "c. 795 - c. 833"); the roll formerly opened in 800, a textbook rounding with no citation, which put these sourced campaigns before his accession.

events.text: Nagabhata II's hill-fort campaigns: the Gwalior inscription of his grandson credits the young Pratihara with forcibly seizing the hill-forts of the kings of Anartta, Malava, Kirata, Turushka, Vatsa and Matsya — the earliest military exploits of the reign, said to have begun in his boyhood, and the first stage of the Pratihara recovery after Vatsaraja's defeat. The record names the six regions but no single action, and no details of the campaigns survive.
events.belligerents: Gurjara-Pratihara Empire vs the rulers of Anartta, Malava, Kirata, Turushka, Vatsa and Matsya
events.outcome: Forts taken across six regions; the advance towards north Gujarat and Malwa brought on the Rashtrakuta conflict of 794-795
events.commanders: Nagabhata II — the local rulers named in the Gwalior inscription
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 24: the Gwalior inscription says he "forcibly seized the hill-forts of the kings of Anartta, Malava, Kirata, Turushka, Vatsa, and Matsya"; "The forcible seizure of the hill-forts of Anartta, Malava, etc. is said to have begun even in his boyhood ... They may, therefore, be regarded as the earliest military exploits of Nagabhata II. The geographical position of the rulers shows that Nagabhata advanced towards North Gujarat (Anartta) and Malwa in the south and east, and this probably brought him into conflict with the Rashtrakutas". Printed p. 25: "His similar enterprises in the north (Matsya), east (Vatsa), and west (Turushka) were probably more successful, but we possess no details of these campaigns." Date approximate: HCIP dates none of the seizures, placing them at the opening of the reign, before the Rashtrakuta conflict of A.D. 794-795 (chronology, printed p. 508). One row for the whole series, because the source names regions rather than engagements. Coordinate approximate: plotted on the Malwa plateau, the Anartta-Malava axis that HCIP alone locates; the six fort groups run from Gujarat to the Himalayan foothills, so the pin stands for the campaign, not for a battlefield. NOT IN WIKIPEDIA's Tripartite Struggle article. The year is placed in the first years of Nagabhata II as this atlas dates them (795-833, Wikipedia "c. 795 - c. 833"); the roll formerly opened in 800, a textbook rounding with no citation, which put these sourced campaigns before his accession.

events.text: Govinda III's northern expedition: marching via Bhopal and Jhansi with Kanauj as his objective, the Rashtrakuta emperor met Nagabhata II probably in Bundelkhand and routed him, the Pratihara fleeing to Rajputana 'nobody knew whither'; Chakrayudha and Dharmapala submitted of their own accord, and Govinda swept on to the Himalayas before returning to the Narmada.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakuta Empire vs Gurjara-Pratihara Empire, Pala Empire
events.outcome: Rashtrakuta victory; Nagabhata II's imperial ambitions shattered
events.commanders: Govinda III — Nagabhata II
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 7-8, 26. date approximate/disputed: long placed c. 806-807, but 'now generally held' to be before 802, most probably A.D. 800 (p. 8)

events.text: Vettuvan Koil at Kalugumalai: The Pandya monolith cut from the top of a granite hill and never finished — the vimana complete, the sanctum below it barely begun; eighth century.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Govinda III scatters the southern confederacy: taking advantage of Govinda's absence in the north, the Pallava, Pandya, Kerala and Ganga rulers formed a confederacy against him; he marched south with lightning speed and scattered them all before the end of 802, occupying Kanchi (c. 804) — a blow that so alarmed the king of Ceylon that he sent statues of himself and his minister in token of submission.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakutas vs confederacy of Pallava, Pandya, Kerala and Ganga rulers
events.outcome: Rashtrakuta victory; Kanchi occupied
events.commanders: Govinda III — Dantivarman Pallava and the confederate kings
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 8; Kanchi invasion c. 804 at p. 151 and chronology p. 508

events.text: Govinda III dies — The Rashtrakuta at the empire’s widest reach, from Kannauj to the Kaveri.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj: Nagabhata II took Kannauj from Chakrayudha, Dharmapala's protege, and moved the Pratihara capital there from Ujjayini - the central prize of the three-way war between Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas. No source gives a year for the seizure; the Buchkala record of 815 that gives Nagabhata II full imperial titles, and the date Schwartzberg gives for the transfer of the capital.
events.belligerents: Gurjara-Pratihara (Nagabhata II) vs Chakrayudha, backed by the Pala Empire (Dharmapala)
events.outcome: Pratihara victory; Kannauj becomes the imperial capital of northern India
events.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers. Dated 816 here so that the map, the capital record and the milestone all give one year; the Buchkala record of 815 and Schwartzberg's "c. 815" are the evidence, and the year is approximate.

events.text: Battle of Monghyr: with Kannauj taken and Chakrayudha put down, Nagabhata II carried the war into the heart of the Pala dominions, where a pitched battle was fought, probably near Monghyr (Mudgagiri), against Dharmapala, ‘a mass of dark, dense cloud of mighty elephants, horses and chariots’; the Pratihara, aided by the feudatories Kakka, Vahukadhavala and Sankaragana, won a great victory. It was a field victory and not a conquest — no Pala district changed hands, and Magadha stayed Pala for another seventy years — but it secured the eastern flank of the city Nagabhata had just made his capital.
events.belligerents: Gurjara-Pratihara Empire vs Pala Empire
events.outcome: Pratihara victory in the field; no territory taken, the Pala hold on Anga and Magadha unbroken
events.commanders: Nagabhata II — Dharmapala
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 25-26, 47-48; the Gwalior prashasti of Bhoja I, which names Chakrayudha first and the Gauda king after. Undated in the sources; the year is approximate, within 816-820. DISPUTED: Majumdar (HCIP) puts both the Kannauj conquest and this battle BEFORE Govinda III’s northern raid of c. 800; this atlas follows the later reading, because its own paint does - HCIP IV p. 26 has Dharmapala and Chakrayudha surrendering to Govinda III of their own accord in c. 800, so Chakrayudha still held Kannauj then, p. 25 has Nagabhata II defeating him "only in the early 9th century", and Schwartzberg has the Ayudhas "c. 815. Overthrown by Pratiharas". On that reading Dharmapala must still be reigning, which is A. M. Chowdhury (1967) 781-821 and B. P. Sinha (1977) 783-820 rather than Majumdar’s 770-810.

events.text: Adi Shankara dies — By tradition at Kedarnath, aged thirty-two; the philosopher of Advaita.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Dharmapala dies — c. 820; founder of Vikramashila, whose armies reached Kannauj.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Battle of Vingavalli: Amoghavarsha I, after recovering his throne with the help of his Gujarat viceroy Karkka, destroyed a large host of the Eastern Chalukyas at Vingavalli near Stambhapuri (Kambham) and drove their army out of Rashtrakuta territory.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakuta Empire vs Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi
events.outcome: Decisive Rashtrakuta victory; Chalukya invasion rolled back and Vengi occupied
events.commanders: Amoghavarsha I — Vijayaditya II (Sastri: Vijayaditya III)
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 9, 134; Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, block 142 of the archive.org text. Date disputed: HCIP implies c. 830 vs Vijayaditya II; Sastri places it against Vijayaditya III in the 850s

events.text: Nagabhata II dies — The Pratihara who took Kannauj from the Palas.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Pandya invasion of Ceylon: Srimara Srivallabha invaded Ceylon in the reign of Sena I, ravaged the northern province and sacked the capital and its monasteries, until Sena submitted and the Pandya forces quit the island.
events.belligerents: Pandya kingdom vs Sinhala kingdom of Anuradhapura
events.outcome: Pandya victory; Sena I submitted and bought peace
events.commanders: Srimara Srivallabha — Sena I
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 170; Sastri, A History of South India, blocks 139-140 of the archive.org text. Date approximate, within Sena I's reign (c. 831-851)

events.text: Bhoja I recovers Gurjaratra: the Daulatpura copper-plate of A.D. 843 shows Bhoja I reasserting Pratihara authority over Gurjaratra (central and eastern Rajputana), lost during Ramabhadra's inglorious reign, aided by loyal feudatories like the Guhilot Harsharaja who 'overcame the kings in the north'.
events.belligerents: Gurjara-Pratihara Empire vs rebellious Jodhpur Pratiharas and northern kings
events.outcome: Pratihara authority restored over Gurjaratra by A.D. 843
events.commanders: Bhoja I; Harsharaja (Guhilot feudatory) — Bauka of Jodhpur
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 29-30 (Daulatpura plate, A.D. 843)

events.text: Devapala defeats Bhoja I: soon after re-establishing his family's fortunes, Bhoja had to measure his strength with the Pala emperor Devapala; Bhoja was defeated and his triumphant career arrested, the Palas remaining supreme in the east while Devapala 'destroyed the haughtiness of the lords of the Gurjaras'.
events.belligerents: Pala Empire vs Gurjara-Pratihara Empire
events.outcome: Pala victory; Pratihara expansion eastward checked until after Devapala's death
events.commanders: Devapala (aided by his cousin-general Jayapala) — Bhoja I
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 30, 50-51. Date approximate (c. 840-850, before Devapala's death c. 850); battle site in the middle Ganga valley uncertain

events.text: Battle of Tellaru: The Battle of Tellaru was fought in 830 between the forces of the Pallava King Nandivarman III and the Pandyan King Srimara Srivallabha.
events.belligerents: Pallava dynasty vs Pandyan Dynasty
events.outcome: Pallava victory
events.commanders: Nandivarman III — Srimara Srivallabha
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07) Re-dated from 830 to 850. The row came from a Wikipedia category sweep that dates the battle to 830 while the same encyclopaedia dates its victor, Nandivarman III, to c. 846-869 - he was not yet king in 830. This atlas paints him from 847, and carries Srimara’s revenge at Kumbakonam in 859 and Nripatunga’s answer at Arisil in 861, so Tellaru belongs between the accession and 859.

events.text: Devapala dies — c. 850; the Pala at the empire’s widest reach.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Bankeya crushes the Ganga revolt: the Western Ganga Nitimarga Ereyanga and other feudatories rose against Amoghavarsha I, whose famous general Bankeya campaigned successfully in Gangavadi before being recalled; the long Ganga war ended only with the marriage alliance of c. 860.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakuta Empire vs Western Gangas and rebel feudatories
events.outcome: Revolt largely suppressed; hostilities ended by the marriage of Amoghavarsha's daughter to the Ganga prince Butuga c. 860
events.commanders: Bankeya (for Amoghavarsha I) — Nitimarga Ereyanga
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 9-10; Sastri, A History of South India, block 143 of the archive.org text. Date approximate (c. 850-860)

events.text: Battle of Kumbakonam: the Pandya Srimara Srivallabha recovered his strength and about 859 defeated the Pallava Nandivarman III and his confederates in a battle near Kumbakonam in the Kaveri delta.
events.belligerents: Pandya kingdom vs Pallava-led confederacy
events.outcome: Pandya victory over the Pallava confederacy
events.commanders: Srimara Srivallabha — Nandivarman III
events.source: Sastri, A History of South India, block 142 of the archive.org text ('about 859')

events.text: Dhruva II repels the Pratihara invasion of Lata: Mihira Bhoja, seeking to avenge Nagabhata II's defeat, invaded the Gujarat Rashtrakuta kingdom, but Dhruva II — reconciled with Amoghavarsha in 860 — held his own and confined the enemy to the other side of the Narmada, being secure on his throne again by 867.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakutas of Gujarat (Lata branch) vs Gurjara-Pratihara Empire
events.outcome: Pratihara invasion checked at the Narmada
events.commanders: Dhruva II — Mihira Bhoja
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 10; Sastri, A History of South India, block 143 of the archive.org text. Date approximate (c. 860-867)
