events.text: Battle of Arisil: soon after his accession the young Pallava Nripatunga avenged his father's defeat at Kumbakonam by a decisive victory over the Pandyas on the banks of the Arisil (Arichit), a distributary of the Kaveri, recorded in his Bahur plates.
events.belligerents: Pallava kingdom vs Pandya kingdom
events.outcome: Decisive Pallava victory; Pandya power in the Kaveri delta broken
events.commanders: Nripatungavarman — Srimara Srivallabha
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 152; Sastri, A History of South India, block 142 of the archive.org text. Date approximate (c. 860-862)

events.text: Sinhalese sack of Madurai: Sena II of Ceylon, allied with the Pallavas and a Pandya pretender, sent an expedition into the Madurai kingdom which was a complete success — the capital was sacked, Srimara Srivallabha died of his wounds, and Varagunavarman II was enthroned by the Sinhalese commander-in-chief.
events.belligerents: Sinhala kingdom (Sena II) and Pandya pretender vs Pandya kingdom of Srimara
events.outcome: Madurai sacked; Srimara died of his wounds; Varagunavarman II installed (862)
events.commanders: Sena II's commander-in-chief — Srimara Srivallabha
events.source: Sastri, A History of South India, block 142 of the archive.org text; The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 170 (Sena II, A.D. 844-79)

events.text: Amoghavarsha I dies — Sixty-four years on the Rashtrakuta throne; author of the Kavirajamarga.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Battle of Soremati: the Nolamba Mahendra I, backed by the Western Gangas, sent his general Kaduvetti Muttarasa to invade Pulinadu, but the Banas and Vaidumbas attacked at Soremati about A.D. 878 and the Nolambas were repulsed.
events.belligerents: Banas and Vaidumbas vs Nolambas and Western Gangas
events.outcome: Bana-Vaidumba victory; the Nolamba invasion repulsed
events.commanders: Kaduvetti Muttarasa (for Mahendra I Nolamba) — Bana and Vaidumba chiefs
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 163, 511 (chronology: 'c. 878'). Locality in the Bana country (Chittoor-Punganur region) approximate

events.text: Battle of Thirupurambiyam: Battle of Thirupurambiyam was fought between the Pandya king Varagunavarman II and a confederacy of the Pallavas, Western Ganga Dynasty and the Medieval Cholas in about 879 CE.
events.belligerents: Pallava dynasty, Western Gangas, Medieval Cholas vs Pandya kingdom, Pallava factions
events.outcome: Alliance victory
events.commanders: Aparajitavarman, Prithvipati I, Aditya I — Varagunavarman II, Nriputungavarman
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Battle of the Narmada: Bhoja I took the offensive against the Rashtrakutas, and a Pratihara record refers to the defeat of Krishna II, probably on the banks of the Narmada, and his retreat to the south of the river, after which Bhoja occupied Malwa and advanced towards Gujarat, taking Khetaka (Kaira).
events.belligerents: Gurjara-Pratihara Empire vs Rashtrakuta Empire
events.outcome: Pratihara victory; Krishna II driven south of the Narmada. The Pratihara record also claims Malwa, but the map keeps Malwa Paramara under Rashtrakuta overlordship until 930
events.commanders: Bhoja I — Krishna II
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 31. Date within c. 878-888 (early in Krishna II's reign); exact site on the Narmada uncertain. Note: HCIP credits the victory to Bhoja, against the older view of a Pratihara defeat DISAGREEMENT INSIDE ONE BOOK: HCIP IV p. 31 (Pratihara chapter) has Bhoja occupying Malwa after this victory; p. 95 (Paramara chapter) has the early Paramaras as Rashtrakuta vassals in Malava throughout and says Nagabhata II "could not reconquer Malava". The map follows p. 95 and gives the Pratiharas Malwa only in 930-946, so the outcome line here no longer states the occupation as fact.

events.text: Avantivarman of Kashmir dies — The Utpala king whose engineer Suyya drained the valley; founder of Avantipur.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Utpala war of succession in Kashmir: on Avantivarman's death in A.D. 883 civil war broke out among the descendants of Utpala; after a strenuous fight Sankaravarman put down the rival Yuvaraja Sukhavarman and other claimants and made himself absolute ruler of the country.
events.belligerents: Sankaravarman's faction vs Sukhavarman and rival Utpala princes
events.outcome: Sankaravarman victorious; sole ruler of Kashmir (r. 883-902)
events.commanders: Sankaravarman — Sukhavarman
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 117

events.text: Battle of Ujjayini: Rashtrakuta records assert that Krishna II recovered Khetaka and fought a sanguinary battle with Bhoja I's host at Ujjayini 'which made a deep impress even upon posterity' — the Begumra plates of 914 say old men still talked of the great battle.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakuta Empire (with Kalachuri allies) vs Gurjara-Pratihara Empire
events.outcome: Claimed as a Rashtrakuta success, but Malwa remained in Pratihara hands (still Pratihara in A.D. 946)
events.commanders: Krishna II — Bhoja I
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 11, 31. Date disputed: 'some time between A.D. 878 and 888' On Malwa the map gives the Pratiharas 930-946 only (HCIP IV p. 95, the Paramara chapter); the sentence "still Pratihara in A.D. 946" is the end of that window, not evidence that they held it from 880.

events.text: Mihira Bhoja dies — The Pratihara who held Kannauj against the Palas and the Rashtrakutas alike.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Mahendrapala's eastern campaign: the Pratihara emperor took Magadha from the Pala Narayanapala and pushed on into northern Bengal, where a pillar of his fifth regnal year stands in the Somapura monastery at Paharpur. How much ground he actually held beyond Bihar is disputed — Majumdar reads the pillar as occupation of part of Varendra, Schwartzberg keeps the whole region inside the Pala core.
events.belligerents: Gurjara-Pratihara Empire vs Pala Empire
events.outcome: Magadha lost to the Pratiharas; the extent of the Bengal push is disputed
events.commanders: Mahendrapala I — Narayanapala
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 33, 53, 57 n.45 Re-dated from 895 to 886 to agree with the map, which has taken Magadha from the Palas in 886 since the 800-1188 layer on HCIP IV p. 33 - "shortly after his accession he conquered Magadha", with records from his 2nd regnal year on. The Paharpur pillar of his 5th year (c. 890) dates the later push into north Bengal, not the conquest of Magadha.

events.text: Sankaravarman's Punjab campaign against Alakhana: the Kashmir king invaded the Gurjara country of the Punjab (modern Gujrat) and forced its king Alakhana to surrender the Takka land east of the Chenab, while Prithivichandra of Trigarta acknowledged his supremacy and even the Pratihara Mahendrapala ceded territories in the Punjab.
events.belligerents: Utpala dynasty of Kashmir (Sankaravarman) vs Gurjaras of the Punjab (Alakhana) and their allies
events.outcome: Kashmiri victory; Takka land ceded, Trigarta submitted, Pratihara territory in the Punjab ceded
events.commanders: Sankaravarman — Alakhana
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 33, 118. Date approximate (within Sankaravarman's reign, 883-902; campaign usually placed c. 885-890)

events.text: Sankaravarman repulsed by Lalliya Shahi: the Kashmir king's military operation against Lalliya Shahi of Udabhanda, who had supported Alakhana against him, did not meet with success; Kalhana says Lalliya's glory outshone all the rulers of the north.
events.belligerents: Kashmir (Utpala dynasty) vs Hindu Shahi kingdom of Udabhanda
events.outcome: Kashmiri failure; the Shahi kingdom remained independent
events.commanders: Sankaravarman — Lalliya Shahi
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 112, 118. Date approximate (c. 885-895, during Sankaravarman's Punjab wars)

events.text: Battle of Niravadyapura: after Vijayaditya III's death (892) the Rashtrakutas under Krishna II occupied Vengi, but Chalukya-Bhima I fought many battles to overthrow the foreign domination — at Niravadyapura his son killed a Rashtrakuta dandesa (general) — and, though Bhima was once taken prisoner, Chalukya rule was restored.
events.belligerents: Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi vs Rashtrakuta Empire
events.outcome: Chalukya independence restored under Bhima I, who thereafter ruled Vengi (at times as a nominal feudatory)
events.commanders: Chalukya-Bhima I and his son — Krishna II's generals
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 12, 136. Date approximate (c. 892-895)

events.text: Aditya I conquers Tondaimandalam: the Chola king attacked and slew the Pallava Aparajita, 'who was seated on the back of a tall elephant', earning the surname Kodandarama; the whole Pallava kingdom became Chola territory, bordering thereafter on the Rashtrakutas.
events.belligerents: Chola kingdom vs Pallava kingdom
events.outcome: Decisive Chola victory; Aparajita killed and Pallava rule extinguished (c. 893-897)
events.commanders: Aditya I — Aparajita Pallava
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 154; Sastri, A History of South India, block 144 of the archive.org text (897 for the completed annexation). Battle site unknown; placed in Tondaimandalam Date dispute: c. 893 (The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 152) vs 897 (Sastri: "the whole of the Pallava kingdom now became Chola territory... (897)"); the atlas follows 897 with the paint.

events.text: Death of Sankaravarman at Urasa: returning from a punitive expedition through Uttarapatha, the Kashmir king was passing through Urasa (modern Hazara) when the inhabitants resisted the quartering of his army; in the affray an arrow shot from a hilltop pierced his neck and he died shortly after, his death concealed until the army reached the Kashmir border.
events.belligerents: Utpala dynasty of Kashmir vs Urasa (Hazara hill kingdom)
events.outcome: Sankaravarman mortally wounded (A.D. 902); Kashmir's expansion into the Punjab collapsed
events.commanders: Sankaravarman — the hillmen of Urasa
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 118

events.text: Prabhakara restores the Shahi throne at Udabhanda: the Kashmiri minister Prabhakara led an expedition against the Shahi kingdom and secured the throne of Udabhanda for Lalliya Shahi's son Toramana-Kamaluka by defeating the usurper Samanta.
events.belligerents: Kashmir expeditionary force and Toramana-Kamaluka vs the usurper Samanta
events.outcome: Samanta defeated; Kamaluka installed as Hindu Shahi king
events.commanders: Prabhakara — Samanta
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 112, 118. Date approximate (c. 900-904, during Gopalavarman's short reign)

events.text: Aditya I dies — The Chola who ended Pallava rule at Tondaimandalam.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Battle of Vallala: on the death of Aditya I, Krishna II invaded the Chola kingdom to secure the throne for his grandson Kannara, but was decisively defeated by Parantaka I at Vallala (modern Tiruvallam in North Arcot District).
events.belligerents: Chola Empire vs Rashtrakuta Empire
events.outcome: Decisive Chola victory; the Rashtrakuta bid to control the Chola succession failed
events.commanders: Parantaka I — Krishna II
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 12. Date approximate (between Parantaka's accession in 907 and Krishna II's death in 914)

events.text: Parantaka I captures Madurai: soon after his accession (907) the Chola king raided Madurai, winning the title Madhurantaka, and by his third regnal year assumed the title Maduraikonda ('captor of Madurai'), driving the Pandya Rajasimha II to seek Sinhalese aid.
events.belligerents: Chola Empire (with Western Ganga, Kerala and Kodumbalur allies) vs Pandya kingdom
events.outcome: Chola victory; Madurai taken and the Pandya king forced to seek Ceylonese help
events.commanders: Parantaka I — Maravarman Rajasimha II
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 154 (title Maduraikonda by the third regnal year, i.e. c. 910)

events.text: Tantrins crush Sugandha's bid for power: the dowager queen Sugandha of Kashmir, backed by the Ekanga troops, marched on the capital in A.D. 914 to regain her sovereignty, but the Tantrin infantry — then the kingmakers of Kashmir — defeated the Ekangas and put Sugandha to death.
events.belligerents: Tantrin infantry (for Partha) vs Sugandha and the Ekanga troops
events.outcome: Tantrin victory; Sugandha executed, Kashmir left to Tantrin king-making
events.commanders: Tantrin corps leaders — Sugandha
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 119

events.text: Battle of Vellur: the defeated Pandya Rajasimha II obtained the aid of the Ceylonese king Kassapa V, but about A.D. 915 Parantaka I beat the combined Pandya and Sinhalese army in a famous battle at Vellur, south-west of Madurai; a third campaign expelled Rajasimha about 920.
events.belligerents: Chola Empire vs Pandya kingdom and Sinhalese expeditionary army
events.outcome: Chola victory; Rajasimha II eventually expelled and Parantaka styled 'captor of Madurai and Ceylon'
events.commanders: Parantaka I — Maravarman Rajasimha II; Kassapa V's generals
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 154, 170

events.text: Rashtrakuta sack of Kannauj: Indra III stormed the Pratihara capital, the deepest southern thrust of the tripartite struggle; Mahipala I recovered the city only after the Rashtrakutas withdrew.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakuta Empire (Indra III) vs Gurjara-Pratihara Empire (Mahipala I)
events.outcome: Kannauj sacked; Pratihara prestige never fully recovered
events.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

events.text: Mahipala recovers Kannauj: after the Rashtrakuta debacle of 916, the Pratihara Mahipala (Kshitipala) regained the imperial throne mainly through his powerful feudatories — a Chandella record says king Harsha 'placed Kshitipala on the throne', and the Guhilot chief Bhatta also fought for him.
events.belligerents: Gurjara-Pratihara Empire with Chandela dynasty and Guhila feudatories vs remnants of the Rashtrakuta occupation
events.outcome: Pratihara restoration at Kannauj (Mahipala attested ruling in A.D. 917)
events.commanders: Mahipala I; Harsha Chandella — Rashtrakuta garrisons
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 33, 36

events.text: Battle of Padmapura: the fugitive Kashmir king Chakravarman enlisted the Damara landholders, whose champion Samgrama inflicted a crushing defeat on the Tantrin infantry near Padmapura; Chakravarman re-entered Srinagar in triumph and the usurper Sambhuvardhana was executed.
events.belligerents: Damaras (for Chakravarman) vs Tantrin infantry (for Sambhuvardhana)
events.outcome: Damara victory; Tantrin power broken and Chakravarman restored (killed by robbers in 937)
events.commanders: Samgrama (Damara); Chakravarman — Sambhuvardhana
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 119. Date c. 935-936

events.text: Battle of Takkolam: The Battle of Takkolam (948–949) was a military engagement involving a contingent of troops led by Rajaditya, crown prince and eldest son of the Chola king Parantaka I (907–955).
events.belligerents: Chola Empire, Cheras vs Rashtrakuta Empire, Western Ganga Dynasty
events.outcome: Rashtrakuta victory
events.commanders: Rajaditya Chola, Vellan Kumaran (Chera/Kerala) — Krishna III, Vaddiga I, Butuga II
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07) Date: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 155: "A decisive engagement took place at Takkolam in A.D. 949".

events.text: The Lakshmana temple at Khajuraho: Yashovarman’s Vaikuntha Vishnu temple, dedicated in 954, the first of the great Chandela temples; the Kandariya Mahadeva followed under Vidyadhara.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Parantaka I dies — Forty-eight years on the Chola throne; roofed the Chidambaram shrine in gold.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Krishna III's second northern expedition: the Rashtrakuta emperor, aided by the Ganga Marasimha, marched into Bundelkhand in c. 963 and then led an expedition into Malwa against the Paramara Siyaka, occupying Ujjayini. The campaign confirmed Rashtrakuta lordship over 'the whole of the Deccan' at its last zenith.
events.belligerents: Rashtrakutas vs Paramaras of Malwa
events.outcome: Rashtrakuta victory; Ujjayini occupied
events.commanders: Krishna III, Marasimha II — Siyaka II
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 15

events.text: Krishna III dies — The last great Rashtrakuta; victor of Takkolam over the Cholas.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Chola recovery of Tondaimandalam: after Krishna III's death (967) the Cholas under Uttama and the young Rajaraja's predecessors pushed the Rashtrakutas out of the northern country they had held since Takkolam; by 973 the bulk of Tondaimandalam was Chola again.
events.belligerents: Chola dynasty vs Rashtrakuta Empire
events.outcome: Chola recovery of Tondaimandalam
events.commanders: Uttama Chola and the Chola princes — Rashtrakuta garrisons after Krishna III
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 156: "The Rashtrakuta interregnum must have lasted for at least fifteen years, A.D. 953 to 968"; Sastri: "by [973] the bulk of Tondaimandalam had been recovered from the Rashtrakutas". Year approximate.

events.text: Battle of Kalighatta and the sack of Manyakheta: Siyaka II threw off the Rashtrakuta yoke, defeated the aged emperor Khottiga at Kalighatta on the Narmada (his ally Kanka of Vagada dying in the fight), pursued him to Manyakheta and plundered the imperial capital in the spring of 972 — even the record-office copper plates were carried off. Khottiga died of a broken heart soon after, and the empire never recovered.
events.belligerents: Paramaras of Malwa vs Rashtrakutas
events.outcome: Paramara victory; Manyakheta plundered
events.commanders: Siyaka II, Kanka (Chachcha) of Vagada — Khottiga, Marasimha II
events.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 15, 96

events.text: Ghaznavid campaigns in India: The Ghaznavid campaigns in India refer to a series of military expeditions lasting over two centuries launched by the Ghaznavid Empire.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs Qarmatians, Chaulukya dynasty
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07) The Gurjara-Pratiharas were struck from the belligerents on 14 September 2026: this row came from a Wikipedia category sweep, and by this date the house was a rump at Kannauj that took no part in the fighting on the Afghan frontier.

events.text: Tailapa II overthrew the Rashtrakutas: the feudatory of Tardavadi rose against Karka II, took Manyakheta, and founded the Western Chalukya empire of Kalyani.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukya (Tailapa II) vs Rashtrakuta Empire (Karka II)
events.outcome: Rashtrakuta empire ends; Kalyani Chalukya rule over the Deccan begins
events.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

events.text: Taila II defeats Panchaladeva: the newly enthroned Chalukya faced the Ganga usurper Panchaladeva, whose kingdom reached the Krishna; after the Chalukya rear fled, the day was saved by the feudatory Bhutigadeva, who defeated and killed Panchaladeva some time before 977. The victory secured Taila's supremacy up to northern Mysore.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukyas of Kalyana vs Gangas under Panchaladeva
events.outcome: Chalukya victory; Panchaladeva killed
events.commanders: Taila II, Bhutigadeva — Panchaladeva
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 161-162; date bracketed as before AD 977. Battle site not recorded; placed in the Gadag-Mulgund country

events.text: Fall of Vilinam: in the opening Chera war of Rajaraja I the Chola stormed and destroyed Vilinam (Vizhinjam) on the Kerala coast — recorded as falling before the naval seizure of Kandalur Salai — while Kollam (Quilon) was attacked separately. His adversary was the Chera Bhaskara Ravivarman (987-1036).
events.belligerents: Cholas vs Cheras of Mahodayapuram
events.outcome: Chola victory; Vilinam destroyed
events.commanders: Rajaraja I — Bhaskara Ravivarman
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 234; sequence (before Kandalur Salai) per source, exact year disputed

events.text: Battle of Kandalur Salai: The battle of Kandalur salai, also spelled Kanthaloor salai, was a decisive military assault carried out by the Cholas under Rajaraja I against the roadstead at Kandalur.
events.belligerents: Chola Empire vs Chera Kingdom (Mahodayapuram) (?) or Pandya Kingdom (?)
events.outcome: Decisive Chola victory
events.commanders: Rajaraja Chola I — Bhaskara Ravi (?) Pandya ruler (?)
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Mahipala I recovers Varendra: ascending a throne reduced to south Bihar in c. 988, the Pala king wrested back his 'paternal kingdom usurped by others' — north Bengal from the Kamboja chiefs and, within his first three regnal years, east Bengal as well, as attested by the Bangarh grant of his ninth year.
events.belligerents: Palas vs Kamboja rulers of Gauda (and Chandras of East Bengal)
events.outcome: Pala victory; North and East Bengal recovered
events.commanders: Mahipala I — Kamboja chiefs
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 24; date c. 988 onwards

events.text: Second Battle of Laghman: The Second Battle of Laghman was fought between the Ghaznavid forces under Sabuktigin and the Hindu Shahi under Jayapala near Laghman in 991 AD.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavid Empire vs Hindu Shahis Chahamanas Tomara dynasty Chandelas
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory
events.commanders: Sabuktigin — Jayapala
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07) The Gurjara-Pratiharas were struck from the belligerents on 14 September 2026: this row came from a Wikipedia category sweep, and by this date the house was a rump at Kannauj that took no part in the fighting on the Afghan frontier.

events.text: Chola conquest of Anuradhapura: Rajaraja I invaded Lanka, sacked Anuradhapura and annexed Rajarata as a Chola province — the beginning of the end for a kingdom that had stood since the fourth century BCE.
events.belligerents: Chola Empire (Rajaraja I) vs Anuradhapura Kingdom (Mahinda V)
events.outcome: Chola victory; northern Lanka annexed, Polonnaruwa made the Chola seat
events.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

events.text: Chola conquest of the Pandyas: following his Kerala victories Rajaraja I conquered Madurai and seized the Pandya king Amarabhujanga, then pressed into Kudamalai-nadu (Coorg) and took the stronghold of Udagai; the Pandya country was absorbed as Rajaraja-mandalam.
events.belligerents: Cholas vs Pandyas of Madurai
events.outcome: Chola victory; Madurai taken, Amarabhujanga captured
events.commanders: Rajaraja I — Amarabhujanga Pandya
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 234; year approximate (early 990s)

events.text: Vakpati Munja dies — The Paramara captured and executed by Tailapa II of Kalyani after crossing the Godavari once too often.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Sabuktigin dies — Founder of the Ghaznavid house; his son Mahmud took the throne the next year.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Chola restoration of Saktivarman in Vengi: Rajaraja I intervened in the Eastern Chalukya succession, ending the twenty-seven-year interregnum (973-999) by placing Saktivarman I on the Vengi throne, partly to forestall Satyasraya's scheme of uniting the two Chalukya houses against the Cholas. Vengi became a Chola protectorate and the cockpit of the century's wars.
events.belligerents: Cholas and Eastern Chalukya loyalists vs rivals backed by the Western Chalukyas
events.outcome: Chola victory; Saktivarman I enthroned
events.commanders: Rajaraja I, Saktivarman I — Jata-Choda Bhima
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 203, 234-235; accession dated 999

events.text: The Mukteshvara at Bhubaneswar: The "gem of Odishan architecture", with its torana; the Lingaraja was raised beside it a century later.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Battle of Peshawar: Mahmud of Ghazni with 15,000 picked cavalry routed the Shahi Jayapala's 12,000 horse, 30,000 foot and 300 elephants outside Peshawar before noon on 27-28 November 1001; Jayapala was captured with his sons and later ransomed. Thrice defeated by the Turks, the old king burnt himself on a pyre, and Anandapala succeeded him.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs Hindu Shahis
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory; Jayapala captured, later self-immolated
events.commanders: Mahmud of Ghazni — Jayapala
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 6-7

events.text: Jayapala dies — The Hindu Shahi, defeated by Mahmud at Peshawar, gave up the throne and burned himself on a pyre.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Didda dies — Queen of Kashmir for half a century, as regent and then in her own name.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Capture of Bhatiya and siege of Multan: Mahmud's capture of Bhatiya and Multan — after a three-day battle Mahmud stormed the walled city of Bhatiya, whose ruler Baji Ray fled and stabbed himself (1004); in 1005-06 he crossed the Punjab against the Ismaili ruler Abu-l Fath Daud and reduced Multan, annexing the lower Indus route to Ghazni.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs Baji Ray of Bhatiya; Ismaili amirate of Multan
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory; Multan annexed
events.commanders: Mahmud of Ghazni — Baji Ray, Abu-l Fath Daud
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 7-8; chronology p. 868

events.text: Battle of Donur: Battle of Donur was fought between the Cholas, during the reign of Raja Raja Chola I, and the Western Chalukya king Satyashraya at the town of Donur in Bijapur district.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukyas vs Chola Empire
events.outcome: Chola victory
events.commanders: Satyashraya — Raja Raja Chola I, Rajendra Chola I
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Battle of Chach (Waihind): Mahmud of Ghazni broke the great confederacy raised by Anandapala — Shahi, Multan and Rajput contingents together — opening the Punjab to annexation.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavid Empire (Mahmud) vs Hindu Shahi confederacy (Anandapala)
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory; the Shahi kingdom reduced to a rump on the Punjab plains
events.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

events.text: Capture of Bhimnagar (Nagarkot): pursuing the Hindu army broken on the plain of Chach, Mahmud besieged the hill fortress-temple of Bhimnagar (Kot Kangra), whose accumulated treasure of generations — gold, silver, pearls and coined wealth — surpassed 'the treasury of any king in India'; it surrendered and was stripped.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs Hindu Shahis and the Kangra temple-fort garrison
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory; fort and treasure taken
events.commanders: Mahmud of Ghazni — Anandapala's forces
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 9

events.text: Military career of Bhoja: The 11th century Paramara king Bhoja ruled from his capital at Dhara.
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: The Brihadisvara at Thanjavur is consecrated: Rajaraja I’s temple to Siva, its vimana sixty metres high, the eighty-tonne cap-stone hauled up a ramp; the 275th day of his 25th year.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Sack of Thanesar: marching before the Rajas of Hindustan could combine, Mahmud forced the river-line held by Rama, chief of Dera, then plundered the sacred city of Thanesar, breaking its idols and carrying the chief image to Ghazni for defilement.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs Rama of Dera and the Raja of Delhi's confederates
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory; Thanesar plundered
events.commanders: Mahmud of Ghazni — Rama of Dera
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 10; HCIP dates it 1011 (often given as 1014)

events.text: Fall of Nandana: in the winter campaign of 1013-14 Mahmud, delayed by snow in the passes, took Nandana in the Salt Range, the last capital of the Shahis, from Trilochanapala, son of Anandapala; the Shahi king fled toward Kashmir, whose minister Tunga was sent — in vain — to his aid.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs Hindu Shahis (with Kashmir's aid)
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory; Nandana annexed
events.commanders: Mahmud of Ghazni — Trilochanapala, Tunga of Kashmir
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 10-11, 97

events.text: Rajaraja I dies — The Chola who built the Brihadisvara and took Ceylon and the Maldives.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Rajendra completes the conquest of Lanka: the Chola fleet captured Mahinda V, last king of Anuradhapura, who died in exile in India; the whole island passed under Chola administration.
events.belligerents: Chola Empire (Rajendra I) vs Anuradhapura Kingdom (Mahinda V)
events.outcome: Chola victory; Mahinda V captured, Anuradhapura kingdom extinguished
events.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

events.text: Ramanuja is born — By tradition at Sriperumbudur, in 1017.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Ghaznavid invasions of Kannauj: The Ghaznavid invasion of Kannauj or the siege of Kannauj in 1018 was a military campaign conducted by Mahmud of Ghazni, the then ruler of the Ghaznavid Empire.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavid Empire vs Pratihara dynasty
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory
events.commanders: Mahmud of Ghazni — Rajyapala
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Jayasimha II repulses the confederate invasion: Bhoja of Dhara made a triple alliance with the Kalachuri Gangeyadeva and Rajendra Chola against the Chalukya Jayasimha II, but the Chalukya dispersed the confederates — an inscription of 1019 records his defeat of Bhoja and the rout of the coalition.
events.belligerents: Paramaras, Kalachuris and Cholas vs Western Chalukyas
events.outcome: Chalukya victory; confederacy dispersed
events.commanders: Bhoja, Gangeyadeva, Rajendra I — Jayasimha II
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 61, 66; dated by inscription of AD 1019, battle site unrecorded

events.text: Battle of Musangi (Maski): Rajendra I crushed the Chalukya Jayasimha II, 'who turned his back at Musangi and hid himself,' claiming the seven-and-a-half-lakh country of Irattapadi; yet Jayasimha soon recovered the Raichur Doab and re-established his line on the Tungabhadra, so the Chola conquest proved rhetorical.
events.belligerents: Cholas vs Western Chalukyas
events.outcome: Chola tactical victory; frontier restored to the Tungabhadra soon after
events.commanders: Rajendra I — Jayasimha II
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 237-238

events.text: Battle of the Rahib: Mahmud defeats Trilochanapala — during the 1020-21 expedition against the Chandella Vidyadhara, Mahmud's men swam the flooded river and routed the last Shahi, who lost 270 elephants and was soon afterwards murdered on his way to join Vidyadhara. With him, Al-Biruni lamented, 'the Hindu Sahiya dynasty is now extinct.'
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs Hindu Shahis and Chandella allies
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory; end of the Shahi kingdom
events.commanders: Mahmud of Ghazni — Trilochanapala
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 16-17. The river: "'Utbi mentions the name of this river as Rahib, and Firishta and Nizam-ud-din Ahmad call it Yamuna" - the books give two identifications and settle neither, so the marker is approximate. Note also that two men of this name meet Mahmud in these years: the SHAHI Trilochanapala, killed after this battle ("the entire Shahi kingdom now formed a part of Mahmud's dominions"), and the PRATIHARA Trilochanapala, son of Rajyapala, who fled Bari soon afterwards. This is the Shahi.

events.text: Mahmud razes Bari: after the Rahib, the Sultan marched on Bari, thirty miles east of Kanauj, where the Pratiharas had moved their capital when their old city was sacked. Trilochanapala, son of Rajyapala, fled before he arrived; the Muslims entered unopposed and levelled the town.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs Gurjara-Pratihara Empire
events.outcome: Bari razed; the Pratiharas driven to the Prayaga country
events.commanders: Mahmud of Ghazni — Trilochanapala the Pratihara
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 17: "Mahmud advanced towards Bari, where the Pratiharas had shifted their capital after the sack of Kanauj... The Muslims entered into the city without any opposition, and at the Sultan's command razed it to the ground."

events.text: Siege of Loharkot: after razing Bari and breaking Trilochanapala Shahi, Mahmud of Ghazni turned on Kashmir a second time and led an army against Lohkot, the hill fortress guarding the Pir Panjal approach to the valley, which had already defied him once; he besieged it fruitlessly for a month and then raised the siege and withdrew, leaving the Lohara kingdom of Kashmir the one north-western state Mahmud never subdued.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs the Loharas of Kashmir
events.outcome: Ghaznavid failure; the siege raised after a month
events.commanders: Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni — the garrison of Lohkot
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 18: "Shortly afterwards, in A.D. 1021, the Sultan led an army against Lohkot, in Kashmir, which he had failed to capture on a previous occasion. However, he did not fare better this time. After making a fruitless attempt for a month to take possession of it, he raised the siege." (Note: Lohkot/Loharkot is placed in the Pir Panjal above the Poonch valley; the coordinates are approximate.)

events.text: Sieges of Gwalior and Kalanjara: in 1021-22 Mahmud invested Gwalior, extracting tribute from the Kachchhapaghata Kirttiraja, then besieged Vidyadhara in Kalanjara; the long siege ended in a negotiated peace, 300 elephants and an exchange of compliments — the Turk's deepest thrust into Bundelkhand was halted at the Chandella walls.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs Chandellas and Kachchhapaghatas
events.outcome: Stalemate; tribute paid, siege raised
events.commanders: Mahmud of Ghazni — Vidyadhara, Kirttiraja
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 18; chronology p. 869

events.text: Chola expedition to North India: Rajendra Chola’s Ganga expedition — a Chola army marched up the east coast, defeated Mahipala I of the Palas in Bengal, and carried Ganga water south to consecrate the new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram — ‘the city of the Chola who took the Ganga’.
events.belligerents: Chola Empire (Rajendra I) vs Pala Empire (Mahipala I), with the Somavamshis and lesser powers en route
events.outcome: Chola victory; Ganga water carried to the new imperial capital
events.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

events.text: South-East Asia campaign of Rajendra I: about 1025 the Chola emperor Rajendra I sent a fleet across the Bay of Bengal against the Sailendra empire, took its ports along the Sumatran coast and down the Malay Peninsula, captured king Sangrama-Vijayottunga-varman, and closed the campaign by taking his capital Kadaram (Kedah).
events.belligerents: Chola Empire vs the Sailendra empire of Srivijaya and Kadaram
events.outcome: Chola victory; Sangrama-Vijayottunga-varman captured and Kadaram taken. Sastri holds the kingdom was then restored to its ruler on his acknowledging Chola suzerainty; HCIP V holds the Cholas kept the position for close to half a century, and a Tamil inscription of 1088 from Sumatra shows the traffic continued.
events.commanders: Rajendra I — Sangrama-Vijayottunga-varman of Kadaram
events.source: HCIP V, The Struggle for Empire, pp. 238–239 and p. 732, chronology p. 869; Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, block 161

events.text: Sack of Somnath: The Sack of Somnath in 1026 was a military campaign orchestrated by Mahmud of Ghazni, the ruler of the Ghaznavid Empire, against the Chaulukya dynasty of Gujarat.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs Chaulukya dynasty, Abhira dynasty
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory
events.commanders: Mahmud of Ghazni — Bhima I, Mandalika
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: The sun temple at Modhera: Bhima I’s temple to Surya on the Pushpavati, with its stepped kund; Vikram Samvat 1083.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Mahmud's river war against the Jats: to punish the Jats who had harassed his retreat from Somnath, Mahmud built a flotilla at Multan and destroyed their 4,000 boats on the Indus; the survivors, whose families had been sent to the islands, were slaughtered or drowned. It was his last Indian campaign.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs the Jats of the Indus
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory
events.commanders: Mahmud of Ghazni — Jat chiefs
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 21-22; chronology p. 869

events.text: Chandihara Yayati recovers Kosala and Utkala: raised to the Somavamsi throne by the ministers after warring chiefs — and probably the Cholas, who had carried off king Indraratha from Yayatinagara — had overrun the realm, Yayati Mahasivagupta III (c. 1025-55) freed both Kosala and Utkala and claimed conquest of Trikalinga, uniting upland and coastal Orissa under one house.
events.belligerents: Somavamsis of Kosala-Utkala vs occupying chiefs, Chola garrisons and encroaching Kalachuris
events.outcome: Somavamsi victory; Kosala and Utkala reunited
events.commanders: Chandihara Yayati Mahasivagupta III — occupying chiefs
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 209-210; date c. 1025-30, reign c. 1025-55

events.text: Gangeyadeva conquers Banaras: the Kalachuri Gangeyadeva 'Vikramaditya' defeated Mahipala I, lord of Anga, and wrested the Banaras region from the Palas some time between 1026 and 1034 — the Muslim chronicler Baihaqi found the city in the possession of 'Gang' in 1034.
events.belligerents: Kalachuris of Tripuri vs Palas
events.outcome: Kalachuri victory; Banaras annexed
events.commanders: Gangeyadeva — Mahipala I
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 25-26, 61; date bracketed 1026-1034

events.text: Mahmud of Ghazni dies — Seventeen raids into Hindustan; Somnath, Kannauj and Mathura among them.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: The Vimala Vasahi at Dilwara: Vimala Shah, Bhima I’s minister, raises the first of the marble Jain temples of Mount Abu.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Ahmad Niyaltigin's raid on Banaras: the Ghaznavid governor of the Punjab dashed across the Gangetic plain and plundered the markets of Banaras, then held by the Kalachuri Gangeyadeva, who bore the brunt of the attack — the first Muslim raid to reach the holy city.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavid governorate of the Punjab vs Kalachuris of Tripuri
events.outcome: Raid successful; no occupation
events.commanders: Ahmad Niyaltigin — Gangeyadeva
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 25, 61; chronology p. 870
Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)
events.text: Battle of Bahraich: Raja Suhaldev of Shravasti, with a league of chiefs from the tarai, destroys the army of Salar Masud - "Ghazi Miyan", the nephew of Mahmud of Ghazni - and ends the Ghaznavid push into Awadh. Known almost wholly from the Mirat-i-Masudi, a romance of c. 1620; the date (14 June 1034) is the romance’s.
events.belligerents: Suhaldev of Shravasti and allied chiefs vs Salar Masud (Ghazi Miyan), Ghaznavid
events.outcome: Ghaznavid army destroyed; Salar Masud killed and buried at Bahraich, where his dargah stands

events.text: Gangeyadeva's expedition to the Kira country: in the same year that the Ghaznavid governor Ahmad Niyaltigin sacked his city of Banaras, the Kalachuri Gangeyadeva Vikramaditya of Tripuri struck back at the far end of the Ghaznavid frontier, leading a successful expedition into the Kira country — the Kangra valley — which was then under Muslim control. It is the first recorded counter-raid by an Indian power into Ghaznavid-held territory, and his son Karna repeated it a decade later.
events.belligerents: Kalachuris of Tripuri vs the Ghaznavid occupation of the Kangra hills
events.outcome: Kalachuri victory; the Kira country raided
events.commanders: Gangeyadeva Vikramaditya — Ghaznavid governors of the Kira country
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 61: "In A.D. 1034 Gangeyadeva had to bear the brunt of an attack of the Muslims. Ahmad Niyaltigin, governor of the Punjab under the Ghaznavids, plundered Banaras, and carried away immense riches. Gangeyadeva launched a successful expedition against the Kira country, modern Kangra valley in the Punjab, which was under the sway of the Muslims." (Note: coordinates are for Kangra/Nagarkot, the centre of the Kira country.)

events.text: Gangaikonda Cholapuram: Rajendra I builds his capital and its temple to mark the Ganga campaign; the vimana a little lower than his father’s at Thanjavur, on purpose.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Siege of Hansi (1037): Mas'ud I's storming of Hansi — against the advice of counsellors who begged him to face the Saljuqs instead, Sultan Mas'ud I marched from Ghazni into the Punjab, encamped on the Jhelum near Dinarkotah, and invested the fort of Hansi in the Hissar district. After a strenuous fight Hansi fell; he then took Sonpat, defeating its governor Dipal Har, and extorted presents from the neighbouring Ram Rai before turning back. It was the deepest Ghaznavid penetration of the Haryana plain since Mahmud, and the effort that fatally weakened Mas'ud in the west.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs the chiefs of Hansi and Sonpat
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory; Hansi and Sonpat taken
events.commanders: Sultan Mas'ud I — Dipal Har of Sonpat
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 93: "Thence he went to Hansi, in the Hissar District, Punjab, and invested the fort. After a strenuous fight Hansi fell into his hands. He then marched to Sonpat and defeated its governor Dipal Har." (Note: coordinates are for Hansi; the campaign ran on to Sonipat, 28.99N 77.02E.)

events.text: Mahipala I dies — The Pala who recovered Bengal and Bihar after the Kamboja interlude; Rajendra Chola’s armies met his.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Siege of Lahore (1043): The Siege of Lahore (1043) was a military engagement during the decline of the Ghaznavid Empire.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavid Empire vs Indian confederacy Tomaras of Delhi Kalachuris of Tripuri Paramara dynasty
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory
events.commanders: Mawdud of Ghazni, Faqih Salti — Bhoja, Mahipal Tomar, Lakshmikarna
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Somesvara I sacks Dhara, Ujjain and Mandu: the Chalukya Somesvara I Ahavamalla, who came to the throne of Kalyana in 1042, avenged his father Jayasimha II's humiliation by the Malava confederacy by driving north into the Paramara heartland with his generals Nagadeva, Gundamaya, Jomarasa and Madhusudana. He plundered Mandapa (Mandu), Ujjayini and Dhara itself, forcing the aged Bhoja to flee his capital — the first of the blows that would leave Malava open to partition a decade later.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukyas of Kalyana vs the Paramaras of Malava
events.outcome: Chalukya victory; Dhara, Ujjain and Mandu plundered and Bhoja put to flight
events.commanders: Somesvara I Ahavamalla, with Nagadeva and Madhusudana — Paramara Bhoja
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 66: "Jayasimha's son Somesvara I, who came to the throne of the Deccan in A.D. 1042, avenged himself of the wrong done to his father by plundering Dhara, Ujjain, and Mandu, and forcing Bhoja to flee away from his capital." (Note: coordinates for Dhara/Dhar; HCIP dates only Somesvara's accession, 1042, so the campaign year is approximate. Corroborated at printed pp. 171-72.)

events.text: The Hindu confederacy recovers Hansi, Thanesar and Nagarkot: with Maudud pinned at Ghazni by the Saljuqs, a league of Indian chiefs under the Tomara raja of Delhi set out to end Muslim rule in the Punjab. They wrested Hansi, Thanesar and other places from Maudud's governors, took Nagarkot, and then marched on Lahore and invested it for seven months before a sortie by the desperate garrison scattered them. They kept Nagarkot, Hansi and the other conquests for years. HCIP names the Paramara Bhoja, the Kalachuri Karna and the Chahamana Anahilla as probable members of the confederacy — the high-water mark of Indian recovery between Mahmud and the Ghurids.
events.belligerents: Confederacy of Indian chiefs under the Raja of Delhi vs the Ghaznavid governors of the Punjab
events.outcome: Indian victory in the field — Hansi, Thanesar and Nagarkot recovered — but the siege of Lahore failed
events.commanders: The Tomara Raja of Delhi, with Paramara Bhoja, Kalachuri Karna and Chahamana Anahilla — governors of Sultan Maudud
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 94: "in A.D. 1043, some Indian chiefs formed a confederacy under the leadership of the Raja of Delhi to put an end to the Muslim rule in the Punjab. They wrested HansI, Thaneswar and other places from governors who were posted there by Maudud. After capturing Nagarkot they marched to Lahore and invested it for seven months." (Note: coordinates are for Thanesar/Kurukshetra, the middle of the recovered belt; Hansi 29.10N 75.96E, Nagarkot 32.10N 76.27E. Corroborated at HCIP V, printed p. 67, for Bhoja's share.)

events.text: Battle of Kollippakkai: after pillaging Kalyana and burning its palace, Rajadhiraja I pressed on to Kollippakkai (Kolanupaka in Telangana), where Somesvara I made a stand with his son Vikramaditya, Vijayaditya of Vengi and the commanders Sangamaya, Gandappaya and Gangadhara. The resistance was stiff but the town fell; Gandappaya and Gangadhara died in the encounter and Somesvara fled. Rajadhiraja then overran the Deccan and went home to celebrate with a virabhisheka as Vijayarajendra.
events.belligerents: Cholas vs the Western Chalukyas of Kalyana
events.outcome: Chola victory; Kollippakkai stormed and two Chalukya commanders killed
events.commanders: Rajadhiraja I — Somesvara I, Vikramaditya, Vijayaditya of Vengi, Gandappaya and Gangadhara
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 168: "Somesvara, along with his son Vikramaditya, Vijayaditya of Vengi and his commanders Sangamaya, Gandappaya, Gangadhara and others, gave the Cholas here a stiff resistance, but Kollippakkai could not be defended. Gandappaya and Gangadhara lost their lives in the encounter and Somesvara I fled away like a coward." (Note: coordinates for Kolanupaka, Nalgonda district.)

events.text: Battle of Koluru on the Bhima: driving into the Deccan immediately after Somesvara I's accession, the Chola Rajadhiraja I brushed aside the Chalukya feudatory Vichchaya at Pundi and the generals Nanni-Nolamba, Chamundaraja, Kalidasa, Kommayya and Villavaraja, and was finally met by Somesvara I in person at Koluru on the bank of the Bhima near Chitapur. The Cholas took heavy losses but forced Somesvara to withdraw, opening the road to Kalyana.
events.belligerents: Cholas vs the Western Chalukyas of Kalyana
events.outcome: Chola victory at heavy cost; Somesvara I forced to withdraw
events.commanders: Rajadhiraja I — Somesvara I Ahavamalla
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 168: "The next resistance to the advance of the Cholas was given by Somesvara I at Koluru, on the bank of the Bhima, near Chitapur Railway Station, in the Shorapur District, Hyderabad Though the Cholas suffered a heavy loss on this occasion, they forced Somesvara I to withdraw." (Note: coordinates approximate, near Chitapur on the Bhima. HCIP dates the campaign to 1043-44.)

events.text: Rajendra I dies — Took the Ganga and sent a fleet to Srivijaya; built Gangaikonda Cholapuram.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Sack of Kalyana: Rajadhiraja's sack of Kalyana — invading immediately on Somesvara I's accession (1043-44), the Chola forced the Bhima crossing at Koluru, marched on the Chalukya capital Kalyana, pillaged the city and burnt the palace, celebrating a virabhisheka there with the title Vijayarajendra before storming on to Kollippakkai.
events.belligerents: Cholas vs Western Chalukyas
events.outcome: Chola victory; Kalyana pillaged
events.commanders: Rajadhiraja I — Somesvara I, Vikramaditya
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 167-168; chronology p. 870 (1043-44)

events.text: Nayapala's defeat of the Kalachuris in Magadha: early in his reign the Kalachuri Karna pushed east into Magadha to take Uddandapura (Bihar Sharif); failing, he sacked the Buddhist monasteries of the open country and destroyed the standing grain. The Pala Nayapala rallied and crushed the invading army. Atisa Dipankara Srijnana, rector of Vikramasila and then at the Mahabodhi monastery, sheltered Karna and his beaten troops, arranged their safe departure, and travelled twice into Kalachuri territory to broker a treaty of mutual restitution — one of the rare recorded instances of a monk mediating between Indian empires.
events.belligerents: Palas of Bengal and Magadha vs the Kalachuris of Tripuri
events.outcome: Pala victory; peace mediated by Atisa Dipankara
events.commanders: Nayapala, with the Brahmana Sudraka — Kalachuri Karna
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 27: "Nayapala soon rallied his forces and inflicted a crushing defeat on the invading army. At this time Dlpankara Srijhana, also known as Atlsa, the Rector of the Vikramasila monastery, was residing in the Mahabodhi monastery at Vajrasana. He gave shelter to Karna and his vanquished forces and made arrangements for their safe departure to their own country." (Note: HCIP places the battle only 'in the early part of the reign' of Karna, who acceded between 1034 and 1042; the year is approximate. Coordinates for Uddandapura/Bihar Sharif.)

events.text: Al-Biruni dies — At Ghazni; the Kitab al-Hind is the first outsider’s account of India written from its sources.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Karna's raid on Kanchi: at the height of his power the Kalachuri Karna of Tripuri carried his arms the length of the peninsula, overrunning the Kanchi district then held by the Chola Rajadhiraja or Rajendradeva and claiming victories over the Nolamba-Pallavas, the Kongus of Salem and Coimbatore, the Muralas of the Malabar coast and the Pandyas of Madura — HCIP suggests these powers formed a confederacy under the Chola king against him. He also claimed a victory over Somesvara I of Kuntala. The whole southern adventure must have closed before 1048, the date of his Rewah inscription.
events.belligerents: Kalachuris of Tripuri vs the Cholas and their southern allies
events.outcome: Kalachuri raid successful; Kanchi-vishaya overrun, but nothing annexed
events.commanders: Kalachuri Karna — Chola Rajadhiraja I or Rajendradeva
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 63: "He overran Kanchl-vishaya, modern Conjeeveram, Madras, which was then ruled by the Chola Rajadhiraja or Rajendradeva... His invasion of Southern India and the Deccan must have been completed before A.D. 1048, the date of the Rewah inscription, which mentions his fight with the people of those countries." (Note: coordinates for Kanchipuram; 1048 is the terminus ante quem, not a dated engagement.)

events.text: Battle of Koppam: The Battle of Koppam was fought between the Medieval Chola kings Rajadhiraja Chola I and Rajendra Chola II with the Chalukya king Someshvara I in 1054, or in 1052 according to Sen.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukyas vs Chola Empire
events.outcome: Chola victory
events.commanders: Someshvara I — Rajadhiraja Chola, Rajendra Chola II
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Karna's conquest of Bundelkhand and Gopala's counterstroke: some time after 1051 the Kalachuri Karna defeated the Chandella Kirttivarman and occupied Jejakabhukti outright. The Chandella recovery was the work not of the king but of his vassal Gopala, who defeated Karna, drove him out and restored Kirttivarman to the throne; the minister Vatsaraja recovered the mandala and built the fort of Kirttigiri, identified with Deogarh in Jhansi. It is the clearest case in the century of a feudatory saving a dynasty.
events.belligerents: Kalachuris of Tripuri vs the Chandellas of Jejakabhukti
events.outcome: Kalachuri occupation, then reversed; Kirttivarman restored by his vassal Gopala
events.commanders: Kalachuri Karna — Chandella Kirttivarman, restored by the vassal Gopala
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 63: "Some time after A.D. 1051 Karna captured Bundelkhand by defeating the Chandella Klrttivarman. Subsequently Gopala, a feudatory of the Chandellas, drove him out, and helped Klrttivarman in regaining his throne." (Note: HCIP gives only 'some time after 1051'; the year is approximate. Coordinates for Mahoba. Corroborated at printed p. 58.)
Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)
events.text: Lal Kot: Anangpal II of the Tomaras raises the first fortified city of Delhi at Mehrauli, c. 1052 by the traditional date; the iron pillar was brought there and set up.

Nushtigin Hajib recovers Nagarkot: the Ghaznavid restoration in the Punjab came under Sultan 'Abd-ur-Rashid, who appointed Nushtigin Hajib governor of the country east of the Indus. Nushtigin recaptured Nagarkot, which the Indian confederacy had held since 1043, closing the nine-year Hindu reoccupation of the Kangra hills. Nushtigin then went on to break the usurper Tughril at Ghazni and set Farrukhzad on the throne.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs the Indian holders of Nagarkot
events.outcome: Ghaznavid victory; Nagarkot retaken after nine years
events.commanders: Nushtigin Hajib, for Sultan 'Abd-ur-Rashid — the Indian garrison of Nagarkot
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 94: "NushtL gin captured Nagarkot, which had been in the possession of the Hindus since A.D. 1043." (Note: HCIP places 'Abd-ur-Rashid's accession in 1051 and his murder in 1052-53, so the recapture falls in 1051-52; coordinates for Kangra.)

events.text: Rajadhiraja I sacks Kolhapur: on his third invasion of the Chalukya kingdom, accompanied by his brother Rajendra, Rajadhiraja I seized Kollapuram, burnt many Jain temples and defiled and damaged the Jain sanctuaries there. Somesvara I checked the Chola advance and pursued the retreating army south, and the two hosts met for the decisive trial at Koppam, where Rajadhiraja was killed on his elephant.
events.belligerents: Cholas vs the Western Chalukyas of Kalyana
events.outcome: Chola sack of Kolhapur; the Chalukyas then counter-attacked, leading to Koppam
events.commanders: Rajadhiraja I and Rajendra II — Somesvara I Ahavamalla
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 168: "In A.D. 1051-52 Rajadhiraja invaded the kingdom of Somesvara I for the third time, and was accompanied by his brother Rajendra on this occasion. He seized Kollapuram, burnt down many Jain temples, and defiled and damaged the Jain sanctuaries." (Note: HCIP dates the campaign 1051-52. Rajendra II later erected a victory pillar at Kolhapur, printed p. 241.)

events.text: Somesvara I captures Kanchi: shortly before the battle of Koppam the Chalukya, with his general Pulikesin, invaded Tondaimandalam and took the old Pallava capital, from which the Chola governor fled — Bilhana's boast of the conquest is corroborated by an inscription of 1058.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukyas vs Cholas
events.outcome: Chalukya victory; Kanchi briefly occupied
events.commanders: Somesvara I, Pulikesin — Chola governor of Kanchi
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 169; date approximate (shortly before Koppam, corroborating inscription AD 1058)

events.text: Bhoja of Malwa dies — c. 1055; the Paramara philosopher-king of Dhar, author of the Samarangana Sutradhara.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Kalachuri-Chaulukya conquest of Malwa: the Chaulukya Bhima I of Gujarat allied with the Kalachuri Karna and invaded Malwa from west and east; fighting the two-front war, the aged Bhoja died of disease and his kingdom fell into the hands of the Kalachuris and Chaulukyas in c. 1055.
events.belligerents: Kalachuris of Tripuri and Chaulukyas of Gujarat vs Paramaras of Malwa
events.outcome: Allied victory; Dhara occupied, Malwa partitioned
events.commanders: Karna, Bhima I — Bhoja
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 67; chronology p. 870 (c. 1055)

events.text: Vikramaditya VI restores the Paramaras in Malava: when Bhoja died of disease in about 1055 and the allied Kalachuri Karna and Chaulukya Bhima I seized Malava between them, Bhoja's successor Jayasimha appealed to Somesvara I of Kalyana. Somesvara sent his son Vikramaditya VI, who drove Karna and Bhima out and set Jayasimha on the throne of Dhara — the intervention that made Jayasimha a permanent Chalukya client and prevented the outright partition of Malava.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukyas and the Paramaras vs the Kalachuris and Chaulukyas
events.outcome: Chalukya victory; Karna and Bhima expelled and Jayasimha enthroned at Dhara
events.commanders: Prince Vikramaditya VI, for Somesvara I — Kalachuri Karna and Chaulukya Bhima I
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 172: "In A.D. 1055, when the Kalachuri Kama and the Chaulukya Bhlma forcibly took possession of Malava, Vikramaditya VI, at the order of his father Somes vara I, defeated them and restored Jaya simha, successor of Bhoja, to power." (Note: HCIP gives 1055 for the seizure of Malava at printed p. 172 and describes the rescue as following it, printed pp. 63 and 68; the year here is approximate. Karna and Bhima then fell out over the spoils and Bhima invaded Dahala.)

events.text: Battle of Mudakaru: between 1059 and 1061 Somesvara I, his son Vikramaditya and the general Valadeva invaded the Chola country but were met at Mudakaru on the Tunga by Rajendra II and prince Rajamahendra; the Chalukyas were defeated and fled, Valadeva dying in the engagement.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukyas vs Cholas
events.outcome: Chola victory
events.commanders: Rajendra II, Rajamahendra — Somesvara I, Vikramaditya, Valadeva
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 169; dated between AD 1059 and 1061

events.text: Battle of Kudal-Sangamam: The First Battle of Kudal-Sangamam was fought in 1062 by the forces of the Chola king Rajendra Chola II and the Western Chalukya king Someshvara I at Kudal-Sangamam.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukyas vs Chola Empire
events.outcome: Chola victory
events.commanders: Someshvara I — Rajendra Chola II
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: The Rani ki Vav at Patan: Queen Udayamati’s stepwell in memory of Bhima I, seven storeys down, five hundred sculptures.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Bhima I dies — The Chaulukya who built the sun temple at Modhera and whose queen dug the Rani ki Vav.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Battle of Gangavadi: the first of the five defeats Chola inscriptions claim Virarajendra inflicted on Somesvara I. The Chalukya king met him in central Mysore with his son Vikramaditya and a body of feudatories, was beaten, and was pushed back to the bank of the Tungabhadra. Virarajendra then carried the war into the Andhra country on behalf of the Eastern Chalukya Vijayaditya, and finally to Kudal-Sangamam.
events.belligerents: Cholas vs the Western Chalukyas of Kalyana
events.outcome: Chola victory; the Chalukyas driven back to the Tungabhadra
events.commanders: Virarajendra I — Somesvara I and prince Vikramaditya
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 169: "Somesvara, along with his son Vikramaditya and some feudatories, met Virarajendra first in the battlefield of Gangavadi, i.e. central Mysore. They were defeated and pushed back to the bank of the Tungabhadra." (Note: HCIP says all these wars fell before the fifth year of Virarajendra, A.D. 1067; the year is approximate and Gangavadi is a province, so the coordinates are a central point in it.)

events.text: Vikramaditya VI's invasion of Gauda: sent east by his father Somesvara I, the Chalukya prince Vikramaditya VI carried a Deccani army across northern India and defeated the Pala Vigrahapala III in Gauda shortly before 1068; on the same sweep he is credited with a successful expedition against Kamarupa. It is the deepest recorded penetration of Bengal by a southern power in the century and one more blow in the sequence that left Mahipala II's Pala kingdom open to the Kaivarta revolt.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukyas of Kalyana vs the Palas of Bengal
events.outcome: Chalukya victory; Vigrahapala III defeated in his own country
events.commanders: Prince Vikramaditya VI, for Somesvara I — Pala Vigrahapala III
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 27: "Shortly before A.D. 1068 Vigrahapala had to suffer a defeat at the hands of the Chalukya Vikramaditya VI, who invaded Gauda on behalf of his father Somesvara I, king of the Deccan." (Note: HCIP gives only 'shortly before 1068'; coordinates are for the Gauda capital region near Malda. The Kamarupa expedition is at printed p. 43.)

events.text: Virarajendra overruns Rattapadi: challenged by Somesvara I to a second trial at Kudal, the Chola waited a month at Kandai for an enemy who never came, then ravaged Rattapadi and planted a pillar of victory on the Tungabhadra before turning to Vengi — all his wars with Ahavamalla being fought before his fifth regnal year (1067).
events.belligerents: Cholas vs Western Chalukyas
events.outcome: Chola victory by default; victory pillar erected
events.commanders: Virarajendra — Somesvara I
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 171; chronology p. 871 (1067)

events.text: Battle of Vijayawada: The Battle of Vijayawada was fought in 1068 between the Chola army under Virarajendra Chola and the Western Chalukya army commanded by Vikramaditya VI.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukyas vs Chola Empire
events.outcome: Chola victory Coronation of Vijayaditya VII as Eastern Chalukya ruler
events.commanders: Vikramaditya VI, Jananatha, Rajamayan — Virarajendra Chola
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Vikramaditya plunders Gangaikondacholapuram: in 1067-68 the Chalukya prince Vikramaditya (later Vikramaditya VI) carried the war into the Chola heartland, marching on the imperial capital Gangaikonda and plundering it — the boldest Chalukya counterstroke of the fifty years' war.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukyas vs Cholas
events.outcome: Chalukya victory; Chola capital plundered
events.commanders: Vikramaditya (VI) — Virarajendra's garrison
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 171; chronology p. 871 (1067-1068)

events.text: Virarajendra burns Kampili and Somesvara II's counterstroke: to win the Deccan throne for his son-in-law Vikramaditya VI, Virarajendra invaded the kingdom of the new Chalukya king Somesvara II, burnt the city of Kampili, planted a pillar of victory at Karadikal in Raichur and proclaimed Vikramaditya king of the Rattapadi seven-and-a-half-lakh country. Somesvara II counter-attacked with his cavalry, routed Virarajendra and restored order; Vikramaditya submitted to his brother and served him loyally until 1074.
events.belligerents: Cholas and prince Vikramaditya vs Somesvara II of Kalyana
events.outcome: Chola raid successful at first, then routed; Somesvara II kept his throne
events.commanders: Virarajendra I — Somesvara II Bhuvanaikamalla
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 173: "Vlrarajendra burnt the city of Kampili, set up a pillar of victory at Karadikal (modern village of Karadi, in the Lingsugur Taluk, Raichur District, Hyderabad), and declared Vikramaditya as the king of Rattapadi seven and a half lakh country. Somesvara II, with the help of his cavalry forces, routed Vararajendra and established peace and order in his kingdom." (Note: HCIP dates the expedition to the sixth year of Virarajendra, A.D. 1068-69. Coordinates for Kampli, Bellary.)

events.text: Vijayabahu I expels the Cholas: after fifteen years of campaigning from Ruhuna, Vijayabahu took Polonnaruwa and ended seventy-five years of Chola rule in Lanka.
events.belligerents: Kingdom of Polonnaruwa (Vijayabahu I) vs Chola Empire
events.outcome: Sinhalese victory; the island reunified under Polonnaruwa
events.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

events.text: Somesvara II and Chaulukya Karna partition Malava: suspecting that the Paramara Jayasimha of Malava was conspiring with his rebellious brother Vikramaditya, Somesvara II of Kalyana allied with the Chaulukya Karna of Gujarat and invaded Dhara. Jayasimha lost his life in the battle and Malava was occupied by the two invaders — the second dismemberment of Bhoja's kingdom in twenty years, and the end of his direct line.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukyas of Kalyana and the Chaulukyas of Gujarat vs the Paramaras of Malava
events.outcome: Allied victory; Jayasimha killed and Malava occupied
events.commanders: Somesvara II Bhuvanaikamalla and Chaulukya Karna — Paramara Jayasimha
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 68: "In order to punish Jayasimha king Somesvara II made an alliance with the Chaulukya Karna, son of Bhima I of Gujarat, and invaded Malava. In the battle that followed Jayasimha lost his life and Malava was occupied by Somesvara II and Karna." (Note: HCIP gives no year; the war falls between Somesvara II's accession, 1068, and the first dated inscription of his supplanter Udayaditya, 1080, so this date is approximate. Corroborated at printed pp. 75 and 173.)

events.text: Yasahkarna's raid on Vengi: in the early part of his reign the Kalachuri Yasahkarna of Tripuri, son of Karna, campaigned against Champaranya in north Bihar and then plundered the Andhra country of the Eastern Chalukya Vijayaditya VII. Coming on top of Kulottunga I's demand for the throne of Andhra, the raid destroyed Vijayaditya's remaining strength; he surrendered Vengi and took refuge with the Ganga Rajaraja I of Kalinganagara. The Chola sources add that the raid was 'without any appreciable results' for the Kalachuris themselves.
events.belligerents: Kalachuris of Tripuri vs the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi
events.outcome: Kalachuri plundering raid; Vengi fatally weakened and lost to the Cholas three years later
events.commanders: Kalachuri Yasahkarna — Eastern Chalukya Vijayaditya VII
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 204: "The situation became worse for Vijayaditya when, shortly before A.D. 1073, the kingdom of Vehgi was plundered by the Kalachuri Yasahkarna of Tripurl." (Note: 1073 is a terminus ante quem. Coordinates for Vengi/Pedavegi. Corroborated at printed p. 243.)

events.text: Kaivarta revolt of Divya: amid a general rising of the samantas, the Pala king Mahipala II was defeated and brought to his death by his own officer Divya, a Kaivarta by caste 'who took to fraudulent practice as a vow'; Divya ascended the throne of Varendri in c. 1075, founding a rebel line that held north Bengal until Ramapala's reconquest.
events.belligerents: Kaivarta rebels and confederate feudatories vs Palas
events.outcome: Rebel victory; Mahipala II slain, Varendri lost
events.commanders: Divya — Mahipala II
events.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 28-29; chronology p. 871 (c. 1070 accession of Mahipala II, c. 1075 Divya)

events.text: Udayaditya recovers Malava: with Jayasimha dead and Malava in the hands of Somesvara II and Chaulukya Karna, Udayaditya — a brother or cousin of Bhoja — appealed to the Chahamanas of Sakambhari. Vigraharaja III sent him a cavalry force, and with it Udayaditya inflicted a severe defeat on the occupiers and recovered the kingdom, refounding Paramara power in a line that ruled at Dhara for another sixty years. His inscriptions run from 1080 to 1086.
events.belligerents: Paramaras of Malava with Chahamana cavalry vs the Chalukyas of Kalyana and the Chaulukyas of Gujarat
events.outcome: Paramara victory; Malava recovered and the Udayaditya line established
events.commanders: Paramara Udayaditya, with horse sent by Chahamana Vigraharaja III — Somesvara II and Chaulukya Karna
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 68: "In that serious situation Udayaditya, a brother or cousin of Bhoja, sought help from the Chahamanas of Sakambharl. He recovered Malava after inflicting a severe defeat on the invaders with the help of the cavalry which the Chahamana Vigraharaja III had sent to his assistance." (Note: HCIP gives no year; the recovery lies between Somesvara II's occupation and Udayaditya's first dated record of 1080, so the date is approximate. Corroborated at printed p. 82.)

events.text: Vikramaditya VI usurps the Chalukya throne: With the help of the Hoysala Ereyanga and a Pandya chief, Vikramaditya VI defeated and imprisoned his elder brother Somesvara II and seized the sovereignty of the Deccan, inaugurating the fifty-year golden age of the Kalyani Chalukyas.
events.belligerents: Vikramaditya VI with Hoysala and Pandya allies vs Chalukya emperor Somesvara II
events.outcome: Somesvara II captured and deposed; Vikramaditya VI enthroned at Kalyani
events.commanders: Vikramaditya VI, Hoysala Ereyanga — Somesvara II
events.source: HCIP V (Struggle for Empire), pp. 173-174; accession 1076 (one inscription suggests 1078)

events.text: Kulottunga I's campaign between Nangili and the Tungabhadra: the long duel of the century's two great survivors. Kulottunga's inscription of 1080 records that he fought Vikramaditya VI across the country between Nangili in the Kolar district and the Tungabhadra and captured the two territories of Gangamandalam and Singanam — the culmination of a series that includes a victory over the king of Kuntala in 1074 and the claim of 1076 that Vikramaditya and Jayasimha, defeated, plunged into the river to escape.
events.belligerents: Cholas vs the Western Chalukyas of Kalyana
events.outcome: Chola claim of victory; Gangamandalam and Singanam taken
events.commanders: Kulottunga I — Vikramaditya VI Tribhuvanamalla
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 174: "His inscription of A.D. 1080 states that he fought with Vikramaditya VI between Nahgili (in the Kolar District) and the Tuhgabhadra and captured two countries Gangamandalam and Singanam." (Note: coordinates are an approximate mid-point of the theatre between Nangili, Kolar district, and the Tungabhadra; the Chalukya records do not agree with the Chola claim.)

events.text: Karunakara's conquest of northern Kalinga: early in the reign of Anantavarman Chodaganga, Kulottunga I sent a great army into Kalinga under his general Karunakara Tondaiman. The Chola army took Visakhapattana and renamed it Kulottungasolapattanam; Anantavarman could not resist, and the whole of Kalinga up to the Orissa border fell to Karunakara — probably shortly after 1083, the date of a Mukhalingam inscription of Anantavarman's reign. It is the campaign that set up the two Kalinga wars of Kulottunga's later years.
events.belligerents: Cholas vs the Eastern Gangas of Kalinganagara
events.outcome: Chola victory; northern Kalinga overrun and Visakhapatnam renamed
events.commanders: Karunakara Tondaiman, for Kulottunga I — Anantavarman Chodaganga
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 205: "The Chola army took possession of Visakhapattana (Visakhapatnam) and changed its name to Kulottuhgasolapattanam. Anantavarman could not resist the advancing Chola army. The whole of Kalinga up to the border of Orissa fell into the hands of Karunakara, probably shortly after A.D. 1083" (Note: HCIP says 'probably shortly after A.D. 1083'; the year is approximate.)

events.text: Vikramaditya VI takes Kanchi: after nearly a decade of peace following his accession, the Chalukya emperor Vikramaditya VI marched against the Cholas and took Kanchi some time before 1085 — the deepest Chalukya thrust into the Tamil country since his father's day, and the opening move of the long contest for Vengi that he would not win until 1118.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukyas of Kalyana vs the Cholas
events.outcome: Chalukya victory; Kanchi taken
events.commanders: Vikramaditya VI Tribhuvanamalla — Kulottunga I's viceroys at Kanchi
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 174: "After a long period of peace following his accession Vikramaditya VI marched against the Cholas and took Kahchl some time before A.D. 1085." (Note: 1085 is a terminus ante quem, not an attested date.)

events.text: Mahmud of Lahore's raid on Kannauj and Kalanjara: after the deaths of Bhoja and Karna removed the two princes who had frightened the Ghaznavids out of Hindustan for half a century, Ibrahim's son Mahmud, governor of the Punjab, drove into the Doab some time between 1086 and 1090. He plundered Kannauj and Kalanjara and invaded Ujjain, took Agra by defeating its chief Jaipal, and found an ally in Kannauj named Chand Rai — HCIP identifies him with Chandradeva, the founder of Gahadavala power, who seized the throne of Kannauj from the Rashtrakuta Gopala in the disorder that followed Mahmud's departure. At Kalanjara the Chandella Kirttivarman fought Mahmud off successfully.
events.belligerents: Ghaznavids of Lahore vs the Rashtrakutas of Kannauj, the Chandellas and the Paramaras
events.outcome: Kannauj and Kalanjara plundered; Kirttivarman repulsed the attack on Kalanjara and Lakshmadeva the attack on Ujjain
events.commanders: Prince Mahmud, governor of the Punjab — Chandella Kirttivarman; Rashtrakuta Gopala of Kannauj
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 51: "Some time between A.D. 1086 and 1090 prince Mahmud, the governor of the Punjab, plundered Kanauj and Kalanjara and invaded Ujjain. On that occasion he found an ally in Kanauj named Chand Rai, who may be identified with Chandradeva." (Note: coordinates for Kalanjara; Kannauj 27.06N 79.92E. Kirttivarman's successful defence is at printed p. 58: 'Some time before A.D. 1090 Kirttivarman fought successfully with Mahmud, governor of the Punjab under the Ghaznavids, who invaded Kalanjara.' Mahmud's conquest of Agra and Kannauj is at printed pp. 94-95.)

events.text: Lakshmadeva repulses Mahmud at Ujjain: when the Ghaznavid prince Mahmud of Lahore pushed on from Kannauj into Malava, the Paramara Lakshmadeva son of Udayaditya beat him back from Ujjain. The same king raided Gauda under the Kaivartas, plundered Anga and Kalinga, defeated the Kalachuri Yasahkarna, plundered the Kalachuri capital Tripuri and encamped on the Reva, and led an army to the Kira country — the most far-ranging Paramara campaigns since Bhoja.
events.belligerents: Paramaras of Malava vs the Ghaznavids of Lahore
events.outcome: Paramara victory; the Ghaznavid attack on Ujjain thrown back
events.commanders: Paramara Lakshmadeva — prince Mahmud, governor of the Punjab
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 68: "He won a victory over the Kalachuri Yasahkarna and repulsed an attack of Mahmud, governor of the Punjab, when the latter invaded Ujjain. On the north he is said to have led his army to the Kira country, i.e. Kangra valley in the Punjab." (Note: HCIP dates Lakshmadeva's reign 1088-1094 and the Ghaznavid raid 1086-1090, so the year is approximate. The plundering of Tripuri is at printed p. 64.)

events.text: Ramapala reconquers Varendra: The Pala king, backed by fourteen feudatory chiefs led by his uncle Mathanadeva of Anga, crossed the Ganga into Varendri and defeated the Kaivarta king Bhima in a pitched battle, capturing him and later killing him with his kin — the war immortalised in Sandhyakara Nandi's Ramacharita.
events.belligerents: Palas and fourteen allied feudatory chiefs vs Kaivarta kingdom of Varendri
events.outcome: Decisive Pala victory; Bhima captured and executed, Varendra restored to the Palas, new capital Ramavati founded
events.commanders: Ramapala, Mathanadeva, Sivaraja — Bhima, Hari
events.source: HCIP V, pp. 29-30; battle undated in source — placed in the last quarter of the 11th century (Ramapala r. 1077-1120)

events.text: Vikramaditya VI burns Vengi: some time between 1091 and 1093 the Chalukya emperor and his general Govindarasa burnt Vengi and defeated the Velananti chief Gonka I, and Chalukya records claim that the Andhra country was wrested from Vira-Choda, son of Kulottunga I. The raid did not change who governed the province. Kulottunga's sons held the Vengi viceroyalty without a break — Vira-Choda to 1092, then his brother Vikrama Chola from 1092 to 1118 — which is why the map does not move here. Vikramaditya VI's object of separating the Eastern Chalukya and Chola crowns was achieved only at the end of his reign, when Vengi passed to him in 1118.
events.belligerents: Western Chalukyas of Kalyana vs the Cholas and the Velanandu chiefs
events.outcome: Chalukya victory in the field; Vengi burnt, but the Chola viceroyalty of the province continued unbroken
events.commanders: Vikramaditya VI and Govindarasa — Vira-Choda and the Velananti Gonka I
events.source: HCIP V, printed p. 174: "Some time between A.D. 1091 and 1093 he, along with his general Govindarasa, burnt Vengi, defeated the Velananti Gonka I, and wrested Andhra from Vira-Choda, son of Kulottunga Chola I. In the latter part of A.D. 1099 Kulottunga reconquered Vengi from the Chalukyas." — DISAGREEMENT ON THE RECORD: this paragraph of the Later Chalukyas chapter stands alone. Sastri, History of South India, block 167, gives an unbroken Chola viceroyalty — "Rajaraja Mummudi Chola (1076-8), Vira Choda (1078-84), Rajaraja Chodaganga (1084-9), Vira Choda again (1089-92), and lastly, Vikrama Chola (1092-1118)" — and block 168 holds that "up to 1115 the extent of the Chola empire remained undiminished under Kulottunga… extending at least up to the Godavari on the east coast." HCIP V's own Chola chapter, p. 244, places the separation of the two crowns in the last decade of Vikramaditya's reign, and its Eastern Deccan chapter, p. 217, gives Vira-Choda's viceroyalties as 1078-84 and 1088-92 with no interruption after; the volume's chronology table lists the 1099 reconquest but no 1091-93 conquest to reconquer from. The atlas follows the majority and treats 1091-93 as a raid — raids never repaint — so the territory changes hands in 1118, where the map already moves.
