events.commanders: Edward Gardner, Jasper Nicolls, Hyder Hearsey — Bam Shah
events.source: HCIP VIII p. 531 (OCR partly garbled): 'Gardner succeeded in pushing the [Gurkh]as up to Almora. But Hearsey advancing up the Kali river [was defeated] by the Gurkhas and taken prisoner ... [the Gurkhas] had to surrender the whole district of Kumaon with all the forts.'

events.text: Battle of Makwanpur: when the Darbar balks at ratifying the treaty, Ochterlony marches on Kathmandu and defeats the Gorkhas at Makwanpur, twenty miles from the capital (February 1816).
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Nepal
events.outcome: East India Company victory; with the capital open to assault the Nepalese Darbar ratifies the Treaty of Sagauli
events.commanders: David Ochterlony — Nepalese Darbar’s commanders
events.source: HCIP VIII p. 532: 'He came up with his enemy at Makwanpur, about 20 miles from Khatmandu and succeeded in defeating them. The rapid success of Ochterlony’s operations and the consciousness that the capital now lay open to assault, induced the Nepalese Darbar to ratify the treaty.'

events.text: Nagpur's subsidiary alliance: after Raghuji II's death, Appa Saheb signs a subsidiary treaty with the Company on 27 May 1816 and accepts a British force stationed permanently in his territory.
events.source: HCIP VIII p. 248: 'Raghuji died in 1816 and soon his nephew Appa Saheb concluded a treaty of subsidiary alliance with the British ... which force shall be stationed in perpetuity in the Raja's territory'; chronology p. 843: '1816, May 27'.

events.text: The Treaty of Sugauli (Sagauli, 'Segowlee'): signed 2 December 1815 and ratified by Nepal on 4 March 1816 after Makwanpur, it ends the Anglo-Nepal war — Nepal cedes Garhwal and Kumaon west of the Kali and much of the Terai (part restored in 1816), accepts a British Resident at Kathmandu and gives up Sikkim.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 1025: 'the Anglo-Gurkha War which broke out in 1814 and was ended by the Treaty of Segowli on 4 March, 1816.' HCIP VIII p. 532: 'The treaty of Sagauli signed in March 1816 made some modification in the terms concerning the cession of the Tarai ... this cession of Garhwal and Kumaon to the west of the Kali river drove a wedge of British territory between Sikh dominion on the one side and Gurkha dominion on the other.' The first signature (2 December 1815) is web-only; the library dates only the March 1816 ratification.

events.text: Battle of Khadki (Kirkee): the Peshwa's attack on the Poona residency fails
events.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs East India Company
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Bapu Gokhale's attack on the small force at Kirkee failed with about 500 Maratha casualties to 86 British
events.source: HCIP VIII pp. 505–506: 'Bapu Gokhale with 18,000 horse, 8,000 foot and 14 guns launched an unsuccessful attack on the small force led by Captain Burr ... In the battle of Kirkee, the British losses were 86 killed and wounded as against 500 of the Marathas.'
events.commanders: Bapu Gokhale — Colonel Burr, Mountstuart Elphinstone

events.text: Battle of Mahidpur: Holkar's army is broken on the Sipra
events.belligerents: Holkar (Indore State) vs East India Company
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Malhar Rao Holkar III's army suffered a decisive defeat, followed by the Treaty of Mandasor
events.source: HCIP VIII p. 506: 'Young Malhar Rao Holkar III, his brave widowed sister Bhima Bai ... fought with desperate courage at Mahidpur on 21 December, 1817, and suffered a decisive defeat. Their artillerymen stood to their guns till they were bayonetted.'

events.text: Battle of Sitabuldi: Nagpur's Bhonsle army is checked at the twin hills
events.belligerents: Nagpur (Bhonsle) vs East India Company
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Appa Saheb's 18,000 men were defeated below the Sitabuldi hills and he surrendered on 16 December 1817
events.source: HCIP VIII p. 506: 'Appa Saheb, who had 18,000 men and 26 guns, was defeated after fierce fighting at the battle of Sitabaldi (2 miles west of the old city of Nagpur) on 27 November, 1817. He surrendered on 16 December, 1817'. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 475.

events.text: Battle of Yerwada: ten days after Khadki, General Smith crosses the Mula-Mutha at Yerwada on 15 November 1817 and defeats Bapu Gokhale. Bajirao II abandons Poona for Purandar, and the British flag goes up over the Peshwa's palace.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Maratha Empire
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Bapu Gokhale defeated and Poona abandoned by the Peshwa
events.commanders: General Lionel Smith — Bapu Gokhale
events.source: HCIP VIII p. 506: 'From Sirur General Smith arrived at Kirkee, defeated Bapu Gokhale at the battle of Yeravda on 15 November, 1817, and compelled the Peshwa to retreat to Purandhar.' Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 490: 'Smith on 15th November crossed the river at Yeravda'.

events.text: First Burmese invasion of Assam: at the invitation of the fugitive Bar Phukan Badan Chandra, Bodawpaya’s army defeats the Assamese and occupies the Ahom capital Jorhat.
events.belligerents: Konbaung (Burmese) Empire vs Ahom Kingdom
events.outcome: Konbaung victory; Jorhat occupied, Badan Chandra installed in power under Chandrakanta Singha
events.commanders: Maha Thilawa — Ruchinath Buragohain
events.source: HCIP IX p. 128: 'Badan succeeded in inducing Bodawpaya, the powerful king of Burma, to send an expedition to Assam (A. D. 1817). The Assamese troops were severely defeated by the Burmese army which occupied Jorhat, the capital of Assam.'

events.text: The Treaty of Poona (1817): on 13 June 1817 Elphinstone forces Bajirao II to hand over Trimbakji Dengle, formally dissolve the Maratha confederacy and give up his claims on Baroda.
events.source: HCIP VIII p. 503: 'The Peshwa was compelled by Elphinstone to sign the treaty of Poona on 13 June, 1817 ... The Peshwa recognised the dissolution in form and substance of the Maratha confederacy'.

events.text: The Treaty of Titalia: the Company restores to the Raja of Sikkim the lands the Gorkhas had taken west of the Tista, and Sikkim becomes a Company protectorate (February 1817).
events.source: HCIP VIII p. 532: 'A portion of the Tarai was given to the Raja of Sikkim. The Raja of Sikkim also signed a protective treaty in February 1817.' HCIP IX p. 1066: 'by a treaty concluded in 1817, restored to the Raja of Sikkim the territory that had been wrested from him by the Nepalese.'

events.text: Third Anglo-Maratha War
events.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent
events.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs East India Company
events.outcome: British victory
events.commanders: Peshwa Baji Rao II, Appa Sahib Bhonsle and Malhar Rao Holkar II / Maratha chiefs — Lord Hastings; Thomas Hislop; Mountstuart Elphinstone and British EIC commanders

events.text: Uva Rebellion: The Uva-Wellassa rising — the Kandyan chiefs rose against the British and were put down by a scorched-earth campaign. Crops, cattle, granaries and irrigation tanks were destroyed and Uva was left depopulated for generations. Keppetipola Disawe was executed in November 1818 and the guarantees of the Kandyan Convention were revoked.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: Kandyan chiefs and the Uva-Wellassa peasantry vs British Ceylon
events.commanders: Keppetipola Disawe (executed 1818)
events.outcome: Rebellion crushed; the province devastated

events.text: Bajirao II surrenders: the last Peshwa surrenders to Malcolm on 3 June 1818. The Peshwaship ends, and he is pensioned off to Bithur.
events.source: HCIP VIII p. 507: 'He surrendered to Malcolm at Mhow near Indore on 3 June, 1818. The Peshwa lost his title ... The Governor-General ... guaranteed the Peshwa a pension of eight lakhs of rupees per annum.' (Place given as Mhow in HCIP; other accounts say Dholkot near Asirgarh.)

events.text: Battle of Ashti: General Smith overtakes the fleeing Peshwa's army at Ashti in February 1818. Bapu Gokhale is killed, Bajirao II flees, and the Raja of Satara and the Peshwa's treasure fall to the British.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Maratha Empire
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Bapu Gokhale killed and the Raja of Satara taken
events.commanders: General Lionel Smith — Bapu Gokhale
events.source: HCIP VIII p. 507: 'On 20 February, 1818, Bapu Gokhale was overtaken by General Smith at Ashta and killed in a hotly contested battle.' Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 493: 'At Ashta Bapu Gokhale was overtaken by General Smith and was killed in a stiff action on 19th February 1818 ... The Raja of Satara and his party ... fell into the British hands.' The two books differ by a day (19 or 20 February).

events.text: Battle of Koregaon: a small Company force holds off the Peshwa's army on the Bhima
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Maratha Empire
events.outcome: Stalemate; strategic Company success
events.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 492: 'Staunton, taken by surprise, took cover in the village where a bitter fight raged throughout the day ... Towards evening they showed signs of exhaustion having lost about 175 men ... Bajirao, however, suddenly resumed his flight, having been apprized of General Smith's approach on his track. Staunton returned to Sirur with his wounded.'

events.text: Conquest of Multan: Misr Diwan Chand's army took the city in February 1818 and stormed the fort on 20 June after a long siege; Nawab Muzaffar Khan and two of his sons fell in the breach, and Multan passed to the Sikh Empire.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Durrani (Afghan) Empire (Nawab Muzaffar Khan of Multan)
events.outcome: Sikh Empire victory; Multan fort stormed, Muzaffar Khan killed, province annexed
events.commanders: Misr Diwan Chand, Sadhu Singh Akali, Hari Singh Nalwa — Nawab Muzaffar Khan
events.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 111: 'On 20 June, 1818, Sadhu Singh Akali, at the head of his Nihangs, rushed into one breach ... Nawab Muzaffar Khan standing in a breach with sword in hand fought hard along with his four sons in a heroic combat, and fell dead.' p. 110: 'The city of Multan fell in February, 1818.'

events.text: Jammu is given to Gulab Singh: the Dogra principality, conquered for Ranjit Singh in 1809, was assigned to Gulab Singh for a tribute of four lakhs a year — the beginning of Dogra rule in Jammu.
events.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 65: 'In 1809 Bhawani Das conquered Jammu, and it became a part of Ranjit Singh's kingdom. Jamadar Khushhal Singh was its first governor. In 1818, Jammu was assigned to Gulab Singh for an annual tribute of Rs. 4 lakhs.'

events.text: The Rajput states accept British protection: in a run of treaties from November 1817 to December 1818 — Karauli, Kota, Jodhpur, Udaipur, Bundi, Bikaner, Kishangarh, Jaipur and others — the Rajput princes acknowledged the Company's supremacy and paid it the tribute once taken by Sindhia, Holkar and Amir Khan.
events.source: Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages III p. 39: 'Karoli—9th Nov. 1817; Kotah—26th Dec. 1817; Jodhpur—6th Jan. 1818; Udaipur—13th Jan. 1818; Bundi—10th Feb. 1818; Bikaner—9th Mar. 1818; Kishangarh—2nd April 1818 ...'. Bakshi I p. 225 (Udaipur): 'The treaty was signed in Delhi on 13 January, 1818 ... By Article 3 the Rana promised to act in subordinate co-operation with the British Government and acknowledge its supremacy'; p. 295 (Jaipur): 'a tardy and ungracious assent to a treaty on 2 April, 1818.' Coordinates: Ajmer, where the Company replaced Sindhia.

events.text: The Third Anglo-Maratha War ends Maratha power; British paramountcy begins
events.source: Stewart Gordon

events.text: The Treaty of Mandasor: after Mahidpur, Malhar Rao Holkar III accepts British supremacy and a subsidiary force on 6 January 1818, and gives up his lands north of Bundi and south of the Satpuras.
events.source: HCIP VIII p. 506: 'By the subsidiary treaty of Mandasor (6 January, 1818), Malhar Rao Holkar III agreed to accept the British suzerainty, limit his troops to three thousand, maintain a British subsidiary force'.

events.text: The principality of Satara: the British set up Chhatrapati Pratap Singh, rescued at Ashti, as ruler of a small state around Satara. The treaty of 1819 formalises it.
events.source: HCIP VIII p. 507: 'Chhatrapati Pratap Singh was set up as a ruler of a small principality "as a sop to Maratha sentiment"'; HCIP IX (British Paramountcy) p. 151: 'The treaty of 1819, by which the principality of Satara was created'.

events.text: Battle of Shopian: The Battle of Shopian took place on 3 July 1819 between an expeditionary force from the Sikh Empire and Jabbar Khan, the governor of the Kashmir Valley province.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Durrani (Afghan) Empire (Jabbar Khan, governor of Kashmir)
events.outcome: Sikh Empire victory; Jabbar Khan routed twice and fled to Kabul; the Sikh army entered Srinagar on 15 July 1819 and Kashmir was annexed
events.commanders: Ranjit Singh, Misr Chand, Hari Nakwa — Jabbar Khan Barakzai, Aghar Khan
events.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V pp. 129–130: 'The Sikh army reached Shupian on 5 July, 1819. In a sharp engagement lasting for a few hours the Afghans were repulsed ... In a fierce fight Jabbar Khan was again defeated ... The Sikh Army entered Srinagar on 15 July, 1819.' (Gupta: 5 July; the row's text has 3 July.)

events.text: Burmese conquest of Manipur: when Marjit Singh, Burma’s vassal since 1812, shows independence and skips Bagyidaw’s coronation, a Burmese army occupies Manipur; Marjit flees to Cachar and the seven-year devastation of Manipur begins.
events.belligerents: Konbaung (Burmese) Empire vs Manipur (Marjit Singh)
events.outcome: Konbaung victory; Marjit expelled and Manipur occupied until 1825
events.commanders: — Marjit Singh
events.source: HCIP IX p. 1027: 'In 1812 Marjit occupied the throne of Manipur as a vassal of Burma. But in 1818-1819, when he showed signs of independence, a Burmese army occupied Manipur. Marjit fled from Manipur.' HCIP IX p. 129: 'the expulsion of the king of Manipur who had failed to attend the coronation ceremony of Bagyidaw.'

events.text: Second Burmese invasion of Assam: a Burmese army wins at Khagarjan (Nowgong), drives out Purandar Singha and Ruchinath and restores Chandrakanta Singha as a Burmese client.
events.belligerents: Konbaung (Burmese) Empire vs Ahom Kingdom (Purandar Singha, Ruchinath)
events.outcome: Konbaung victory; Chandrakanta reinstated, Purandar and Ruchinath flee to Bengal
events.commanders: Kiamingi — Purandar Singha, Ruchinath Buragohain
events.source: HCIP IX p. 129: 'A Burmese army successfully invaded Assam in 1819, and reinstated Chandrakanta on the throne. Both Ruchinath and his protege fled to Bengal.' Acharyya, History of Medieval Assam p. 27: 'the victory of the Burmese army at Khagarjan (Nowgong) in 1819.'

events.text: Siege of Asirgarh (1819): General Doveton and Malcolm take Asirgarh from Scindia's commandant Yashwant Rao Lad, who had sheltered the fugitive Appa Saheb. This is the last fortress action of the war.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Gwalior (Scindia) garrison
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Asirgarh taken on 8 April 1819
events.commanders: General Doveton, Sir John Malcolm — Yashwant Rao Lad
events.source: HCIP VIII p. 506: 'On 8 April, 1819, General Doveton, with the help of Sir John Malcolm, wrested Asirgarh from its commandant Yashwant Rao Lad.'

events.text: Battle of Mangal: The Battle of Mangal was fought between the Sikh forces led by Hari Singh Nalwa and the Jadoon, led by Muhammad Khan
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Jadoon, Tareen, Awan
events.outcome: Sikh victory
events.commanders: Hari Singh — Bostan Khan, Muhammad Awan
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Battle of Mangrol (1821): Maharao Kishore Singh of Kota, trying to recover real power from the regent Zalim Singh, was defeated in October 1821 by a British force sent to support the regent under the 1817–18 treaty; his brother Prithvi Singh was killed.
events.belligerents: East India Company, Kota (regent Zalim Singh) vs Kota (Maharao Kishore Singh)
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Kishore Singh retreats to Mewar and later submits
events.source: Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages I p. 338: 'Kishore Singh returned from Brindaban to Kotah at the head of a force; but he was defeated (October 1821) by a British force which had been sent to co-operate with the Regent. Prithvi Singh was killed.' (The book does not name the field; Mangrol is the usual name.)

events.text: Siege of Mankera (1821–1822): The Siege of Mankera, also known as the Fall of Mankera, was a military conflict from 7 December 1821 to 1 January 1822, fought by the Sikh forces led by Ranjit Singh.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire, Assisted by, Tiwanas of Mitha Tiwana vs Mankera State
events.outcome: Sikh victory
events.commanders: Ranjit Singh, Hari Singh, Khushal Singh — Hafiz Khan
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Battles of Kaliani Pathar and Assam Choky: Maha Bandula’s army of some 20,000 defeats Chandrakanta Singha on 17 April 1822 and again on 21 June 1822, and Burma annexes Assam.
events.belligerents: Konbaung (Burmese) Empire vs Ahom Kingdom (Chandrakanta Singha)
events.outcome: Konbaung victory; Chandrakanta flees to British territory — 'the end of the Ahom sovereignty in Assam'
events.commanders: Maha Bandula — Chandrakanta Singha
events.source: HCIP IX p. 130: 'A severe engagement took place at Kaliani Pathar on April 17, 1822, and though Chandrakanta fought with great valour he was defeated ... Being defeated there in another engagement on June 21, 1822, he took refuge in the British territory. The defeat of Chandrakanta on June 21, 1822, marks the end of the Ahom sovereignty in Assam.'

events.text: Akali Phula Singh dies — the Nihang leader who stormed Kasur and Multan for Ranjit Singh, killed at the battle of Nowshera.
events.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 151: 'The Sikhs also suffered heavily. Their two notable commanders, Akali Phula Singh and General Balbhadra Singh Gorkha, with about 2,000 men lost their lives.'

events.text: Battle of Nowshera: The Battle of Nowshera, also called the Battle of Tihri, Battle of Naushahra, or Battle of Pir Sabaq, was fought in March 1823 near Nowshera by the forces of Ranjit Singh.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Peshawar Sardars (Barakzai), Azim Khan's Afghans and Yusafzai tribesmen
events.outcome: Sikh victory
events.commanders: Ranjit Singh, Sher Singh, Kharak Singh — Mohammad Azim Khan, Dost Mohammad Khan, Nawab Jabbar Khan
events.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 151 ('The Battle of Tihri or Naushahra, 14 March, 1823'): 'Azim Khan was so much frightened that leaving his guns, tents and other equippage, fled to Peshawar and then to Kabul ... The Sikhs also suffered heavily. Their two notable commanders, Akali Phula Singh and General Balbhadra Singh Gorkha, with about 2,000 men lost their lives.'

events.text: Battle of Ramu: Maha Bandula, advancing from Arakan, overwhelms the Company’s detachment at Ramu in Chittagong district on 17 May 1824 — the Company’s worst defeat of the first Burmese war.
events.belligerents: Konbaung (Burmese) Empire vs East India Company
events.outcome: Konbaung victory; the British retreat 'turned out to be a veritable rout', the captain and most officers killed, and troops pulled back from Sylhet to cover Chittagong
events.commanders: Maha Bandula — Captain Noton
events.source: HCIP IX p. 102: 'On May 17, 1824, Maha Bandula attacked this post ... the British detachment had to retreat; and the retreat turned out to be a veritable rout ... the Captain and the rest were all killed.'

events.text: Dayananda Saraswati, founder of the Arya Samaj, is born
events.source: R. C. Majumdar

events.text: First Anglo-Burmese War
events.source: HCIP IX pp. 101–110: 'The British Government issued a formal declaration of war on February 24, 1824' (p. 101); 'The treaty was signed at Yandabo on February 24, 1826' (p. 107); '40,000 men passed through the cadres, 15,000 died, and the war cost £5,000,000' (p. 110).
events.belligerents: East India Company and Manipur (Gambhir Singh) vs Konbaung (Burmese) Empire
events.outcome: East India Company victory; by the Treaty of Yandabo (24 February 1826) Ava renounces Assam, Cachar and Jaintia, recognises Gambhir Singh in Manipur, cedes Arakan and Tenasserim and pays one crore — at a cost of some 15,000 Company dead, mostly of disease
events.commanders: Lord Amherst; Sir Archibald Campbell and East India Company forces — King Bagyidaw of Burma; General Maha Bandula

events.text: Zalim Singh of Kota dies — the regent who ruled Kota for half a century in the Maharao's name and kept it out of Maratha hands.
events.source: Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages I p. 340: 'Zalim Singh died in 1824. Madho Singh succeeded him "with the full power exercised by his father".' p. 338: 'But for the able management of Zalim Singh, Kotah would have long since fallen an easy prey to Sindhia and Holkar.'

events.text: Gambhir Singh recovers Manipur: with Company sanction and his own Manipur Levy, the exiled prince drives the Burmese out of Manipur and takes the capital.
events.belligerents: Manipur (Gambhir Singh) vs Konbaung (Burmese) Empire
events.outcome: Manipur victory; Burmese driven out and Gambhir Singh’s title recognised at Yandabo
events.commanders: Gambhir Singh, Nar Singh — Burmese garrison
events.source: HCIP IX p. 103: 'Gambhir Singh, who had joined the British camp with his troops, was permitted to conquer it on his own account. He did so and occupied the capital.' HCIP IX p. 1028: 'The Burmese forces were driven out of Manipur.' (Year from the course of the war: the book narrates it after the 1824 rains; web accounts give June 1825.)

events.text: Maha Bandula dies — The Burmese general who conquered Assam (1822) and won at Ramu (1824), killed by a rocket defending Danubyu on 1 April 1825.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 105: 'on April 1, 1825, attacked the enemy’s position. The Burmese General Maha Bandula was killed by a rocket and that was the signal for the general retreat of the Burmese.'

events.text: Battle of Akora Khattak: The Battle of Akora Khattak was the first significant clash between the Mujahidin movement led by Syed Ahmad Barelvi and the Sikh Empire.
events.belligerents: Mujahideen vs Sikh Empire
events.commanders: Syed Ahmad, Khadi Khan, Baqar Ali — Budh Singh, Atar Singh
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Siege of Bharatpur (1825–26): to unseat the usurper Durjan Sal and erase the memory of Lake's failure, Combermere breaches the 'impregnable' Jat fortress with mines and storms it.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Bharatpur (Durjan Sal)
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Bharatpur stormed, Durjan Sal deposed and the minor Balwant Singh installed
events.commanders: Lord Combermere, Sir Charles Metcalfe — Durjan Sal
events.source: HCIP IX (British Paramountcy) p. 30-31: 'The General reached Bharatpur on December 10, and after a breach was effected by bombardment from the artillery and by laying undergound mines, the fort of Bharatpur was taken by assault on December 18, 1825. The failure of Lord Lake in 1805 was thus avenged.'; HCIP IX chronology p. 1186 lists 'Fall of Bharatpur' under 1826. DATE CONFLICT: HCIP body says 18 Dec 1825; the storm is generally dated 18 January 1826 — year kept at 1826 per the chronology

events.text: The Treaty of Yandabo: signed 24 February 1826 within sixty miles of Ava, it ends the first Anglo-Burmese war — Burma renounces Assam, Cachar and Jaintia, recognises Gambhir Singh in Manipur, cedes Arakan and Tenasserim and pays one crore.
events.source: HCIP IX pp. 107–108: 'The treaty was signed at Yandabo on February 24, 1826 ... provided for the abrogation of all claims on the part of the Burmese king to Assam, Cachar, and Jaintia. As regards Manipur, it was agreed that should Gambhir Singh desire to return to that country, he should be recognised as its ruler ... The indemnity was fixed at one crore of Rupees.'

events.text: Battle of Shaidu: The Battle of Shaidu, also known as the Battle of Pirpai, was fought in March 1827 between the Sikh forces led by Hari Singh Nalwa and the Mujahideen troops.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Mujahideen
events.outcome: Sikh victory
events.commanders: Budh Singh — Syed Ahmad
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Battle of Haidru (1828): The Battle of Haidru, also called Battle of Attock, was fought in 1828 by the Sikh forces led by Hari Singh Nalwa and the Mujahideen forces led by Syed Ahmad Barelvi.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Mujahideen
events.outcome: Sikh victory
events.commanders: Hari Singh — Syed Ahmad
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Rani Lakshmibai is born — At Varanasi, as Manikarnika.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Kittur Chennamma dies — In prison at Bailhongal, five years after her rising against the Company.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: The Khasi rising of U Tirot Singh: the Khasi chiefs, resenting the Company’s road through their hills, massacre the post at Nongkhlaw on 5 May 1829 and fight a four-year guerrilla war from the hills.
events.belligerents: Khasi States (U Tirot Singh of Nongkhlaw, Bar Manik) vs East India Company
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Tirot Singh surrenders in January 1833 on promise of his life
events.commanders: David Scott — U Tirot Singh, Bar Manik
events.source: HCIP IX pp. 453: 'On 5 May, 1829, a strong party of Khasis, aided by the Garos, raided Nunklow and massacred the European and Bengali inmates ... The long and harassing warfare with the Khasis continued for four years ... Tirut Singh surrendered in January, 1833, on condition that his life should be spared.'

events.text: Battle of Balakot: The Battle of Balakot was the final battle fought between the Sikh forces under prince Sher Singh and mujahideen under Syed Ahmad Barelvi at Balakot on 6 May 1831.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Mujahideen
events.outcome: Sikh victory
events.commanders: Sher Singh, Akali Singh — Syed Ahmad, Shah Dehlvi, Mirza Dehlvi
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: The Company takes over Mysore: after the Nagar rising, Bentinck (7 September 1831) removes Krishnaraja Wodeyar III from power and puts the whole state under British Commissioners — an act he later admitted went beyond the 1799 treaty.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 38: 'On September 7, 1831, Bentinck ... transferred the entire administration of the country into the hands of British officers'; p. 40: Bentinck 'could not help entertaining doubts, both as to the legality and the justice of the course that has been pursued.'

events.text: The Kol rising: the Mundas of Chota Nagpur, joined by the Hos, rise against revenue-farmers from outside and the new Bengal regulations; the revolt spreads over Ranchi, Hazaribagh, Palamau and Manbhum and about a thousand settlers are killed.
events.belligerents: Kols (Mundas and Hos) of Chota Nagpur vs East India Company
events.outcome: East India Company victory; suppressed in March 1832 after extensive operations — Buddho Bhagat died defending his village with 150 followers
events.commanders: Captain Wilkinson — Buddho Bhagat, Sindrai Manki
events.source: HCIP IX p. 455: 'when the Mundas of Chota Nagpur broke out into revolt in 1831, the Hos joined them ... After extensive military operations the insurrection was suppressed in March, 1832 ... one, Buddho Bhagat, rather than surrender, perished with his whole family and 150 followers in defending his village.'

events.text: Annexation of Cachar: after Raja Govinda Chandra is assassinated (24 April 1830) — a murder the Company traced to Gambhir Singh of Manipur — the Company refuses every claimant and annexes the Kachari kingdom of the plains.
events.source: HCIP IX pp. 136–137: 'Govinda Chandra was assassinated on April 24, 1830 ... Having thus disposed of all the claims the British Government annexed Cachar.' Year 1832 (proclamation of 14 August 1832) is web-only; the book gives no year.

events.text: The Bhumij rising of Ganganarayan: a disappointed claimant to Barabhum kills the diwan, sacks Barabazar and, with Chuar and Bhumij levies, drives the government force back to Bankura in June 1832.
events.belligerents: Bhumij and Chuars (Ganganarayan) vs East India Company
events.outcome: East India Company victory; troops scour the country late in 1832 and Ganganarayan’s death ends the rising
events.commanders: — Ganganarayan Singh
events.source: HCIP IX pp. 455–456: 'in the first week of June, 1832, government force had to retire to Bankura leaving Barabhum to the possession of the rebel chief. Ganganarayan assumed the title of raja ... the death of Ganganarayan, shortly after, put an end to the insurrection.'

events.text: Capture of Peshawar (1834): The city of Peshawar was formally annexed on 6 May 1834 by the Sikh Empire.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Peshawar Sardars (Barakzai)
events.outcome: Sikh Empire victory; Sultan Muhammad Khan fled to Kabul and Peshawar came under direct Sikh rule, Hari Singh Nalwa governor (May 1834)
events.commanders: Hari Singh, Ranjit Singh, Mahan Singh — Sultan Mohammad Khan
events.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 174: 'Prince Nau Nihal Singh, Ventura and Court were sent from Lahore to Peshawar ... Sultan Muhammad Khan fled away to Kabul ... The Maharaja established his own administration at Peshawar in May, 1834, and appointed Hari Singh Nalwa its governor.'

events.text: Coorg War: after a quarrel over fugitives and a detained envoy, four Company columns invade Coorg; Madikeri falls on 6 April 1834, Coorg is annexed five days later and Chikka Virarajendra goes into exile.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Kingdom of Coorg
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Coorg annexed (April 1834)
events.commanders: Lord William Bentinck (four Company columns) — Chikka Virarajendra (Viraraja the Younger)
events.source: HCIP IX p. 43: 'On April 6, the British force entered the capital of Coorg, Madikeri or Mercara, and five days later Coorg was annexed to the British dominions by a formal Proclamation. The Raja, Viraraja the Younger, surrendered with his family on April 23.'

events.text: Dogra conquest of Ladakh: Zorawar Singh, Gulab Singh's governor of Kishtwar, marched through the Suru valley, beat the Ladakhis and forced the Gyalpo to pay a war indemnity and tribute; a Dogra fort was built outside Leh.
events.belligerents: Dogra J&K (Sikh Empire) vs Ladakh (Namgyal)
events.outcome: Dogra victory; the Gyalpo pays Rs 50,000 and an annual tribute of Rs 20,000, Ladakh annexed to Jammu
events.commanders: Zorawar Singh Kahluria, Mehta Basti Ram — the Gyalpo of Ladakh
events.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 195: 'Zorawar Singh at the head of troops marched from Kishtwar ... The advance guard under Mehta Basti Ram fought against the Ladakhis ... Eventually Gyalpo agreed to pay Rs. 50,000 as the cost of war and an annual tribute of Rs. 20,000. A fort was built outside the city of Leh.'

events.text: Gambhir Singh dies — The Manipuri prince who drove the Burmese out of Manipur in the first Burmese war and ruled it as an ally of the Company.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 1029: 'Gambhir Singh died in 1834, leaving a son, Chandrakirti, only two years old.'

events.text: Standoff at the Khyber Pass (1834–1835): The Standoff at the Khyber Pass (1834–1835) was a short conflict from May 1834 to May 1835 between the Sikh forces led by Maharaja Ranjit Singh and the Afghan forces.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire, Peshawar Sardars vs Emirate of Kabul
events.outcome: Inconclusive
events.commanders: Ranjit Singh Hari Singh Gulab Singh Dhian Singh Lehna Singh Tej Singh Jean Allard Paolo Avitabile Josiah Harlan Jean Ventura Faqir Azizuddin Claude Court Attar Singh Khushal Singh Misr Raj Jawala Singh Sultan Khan — Dost Khan, Wazir Khan, Abdul Khan
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: The Kabaw valley returned to Burma: the Company awards the Shan valley Gambhir Singh had occupied in the war to Ava and pays Manipur Rs 500 a month in compensation.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 1029: 'the Kubo valley was transferred to Burma in 1834. The Government of India, conscious of the just claims of Gambhir Singh which had to be sacrificed for placating Burma, agreed to pay Rs. 500 per month to Manipur State as compensation.'

events.text: Annexation of Jaintia: on the pretext of human sacrifices at Gobha, the Company confiscates Raja Rajendra Singh’s plains (proclamation of 15 March 1835); he gives up the hills, and the Court of Directors condemns the act but does not reverse it.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 139: 'On March 15, 1835, Jaintia Pargana was formally annexed to the British dominion by a formal proclamation, and Gobha was annexed a few weeks later. Rajendra Singh thereupon voluntarily gave up the hilly tracts of his dominion.'

events.text: Battle of Ramkani: The Battle of Ramkani was fought on 4 May 1835 by the Sikh forces led by Maharaja Ranjit Singh and Barakzai forces including Ghazis.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Barakzais, Assisted by Ghazis
events.outcome: Sikh victory Afghan withdrawal
events.commanders: Ranjit Singh, Misr Raj — Unknown
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Darjeeling ceded: the Raja of Sikkim is induced to grant the Darjeeling tract to the Company unconditionally by a Deed of Grant (February 1835).
events.source: HCIP IX p. 1066: 'This was effected about a decade later in February, 1835, when the Raja of Sikkim was induced to cede unconditionally the Darjeeling tract under a Deed of Grant.'

events.text: Battle of Panjtar: The Battle of Panjtar was fought in November 1836 as part of the Afghan–Sikh Wars.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Panjtar Pashtuns
events.outcome: Afghan Victory
events.commanders: Hari Singh, Zorawar Singh — Fateh Khan
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Ramakrishna is born — At Kamarpukur in Hooghly.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: The Mappila outbreaks: twenty-two violent outbreaks in Ernad and Valluvanad against Hindu landlords and the Company's order; in 1855 the Malabar District Magistrate H. V. Conolly is murdered at Calicut.
events.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 280: 'Twenty-two such riots were reported from different parts of Malabar, particularly the Ernad and Valluvanad taluks, during the period 1836-1856'; p. 281: 'in 1855 H.V. Connolly, the District Magistrate of Malabar, was murdered by four Mappila convicts in his bungalow at Calicut.'

events.text: Battle of Jamrud: The Battle of Jamrud was fought between the forces of the Emirate of Afghanistan under Wazir Akbar Khan, and the Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh on 30 April 1837.
events.belligerents: Emirate of Kabul (Barakzai) vs Sikh Empire
events.outcome: Inconclusive — books disagree: the Afghans won the first day's fighting and killed Hari Singh Nalwa, but withdrew to Jalalabad without taking Jamrud or Peshawar
events.commanders: Akbar Khan, Afzal Khan, Shams Khan — Hari Singh, Mahan Singh, Mangal Singh
events.source: Books disagree. HCIP IX p. 165: 'He sent an army under his two sons who defeated the Sikh army at Jamrud (A.D. 1837), but did not follow up their victory.' HCIP IX p. 245: 'The Afghans, after watching for five or six days, finally retired, without achieving any conspicuous success.' Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 181: 'the Afghans hurriedly retired to Jalalabad ... The two sides lost heavily, about 7,000 men'; p. 308: 'Hari Singh Nalwa was killed, but neither Jamrud fort nor Peshawar was taken.'

events.text: Hari Singh Nalwa dies — Ranjit Singh's great frontier general, governor of Hazara and Peshawar, mortally wounded at Jamrud.
events.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 180: 'Hari Singh Nalwa rallied his men and rode to the front. He was struck by two balls, one in the stomach and the other in the side ... Hari Singh then expired.' p. 153: 'Hari Singh Nalwa who was killed on 30 April, 1837, in the battle of Jamrud.'

events.text: Siege of Herat
events.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent
events.belligerents: Emirate of Herat, East India Company, British Empire and allied tribes/khanates vs Qajar Iran supported by Russian Empire and Qandahar
events.outcome: Company victory
events.commanders: Kamran Shah Durrani of Herat; British agent Eldred Pottinger and allied defenders — Mohammad Shah Qajar of Iran; Russian advisers/support; Qandahar allies

events.text: End of the Ahom kingdom: Purandar Singha, installed by the Company as ruler of Upper Assam on 2 March 1833 and reduced to a jagirdar that June, is deposed in October 1838 and Upper Assam annexed.
events.source: HCIP IX pp. 134–135: 'a treaty was concluded on March 2, 1833, at Gauhati by which Purandar Singh became the ruler of Upper Assam ... So Purandar Singh was formally dethroned or discharged from his Jagir in October 1838, and retired on a pension of Rs. 1,000 a month.'

events.text: The Tripartite Treaty: the Company, Ranjit Singh and Shah Shuja agreed to restore Shah Shuja at Kabul, with Ranjit Singh to support him with money and material; the Army of the Indus then marched from Firozpur through Bahawalpur, Sindh and the Bolan — the Indian side of the First Anglo-Afghan War.
events.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V pp. 304–305: 'In July, 1838, a Tripartite Treaty was made between Shah Shuja-ul-Mulk, Ranjit Singh and the British Government. Shah Shuja was to be placed on the throne at Kabul by the British army. Ranjit Singh was to support Shah Shuja with money and material. The British army marched from Firozpur via Bahawalpur, Shikarpur, Quetta, Kandhar and Ghazni to Kabul.' Also p. 288: 'Ranjit Singh did not like it because it was mainly aimed against him.'

events.text: Annexation of Matak: when Bar Senapati’s heirs refuse a tribute and the separation of Moran, the Company annexes the Moamaria (Matak) chiefdom to Lakhimpur district in November 1839.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 142: 'This was strenuously opposed not only by Maju Gohain but all the other brothers ... So the British Government annexed Matak to the Lakhimpur district in November, 1839.'

events.text: Battle of Kalat: The storming of Kalat — a British column takes the Khanate capital; Mehrab Khan dies defending it
events.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Kalat (Khanate)
events.outcome: Company victory — a puppet khan installed

events.text: First Anglo-Afghan War
events.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Emirate of Afghanistan
events.outcome: Afghan victory
events.commanders: Lord Auckland; Shah Shuja Durrani; William Elphinstone and British/EIC commanders — Dost Mohammad Khan and Wazir Akbar Khan of Afghanistan

events.text: First Opium War
events.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent
events.belligerents: Great Britain / East India Company vs Qing dynasty
events.outcome: Company victory
events.commanders: Queen Victoria's Britain; Charles Elliot and British/EIC commanders — Daoguang Emperor; Lin Zexu and Qing officials

events.text: Pratap Singh of Satara deposed: the Raja refuses to sign an admission of treason, is dethroned on 5 September 1839 and exiled to Banaras. His brother Appa Sahib replaces him.
events.source: HCIP IX (British Paramountcy) p. 157: 'the Raja refused to sign the memorandum. He was dethroned on September 5, 1839, and deported to Banaras, where he died in A.D. 1847.' p. 24 calls the charges 'allegations, which appear to be unfounded to a very large extent'.

events.text: Ranjit Singh dies — At Lahore on 27 June 1839, after years of illness following a stroke in 1834; the Sikh empire outlived him by ten years.
events.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 534: '27 June, 1839. On Thursday morning, 27 June ... The soul flew out of his body through the eyes at 5 p.m.' HCIP IX p. 249: 'Ranjit Singh died on June 27, 1839, and was succeeded by Kharak Singh, his eldest son.'

events.text: The Amirs of Sindh accept a subsidiary force: to open the road for the Army of the Indus, Khairpur became a protected state (treaty ratified 10 January 1839); Sir John Keane marched on Hyderabad, Karachi was seized, and the Hyderabad Amirs signed away Karachi on 3 February and took a subsidiary force on 11 March 1839.
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 207: 'A treaty was concluded with the Khairpur State on December 24, 1838, and ratified by the Governor-General on January 10, 1839, by which it became a protected State'; p. 208: 'the recalcitrant Amirs who signed a treaty on February 3, 1839, surrendering Karachi (fort and town), and another on March 11, 1839, agreeing to receive a subsidiary force, not exceeding 5,000 men, and pay three lakhs yearly.'

events.text: The Khamti rising at Sadiya: the Khamtis surprise the Company’s post at Sadiya, destroy its garrison and kill Political Agent Major White; the Singphos rise alongside them.
events.belligerents: Khamtis (and Singphos) vs East India Company
events.outcome: East India Company victory; order restored with the Matak chief’s help, the Khamtis withdraw to the Mishmi hills and the last surrender in December 1843
events.commanders: — Khamti chiefs
events.source: HCIP IX p. 141: 'They suddenly attacked Sadiya, destroyed the British regiment stationed there, and burnt the barracks. Major White himself was killed in action. With the help of the Matak Chief, order was restored ... The rising was not however put down till December 1843.' (p. 454 dates the Singpho rising 1839 and calls White 'Col.')

events.text: Kharak Singh dies — Ranjit Singh's eldest son and successor, dead after little more than a year on the throne.
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 250: 'Kharak Singh died on 5 November, 1840.'

events.text: Nau Nihal Singh dies — Ranjit Singh's grandson and the real power under Kharak Singh, killed by a falling gateway returning from his father's cremation, the same day; the Jammu Rajas were widely suspected.
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 250: 'Nao Nihal Singh duly performed the funeral rites of his father, but on his way back, while passing under a covered gateway, a portion of the structure fell down and caused his death. Although positive evidence was lacking, it was generally believed that Nao Nihal's death was due to a deliberate conspiracy on the part of the Rajas of Jammu.'

events.text: Dogra–Tibetan war: The Dogra–Tibetan war, also called the Sino–Sikh war, was fought from May 1841 to August 1842 by the Dogra-led Kingdom of Jammu, a federal subject of the Sikh Empire.
events.belligerents: Qing dynasty Tibet vs Sikh Empire Dogra dynasty
events.outcome: Inconclusive — status quo ante; Ladakh confirmed under the Dogras by the Treaty of Chushul
events.commanders: Khedrup Gyatso Palden Nyima Minister Pellhün General Pi-Hsi Banka Kahloon Bazgoo Kahloon Moru Tadsi General Mandal General Ragasha — Sher Singh Gulab Singh Zorawar Singh Hari Chand Wazir Lakhpat Jawahir Singh Basti Ram
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: The Assam Duars annexed: Auckland takes over the seven Bhutan-held passes on the Assam frontier, paying Bhutan Rs 10,000 a year in compensation.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 1022: 'Lord Auckland, the Governor-General of India, authorized the annexation of the Assam Duars in 1841 on payment of Rs. 10,000 per annum to the Bhutan Government as compensation.'

events.text: Zorawar Singh dies — Gulab Singh's general, conqueror of Ladakh and Baltistan, killed in western Tibet when Tibetan and Chinese troops surrounded his army.
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 1060: 'before Zorawar Singh could retrace his steps he was surrounded by 10,000 Tibetan and 2,000 Chinese soldiers. Zorawar Singh had about 2,500 soldiers, but he died fighting on 12 December, 1841.' (Coordinates approximate, near Taklakot.)

events.text: Battle of Chushul: The Battle of Chushul was one of the major engagements of the Dogra–Tibetan war fought between the Dogra dynasty against the Tibetans under the Qing dynasty.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire Dogra dynasty vs Qing dynasty Tibet
events.outcome: Tibetan attack on Ladakh repulsed by Rajputs Dogra dynasty annexes Ladakh
events.commanders: Gulab Singh, Jawahar Singh, Wazir Lakhpat — Gen. Ragasha
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Pollock forces the Khyber: after waiting two months at Peshawar, General Pollock marched through the Khyber in early April 1842, with Sikh help in carrying the pass, and relieved Jalalabad on 16 April.
events.belligerents: East India Company, Sikh Empire vs Emirate of Kabul (Afridi and Afghan forces)
events.outcome: East India Company victory; the pass carried and Jalalabad relieved
events.commanders: George Pollock — Afridi tribesmen
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 196: 'It was not till the beginning of April that he could commence his march through the Khyber Pass towards Jalalabad, and relieve that garrison on April 16.' p. 249: 'when they again proceeded to Kabul, under General Pollock ... the Sikh army offered valuable aid in carrying the Khyber Pass.'

events.text: Repulse at the Khyber: Brigadier Wild, trying to force the Khyber to relieve Jalalabad, was beaten at the mouth of the pass on 19 January 1842; he fell back on Jamrud and Ali Masjid fell to the Afghans.
events.belligerents: Emirate of Kabul (Afridi and Afghan forces) vs East India Company
events.outcome: Afghan victory; Wild falls back on Jamrud, Ali Masjid lost
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 196: 'Wild advanced to the Pass, but was decisively defeated on January 19, at the entrance of the Pass, as his sepoys had no heart in the fight. He fell back on Jamrud, and Ali Masjid fell into the hands of the Afghans.'

events.text: Battle of Dubba (Hyderabad): Napier beats Sher Muhammad of Mirpur, the last Talpur Amir still in the field, six miles from Hyderabad on 24 March 1843; Mirpur and Umarkot fall and Sindh is annexed.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Sindh (Talpur Amirs)
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Mirpur taken 27 March, Umarkot soon after; Sindh annexed (notification of 5 March 1843)
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 214: 'Napier marched against him and defeated him at Dabo, six miles from Hyderabad, on March 24, 1843 ... Mirpur was taken on March 27, and Amarkot fell shortly after ... Already, on March 5, the annexation of Sindh had been virtually proclaimed by a notification.'

events.text: Battle of Maharajpore: Gwalior's army is defeated in a single afternoon
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Gwalior (Scindia)
events.outcome: Company victory
events.source: HCIP IX (British Paramountcy) p. 231-232: 'on 29 December, the British troops, under the Commander-in-Chief, Hugh Gough, came into clash with the Gwalior troops... they unexpectedly met with the enemy troops at Maharajpur... though the Maratha troops fought with courage, they were dislodged... The British army gained a complete victory but suffered heavy losses'

events.text: Battle of Miani: Napier defeats the Talpur Amirs and conquers Sindh
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Sindh (Talpur Amirs)
events.outcome: East India Company victory; about 6,000 Baluchis and 275 British killed; six Amirs surrender and Hyderabad is occupied on 20 February
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 214: 'He marched with his army of 2,800 and defeated the enemy after a severely contested battle on February 17, 1843 ... The casualties were 275 British and 6,000 Baluchis. Six of the Amirs now surrendered as prisoners of war and Hyderabad was occupied on the 20th.'

events.text: Battle of Punniar: on the same day as Maharajpur (29 December 1843), Grey's wing of the Gwalior expedition defeats a second Gwalior army at Punniar south-west of Gwalior.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Gwalior (Scindia)
events.outcome: East India Company victory; a large body of Gwalior troops defeated
events.commanders: Maj.-Gen. John Grey — Gwalior darbar's army
events.source: HCIP IX p. 232: 'On the same day, another wing of the British army defeated a large body of Gwalior troops near Punniar... It seems to be certain, however, that the British army took the aggressive and attacked the Maratha force without any formal declaration of war on either side.'

events.text: Maharaja Sher Singh is murdered — with his son Pratap Singh and the minister Dhian Singh, by the Sandhanwalia sardars; the Lahore state slid into army rule.
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 262: 'on September 15, 1843, Sher Singh, his son Pratap Singh, as well as the Prime Minister Dhian Singh were all murdered by the Sandhanwalia Sardars, Attar Singh and his nephew Ajit Singh.'

events.text: Battle of Ferozeshah: The Battle of Ferozeshah was fought on 21 December and 22 December 1845 between the British East India Company and the Sikh Empire, at the village of Ferozeshah in Punjab.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs East India Company
events.outcome: British victory
events.commanders: Lal Singh, Tej Singh — Hugh Gough, Henry Hardinge
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Battle of Mudki: the first clash of the First Anglo-Sikh War
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Sikh Empire
events.outcome: Company victory
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 49: 'the four successive battles of Mudki (December 18, 1845), Firozshah (December 21-22), Aliwal (January 28, 1846) and Sobraon (February 10, 1846)'; p. 270: 'After the battle had begun, Lal Singh, according to plan, deserted the army ... the Sikh force was repulsed.'

events.text: First Anglo-Sikh War
events.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs East India Company and Patiala
events.outcome: Company victory
events.commanders: Sikh Empire under Maharaja Duleep Singh's regency; Rani Jind Kaur; generals Lal Singh and Tej Singh — Governor-General Henry Hardinge; Hugh Gough; East India Company and Patiala allies

events.text: Battle of Aliwal: Harry Smith's "battle without a mistake" on the Sutlej
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Sikh Empire
events.outcome: Company victory
events.source: Curated sweep (Sarkar; Majumdar; Schwartzberg)

events.text: Battle of Baddowal: The battle of Baddowal was an engagement between the Sikh Khalsa Army and British forces which occurred on 21 January 1846 during the First Anglo-Sikh War.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs East India Company
events.commanders: Ranjodh Singh — Harry Smith
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 271: 'Sir Harry Smith, while proceeding to relieve Ludhiana, was surprised at Baddowal (January 21, 1846). His losses in men were very heavy, and even his baggage and hospital stores were captured by the Sikhs. He was saved by the timely arrival of a British detachment.'
events.outcome: Sikh Empire victory; Harry Smith surprised on the march to Ludhiana, with heavy losses and his baggage and hospital stores captured

events.text: Battle of Sobraon: The Battle of Sobraon was fought on 10 February 1846, between the forces of the East India Company and the Sikh Khalsa Army.
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs British Empire, East India Company
events.outcome: British victory
events.commanders: Tej Singh, Lal Singh, Sham Singh — Sir Hugh Gough, Henry Hardinge, Robert Dick
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Jang Bahadur Kunwar becomes Prime Minister of Nepal, founding the Rana ascendancy that turned Nepal into a firm British ally.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 1025: 'The British relations with Nepal were still further improved when Jang Bahadur became the Prime Minister in 1846. He was by far the most remarkable Prime Minister of Nepal.' (The Kot massacre of September 1846 that brought him to power is web-only.)

events.text: The Khond rising: the Khonds of Gumsur and the Khondmals, fearing for their lands, rise against the Company’s campaign against Meriah sacrifice and hold out in the hills for three years under Chakra Bisayi.
events.belligerents: Khonds (Chakra Bisayi) vs East India Company
events.outcome: East India Company victory; suppressed in 1848 and the exiled Khond chief recalled, though Chakra Bisayi fought on to 1855
events.commanders: John Campbell, Samuel Macpherson — Chakra Bisayi
events.source: HCIP IX p. 456: 'made the Khonds to break into an open rebellion in 1846 ... the Khonds, undaunted by defeat, held out in the depths of their highland lairs. When, in 1848, the rebellion was suppressed, the exiled Khond Chief was recalled and placed at the head of Khonds.'

events.text: The Treaty of Amritsar (16 March 1846): the Company made over Kashmir and the hill country to Gulab Singh of Jammu as an independent Maharaja, for cash — the founding charter of the Dogra state of Jammu and Kashmir.
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 273: 'Gulab Singh got his promised reward of sovereignty over Kashmir and Jammu on payment of fifty lakhs in cash ... A treaty was concluded on March 16, 1846, recognizing Maharaja Gulab Singh independent sovereign of Kashmir.'

events.text: The Treaty of Bhyrowal (16 December 1846): a British Resident at Lahore was given 'full authority to direct and control all matters in every department of the State' during Dalip Singh's minority, with a Council of Regency and a British garrison — the Punjab in all but name a protectorate.
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 275: 'the Treaty of Bhyrowal was signed on the following day, December 16, 1846. This treaty provided that "a British officer ... shall be appointed by the Governor-General to remain at Lahore, which officer shall have full authority to direct and control all matters in every department of the State."'

events.text: The Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846): ending the first Anglo-Sikh war, the Lahore state ceded the Jullundur Doab and everything south of the Sutlej, gave up the hill country between the Beas and the Indus in lieu of indemnity, cut its army and surrendered its war guns; Dalip Singh kept the throne.
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 272: 'On March 9 a treaty was concluded at Lahore ... The British annexed the Jullundur Doab to their dominions ... they took possession of the entire hill country between the Beas and the Indus, to be alienated to Gulab Singh'; p. 49: 'The Sikh Government had to cede the Jalandar doab between the Beas and the Sutlej and all the territories lying to the south of the last-named river.'

events.text: Battle of Ramnagar: Sikh cavalry checks Gough on the Chenab
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs East India Company
events.outcome: Sikh Empire victory; Gough's attack on the Sikh detachments at Nawala near Ramnagar was beaten off with heavy British loss (22 November 1848)
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 285: 'a few small scattered groups were on the left bank, at Nawala near Ramnagar. Lord Gough sent troops to drive these Sikhs, but the British suffered defeat with a heavy loss of life (November 22).'

events.text: Matale Rebellion: a peasant rising against new taxes, crushed within weeks under martial law. Puran Appu was executed on 8 August. The severity of the repression caused a parliamentary inquiry in London and the recall of the governor.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: Peasant rebels under Gongalegoda Banda and Puran Appu vs British Ceylon
events.outcome: Suppressed; the governor recalled after a parliamentary inquiry

events.text: Satara annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse: Raja Appa Sahib dies on 5 April 1848 with only an adopted son. Dalhousie's council, upheld by the Court of Directors, sets the adoption aside and annexes the state.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 68: 'when Appa Sahib, the Raja of Satara, died on April 5, 1848'; p. 65: 'He had no male issue, but adopted a son without the previous consent of the British Government ... Satara was accordingly annexed and the claim of adopted son set aside.' (The annexation took effect in 1848–49 after the reference to London.)

events.text: Second Anglo-Sikh War
events.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs East India Company
events.outcome: Company victory
events.commanders: Sikh Empire forces under Sher Singh Attariwala and Chattar Singh; nominally Duleep Singh — Lord Dalhousie; Hugh Gough and East India Company forces

events.text: Siege of Multan: Mulraj's revolt ignites the Second Anglo-Sikh War
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Multan (Diwan Mulraj) and Sikh rebels
events.outcome: East India Company victory; the city carried by assault on 2 January 1849 and Mulraj surrendered on 22 January
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy pp. 277–278 (murder of Agnew and Anderson at Multan, April 1848) and p. 286: 'the city was carried by assault on January 2, 1849, and Mulraj unconditionally surrendered on January 22.'

events.text: Annexation of the Punjab: after Gujrat and the Sikh army's surrender at Rawalpindi (12 March), Dalhousie's treaty of 29 March 1849 made Dalip Singh resign the sovereignty of the Punjab for a pension; the Sikh Empire ended.
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 287: '... March 29, 1849, and ratified by the Governor-General on April 5. By this treaty Dalip Singh resigned the sovereignty of the Panjab and the British agreed to give him a pension between four and five lakhs of Rupees a year.' p. 286: 'On March 12, 1849, there was a general surrender of the Sikhs ... The Sikh army ceased to exist.'

events.text: Battle of Chillianwala: the Sikhs maul the Company army in one of its hardest-fought battles
events.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs East India Company
events.outcome: Inconclusive — the British lost 2,446 men and the colours of three regiments; some count it a British victory, others a defeat, many a drawn battle
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 285: 'When night fell the British had lost 2,446 men and the colours of three regiments ... The result of the battle of Chilianwala has been estimated in various ways. Some regard it as a victory of the British; others, including many Englishmen, look upon it as a defeat; while many describe it as a drawn battle.'

events.text: Battle of Gujrat: the Khalsa army is destroyed; Punjab is annexed
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Sikh Empire
events.outcome: East India Company victory; the Sikh army routed and pursued fifteen miles (21 February 1849); general surrender on 12 March
events.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 286: 'a pitched battle was fought on February 21, 1849. The Sikh army was defeated and completely routed, and the British cavalry pursued them for fifteen miles. On March 12, 1849, there was a general surrender of the Sikhs.'

events.text: Annexation of the Sikkim Terai: after Campbell and Hooker are seized in Sikkim (November 1849), Dalhousie annexes the Morang (Terai) and the Darjeeling hills west of the Tista — about 1,670 square miles — and stops the Raja’s allowance.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 1068: 'Lord Dalhousie took very strong measures against the Raja and annexed the hill tracts of Darjeeling west of the Tista and the Murung (Terai) district. The Raja’s allowance was also stopped.' HCIP IX p. 90: 'an outlying tract of Sikkim, about 1670 sq. miles in area, was added to British India'; p. 47: 'partly by a military expedition in 1850.'

events.text: Bajirao II dies — the last Peshwa, at Bithur after thirty-three years on a British pension.
events.source: HCIP VIII p. 507: 'Baji Rao II was allowed to live at Bithur, 12 miles north-west of Kanpur, for more than thirty years in splendid isolation till his death on 14 January, 1851.'

events.text: Second Anglo-Burmese War
events.source: HCIP IX p. 126: 'the Commissioner-designate of Pegu, issued a proclamation on December 19, 1852, annexing Pegu.'
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Konbaung (Burmese) Empire
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Pegu annexed by proclamation of December 1852
events.commanders: Lord Dalhousie; Commodore Lambert; General Henry Godwin and East India Company forces — King Pagan Min of Burma

events.text: The Nizam assigns Berar: by the treaty of 21 May 1853, the Nizam hands Berar, the Raichur doab and other districts to British management to pay for the Hyderabad Contingent.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 86: 'A new treaty was concluded with the Nizam On May 21, 1853 ... the Nizam assigned the fertile districts of Berar, the cotton garden of Hindustan, the Raichur doab ... to the exclusive management of the British'; p. 647: 'the Nizam who was compelled to cede Berar by force and fraud in 1853'.
Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)
events.text: The first railway: On 16 April the first train in India runs the thirty-four kilometres from Bori Bunder to Thane, three engines and fourteen carriages, four hundred passengers.
Annexation of Jhansi: Raja Gangadhar Rao dies on 21 November 1853 after adopting a son; Dalhousie refuses to recognise the adoption and annexes Jhansi by lapse, setting aside Rani Lakshmibai.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 65: '2. Jhansi. Gangadhar Rao, Raja of Jhansi, died on November 20, 1853. On November 19, he decided to adopt a son'; HCIP IX chronology p. 1187: '1854 Annexation of Jhansi.'

events.text: Annexation of North Cachar: Tularam’s hill kingdom, left to him in 1834 and kept by his sons after his death in 1851, is annexed when Nakulram attacks a Naga village without Company consent.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 138: 'The act of Nakulram was a violation of article 7 of the treaty whereby he had agreed not to make war without the consent of the British. Accordingly, the country was formally annexed to the British dominions in 1854.'

events.text: Nagpur annexed: Raghuji III dies in 1853 without a natural or adopted heir. Dalhousie's minute of 28 January 1854 treats Nagpur as a British grant, and the state lapses to the Company.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 67: 'The Raja of Nagpur died in 1853. He had no male heir and did not actually adopt any son'; p. 70: Dalhousie's 'minute, dated January 28, 1854, in which he proved, to his own satisfaction, that Nagpur was a dependent State'. De Brett, Central Provinces Gazetteer (Chhattisgarh Feudatory States), block 148 of the archive.org text: 'In 1854 the Nagpur Raj lapsed'. HCIP VIII chronology p. 844 puts the annexation in 1853.

events.text: The Carnatic and Tanjore titles extinguished: when Nawab Muhammad Ghaus dies childless (17 October) and Raja Shivaji of Tanjore dies leaving only daughters (29 October 1855), Dalhousie abolishes the nawabship and declares the Tanjore Raj extinct.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 81: 'On October 17, 1855, Muhammad Ghaus, the Nawab of the Carnatic, died without leaving any issue ... It was, however, decided that the title of Nawab should be abolished.' p. 82: 'On 29 October, 1855, died Shivaji, the Raja of Tanjore ... The Council of Madras ... decided that the Tanjore Raj was extinct'.

events.text: The Nepal–Tibet war of Jang Bahadur: Nepal invades Tibet and by the treaty signed at Kathmandu (Thapathali) on 24 March 1856 wins an annual payment, free trade and a Nepalese representative at Lhasa.
events.belligerents: Nepal vs Tibet
events.outcome: Nepal victory; Tibet pays 10,000 rupees a year, abolishes duties on Nepalese goods and admits a Nepalese envoy at Lhasa
events.commanders: Jang Bahadur, Dhir Shamsher — Tibetan commanders
events.source: HCIP IX p. 1026: 'Jang Bahadur tried to increase the influence of Nepal by declaring war on Tibet. The war was ended by the treaty signed at Katmandu on the 24th March, 1856. Nepal gained valuable concessions — the payment of an annual indemnity by the Tibetans of ten thousand Rupees, freedom of trade to Nepalese subjects in Tibet ...'

HCIP IX pp. 456–458: 'Under the leadership of two brothers, Sidhu and Kanhu ... ten thousand Santals met in June 1855, and declared their intention ‘to take possession of the country and set up a Government of their own’ ... A British force under Major Burrough was defeated ... Even in August, the number of insurgents exceeded 30,000 men in arms. They ... were openly at war with the British till February, 1856, when their leaders were arrested.' The 15,000 dead and the creation of the Santal Parganas are web-only.
events.text: The Santhal Hul: Sido and Kanhu Murmu raise the Santhals at Bhognadih on 30 June against the zamindars, moneylenders and the Company; ten thousand march on Calcutta. Put down by 1856 with martial law and the deaths of some fifteen thousand; the Santhal Parganas were made a separate district after it.
events.belligerents: Santhals (Sido and Kanhu Murmu) vs East India Company and the zamindars
events.outcome: East India Company victory; after routing Major Burrough’s column and holding the Bhagalpur–Rajmahal country, the Santals, over 30,000 in arms in August 1855, fought on until their leaders were taken in February 1856

events.text: Anglo-Persian War
events.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent
events.belligerents: East India Company & Britain vs Qajar Persia
events.outcome: Company victory
events.commanders: Lord Canning's British India; James Outram and British/EIC forces — Naser al-Din Shah Qajar of Iran; Herat/Afghan-linked forces

events.text: Annexation of Awadh: Wajid Ali Shah refuses to sign away his kingdom, taking off his turban and placing it in Outram's hands; the Company proclaims Oudh British territory (February 1856) and exiles the king to Calcutta.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 308-309: 'On 4 February, 1856, the Resident had an interview with “His Majesty” Wajid Ali... Outram could not, by any means, persuade him to sign the treaty... Thereupon a proclamation... was issued, “declaring the province of Oude to be thenceforth, for ever, a component part of the British Indian Empire.”'

events.text: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, nationalist leader ('Lokmanya'), is born
events.source: R. C. Majumdar

events.text: Battle of Cawnpore (1857): Tantia Tope's Gwalior Contingent defeats Windham and takes Kanpur city (27–28 November), but Campbell, hurrying back from Lucknow, routs him on 6 December — the last battle for Kanpur.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Tantia Tope's army (Gwalior Contingent rebels, Nana Sahib's forces)
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Tantia Tope routed and driven back on Kalpi, after first beating Windham
events.commanders: Colin Campbell, Charles Windham — Tantia Tope
events.source: HCIP IX p. 568: 'Though Tantia was defeated on the Pandu-nadi on 26 November, he attacked Kanpur the next day, and after a strenuous fight for two days repulsed the British troops... Sir Collin Campbell... hastened back to Kanpur and won a complete victory over Tantia’s troops on 6 December. That was the last battle fought for Kanpur.'

events.text: Indian Rebellion of 1857: the great revolt across north and central India
events.source: R. C. Majumdar
events.belligerents: Mughal Empire, Oudh, forces of Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, Nana Sahib, various rajas/nawabs/zamindars/taluqdars/chieftains vs East India Company, United Kingdom, Nepal, allied princely/chiefly forces
events.outcome: Company victory
events.commanders: Bahadur Shah II, Nana Sahib, Rani Lakshmibai, Begum Hazrat Mahal, Tatya Tope, Kunwar Singh and many local leaders — East India Company and British Crown forces under Lord Canning, Colin Campbell, Henry Havelock; Nepal under Jung Bahadur Rana; loyal princely allies

events.text: Mangal Pandey dies — Hanged at Barrackpore on 8 April; the first shot of the rising.
events.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

events.text: Siege of Arrah: The siege of Arrah took place during the Indian Mutiny.
events.belligerents: East India Company, United Kingdom vs Jagdishpur estate, Mutinying Sepoys
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Boyle’s house held out from 27 July, Dunbar’s relief column was cut up on 29 July, and Vincent Eyre relieved Arrah on 3 August 1857 and sacked Jagdishpur
events.commanders: Herwald Wake, Hooken Singh, Charles Dunbar — Kunwar Singh, Babu Amar Singh, Hare Krishna Singh
events.source: HCIP IX p. 551: 'On July 27 the Danapur mutineers reached Arrah ... attacked Boyle’s house, under the leadership of Kunwar Singh ... On the 29th a detachment under Captain Dunbar ... was attacked at night ... and forced to retreat with heavy loss ... Arrah was relieved, on August 3, by Vincent Eyre.'

events.text: Siege of Cawnpore: The siege of Cawnpore was a key episode in the Indian Rebellion of 1857.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Nana Sahib's forces, Rebel Company soldiers
events.outcome: Rebel victory
events.commanders: Hugh Wheeler, John Moore — Nana Sahib, Tantya Tope, Bala Rao
events.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

events.text: Siege of Delhi (1857): The siege of Delhi was a decisive conflict of the Indian Rebellion of 1857.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Mughal Empire (Bahadur Shah II), rebel sepoys
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Delhi stormed 14–20 September 1857, Nicholson mortally wounded, Bahadur Shah surrendered to Hodson on 21 September and his sons were shot
events.commanders: George Anson Sir Henry William Barnard, Archdale Wilson John Nicholson William Hodson James Hope Grant — Bahadur Shah II Mirza Mughal Mirza Khizr Sultan Bakht Khan
events.source: HCIP IX p. 567: 'the British force made a full-scale attack on Delhi on September 14. The Kashmir Gate was forced... On September 20, the British troops took the Lahore Gate and the Jumma Masjid, and finally the gates of the Red Fort were blown in... Bahadur Shah surrendered to Hodson on the sole condition that his life should be spared.'

events.text: Siege of the Lucknow Residency: Awadh's rebels besiege the British garrison from 30 June 1857; Havelock and Outram fight their way in on 25 September but are themselves shut up, and Colin Campbell breaks through on 17 November and evacuates the Residency, leaving the city to the rebels until March 1858.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Awadh (Begum Hazrat Mahal's government), rebel sepoys
events.outcome: East India Company victory; the Residency held and its garrison relieved and withdrawn, though the city stayed in rebel hands
events.commanders: Henry Lawrence (killed), John Inglis, Henry Havelock, James Outram, Colin Campbell — Begum Hazrat Mahal, Maulavi Ahmadullah
events.source: HCIP IX p. 568-570: 'the tiny besieged garrison at the Residency were heroically defending themselves against enormous odds since June 30... joined the garrison at Lakhnau on the evening of the 25th... he joined the besieged in the Residency on November 17... The Residency was vacated, and Outram took his position at Alambagh outside the city.'

events.text: The Meerut rising and the seizure of Delhi: on 10 May 1857 the 3rd Cavalry and two infantry regiments at Meerut free their imprisoned comrades and kill their officers; next morning they reach Delhi, and on 12 May Bahadur Shah II places himself at their head as Emperor of Hindustan.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 473: 'On May 10, Sunday, at about sunset... several hundreds of them galloped to the jail and released not only their comrades but also its other inmates'; p. 505: 'On reaching Delhi on the morning of May 11, they went straight to the Red Fort... Bahadur Shah placed himself at the head of the sepoys and assumed the title of the Emperor of Hindusthan.'

events.text: Battle of Bareilly (1858): Campbell's converging columns reach Rohilkhand's rebel capital; Khan Bahadur Khan's army, with its charges of Ghazis, is beaten on 5 May and Bareilly occupied next day, though Khan Bahadur escapes to fight on.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Rohilkhand rebels (Khan Bahadur Khan)
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Bareilly occupied on 6 May, Khan Bahadur Khan escaped with most of his army
events.commanders: Colin Campbell — Khan Bahadur Khan
events.source: HCIP IX p. 572-573: 'Sir Colin reached the city on May 4... A fierce battle took place the next day, but though he was defeated, his men gave a good account of themselves... After six hours’ severe fighting the British gained a complete victory and occupied Bareilly the next day (May 6). Khan Bahadur Khan effected his escape'

events.text: Battle of Gwalior (1858): Rose takes Morar on 16 June; at Kotah-ki-Serai on 17 June Rani Lakshmibai, leading her troops in man's dress, is cut down; the rebels are driven from the city on 19 June and the fort stormed on 20 June, and Sindhia is restored.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Tantia Tope, Rao Sahib, Gwalior Contingent rebels
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Gwalior city and fort retaken, the Rani of Jhansi killed, Tantia Tope escaped
events.commanders: Sir Hugh Rose, Brig. Smith — Rani Lakshmibai (killed), Tantia Tope, Rao Sahib
events.source: HCIP IX p. 583-584: 'He left Kalpi on June 6... arrived on the 16th within five miles of the Morar cantonments... carried the cantonments by assault'; 'Thus died the Rani of Jhansi... Rose immediately attacked them, and after a short but sharp engagement, drove away the rebels and occupied the city. Next morning, June 20... Rose attacked the strong fortress and carried it by assault.'

events.text: Battle of Jagdishpur: back in his home village after his Azamgarh campaign, the aged Kunwar Singh routs Le Grand’s column from Arrah on 23 April 1858 — his last victory, three days before his death.
events.belligerents: Jagdishpur (Kunwar Singh, Amar Singh) vs East India Company
events.outcome: Jagdishpur victory; two-thirds of the British force, including Le Grand, killed and the rest flee to Arrah
events.commanders: Kunwar Singh, Amar Singh — Captain Le Grand
events.source: HCIP IX p. 579: 'Next day Kunwar was attacked by a detachment of British troops from Arrah led by Le Grand ... the British were forced to retreat and the retreat was soon converted to a rout. It was a veritable disaster. Two-thirds of the British force, including the commander, were killed ... this was the last great victory of the old veteran.'

events.text: Battles of Kunch and Kalpi (Golauli): Rose defeats the Rani of Jhansi and Tantia Tope at Kunch, then at Golauli before Kalpi on 22 May 1858, and enters the deserted fortress next day.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Rao Sahib, Nawab of Banda, Tantia Tope's army
events.outcome: East India Company victory; the rebels defeated at Golauli and Kalpi abandoned
events.commanders: Sir Hugh Rose, Maxwell — Rani Lakshmibai, Rao Sahib, Nawab of Banda, Tantia Tope
events.source: HCIP IX p. 581-582: 'On the way, he was met by the Rani and Tantia at a town called Koonch... they were severely defeated by Rose... On May 22, Rose was attacked by the rebels, but they were completely defeated. Next day when the British advanced through the ravines to Kalpi, they found that the enemy had fled'

events.text: Capture of Lucknow (1858): Campbell's army, joined by Jang Bahadur's Gurkhas, fights its way through the fortified city street by street from 3 March and holds all of Lucknow by 21 March, though some sixty thousand rebels escape into the Awadh countryside.
events.belligerents: East India Company, Nepal vs Awadh (Begum Hazrat Mahal's government), rebel sepoys
events.outcome: East India Company victory; Lucknow retaken, but the rebel army was allowed to disperse unpursued
events.commanders: Colin Campbell, James Outram, Jang Bahadur Rana — Begum Hazrat Mahal, Maulavi Ahmadullah
events.source: HCIP IX p. 571: 'On March 3 and 4, the advanced section of the British army reached the outskirts of the city, and though the sepoys fought with stubborn courage... the British gained possession of the whole city by 21 March. The Gurkha troops under Jang Bahadur had joined the British army on 11 March, and took part in the assault on Lakhnau.'

events.text: Kunwar Singh dies — At Jagdishpur, days after routing Le Grand’s column there, of the wound (his right wrist amputated) taken as he crossed the Ganga; the old general of the rising in Bihar.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 579: 'But this was the last great victory of the old veteran. Three days later Kunwar Singh died at his own house at Jagdishpur. He had been hit by a cannon ball and his right wrist was amputated ... Evidently this brought about the end on 9 May, 1858.' The page gives both 'three days later' (i.e. c. 26 April) and 9 May 1858.

events.text: Maniram Dewan is hanged — The Assamese noble and tea pioneer executed at Jorhat for plotting a rising in Assam in 1857.
events.source: Acharyya, History of Medieval Assam p. 27: the chronicle 'continues his account up to the execution of Mani Ram Dewan in 1858.' (Place, Jorhat, and the 1857 plot are web-only.)

events.text: Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah dies — The Faizabad maulavi who led the siege of the Lucknow Residency and styled himself King of Hindustan, shot at the gate of Powain and beheaded for the Company's reward.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 573: 'On June 5, the Maulavi went to Powain... the Raja’s followers fired a volley and shot the Maulavi dead... Thus ended the career of one of the greatest patriots and leaders of the revolution of 1857'

events.text: Rani Lakshmibai dies — Killed in the fighting at Kotah-ki-Serai outside Gwalior, in uniform, on 17 June.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 584: '“Clad in the attire of a man and mounted on horseback, the Rani of Jhansi might have been seen animating her troops throughout the day... A hussar, close upon her track, ignorant of her sex and rank, cut her down.” According to another account the Rani was struck by a bullet.'

events.text: Rebel seizure of Gwalior: the fugitives from Kalpi — Rao Sahib, Tantia Tope and the Rani of Jhansi — march on Gwalior; on 1 June 1858 Jayaji Rao Sindhia's army goes over to them, he flees to Agra, and Nana Sahib is proclaimed Peshwa in the fort.
events.belligerents: Rao Sahib, Tantia Tope, Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai) vs Gwalior (Scindia)
events.outcome: Tantia Tope and Rao Sahib victory; Sindhia's army deserted to the rebels and Gwalior with its treasury and arsenal was seized
events.commanders: Tantia Tope, Rani Lakshmibai, Rao Sahib — Jayaji Rao Sindhia
events.source: HCIP IX p. 582-583: 'On June 1, Sindhia marched out with his army to oppose them... Sindhia’s infantry and cavalry, his bodyguards alone excepted, either joined the rebels... Sindhia turned and fled... He did not draw rein till he reached Agra... entered the fort of Gwalior, seized the treasury and the arsenal, and proclaimed Nana Sahib as Peshwa.'

events.text: Siege of Jhansi (1858): Hugh Rose invests Jhansi on 22 March, beats Tantia Tope's 22,000-man relief army on the Betwa on 1 April and storms the city on 3 April; Rani Lakshmibai escapes by night to Kalpi.
events.belligerents: East India Company vs Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Tantia Tope's army
