events.outcome: East India Company victory; Tantia's relief force routed and Jhansi taken by assault
events.commanders: Sir Hugh Rose — Rani Lakshmibai, Tantia Tope
events.source: HCIP IX p. 580-581: 'the city and the fort with his cavalry on 22 March'... 'defeated the host of Tantia who fled towards Kalpi (April 1, 1858). Two days later Rose took the city of Jhansi by assault... The Rani left the fort with a few attendants on the night of the 4th April' (the page's OCR is damaged)

events.text: The Crown takes over from the East India Company; the British Raj begins
events.source: R. C. Majumdar

events.text: Tantia Tope dies — Hanged at Shivpuri after his betrayal by Man Singh of Narwar; the last general of 1857 in the field.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 585: 'Man Singh not only surrendered, but led a few sepoys of the British detachment to the hiding place of Tantia Topi... carried him to the British camp at Sipri. He was tried by a court martial on April 15, 1859, and was hanged on the 18th'

events.text: The Naya Muluk restored to Nepal: for Jang Bahadur’s help in 1857–58 the Government of India returns a large part of the western Terai ceded at Sugauli (Banke, Bardiya, Kailali, Kanchanpur).
events.source: HCIP IX p. 1026: 'As a reward for his services the Government of India restored to Nepal a large part of the former Gurkha possessions in the Terai, which had been ceded to the British in 1816.' Year 1860 (treaty of 1 November 1860) is web-only; the book gives no year.

events.text: The reverse at Rinchenpong: Campbell’s levy, occupying Sikkim west of the Rangit to force the return of kidnapped subjects, is attacked by Sikkimese and Tibetan Bhutias on 27 November 1860 and flees to Darjeeling.
events.belligerents: Kingdom of Sikkim (Namgyal) vs British Raj
events.outcome: Sikkim victory; Campbell’s Sebundy Sappers routed, a havildar and nineteen sepoys captured with all arms and ammunition
events.commanders: the Sikkim Diwan Namgay — Archibald Campbell, Captain Murray
events.source: HCIP IX pp. 1068–1069: 'established his outpost at Ringchingpong. They were attacked on November 27 by a mixed force of Tibetan and Sikkim Bhutias under the direction of the Diwan and forced to retreat ... one Havildar and nineteen sepoys were captured by the Sikkim army, and all the arms and ammunition of Campbell’s force fell into their hands.'

events.text: Rabindranath Tagore, poet and future Nobel laureate, is born in Calcutta
events.source: R. C. Majumdar

events.text: The Treaty of Tumlong: Gawler’s column reaches the Sikkim capital almost unopposed and on 28 March 1861 the heir Sidkyong Namgyal signs a treaty that fines Sikkim, expels the Diwan, bans slave-dealing and opens the road to Tibet — 'practically reduced to vassalage'.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 1069: 'On 28 March, 1861, a new treaty was concluded with the heir apparent, Sidkyong Nam Gyal ... all former treaties were abrogated ... which meant that Sikkim was practically reduced to vassalage. The Raja was fined Rs. 7,000.'

events.text: Bahadur Shah II dies — The last Mughal emperor, figurehead of the 1857 rising, dies in exile at Rangoon on 7 November 1862.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 568: 'He was found guilty and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He was exiled to Rangoon with his favourite queen, and died after four years, on November 7, 1862.'

events.text: Swami Vivekananda is born in Calcutta
events.source: R. C. Majumdar

events.text: The Bhutan (Duar) War: after Ashley Eden’s mission is humiliated at Punakha, the Government of India annexes the Bengal Duars and occupies Dalingkot, Pasakha and Dewangiri; the Bhutanese retake Dewangiri before being driven out again.
events.belligerents: British Raj vs Bhutan (Deb Raja)
events.outcome: British Raj victory; the eighteen Duars ceded to India by the Treaty of Sinchula for an annual subsidy — though the Bhutanese 'scored two notable successes', retaking Dewangiri and occupying Tazigong
events.commanders: Henry Tombs, Mulcaster — Jigme Namgyal, Tongsa Penlop
events.source: HCIP IX pp. 1023–1024: 'all the above forts were occupied, without much resistance, by the middle of January, 1865. The Bhutiyas, however, scored two notable successes; they recaptured Dewangiri and occupied Tazigong by forcing the British to evacuate them. Both these places were afterwards re-taken, and the newly annexed Duars of Bhutan were occupied by a strong military force.'

events.text: The Treaty of Sinchula (11 November 1865): Bhutan cedes the eighteen Duars and the Dewangiri hills to British India for a subsidy rising to Rs 50,000 a year, and submits disputes with Cooch Behar and Sikkim to Indian arbitration.
events.source: HCIP IX p. 1024: 'a treaty was made on 11th November, 1865. The Government of India agreed, in return for the Duars, to pay to the Bhutan Government an annual sum of Rs. 25,000 in the first year ... and Rs. 50,000 on every succeeding year ... The 18 Duars was ceded to the Government of India.' The name Sinchula is web-only; the book gives only the date.

events.text: 1915 Ceylonese riots: The hundred days of martial law — communal rioting between Sinhalese and Muslim communities was answered with shoot-on-sight martial law that killed far more than the riots had. The repression, and the execution of Henry Pedris, turned a generation of the Ceylonese elite towards the independence movement.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: Sinhalese rioters and Muslim communities; then the British military and the population
events.outcome: Riots suppressed; the governor recalled; a catalyst for the independence movement

events.text: Mohandas Gandhi returns to India from South Africa

events.source: R. C. Majumdar

events.text: The Rowlatt Act and the Government of India Act (Montagu-Chelmsford reforms)
events.source: R. C. Majumdar

events.belligerents: British Raj vs Emirate of Afghanistan
events.outcome: Stalemate; Treaty of Rawalpindi

events.text: Easter Sunday Raid: The Japanese carrier strike on Colombo — Japanese carrier aircraft struck the harbour on 5 April and sank the cruisers Dorsetshire and Cornwall the same day. On 9 April they struck Trincomalee and sank the carrier Hermes off Batticaloa. The Eastern Fleet withdrew to East Africa - the heaviest attack ever made on the island.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: Imperial Japanese Navy vs the Royal Navy and RAF
events.outcome: Japanese tactical victory; the Eastern Fleet withdraws from Ceylon

The Bengal famine kills an estimated three million people

events.text: Black July: after an LTTE ambush killed thirteen soldiers at Thirunelveli on 23 July, organised mobs attacked Tamil civilians in Colombo, Kandy and elsewhere for a week, using electoral rolls to find homes and businesses. Fifty-three Tamil detainees were killed inside Welikada prison on 25 and 27 July. About 150,000 people were displaced and mass Tamil emigration began. No one has ever been convicted for any of it. This was not a battle, and it is where the civil war starts.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: Organised mobs, with documented state facilitation, against Tamil civilians
events.outcome: The pogrom that began the twenty-six-year civil war

events.text: 1987–1989 JVP insurrection: fought as reciprocal assassination rather than as battles, and answered by state-linked death squads. Over ten thousand bodies were recovered and the claims of enforced disappearance run far higher. The JVP leadership was captured and killed in November 1989.

events.text: IPKF war: the Indian Peace Keeping Force arrived under the Indo-Lanka Accord to disarm the LTTE and ended up fighting it for three years. India took Jaffna at heavy cost, lost some twelve hundred dead and withdrew in March 1990 without disarming anyone; the LTTE walked back into Jaffna behind it. Independent Tamil human-rights monitors documented the killing of some sixty to seventy patients and staff at Jaffna Teaching Hospital in October 1987; India has never acknowledged it or held an inquiry.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: Indian Peace Keeping Force vs the LTTE
events.outcome: India withdraws; the LTTE returns to Jaffna stronger

events.text: Vadamarachchi Operation (Operation Liberation): the army recovered LTTE-held ground in the Jaffna peninsula for the first time, and was stopped not by the Tigers but by India, which turned back a relief flotilla and then airdropped supplies into the peninsula under fighter escort on 4 June.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: Sri Lanka Army and Air Force vs the LTTE
events.outcome: Vadamarachchi taken; the offensive halted under Indian pressure

events.text: General Zia-ul-Haq's C-130 crashes minutes after take-off from Bahawalpur, killing him, the American ambassador and the army's senior command; elections follow within months
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: Eelam War II: talks collapsed and the LTTE killed several hundred policemen who had surrendered on government orders in the Eastern Province. In October it expelled the entire Muslim population of the Northern Province, about seventy-two thousand people, at forty-eight hours notice - ethnic cleansing on any definition, and never redressed.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: LTTE vs the Sri Lanka Police; and the LTTE against the Northern Muslim population
events.outcome: Several hundred surrendered police killed; the north emptied of Muslims

events.text: Jana Andolan, the People's Movement: seven weeks of protest force King Birendra to lift the ban on parties and accept a constitutional monarchy
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: The mass uprising forces General Ershad to resign after nine years; parliamentary rule returns
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: First Battle of Elephant Pass: the LTTE besieged the base commanding the isthmus into the Jaffna peninsula and a seaborne relief force broke through after a month. The largest set-piece battle of the war to that point, and a government victory.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: LTTE vs the Sri Lanka Army
events.outcome: Government victory; the base held

events.text: President Ranasinghe Premadasa is killed by an LTTE suicide bomber at the May Day rally in Colombo
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: Operation Riviresa and the fall of Jaffna: the army took Jaffna city in early December and held it for the rest of the war. Between a third and half a million civilians left the peninsula in an exodus the LTTE ordered.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: Sri Lanka Army vs the LTTE
events.outcome: Jaffna taken and held; mass civilian displacement

events.text: Battle of Mullaitivu (1996): the LTTE overran the army base in four days and killed more than a thousand soldiers, one of the worst defeats the army suffered. Six months earlier a suicide bombing at the Central Bank in Colombo had killed about a hundred civilians and injured fourteen hundred.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: LTTE vs the Sri Lanka Army
events.outcome: LTTE victory; the base destroyed

events.text: Nepalese Civil War: The Maoist insurgency begins — the CPN (Maoist) attacks police posts in Rolpa, Rukum and Sindhuli on 13 February, opening a ten-year "People's War" that kills some 17,000
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)
events.belligerents: Government of Nepal vs Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist)
events.outcome: Comprehensive Peace Accord, November 2006; the Maoists enter parliament

events.text: Operation Jayasikurui: an eighteen-month attempt to force a land corridor up the A9 to Kilinochchi, the longest and costliest operation of the war. It was abandoned in December 1998 without reaching its objective.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: Sri Lanka Army vs the LTTE
events.outcome: Government failure; the corridor never opened

events.text: Capture of Tiger Hill: the summit is retaken in a night assault, the most publicised action of the Kargil war
events.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India
events.belligerents: India vs Pakistan
events.outcome: Indian victory — Tiger Hill recaptured
events.commanders: Yogendra Singh Yadav

events.text: Capture of Tololing: the six-week fight for the ridge overlooking the Srinagar-Leh highway turns the Kargil war
events.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India
events.belligerents: India vs Pakistan
events.outcome: Indian victory — Tololing recaptured

events.text: Kargil War (Operation Vijay): Indian forces evict intruders from the heights above the Srinagar-Leh highway
events.source: Wikipedia: List of wars involving India
events.belligerents: India vs Pakistan
events.outcome: Indian victory — all positions on the Indian side of the LoC recaptured

events.text: The fourth coup: General Pervez Musharraf's army takes Islamabad after Nawaz Sharif tries to dismiss him while his flight is in the air
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: Second Battle of Elephant Pass: The fall of Elephant Pass — an LTTE offensive rolled back everything the army had gained in the Vanni and took the isthmus in April, reaching the outskirts of Jaffna before it was halted. The high-water mark of the Tigers as a conventional force.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: LTTE vs the Sri Lanka Army
events.outcome: LTTE victory; the army loses the Vanni and the isthmus

events.text: Bandaranaike Airport attack: The raid on Katunayake — LTTE commandos destroyed half the air force combat fleet and several airliners on the ground beside the international airport. The insurance and tourism consequences pushed both sides towards the ceasefire.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: LTTE Black Tigers vs the Sri Lanka Air Force
events.outcome: Half the combat fleet destroyed; a direct pressure toward the 2002 ceasefire

events.text: The Narayanhiti palace massacre: Crown Prince Dipendra shoots King Birendra, Queen Aishwarya and seven others of the royal family at a family dinner, then himself; his uncle Gyanendra takes the throne
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: The Norwegian-brokered ceasefire: signed on 22 February and monitored by a Nordic mission. It held in form for six years. The LTTE left the talks in 2003 and split in 2004 when its eastern commander defected to the government side, taking the East with him.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: Government of Sri Lanka and the LTTE, brokered by Norway
events.outcome: Four years of formal truce; the LTTE splits in 2004

events.text: The Indian Ocean tsunami strikes the eastern and southern coasts on Boxing Day, killing some 35,000 in Sri Lanka
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: King Gyanendra's coup: the government is dismissed, the king assumes direct rule and cuts the country's telephone lines
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: Battle of Mavil Aru: the LTTE closed the sluice gates of an irrigation channel in July, cutting water to some fifteen thousand farming families, and the army went in to reopen them. The ceasefire was never formally revoked at this point, but this is where it ended and the final war began.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: Sri Lanka Army and Air Force vs the LTTE
events.outcome: Gates reopened; the ceasefire collapses in practice

events.text: Loktantra Andolan: nineteen days of protest in April force King Gyanendra to restore parliament; in November the Comprehensive Peace Accord ends the civil war
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: Battle of Thoppigala: The clearing of the East — the last major LTTE stronghold in the Eastern Province fell in July after thirteen years. The army then turned north with its whole weight.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: Sri Lanka Army vs the LTTE
events.outcome: The Eastern Province declared cleared

events.text: Benazir Bhutto is assassinated leaving a rally at Liaquat Bagh, Rawalpindi, the park where Liaquat Ali Khan was shot in 1951
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: Siege of Lal Masjid: after a week-long stand-off the army storms the Red Mosque in the capital; over a hundred die, and the Pakistani Taliban's war on the state begins
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)
events.belligerents: Pakistan Army vs the Lal Masjid militants
events.outcome: The mosque is taken; a wave of suicide bombings follows

events.text: Nepal becomes a republic: the Constituent Assembly abolishes the 240-year Shah monarchy at its first sitting
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: Battle of Kilinochchi: The fall of Kilinochchi — the LTTE lost its administrative capital on 2 January, Elephant Pass and the A9 a week later, and Mullaitivu town on 25 January. Within a month it held no town at all and was confined to a shrinking strip of coast.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: Sri Lanka Army vs the LTTE
events.outcome: The LTTE loses its capital, the isthmus and its last town

events.text: Battle of Mullivaikkal and the end of the war: the last months were fought in a strip of coast a few kilometres across holding something over 300,000 civilians. Successive government-declared no-fire zones were shelled and hospitals inside them struck more than two dozen times; the LTTE held the population as a buffer and shot people who tried to leave. Fighting ended on 18 May and Prabhakaran was found dead the next day. The LTTE was destroyed and the war was over after twenty-six years. Civilian deaths in this phase are disputed and no independent forensic accounting has ever been allowed: a contemporaneous UN field tally counted 7,721 killed to 13 May, the UN Secretary-General's Panel of Experts held in 2011 that a figure as high as 40,000 could not be ruled out, and the state has never published a count of its own. The Panel found credible allegations of war crimes against both sides; none has been adjudicated.
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)
events.belligerents: Sri Lanka Armed Forces vs the LTTE, with over 300,000 civilians inside the pocket
events.commanders: Velupillai Prabhakaran (killed 18-19 May 2009)
events.outcome: The LTTE destroyed and the civil war ended; the civilian death toll disputed

events.text: Peshawar school massacre: The Army Public School attack — Tehrik-i-Taliban gunmen kill 149 people at a school in Peshawar, 132 of them children; the state answers with the National Action Plan and the Zarb-e-Azb offensive
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)
events.belligerents: Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan against schoolchildren
events.outcome: The deadliest terrorist attack in Pakistan's history

events.text: The Gorkha earthquake of 25 April kills nearly 9,000; the new federal constitution is promulgated on 20 September
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: 2019 Easter bombings: suicide attacks on three churches and three hotels in Colombo, Negombo and Batticaloa kill 269
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)
events.belligerents: National Thowheeth Jama'ath against worshippers and hotel guests
events.outcome: The deadliest attack since the war; a state of emergency

events.text: Imran Khan becomes the first prime minister removed by a vote of no confidence
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: The Aragalaya: months of protest at Galle Face over the economic collapse end with crowds inside the President's House on 9 July; Gotabaya Rajapaksa flees and resigns
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: The July uprising: student protests over job quotas grow into a national revolt; Sheikh Hasina flees to India on 5 August after fifteen years in power
events.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

events.text: Operation Sindoor: Indian strikes on terrorist infrastructure across the border after the Pahalgam attack; ceasefire after four days of exchanges
events.source: Wikipedia: List of wars involving India
events.belligerents: India vs Pakistan
events.outcome: Indian victory — stated objectives against terror infrastructure achieved

milestones.detail: The Kushans are fading in the north-west, the Western Kshatrapas still hold Malwa and Gujarat, the Vakatakas rule the Deccan and the Kalabhras are about to upset the Tamil south; in Magadha a small house called Gupta is two generations from empire. The atlas’s paint begins here.

"Some time about A.D. 300 or a little later the whole country was upset by the predatory activities of the Kalabhras" — the three Tamil crowns eclipsed for nearly three centuries; a Buddhist Kalabhra king Achchutavikkanta patronises monasteries in the Chola country.
milestones.source: Sastri, A History of South India scan 12, 130; HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 265-266

milestones.text: Rudrasimha II seizes the Western Kshatrapa throne
milestones.detail: A usurper from a collateral line ousts the legitimate heir at Ujjain; the Saka satrapy limps on for another century under his line.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 46 (chronology p. 707)

milestones.text: Sridharavarman sets up an independent kingdom
milestones.detail: A Saka chief, once a Kshatrapa officer, rules independently in the Sanchi–Eran country of eastern Malwa — a sign of the Kshatrapa break-up before the Guptas arrive.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 47 (Kanakhera and Eran inscriptions)

milestones.text: The Gupta era begins: Chandragupta I is crowned Maharajadhiraja
milestones.detail: On 26 February 320 the reckoning later used from Bengal to Kathiawad commences — most probably the coronation of Chandragupta I, whose marriage to the Licchavi Kumaradevi united two principalities of Bihar into the kingdom his son would make an empire.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 4-5

milestones.text: Samudragupta succeeds to the Gupta throne
milestones.detail: Chosen by his father over other claimants, the "hero of a hundred battles" begins the reign that gives the Allahabad prasasti its subject.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 6-7

milestones.text: Mayurasarman founds the Kadamba kingdom at Banavasi
milestones.detail: The first Kannada royal house — a Brahmana who "took to the sword" against the Pallavas and was crowned by them.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 270-272 (Talagunda pillar); chronology p. 707 (c. 340-70)

milestones.detail: Harishena's eulogy of Samudragupta, engraved on the Asokan pillar at Prayaga — the single most important political document of the age, naming the kings of Aryavarta and Dakshinapatha, the frontier kingdoms and the tribal republics.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 7-12; Sircar, Select Inscriptions no. 2

milestones.text: Konganivarman Madhava founds the Western Ganga line
milestones.detail: The Gangas of Kuvalala (Kolar) and later Talakad, who will hold southern Karnataka for six centuries, begin "about the middle of the fourth century", perhaps in the confusion left by Samudragupta's southern march.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 268-269; Sastri, A History of South India scan 104

milestones.text: Pushyavarman founds the Varman dynasty of Kamarupa
milestones.detail: The first historical king of Assam, whose kingdom the Allahabad prasasti lists among the frontier states paying tribute to Samudragupta; thirteen generations follow to Bhaskaravarman.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 89 (Nidhanpur and Doobi plates); chronology p. 707

milestones.detail: The twin Tamil epics of the merchant's daughter Kannaki and the Buddhist nun Manimekalai are generally placed in the post-Sangam centuries, c. 300-500 — the last flowering before the Kalabhra dark age.
milestones.source: Sastri, A History of South India ch. on literature (date debated); HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 327

milestones.text: Meghavarna of Ceylon sends a mission to Samudragupta
milestones.detail: The Sinhalese king asks leave to build a monastery for Ceylonese pilgrims at Bodh Gaya; the Mahabodhi sangharama Hiuen Tsang later saw was the result.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 11; chronology p. 707 (352-79)

milestones.detail: After the shadowy Ramagupta episode, the son of Samudragupta takes the throne he will hold to c. 414 — the reign of the Saka conquest, Fa-hien's visit and Kalidasa's tradition.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 15-18; chronology p. 708

milestones.text: Prabhavatigupta rules the Vakataka kingdom as regent
milestones.detail: The daughter of Chandragupta II, widowed by Rudrasena II, governs Vidarbha for her minor sons for some twenty years — Gupta influence reaches the Deccan through her.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 179-181

milestones.detail: The Chinese monk travels the Gupta empire 400-411 — Mathura, Kanauj, Pataliputra, Tamralipti — and Ceylon 411-12, and leaves the earliest outsider's picture of the Classical Age: mild government, no death penalty, prosperous cities.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 22, 613-614; chronology p. 708

milestones.detail: The rustless pillar of "king Chandra", raised as a standard of Vishnu on a hill called Vishnupada and later moved to Delhi — the record of Chandragupta II's Vanga and Vahlika wars.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 20; CII III no. 32

milestones.text: The Udayagiri caves are cut under Chandragupta II
milestones.detail: The Varaha and Vishnu cave-temples at Udayagiri near Vidisa, with an inscription of the emperor's minister Virasena dated 401 — the earliest datable monuments of Gupta art.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 19-20 (Udayagiri inscription, Gupta year 82)

milestones.detail: Forty years of peace and asvamedha — the reign in which Nalanda is founded and the Gupta silver coinage spreads through the west; it ends with the Pushyamitra and Hun wars.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 23-25; chronology p. 708 (415-55)

milestones.detail: Hiuen Tsang attributes the first monastery at Nalanda to "Sakraditya" — identified with Kumaragupta I — on which five kings built in turn; the university of the Classical Age.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) ch. XX; Hiuen Tsang (Beal II, 167-170). Year conventional.

milestones.text: The king of Ka-pi-li sends an embassy to China
milestones.detail: A ruler of Kapilavastu — or Davaka — writes to the Sung court; the first Indian embassy to China of the period, followed by Mahanaman of Ceylon's letter the same year.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 90; chronology p. 709

milestones.text: The silk-weavers of Dasapura build a sun temple
milestones.detail: A guild of weavers migrated from Lata raises a temple of the Sun at Mandasor under Kumaragupta and the Aulikara Bandhuvarman; restored by the same guild in 473 — the classic record of Gupta-age guild life.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 442; chronology p. 709 (437-38, 473)

milestones.text: The Talagunda pillar records the Kadamba origins
milestones.detail: Kakusthavarman's prasasti at Talagunda tells how Mayurasarman won a kingdom and how the Kadamba princesses married Guptas and Vakatakas — the foundation text of Karnataka's dynastic history.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 270-272

milestones.text: The Sudarsana lake bursts at Girnar
milestones.detail: The Mauryan reservoir, repaired by Rudradaman in 150, breaks its embankment "in a night"; Skandagupta's governor Parnadatta and his son Chakrapalita rebuild it in 456-58 and record it beside Asoka's edicts.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 61 (Junagadh inscription of Skandagupta, Gupta years 136-138)

milestones.detail: Skandagupta's own account of the tottering fortunes of his house, the Pushyamitra war and the Hun victory, set up at Bhitari in Ghazipur.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 25-27

milestones.text: Manadeva raises the Changu Narayan pillar
milestones.detail: The earliest dated inscription of Nepal (Saka 386): the Licchavi king Manadeva records his father's death and his own campaigns east and west of the valley.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 83-84

milestones.text: The Ajanta caves of the Vakataka age
milestones.detail: Under Harishena of Vatsagulma and his minister Varahadeva the great painted viharas — caves XVI, XVII, I and II — are excavated: the Bodhisattva Padmapani, the Jatakas, the "Persian embassy" scene.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 184-186 (Ajanta cave XVI inscription); art chapter

milestones.text: Bhatarka founds the Maitraka state of Valabhi
milestones.detail: The Gupta senapati of Saurashtra makes himself master of the peninsula as the empire loosens; his descendants rule from Valabhi for three centuries.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 61-62; chronology p. 709 (c. 465-75)

milestones.text: Sigiriya: Kasyapa builds his rock fortress
milestones.detail: The patricide king of Ceylon raises palace, gardens and the Lion-gate on the rock of Sigiriya, with the painted "cloud maidens"; abandoned after his death in battle.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 285-286

milestones.detail: Maharaja Matrivishnu's pillar at Eran, dated Gupta year 165, shows Budhagupta still sovereign in Malwa "between the Kalindi and the Narmada" — the last firm date of imperial Gupta rule in the west.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 30-31

milestones.text: The Ganga era begins in Kalinga
milestones.detail: Indravarman I of the Eastern Gangas founds the reckoning used by the dynasty for five centuries; Kalinganagara becomes their seat.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 215; chronology p. 710

milestones.detail: The finest surviving Gupta structural temple, with its Anantasayana, Gajendramoksha and Nara-Narayana panels, c. 500. The Bhitargaon brick temple in Kanpur is of the same generation.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) art chapter (ch. XVIII); date conventional

milestones.detail: Maharaja Dronasimha of Valabhi, "anointed by the paramount sovereign in person", issues the first of the great series of Valabhi copper plates.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 61; chronology p. 710

milestones.detail: The Gunaighar plate of Maharaja Vainyagupta (Gupta year 188) shows a Gupta prince holding Samatata with the imperial titles — the seed of Bengal's separate kingdom.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 33, 40; chronology p. 710

milestones.text: Sung Yun visits the Hun court in Gandhara
milestones.detail: The Wei envoy sent for Buddhist books finds the Hephthalite king ruling Gandhara "in the third generation" of conquest, cruel and hostile to the Law — the eyewitness account of Hun India.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 35-36, 615; chronology p. 710

milestones.detail: The monk "third son of an Indian king, probably the Pallava king of Kanchi", received by Emperor Wu of Liang, brings the meditative school to China — Chan, and later Zen. Date and person semi-legendary.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 612, 616

milestones.text: Gopachandra founds an independent kingdom of Vanga
milestones.detail: South and east Bengal "shook off the suzerainty of the Guptas" under Gopachandra, Dharmaditya and Samacharadeva, who "assumed the title Maharajadhiraja and issued gold coins like the Gupta emperors".
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 40-41, 77; chronology p. 711 (c. 525-75)

milestones.detail: Two pillars at Sondani proclaim the Aulikara "who rules from the Lauhitya to the western ocean" and to whose feet Mihirakula bowed — the record of the Hun defeat.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 39-40 (Mandasor inscription, Malava year 589 = 532)

milestones.text: Cosmas Indicopleustes describes India and Ceylon
milestones.detail: The Alexandrian merchant-monk who had sailed the Indian Ocean writes his Christian Topography: the Hun "Lord of India", the pepper ports of Male (Malabar), the Persian Christians and the king of Taprobane.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 36; chronology p. 711

milestones.text: Pulakesin I fortifies Badami and founds the Chalukya kingdom
milestones.detail: The Chalukya makes the hill-fort of Vatapi his capital and performs the asvamedha — the dynasty that will rule the Deccan for two centuries steps out of Kadamba vassalage.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 231 (Badami cliff inscription, Saka 465 = 543)

milestones.text: Paramartha sails from India to China
milestones.detail: The scholar-monk of Ujjain and Pataliputra reaches China in 546 and translates the Yogachara texts of Asanga and Vasubandhu; he dies there in 569.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 611; chronology p. 711

milestones.text: Elephanta: the great cave of Siva
milestones.detail: The Mahesamurti and the Siva cave on the island of Gharapuri are cut in the sixth century, under the Kalachuris of Mahishmati or the Konkan Mauryas.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) art chapter; attribution debated

milestones.text: Tirumular and Karaikkal Ammaiyar: the first Saiva saints
milestones.detail: A sixth-century Saiva yogi, Tirumular, composes the Tirumantiram; the poetess of Karaikkal is remembered as the earliest of the sixty-three Nayanars — the Bhakti movement stirs in the Tamil south.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 328; Sastri, A History of South India ch. on religion

milestones.detail: The Haraha inscription of Vikrama 611 proclaims the Maukhari Maharajadhiraja after his victories over the Andhras, Sulikas and Gaudas — a new imperial house at Kanauj.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 68-69

milestones.text: Guhadatta founds the Guhila principality of Mewar
milestones.detail: A chief "established a small principality in the western part of the old State of Udaipur" after the Gupta collapse — the ancestor of the Ranas of Mewar. Date traditional.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 157-159 (Atpur inscription of 977)

milestones.text: The Sumandala plate: Gupta suzerainty still acknowledged in Orissa
milestones.detail: King Prithivivigraha rules Kalinga "in the dominion of the Guptas" in Gupta year 250 — the last echo of the empire, half a century after Yasodharman claimed to have swept it away.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 42, 92

milestones.text: Mangalesa dedicates Cave III at Badami
milestones.detail: The great Vishnu cave, "the earliest dated Hindu cave temple in India" (Saka 500), with its Varaha, Trivikrama and Narasimha reliefs — the Chalukya style is born.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 233-234 (Badami cave inscription of Mangalesa, Saka 500)

milestones.detail: The first Pushyabhuti to take the title Maharajadhiraja — "a lion to the Huna deer, a burning fever to the king of Sindhu, a troubler of the sleep of the Gurjara king" (Bana).
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 96-98; chronology p. 712

milestones.detail: Sankaragana's Abhona plates (Kalachuri year 347) are issued from Ujjayini — northern Maharashtra, Gujarat and western Malwa under one Kalachuri king.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 74, 195

milestones.text: The Mahabodhi temple at Bodh Gaya
milestones.detail: The tall brick temple over the seat of enlightenment, described by Hiuen Tsang, takes its present form in the Gupta and post-Gupta centuries.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) art chapter; Hiuen Tsang (Beal II)

milestones.text: Sirpur: the Lakshmana temple of the Panduvamsis
milestones.detail: Queen Vasata's brick temple to Vishnu at Sripura, the Panduvamsi capital on the Mahanadi — the finest brick shrine of the age. Date approximate.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 220-221 (Sirpur inscriptions of Vasata and Balarjuna)

milestones.text: Chach seizes the throne of Sindh
milestones.detail: The Brahmin minister marries the widow of Rai Sahasi II and founds the dynasty that Muhammad ibn Qasim will destroy — 602 by the Chach-nama's own reckoning, which modern scholars place a generation later.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 166 (Chach-nama; chronology uncertain)

milestones.text: Harsha ascends the throne of Thanesar
milestones.detail: At sixteen, after the murders of his brother-in-law and brother, Harshavardhana takes the crown "without any hesitation" and vows vengeance on Gauda; the Harsha era begins.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 100-102

milestones.detail: The envoy Hamsavega brings the Kamarupa king's offer of "perpetual friendship" to Harsha's camp — the eastern alliance that outflanks Sasanka.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 91, 100 (Harshacharita)

milestones.detail: After the civil war that killed his uncle Mangalesa, the greatest of the Badami Chalukyas begins the reign that will face Harsha, take Vengi and end at Vatapi.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 234; chronology p. 713 (610-11 to 642)

milestones.text: Mahendravarman I cuts the first Pallava rock temples
milestones.detail: The Mandagapattu cave records the "curious-minded" king's boast of a temple without brick, timber, metal or mortar — the beginning of Tamil stone architecture, continued at Tiruchirappalli and Mamallapuram.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 259-260; Sastri, A History of South India scan 134

milestones.detail: The Ganjam grant of Madhavaraja II of Kongoda acknowledges the Gauda king's suzerainty in Gupta year 300 — Sasanka's power then reached the Orissa coast; he is dead by the mid-620s.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 107; chronology p. 713

milestones.text: The Eastern Chalukya kingdom of Vengi is founded
milestones.detail: Pulakesin II installs his younger brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana as ruler of the conquered Andhra country — a line that will last five centuries.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 238, 252

milestones.text: Pulakesin II and Khusrau II exchange embassies
milestones.detail: Tabari records an embassy from "the king of India" to the Sasanian court in 625-26; tradition sees the Persian embassy in return painted on the walls of Ajanta cave I.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 240 (Tabari); chronology p. 713

milestones.text: Durlabhavardhana founds the Karkota dynasty of Kashmir
milestones.detail: The son-in-law of the last Gonanda king takes the throne; Hiuen Tsang will find the dynasty ruling "five other countries" from the valley.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 132

milestones.detail: At Bhillamala under the Chapa king Vyaghramukha, the thirty-year-old astronomer writes the treatise that first treats zero as a number and gives rules for negative quantities — carried to Baghdad a century later as the Sindhind.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 161, 323; chronology p. 713

milestones.detail: The Chinese Master of the Law crosses the Hindu Kush in 630 and spends fourteen years in India — Kashmir, Kanauj, Nalanda, Kamarupa, Kanchi, Badami — leaving the fullest description of the subcontinent before the Mughals.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 100, 618; chronology pp. 712-714

milestones.text: Appar and Sambandar lead the Saiva revival
milestones.detail: Tirunavukkarasar (Appar), who turned Mahendravarman I from Jainism, and the boy-saint Tirujnanasambandar, who reconverted the Pandya court, sing the Tevaram hymns through the Tamil country — the Bhakti movement in full voice.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 328; Sastri, A History of South India scan 134, 370

milestones.text: The rathas and reliefs of Mamallapuram
milestones.detail: Narasimhavarman I Mamalla gives his name to the port where the monolithic rathas, the Arjuna's Penance relief and the cave-temples are cut — the seaboard workshop of Pallava art.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 260-261; art chapter

milestones.text: Hiuen Tsang at Kashmir and Taxila
milestones.detail: The pilgrim spends two years (631-33) in Kashmir, where the Karkota king lends him twenty scribes, and finds Taxila a dependency of Kashmir and Gandhara desolate.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 132-133

milestones.text: The Aihole prasasti of Pulakesin II
milestones.detail: Ravikirti's Sanskrit eulogy on the Meguti Jain temple (Saka 556) records the Chalukya's conquests from the Konkan to Kanchi and his check of Harsha — and dates itself by the Mahabharata war.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 235-237

milestones.text: Harsha exchanges embassies with the Tang court
milestones.detail: Harsha's envoy reaches Chang-an and Tai-tsung sends Liang Huai-ching in return — the first of four Chinese missions to Kanauj in seven years.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 120; chronology p. 714

milestones.detail: The pilgrim finds the Pallava capital "the birthplace of Dharmapala", with a hundred monasteries, and hears of Ceylon from the monks who fled its civil war.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 260

milestones.detail: Twenty kings, three thousand monks and the Chinese pilgrim attend the great religious assembly in honour of Mahayana; a fire in the tower and an attempt on the king's life mar it.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 116-119

milestones.detail: At the confluence Harsha gives away the accumulated wealth of five years to Buddhists, Brahmanas and the poor, ending with the clothes on his back — the sixth such Mahamoksha-parishad of his reign.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 119-120

milestones.text: Chinese envoys find Narendradeva on the throne of Nepal
milestones.detail: The Licchavi restored with Tibetan help receives the Tang mission bound for Magadha; Nepal is now within the Tibetan orbit.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 85, 137

milestones.text: Hiuen Tsang at the court of Bhaskaravarman
milestones.detail: The Kamarupa king, "a devout Brahmana", entertains the pilgrim for a month and then escorts him to Harsha's assembly with twenty thousand elephants and thirty thousand boats.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 91-92, 116

milestones.detail: The last great emperor of the north dies without an heir; his minister Arjuna usurps the throne and "the history of Kanauj is wrapt in obscurity" for half a century.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 121, 124; HCIP IV p. xii

milestones.text: Valabhi conquers the Gurjara kingdom of Nandipuri
milestones.detail: Dharasena IV Chakravartin of Valabhi issues grants from Broach in 648 — the Maitrakas briefly master the Gurjaras of Lata.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 147; chronology p. 714

milestones.detail: Jayaditya and Vamana's commentary on Panini's grammar — the standard gloss for thirteen centuries — is composed about the middle of the seventh century.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 311, 319; chronology p. 715

milestones.text: Narendradeva of Nepal sends a mission to China
milestones.detail: The Licchavi king's embassy reaches the Tang court; Nepal is described as a country of merchants and copper coinage.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 137; chronology p. 715

milestones.text: Vikramaditya I restores the Chalukya kingdom
milestones.detail: Thirteen years after the sack of Badami the son of Pulakesin II recovers the throne and turns on the Pallavas.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 241; chronology p. 715 (655-81)

milestones.text: Adityasena of Magadha performs the horse-sacrifice
milestones.detail: The Later Gupta king assumes the imperial titles and celebrates the asvamedha; his Aphsad inscription rehearses his line back to Krishnagupta. "Magadha rose to a position of imperial greatness."
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 126-127, 358 (Aphsad inscription)

milestones.detail: The Chinese pilgrim comes by sea in 671, studies ten years at Nalanda and writes the Record of the Buddhist Religion — the picture of Indian monastic life after Harsha.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 2, 620; chronology p. 715

milestones.detail: Vikramaditya I's Gadval plates, issued from Uragapura on the Kaveri, show the Chalukya army in the heart of the Chola country after the capture of Kanchi.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 241, 261

milestones.detail: The earliest dated Guhilot record: a chief of the Chatsu branch in eastern Rajasthan, Vikrama 741.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 160; chronology p. 716

milestones.detail: Siladitya III of Valabhi issues grants from the Gurjara capital in 685 — the second Maitraka occupation of Lata.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 149; chronology p. 716

milestones.detail: The Rashtrakutas of Berar — Durgaraja, Govindaraja, Svamikaraja, Nannaraja Yuddhasura — hold Elichpur under the Chalukyas; the Multai grant of 709 is Nanna's. The kin, perhaps, of Dantidurga's line.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 201-202; chronology p. 716

milestones.text: Rajasimha begins the Kailasanatha of Kanchi
milestones.detail: Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha (695-722) raises the first great structural temple of the Pallavas at Kanchi and the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram.
milestones.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 262, 281

milestones.detail: Fifty years after Harsha’s death the north lies fragmented among local chiefs; the Chalukyas rule the Deccan, the Pallavas the Tamil country, and in Sindh the last Hindu kings face the armies of the caliphate. The Classical Age has ended; the age of imperial Kanauj is about to begin.
Muhammad ibn Qasim defeated Raja Dahir at Aror; the lower Indus became the easternmost province of the Umayyad caliphate.
milestones.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

milestones.detail: Kannauj returned to power under Yashovarman, patron of Vakpati and Bhavabhuti, until Lalitaditya of Kashmir broke him c. 740.
milestones.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

milestones.detail: From Avanti, Nagabhata I built the power that repelled the Arab campaigns and grew into the Gurjara-Pratihara empire.
milestones.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

milestones.detail: Yashovarman of Kanauj (the 'I-cha-fan-mo' of the Chinese annals) sent his minister, the Buddhist monk Buddhasena, as ambassador to the Tang court in 731, probably seeking common cause against the Arabs and Tibetans pressing on India.
milestones.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), p. 130; chronology p. 717 (731)

milestones.detail: Lalitaditya Muktapida of Kashmir sent a diplomatic mission to the Tang emperor to induce him to make common cause against the Tibetans; the emperor received it with honour and recognised the Kashmir king as his royal ally, though no military aid was sent.
milestones.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), p. 133. date approximate/disputed: A.D. 733 on p. 133, but 736 on p. 130 and in the chronology p. 717

milestones.detail: Vakpati, court poet of Yashovarman of Kanauj, composed the Prakrit epic Gaudavaho ('the slaying of the Gauda king') celebrating his patron's conquests — a key literary monument and historical source for the age.
milestones.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), pp. 128-129. date approximate: composed during Yashovarman's reign, after his Gauda victory of c. 725-735 and before his fall to Lalitaditya

milestones.detail: After the Arab reverses that followed Junaid, a fortified refuge-city was begun in Sindh on the ruins of Brahmanabad — built, according to Baladhuri, by a son of Muhammad ibn Qasim under governor Hakam and finished under Caliph al-Mansur, it became Mansura, the great Muslim capital of Sindh.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 127; The Classical Age (HCIP III), p. 173. date approximate/disputed: begun under governor Hakam (c. 731-740), completed under Caliph al-Mansur (754-775)

milestones.text: The Arab advance is turned back
milestones.detail: Nagabhata I, the Chalukya viceroy Pulakeshin and allied powers broke the Umayyad push beyond Sindh; the frontier held for three centuries.
milestones.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

milestones.detail: According to the Gujarat chronicles, the Chapotkata (Chavda) king Vanaraja built Anahilapataka (Anahilwara-Patan), the city that would remain the political centre of Gujarat for six centuries.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 103 and chronology p. 506 (745); The Classical Age (HCIP III) chronology p. 717 gives 746. date approximate/disputed: 745 or 746

milestones.detail: Gao Xianzhi’s expedition over the Pamirs restored the Patola Shahis — Tang China’s furthest reach toward India, undone within a decade.
milestones.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

milestones.detail: The chiefs of Gauda ended the century of matsyanyaya by raising Gopala — the founding of the Pala empire.
milestones.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

milestones.detail: Dantidurga overthrew Kirtivarman II of Badami; his successors would carve the Kailasa at Ellora and raid the Ganga.
milestones.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

milestones.detail: Lalitaditya Muktapida, the greatest of the Karkota emperors of Kashmir, died about 760 after a reign of conquest stretching from Bengal to Central Asia; his most famous monument, the Martanda sun temple, remains 'the most striking of the ancient architecture of Kashmir'.
milestones.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), pp. 133-135; chronology p. 718 (c. 760). date approximate

milestones.detail: The stupendous rock-cut Kailasa temple of Shiva at Ellora was excavated at the orders of the Rashtrakuta emperor Krishna I — 'a marvel of architecture' that will keep alive for ever the name of its builder.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 3, 17. date approximate: within Krishna I's reign, c. 758-773

milestones.detail: Jatila Parantaka of the Pandyas stormed the Ay port — the far south’s wars now reach the atlas.
milestones.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

milestones.detail: The Maitraka dynasty of Saurashtra, patrons of a university ranked with Nalanda, ends; tradition blames Arab sea-raids.
milestones.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

milestones.detail: Udyotana Suri completed the Prakrit romance Kuvalayamala at Javalipura (Jalor) in Saka 700 (A.D. 778), during the reign of the Pratihara Vatsaraja — a landmark of Jain literature and a dated anchor for Pratihara chronology.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 21, 209; chronology p. 507 (778)

milestones.detail: Vatsaraja took Kannauj, Dharmapala installed his own king there, and Dhruva the Rashtrakuta beat them both — three empires locked on one city.
milestones.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

milestones.detail: The aged Dhruva, having chosen his ablest son over the elder Stambha, abdicated in favour of Govinda III, who ascended the Rashtrakuta throne in 793 and would carry the empire's arms from Kanauj to Cape Comorin.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 5-6; chronology p. 508 (793-814)

milestones.detail: Dharmapala convoked a great durbar at Kanauj to proclaim himself suzerain of Northern India and install Chakrayudha on its throne; the vassal rulers of Bhoja, Matsya, Madra, Kuru, Yadu, Yavana, Avanti, Gandhara and Kira attended, 'bowing down respectfully with their diadems trembling'.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 46. date approximate: undated in HCIP; between Dhruva's withdrawal (c. 790) and Nagabhata II's capture of Kanauj

milestones.detail: Dharmapala, a great patron of Buddhism, founded the Vikramashila monastery on a hill above the Ganga in Magadha (probably Patharghata near Bhagalpur), which grew into a university second only to Nalanda; Tibetan tradition also credits him with the great monasteries of Odantapuri in Bihar and Somapuri (Paharpur) in Varendra.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 49. date approximate: within Dharmapala's reign, c. 770-810; Odantapuri also attributed by some to Gopala or Devapala

milestones.detail: Shankara of Kaladi, the Acharya par excellence of Advaita Vedanta, is assigned by tradition to c. 788-820; in his brief life he composed the great commentaries and, in the course of his digvijaya, carried his philosophy across the subcontinent.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 304; chronology p. 507 (c. 788-820). date approximate/disputed: traditional dates c. 788-820 (midpoint given)

milestones.detail: The colossal stupa of Borobudur in Central Java, whose artists 'conceived like giants and finished like jewellers', was built towards the close of the 8th or the beginning of the 9th century under the patronage of the Shailendras, then the dominant power of Suvarnadvipa; a Shailendra king had already raised the Tara temple of Chandi Kalasan in 778, with the Gauda monk Kumaraghosha attested as royal guru in 782.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 440-441 (Borobudur), 440 (Kalasan, 778); chronology p. 507. date approximate: late 8th-early 9th century

milestones.detail: Dharmapala, 'the hero of a hundred fights' who raised Bengal to imperial power, died at an advanced age after a reign of 32 years or more, leaving his dominions intact to his son Devapala, under whom the Pala empire reached its widest extent.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 48, 50 (Dharmapala c. 770-810; Devapala c. 810-850). date approximate

milestones.detail: On the death of Govinda III in 814, his son Sarva, better known as Amoghavarsha I Nripatunga, succeeded to the Rashtrakuta throne as a boy of 13 or 14 under the regency of his cousin Karkka; his 64-year reign became famous for letters and religion rather than war, and he himself wrote the Kavirajamarga, the earliest Kannada work on poetics.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 8; chronology p. 508 (814-878)

milestones.detail: Nagabhata II, having broken Chakrayudha and then been broken in his turn by Govinda III, recovered Kannauj at the second attempt and moved the Pratihara seat of government from Ujjayini to Kanyakubja; HCIP will not commit to a year, but Schwartzberg dates the overthrow of the Ayudha line and the transfer of the capital to c. 815.
milestones.source: Schwartzberg, Historical Atlas of South Asia, plate IV.1, map note at Kanyakubja: "Successively subject to Pratihara, Pala and Rastrakuta power. c. 815. Overthrown by Pratiharas who then transfer their capital from Ujjayini to Kanyakubja."; The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 25, 27-28. date approximate: HCIP gives no year and would place the transfer no earlier than the end of Nagabhata II's reign

milestones.detail: Amoghavarsha built the city of Manyakheta (modern Malkhed) and established his capital there, giving the Rashtrakuta empire the seat from which it would rule the Deccan for a century and a half.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 10. date approximate: undated in HCIP; placed here at Amoghavarsha's assumption of the government (c. 821)

milestones.detail: The Kollam or Malayalam era, still in use in Kerala, originated in A.D. 824-25 — connected by some with the end of Cheraman Perumal's rule and by others with the foundation of the port city of Kollam (Quilon).
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 165; chronology p. 508 (824-825). date approximate/disputed: origin explained variously

milestones.text: Bhoja I's accession; first firm evidence of Kannauj as the Pratihara capital
milestones.detail: The Barah copper-plate of A.D. 836, issued from Bhoja's camp (skandhavara) at Mahodaya to confirm an endowment in the Kalanjara mandala of the Kanyakubja bhukti, shows that he had ascended the throne in or before 836 and had recovered the region round Kannauj lost in his father's reign; it is the earliest document that ties a Pratihara king's own seat to the city.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 29: "On the whole it is likely, though not certain, that as early as A.D. 836, Bhoja had fixed his capital at Kannauj, and obtained mastery of the region round it, which had been probably lost during his father's reign."; cf. printed p. 27: "although Kanauj was the capital of Bhoja, we have no independent evidence that it was the Pratihara capital before his time."

milestones.detail: Amoghavarsha I is celebrated as the maker of the city of Manyakheta (Malkhed), 'built to excel the city of Indra', with a palace full of fine workmanship; it remained the imperial Rashtrakuta capital until its sack in 972.
milestones.source: Sastri, A History of South India, block 143 of the archive.org text; The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 12. Date approximate — early-to-mid reign of Amoghavarsha (814-878)

milestones.detail: The Digambara acharya Jinasena, author of the Adipurana, adorned the court of Amoghavarsha I, who revered him profoundly; the work became the foundation of Kannada-country Jain purana literature.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 11, 294. Date approximate, mid-9th century

milestones.text: The Kavirajamarga, first landmark of Kannada letters
milestones.detail: Amoghavarsha I (Nripatunga) was himself the author of the Kavirajamarga, the earliest Kanarese work on poetics and the first major landmark of Kannada literature.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 11, 223. Date approximate, mid-9th century

milestones.detail: Mahaviracharya, author of the Ganitasarasamgraha — the most celebrated Indian arithmetic treatise of the age — flourished at the court of Amoghavarsha I.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 11. Date approximate, mid-9th century

milestones.detail: Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyar chiefs, founding the imperial Chola line that would dominate the south for four centuries.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.text: Sulaiman's account of the king of Juzr
milestones.detail: An Arab account composed in A.D. 851 and attributed to the merchant Sulaiman describes Bhoja I, 'king of Juzr', as maintaining the finest cavalry in India, the greatest foe of the Muhammadan faith among Indian princes, and ruler of the country safest from robbers — testimony to the Pratihara bulwark against Arab expansion from Sindh.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 32

milestones.detail: In c. A.D. 855-56 the rule of the Karkota dynasty of Kashmir came to an end and Avantivarman (855/56-883), founder of the Utpala dynasty, took the throne, devoting his reign to economic recovery and patronising Anandavardhana and Ratnakara.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 116-117, 510 (chronology, c. 855-856)

milestones.detail: Avantivarman's engineer-minister Suyya cleared the boulder-choked bed of the Vitasta (Jhelum), embanked the river, and shifted its confluence with the Sindhu, draining the flood-lands of the Valley so that grain output soared and prices fell — Kalhana's most remarkable account of public works.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 117, 244. Date approximate, within Avantivarman's reign (855/56-883)

milestones.text: Kallar-Lalliya founds the Hindu Shahi dynasty
milestones.detail: The Brahmana minister Kallar, identified with Kalhana's Lalliya Shahi, overthrew the last Turkish Shahi of Kabul in the second half of the ninth century; after Kabul fell to the Saffarid Ya'qub ibn Layth in A.D. 870, Lalliya fixed his capital at Udabhanda (Und) on the Indus.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 112

milestones.text: Aditya I begins the Chola ascent
milestones.detail: Aditya I succeeded Vijayalaya; by 897 he had defeated and killed the last Pallava, Aparajita, and annexed Tondaimandalam.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.detail: Amoghavarsha I died about A.D. 878 after a 64-year reign of peace-loving statesmanship and patronage of letters, and was succeeded by his son Krishna II (Akalavarsha), whose reign was full of wars.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 11, 511 (chronology, c. 878). Sastri (block 143) gives 880

milestones.text: Death of Bhoja I; Mahendrapala extends the empire east
milestones.detail: Bhoja I probably died about A.D. 885 and was succeeded by Mahendrapala I, who not only kept the vast empire intact but conquered Magadha and part of northern Bengal soon after his accession, his records stretching from Kathiawar to North Bengal — 'from the Himalayas to the Vindhyas'.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 33 (accession c. 885; eastern conquests dated by records of regnal years 2-19)

milestones.text: Rajashekhara at the court of Mahendrapala
milestones.detail: The poet Rajashekhara, guru of the Pratihara emperor Mahendrapala I, flourished at Kannauj about A.D. 900; his Kavyamimamsa gives invaluable glimpses of the life, letters and geography of the age and celebrates the grandeur of the imperial city.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 33

milestones.detail: Parantaka I succeeded Aditya I in A.D. 907 — a date so securely fixed that it is called the bed-rock of Chola chronology — and in a 46-year reign of incessant campaigning built the Chola kingdom into an empire.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 154

milestones.detail: Before his 54th regnal year the Pala king had "recovered North Bengal and South Bihar from the Pratiharas", ending Mahendrapala's eastern gains and restoring the Ganga valley from Munger westward to Pala rule.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 53

milestones.detail: The Rashtrakuta emperor stormed the Pratihara capital — the deepest southern blow of the tripartite struggle.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.text: The Uttaramerur constitution of village self-government
milestones.detail: Two inscriptions of Parantaka I at the Brahmana village of Uttaramerur, of A.D. 919 and 921, record the sabha's resolutions fixing appointment to its executive committees (variyams) by a mixed method of lot and election — the classic charter of Chola village self-government.
milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 252 (records of A.D. 919 and 921); The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 248-249

milestones.text: Parantaka I gilds the Chidambaram shrine
milestones.detail: Parantaka I, a devoted Saiva and builder of many temples, provided the Nataraja shrine at Chidambaram with a roof of gold, an act remembered in his title 'who covered with gold the hall of Siva'.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 155. Date approximate, within Parantaka's reign (907-953)

milestones.detail: An inscribed pillar from Dinajpur names a 'lord of Gauda' of the Kamboja family, and a Kamboja line of Rajyapala, Narayanapala and Nayapala ruled North and West Bengal with imperial titles — probably a Pala official who carved out an independent kingdom during Pala weakness.
milestones.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 54. Date disputed: the pillar's date has been read as Saka 888, but HCIP assigns both records to the latter half of the 10th century

milestones.detail: Tailapa II took Manyakheta and founded the Western Chalukya empire of Kalyani, ending the dynasty Arab travellers had counted among the four great empires of the world.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.detail: The accession of Rajaraja I opened the Chola imperial century: Kerala, Lanka, the Gangavadi and finally the seas to Srivijaya.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.detail: Rajaraja I sacked Anuradhapura and annexed northern Lanka — the end of a royal city inhabited since the fourth century BCE.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.detail: In AD 1000 Rajaraja I ordered a great survey and assessment of the land of the Chola empire, the basis of the revenue system recorded in his Thanjavur inscriptions and the administrative backbone of Chola imperial government.
milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 235; chronology p. 868

milestones.text: Didda's reign ends; the Loharas take Kashmir
milestones.detail: Queen Didda, who had dominated Kashmir as regent and sovereign since 958, died in 1003, and the throne passed to her nephew Samgramaraja, first king of the Lohara dynasty — whose minister Tunga would soon be fighting Mahmud beside the last Shahis.
milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 97; chronology p. 868 (980-1003)

milestones.detail: In 1006 the Sailendra king Mara-Vijayottungavarman of Srivijaya founded a Buddhist monastery, the Chudamani-vihara, at Negapatam, endowed with a village by Rajaraja I — a monument to the friendly maritime intercourse that preceded the Chola-Srivijaya war of 1025.
milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 239; chronology p. 868

milestones.detail: Rajaraja I completed the great granite temple at Thanjavur, the largest in India at its consecration and still the emblem of Chola power.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.detail: Rajaraja I, architect of the Chola empire, died in 1014, two years after associating his son Rajendra in the government (1012); the transition passed without a tremor, and Rajendra carried the empire to its widest bounds.
milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 235-236, 239; chronology p. 869

milestones.detail: The Chola monarchs sent embassies, part diplomatic and part commercial, to Sung China, which reached that country in 1016, 1033 and 1077 — the war with Srivijaya (1025) falling between the first and second missions over control of the China sea-route.
milestones.source: Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, p. 177 (embassy years 1016, 1033, 1077)

milestones.text: The conquest of Lanka is complete
milestones.detail: Rajendra I captured Mahinda V, last king of Anuradhapura; the whole island passed under Chola administration for half a century.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.detail: Mahmud of Ghazni took the imperial city almost unopposed; Rajyapala’s flight broke the Pratihara empire and reordered northern India.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.detail: The Chola expedition defeated Mahipala of Bengal and carried Ganga water south to consecrate Gangaikonda Cholapuram, the new imperial capital.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.text: The Chola fleet sails to Srivijaya
milestones.detail: Rajendra I’s navy raided Kadaram and the ports of Srivijaya across the Bay of Bengal — the one great overseas expedition in Indian dynastic history.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.detail: About 1025 Rajendra I raised, in the new capital city he had founded to commemorate his march to the Ganga, a second colossal Siva temple to stand beside his father's at Tanjore. Built within a quarter of a century, it fundamentally resembles the great conception of Rajaraja, and beside it Rajendra dug the Cholagangam, the vast irrigation tank filled with water brought from the Ganga by his returning army. Gangaikondacholapuram remained the imperial Chola capital from Rajendra's day until the end of the line.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 620: "About A.D. 1025 Rajendra Chola constructed another stupendous monument in his new capital city of Gangaikondacholapuram. Built within a quarter of a century, it resembles fundamentally the great conception of his father." (The Cholagangam tank and the founding of the city are at printed p. 238.)

milestones.text: Extinction of the Hindu Shahi dynasty
milestones.detail: The house that had held the gate of India against Ghazni for more than twenty-five years came to an end in the 1020s. Trilochanapala, beaten on the Rahib, tried to reach the Chandella Vidyadhara and was killed on the road by Hindus; his son Bhimapala, who had escaped from Sharva when Mahmud plundered the fort in 1019, survived him five years without ever holding royal position, and the entire Shahi kingdom passed into Mahmud's dominions. Al-Biruni, who knew them, wrote the epitaph, and Kalhana echoed it a century later.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 17: "His son Bhimapala, who had obviously effected his escape from Sharva at the time when Mahmud plundered the fort in A.D. 1019, survived him for five years without holding any royal position. The entire Shahi kingdom now formed a part of Mahmud's dominions... Al-Blruni remarks with a note of pathos: “The Hindu Sahiya dynasty is now extinct, and of the whole house there is no longer the slightest remnant in existence.”" (Note: HCIP places Trilochanapala's death about 1021-22 and Bhimapala's five surviving years after it, so c. 1026 is a reconstruction. Coordinates are for Nandana in the Salt Range, the last Shahi capital.)

milestones.detail: The Ghaznavid army stormed the temple of Somnath on the Saurashtra coast; the raid echoed through Indian memory for nine centuries.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.detail: Under Bhima I the Solanki style reached its supreme expression in the Sun temple at Modhera, with its sacred kunda, kirti-torana and 'magnificent pile of pillared splendour'; an inscribed date of VS 1083 (AD 1026-27) conventionally fixes it in the very years after Mahmud's Somnath raid.
milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 594-595 (11th century); precise date 1026-27 conventional, from inscription

milestones.text: Al-Biruni completes his study of India
milestones.detail: About 1030 Al-Biruni, who had travelled north-western India in Mahmud's train and saw Kannauj already in ruins, completed his Tahqiq-i-Hind, the profoundest survey of Indian science, religion and society written by any foreign observer of the age.
milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 17, 50 (his testimony 'some time before AD 1030'); composition c. 1030

milestones.detail: Mahmud died at Ghazni in 1030 after some seventeen Indian expeditions; his raids left Thanesar, Mathura, Kannauj and Somnath 'smoking ruins' but no empire beyond the Punjab, which his weaker successors held from Lahore.
milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 16, 22, 92; chronology p. 869

milestones.detail: The Chandella temple-city of Khajuraho culminated in the Kandariya Mahadeva, whose sikhara clustered with miniature replicas is the most emphatic expression of the central Indian mode; dated inscriptions at the site run from 953 to 1001 and the usual chronology placing the Kandariya c. 1030 is admittedly tentative.
milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 564-565 (chronology tentative), 657; date c. 1030 conventional

milestones.text: Vimala Vasahi completed on Mount Abu
milestones.detail: In 1031, within seven years of Mahmud's demolition of Somnath, the minister Vimala of the Porwad caste completed the marble Adinatha temple (Vimala Vasahi) at Dilwara on Mount Abu — 'unique in the world' for its delicate carving, and read by tradition as Gujarat's answer to the Muslim sack.
milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 428; chronology p. 870

milestones.text: Death of Mahipala I and the accession of Nayapala
milestones.detail: Mahipala I died about 1038 after a reign of nearly half a century, having recovered his ancestral dominions, saved the Pala kingdom from ruin and restored much of its old glory against the twin pressure of the Kalachuris and the Cholas. HCIP calls him the founder of the second Pala Empire and the greatest Pala emperor since Devapala — the one whose name alone survives in the popular ballads of Bengal. He rebuilt and repaired hundreds of shrines at Sarnath, Bodh-Gaya and Nalanda. His son Nayapala inherited a kingdom reaching west to Magadha and at once faced Kalachuri invasion.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 27: "After the death of Mahipala I in c. A.D. 1038 his son Nayapala ascended the throne. Nayapala's kingdom extended on the west up to Magadha, beyond which lay the kingdom of the Kalachuris of Tripurl." (The assessment of Mahipala is at printed p. 26: 'Mahipala may justly be regarded as the founder of the second Pala Empire.')

milestones.text: Karna ends Pratihara rule at Allahabad
milestones.detail: The last territorial remnant of the Gurjara-Pratihara empire disappeared in the 1040s. After Mahmud razed Bari in 1021 the dynasty survived only as lords of the Allahabad region under Yasahpala — a survival attested by Gangeyadeva's inability to push west of Banaras before 1034. Some time after 1037 the Kalachuri Karna wrested Allahabad from Yasahpala and annexed it; HCIP notes that Allahabad was the only country Karna ever permanently added to his paternal kingdom. With that, the imperial house of Kannauj vanished from the map entirely.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 62: "He wrested Allahabad from Pratihara Yasahpala some time after A.D. 1037 and, in course of conquest, reached the Kira country where he won a victory over the Muslims." (Note: HCIP gives only 'some time after A.D. 1037', so the year is approximate. Yasahpala's hold on Allahabad before 1034 is at printed p. 61; Karna's gain of Allahabad alone is at printed p. 63.)

milestones.text: The fall of Mas'ud I and the Ghaznavid crisis
milestones.detail: Mas'ud I paid for wasting his strength in Hindustan. Hard pressed by the Saljuqs in 1040, he abandoned Ghazni for India with his family, his blind brother Muhammad and his treasure; in the pass of Marigala his Turkish and Hindu slaves revolted, took him prisoner and proclaimed Muhammad king, and Mas'ud was slain in the fort of Giri the same year. His son Maudud came down from Balkh, destroyed Muhammad at Nangrahar, killed his brother Nami at Multan, and inherited the Punjab when his brother Majdud was found poisoned at Lahore on the eve of battle. Ghaznavid India was never again ruled from a secure Ghazni.
milestones.region: The Punjab and the north-west passes
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 93: "In A.D. 1040, being hard pressed by the Saljuqs, he left Ghazni and proceeded towards Hindustan with his family, including his blind brother Muhammad, and treasure. On his way, in the pass of Marigala, his Turkish and Hindu slaves revolted, took him prisoner, and declared Muhammad as king. In the same year Mas'ud was slain in the fort of Girl." (Note: coordinates are approximate, for the Margalla pass near Taxila.)

milestones.text: Atisha Dipankara sets out for Tibet
milestones.detail: The great Vikramashila master Atisha Dipankara, who had worked at Somapura translating Bhavaviveka into Tibetan, passed through Nepal in c. 1039 on his way to Tibet, where his mission renewed Buddhist learning and founded the Kadampa tradition.
