milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 45 (Nepal, c. 1039), 415; departure c. 1040-42

milestones.text: Death of Rajendra I; Rajadhiraja's ashvamedha
milestones.detail: Rajendra I, conqueror of Lanka, the Ganga and Kadaram, died in 1044 after a thirty-two-year reign; his son Rajadhiraja, co-regent since 1018, marked his full sovereignty by performing a horse-sacrifice the same year.
milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 236, 240-241; chronology pp. 869-870 (1012-1044; 1044 ashvamedha)

milestones.detail: Bhoja Paramara, warrior-king and polymath credited with more than twenty-three works including the Samarangana-sutradhara, patron of Dhanapala and founder of schools and of the city of Bhojapura, died c. 1055 as enemy armies closed on Malwa — mourned in the verse that with him gone 'Dhara is without support.'
milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 66-67, 331; chronology p. 870 (c. 1055)

milestones.detail: The majestic Lingaraja at Bhubaneswar, shrine of Siva Tribhuvanesvara from whom the city takes its name, represents the Orissan Nagara temple 'in its full maturity'; it is conventionally assigned to the mid-11th century under the later Somavamsis, the precise date being unrecorded.
milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 547-549; date c. 1060 conventional

milestones.text: Anmakonda granted to the Kakatiya Prola I
milestones.detail: The seed of the Kakatiya kingdom was a war-grant. Prola I, a Mahamandalesvara under Somesvara I Trailokyamalla of Kalyana, fought for his overlord against the Nagas of Chakrakota, the Silaharas of Konkana and the chiefs of Kadparti, and killed Gonna of Purakuta in battle. In recognition of that service he 'obtained permanently from king Trailokyamalla, by way of grant, Anmakonda-vishaya' — the country round Hanamkonda in the Warangal district. His son Beta II moved his capital there, built the Sivapuri tank and a temple in his own name, and within a century Anmakonda's lords were the sovereigns of Telangana.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 198: "Probably in recognition of this military service he “obtained permanently from king Trailokyamalla, by way of grant, Anmakonda-vishaya,” the country round Hanamkonda, in the Warangal Taluk" (Note: HCIP dates only Somesvara I's reign, 1043-1068, so the year of the grant is approximate. Corroborated at printed p. 172; Beta II's capital at printed p. 199.)

milestones.text: The Brahmesvara temple built by queen Kolavati
milestones.detail: The Bhubaneswar inscription of Uddyotakesari's eighteenth regnal year records that his mother Kolavati, born of the solar line, built the temple of Brahmesvara at Ekamra (Bhubaneswar) — a securely dated landmark (c. 1058-60) on the road to the Lingaraja.
milestones.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 211 (18th year of Uddyotakesari, r. c. 1055-80)

milestones.text: The college, hostel and hospital at Tirumukkudal
milestones.detail: An inscription of 1067, in the reign of Virarajendra, records the endowment at Tirumukkudal in Chingleput of a Vedic college with a hostel and a hospital attached. The medical staff comprised two doctors, two nurses and others; there were beds for fifteen in-patients, and water scented with cardamom and khas-khas root was fetched for them from Perambalur. It is the fullest surviving account of an endowed hospital in medieval India, and one of a chain of Chola foundations that includes the 340-student college at Ennayiram of about 1025 and the college at Tribhuvani of 1048.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 242: "An inscription of A.D. 1067 mentions the provision made for a Vedic college with a hostel and hospital at Tirumukkudal (Chingleput District), and the medical staff consisted of two doctors, two nurses and others. There were beds for fifteen in-patients, and water scented with cardamoms and Khas Khas (cus cus) roots was brought from Perambalur" (Ennayiram at printed p. 240; Tribhuvani at printed p. 241.)

milestones.text: Death of Somesvara I by drowning in the Tungabhadra
milestones.detail: Somesvara I Ahavamalla, who had fought the Cholas for a quarter of a century and yielded to them on many occasions without ever losing a province, ended by drowning himself. Suffering from an incurable fever, he had challenged Virarajendra to meet him again at Kudal-Sangamam in 1067 and then failed to appear; the Chola army waited a month, overran Rattapadi, planted a pillar of victory on the Tungabhadra and insulted his effigy. HCIP records his death in March 1068 and the Chola account that the fever 'subsequently led to his suicide by drowning in the Tungabhadra'. His four sons had all held governorships; the eldest, Somesvara II, succeeded, and the second, Vikramaditya VI, would take the throne eight years later.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 241: "the Chola army returned home after erecting a pillar of victory on the banks of the Tungabhadra and offering insults to the effigy of Somesvara, who was then suffering from an incurable fever which subsequently led to his suicide by drowning in the Tungabhadra." (Note: HCIP states at printed p. 173 that he 'died in March, 1068'. Coordinates are an approximate point on the Tungabhadra.)

milestones.text: Extinction of the Vijayalaya line of Cholas
milestones.detail: Virarajendra's son Adhirajendra, who had ruled with his father from 1068, reigned alone only a few months. His unnatural death in a popular commotion, and the accession of the Eastern Chalukya prince Rajendra as Kulottunga I, ended the male line of Vijayalaya that had held Tanjore since the ninth century. HCIP calls the confusion of these months hard to explain: Vikramaditya VI intervened to place Adhirajendra on the throne and then withdrew; Adhirajendra died in the rebellion that followed; Kulottunga, three-quarters Chola by blood through two descents from Rajaraja I, took the crown and founded the Chalukya-Chola dynasty that ruled until 1271.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 242: "Virarajendra I was succeeded by his son Adhirajendra, who ruled from A.D. 1068 to 1070 with his father, and only for a few months as a sole monarch. His unnatural death and the accession of Kulottunga I resulted m the extinction of the Vijayalaya line." (The descent of Kulottunga is at printed p. 242; the Chalukya-Chola tenure to 1271 at printed p. 204.)

milestones.detail: The Eastern Chalukya prince Rajendra took the Chola throne as Kulottunga I, joining Vengi to the Chola empire and founding the Later Chola line that ruled for two more centuries.
milestones.source: Cross-referenced against Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, and the Chola Empire literature (Aug 2026).

milestones.text: Death of al-Hujwiri, Data Ganj Bakhsh, at Lahore
milestones.detail: Three centuries after the first Muslim settlements on the Indian coast, the Ghaznavid conquest of the Punjab produced the first Indian Sufis. Shaikh Isma'il of Lahore was the first; he was followed by Shaikh 'Ali bin 'Usman al-Hujwairi, known as Data Ganj Bakhsh, who died at Lahore in 1072. He wrote the Kashf al-Mahjub, the earliest Persian treatise on Sufism composed in India, and HCIP describes him as the founder of the Sufi cult in India. His tomb at Lahore became one of the most popular Muslim shrines in the Punjab.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 467: "He was followed by Shaikh ‘Ali bin ‘Usman al-Hujwairi, better known under his sobriquet of Data Ganj Bakhsh, who died in A.D. 1072 and whose tomb at Lahore is one of the most popular Muslim shrines in the Punjab. He was the author of several works, the best known of which is the Kashf al-Mahjub, and might be described as the founder of the Sufi cult in India"

milestones.text: End of the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi
milestones.detail: The dynasty that had ruled Andhra since the seventh century ended in 1076. Vijayaditya VII, who had usurped the Vengi throne from his half-brother Rajaraja I and been twice rescued by Chola arms, was ruined by the Kalachuri raid of 1073 and by the demand of his own nephew Kulottunga I for the throne of Andhra. He surrendered the country and took refuge with the Ganga Rajaraja I of Kalinganagara, who gave him a corner of his kingdom to rule. Kulottunga annexed Andhra to the Chola empire in 1076 and set his sons over it as viceroys — the union of the two crowns that Vikramaditya VI spent his life trying to break.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 204: "He surrendered the Andhra country to Kulottunga and took shelter with the Ganga Rajaraja I of Kalinganagara, who allowed him to rule over a small territory on the western part of his kingdom. Kulottunga annexed the Andhra country to the Chola empire in A.D. 1076." (Corroborated at printed p. 243: 'After the death or ejection of Vijayaditya VII Eastern Chalukya in A.D. 1076, Kulottunga appointed his sons as viceroys of Vengi.')

milestones.detail: Immediately after seizing the throne, Vikramaditya VI abolished the Saka reckoning at his court and started a new era named after himself, the Chalukya-Vikrama era of 1076 — a rare imperial assertion imitated across the Deccan for half a century.

Anantavarman Chodaganga, son of the Eastern Ganga Rajaraja I and of the Chola princess Rajasundari, daughter of Kulottunga I, was anointed king in 1078 and reigned for seventy-two years. He survived Karunakara's Chola conquest of northern Kalinga in the 1080s, restored and then supplanted the fallen lords of Utkala, took tribute as far as the Ganga in the east, and by 1112 had ended independent Somavamsi rule in lower Orissa. His accession begins the imperial Ganga age that would raise the great temples of Puri and Konarak.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 205: "Anantavarman Chodaganga was anointed king in A.D. 1078." (His absorption of Utkala and the end of Somavamsi rule are at printed p. 212.)

milestones.detail: Udayaditya, the brother or cousin of Bhoja who recovered Malava from its conquerors, built the temple of Nilakanthesvara at Udayapur in the Bhilsa country. It is the great surviving monument of Paramara Saivism — Bhoja himself had been not merely a follower but an exponent of the faith, and the author of the Tattvaprakasa — and one of the finest examples of the Bhumija sikhara in central India. Udayaditya's inscriptions run from 1080 to 1086 and his kingdom reached from Nimar to Jhalawar and Bhilsa.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 443: "His brother or cousin Udayaditya built the Nilakanthesvara temple at Udayapur. The later Paramaras were also adherents of Saivism." (Note: HCIP gives no date for the temple; Udayaditya's dated inscriptions are 1080 and 1086, printed p. 68, so the year is approximate.)

milestones.detail: The Kashmirian poet Bilhana, court laureate (vidyapati) of Vikramaditya VI at Kalyani, composed the Vikramankadevacharita, a mahakavya glorifying his patron's battles and pleasures — with Kalhana's work, the summit of the Sanskrit historical kavya.
milestones.source: HCIP V, pp. 177, 307; composed c. 1085 (approximate, within Vikramaditya's reign)

milestones.text: The eight hill kings assemble at Srinagar
milestones.detail: Kashmir's hegemony over the western Himalaya was displayed in 1087, when the rulers of eight hill states assembled in Kalasa's capital: Kirtti of Baddhapura, Asata of Champa (Chamba), Kalasa of Vallapura, Samgramapala of Rajapuri, Utkarsha of Lohara, Sangata of Urasa, Gambhirasiha of Kanda and Uttamaraja of Kashthavata. Kalasa, whom his father Ananta had thought worthless, had twice sent armies to protect the young king of Rajapuri, conquered Urasa and raided across the Kishanganga; HCIP judges his foreign policy a conspicuous success even as his household destroyed him.
milestones.region: Kashmir and the western Himalayan hill states
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 98: "In A.D. 1087 the rulers of eight hill states, viz. Kirtti of Baddhapura (?), Asata of Champa (Chamba), Kalasa of Vallapura, Samgramapala of Rajapuri, Utkarsha of Lohara, Sangata (?) of Urasa, Gambhirasiha of Kanda, and Uttamaraja of Kashthavata assembled in his capital."

milestones.detail: The Gahadavala dynasty established itself at Kannauj, restoring settled rule to the Ganga heartland after seventy years of fragmentation.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.text: Harsha seizes the throne of Kashmir
milestones.detail: Kalasa died in 1089 after his ministers had fetched his second son Utkarsha from Lohara and inaugurated him king. Within days Utkarsha had alienated the ministers; his step-brother Vijayamalla revolted and stormed the palace, and Utkarsha released his imprisoned brother Harsha to win his support. Harsha joined the rebels instead, took the throne for himself and imprisoned Utkarsha, who killed himself in captivity. Harsha's twelve-year reign began with energy and prosperity and ended in famine, systematic plunder of temple property and his own violent death — the reign Kalhana would make the tragic centrepiece of the Rajatarangini.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 99: "In order to secure the support of Harsha he released him, but Harsha joined Vijayamalla, captured the throne for himself, and took Utkarsha prisoner. Utkarsha committed suicide in his captivity." (The temple plunder, the famine of 1099 and Harsha's death in 1101 are at printed p. 99.)

milestones.text: The Turushkadanda appears in Gahadavala charters
milestones.detail: From 1090 onward the inscriptions of the Gahadavalas of Kannauj mention a tax called the Turushkadanda, the 'Turk-levy'. Scholars have read it two ways: as an impost on the subjects to meet the cost of resisting Muslim invasion, or as the money by which the Gahadavalas paid annual tribute to the Sultans of Ghazni. HCIP prefers the second reading, since Chandradeva appears to have owed his throne partly to the favour of the Ghaznavid prince Mahmud — and it suggests the periodic Muslim expeditions into northern India were sent to enforce payment.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 51: "The inscriptions of the Gahadavalas, dating from A.D. 1090, mention a tax called Turushkadanda. Some suggest that it was an impost on the subjects of the Gahadavalas to meet the expenses of resisting the invasion of the Muslims. Others think that the Gahadavala kings realised this tax from the people in order to make annual payment of tribute to the Sultans of Ghazni."

milestones.text: Chandradeva takes Banaras and Allahabad; Kasi becomes the second Gahadavala capital
milestones.detail: Chandradeva, whose dated inscriptions run from 1090 to 1100, did not stop at Kannauj. He conquered all the country from Allahabad to Banaras from the Kalachuri Yasahkarna of Dahala, and made Banaras the second capital of the Gahadavalas — the beginning of the Kasi kingdom that lasted a century until Muhammad of Ghur. He claimed to be the protector of the holy places of Kusika, Kasi, Uttara-Kosala and Indrasthana; his advance east was checked only by Bhimayasas of Magadha.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 52: "The inscriptions of Chandradeva, the dates of which range from A.D. 1090 to 1100, prove that he was in possession of Kanauj, Banaras, and Ayodhya. He conquered all the countries from Allahabad to Banaras from the Kalachuri Yasahkarna, king of Dahala. Banaras (Kasi) was made the second capital of the Gahadavalas." (Note: HCIP gives only the inscription range 1090-1100, so the year is approximate.)

milestones.detail: Karna of Gujarat — who had killed Paramara Jayasimha and briefly held Malava, subdued the Bhilla chief Asa at Asapalli near modern Ahmedabad, and married Mayanalladevi, daughter of the Kadamba Jayakesin of Goa — was succeeded about 1094 by his minor son Jayasimha, with his mother acting as regent. Jayasimha, who took the title Siddharaja, became the greatest king of his line: his kingdom would reach Bali in Jodhpur and Sambhar in Jaipur, Bhilsa in the east and Kutch and Kathiawar in the west, and he would take the Paramara Naravarman prisoner after a twelve-year war and annex the whole of Malava.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 75: "He married MayanalladevI, the daughter of the Kadamba Jayakesin, king of Goa, and was succeeded by his minor son Jayasimha in c. A.D. 1094. MayanalladevI acted as a regent for her son for some time."

milestones.text: Accession of Vijayasena and the rise of the Senas
milestones.detail: Hemantasena, who had consolidated the family's position in Radha in the troubled years after the Kalachuri Karna's occupation and who is called 'the skilful protector of kings' — perhaps for sheltering Surapala and Ramapala when they escaped the Kaivarta prison — was succeeded by his son Vijayasena about 1095. Vijayasena would be the greatest king of the Sena dynasty: allying with Anantavarman Chodaganga, he made his bid for the whole of Bengal as the Pala kingdom disintegrated after Ramapala's death, and supplanted them in Gauda.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 36: "He was succeeded by his son Vijayasena in c. A.D. 1095. Vijayasena was the greatest king of the Sena dynasty."

milestones.text: Ramanuja takes refuge at the Hoysala court
milestones.detail: Ramanuja, born about 1016-17 and successor of Yamunacharya at Srirangam, was persecuted in his later years by a Chola prince of the Saiva faith. HCIP records that he took refuge in 1096 at the court of the Hoysala prince Vishnuvardhana, whom he converted to Vaishnavism, and that he lived in Mysore more than twenty years before he could return. It is the decisive migration in the history of Srivaishnavism: it carried the Visishtadvaita — the qualified monism of chit, achit and Isvara set out in his commentary on the Brahma-sutra — into the Kannada country, and turned the Hoysalas into its patrons.
milestones.source: HCIP V, printed p. 437: "As a result Ramanuja is said to have taken refuge in A.D. 1096 at the court of the Hoysala prince Vishnuvardhana whom he converted to Vaishnavism." (Ramanuja's birth in Saka 938 = A.D. 1016-17 is on the same page; his death about 1137 at printed p. 438; the persecution and twenty-year exile at printed p. 404.)

milestones.detail: The Karnata dynasty of Mithila — this atlas’s Tirhut — began on a date preserved exactly on the Simraungadh stone pillar.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.detail: On the death of his elder brother Ballala I, Bittiga (better known by his title Vishnuvardhana) became Hoysala king. HCIP V calls him 'the real maker of the Hoysala kingdom': over the next thirty years he conquered Gangavadi and much of Nolambavadi, built Belur and Halebid, and turned a hill chiefdom into the dominant power of southern Karnataka.
Loiyumba’s written constitution, the Loiyumba Shinyen, organised the Meitei state — the administrative foundation Manipur carries into the modern era.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.detail: Jayangondar, court poet of Kulottunga I, composed the Kalingattupparani on the 1110 Kalinga war of the general Karunakara Tondaiman, a war-poem unflinching about both the bright and seamy sides of battle and a landmark of Tamil literature.
milestones.source: HCIP V, p. 243; composed shortly after the 1110 war, c. 1112 (approximate)

milestones.detail: The Hoysala king drove the Cholas from Talakad, the victory that made his house a Deccan power and filled Karnataka with its star-shaped temples.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.detail: The Hoysala Vishnuvardhana founded the Chenna Kesava (Vijayanarayana) temple at Belur, dating from 1117 in the flush of his Gangavadi conquests — the masterpiece that inaugurated the star-planned, sculptor-dominated Hoysala style continued at Halebid.

milestones.text: The Eastern Gangas annex all of Orissa
milestones.detail: Anantavarman Chodaganga completed the absorption of Utkala (Orissa) into his Kalinga kingdom, and from this point the Ganga kings added 'lord of Utkala' to their older title 'lord of Trikalinga'. His realm now ran from the Ganga to the Godavari, and he founded the great Jagannatha temple at Puri.

milestones.text: Ramapala drowns himself in the Ganga
milestones.detail: Broken by the news that his beloved maternal uncle and chief ally Mathanadeva of Anga had died, the last great Pala emperor drowned himself in the Ganga near Monghyr. He had spent a lifetime rebuilding a shattered dynasty; within a generation of his death almost everything he recovered was lost to the Senas, the Gahadavalas and the Gangas.

Vijnaneshvara, writing at Kalyani while 'king Vikramarka' (Vikramaditya VI) ruled, completed the Mitakshara, a digest-commentary on the Yajnavalkya-smriti that became the paramount authority on Hindu property and inheritance law in courts across India (outside Bengal) into the twentieth century.
milestones.source: HCIP V, pp. 332-333, 177; dated c. 1100-1120 (Kane) or 1118-27 (Rangaswami Aiyangar) — disputed

milestones.detail: Kulottunga Chola I, the Chalukya-Chola who ruled for fifty years, ordered Domesday-style land surveys (1086, 1110) and abolished tolls, died; his son Vikrama Chola, already co-ruler since 1118, became sole ruler of a Chola empire shorn of Ceylon, Gangavadi and Vengi.
milestones.source: HCIP V, pp. 242, 244-245 (reign 1070-1120; some scholars extend to 1122)

milestones.detail: Basava, the organiser of the Virasaiva or Lingayat movement, was born into a Brahmana family at Ingaleshwar-Bagevadi in the Bijapur country. He refused the sacred-thread ceremony, later became chief minister to the Kalachuri king Bijjala of Kalyana, and founded the Anubhava Mantapa, an academy of religious experience that produced the vachana literature of Kannada.

milestones.text: Death of Pala Kumarapala; Gopala III succeeds
milestones.detail: Ramapala's son Kumarapala died leaving a kingdom already coming apart: petty chiefs in Magadha had declared themselves kings, the Gahadavala Govindachandra had taken western Magadha, and the Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga had overrun south-west Bengal. His son Gopala III ruled for fourteen troubled years and died an unexplained, unnatural death.

Vikramaditya VI Tribhuvanamalla, greatest of the Kalyani Chalukyas, patron of Bilhana and Vijnaneshvara and master of the Deccan from the Narmada to the Tungabhadra for fifty years, died in 1126; his son Somesvara III succeeded, and the Cholas promptly recovered Vengi.

milestones.text: Somesvara III Bhulokamalla succeeds Vikramaditya VI
milestones.detail: The son of the great Vikramaditya VI took the Chalukya throne of Kalyana. Nicknamed Sarvajna-bhupa, the all-knowing king, he was a scholar rather than a soldier: he compiled the encyclopaedic Manasollasa but had to surrender the Andhra country to the Cholas and watch his Hoysala vassal Vishnuvardhana grow ever stronger.

Madanavarman came to the throne of Jejakabhukti (Bundelkhand) and ruled until 1163, one of the longest Chandella reigns. He seized the Bhilsa region from the Paramaras, fought the Gahadavala Govindachandra and the Kalachuri Gayakarna, and successfully defended Mahoba when Jayasimha Siddharaja of Gujarat invaded, though he had to give up Bhilsa.

The scholar-emperor Somesvara III 'Sarvajna-chakravarti' composed the Manasollasa (Abhilashitartha-chintamani), a vast Sanskrit encyclopaedia of statecraft, cuisine, music, medicine and the arts — a unique window on twelfth-century courtly life.

milestones.text: Kulottunga II installed on the Chola throne
milestones.detail: Vikrama Chola's son was formally installed in 1133 and became sole ruler on his father's death about 1135. His short reign is remembered less for war than for the rebuilding of the Nataraja temple at Chidambaram — and for his religious intolerance: he had the Vaishnava image of Govindaraja thrown into the sea, which Vaishnava tradition repaid by remembering him as the leprous 'Krimikantha' Chola.

The Chola emperor who had exploited Vikramaditya VI's death to win back Vengi and parts of Gangavadi died about 1135. His reign saw floods and famine in the Arcot country about 1125, lavish gifts to Chidambaram in 1128, and a medical school at Tiruvaduturai teaching the Charaka and Vagbhata compendia — recorded in an inscription of 1121.

The philosopher who gave Vaishnavism its intellectual armour died about 1137. His Visishtadvaita or 'qualified monism' held that souls and the material world are real attributes forming the body of the Supreme Soul — a direct answer to Sankara's doctrine that the visible world is illusion. His commentary on the Brahma-sutra made devotional religion philosophically respectable and shaped every later bhakti school.

The Hoysala king performed the Tulapurusha, the ceremony in which a ruler is weighed against gold and the gold given away. HCIP V reads it as his symbolic assumption of royal rank: still nominally a Chalukya feudatory, Vishnuvardhana was now behaving as a sovereign, with fortified capitals at Talakad in the south and Bankapura in the north.

The scholar-king Somesvara III died and his son Jagadekamalla II took the Chalukya throne of Kalyana. He inherited a revolt of the Hoysalas, the Kadambas of Goa and other vassals, put down with the help of the Sinda chief Permadideva of Erambarage, whose inscription boasts of pursuing Vishnuvardhana as far as Belupura.

The Tiruttondar-puranam or Periya Puranam, composed by Sekkilar in the reign of Kulottunga II, tells the lives of the sixty-three canonised Saiva saints. Accepted as the twelfth Tirumurai, it closed the Tamil Saiva canon and became the classic account of Tamil devotional sainthood. HCIP V assigns Sekkilar to 'the middle of the twelfth century' and Sastri places the work in Kulottunga II's reign of 1133-50.
milestones.source: HCIP V, pp. 245, 365; Sastri, A History of South India, ch. on Late Chola literature

milestones.text: Chodaganga crowns his son Kamarnava VII
milestones.detail: Anantavarman Chodaganga, by then more than sixty years on the throne of Kalinga, had his son Kamarnava VII anointed king in 1142 — an associate kingship meant to secure the succession of a realm that now stretched from the Ganga to the Godavari. Chodaganga himself lived until at least 1150; Kamarnava exercised the kingship from 1148 to 1155.

milestones.text: The disputed Chaulukya succession in Gujarat
milestones.detail: Jayasimha Siddharaja, the greatest of the Gujarat kings, closed his reign about 1143 without a son. He had refused to recognise Kumarapala, a great-grandson of Bhima I by a concubine, and adopted his minister's son Bahada instead; Kumarapala's father was killed and Kumarapala driven into exile. Between 1143 and 1145 Kumarapala nonetheless seized the throne with Jain backing and the help of his brother-in-law Krishna.

milestones.text: Madanapala, last of the Palas, takes the throne
milestones.detail: Gopala III died an unnatural death and was succeeded not by a son but by his uncle Madanapala, the youngest son of Ramapala. He fought Gahadavalas, Gangas and Senas for seventeen years, but after losing Varendra he withdrew to Anga, where he ruled until about 1161. He is the last known king of the line of Gopala and Dharmapala.

Sandhyakara Nandi, the 'Kalikala-Valmiki' of Varendra, completed the Ramacharita, a tour-de-force telling simultaneously, verse by verse, the story of Rama and the history of Ramapala's recovery of Varendra from the Kaivartas — the prime contemporary source for Pala Bengal.
milestones.source: HCIP V, pp. 31, 308; narrative ends with Madanapala (acc. 1144), so completed c. 1145 (approximate)

milestones.text: Rajaraja II joins his father on the Chola throne
milestones.detail: Kulottunga II associated his son Rajaraja II with the administration in 1146, and Rajaraja ruled in his own right until 1173. His long reign is the hinge of Chola decline: the feudatories grew stronger, and the Pandya civil war of about 1169 dragged the empire into an exhausting war with Ceylon.

Jina Vallabha, pupil of Jinesvara Suri, founded the Kharatara-gachchha at Chitrakuta (Chittorgarh) in 1147. It was the most important of a series of splits inside the Svetambara Jain community in these decades — the Anchalaka-mata followed nine years later, the Sardha-Paurnamiyaka in 1169 — and its chroniclers, notably Jinapala's Kharataragachchha-pattavali, became a major source for the political history of Rajasthan.

The Kashmirian Kalhana completed the Rajatarangini, the 'River of Kings', carrying the chronicle of Kashmir from its beginnings down to 1148-49 in the reign of Jayasimha — built from inscriptions, eulogies and family records, and without rival as a work of critical history in premodern India.
milestones.source: HCIP V, pp. 307-308 and p. 103 n. 30 (narrative closes 1148-49); conventionally dated 1148-50

milestones.detail: Jagadekamalla II's last known date is 1151, in which year his brother Taila III succeeded him at Kalyana. Taila still held Shimoga, Cuddapah and Kurnool, and before 1153 beat off attacks by Kumarapala of Gujarat and Kulottunga II of the Cholas — but his reign would end in the humiliation that destroyed the dynasty's prestige.

After a tripartite civil war in which he was at one point driven out of Polonnaruva altogether, Parakramabahu I emerged as sole king of Lanka and ruled for thirty-three years. He rebuilt Polonnaruva and Anuradhapura, reorganised the Buddhist church, and built the irrigation works that made his reign a byword for prosperity — paid for, the chronicles admit, by crushing taxation.

The king who finally broke the Damara barons and gave Kashmir nearly three decades of peace died in 1155 after a reign of thirty-two years. It was at his court that Kalhana wrote the Rajatarangini. Jayasimha exchanged embassies with the Gahadavala Govindachandra and with the Silahara Aparaditya of Konkan; his son Paramanuka and grandson Vantideva ended the Lohara line by 1172.
The Bhati capital moved from thrice-sacked Lodhruva to the golden fort on Trikuta hill.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.text: The Ghaznavids lose Ghazni for ever
milestones.detail: Shortly after 1157 the Ghuzz Turks drove Sultan Khusrav Shah out of Ghazni, and the city was never recovered by the house of Mahmud. Khusrav Shah withdrew to Lahore and ruled there until 1160. From this point the Ghaznavid state was simply a Punjab kingdom, and its fall to the Ghurids thirty years later was only a matter of time.

Vijayasena, the real founder of Sena power, was succeeded by his son Vallalasena (Ballalasena), who took the title Nihsanka-Sankara. He completed his father's work by ending the rule of Govindapala, the last claimant styling himself lord of Gauda, in 1162, and was a scholar of standing who wrote the Danasagara and began the Adbhutasagara.

Basava, minister of the Kalachuri usurper Bijjala at Kalyana, organised and inspired the Virashaiva (Lingayat) movement, preaching devotion to Shiva through the vachanas and rejecting caste and ritual — a religious and social upheaval that reshaped the Kannada country and its literature.
milestones.source: HCIP V, pp. 180-181, 367, 445-446; movement at its height c. 1160 under Bijjala (r. 1156-68)

milestones.text: Collapse of Govindapala and the end of Pala Magadha
milestones.detail: Govindapala, who styled himself lord of Gauda and ruled in the Gaya district, saw his power collapse in 1162 — a defeat Vallalasena of Bengal claimed for himself. So decisive was it that manuscripts and inscriptions afterwards dated themselves not by a reign but by years counted from 'the destruction of the kingdom of Govindapala'. Four hundred years of Pala rule were over.

milestones.text: Ghiyas-ud-din Muhammad becomes Sultan of Ghur
milestones.detail: The nephew of Ala-ud-din 'the World-burner' ascended the throne of Ghur in 1163. Ten years later he drove the Ghuzz from Ghazni and made his brother Shihab-ud-din — later famous as Muizz-ud-din Muhammad — its ruler. The partnership of these two brothers destroyed the Ghaznavids and carried Muslim power to the Ganga.

A Hanamkonda inscription of 1163 says the Chalukya emperor 'with body completely overcome by dysentery died' out of fear of the Kakatiya Rudradeva. Whatever the truth of the taunt, his death removed the last figure to whom Bijjala and the other usurping feudatories had paid even nominal allegiance, and the Deccan passed to the Kalachuris for a quarter of a century.
Rudradeva’s Anumakonda inscription is the first to drop the Chalukya overlord — Telangana’s own dynasty steps onto the map.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.text: Accession of Rajadhiraja II of the Cholas
milestones.detail: Rajaraja II's successor, another grandson of Vikrama Chola, ruled from 1163 to 1179. His achievement was to bring the ruinous Pandya civil war to a close, but by his reign the Chola empire was visibly living on the loyalty of feudatories — Telugu-Chodas, Kadavas, Banas and Sambuvarayas — who were becoming powers in their own right.

The Chaulukya Kumarapala, under the influence of the polymath Hemachandra 'Kalikala-Sarvajna' (1088-1172), embraced Jainism before 1164, banning animal slaughter and gambling across Gujarat and its dependencies — the high noon of royal Jain patronage in western India.
milestones.source: HCIP V, pp. 77-78, 345; conversion epigraphically fixed before A.D. 1164

milestones.text: Paramardi succeeds to the Chandella throne
milestones.detail: Madanavarman was succeeded by his grandson Paramardi, whose inscriptions run from 1165 to 1201; the HCIP chronology table gives the accession as about 1163. He held Jejakabhukti intact for decades and recovered Bhilsa from Gujarat, but is remembered chiefly for his defeat by Prithviraja III in 1182 and for his surrender of Kalanjara to Qutb-ud-din in 1202.

milestones.text: Bijjala abdicates in favour of Sovideva
milestones.detail: An inscription records that in 1168 the Kalachuri king Bijjala handed the throne to his son Somesvara, also called Sovideva, who had been associated in the government since about 1165. The contemporary evidence of an abdication undercuts the later Virasaiva legend that Basava had Bijjala assassinated.

The Sena king Vallalasena, pupil of Aniruddha and a Smriti scholar in his own right, completed the Danasagara, his great digest on religious gifts, in Saka 1091 (A.D. 1169), and began the Adbhutasagara, finished after his death by Lakshmanasena.

milestones.text: Death of Kumarapala and the Gujarat succession struggle
milestones.detail: The Chaulukya king who had made Gujarat the leading power of western India died in 1171-72. A fight followed between his sister's son Pratapamalla, backed by the Jains, and Ajayapala, son of his brother Mahipala, backed by the Brahmanas. Ajayapala won, and the Jain chronicles accuse him of demolishing Jain temples and executing the scholar Ramachandra.

Ghiyas-ud-din wrested Ghazni from the Ghuzz Turks in 1173 and placed his younger brother Shihab-ud-din — thereafter styled Muizz-ud-din Muhammad bin Sam — on its throne. From this base the younger brother set out to emulate Mahmud, raiding India almost every year; within twenty years his victories would put a Turkish sultanate at Delhi.

Vijaya Narasimha I died in 1173 and his son Ballala II succeeded. After twenty years of hard fighting against the Nolambas, the Kalachuris, the Kadambas and above all the Yadavas of Devagiri, he declared himself an independent sovereign in 1193, ending the Hoysalas' long formal subordination to the Chalukyas.

Sriharsha, who according to tradition lived at the court of the Gahadavala Jayachandra of Kannauj, composed the Naishadhiyacharita on the Nala-Damayanti story — reckoned the last of the great Sanskrit mahakavyas.
milestones.source: HCIP V, pp. 54, 337; within Jayachandra's reign (1170-1193), c. 1175 (approximate; court attribution 'according to some scholars')

milestones.detail: Ajayapala lost his life at the hands of the Pratihara Vayajaladeva about 1176. His young son Mularaja II succeeded, with his mother Naikidevi — daughter of the Kadamba king Paramardin of Goa — acting as regent. It was Naikidevi who two years later led the Gujarat army in person against Muizz-ud-din Muhammad.

The Chahamana Somesvara died about 1177 leaving a son still a minor; HCIP V places Prithviraja III's birth between 1162 and 1165. His mother Karpuradevi acted as regent with the minister Kadambavasa and the Kalachuri-descended general Bhuvanaikamalla, and the king took charge of the government himself in 1178.

Lakshmanasena, already a proven general against Gauda and Kalinga, ascended the Sena throne of Bengal in 1178; his court at Vikramapura and Nadia, graced by Jayadeva, Dhoyi and Halayudha, was the last great center of independent Hindu Bengal before the Turkish conquest.

Kamban, greatest of Tamil poets, who flourished in the reign of Kulottunga III, composed the Ramavataram (the Tamil Ramayanam) — no translation of Valmiki but a re-creation colored by the Chola country, and the supreme epic of Tamil literature.
milestones.source: Sastri, A History of South India, pp. 367-368 (reign of Kulottunga III, 1178-1216); traditional date c. 1178-80, disputed

milestones.detail: Jayadeva, ornament of Lakshmanasena's court, composed the Gita Govinda, the lyric cycle of Radha and Krishna that is unique in Sanskrit poetry for its novelty and completeness of effect — the fountainhead of a new genre and of centuries of Vaishnava devotional art and music.
milestones.source: HCIP V, pp. 40, 337; composed at Lakshmanasena's court (acc. 1178), c. 1185 (approximate)

milestones.detail: Mu’izz al-Din Ghuri deposed the last Ghaznavid, Khusrau Malik; the road to Delhi lay open.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.text: Death of Parakramabahu I of Ceylon
milestones.detail: The greatest of the Polonnaruva kings died after thirty-three years, and was succeeded by his sister's son Vijayabahu II, a scholar who reigned barely a year and made a treaty of friendship with the Burmese king of Pagan. Parakramabahu's death ended Ceylon's brief career as an aggressive power in south India.
The Seuna king seized Kalyani, declared sovereignty and built a new capital at Devagiri — the fortress later ages would call Daulatabad.
milestones.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and regional sources.

milestones.text: Earliest dated Vithoba shrine at Pandharpur is recorded
milestones.detail: A temple inscription dated 1189 records the establishment of a small shrine to Vithoba at the site of today’s Pandharpur temple, providing early epigraphic evidence for Vithoba worship there.
milestones.source: Pandharpur historical summary / cited epigraphic scholarship

milestones.detail: Chakradhara Swami, the philosopher and founder associated with the Mahanubhava tradition, was born.

milestones.text: Rajaraja Deva III begins rule of Eastern Ganga kingdom of Kalinga
milestones.detail: Rajaraja Deva III began ruling Eastern Ganga kingdom of Kalinga. Its territory is approximately associated with Odisha, north Andhra, parts of Bengal/Telangana/Chhattisgarh at peak. Capital or principal centres: Kalinganagara; Cuttack; Puri/Khurda later.
milestones.region: Odisha, north Andhra, parts of Bengal/Telangana/Chhattisgarh at peak

milestones.text: The Qutb Minar rises at Delhi
milestones.detail: The Qutb Minar was mostly built between 1199 and 1220: Qutb-ud-din Aibak began the tower and Iltutmish extended the early structure. Later rulers repaired and added to it, but this first construction phase created one of South Asia’s defining Indo-Islamic monuments.
Razia, the Delhi ruler remembered as one of the earliest women to exercise sovereign authority in the subcontinent, was born.
Qutb al-Din Aibak died after a polo accident and was succeeded in the Mamluk political order.

milestones.text: Ganapavaram inscription records the founding of Ganapatipura
milestones.detail: A Kakatiya-period inscription dated 1214 records the establishment of a new village named Ganapatipura and the installation of the deity Rudresvara under Ganapati Deva’s reign.
Maravarman Sundara Pandya burned the Chola capital and Uraiyur — the revenge of Madurai, and the beginning of the Chola end.
milestones.source: Cross-referenced against Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, and the Chola Empire literature (Aug 2026).

milestones.text: Yadava power absorbs the Kolhapur Shilahara realm
milestones.detail: Epigraphic evidence indicates that Simhana’s Seuna (Yadava) kingdom had annexed the Kolhapur Shilahara realm by 1217; a 1217 inscription describes him as a 'thunderbolt' to the Panhala fort.
milestones.source: Simhana historical summary, citing epigraphic scholarship

milestones.text: Kundamamba builds the Nidigonda Trikuta temple
milestones.detail: An inscription dated 1219 records that Kundamamba, sister of Kakatiya king Ganapati Deva, commissioned the Shaiva Trikuta temple at Nidigonda in present-day Jangaon district.
milestones.source: Times of India, citing Warangal District Inscriptions

milestones.text: Sultan Ghari, an early monumental Islamic tomb, is completed
milestones.detail: The mausoleum of Nasiruddin Mahmud was completed near Delhi and is generally regarded as the first monumental Islamic mausoleum built in India.
Mu'in al-Din Chishti, the Chishti Sufi teacher whose shrine at Ajmer became one of South Asia’s most important pilgrimage centres, died.
Madhvacharya, the philosopher who systematised the Dvaita school of Vedanta, was born.
Nizamuddin Auliya, the Chishti Sufi master whose Delhi khanqah became a major centre of spiritual and cultural life, was born.
Sarngadeva, the musicologist who composed the influential Sangita Ratnakara, died.

milestones.text: The Sangita Ratnakara becomes a foundational musicological text
milestones.detail: Sarngadeva’s Sanskrit treatise synthesised earlier theories of music, rhythm and dance and became a common intellectual ancestor of later Hindustani and Carnatic traditions.

milestones.text: The Konark Sun Temple is built
milestones.detail: The monumental temple complex at Konark was created as a stone chariot of the solar deity and became one of the masterpieces of Kalinga architecture.
Amir Khusrau, the poet, musician and multilingual literary innovator associated with the Delhi Sultanate and the Chishti tradition, was born.
Baba Farid, the Chishti Sufi poet whose Punjabi verses were later included in the Guru Granth Sahib, died.
Vedanta Desika, the theologian, poet and philosopher of the Sri Vaishnava tradition, was born.
Namdev, the Marathi bhakti poet-saint whose compositions circulated widely across northern and western India, was born.
Jnaneshwar, the Marathi philosopher-poet and author of the Jnaneshwari, was born.
After Kannanur Kuppam, Rajendra III vanishes from the record; the dynasty of Rajaraja and Rajendra, four centuries old, ceases to exist.
milestones.source: Cross-referenced against Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, and the Chola Empire literature (Aug 2026).

milestones.detail: Ziauddin Barani, the historian and political thinker who chronicled the Delhi Sultanate, was born.

milestones.text: The Jnaneshwari is composed in Marathi
milestones.detail: Jnaneshwar’s poetic commentary on the Bhagavad Gita helped establish Marathi as a major vehicle for philosophy and devotional literature.
Jnaneshwar, the Marathi philosopher-poet whose Jnaneshwari transformed regional devotional literature, died.

milestones.text: Siri is established as a new fortified city of Delhi
milestones.detail: The new urban centre expanded the Delhi metropolitan complex and introduced major works of hydraulic and monumental construction.
The ceremonial gateway introduced highly refined arcuate construction, calligraphy and geometric decoration into the Qutb complex.
Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani, the Sufi scholar associated with the spread of Persianate crafts and religious learning in Kashmir, was born.
Madhvacharya, the philosopher who systematised the Dvaita school of Vedanta, died.
Lal Ded, the Kashmiri mystic poet whose vakhs became foundational to Kashmiri literary and spiritual culture, was born.
The massive stone city and fort represented a new scale of planned urban and defensive architecture in the Delhi region.
Amir Khusrau, the poet, musician and multilingual literary innovator of the Delhi Sultanate, died.
Nizamuddin Auliya, the Chishti Sufi master whose Delhi shrine remains a major cultural and devotional centre, died.

milestones.text: Muhammad bin Tughluq shifts the Delhi Sultanate’s capital to Daulatabad
milestones.detail: In 1327 Muhammad bin Tughluq ordered the transfer of the capital from Delhi to Devagiri, renamed Daulatabad. The migration of courtly, scholarly and administrative groups continued over the following years before the experiment was reversed, deepening north–Deccan political and cultural links.

milestones.text: Muhammad bin Tughluq introduces copper token currency
milestones.detail: Muhammad bin Tughluq experimented with copper and brass token money assigned the face value of silver coinage. Widespread counterfeiting undermined the scheme and it was withdrawn after a short period.
milestones.source: Sarmaya — Muhammad bin Tughlaq copper tanka

milestones.detail: The Moroccan traveller entered the service of the Delhi court and later left one of the most detailed foreign descriptions of fourteenth-century India and the Indian Ocean world.
Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan, the Delhi Sultanate’s governor in Ma'bar, declared independence at Madurai in 1335, creating the short-lived Madurai Sultanate in southern Tamil country.
The new capital developed into one of the world’s largest premodern cities and a major centre of trade, temple architecture, literature and court culture.

milestones.text: Delhi abandons its campaign to reconquer Madurai
milestones.detail: Muhammad bin Tughluq’s attempt to suppress the breakaway Madurai Sultanate collapsed in 1337 amid disease and wider rebellions, leaving the far south outside direct Delhi control.
milestones.person: Muhammad bin Tughluq; Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan

milestones.text: Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah establishes independent rule at Sonargaon
milestones.detail: Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah emerged as the independent Sultan of Sonargaon in 1338, founding one of the earliest independent Muslim sultanates in Bengal with its centre in eastern Bengal.

milestones.text: Shah Mir establishes the Kashmir Sultanate
milestones.detail: Shah Mir took the throne of Kashmir in 1339, founding the Shah Mir dynasty and inaugurating the Kashmir Sultanate.
Madhava, founder of the Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics, was born. The year is an estimate; MacTutor gives a range of 1350–1425.

milestones.text: Ibn Battuta travels from Delhi through India to the Maldives and Sri Lanka
milestones.detail: After years at Muhammad bin Tughluq’s court, Ibn Battuta left Delhi in 1341 on a diplomatic mission and travelled through Daulatabad, Gujarat and Calicut before spending time in the Maldives and visiting Sri Lanka. The journey, completed by 1344, produced one of the richest eyewitness accounts of fourteenth-century South Asia.
milestones.region: Delhi / Gujarat / Kerala / Maldives / Sri Lanka
milestones.source: UC Berkeley ORIAS — The Travels of Ibn Battuta

milestones.text: A major Periyar flood is traditionally dated to 1341
milestones.detail: A major flood or deluge is traditionally dated to 1341 in the Periyar delta. Archaeological and geological reconstructions associate it with major changes around Muziris, Vypin and waterways leading to Kochi; no direct contemporary written account survives.
milestones.source: 1341 Kerala floods — historical and geological summary

milestones.detail: Hoysala ruler Veera Ballala III was captured and killed after the Battle of Kannanur.

milestones.text: End of Vira Pandyan IV's reign over Pandya kingdom / Tenkasi Pandyas
milestones.detail: The recorded reign of Vira Pandyan IV over Pandya kingdom / Tenkasi Pandyas ended. Civil-war claimant/branch
milestones.region: Madurai, southern Tamil Nadu, Tirunelveli, Ramanathapuram, parts of Kerala/Sri Lanka influence

milestones.text: A Sambhuvaraya inscription records a major temple land sale
milestones.detail: An inscription dated 27 April 1348 records residents of Puduppattinam selling the village of Mangalam for 350 pon to the temple at Tirukkalukkunram, providing a dated record of landholding and temple economy under the Sambuvarayas.
Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah, founder of the independent Sonargaon sultanate, died at Sonargaon in 1349 and was succeeded by Ikhtiyaruddin Ghazi Shah.
Namdev, the Marathi bhakti poet-saint whose verses influenced devotional traditions across several languages, died.

milestones.text: Firuz Shah Tughlaq begins a reign defined by canals and public works
milestones.detail: Firuz Shah Tughlaq took the Delhi throne in 1351 and made irrigation and public construction major features of his long reign. His government dug and restored canals, founded towns, built public institutions and repaired monuments, making infrastructure a conspicuous part of Tughlaq rule.
milestones.source: Firuz Shah Tughlaq — infrastructure and education

milestones.detail: Vidyapati, the Maithili and Sanskrit poet whose songs shaped eastern Indian literary and devotional traditions, was born.

milestones.text: Firoz Shah Kotla and new canal works reshape Delhi
milestones.detail: The new citadel and associated waterworks reflected a sustained programme of urban construction, irrigation repair and public architecture.

milestones.text: End of Veera Ballala IV's reign over Hoysala Empire
milestones.detail: The recorded reign of Veera Ballala IV over Hoysala Empire ended. Late claimant/successor; chronology overlaps

milestones.text: Bukka I begins the consolidation and expansion of Vijayanagara
milestones.detail: Bukka I succeeded Harihara I in 1356. During his reign the still-young Vijayanagara state substantially expanded its territorial reach and consolidated the political structure that would make it the dominant power of much of southern India.
Ziauddin Barani, the historian and political thinker whose writings are central sources for the Delhi Sultanate, died.

milestones.text: Ziauddin Barani completes the Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi
milestones.detail: The Persian chronicle became one of the principal narrative sources for the political and social history of the Delhi Sultanate.

milestones.text: Muhammad Shah I begins rule of Bahmani Sultanate
milestones.detail: Muhammad Shah I began ruling Bahmani Sultanate. Its territory is approximately associated with Northern Deccan: Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra. Capital or principal centres: Gulbarga/Ahsanabad; Bidar.
milestones.region: Northern Deccan: Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra

milestones.detail: Srinatha, the Telugu poet who became one of the leading literary figures of the late medieval Deccan, was born.
Vedanta Desika, the Sri Vaishnava theologian and multilingual poet-philosopher, died.

milestones.text: Ranganatha worship is restored at Srirangam
milestones.detail: Following Vijayanagara advances into Tamil country, the image of Ranganatha was restored to the Srirangam temple in 1371, marking the re-establishment of the major Vaishnava centre after decades of disruption.
milestones.source: Kampana’s invasion / Srirangam restoration historical summary

milestones.text: A Vijayanagara inscription records a temple land endowment at Kotesvara
milestones.detail: A dated inscription from Bukka Raya’s reign records the purchase of specified plots at Kotesvara and their grant to the temple to support festival feeding, illustrating the land-and-temple economy of early Vijayanagara rule.

milestones.text: Death of Sultan Shihab-ud-Din of Kashmir
milestones.detail: Shihab-ud-Din Shah, a powerful Shah Mir ruler under whom the Kashmir Sultanate expanded widely, died at Srinagar in 1373 and was succeeded by Qutbu'd-Din.

milestones.text: Rao Viram Dev begins rule of Marwar / Jodhpur State
milestones.detail: Rao Viram Dev began ruling Marwar / Jodhpur State. Its territory is approximately associated with Rajasthan: Jodhpur, Pali, Nagaur, Barmer, Jalore influence. Capital or principal centres: Mandore; Jodhpur.
milestones.region: Rajasthan: Jodhpur, Pali, Nagaur, Barmer, Jalore influence

milestones.text: Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani returns to Kashmir
milestones.detail: The Persian Sufi scholar Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani returned to Kashmir around 1379–1380 and spent about a year teaching and preaching, strengthening the Kubrawiya Sufi tradition’s influence in the valley.
milestones.source: Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani historical summary

milestones.text: Tyao Khamti begins rule of Ahom Kingdom
milestones.detail: Tyao Khamti began ruling Ahom Kingdom. Its territory is approximately associated with Assam/Brahmaputra valley. Capital or principal centres: Charaideo; Garhgaon; Rangpur; Jorhat.

milestones.text: Tradition dates the establishment of Koratty Muthy Church to 1381
milestones.detail: Kerala Tourism dates St. Mary’s Forane Church at Koratty, a major Christian pilgrimage centre in Thrissur, to 1381. The medieval foundation date is traditional.

milestones.text: Rana Lakha’s reign opens a new phase of mining and public works in Mewar
milestones.detail: Rana Lakha began ruling Mewar in 1382. His reign is associated with exploitation of the silver and zinc deposits at Zawar and with rebuilding and public works, resources that strengthened the fiscal base of the kingdom.

milestones.text: Karmadhwajpal begins rule of Chutia / Sadiya kingdom
milestones.detail: Karmadhwajpal began ruling Chutia / Sadiya kingdom. Its territory is approximately associated with Upper Assam: Sadiya, Dhemaji, Tinsukia, Lakhimpur. Capital or principal centres: Sadiya/Ratnapur.
milestones.region: Upper Assam: Sadiya, Dhemaji, Tinsukia, Lakhimpur

milestones.detail: Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani, the Sufi scholar associated with Kashmir’s Persianate religious and craft traditions, died.

milestones.text: Ganagitti Jain temple at Hampi is dated by inscription to 1385
milestones.detail: The Ganagitti Jain temple at Hampi is dated to 1385 during Harihara II’s reign on the basis of an inscription and is associated with Irugappa, a Vijayanagara commander. Some modern site guides give 1386, so the date is retained as inscription-based.

milestones.text: Kumaragiri Reddy makes Vasantha Utsavam a hallmark of Kondavidu court culture
milestones.detail: Kumaragiri Reddy, who came to power in 1386, was celebrated as Vasantaraya. Accounts of his reign emphasise learning, performance and his revival or elaborate patronage of the Vasantha Utsavam spring festival, making courtly culture a defining feature of the period.

milestones.text: A Vijayanagara land-grant inscription is recorded at Madhukeshwara Temple
milestones.detail: A pillar inscription at Madhukeshwara Temple in Banavasi, dated 1387 and attributed to Vijayanagara rule, records a land gift to a deity, apparently by the governor of Goa.
milestones.source: Archaeological Survey of India, Dharwad Circle

milestones.detail: Firoz Shah Tughlaq, the Delhi ruler noted for canals, gardens, colleges, hospitals and the repair of older monuments, died.

milestones.text: Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah begins Bengal’s cosmopolitan diplomatic and literary high point
milestones.detail: Around 1390–91 Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah became Sultan of Bengal. His reign is remembered for consolidation, diplomatic contact with Ming China and cultural links with the Persian world, helping position Bengal within wider Asian intellectual and commercial networks.

milestones.text: Zafar Khan is appointed governor of Gujarat
milestones.detail: Zafar Khan, later Muzaffar Shah I, became governor of Gujarat in 1391 and established the Muzaffarid power base that evolved into the independent Gujarat Sultanate.
milestones.source: Gujarat under the Delhi Sultanate historical summary

milestones.detail: Lal Ded, the Kashmiri mystic poet whose vakhs remain central to Kashmiri language and spiritual culture, died.
After the Rao of Idar refused the customary tribute, Gujarat governor Zafar Khan led an expedition against Idar in 1393 and compelled submission.
milestones.source: Gujarat under the Delhi Sultanate historical summary

milestones.text: The Jaunpur Sultanate emerges as an independent Sharqi power
milestones.detail: In 1394 Malik Sarwar was appointed governor of Jaunpur and soon established himself as an independent ruler. The Sharqi state became one of north India’s most important regional powers and later a major centre of scholarship and a distinctive school of architecture.
milestones.source: Brill — The Rise of the Jaunpur Sultanate

milestones.text: Kataya Vema Reddy begins rule of Reddy Kingdom
milestones.detail: Kataya Vema Reddy began ruling Reddy Kingdom. Its territory is approximately associated with Coastal Andhra: Guntur, Prakasam, Krishna, Godavari; Telangana fringe. Capital or principal centres: Addanki; Kondavidu; Rajahmundry.
milestones.region: Coastal Andhra: Guntur, Prakasam, Krishna, Godavari; Telangana fringe

milestones.text: Zafar Khan campaigns in Rajasthan and returns to Patan
milestones.detail: In 1396 Gujarat governor Zafar Khan campaigned against chiefs around Sambhar and Dandwana and against Rajput rulers of Delvada and Jhalavad before returning to Patan.
milestones.source: Gujarat under the Delhi Sultanate historical summary

milestones.text: Firuz Shah Bahmani begins a cosmopolitan intellectual era in the Deccan
milestones.detail: Firuz Shah Bahmani came to the throne in 1397. He cultivated scholarship and languages and showed a marked interest in astronomy, including ordering an observatory at Daulatabad, making his court one of the Bahmani Sultanate’s notable intellectual centres.
milestones.source: Taj ud-Din Firuz Shah historical summary

milestones.text: Maha Manikya begins rule of Tripura / Manikya kingdom
milestones.detail: Maha Manikya began ruling Tripura / Manikya kingdom. Its territory is approximately associated with Tripura; parts of present Bangladesh plains historically. Capital or principal centres: Udaipur; Agartala.
milestones.region: Tripura; parts of present Bangladesh plains historically

milestones.detail: Dilawar Khan established an independent sultanate in Malwa.

milestones.text: Ibrahim Shah Sharqi begins Jaunpur’s cultural and architectural high point
milestones.detail: Ibrahim Shah Sharqi’s long reign from 1402 made Jaunpur a major centre of Islamic learning and Sharqi architecture. Colleges, theological scholarship and monumental building turned the city into a celebrated regional capital.

milestones.text: Tatar Khan deposes Zafar Khan and proclaims himself Sultan in Gujarat
milestones.detail: In 1403 Tatar Khan imprisoned his father Zafar Khan at Ashaval and declared himself Sultan as Muhammad Shah I, briefly interrupting Zafar Khan’s rule.

milestones.text: Virupaksha Raya I begins rule of Vijayanagara Empire
milestones.detail: Virupaksha Raya I began ruling Vijayanagara Empire. Its territory is approximately associated with Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Goa, Kerala parts, south Maharashtra at peak. Capital or principal centres: Vijayanagara/Hampi; Penukonda; Chandragiri; Vellore.
milestones.region: Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Goa, Kerala parts, south Maharashtra at peak

milestones.text: Zheng He’s first treasure voyage links Ming China with Calicut
milestones.detail: Zheng He’s first great Indian Ocean voyage left China in 1405 and reached the Malabar coast during the voyage. Calicut became a recurring destination in the Ming treasure-voyage network, strengthening diplomatic and commercial links across the Indian Ocean.
milestones.source: Live History India — Zheng He at Calicut

milestones.detail: Muzaffar Shah I declared independence and founded the Gujarat Sultanate.
Annamacharya, the Telugu poet-composer whose devotional songs became central to the musical tradition of Tirumala, was born.

milestones.text: Zheng He’s trilingual inscription is dated to 1409
milestones.detail: A stone tablet prepared for Zheng He’s Indian Ocean voyage bears Chinese, Persian and Tamil texts praising Buddhist, Islamic and Hindu traditions. Dated 15 February 1409, it reflects the maritime networks linking South India and Sri Lanka with Ming China.
milestones.region: Indian Ocean / Tamil maritime world / Sri Lanka

milestones.text: Deva Raya I builds a Tungabhadra barrage and aqueduct for Vijayanagara
milestones.detail: In 1410 Deva Raya I ordered a barrage across the Tungabhadra and a long aqueduct to the Vijayanagara capital, strengthening urban water supply and irrigation.

milestones.text: Ahmedabad is founded as a new capital
milestones.detail: The planned city on the Sabarmati developed into a major centre of textile production, trade, architecture and urban culture.

milestones.text: A 1412 inscription records additions to Mylara Lingeshwara Temple
milestones.detail: A Vijayanagara inscription dated 1412 at Mylara Lingeshwara Temple records architectural additions to the complex during the Devaraya period, preserving a dated record of temple patronage in the Tungabhadra region.

milestones.text: Nasiruddin Muhammad Shah begins rule of Bengal Sultanate
milestones.detail: Nasiruddin Muhammad Shah began ruling Bengal Sultanate. Its territory is approximately associated with West Bengal, Bangladesh, Bihar/Odisha/Assam frontiers. Capital or principal centres: Pandua/Firozabad; Gaur/Lakhnauti.
Narsinh Mehta, the Gujarati bhakti poet associated with some of the language’s earliest major devotional literature, was born.

milestones.text: The House of Ganesha reshapes Bengal’s succession politics
milestones.detail: The rise of Raja Ganesha and the House of Ganesha transformed Bengal’s ruling order in the mid-1410s. By 1416 the contested sequence involving Raja Ganesha and his son Jalaluddin Muhammad Shah had become the defining dynastic crisis of the sultanate.

milestones.text: Kashmir’s craft and translation traditions expand under Zain-ul-Abidin
milestones.detail: Court patronage encouraged manuscript culture, music, translation and crafts such as papier-mâché, shawl weaving and woodwork.
Kabir, the poet-saint whose vernacular verses challenged sectarian boundaries and shaped bhakti and nirguna traditions, was born.

milestones.text: The Vijay Stambha is completed at Chittorgarh
milestones.detail: The monumental victory tower became an outstanding example of late medieval Rajput stone architecture and sculptural programme.
Shankaradeva, the Assamese saint, playwright and cultural reformer who founded the Ekasarana devotional movement, was born.
Ravidas, the bhakti poet-saint whose teachings on equality influenced North Indian devotional and social thought, was born.
Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism and the first of the Sikh Gurus, was born.
Krishnadevaraya, the Vijayanagara ruler, writer and patron associated with a high point of Telugu and Sanskrit court culture, was born.
Gujarat Sultan Mahmud Begada captured the fortified Girnar-Junagadh stronghold in 1472, one of the major fort conquests associated with his long reign.

milestones.text: Shamsuddin Yusuf Shah begins rule of Bengal Sultanate
milestones.detail: Shamsuddin Yusuf Shah began ruling Bengal Sultanate. Its territory is approximately associated with West Bengal, Bangladesh, Bihar/Odisha/Assam frontiers. Capital or principal centres: Pandua/Firozabad; Gaur/Lakhnauti.

milestones.text: Bhimraj’s revolt at Kondavidu opens a new Bahmani–Gajapati conflict
milestones.detail: In 1475 the rebel officer Bhimraj seized Kondavidu and killed Bahmani officials, then sought Gajapati support, helping trigger a wider Bahmani–Gajapati conflict across the eastern Deccan.
milestones.source: Bahmani invasion of Orissa historical summary

milestones.text: Gajapati forces recover Rajahmundry and Kondapalli
milestones.detail: In 1476 Purushottama Deva exploited Bahmani weakness to advance south; inscriptional evidence places him at Rajahmundry, and Gajapati forces recovered Rajahmundry and Kondapalli during the conflict.
milestones.source: Bahmani invasion of Orissa historical summary

milestones.detail: Malik Muhammad Jayasi, the Awadhi Sufi poet best known for the epic Padmavat, was born.

milestones.text: Chamaraja Wodeyar II begins rule of Kingdom of Mysore
milestones.detail: Chamaraja Wodeyar II began ruling Kingdom of Mysore. Its territory is approximately associated with Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Andhra parts under Hyder-Tipu. Capital or principal centres: Mysore; Srirangapatna; Bangalore administrative centre later.
milestones.region: Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Andhra parts under Hyder-Tipu

milestones.detail: Vallabhacharya, the philosopher who founded the Pushtimarg tradition of Krishna devotion, was born.

milestones.text: Kalyanamalla begins rule of Tomara kingdom of Gwalior
milestones.detail: Kalyanamalla began ruling Tomara kingdom of Gwalior. Its territory is approximately associated with Gwalior/Chambal, northern MP. Capital or principal centres: Gwalior Fort.

milestones.text: Jalaluddin Fateh Shah begins rule of Bengal Sultanate
milestones.detail: Jalaluddin Fateh Shah began ruling Bengal Sultanate. Its territory is approximately associated with West Bengal, Bangladesh, Bihar/Odisha/Assam frontiers. Capital or principal centres: Pandua/Firozabad; Gaur/Lakhnauti.

milestones.text: Mahmud Shah Bahmani II begins rule of Bahmani Sultanate
milestones.detail: Mahmud Shah Bahmani II began ruling Bahmani Sultanate. Its territory is approximately associated with Northern Deccan: Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra. Capital or principal centres: Gulbarga/Ahsanabad; Bidar.
milestones.region: Northern Deccan: Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra

milestones.detail: Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire in India, was born in Andijan.
Purandara Dasa, the composer-saint widely regarded as a foundational figure in the teaching system of Carnatic music, was born.

milestones.text: Saluva Narasimha’s coup ends the Sangama dynasty at Vijayanagara
milestones.detail: In 1485 Saluva Narasimha seized the Vijayanagara throne as the old Sangama line collapsed, founding the Saluva dynasty. The coup was a major dynastic reorganisation of the empire rather than an ordinary accession.
milestones.source: Saluva Narasimha Deva Raya historical summary

milestones.detail: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, the Bengali Vaishnava teacher whose ecstatic devotional movement spread across eastern India, was born.
Sher Shah Suri, the ruler and administrator associated with currency, road, postal and revenue reforms, was born.

milestones.text: Pratap Manikya begins rule of Tripura / Manikya kingdom
milestones.detail: Pratap Manikya began ruling Tripura / Manikya kingdom. Its territory is approximately associated with Tripura; parts of present Bangladesh plains historically. Capital or principal centres: Udaipur; Agartala.
milestones.region: Tripura; parts of present Bangladesh plains historically

milestones.text: Suhenphaa begins rule of Ahom Kingdom
milestones.detail: Suhenphaa began ruling Ahom Kingdom. Its territory is approximately associated with Assam/Brahmaputra valley. Capital or principal centres: Charaideo; Garhgaon; Rangpur; Jorhat.
Madhavdeva, the Assamese poet, dramatist and organiser who consolidated the Ekasarana tradition, was born.

milestones.text: Bahmani realm fragments into Deccan sultanates
milestones.detail: Ahmadnagar, Bijapur and Berar asserted independence as the Bahmani political order fragmented.

milestones.text: Narasimha Raya II begins rule of Vijayanagara Empire
milestones.detail: Narasimha Raya II began ruling Vijayanagara Empire. Its territory is approximately associated with Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Goa, Kerala parts, south Maharashtra at peak. Capital or principal centres: Vijayanagara/Hampi; Penukonda; Chandragiri; Vellore.
milestones.region: Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Goa, Kerala parts, south Maharashtra at peak

milestones.text: Rao Suja begins rule of Marwar / Jodhpur State
milestones.detail: Rao Suja began ruling Marwar / Jodhpur State. Its territory is approximately associated with Rajasthan: Jodhpur, Pali, Nagaur, Barmer, Jalore influence. Capital or principal centres: Mandore; Jodhpur.
milestones.region: Rajasthan: Jodhpur, Pali, Nagaur, Barmer, Jalore influence

milestones.text: Supimphaa begins rule of Ahom Kingdom
milestones.detail: Supimphaa began ruling Ahom Kingdom. Its territory is approximately associated with Assam/Brahmaputra valley. Capital or principal centres: Charaideo; Garhgaon; Rangpur; Jorhat.

milestones.text: Alauddin Hussain Shah inaugurates the Hussain Shahi high point in Bengal
milestones.detail: Hussain Shah’s accession in 1494 began a long reign remembered for territorial strength and for patronage that coincided with a major phase of Bengali literary, religious and artistic culture.

milestones.text: Gujarat launches a major expedition against Bahadur Khan Gilani
milestones.detail: In 1494–1495 Mahmud Begada sent a land force and a large naval force toward Dabhol against Bahadur Khan Gilani, whose forces had harassed Gujarat’s ports; the crisis ended after the Bahmani Sultan captured and executed Gilani.

milestones.text: Qutb Shahi power begins to emerge around Golconda
milestones.detail: Harvard’s South Asian chronology dates the Qutb Shahi polity from about 1496. Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk rose through Bahmani service to govern Telangana/Golconda, laying the political foundation for the later independent Qutb Shahi state.

milestones.text: Vasco da Gama departs Lisbon on the voyage that will reach India
milestones.detail: Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon with four ships on 8 July 1497 to find a sea route around Africa to India. The expedition reached Calicut in May 1498 and permanently transformed the maritime history of the Indian Ocean.
milestones.source: EBSCO Research Starters — Vasco da Gama’s voyage

milestones.detail: Mirabai, the Rajput poet-saint whose Krishna devotional songs became part of the shared literary culture of North India, was born.

milestones.text: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut by sea
milestones.detail: The Portuguese expedition established the first direct maritime route between Western Europe and India around the Cape of Good Hope.

milestones.text: The Keladi Nayaka state emerges in western Karnataka
milestones.detail: Around 1499 Chaudappa Nayaka established the Keladi/Ikkeri line, which grew from a Vijayanagara subordinate into an important regional power controlling parts of the Malnad and coastal Karnataka.
Annamacharya, the Telugu poet-composer whose songs remain central to the Tirumala devotional tradition, died.
Guru Angad, the second Sikh Guru, associated with the standardisation and promotion of the Gurmukhi script, was born.
Humayun, the Mughal ruler whose exile and restoration shaped Indo-Persian cultural exchange, was born.
Kanaka Dasa, the Kannada poet-saint and composer of the Haridasa movement, was born.
The Telugu poem combined devotional narrative with reflections on kingship and is regarded as a major work of classical Telugu literature.
Kabir, the poet-saint whose vernacular verses became foundational to bhakti, Sikh and nirguna traditions, died.
Ravidas, the bhakti poet-saint whose teachings on equality influenced devotional and social traditions, died.

milestones.text: Portuguese rebuild the St Thomas shrine at Mylapore
milestones.detail: Portuguese builders began a new church over the traditional tomb of St Thomas at Mylapore in 1522. In 1523 the tomb was opened and the church rebuilt/opened, establishing the San Thome institution that later became Chennai’s cathedral basilica.
Rani Durgavati, the Gond ruler remembered for governance, patronage and resistance in central India, was born.

milestones.text: Babur begins the final invasion that leads to Panipat
milestones.detail: At the end of 1525 Babur returned to northern India, crossed the Indus, secured Punjab and advanced toward Delhi; the campaign culminated in his victory over Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in April 1526.
milestones.source: First Battle of Panipat historical summary

milestones.detail: Krishnadevaraya, the Vijayanagara ruler, writer and patron associated with a high point of south Indian court culture, died.
Babur died and was succeeded by Humayun as Mughal emperor.
Vallabhacharya, the philosopher and founder of the Pushtimarg tradition, died.
Tulsidas, the Awadhi poet traditionally credited with the Ramcharitmanas, was born.
Eknath, the Marathi poet-saint whose works expanded vernacular bhakti literature, was born.
Guru Ram Das, the fourth Sikh Guru and founder associated with the city of Amritsar, was born.
Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, the Bengali Vaishnava teacher whose devotional movement reshaped eastern Indian religious culture, died.

milestones.text: Bahadur Shah of Gujarat dies during negotiations with the Portuguese off Diu
milestones.detail: Sultan Bahadur Shah of Gujarat died in 1537 during a shipboard encounter with Portuguese representatives near Diu. His death deepened the Portuguese position on the Gujarat coast and destabilised one of western India’s major sultanates.
milestones.source: Indian History Congress / JSTOR — Khwaja Safar, the merchant governor of Surat

milestones.text: Gaur falls to Sher Khan, ending the Hussain Shahi Sultanate’s rule in Bengal
milestones.detail: In 1538 Sher Khan’s forces took Gaur, the Bengal capital. The fall displaced Sultan Ghiyasuddin Mahmud Shah and marked a decisive transfer of power in Bengal during Sher Khan’s rise toward the Sur Empire.
milestones.person: Sher Khan (Sher Shah Suri); Ghiyasuddin Mahmud Shah

milestones.detail: Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism and the first Sikh Guru, died.

milestones.text: Sher Shah’s standardised silver rupiya enters circulation
milestones.detail: A high-quality silver coin called the rupiya became an important ancestor of the modern rupee and influenced later Mughal and colonial currency systems.

milestones.text: The imperial road later called the Grand Trunk Road is reorganised
milestones.detail: Sher Shah Suri improved and linked older routes with serais, milestones, policing and postal arrangements across northern India.
Akbar, the Mughal ruler associated with administrative consolidation, translation projects and a major flowering of architecture and painting, was born.

milestones.text: St Paul’s College is founded in Goa
milestones.detail: The Jesuit institution became one of the earliest European-style colleges in India and an important centre for languages, theology and printing.
Malik Muhammad Jayasi, the Awadhi Sufi poet best known for Padmavat, died.
Dadu Dayal, the nirguna bhakti teacher whose followers formed the Dadu Panth, was born.
Sher Shah Suri, the ruler and administrator associated with road, currency, postal and revenue reforms, died.
Mirabai, the Rajput poet-saint whose Krishna songs became part of North India’s shared devotional culture, died.
Faizi, the Persian poet and scholar of Akbar’s court, was born.
Abu'l-Fazl, the historian and statesman who authored the Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari, was born.
Guru Angad, the second Sikh Guru, associated with the promotion of Gurmukhi, died.

milestones.text: The first printing press in India begins operating in Goa
milestones.detail: Movable-type printing arrived in Goa and inaugurated a new era in the production and circulation of books in South Asia.
milestones.source: Government of Goa, Directorate of Art and Culture

milestones.detail: Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan, the poet, translator and statesman remembered for Hindi dohas and Persianate scholarship, was born.

milestones.text: Garcia da Orta’s Colóquios is printed in Goa
milestones.detail: The book recorded medicinal plants, drugs and medical knowledge of the Indian Ocean world and was among the earliest scientific works printed in India.
Purandara Dasa, the composer-saint widely regarded as a foundational figure in Carnatic music pedagogy, died.
Rani Durgavati, the Gond ruler remembered for governance and resistance in central India, died.
Shankaradeva, the Assamese saint, playwright and cultural reformer who founded the Ekasarana movement, died.

milestones.text: Akbar establishes the Maktab Khana translation bureau
milestones.detail: The imperial translation department sponsored Persian versions of Sanskrit works and fostered sustained intellectual exchange across languages and traditions.

milestones.text: The Ibadat Khana opens at Fatehpur Sikri
milestones.detail: The house of worship became a forum for debates among Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Christian and Zoroastrian scholars at Akbar’s court.

Mehr-un-Nissa, later Empress Nur Jahan, was born in 1577. She became one of the most politically influential women of the Mughal period and a major patron of art, architecture and court culture. Sources differ on the day: 31 May 1577 at Kandahar is the conventional date, while Ruby Lal’s biography places the birth in the winter of 1577.

milestones.text: The first surviving book printed in an Indian language appears
milestones.detail: Thambiran Vanakkam, a Tamil Christian text printed at Kollam, is generally regarded as the earliest surviving printed book in an Indian language.

milestones.text: The first Jesuit mission reaches Akbar’s court
milestones.detail: Jesuit scholars from Goa entered sustained theological and cultural dialogue with the Mughal court at Fatehpur Sikri.
Guru Ram Das, the fourth Sikh Guru and founder associated with Amritsar, died.

milestones.text: Akbar propounds the Tawhid-i-Ilahi / Din-i Ilahi
milestones.detail: In 1582 Akbar propounded the courtly ethical-spiritual fellowship later known as Din-i Ilahi at Fatehpur Sikri, drawing on debates among multiple religious traditions at his court.
Surdas, the Braj poet traditionally associated with the Sursagar and Krishna devotional literature, died.

milestones.text: English traveller Ralph Fitch reaches India
milestones.detail: Fitch’s long journey through Goa, the Mughal territories, Bengal and Southeast Asia provided England with influential commercial information about Asian trade.

milestones.text: Akbar introduces the Tarikh-i Ilahi calendar era
milestones.detail: Akbar introduced the Tarikh-i Ilahi ('Divine Era') in 1584, using a solar reckoning whose epoch was tied to the vernal equinox near his accession in 1556.
milestones.source: Cambridge University Press — Time in Early Modern Islam

milestones.detail: Tansen, the musician whose legacy became foundational to later Hindustani classical traditions, died.

milestones.text: The Persian Mahabharata, the Razmnama, is completed
milestones.detail: The illustrated translation brought the Sanskrit epic into the Persian-reading world and became a landmark of Mughal translation and manuscript art.
Prince Khurram, later Mughal emperor Shah Jahan and patron of the Taj Mahal, was born at Lahore on 5 January 1592.
Arjumand Banu Begum, later titled Mumtaz Mahal and the empress for whom Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal, was born in April 1593.

milestones.text: Akbar’s Tarikh-i Alfi millennial history is completed
