c. dates. Alias Jejjaka - Jejakabhukti (Bundelkhand) is named after him. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 83.
c. dates. Younger brother and successor of Jayasakti (The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 83).
c. dates. No independent date; bracketed between Vijayasakti and Harsha (The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 84).
The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 84 and chronology p. 512: 'c. 900-925'. Restored the Pratihara Mahipala I to his throne c. 914.
Alias Lakshavarman. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV) chronology p. 513: accession c. 925. Took Kalanjara from the Pratiharas and pushed the frontier to the Yamuna.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV) chronology p. 514 gives 950-1000; text p. 87 has inscription dates 954-1002. The first fully independent Chandela; issued an inscription from Kasika (Banaras) in 998.
c. dates. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 58: succeeded Dhanga 'some time after A.D. 1002'; end bracketed by Vidyadhara on the throne in 1019.
c. dates. Fixed points only: Mahmud of Ghazni's attacks on Kalanjara in 1019 and 1021-22 (The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 58).
c. dates. Defeated the Kalachuri Gangeyadeva; his successor was ruling in 1050 (The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 58).
c. dates. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 58 (as Devendravarman) gives one fixed date: 'known to have been ruling in A.D. 1050'.

c. dates. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 58: ascended 'some time before A.D. 1073'; fought Mahmud, Ghaznavid governor of the Punjab, before 1090. Briefly lost his kingdom to the Kalachuri Karna.
c. dates. Defeated the Paramara Naravarman and the Kalachuri Yasahkarna (The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 58).
c. dates. Acceded in or before 1117 and 'after a short reign abdicated in favour of his uncle' (The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 58).
c. dates. End fixed by Madanavarman's earliest date, 1129 (The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 58-59).
The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 59 and chronology p. 872: extreme known dates 1129 and 1163. Annexed Bhilsa from the Paramara Yasovarman.

Gurjara-Pratihara Empire.note: Nephew of Nagabhata I, who was succeeded by his brother's sons Kakkuka and Devaraja. HCIP IV says of the pair only that nothing is known of them, and the Gwalior prasasti records merely that Kakkuka had a keen sense of humour, so both dates are inferred from the roll's neighbouring reigns. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 21 (also p. 19 of the prasasti summary; genealogy p. 520).

The other nephew of Nagabhata I and the father of Vatsaraja, so his reign closes the interval before Vatsaraja, whose accession HCIP IV's chronology puts at c. A.D. 778 or earlier. The volume records no dates or events for him, so the years are an estimate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 21 (chronology p. 507; genealogy p. 520).

Son of Mahendrapala I by the queen Dehanagadevi, he held the throne between his father's last known date of A.D. 907-8 and Mahipala I's accession about A.D. 912, and the grant of A.D. 931 names him as his younger brother's predecessor; no year of his own is recorded, so the single year given here is only the width of the gap on this roll. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 33-35 and 520.

Son of Vinayakapala (Mahipala I), whose own rule ran till at least A.D. 942. Mahendrapala II's known date is A.D. 945-6 and the Pratihara empire still included Malwa in A.D. 946; the end year is a boundary set against Devapala's known date of A.D. 948-9, not a recorded one. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 36-37.

HCIP IV counts four kings in the fifteen years after Mahendrapala II and gives Mahipala II the known date A.D. 955, with Vijayapala on the throne early in A.D. 960; it adds that whether all four were distinct rulers, or two or more of them the same man, cannot be said. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 37, 514 and 520.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 38: 'Trilochanapala, the successor of Rajyapala, ruling in A.D. 1027, is the last of the Imperial Pratiharas known to us' - known from the Jhusi copper-plate (p. 43 n. 108); the genealogy (p. 520) numbers him seventeenth. By this date the Pratihara dominion had contracted to the small kingdom of Kanauj. Dates approximate - A.D. 1027 is his only recorded date.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), genealogy p. 520, enters him as '18 (?) Yasahpala', and p. 43 n. 108 cautions: 'Another king Yasahpala is known from Kara Ins. ... but it is not definitely known whether he belonged to the Imperial Pratihara family.' The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 62: the Kalachuri Karna 'wrested Allahabad from Pratihara Yasahpala some time after A.D. 1037'. Dates approximate.

Pala Empire.note: Eldest son of Vigrahapala III, who died about A.D. 1070. He imprisoned his brothers Surapala and Ramapala on a report that they were conspiring against him, faced a general revolt of the vassals, and lost his life when the state officer Divya took Varendri; Divya's accession there is put at about A.D. 1075, which is the only bound on the end of this reign. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), printed pp. 28-29.

Brother of Mahipala II, he escaped from prison during the loss of Varendri and ruled the remnant of the Pala kingdom in northern and central Bihar for about a couple of years, until his younger brother Ramapala succeeded about A.D. 1077. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), printed p. 28.
R.C. Majumdar (gen. ed.), The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), printed p. 31.

Son of Ramapala; HCIP V dates Ramapala's death to c. A.D. 1120 and Kumarapala's to c. A.D. 1125. His minister Vaidyadeva held off Anantavarman Chodaganga for a time and put down the revolt of Timgyadeva in Kamarupa, but Magadha chiefs broke away and the Gahadavalas took western Magadha. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), printed pp. 31-32.

Son of Kumarapala; HCIP V says he ruled more than fourteen years and died an unnatural death whose circumstances are unknown, and that his uncle Madanapala succeeded him in A.D. 1144. See fixes.json: this entry sits correctly only if Ramapala's end date is also moved back to 1120. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), printed p. 32 (chronology p. 872).

Hindu Shahi kingdom.note: Son of Lalliya. After Lalliya's death the throne was taken by a kinsman named Samanta, known from coins reading Sri-Samanta; Prabhakara, minister of the Kashmir king Gopalavarman, took Udabhanda and installed Toramana there, giving him the new name Kamaluka. Al-Biruni calls him Kamalu. He mustered an army against the governor of Zabulistan after the sack of Sakawand but stood the plan down; his son Bhima followed him. HCIP IV does not fix his accession or death years, so the span is set by the roll's neighbouring reigns. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 113 (genealogy p. 528).

Turk Shahi kingdom.note: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 112: Lagaturman was overthrown by his minister Kallar/Lalliya "in the second half of the ninth century", and Lalliya lost Kabul to Ya'qub ibn Layth in 870 — so this reign ends about 865, not 822. Dates approximate.

Ghaznavid Empire.title: Sultan of Ghazni
Ghaznavid Empire.note: 'Ali Abu-'l-Hasan, son of Mas'ud I. On Mawdud's death in A.D. 1049 the royal servants first raised Mawdud's young son Mas'ud II, whom the ministers and nobles set aside after a few days in favour of 'Ali; he was himself deposed in A.D. 1051. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), printed p. 94.

Ghaznavid Empire.title: Sultan of Ghazni
Ghaznavid Empire.note: 'Izz-ud-daulah 'Abd-ur-Rashid, sixth son of Mahmud, released from a long confinement and raised to the throne in A.D. 1051; his officer Nushtigin Hajib took Nagarkot, held by Indian chiefs since A.D. 1043. He was deposed and killed by Tughril Hajib, who held Ghazni for forty days before the nobles placed Farrukhzad on the throne. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), printed p. 94.

Ghaznavid Empire.title: Sultan of Ghazni
Ghaznavid Empire.note: Arsalan 'Abd-ul-Malik, son of Mas'ud III. His elder brother Shirzad succeeded their father in A.D. 1115 and ruled only for a year, after which Arsalan took the throne; Ghazni then passed back and forth with his half-brother Bahram Shah, who held it finally in A.D. 1118. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), printed p. 95.

Western Chalukya Empire.note: HCIP V heads his reign c. A.D. 1008-1014 and notes that the dates of his inscriptions run from A.D. 1008 to 1013-14; his sister Akkadevi governed Kisukad in A.D. 1012. The start here is set to follow Satyashraya on this roll. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), printed p. 166.

Younger brother of Vikramaditya V, whom he succeeded in A.D. 1014; he did not rule for more than a year and was followed by his youngest brother Jayasimha II in or before A.D. 1015. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), printed p. 166.

The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), printed p. 182: "11. SOMESVARA IV (A.D. 1181-c. 1189), THE LAST CHALUKYA RULER ... In any case he ascended the throne in A.D. 1181-82 and assumed the title Tribhuvanamalla." The same page adds that "In A.D. 1181 Somesvara IV succeeded in wresting from Ahavamalla the larger portion of the Deccan including Kalyana", and that an inscription from Kurgod places him on the throne of Kalyana in A.D. 1181-82.

Eastern Chalukya dynasty.note: viceroy from 631, king 624/633 by different theories

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 137: 'Vijayaditya IV defeated the Rashtrakuta forces but lost his life after a reign of 6 months, at the battle of Virajapuri to the south of the Krishna.' His reign fell in A.D. 921-22.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 137: son of Vijayaditya IV, he 'succeeded him about the end of A.D. 922 with the virudas Rajamahendra and Sarvalokasraya. Amma I ruled for 7 years, i.e. till about A.D. 929.'

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 137: son of Amma I, 'the former succeeded (A.D. 929) him under the name Kanthika-Vijayaditya or Kanthika-Beta. A fortnight after the installation of Vijayaditya V, the young king was overthrown by Tala.' He escaped and took shelter with Arikesarin II of Vemulavada.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 137: son of Yuddhamalla, he took the throne in A.D. 929 with the support of the Rashtrakuta Govinda IV and of Ayyappa of Nolamba-rashtra, and 'was, however, ousted after only a month by another claimant to the throne named Vikramaditya (II)'.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 137: a son of Chalukya-Bhima I, he 'is said to have ruled over the Vengi country together with Trikalinga for nine or eleven months or for a year (A.D. 929) when he was himself overthrown by Bhima II'.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 137: a son of Amma I and brother of Vijayaditya V; 'after a rule of 8 months (A.D. 930) Bhima II was killed by one Malla, Mallapa or Yuddhamalla (II)'. Called Bhima II by HCIP at this point, but distinct from Chalukya-Bhima II below, who was a son of Vijayaditya IV.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 137-38: son of Tala; 'This king, who ruled for seven years (A.D. 930-36), built the Mallesvarasvami temple at Vijayawada.' An inscription of Amma II records that during those seven years Rashtrakuta commanders and Sabara chiefs apportioned the kingdom among themselves. He was ousted by Chalukya-Bhima II. End year set at 935 to abut the '12 years (A.D. 935-46)' HCIP gives his successor; HCIP's own two figures overlap by a year.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 138: son of Vijayaditya IV and step-brother of Amma I; a record 'says that Bhima (Chalukya-Bhima II) ruled for 12 years (A.D. 935-46) after having extirpated Yuddhamalla and other claimants to the throne'. He died in Saka 867 = A.D. 946 and was succeeded by his son Amma II, whom the existing roll enters from 947.

Eastern Chalukya dynasty.title: Telugu-Choda occupant of Vengi
Eastern Chalukya dynasty.note: Not an Eastern Chalukya but the ruler in possession of Vengi through the whole gap. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 139: 'Amma's death was avenged by his wife's brother Jata Choda-Bhima who defeated and killed Danarnava in A.D. 973 and made himself king of Vengi.' HCIP IV, p. 140: the sons of Danarnava stayed in exile at the Chola court 'until Rajaraja conquered Vengi for them from Jata Choda-Bhima in A.D. 999', and the dynasty's own inscriptions instead say that 'after Danarnava... the country of Vengi was without a ruler for 27 years (c. A.D. 973-99)'. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 235, calls it 'the long interregnum from A.D. 973 to 999'.

Western Ganga dynasty.note: The Classical Age (HCIP III), chronological table p. 715: '670-713 Sivamara I, W. Ganga'; narrative p. 270: 'Sivamara I, the great-grandson of Durvinita, ruled probably from A.D. 670-713.' HCIP III adds that 'He was succeeded by a ruler whose name is uncertain' before Sripurusha (725-788), so 713-725 is left blank here rather than filled with a guess.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 161: 'Rajamalla I was succeeded by his son Nitimarga I (A.D. 853-870) who continued with success the struggle for Western Ganga independence.' Sastri, block 143 (printed p. 155), calls him 'Eraya, known also as Nitimarga and Ranavikrama (837-70), son of Rachamalla I' - the two books differ on the accession year.
The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 161: 'His elder son, Rajamalla II (A.D. 870-907), was ably assisted by his younger brother, Butuga I, in the wars with the Eastern Chalukyas.'

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 161: Rajamalla II 'was consequently succeeded by Nitimarga II (A.D. 907-935), the son of Butuga I. Nitimarga II consolidated his position in Gangavadi, and had three sons, Narasimha, Rajamalla III, and Butuga II.'

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 161: 'After a short reign, Narasimha was followed by Rajamalla III.' Dates approximate - HCIP gives no regnal years, only that the reign was short and fell between Nitimarga II (to 935) and the ousting of Rajamalla III in 937.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 161: Narasimha 'was followed by Rajamalla III, who was ousted by Butuga II in A.D. 937'; HCIP IV, p. 162, adds that Butuga II 'killed his brother Rajamalla III, and became king of Gangavadi', taking the throne with Rashtrakuta help after the death of Prithvipati II in 940. Start date approximate.

Pallava dynasty.note: Sanskrit-charter Pallavas; order per HCIP pp. 282-283

Karkota dynasty of Kashmir.note: Son of the dynasty's founder Durlabhavardhana, who succeeded about A.D. 627; Kalhana allots the two of them reigns of 36 and 50 years, which puts Durlabhaka from about A.D. 663 to the accession of his eldest son Chandrapida around A.D. 712. Nothing of his reign is otherwise recorded, and the end year here is set to meet Chandrapida's start on this roll. The Classical Age (HCIP III), printed p. 132.

Karkota dynasty of Kashmir.title: King of Kashmir
Karkota dynasty of Kashmir.note: Younger brother of Chandrapida, who died after a reign of eight and a half years; Tarapida then ruled four years and was followed by his younger brother Lalitaditya Muktapida, who came to the throne about A.D. 724. The Classical Age (HCIP III), printed p. 133.

Elder of Lalitaditya Muktapida's two sons; he and his brother Vajraditya held the throne one after the other. HCIP IV gives him no regnal years of his own, so this short span is bracketed by Lalitaditya's close on the roll (760) and Vajraditya's accession, which the volume's chronology places at c. A.D. 762. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 115 (narrative and genealogy p. 528; chronology p. 507).

Second son of Lalitaditya; HCIP IV's chronology dates his accession to c. A.D. 762, and the raid on Kashmir by Hisham ibn Amr at-Taghlibi, governor of Sindh A.D. 768-772, is assigned to his reign. His end year is inferred from the fact that two more of his sons reigned before Jayapida, so treat it as approximate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 115 (chronology p. 507).

Eldest son of Vajraditya; he took the throne on his father's death and was later removed by his step-brother Samgramapida. HCIP IV supplies the order but no regnal years, so this span is an estimate fitted between Vajraditya and Jayapida. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 115 (genealogy p. 528).

Second son of Vajraditya; HCIP IV states he died seven days after his accession, whereupon his brother Jayapida took the sovereignty. The year given here is nominal, marking the handover rather than a full reign. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 115 (genealogy p. 528).

Son of Jayapida Vinayaditya; HCIP IV says Jayapida's sons Lalitapida and Samgramapida II held the throne in succession after his death. The volume gives neither of them regnal years, so the split of the 810-826 interval between the two is approximate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 116 (genealogy p. 528).

Second son of Jayapida, also named Prithivyapida; on his death the throne passed to Chippatajayapida. HCIP IV's own chronology runs about a decade earlier than this roll and puts Chippatajayapida's death at c. A.D. 813, so the absolute years here follow the roll's framework rather than the volume's. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 116 (chronology p. 509).

Grandson of Vajraditya Bappiyaka, placed on the throne by Utpalaka, one of the late king's maternal uncles who ran the state through a succession of nominal rulers for close to forty years. HCIP IV records the sequence but no regnal years, so the dates are fitted to the roll's surrounding entries. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 116 (genealogy p. 528).

Son of Samgramapida II; a rival faction removed Ajitapida and set him up in his place, before Sukhavarman replaced him with Utpalapida. HCIP IV gives the order without regnal years, so these dates are fitted between Ajitapida and the roll's Utpalapida. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 116 (genealogy p. 528).

Utpala dynasty of Kashmir.note: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 118: son of Shankaravarman, he 'ascended the throne shortly before A.D. 900. As he was still young, his mother Sugandha carried on the administration of the State'; the minister Prabhakara later killed him. End date approximate - HCIP fixes only that his death preceded the ten-day reign of Sankata and Sugandha's own accession.
The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 118-19: Prabhakara 'placed Sankata, an alleged son of Sankara-varman, on the throne. This new king died ten days after his accession.' Year approximate.

Utpala dynasty of Kashmir.title: Queen regnant
Utpala dynasty of Kashmir.note: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 119: 'As there was no direct heir to the throne, the queen Sugandha assumed the royalty at the wishes of the people.' The Tantrin infantry deprived her of her sovereignty and set Partha on the throne in A.D. 908; she withdrew to Hushkapura and was put to death in 914 after a failed attempt to return. Start year approximate.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 119: the Tantrins 'placed Partha, the son of Nirjita-varman, who was ten years old, on the throne in A.D. 908'; his father acted as guardian. 'In A.D. 921 Nirjita-varman deposed Partha with the help of the Tantrins and himself assumed the royalty.' A famine struck Kashmir in 917.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 119: grandson of Suravarman, half-brother of Avantivarman; ruled from A.D. 921 and 'In A.D. 923 he placed his other son named Chakra-varman on the throne, and died soon after.'

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 119: 'Chakra-varman ruled for ten years under the guardianship of his mother and grandmother. The Tantrins, eager for more money, overthrew him and placed his half-brother Sura-varman I on the throne.'

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 119: half-brother of Chakravarman, raised by the Tantrins; 'After a year, Sura-varman had to yield his throne to Partha, who had regained the favour of the Tantrins.' Dates approximate.
The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 119: restored by the Tantrins; 'A year later, in A.D. 935, Chakra-varman got back the sovereignty by paying a higher price.'

Utpala dynasty of Kashmir.title: Minister who took the throne
Utpala dynasty of Kashmir.note: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 119: after Chakravarman fled, 'the minister Sambhuvardhana, by offering handsome bribes, purchased the throne for himself'. He was taken prisoner and executed when Chakravarman returned with Damara support after the Damara Samgrama defeated the Tantrins near Padmapura.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 119: he re-entered Srinagara with the backing of the Damaras and was received by the feudal lords, ministers and Ekangas; 'In A.D. 937 he lost his life at the hands of robbers.'

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 119-20: son of Partha, raised to the throne by the ministers in A.D. 937. His subordinates killed his father at his instigation. 'Just before his death in A.D. 939 he declared a child named Sura-varman II as his son and placed him on the throne.'

Utpala dynasty of Kashmir.title: Child king
Utpala dynasty of Kashmir.note: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 120: placed on the throne by Unmattavanti and dethroned within the year by the minister Kamalavardhana, who left the choice of a king to an assembly of Brahmanas; the assembly chose Yasaskara. 'The rule of the Utpala dynasty thus came to an end in A.D. 939.'

Somavamshi dynasty.note: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), printed p. 212: "Uddyotakesari, whose latest known date is his eighteenth regnal year, appears to have been a contemporary of the Ganga king Anantavarman Vajrahasta III (A.D. 1038-70) ... and the latter's son Rajaraja I (A.D. 1070-78)", and "by A.D. 1112, which is the date of Chodaganga's Korni grant, independent Somavamsi rule must have been terminated in lower Orissa by the Gangas and ... Uddyotakesari's rule had ended some time before that date."

Somavamshi dynasty.title: Lord of Paschima-Lanka
Somavamshi dynasty.note: He issued the Kelga plates from Suvarnapura (Sonpur) and held that district after the other parts of the Somavamshi dominions had been occupied, taking the titles Paramesvara and Paramabhattaraka; HCIP V places him in the early years of the twelfth century and identifies him with the Somesvara defeated by the Kalachuri Jajalla I, whose Ratanpur inscription is dated A.D. 1114. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), printed pp. 213-214.

Bhauma-Kara dynasty.title: Not individually recorded
Bhauma-Kara dynasty.note: No king of the house is named before Kshemankaradeva, whose accession is year one of the Bhauma era. But the family is in Tosali before that: it is from Tosali that they drove the Shailodbhavas out of Kongoda about 736, which means they were already established to the north. This entry stands for those unnamed predecessors so that the ruler roll and the map agree; it is not a reign, and no source names anyone in it.

The roll ends Kshemankaradeva in 748 and starts his son Shivakara I in 756, leaving an eight-year hole that no source supports. HCIP IV lists the family as No. I Kshemankaradeva followed directly by No. II Shivakaradeva I and states that all the monarchs 'ruled in an unbroken line of succession'; no ruler is known between them. Shivakara I's earliest date is year 20 of the Bhauma era, which is A.D. 756 on the 736 epoch this roll uses, so the founder's reign should simply run to his son's accession. This closes the hole without inventing a ruler.

Bhauma-Kara dynasty.title: Paramabhattaraka Maharajadhiraja Paramesvara
Bhauma-Kara dynasty.note: No. V in the family's genealogy, also called Gayada I and Lalitahara I; younger brother of Shivakara II. His firm date is year 93 of the Bhauma era, which is A.D. 829 on the era-epoch of 736 that the rest of this roll already uses. He married Tribhuvana Mahadevi I, daughter of the Naga chief Rajamalla, and it was either in his reign or his brother's that the Pala king Devapala overran Utkala; the Dhenkanal plate of year 110 says that after the deaths of Unmattakesari and Gayada the Kara kingdom 'looked like the sky bereft of refulgent stars'. Start and end are inferred from the neighbouring dated plates, not recorded. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 63, 67.

Bhauma-Kara dynasty.title: Paramabhattaraka Maharajadhiraja Paramesvara
Bhauma-Kara dynasty.note: No. VI, son of Shivakara II, known from a single plate of year 100 of the Bhauma era (A.D. 836). The later charters of the house pass over him in silence, which suggests a short and possibly contested reign; his dates here are bracketed by the year-93 record of Shantikara I and the year-103 record of Shubhakara III, so they are approximate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 63, 67, 80 n. 32.

Bhauma-Kara dynasty.title: Paramabhattaraka Maharajadhiraja Paramesvara
Bhauma-Kara dynasty.note: No. VII, also called Simhaketu and Kusumahara I; son of Shantikara I and Tribhuvana Mahadevi I. His dated record is year 103 of the Bhauma era (A.D. 839). The Talcher plate of year 141 records that on his death his mother took up the burden of administration, which fixes his end at her accession. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 63, 67.

Bhauma-Kara dynasty.title: Paramabhattaraka Maharajadhiraja Paramesvara
Bhauma-Kara dynasty.note: No. IX, also called Gayada II and Lonabhara I; grandson of Tribhuvana Mahadevi I, who according to the Talcher plate of year 141 of the Bhauma era (A.D. 877) abdicated in his favour once he had come of age. He has no dated charter of his own, so this long reign is simply the stretch between her charter of year 110 (A.D. 846) and Shubhakara IV's of year 145 (A.D. 881); the length is an inference from the succession, not a recorded figure. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 64, 67.

Bhauma-Kara dynasty.title: Paramabhattaraka Maharajadhiraja Paramesvara
Bhauma-Kara dynasty.note: No. XI, also called Lalitahara II; brother of Shubhakara IV. His Talcher plate is dated year 149 of the Bhauma era (A.D. 885). Nothing else is recorded of him, and the end date is set at the first charter of his successor, so it is approximate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 64, 66, 67.

Bhauma-Kara dynasty.title: Paramabhattarika Maharajadhiraja Paramesvari; also styled Prithvi Mahadevi
Bhauma-Kara dynasty.note: Queen of Shubhakara IV and daughter of the Somavamsi king Yayati Mahasivagupta I (Svabhavatunga) of Kosala. Her unpublished Baud plates are dated year 158 of the Bhauma era (A.D. 894 on this roll's epoch) and claim that Shubhakara IV and Shivakara III died without issue so that the throne passed to her; later records instead name two sons of Shivakara III who did reign, so she is best read as a rival claimant who held the throne briefly, probably with her father's military help, and was then removed. Authorities differ sharply here: the same volume dates her father Yayati to about A.D. 970-1000, which cannot be reconciled with a 736 era-epoch, so her absolute date may be as much as eight decades later than shown. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 64, 80 n. 33, 148-149.

Bhauma-Kara dynasty.title: Paramabhattaraka Maharajadhiraja Paramesvara
Bhauma-Kara dynasty.note: No. XII, also called Lavanabhara II; elder son of Shivakara III and husband of Dharma Mahadevi, who later reigned in her own right. No charter of his is dated - the volume states plainly that 'nothing is known of the four successors of Lonabhara' - so the span shown is an even division of the undated interval between Prithvi Mahadevi's plate of year 158 and Dandi Mahadevi's of year 180. Treat the years as placeholders for an attested reign of unknown length. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 64, 67.

Bhauma-Kara dynasty.title: Paramabhattaraka Maharajadhiraja Paramesvara
Bhauma-Kara dynasty.note: No. XIII, younger son of Shivakara III and the last male ruler of the house; on his death his queen Gauri took the throne. He has no dated record, so the years shown are an even division of the undated stretch between year 158 and year 180 of the Bhauma era; dates approximate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 64, 67.

Bhauma-Kara dynasty.title: Queen regnant
Bhauma-Kara dynasty.note: No. XIV, queen of Shubhakara V, who succeeded her husband and was in turn succeeded by her own daughter Dandi Mahadevi. She is the first of the closing run of four reigning queens and, unlike Tribhuvana Mahadevi I, Dandi Mahadevi and Dharma Mahadevi, has left no charter of her own, so no date can be attached to her directly; the years shown run from the estimated end of her husband's reign to Dandi Mahadevi's first dated plate of year 180 (A.D. 916). The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 64, 67-68.

Bhauma-Kara dynasty.title: Queen regnant
Bhauma-Kara dynasty.note: No. XVI, step-mother of Dandi Mahadevi and, on the evidence of the newly found Taltali plate, her successor. A verse describes her as an ornament in the family of the Bhanja kings, so she was almost certainly a Bhanja by birth, and her relatives may well have had a hand in the succession. Her plate carries no year, but its script has been compared with Somavamsi records datable to about the middle of the tenth century A.D., which is the only anchor available; dates approximate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 64, 67-68, 80 n. 47.

Bhauma-Kara dynasty.title: Paramabhattarika Maharajadhiraja Paramesvari
Bhauma-Kara dynasty.note: No. XVII, queen of Shantikara III (Lavanabhara II) and the last known ruler of the house; she closes a remarkable sequence of four queens who held the throne one after another. Nothing is recorded of the Karas after her, and she 'probably flourished about the year 200 of the Kara era, i.e. about A.D. 950', after which the family was most likely displaced by the Somavamsis, who are known to have taken Orissa about the middle of the tenth century. Note the slack in the arithmetic: year 200 on the 736 epoch used by this roll would be A.D. 936, while the volume itself says about 950, so her absolute dates are good only to within about fifteen years. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 64, 67-68.

Panduvamshi dynasty.note: The Classical Age (HCIP III), pp. 221-22: 'The son and successor of Chandragupta was Harshagupta who married Vasata, daughter of a ruler named Surya-varman'; 'Harshagupta's son and successor Balarjuna assumed the title Sivagupta'. The genealogy (p. 727) numbers him sixth in the Panduvamshi line of South Kosala. Dates approximate: HCIP III places Balarjuna in the early seventh century, whereas this roll dates him 730-790; the span here is simply the stretch immediately before this roll's date for his son, and no regnal years of Harshagupta's own survive.

Chera Perumal kingdom.note: Sastri, A History of South India, block 175 (printed p. 192): 'Sthanuravi was perhaps succeeded by Vijayaragadeva, described as manager of the temple or palace (koyil adigarigal) in the Kottayam plates, and as Kerala raja in the Tiruvorriyur epigraph.' He is the ONLY Perumal the library names between Rama Rajasekhara and Bhaskara Ravi. Dates approximate: no regnal years for him survive in the library, and the span here is a placeholder covering the head of the 883-962 gap, not an attested reign-length. Sastri, block 143 (printed p. 155), states that through this period 'the land continued under the Perumals' - the gap is a gap in the record, not a change of dynasty.

Habbarid Emirate.title: Ruler of Mansura
Habbarid Emirate.note: Khafif is named as the ruler of Mansura when Mahmud of Ghazni, marching home from Somanatha up the Indus, reached the town and defeated him; Mahmud's column got back to Ghazni in A.D. 1026. The date of Khafif's accession is not recorded, so these years mark only the single moment at which he is attested, not the true length of his reign. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), printed p. 21.

Saindhava dynasty.note: The roll dates this entry 776-799, but 776-799 is the reign of Agguka I, the third king, not of Pushyadeva. HCIP IV says Pushyadeva is the earliest known king of the dynasty and 'flourished in the second quarter of the eighth century'; the Arabs of Sindh invaded his kingdom in or before A.D. 739, and he also suffered a defeat at the hands of the Rashtrakuta Dantidurga. HCIP III adds that a record dated A.D. 738 names a Jaikadeva as lord of Surashtra-mandala ruling at Bhumilika, though the genuineness of that record has been doubted. Moving this entry back to c. 735-755 puts Pushyadeva where the sources put him and frees 755 onward for the separately named successors added in rulers.json.

Son and successor of Pushyadeva, and second in the Ghumli genealogy. About A.D. 756 Hisham, the newly appointed Arab governor of Sindh, sent Amru bin Jamal with a fleet against the coast of Barada, the tract along the Barda hills; no Arab victory is claimed, and the fleet was evidently beaten off by the Saindhavas under Krishna, who styled themselves lords of the western sea. His reign has no dated record and is placed by position between his father in the second quarter of the eighth century and Agguka I in the last quarter, so the years are approximate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 99, 524.

Saindhava dynasty.title: Mahasamanta
Saindhava dynasty.note: Son of Krishnaraja I; the volume places his rule in the last quarter of the eighth century. About A.D. 776 a second Arab naval expedition attacked Barada and took a town, probably Ghumli itself, before withdrawing; the Arab account blames an epidemic, but a Saindhava inscription credits Agguka with having 'showed the greatness of Varaha when he easily rescued his country, which was being drowned in an ocean of naval force sent by powerful enemies', which reads as the real reason. Dates approximate; no year-dated charter of his survives. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 99-100, 524.

Son of Agguka I, fourth in the Ghumli genealogy, and placed in the first quarter of the ninth century. It was in his time that the Pratihara Nagabhata II led an expedition into Saurashtra and won a victory over the Saindhavas, after which the house probably held Bhutambilika as Pratihara feudatories. He had two sons by two queens, Krishnaraja II and Jaika I. The name is printed as Kanaka in some places in the volume and as Ranaka in others; the chronological table uses Ranaka. Dates approximate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 100-101, 524, 559.

Saindhava dynasty.title: Raja
Saindhava dynasty.note: Elder son of Ranaka I. His reign opened the long war between the Saindhavas and the Chapas of Vardhamana, and he fought successfully against the Chapa chief, probably Vikramarka, and is said to have brought happiness to the people of Parvata, meaning the Barda hills. He died young and left a boy heir, which is why the regency of 832 follows immediately; his years are inferred from that fixed point backwards and are approximate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 100.

Young son of Krishnaraja II, who came to the throne as a minor under the regency of his uncle Jaika I. Jaika issued a charter as regent in A.D. 832 professing that although Royal Fortune was willing to attach herself to him in preference to Agguka, 'her rightful lord', he would remain the disinterested guardian of his young nephew - but Jaika is later found on the throne himself, and it is not unlikely that he displaced the boy. Only the regency date of 832 is fixed; the end year is an estimate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 100.

Step-brother of Krishnaraja II and uncle of Agguka II, whose regent he was from A.D. 832 before taking the throne of Bhutambilika himself. He is credited with a victory over the Chapas of Vardhamanapura and left two sons, Chamundaraja and Agguka III. His own dates are not recorded; some scholars number him Jaika II, counting the Jaikadeva of the disputed Dhiniki plate of A.D. 738 as the first of the name, so the roman numeral varies between authorities. Dates approximate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 100, 524.

Elder son of Jaika I, who came to the throne after his father and was followed by his younger brother rather than by his own son, a break that later caused a contested succession. He has no dated record; the years shown fall between Jaika I's regency charter of 832 and Ranaka II's known date of 874 and are approximate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 100-101, 524.

Younger brother of Chamundaraja. He is said to have been on the throne a long time before deciding to crown his son, noticing how Lakshmi 'had become eager to be united with his son Ranaka, who had become quite capable of bearing the burden of administration'; the abdication looks like a move to secure the throne for his own son against the claim of his nephew Agguka IV. No dated charter is his; the end is fixed by Ranaka II's date of A.D. 874 and the start is an estimate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 100-101.

Son of Agguka III, raised to the throne by his father's abdication; his known date is A.D. 874. His own son took the title of Yuvaraja but never reigned, because after Ranaka II the throne is found in the hands of his cousin Agguka IV, which suggests the displaced branch won the quarrel. The 874 date is firm; the end year is set at his cousin's known date and is approximate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 101, 524, 559.

Son of Chamundaraja and cousin of Ranaka II, whom he appears to have supplanted. He was ruling in A.D. 886, the one firm point in his reign; the start is taken from that date and the end from his son's first known date, so both bounds are approximate. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 101, 524, 559.

Saindhava dynasty.title: Mahasamantadhipati
Saindhava dynasty.note: Son of Agguka IV and the last king of the house of whom anything is known; his recorded dates are A.D. 904 and 915. Nothing survives about his successors, who were probably overthrown by the Abhira chief Graharipu when the Abhiras established themselves over southern and western Saurashtra in the second half of the tenth century. The end year of 920 is an estimate a little past his last dated charter, not a recorded date; some scholars number him Jaika III under the alternative reckoning that begins the series with the Dhiniki-plate Jaikadeva. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 101-102, 524, 560.

Ayudha dynasty of Kannauj.note: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), Foreword, printed p. x: "Nagabhata II, in his turn, marched against Chakrayudha, overthrew him and made Kanauj his capital. Soon after Rashtrakuta Govinda III invaded Kanauj and inflicted a defeat on Nagabhata which, however, did not cripple his strength. Ultimately Kanauj passed into the hands of the Pratiharas. About A.D. 815 it became the capital of the Pratihara empire." Compare printed p. 25 (Nagabhata defeats Chakrayudha) and printed p. 48 (Dharmapala and Chakrayudha submit to Govinda III).

Brahmin dynasty of Sindh.note: Son of Raja Dahir. He commanded the force that met Budail's seaborne expedition before the main invasion - "He was met by Jaisimha, son of Dahar. A pitched battle ensued, which lasted a whole day. At the end, the Muslim army was routed and Budail was killed" - and after his father fell at Raor in 712 he "retreated to Brahmanabad" and prepared to defend it and the capital Alor. On the recall and death of Muhammad ibn Qasim, which followed the deaths of Hajjaj in 714 and Caliph Walid in 715, "the chiefs of Sindh... threw off the Muslim yoke. Dahar's son Jaisimha re-occupied Brahmanabad", while Habib, sent by the Caliph, "conquered Alor and made some minor conquests". Caliph Umar II (717-720) then "offered virtual independence to the chiefs of Sindh, under his suzerainty, on condition of their accepting Islam. Many chiefs including Jaisimha accepted the offer"; HCIP adds elsewhere that he took an Arab name, and that "within a few years of his conversion Jaisimha quarrelled with the governor of Sindh". Under Hisham (acceded 724) he declared war on the governor Junaid, who "defeated him and took him prisoner. With Jaisimha ended the Hindu royal dynasty of Sindh." HCIP III names no second son of Dahir and no co-ruler beside Jaisimha - the two daughters of Dahir appear only in a Chach-nama story the volume rejects, and the divided kingship belongs a generation earlier, to Chach's two sons Daharsiah and Dahar, who held the kingdom between them until Daharsiah's death, dated "about A.D. 700". The Classical Age (HCIP III), printed pp. 166, 170-172 and 460.

Caliphal Sindh (Umayyad–Abbasid).title: Governor of Sindh
Caliphal Sindh (Umayyad–Abbasid).note: Sent by the Caliph to recover Sindh after Muhammad ibn Qasim's recall, he took Alor and made some minor conquests; HCIP III gives him no dates, and records that the next Caliph 'Umar II (A.D. 717-720) left many chiefs of Sindh, Jaisimha among them, in virtual independence under caliphal suzerainty. The years here run from the recall to Junayd's arrival and are not recorded ones. The Classical Age (HCIP III), printed p. 172.

Caliphal Sindh (Umayyad–Abbasid).title: Governor of Sindh
Caliphal Sindh (Umayyad–Abbasid).note: Junayd's successor as governor, in whose time the Arabs gave up the territories taken east and south of Sindh and fell back on the province itself; a new city was built beyond the lake, on the site where Mansurah later stood, as a refuge. HCIP III gives no dates for him, so the years here are bounded by Junayd and al-Hakam ibn Awana on this roll. The Classical Age (HCIP III), printed p. 173.

Tibetan Empire.note: Mu-Khri-btsan-po or Mu-tig-btsan-po, son of Khri-sron-lde-btsan. HCIP IV gives his reign as A.D. 798 to 804 and reports the Tibetan chronicles' claim that he subjugated parts of Jambudvipa and took tribute from the Pala king Dharmapala; the end year is trimmed here to meet Sadnalegs on this roll, and HCIP adds that no Indian source records any such campaign. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 446 and 508.

The Classical Age (HCIP III), p. 158 follows Ojha's 734 and 753 for his accession and abdication and notes Tod's rival 728 and 784; the atlas paints the seizure of Chitor at c. 740 because Maurya Dhavala was still honoured there in 738-39 (The Classical Age (HCIP III), p. 162).
c. dates; no regnal years in The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 109.
c. dates; no regnal years in The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 109.
c. dates; no regnal years in The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 109.
c. dates. Joined the Pratihara Nagabhata II and the Chahamana Guvaka I against Bashar, Arab governor of Sindh (The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 106, 109).
c. dates; no regnal years in The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 109.
c. dates; no regnal years in The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 109.
Titled Maharajadhiraja; a grant of A.D. 942 and a stone inscription of 943 from Ahar, which became the capital in this reign (The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 109).
'Known dates are A.D. 951 and 953'; killed the Pratihara Devapala in battle; married the Huna lady Hariyadevi (The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 109).
'Ruled till at least A.D. 971' (The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 109).
c. dates; no regnal years in The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 109.
Three Ahar inscriptions, one dated A.D. 977; 'he ruled up to the close of the tenth century'. Aghata was sacked by the Paramara Munja in his reign (The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 109-110).
c. dates. 'Lost his life in a battle with the Chahamana Vakpati II of Sakambhari' (The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 89).

APPROXIMATE. The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 89 lists Suchivarman, Naravarman, Anantavarman, Kirttivarman, Yogaraja, Vairata, Hamsapala and Vairisimha in bare succession with NO dates at all; these spans are distributed evenly between two fixed points, Saktikumara (to c. 1000) and Vijayasimha (1108-1116).

The one firmly dated ruler of this stretch: 'definitely known to have been ruling in A.D. 1108 and 1116'. Father-in-law the Paramara Udayaditya; son-in-law the Kalachuri Gayakarna (The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 89).
APPROXIMATE. A bare name in The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 89; spans to Samantasimha are evenly distributed over HCIP's succession order.

c. dates. His son Kshemasimha founded the Raval line and his son Rahapa the Sisodiya line at Sisoda (The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 89).
APPROXIMATE - see the note on Arisimha (The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 89).
'Known to have been ruling in Mewar in A.D. 1171'; wounded the Chaulukya Ajayapala, then lost Medapata to Kirttipala of Nadol (The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 78, 89).
c. dates. Younger brother of Samantasimha; drove Kirttipala out and 'occupied Mewar before A.D. 1182' with Chaulukya help (The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 89).

Thakuri dynasty of Nepal.note: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 108. Dated 1187.
The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 109. Dated 1196-97.

Kamarupa.note: Salastambha dynasty. The Classical Age (HCIP III), p. 141: 'A king of this dynasty, called both Harsha and Harsha-varman, has been identified with king Harshadeva of the Bhagadatta dynasty, who is referred to in a Nepal inscription as the father of Rajyamati (queen of Jayadeva)'; HCIP notes the identification 'must remain doubtful'. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 60, begins its account with 'King Harsha of Salastambha family'. Dates approximate and unattested - HCIP gives no regnal years and calls the century after Bhaskaravarman 'a dark period in the history of Kamarupa'; the span here is anchored only to the Nepalese connection with Jayadeva.

Salastambha dynasty. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 60: 'King Harsha of Salastambha family was followed by Balavarman, and probably one or two others, after whom we find a king Salambha on the throne of Kamarupa.' Dates approximate and unattested - HCIP gives no regnal years, and the 'one or two others' between him and Salambha are not named, so 760-790 is left blank here rather than filled.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 60: 'We are not also quite sure about the name of the ruler, for another copper-plate gives the name as Pralambha. He probably flourished about the end of the eighth or the beginning of the ninth century A.D.' HCIP suggests the change of dynasty may have followed the Pala invasion. His son or nephew Harjaravarman, already in the roll, took full imperial titles in a record of A.D. 829 (HCIP IV, p. 61). Dates approximate.

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 61: 'Vanamala was succeeded by his son Jayamala, who assumed the name of Viravahu after his accession to the throne.' Dates approximate - HCIP records no regnal years for him. (Fills a hole the brief did not list, between Vanamalavarmadeva and Brahmapala.)

The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 61: 'Nothing is known of him or of his son and successor Bala-varman', from whom the Nowgong and Howraghat plates survive. The dynasty of Salambha 'ruled from A.D. c. 800 to c. 1000' and ended with Tyagasimha, after whom the people chose Brahmapala - already in the roll from 900. Dates approximate.
The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 43. Set up by Ramapala as governor of Kamarupa and later ruled in his own right.

HCIP IV gives no regnal years for any of the three, placing them only in the latter half of the tenth century, so these dates are an apportionment of the interval and not recorded ones. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 54 and 85.

One of the two sons of Rajyapala of the Kamboja family of Gauda. HCIP IV supplies no regnal years, so these dates are an apportionment of the interval, not recorded ones. The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 54.

HCIP V p. 41: "Harikaladeva or his successor was overthrown by the Deva dynasty."

Deva dynasty of Samatata and Vanga.note: HCIP V p. 42: inscriptions dated A.D. 1234 and 1243; the Mehara grant in the Samatata-mandala. Dates approximate.
HCIP V p. 42: the Danuj Rai who met Balban at Sonargaon in 1283. Dates approximate.
HCIP V p. 42 has the kingdom passing to the Muslims in the later thirteenth century; HCIP VI p. 388 dates the conquest of Tippera and Chittagong to 1326-27.

Gohad (Jat Ranas).note: Took Gwalior fort in 1740 and held it until the Marathas took it in 1754-55. (Web-sourced; the library does not name him.)
A short reign between Bhim Singh and Chhatra Singh. (Web-sourced.)

Sarkar III p. 273: Mahadji crushed 'Rana Chhatra Singh of Gohad, by storming Gwalior fort (31 July 1783) and seizing Gohad and the Rana's person (25 Feb. 1784)'. Bought peace from Raghunath Rao for 15 lakhs in December 1766 (HCIP VIII p. 218); held Gwalior again 1780-83 by Hastings's gift. The end year is web-sourced.

Restored to Gohad by the British after Laswari and moved to Dholpur when Gohad went back to Sindia by the treaty of Mustafapur, 21 November 1805 (HCIP VIII p. 499). Continues as the first Rana of Dholpur.

Farrukhabad (Bangash).note: Founded Farrukhabad in 1714; imperial viceroy of Allahabad and Malwa. Sarkar I p. 39 has him die in 1743, p. 29 in 1748; the roll follows p. 39 and records the disagreement.
'A fine soldier and sportsman, but too much obsessed by religiosity to pursue a career of ambition' (Sarkar I p. 39). Killed fighting the Rohillas at Daunri, November 1749 (Sarkar I p. 240).
Raised by his mother Bibi Sahiba; Safdar Jang seized the state within months (Sarkar I pp. 240-241).

Led the Afghan rising that swept Safdar Jang's rule off the country, beat him at Ram Chatauni (September 1750), lost to the Marathas in 1751 and kept Farrukhabad by the peace of 1752 (Sarkar I pp. 241-257; HCIP VIII p. 137). The end year is web-sourced.
(Web-sourced; the library does not name him.)
Ceded the state to the Company in 1802 (Sarkar IV p. 266). Web-sourced dates.

PK-JHELUM.detail: Alexander defeats Porus on the Jhelum, the first major recorded battle in Indian history

in the winter campaign of 1013-14 Mahmud, delayed by snow in the passes, took Nandana in the Salt Range, the last capital of the Shahis, from Trilochanapala, son of Anandapala; the Shahi king fled toward Kashmir, whose minister Tunga was sent — in vain — to his aid.

IN-THIRUVARUR.outcome: Pandyan victory; the seven-ruler coalition defeated, Chera ruler captured

IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.detail: "Some time about A.D. 300 or a little later the whole country was upset by the predatory activities of the Kalabhras" — the three Tamil crowns eclipsed for nearly three centuries; a Buddhist Kalabhra king Achchutavikkanta patronises monasteries in the Chola country.
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.source: Sastri, A History of South India scan 12, 130; HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 265-266

IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.detail: the Pallava 'not only suppressed the Kalabhras but conquered the whole country up to the Kaveri and even came into conflict with the Pandyas and the ruler of Ceylon' — the beginning of the Greater Pallavas.
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.belligerents: Pallava dynasty (Simhavishnu) vs Kalabhra dynasty; vs Pandya and Ceylon
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.outcome: Pallava rule extended to the Kaveri; Kalabhra power in Tondaimandalam and the Chola country ended
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.source: Sastri, A History of South India scan 134; HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 258, 266

IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.detail: Paramesvaravarman I turns the tide — Vikramaditya I, 'although his army consisted of several lakhs, was obliged to flee covered only by a rag' at Peruvalanallur near Lalgudi; the Chalukya withdraws from the Pallava country.
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.belligerents: Pallava dynasty (Paramesvaravarman I) vs Chalukya (Badami) (Vikramaditya I)
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 261-262 (Kuram plates)

IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.detail: Vikramaditya I's Gadval plates, issued from Uragapura on the Kaveri, show the Chalukya army in the heart of the Chola country after the capture of Kanchi.
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 241, 261

IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.text: Ramanuja dies — By tradition at Srirangam, aged 120
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.detail: The Battle of Srirangam was a major conflict between the Pandya dynasty under Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan I and the Hoysala Empire led by Vira Someshvara.

Maravarman Kulasekhara Pandya defeated the Hoysalas at Kannanur Kuppam and, in the same war, the last Chola emperor Rajendra III disappears from the record — four hundred and thirty years after Vijayalaya took Thanjavur.
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.belligerents: Pandya dynasty (Maravarman Kulasekhara) vs Hoysala Kingdom and the last Cholas (Rajendra III)
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.outcome: Pandya victory; the Chola state ceases to exist
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.source: Cross-referenced against Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, and the Chola Empire literature (Aug 2026).

IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.detail: The Battle of Kannanur took place in 1342, in what is now Kannanur, Tamil Nadu, India.
the last great Hoysala is captured and executed by the Madurai Sultanate
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.outcome: Madurai victory — the last great king captured and executed
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.detail: a Bijapuri army under Shahaji, joined by Lingama Nayaka and Tanjore, besieged Chokkanatha Nayak in Trichinopoly and was beaten off — the first of two sieges of the fort in his reign.
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.belligerents: Madurai Nayakas vs Bijapur Sultanate, Tanjore Nayaks

IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.detail: a second Bijapuri siege of Trichinopoly, under Vanamian and with Tanjore's Vijaya Raghava Nayak, three years after the 1660 attempt.
Battle of Trichinopoly (1682) was fought between the Maratha Empire and the Kingdom of Mysore.
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.belligerents: Maratha Kingdom, Thanjavur Maratha kingdom, Golkonda Sultanate vs Kingdom of Mysore, Madurai Nayaks
Maratha Empire, Thanjavur (Maratha) vs Chanda Sahib (Trichinopoly)
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.outcome: Maratha victory; Chanda Sahib surrenders Trichinopoly on 14 March 1741 and is taken prisoner, and Murari Rao is left in charge
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II p. 255: 'Chanda Saheb ... delivered the place to Raghuji on 14th March (Ramnavami). It was a grand success for the Marathas ... Chanda Saheb was taken into custody.' HCIP VIII p. 313.

IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.detail: the Nizam marches into the Karnatak, restores order at Arcot and after six months forces Murari Rao's Maratha garrison out of Trichinopoly, ending the Maratha hold won in 1741.
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.outcome: Hyderabad victory; Murari Rao evacuates Trichinopoly and Mughal authority is re-established in the Karnatak
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.source: HCIP VIII p. 313: 'He then proceeded to Trichinopoly which he contrived to secure, after six months of desultory operations.' p. 336 n. 4: 'Murar Rao, was left in charge of Trichinopoly till he was forced by Nizam-ul-Mulk to evacuate it in the latter part of 1743.'

IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.text: Chanda Sahib dies — the Nawayat adventurer who took Madurai, was Dupleix's Nawab of Arcot from 1749, and was killed after surrendering to the Tanjore general at Srirangam.
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.source: HCIP VIII p. 325: 'Ultimately Chanda Sahib was killed, it is said, at the instigation of Muhammad Ali (June 1752).'

IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.text: Surrender at Srirangam and death of Chanda Sahib
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.detail: Law's French army, cut off on Srirangam island by Lawrence and Clive, surrenders; Chanda Sahib gives himself up to the Tanjore general and is killed, ending the French siege of Trichinopoly.
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.belligerents: East India Company, Carnatic (Arcot Nawab), Mysore, Thanjavur (Maratha) vs French India, Chanda Sahib
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.outcome: East India Company victory; the French force surrenders and Chanda Sahib is put to death (June 1752)
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.source: HCIP VIII p. 325: 'Ultimately Chanda Sahib was killed, it is said, at the instigation of Muhammad Ali (June 1752). Thus ended the French siege of Trichinopoly. No such blow had fallen on the French since they entered the field of Indian politics.'

IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.detail: The Battle of Seringham was fought on the island of Srirangam by 1,000 troops of the British East India Company commanded by Stringer Lawrence.
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.belligerents: Kingdom of Great Britain East India Company Maratha Empire Thanjavur Marathas vs France French East India Company Nawab of Arcot

IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.detail: Lawrence checks the French–Mysore alliance at Trichinopoly
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.belligerents: East India Company, Thanjavur (Maratha) vs French India, Mysore
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.outcome: East India Company victory; Lawrence's surprise attack on the rock position throws the French and Mysoreans into panic
IN-TIRUCHIRAPPALLI.source: HCIP VIII p. 328: 'The latter however launched an unexpected attack against a strong rock position which struck the French with panic and created dissensions between them and their allies.'

IN-UJJAIN.text: Rudrasimha II seizes the Western Kshatrapa throne
IN-UJJAIN.detail: A usurper from a collateral line ousts the legitimate heir at Ujjain; the Saka satrapy limps on for another century under his line.
IN-UJJAIN.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 46 (chronology p. 707)

IN-UJJAIN.text: Rudrasimha III dies — Last Western Kshatrapa, defeated by Chandragupta II
IN-UJJAIN.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 19

IN-UJJAIN.text: Paramartha is born — Born at Ujjain
IN-UJJAIN.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 611 (Chinese biographies)

IN-UJJAIN.detail: in 533 Malwa is 'being ruled by the governor of Isanavarman, the Maukhari'; two years later Kumaragupta III re-establishes Gupta sway and styles himself 'Lord of the three seas'.
IN-UJJAIN.belligerents: Maukhari dynasty (Isanavarman) vs Gupta Empire (Kumaragupta III)
IN-UJJAIN.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. xvi (introduction)

IN-UJJAIN.text: Paramartha sails from India to China
IN-UJJAIN.detail: The scholar-monk of Ujjain and Pataliputra reaches China in 546 and translates the Yogachara texts of Asanga and Vasubandhu; he dies there in 569.
IN-UJJAIN.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 611; chronology p. 711
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 317; chronology p. 712

IN-UJJAIN.detail: Sankaragana's Abhona plates (Kalachuri year 347) are issued from Ujjayini — northern Maharashtra, Gujarat and western Malwa under one Kalachuri king.
IN-UJJAIN.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 74, 195

IN-UJJAIN.detail: Sankaragana, son of Krishnaraja, is 'in possession of Ujjayini' by 595 — the Later Guptas of Malwa are pushed out and the Kalachuris hold northern Maharashtra, Gujarat and parts of Malwa.
IN-UJJAIN.belligerents: Kalachuri of Mahishmati (Sankaragana) vs Later Gupta dynasty (Mahasenagupta)
IN-UJJAIN.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 74, 191, 195 (Abhona plates, Kalachuri year 347 = 595)

IN-UJJAIN.text: Bhartrihari dies — Forty years before I-tsing wrote (691).
IN-UJJAIN.source: I-tsing, Record (Takakusu); HCIP III ch. XIX

IN-UJJAIN.detail: Junaid, the Umayyad governor of Sindh, crushed Jaisimha, who had renounced the treaty submission his family had made to the caliphate and then pushed far beyond Sindh, his columns overrunning Marumada (Jaisalmer-Jodhpur), Vallamandala, Broach and Malwa as far as Ujjain, and defeating the Saindhava, Kachchhella, Saurashtra, Chavotaka, Maurya and Gurjara kings. The gains proved short-lived and were lost under his successor Tamim.
IN-UJJAIN.belligerents: Caliphal Sindh (Umayyad–Abbasid) (Junaid) vs the kingdoms of Rajasthan, Gujarat and Malwa - Gurjaras of Bhillamala, Pratiharas of Avanti, Chalukya (Badami) viceroys of Lata
IN-UJJAIN.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), pp. 172-173; raids dated A.D. 724-738 in chronology p. 717. date approximate: raids spread over c. 724-738

IN-UJJAIN.detail: after the death of his Chalukya overlord in 747 the Rashtrakuta Dantidurga marched north, extinguished the Gurjara kingdom of Nandipuri in southern Gujarat, and proclaimed the conquest of Malwa by performing the Hiranyagarbha-dana ceremony at its capital Ujjayini, where the defeated Gurjara king is said to have served him as door-keeper. The victory was not followed by annexation: Nagabhata I was still acknowledged as suzerain at Broach in 756 and left a kingdom in Malwa and Rajputana to his successors.
IN-UJJAIN.outcome: Rashtrakuta victory and the submission of the Gurjara king, but no lasting conquest north of the Kim
IN-UJJAIN.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 20: "The Rashtrakuta king Dantidurga, who reigned between c. A.D. 733 and 758, is said to have defeated the Gurjara king and made him serve as a door-keeper (pratihara) when he performed the Hiranyagarbha-dana ceremony at Ujjain"; same page, "it is more or less certain that his Gurjara adversary could not have been anybody else but Nagabhata I" and "it does not appear that Dantidurga's military victory was followed by any permanent conquest". Printed p. 2 places the expedition after A.D. 747: "Then he led an expedition into Malwa; and proclaimed its conquest by performing Hiranyagarbha-dana ceremony at its capital Ujjayini." Date approximate (c. 748-750). DISAGREEMENT ON THE RECORD: Wikipedia states flatly that Dantidurga defeated and subdued Nagabhata I in Gujarat and Malwa; HCIP IV reports the door-keeper episode only as a claim ("is said to have"), notes that the identification with the Pratihara rests on a pun on pratihara that "is not accepted by all" (printed p. 20), and holds at printed p. 21 that "in spite of initial discomfiture Nagabhata was able to leave to his successors a powerful principality comprising Malwa and parts of Rajputana and Gujarat".

IN-UJJAIN.detail: Rashtrakuta records assert that Krishna II recovered Khetaka and fought a sanguinary battle with Bhoja I's host at Ujjayini 'which made a deep impress even upon posterity' — the Begumra plates of 914 say old men still talked of the great battle.
IN-UJJAIN.belligerents: Rashtrakuta Empire (with Kalachuri allies) vs Gurjara-Pratihara Empire
IN-UJJAIN.outcome: Claimed as a Rashtrakuta success, but Malwa remained in Pratihara hands (still Pratihara in A.D. 946)
IN-UJJAIN.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 11, 31. Date disputed: 'some time between A.D. 878 and 888' On Malwa the map gives the Pratiharas 930-946 only (HCIP IV p. 95, the Paramara chapter); the sentence "still Pratihara in A.D. 946" is the end of that window, not evidence that they held it from 880.

IN-UJJAIN.detail: the Rashtrakuta emperor, aided by the Ganga Marasimha, marched into Bundelkhand in c. 963 and then led an expedition into Malwa against the Paramara Siyaka, occupying Ujjayini. The campaign confirmed Rashtrakuta lordship over 'the whole of the Deccan' at its last zenith.
IN-UJJAIN.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 15

IN-UJJAIN.detail: when the Ghaznavid prince Mahmud of Lahore pushed on from Kannauj into Malava, the Paramara Lakshmadeva son of Udayaditya beat him back from Ujjain. The same king raided Gauda under the Kaivartas, plundered Anga and Kalinga, defeated the Kalachuri Yasahkarna, plundered the Kalachuri capital Tripuri and encamped on the Reva, and led an army to the Kira country — the most far-ranging Paramara campaigns since Bhoja.
IN-UJJAIN.belligerents: Paramaras of Malava vs the Ghaznavids of Lahore
IN-UJJAIN.outcome: Paramara victory; the Ghaznavid attack on Ujjain thrown back
IN-UJJAIN.source: HCIP V, printed p. 68: "He won a victory over the Kalachuri Yasahkarna and repulsed an attack of Mahmud, governor of the Punjab, when the latter invaded Ujjain. On the north he is said to have led his army to the Kira country, i.e. Kangra valley in the Punjab." (Note: HCIP dates Lakshmadeva's reign 1088-1094 and the Ghaznavid raid 1086-1090, so the year is approximate. The plundering of Tripuri is at printed p. 64.)

IN-UJJAIN.detail: Jai Singh, as Mughal governor, makes Peshwa Balaji Rao deputy governor of Malwa in July 1741 and grants him its chauth and sardeshmukhi in September. With this, Malwa is cut off from the Mughal empire in law as well as in fact.
IN-UJJAIN.source: HCIP VIII p. 145: 'when in July 1741 the Peshwa (Balaji Rao) was granted the deputy-governorship of Malwa. Thus, Malwa ceased to be a part of the empire ... it was finally and completely cut off from the Mughul empire.' Chronology p. 821.

IN-UJJAIN.detail: Holkar's army is broken on the Sipra
IN-UJJAIN.belligerents: Holkar (Indore State) vs East India Company
IN-UJJAIN.outcome: East India Company victory; Malhar Rao Holkar III's army suffered a decisive defeat, followed by the Treaty of Mandasor
IN-UJJAIN.source: HCIP VIII p. 506: 'Young Malhar Rao Holkar III, his brave widowed sister Bhima Bai ... fought with desperate courage at Mahidpur on 21 December, 1817, and suffered a decisive defeat. Their artillerymen stood to their guns till they were bayonetted.'

IN-RAISEN.text: Sridharavarman sets up an independent kingdom
IN-RAISEN.detail: A Saka chief, once a Kshatrapa officer, rules independently in the Sanchi–Eran country of eastern Malwa — a sign of the Kshatrapa break-up before the Guptas arrive.
IN-RAISEN.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 47 (Kanakhera and Eran inscriptions)

IN-RAISEN.detail: The siege of Raisen was a six-month siege led by Sher Shah Suri of the Sur Empire in 1543 against the Rajput leader, Raja Puran Mal of Chanderi.

IN-PATNA.detail: Chandragupta I is crowned Maharajadhiraja: On 26 February 320 the reckoning later used from Bengal to Kathiawad commences — most probably the coronation of Chandragupta I, whose marriage to the Licchavi Kumaradevi united two principalities of Bihar into the kingdom his son would make an empire.
IN-PATNA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 4-5

IN-PATNA.text: Chandragupta I dies — Succeeded by Samudragupta, chosen over other claimants.
IN-PATNA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 5-6

IN-PATNA.text: Samudragupta succeeds to the Gupta throne
IN-PATNA.detail: Chosen by his father over other claimants, the "hero of a hundred battles" begins the reign that gives the Allahabad prasasti its subject.
IN-PATNA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 6-7
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 15

IN-PATNA.detail: After the shadowy Ramagupta episode, the son of Samudragupta takes the throne he will hold to c. 414 — the reign of the Saka conquest, Fa-hien's visit and Kalidasa's tradition.
IN-PATNA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 15-18; chronology p. 708

IN-PATNA.detail: The Chinese monk travels the Gupta empire 400-411 — Mathura, Kanauj, Pataliputra, Tamralipti — and Ceylon 411-12, and leaves the earliest outsider's picture of the Classical Age: mild government, no death penalty, prosperous cities.
IN-PATNA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 22, 613-614; chronology p. 708
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 22; chronology p. 708 (376-414)

IN-PATNA.detail: Forty years of peace and asvamedha — the reign in which Nalanda is founded and the Gupta silver coinage spreads through the west; it ends with the Pushyamitra and Hun wars.
IN-PATNA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 23-25; chronology p. 708 (415-55)
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 25 (inferred)

IN-PATNA.text: Kumaragupta I dies — Died during the Pushyamitra and Hun crises.
IN-PATNA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 25
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 28

IN-PATNA.detail: aged 23 in Kali 3600 = 499. Born, by tradition, at Kusumapura or in Asmaka.
IN-PATNA.source: Aryabhatiya, Kalakriya 10; HCIP III ch. XX
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 32
Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)
Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PATNA.text: Guru Gobind Singh is born — At Patna
IN-PATNA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PATNA.detail: The Battle of Naubatpur was a military confrontation during the Maratha invasions of Bengal in 1745.
IN-PATNA.belligerents: Bengal Subah vs Maratha Empire Kingdom of Nagpur Afghan rebels

IN-PATNA.detail: The Battle of Rani Sarai, also known as the Battle of Kaladiara, fought on 16 April 1748 near Rani Sarai, eight miles west of Barh in Bihar, was a decisive engagement.
IN-PATNA.belligerents: Bengal Subah vs Afghan rebels (Shamshir Khan, Murad Sher Khan), with Janoji’s Marathas standing off
IN-PATNA.outcome: Bengal Subah victory; Shamshir Khan and Murad Sher Khan killed and Bihar recovered — the Marathas watched from the flank and slipped away
IN-PATNA.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I pp. 91–92: 'It was the 16th of April 1748. Alivardi advanced to the village of Ranisarai, eight miles west of Barh ... The Marathas could be seen on the left hand some distance behind, waiting to plunder whichever side should lose the day. Ignoring the Maratha light horse as beneath his notice and pointing to the Afghans as “There are my enemies,” the Nawab advanced'; HCIP VIII p. 110: 'The Afghans were ultimately vanquished by ‘Ali Vardi in a battle with them at Ranichak or Ranisarai, near Barh, in 1748.'

IN-PATNA.detail: Major Caillaud and Miran defeat Shah Alam II near Bakhtiyarpur on 22 February 1760; the emperor’s raid on Murshidabad that followed failed.
IN-PATNA.belligerents: East India Company and Bengal (Nawab) vs Mughal Empire (Shah Alam II)
IN-PATNA.outcome: East India Company victory; Shah Alam beaten but, the Nawab’s cavalry refusing to pursue, retires unbroken to Bihar city
IN-PATNA.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 540: 'Major Caillaud pushed up and on the 22nd completely defeated him at Sherpur. The refusal of the Nawab’s cavalry to obey the English commander enabled the Emperor to retire unbroken to Bihar city.' HCIP VIII p. 342: 'The Shahzada was beaten in an engagement at Sirpur, but Miran would not follow up the victory.'

IN-NAGPUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 177

IN-NAGPUR.text: Prabhavatigupta rules the Vakataka kingdom as regent
IN-NAGPUR.detail: The daughter of Chandragupta II, widowed by Rudrasena II, governs Vidarbha for her minor sons for some twenty years — Gupta influence reaches the Deccan through her.
IN-NAGPUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 179-181
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 180; chronology p. 708

IN-NAGPUR.detail: The siege of Nagpur was laid by Khan-i-Dauran, a high-ranking Mughal official to the fort of Nagpur, ruled by the Gond king of Deogarh, Kok Shah.
IN-NAGPUR.belligerents: Kingdom of Deogarh vs Mughal Empire

IN-NAGPUR.text: Raghuji Bhonsle I dies — founder of the Bhonsle kingdom of Nagpur, which reached from Berar to Orissa.
IN-NAGPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 244: 'Raghuji died on 14 February, 1755 at the age of 60'; p. 243: 'a kingdom extending from Berar in the west to Orissa in the east'.

IN-NAGPUR.detail: after Raghuji II's death, Appa Saheb signs a subsidiary treaty with the Company on 27 May 1816 and accepts a British force stationed permanently in his territory.
IN-NAGPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 248: 'Raghuji died in 1816 and soon his nephew Appa Saheb concluded a treaty of subsidiary alliance with the British ... which force shall be stationed in perpetuity in the Raja's territory'; chronology p. 843: '1816, May 27'.

IN-NAGPUR.detail: Nagpur's Bhonsle army is checked at the twin hills
IN-NAGPUR.outcome: East India Company victory; Appa Saheb's 18,000 men were defeated below the Sitabuldi hills and he surrendered on 16 December 1817
IN-NAGPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 506: 'Appa Saheb, who had 18,000 men and 26 guns, was defeated after fierce fighting at the battle of Sitabaldi (2 miles west of the old city of Nagpur) on 27 November, 1817. He surrendered on 16 December, 1817'. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 475.

IN-NAGPUR.detail: Raghuji III dies in 1853 without a natural or adopted heir. Dalhousie's minute of 28 January 1854 treats Nagpur as a British grant, and the state lapses to the Company.
IN-NAGPUR.source: HCIP IX p. 67: 'The Raja of Nagpur died in 1853. He had no male heir and did not actually adopt any son'; p. 70: Dalhousie's 'minute, dated January 28, 1854, in which he proved, to his own satisfaction, that Nagpur was a dependent State'. De Brett, Central Provinces Gazetteer (Chhattisgarh Feudatory States), block 148 of the archive.org text: 'In 1854 the Nagpur Raj lapsed'. HCIP VIII chronology p. 844 puts the annexation in 1853.

IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.text: Mayurasarman founds the Kadamba kingdom at Banavasi
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.detail: The first Kannada royal house — a Brahmana who "took to the sword" against the Pallavas and was crowned by them.
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 270-272 (Talagunda pillar); chronology p. 707 (c. 340-70)

IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.detail: the Vatsagulma Vakataka Vindhyasakti II (Vindhyasena) is 'represented as having defeated the king of Kuntala' — the Kadamba Kakusthavarman, who nonetheless married his daughters to the Vakataka and Gupta houses.
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.belligerents: Vakataka dynasty (Vatsagulma branch) vs Kadamba dynasty (Kakusthavarman)
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.outcome: Vakataka victory claimed; alliance by marriage follows
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 183, 185 (Ajanta cave XVI inscription; Talagunda pillar)

IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.detail: the Kadamba Ravivarman 'secured the throne by defeating a combination of his enemies, including Vishnuvarman of the younger branch', whom he killed; Vishnuvarman's overlord, the Pallava Chandadanda (Santivarman), was also fought.
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.belligerents: Kadamba dynasty (Ravivarman) vs the younger Kadambas (Vishnuvarman) and Pallava dynasty (Santivarman/Chandadanda)
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.outcome: Ravivarman sole Kadamba king; later triumphs over the Western Gangas
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 273, 278 Re-dated from 497 to 500: the row names the Pallava Santivarman (Chandadanda), whom this atlas dates 500-525, so 497 put him in the field three years before his accession. HCIP gives no year for the war; both dates are approximate and 500 is the first that holds all the parties at once.
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 273

IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.text: Harivarman (Kadamba) dies — The last Kadamba of Banavasi
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 273

IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.detail: the Chalukya 'was the night of doom to the Nalas, the Mauryas and the Kadambas' — Vanavasi and the Kadamba domain absorbed, the Konkan Mauryas and the Nalas of Bastar defeated.
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Kirtivarman I) vs Kadamba, Mauryas of Konkan and Nala dynasty
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.outcome: Chalukya expansion over Kuntala, Konkan and the Nala country
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 232-233 (Aihole prasasti; Mahakuta pillar)

IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.detail: Appayika and Govinda, who came 'with elephant troops' from north of the Bhima, are broken by bheda — Govinda won over, Appayika 'defeated and expelled'; then Vanavasi, the Kadamba capital, is besieged and reduced, and the Gangas and Alupas submit.
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Pulakesin II) vs Appayika and Govinda; vs Kadamba (Banavasi); Ganga and Alupa
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.outcome: Chalukya victory; Kadambas, Gangas, Alupas subdued
IN-UTTARA-KANNADA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 235 (Aihole prasasti)

IN-SHIMOGA.detail: the Brahmana student insulted at Kanchi 'took to the sword', defeated the Pallava frontier guards and the Banas, and forced the Pallavas to crown him — the Talagunda pillar tells the story. He also fought the Abhiras and Traikutakas.
IN-SHIMOGA.belligerents: Kadamba dynasty (Mayurasarman) vs Pallava dynasty; vs the Banas, Abhiras and Traikutakas
IN-SHIMOGA.outcome: Kadamba kingdom established at Banavasi with Pallava recognition
IN-SHIMOGA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 192, 270-272 (Talagunda pillar; Chandravalli inscription)
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 272; chronology p. 709

IN-SHIMOGA.text: The Talagunda pillar records the Kadamba origins
IN-SHIMOGA.detail: Kakusthavarman's prasasti at Talagunda tells how Mayurasarman won a kingdom and how the Kadamba princesses married Guptas and Vakatakas — the foundation text of Karnataka's dynastic history.
IN-SHIMOGA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 270-272

IN-SHIMOGA.detail: Haidar takes the Keladi (Ikkeri) capital in the name of a pretender, renames it Haidar-Nagara and ends the Nayaka state; the loot finances his rise and brings him to the borders of Kerala.
IN-SHIMOGA.belligerents: Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu) vs Ikkeri (Keladi) Nayak
IN-SHIMOGA.outcome: Mysore victory; Bednur falls (c. third week of January 1763) and the Keladi Nayaka kingdom is annexed
IN-SHIMOGA.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore II p. 470 (block 443): 'bestowed on Bednur the new name of Haidar-Nagara ... Bednur fell, as we have seen, about the third week of January 1763'. HCIP VIII p. 455: 'After the conquest of Bednur was completed in the name of the boy-king, Haidar declared him an impostor'.

IN-SHIMOGA.detail: The siege of Bednore was a battle of the Second Anglo-Mysore War.
IN-SHIMOGA.belligerents: Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu) vs East India Company
IN-SHIMOGA.outcome: Mysore victory; Tipu invests Bednur and forces Mathews's army to capitulate
IN-SHIMOGA.source: HCIP VIII p. 460: 'Tipu now advanced with his full force, invested Bednur and compelled the British to capitulate. It is said that safe conduct was promised to the British but Tipu violated the terms.'

IN-SHIMOGA.detail: The Capture of Shimoga, a town and fortress held by forces of the Kingdom of Mysore, occurred on 3 January 1792, after a preliminary battle.
IN-SHIMOGA.belligerents: Maratha Empire, East India Company vs Kingdom of Mysore

IN-SHIMOGA.detail: The Capture of Hooly Honore, a town and fortress held by forces of the Kingdom of Mysore, occurred on 21 December 1791, after two days of siege.
IN-SHIMOGA.belligerents: Maratha Confederacy, British East India Company vs Kingdom of Mysore

IN-EAST-GODAVARI.detail: twelve southern kings — Mahendra of Kosala, Vyaghraraja of Mahakantara, Mahendragiri of Pishtapura, Hastivarman of Vengi, Vishnugopa of Kanchi, Ugrasena of Palakka and others — were 'captured and then released' to rule as tributaries.
IN-EAST-GODAVARI.belligerents: Gupta Empire (Samudragupta) vs Kosala, Mahakantara, Pishtapura, Vengi (Salankayana), Kanchi (Pallava) and others
IN-EAST-GODAVARI.outcome: Gupta victory; the southern kings reinstated as tributaries — grahana-moksha
IN-EAST-GODAVARI.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 7, 9-10; p. 258 (the Pallava Vishnugopa)

IN-EAST-GODAVARI.text: Kulottunga II drives the Gangas off the Godavari
IN-EAST-GODAVARI.detail: after Vikramaditya VI died in 1126 the Eastern Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga had pushed west and taken the country up to the Godavari.
