Some time before 1134 the Chola emperor Kulottunga II, helped by his feudatories Manda II and the Velananti chief Rajendra-Choda, expelled the Gangas from the Godavari district and restored Chola authority in coastal Andhra.
IN-EAST-GODAVARI.belligerents: Cholas and their Velananti feudatories vs the Eastern Gangas of Kalinga
IN-EAST-GODAVARI.outcome: Chola victory; Gangas pushed back out of the Godavari delta

IN-EAST-GODAVARI.detail: Mukund Raj of Kasimkota, backed by Vijayanagara, defeated a Golconda army near Rajahmundry.
IN-EAST-GODAVARI.belligerents: Kasimkota (backed by Vijayanagara Empire) vs Golconda Sultanate
IN-EAST-GODAVARI.outcome: Kasimkota–Vijayanagara victory; Golconda force defeated with heavy losses

IN-KOLAR.text: Konganivarman Madhava founds the Western Ganga line
IN-KOLAR.detail: The Gangas of Kuvalala (Kolar) and later Talakad, who will hold southern Karnataka for six centuries, begin "about the middle of the fourth century", perhaps in the confusion left by Samudragupta's southern march.
IN-KOLAR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 268-269; Sastri, A History of South India scan 104

IN-KOLAR.detail: Vijayanagara commanders defeated Tammappa Gauda, captured Kolar and restored imperial authority in Morasunadu.
IN-KOLAR.belligerents: Vijayanagara Empire (Thanjavur Nayaks, Venkatagiri, Matli chiefs) vs the Chief of Morasunadu
IN-KOLAR.outcome: Vijayanagara victory; Kolar fell and Tammappa Gauda submitted and paid tribute

IN-KOLAR.detail: The Battle of Masti was a conflict between Vijayanagara Empire and Bijapur Sultanate fought in 1646 during the Bijapur invasion of the Vijayanagara Empire.
IN-KOLAR.belligerents: Vijayanagar Empire Kingdom of Mysore, Chennapatnam Nayaks Kangundi Chiefs vs Bijapur Sultanate

IN-KOLAR.text: Haidar Ali born — the Mysore soldier who rose under Nanjaraj, made himself master of the kingdom in 1761 and fought the Company, the Marathas and the Nizam. (Birth year uncertain: Rao gives '1717? 1722'.)
IN-KOLAR.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore II p. 205 (block 205): 'two sons, Muhammad Sabas Sahib and Haidar Ali (b. 1717? 1722)'; p. 206: 'Haidar's place of birth is not known for certain. It was either Budikote ... or Kolar'; Rao III p. 393-394: died December 1782 'at the age of sixty'.

IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.text: Pushyavarman founds the Varman dynasty of Kamarupa
IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.detail: The first historical king of Assam, whose kingdom the Allahabad prasasti lists among the frontier states paying tribute to Samudragupta; thirteen generations follow to Bhaskaravarman.
IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 89 (Nidhanpur and Doobi plates); chronology p. 707

IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.detail: The envoy Hamsavega brings the Kamarupa king's offer of "perpetual friendship" to Harsha's camp — the eastern alliance that outflanks Sasanka.
IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 91, 100 (Harshacharita)

IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.text: Hiuen Tsang at the court of Bhaskaravarman
IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.detail: The Kamarupa king, "a devout Brahmana", entertains the pilgrim for a month and then escorts him to Harsha's assembly with twenty thousand elephants and thirty thousand boats.
IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 91-92, 116
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 141

IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.detail: The Battle of Duimunsilla took place at Duimunisila, Assam in 1533, was an engagement which was the part of Turbak's invasion of Assam.
IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.belligerents: Ahom Kingdom Kachari Kingdom vs Bengal Sultanate

IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.detail: The Battle of Bharali, fought in 1615, was a significant conflict of the Ahom–Mughal wars, resulting in a decisive Ahom victory.
IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.belligerents: Ahom Kingdom vs Mughal Empire Bengal Subah
Ahom Kingdom (Lachit Borphukan) vs Mughal Empire (Raja Ram Singh of Amber)

IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.text: Rudra Singha dies — The Ahom king (r. 1696–1714) who brought his neighbours under Ahom rule and planned a league of eastern rajas to drive out the Mughals
IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.source: Acharyya, History of Medieval Assam p. 131 (chronology of Ahom kings): 'Sukhrungpha or Rudra Singha ... 1696 1714'; p. 275: 'the Ahom king Rudra Singha, a man of great ability and ambition, organised a confederacy of the Rajas of Eastern India with a view to oust the Mughals. After this king, the history of the Ahoms is one of internal strifes.' (Place of death, Gauhati, is web-only.)

IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.detail: The Moamoria rebellion (1769–1805) was an 18th-century uprising in the Ahom kingdom of present-day Assam that began as a power struggle involving the Moamorias (Mataks).
IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.outcome: Severe weakening of the Ahom kingdom; near-end of the Paik system.

IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.text: Battles of Kaliani Pathar and Assam Choky
IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.detail: Maha Bandula’s army of some 20,000 defeats Chandrakanta Singha on 17 April 1822 and again on 21 June 1822, and Burma annexes Assam.
IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.belligerents: Konbaung (Burmese) Empire vs Ahom Kingdom (Chandrakanta Singha)
IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.outcome: Konbaung victory; Chandrakanta flees to British territory — 'the end of the Ahom sovereignty in Assam'
IN-KAMRUP-METROPOLITAN.source: HCIP IX p. 130: 'A severe engagement took place at Kaliani Pathar on April 17, 1822, and though Chandrakanta fought with great valour he was defeated ... Being defeated there in another engagement on June 21, 1822, he took refuge in the British territory. The defeat of Chandrakanta on June 21, 1822, marks the end of the Ahom sovereignty in Assam.'

IN-ALLAHABAD.detail: Harishena's eulogy of Samudragupta, engraved on the Asokan pillar at Prayaga — the single most important political document of the age, naming the kings of Aryavarta and Dakshinapatha, the frontier kingdoms and the tribal republics.
IN-ALLAHABAD.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 7-12; Sircar, Select Inscriptions no. 2

IN-ALLAHABAD.text: Kumaragupta III dies — Died at Prayaga after his victory over Isanavarman (Aphsad inscription)
IN-ALLAHABAD.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 43, 75

IN-ALLAHABAD.detail: Isanavarman is 'defeated by Kumaragupta and probably also by Damodaragupta' in the struggle for the remnants of the Gupta empire; Kumaragupta III dies at Prayaga after his victory.
IN-ALLAHABAD.belligerents: Later Gupta dynasty (Kumaragupta III, Damodaragupta) vs Maukhari dynasty (Isanavarman)
IN-ALLAHABAD.outcome: Later Gupta victories; Kumaragupta III dies at Prayaga
IN-ALLAHABAD.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 68, 75-76 (Aphsad inscription)

IN-ALLAHABAD.detail: At the confluence Harsha gives away the accumulated wealth of five years to Buddhists, Brahmanas and the poor, ending with the clothes on his back — the sixth such Mahamoksha-parishad of his reign.
IN-ALLAHABAD.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 119-120

IN-ALLAHABAD.detail: Jayaditya and Vamana's commentary on Panini's grammar — the standard gloss for thirteen centuries — is composed about the middle of the seventh century.
IN-ALLAHABAD.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 311, 319; chronology p. 715

IN-ALLAHABAD.detail: soon after re-establishing his family's fortunes, Bhoja had to measure his strength with the Pala emperor Devapala; Bhoja was defeated and his triumphant career arrested, the Palas remaining supreme in the east while Devapala 'destroyed the haughtiness of the lords of the Gurjaras'.
IN-ALLAHABAD.outcome: Pala victory; Pratihara expansion eastward checked until after Devapala's death
IN-ALLAHABAD.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 30, 50-51. Date approximate (c. 840-850, before Devapala's death c. 850); battle site in the middle Ganga valley uncertain

IN-ALLAHABAD.text: The Treaty of Allahabad and the Diwani
IN-ALLAHABAD.detail: Shah Alam II’s farman of 12 August 1765 grants the Company the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa; the treaty of 16 August restores Awadh to Shuja-ud-daulah less Kora and Allahabad (given to the emperor) and Chunar.
IN-ALLAHABAD.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 547: 'the Emperor, by a farman signed on 12th August ... granted them the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa (the last subah now comprising the Midnapur district only.)' HCIP VIII p. 116: 'By the Treaty of Allahabad dated 16 August, 1765, all the territories of Shuja-ud-daulah were restored to him, with the exception of the districts of Kora and Allahabad ... Chunar which was retained by the English.' (Milestone M496 carries the Diwani; the event layer has no row for it.)

IN-ALLAHABAD.text: The Treaty of Allahabad with Awadh (16 August 1765)
IN-ALLAHABAD.detail: Clive restores Shuja-ud-Daula to Awadh minus Kora and Allahabad (given to Shah Alam II), keeps Chunar, puts Banaras under Balwant Singh and takes fifty lakhs indemnity and a defensive-treaty charge — the start of Awadh's subordination to the Company. (The same month's diwani farman is milestone M496.)
IN-ALLAHABAD.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 830: '1765, August 16 The treaty of Allahabad concluded between Nawab Shuja-ud-daulah and the English, terms being (1) restoration of all the territories held by the Nawab with the exception of Allahabad and Kora districts given to the emperor, (2) Chunar to be retained by the English'

IN-THANJAVUR.detail: The twin Tamil epics of the merchant's daughter Kannaki and the Buddhist nun Manimekalai are generally placed in the post-Sangam centuries, c. 300-500 — the last flowering before the Kalabhra dark age.
IN-THANJAVUR.source: Sastri, A History of South India ch. on literature (date debated); HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 327

IN-THANJAVUR.detail: shortly after the boy-king Nandivarman II Pallavamalla was chosen by the people (730), a hostile combination organised by the Pandyas championed the pretender Chitramaya and besieged Nandivarman at Nandipura near Kumbakonam; his general Udayachandra raised the siege, beheaded Chitramaya and won several victories in the Tanjore country.
IN-THANJAVUR.belligerents: Nandivarman II Pallavamalla vs Chitramaya and the Pandyas
IN-THANJAVUR.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), pp. 262-263; also Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India (siege of Nandipuram). date approximate: war fought in the years after Nandivarman's accession in 730

IN-THANJAVUR.detail: the Pandya king Nedunjadaiyan (Varaguna I) won a great victory over the Kadava (Pallava) at Pennagadam near Tanjore, on the southern bank of the Kaveri, and went on to crush a rising of petty chieftains headed by Ay-vel, ruler of the hill country between Tirunelveli and Travancore.
IN-THANJAVUR.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 158. date approximate: early in Nedunjadaiyan's reign (acc. c. 765); recorded in the Velvikudi grant of his 3rd regnal year

IN-THANJAVUR.detail: the Pandya Srimara Srivallabha recovered his strength and about 859 defeated the Pallava Nandivarman III and his confederates in a battle near Kumbakonam in the Kaveri delta.
IN-THANJAVUR.outcome: Pandya victory over the Pallava confederacy
IN-THANJAVUR.source: Sastri, A History of South India, block 142 of the archive.org text ('about 859')

IN-THANJAVUR.detail: soon after his accession the young Pallava Nripatunga avenged his father's defeat at Kumbakonam by a decisive victory over the Pandyas on the banks of the Arisil (Arichit), a distributary of the Kaveri, recorded in his Bahur plates.
IN-THANJAVUR.outcome: Decisive Pallava victory; Pandya power in the Kaveri delta broken
IN-THANJAVUR.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 152; Sastri, A History of South India, block 142 of the archive.org text. Date approximate (c. 860-862)

IN-THANJAVUR.detail: Battle of Thirupurambiyam was fought between the Pandya king Varagunavarman II and a confederacy of the Pallavas, Western Ganga Dynasty and the Medieval Cholas in about 879 CE.
IN-THANJAVUR.belligerents: Pallava dynasty, Western Gangas, Medieval Cholas vs Pandya kingdom, Pallava factions

IN-THANJAVUR.text: Aditya I dies — The Chola who ended Pallava rule at Tondaimandalam.
IN-THANJAVUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-THANJAVUR.text: Parantaka I dies — Forty-eight years on the Chola throne
IN-THANJAVUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-THANJAVUR.text: The Brihadisvara at Thanjavur is consecrated
IN-THANJAVUR.detail: Rajaraja I’s temple to Siva, its vimana sixty metres high, the eighty-tonne cap-stone hauled up a ramp; the 275th day of his 25th year.
IN-THANJAVUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-THANJAVUR.text: Rajaraja I dies — The Chola who built the Brihadisvara and took Ceylon and the Maldives.
IN-THANJAVUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-THANJAVUR.detail: Rajaraja II’s temple, a stone chariot with wheels and horses; the last of the great Chola temples.
IN-THANJAVUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-THANJAVUR.detail: Maravarman Sundara Pandya stormed the Chola country, burned Thanjavur and Uraiyur, and drove Rajaraja III into exile — vengeance for a century of Chola overlordship, and the blow the dynasty never recovered from.
IN-THANJAVUR.belligerents: Pandya dynasty (Maravarman Sundara) vs Chola Empire (Rajaraja III)
IN-THANJAVUR.outcome: Pandya victory; the Chola heartland devastated, Chola kingship restored only as a dependent
IN-THANJAVUR.source: Cross-referenced against Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, and the Chola Empire literature (Aug 2026).

IN-THANJAVUR.detail: The siege of Thanjavur was a conflict between the Madurai army led by Venkata Krishna Nayak, and the Thanjavur army under King Vijaya Raghava Nayak.
The Madurai invasion of Thanjavur (1700–1701) took place during the rule of Mangammal, the queen-regent of Madurai.
a Company army takes Tanjore on 17 September 1773 and hands it to Nawab Muhammad Ali; Raja Tulaji is deposed until the Directors order his restoration in April 1776.
IN-THANJAVUR.belligerents: Carnatic (Arcot Nawab), East India Company vs Thanjavur (Maratha)
IN-THANJAVUR.outcome: Carnatic victory; Tanjore annexed to the Nawab's dominions until restored to Tulaji on 11 April 1776
IN-THANJAVUR.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 39 n. (block 31; running head of p. 40 follows the note): 'It was seized by Md. Ali on 17th September 1773 and restored to Raja Tulaji on 11th April 1776 by a special order from the Authorities in England.' Hayavadana Rao II p. 657: 'Tanjore was taken and given to Muhammad Ali in 1773'.

IN-THANJAVUR.detail: Tipu and Lally surround Colonel Braithwaite's detachment near Kumbakonam on 17–18 February 1782; after twenty-six hours of fighting it is destroyed and Braithwaite taken.
IN-THANJAVUR.belligerents: Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu), French India vs East India Company
IN-THANJAVUR.outcome: Mysore victory; the English detachment 'completely defeated' and Braithwaite captured
IN-THANJAVUR.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III p. 371: 'The action lasted for the space of twenty-six hours, when the English detachment was completely defeated'. HCIP VIII p. 459: 'Col. Braithwaite ... was surprised and cut down by an army led by Tipu. Braithwaite was taken prisoner.'

IN-THANJAVUR.detail: by treaty with Wellesley, Raja Serfoji II hands his whole territory except the fort to the Company and becomes a pensioned titular king.
IN-THANJAVUR.source: HCIP IX (British Paramountcy) p. 82: 'By a treaty concluded in 1799 with Lord Wellesley, Raja Sarfoji of Tanjore transferred the whole of his territory, except the fort, to the British Government.' HCIP VIII p. 626: 'Tanjore was annexed in 1799'.

IN-GAYA.text: Meghavarna of Ceylon sends a mission to Samudragupta
IN-GAYA.detail: The Sinhalese king asks leave to build a monastery for Ceylonese pilgrims at Bodh Gaya; the Mahabodhi sangharama Hiuen Tsang later saw was the result.
IN-GAYA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 11; chronology p. 707 (352-79)

IN-GAYA.text: The Mahabodhi temple at Bodh Gaya
IN-GAYA.detail: The tall brick temple over the seat of enlightenment, described by Hiuen Tsang, takes its present form in the Gupta and post-Gupta centuries.
IN-GAYA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) art chapter; Hiuen Tsang (Beal II)

LK-ANURADHAPURA.text: Mahasena of Ceylon dies — Builder of the Jetavana
LK-ANURADHAPURA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 407; chronology p. 708

LK-ANURADHAPURA.text: Mahanaman of Ceylon dies — Murdered by his son Svastisena
LK-ANURADHAPURA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 285

LK-ANURADHAPURA.text: Mitrasena of Ceylon dies — Killed by the Damila Pandya.
LK-ANURADHAPURA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 285

LK-ANURADHAPURA.detail: Mitrasena, newly crowned, 'was killed by a Damila named Pandya who came from the coast of South India' — six Tamil kings rule the north for twenty-seven years while the Sinhalese nobles hold out in Rohana.
LK-ANURADHAPURA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 285 (Mahavamsa / Culavamsa)

LK-ANURADHAPURA.detail: the Moriya prince from Rohana defeats the six Damila kings one after another and restores Sinhalese rule at Anuradhapura; he builds the Kalawewa and the great Avukana Buddha.
LK-ANURADHAPURA.belligerents: Anuradhapura Kingdom (Dhatusena) vs the Damila kings
LK-ANURADHAPURA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 285

LK-ANURADHAPURA.text: Dhatusena dies — Murdered — walled up alive — by his son Kasyapa.
LK-ANURADHAPURA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 285

LK-ANURADHAPURA.text: Kumaradasa of Ceylon dies — The poet-king.
LK-ANURADHAPURA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 286

LK-ANURADHAPURA.text: Aggabodhi I of Ceylon dies — Thirty-three years of building and irrigation.
LK-ANURADHAPURA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 287

LK-ANURADHAPURA.detail: the usurper Silameghavanna kills Moggallana III (608); the general Srinaga 'fled to South India and came back with a large army of Damilas' to seize the Northern Province, but the king 'succeeded in crushing the invading army completely'.
LK-ANURADHAPURA.belligerents: Anuradhapura Kingdom (Silameghavanna) vs Srinaga with Damila (Tamil) troops
LK-ANURADHAPURA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 287-288

LK-ANURADHAPURA.detail: the throne changes hands by battle four times — Jetthatissa III defeats Aggabodhi III, who returns 'with a contingent of Damila troops' and kills him; Dathopatissa 'came with a great South Indian force' and was killed by Kasyapa II.
LK-ANURADHAPURA.belligerents: Anuradhapura factions with South Indian (Pallava/Pandya) mercenaries
LK-ANURADHAPURA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 288

LK-ANURADHAPURA.text: The first Pallava expedition to Ceylon
LK-ANURADHAPURA.detail: Narasimhavarman I gives the exiled Sinhalese prince Manavamma an army; 'in spite of a victory over the forces of Dathopatissa II, the expedition was a failure' and Manavamma returns to Kanchi.
LK-ANURADHAPURA.belligerents: Pallava dynasty for Manavamma vs Anuradhapura Kingdom (Dathopatissa II)
LK-ANURADHAPURA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 261, 289 Re-dated from 668 to 663. Both Ceylon expeditions sat on 668, twenty years apart. The first is Narasimhavarman I’s (r. 630-668) against Dathopatissa II (r. 659-667), so 663 is inside both reigns.

LK-ANURADHAPURA.detail: the second Pallava expedition, 'which sailed from Mahabalipuram', lands Manavamma with a great army; he 'succeeded in defeating totally the titular king Hastadamshtra II and the administrator Pustakushtha' and seizes the throne he holds for thirty-five years.
LK-ANURADHAPURA.belligerents: Pallava dynasty (Narasimhavarman I / Paramesvaravarman I) for Manavamma vs Anuradhapura Kingdom (Hatthadatha II)
LK-ANURADHAPURA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 261, 289 (Culavamsa; Geiger dates 676) Re-dated from 668 to 676, the date this row’s own source already gives (Geiger). The revised Sinhalese chronology puts Manavamma’s accession at 684; on either reckoning 668 is too early, and the second expedition cannot share a year with the first.

LK-ANURADHAPURA.detail: Srimara Srivallabha invaded Ceylon in the reign of Sena I, ravaged the northern province and sacked the capital and its monasteries, until Sena submitted and the Pandya forces quit the island.
LK-ANURADHAPURA.belligerents: Pandya kingdom vs Sinhala kingdom of Anuradhapura
LK-ANURADHAPURA.outcome: Pandya victory; Sena I submitted and bought peace
LK-ANURADHAPURA.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 170; Sastri, A History of South India, blocks 139-140 of the archive.org text. Date approximate, within Sena I's reign (c. 831-851)

LK-ANURADHAPURA.detail: Rajaraja I invaded Lanka, sacked Anuradhapura and annexed Rajarata as a Chola province — the beginning of the end for a kingdom that had stood since the fourth century BCE.
LK-ANURADHAPURA.belligerents: Chola Empire (Rajaraja I) vs Anuradhapura Kingdom (Mahinda V)
LK-ANURADHAPURA.outcome: Chola victory; northern Lanka annexed, Polonnaruwa made the Chola seat
LK-ANURADHAPURA.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

IN-JUNAGADH.detail: Chandragupta II destroys the Western Kshatrapas — the Saka ruler Rudrasimha III is defeated and his kingdom of Malwa, Gujarat and Kathiawad annexed — the end of three centuries of Saka rule in the west.
IN-JUNAGADH.belligerents: Gupta Empire (Chandragupta II) vs Western Kshatrapas (Rudrasimha III)
IN-JUNAGADH.outcome: Gupta victory; Malwa and Saurashtra annexed; Gupta silver coinage begins in the west
IN-JUNAGADH.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 18-20 (Udayagiri and Sanchi records of 401 and 412; Rudrasimha III defeated and his kingdom annexed)

IN-JUNAGADH.text: The Sudarsana lake bursts at Girnar
IN-JUNAGADH.detail: The Mauryan reservoir, repaired by Rudradaman in 150, breaks its embankment "in a night"; Skandagupta's governor Parnadatta and his son Chakrapalita rebuild it in 456-58 and record it beside Asoka's edicts.
IN-JUNAGADH.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 61 (Junagadh inscription of Skandagupta, Gupta years 136-138)

IN-JUNAGADH.text: The revolt of Sumvara in Saurashtra
IN-JUNAGADH.detail: while Kumarapala was busy in Malwa a chief named Sumvara rose in Saurashtra, and the veteran Chaulukya minister Udayana lost his life trying to put him down. Kumarapala sent a second army which brought Sumvara to heel; the Chahamana prince Ahladana of Nadol gave decisive help and was rewarded with Kiratakupa near Barmer and other territory.
IN-JUNAGADH.belligerents: Chaulukyas of Gujarat vs Sumvara of Saurashtra
IN-JUNAGADH.outcome: Revolt crushed at the cost of the minister Udayana's life

IN-JUNAGADH.detail: the Nawab accedes to Pakistan against his people; Indian forces enter and a plebiscite confirms the union
IN-JUNAGADH.outcome: Indian victory — Junagadh integrated after the February 1948 plebiscite
IN-JUNAGADH.source: Wikipedia: List of wars involving India

IN-SOUTH-DEL.text: Chandragupta II's Vanga and Vahlika campaigns
IN-SOUTH-DEL.detail: the Mehrauli iron-pillar record of 'Chandra' claims the defeat of a confederacy of hostile chiefs in Vanga and a crossing of the seven mouths of the Sindhu to conquer the Vahlikas.
IN-SOUTH-DEL.belligerents: Gupta Empire (Chandragupta II) vs the Vanga chiefs; vs the Vahlikas
IN-SOUTH-DEL.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 20 (Mehrauli iron pillar, CII III no. 32)

IN-SOUTH-DEL.detail: The rustless pillar of "king Chandra", raised as a standard of Vishnu on a hill called Vishnupada and later moved to Delhi — the record of Chandragupta II's Vanga and Vahlika wars.
IN-SOUTH-DEL.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 20; CII III no. 32

IN-SOUTH-DEL.detail: Anangpal II of the Tomaras raises the first fortified city of Delhi at Mehrauli, c. 1052 by the traditional date; the iron pillar was brought there and set up.
IN-SOUTH-DEL.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SOUTH-DEL.detail: Prithviraj Chauhan throws a second wall round Lal Kot, c. 1180; the city that Muhammad of Ghor’s slaves took in 1192 and built the Qutb inside.
IN-SOUTH-DEL.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SOUTH-DEL.detail: Aibak lays the first storey of the victory tower at Delhi; Iltutmish adds three more, Firuz Shah the fifth.
IN-SOUTH-DEL.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SOUTH-DEL.detail: Alauddin Khalji’s gateway to the Quwwat-ul-Islam, the first true arch and dome in India.
IN-SOUTH-DEL.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-VIDISHA.text: The Udayagiri caves are cut under Chandragupta II
IN-VIDISHA.detail: The Varaha and Vishnu cave-temples at Udayagiri near Vidisa, with an inscription of the emperor's minister Virasena dated 401 — the earliest datable monuments of Gupta art.
IN-VIDISHA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 19-20 (Udayagiri inscription, Gupta year 82)

IN-VIDISHA.detail: As a general of Jalal-ud-din Khalji, his nephew and son-in-law Alauddin Khalji raided the Paramara city of Bhilsa in 1293 CE.

IN-NALANDA.detail: Hiuen Tsang attributes the first monastery at Nalanda to "Sakraditya" — identified with Kumaragupta I — on which five kings built in turn; the university of the Classical Age.
IN-NALANDA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) ch. XX; Hiuen Tsang (Beal II, 167-170). Year conventional.

IN-NALANDA.text: Dharmakirti is born — Approximate — "beginning of the seventh century".
IN-NALANDA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 391

IN-NALANDA.text: Hiuen Tsang is born — Born at Lo-yang
IN-NALANDA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 618; chronology p. 712

IN-NALANDA.detail: The Chinese Master of the Law crosses the Hindu Kush in 630 and spends fourteen years in India — Kashmir, Kanauj, Nalanda, Kamarupa, Kanchi, Badami — leaving the fullest description of the subcontinent before the Mughals.
IN-NALANDA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 100, 618; chronology pp. 712-714

IN-NALANDA.detail: The Chinese pilgrim comes by sea in 671, studies ten years at Nalanda and writes the Record of the Buddhist Religion — the picture of Indian monastic life after Harsha.
IN-NALANDA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 2, 620; chronology p. 715

IN-NALANDA.text: Nayapala's defeat of the Kalachuris in Magadha
IN-NALANDA.detail: early in his reign the Kalachuri Karna pushed east into Magadha to take Uddandapura (Bihar Sharif); failing, he sacked the Buddhist monasteries of the open country and destroyed the standing grain. The Pala Nayapala rallied and crushed the invading army. Atisa Dipankara Srijnana, rector of Vikramasila and then at the Mahabodhi monastery, sheltered Karna and his beaten troops, arranged their safe departure, and travelled twice into Kalachuri territory to broker a treaty of mutual restitution — one of the rare recorded instances of a monk mediating between Indian empires.
IN-NALANDA.belligerents: Palas of Bengal and Magadha vs the Kalachuris of Tripuri
IN-NALANDA.outcome: Pala victory; peace mediated by Atisa Dipankara
IN-NALANDA.source: HCIP V, printed p. 27: "Nayapala soon rallied his forces and inflicted a crushing defeat on the invading army. At this time Dlpankara Srijhana, also known as Atlsa, the Rector of the Vikramasila monastery, was residing in the Mahabodhi monastery at Vajrasana. He gave shelter to Karna and his vanquished forces and made arrangements for their safe departure to their own country." (Note: HCIP places the battle only 'in the early part of the reign' of Karna, who acceded between 1034 and 1042; the year is approximate. Coordinates for Uddandapura/Bihar Sharif.)

IN-NALANDA.belligerents: Ghurid Empire vs States and inhabitants of Bihar
IN-NALANDA.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-NALANDA.detail: c. 1193-1200, Bakhtiyar Khalji’s raiders destroy the great monastery-university of Magadha, and Odantapuri and Vikramashila with it; the libraries burn. Minhaj describes the taking of a "fortress" whose inmates were all shaven-headed - usually read as Odantapuri. The Tibetan pilgrim Dharmasvamin found Nalanda nearly deserted in 1235.
IN-NALANDA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-NALANDA.detail: on Shah Alam’s third Bihar campaign Colonel Carnac defeats the imperial army six miles west of Bihar city on 15 January 1761 and captures Jean Law and his Frenchmen; the emperor then treats with the English.
IN-NALANDA.belligerents: East India Company vs Mughal Empire (Shah Alam II) with Jean Law’s French
IN-NALANDA.outcome: East India Company victory; Law and his officers captured, Shah Alam sues for terms and visits Carnac at Gaya
IN-NALANDA.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 542: 'The end came on 15th January 1761, when at the village of Suan (6 miles west of Bihar city) Col. Carnac defeated the imperialists and captured Law and his French officers.' HCIP VIII p. 344: 'On 15 January, 1761, Carnac inflicted a severe defeat on the Shahzada.'

NP-KAPILBASTU.text: The king of Ka-pi-li sends an embassy to China
NP-KAPILBASTU.detail: A ruler of Kapilavastu — or Davaka — writes to the Sung court; the first Indian embassy to China of the period, followed by Mahanaman of Ceylon's letter the same year.
NP-KAPILBASTU.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 90; chronology p. 709

IN-MANDSAUR.text: The silk-weavers of Dasapura build a sun temple
IN-MANDSAUR.detail: A guild of weavers migrated from Lata raises a temple of the Sun at Mandasor under Kumaragupta and the Aulikara Bandhuvarman; restored by the same guild in 473 — the classic record of Gupta-age guild life.
IN-MANDSAUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 442; chronology p. 709 (437-38, 473)

IN-MANDSAUR.detail: Yasodharman of Dasapura shatters Mihirakula — the Hun king 'whose head had never been brought to obeisance to any other save Sthanu' pays respect to the Aulikara's feet. Two victory pillars stand at Sondani near Mandasor.
IN-MANDSAUR.outcome: Decisive Aulikara victory; Hun power in Malwa broken
IN-MANDSAUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 37, 40 (Mandasor pillars of Yasodharman, c. 532)

IN-MANDSAUR.detail: after Sondani the Aulikara claims dominion 'from the Lauhitya to the western ocean, from the Himalaya to Mahendra' and defeats Gupta feudatories — 'he rose and fell like a meteor between 530 and 540'.
IN-MANDSAUR.belligerents: Aulikara dynasty (Yasodharman) vs Gupta Empire and its feudatories
IN-MANDSAUR.outcome: Short-lived Aulikara supremacy in Malwa and the north
IN-MANDSAUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 39-42 (Mandasor pillars; Sumandala plate contra)

IN-MANDSAUR.detail: Two pillars at Sondani proclaim the Aulikara "who rules from the Lauhitya to the western ocean" and to whose feet Mihirakula bowed — the record of the Hun defeat.
IN-MANDSAUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 39-40 (Mandasor inscription, Malava year 589 = 532)

IN-MANDSAUR.text: Yasodharman dies — "Vanished into darkness" — his empire perished with him, c. 540.
IN-MANDSAUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 40-41

IN-MANDSAUR.detail: The siege of Mandsaur was a siege laid by Kingdom of Mewar forces under Rana Sanga against Gujarat Sultanate and Malwa Sultanate.
IN-MANDSAUR.belligerents: Kingdom of Mewar vs Gujarat Sultanate, Malwa Sultanate

IN-MANDSAUR.detail: after Mahidpur, Malhar Rao Holkar III accepts British supremacy and a subsidiary force on 6 January 1818, and gives up his lands north of Bundi and south of the Satpuras.
IN-MANDSAUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 506: 'By the subsidiary treaty of Mandasor (6 January, 1818), Malhar Rao Holkar III agreed to accept the British suzerainty, limit his troops to three thousand, maintain a British subsidiary force'.

IN-GHAZIPUR.detail: the Bhitari pillar records the crown prince's 'complete victory' over the Hunas who had broken into Gandhara — the struggle 'was severe' and the empire was saved for a generation.
IN-GHAZIPUR.outcome: Gupta victory; Hun advance halted c. 460
IN-GHAZIPUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 25-27, 35 (Bhitari inscription; Junagadh inscription; the Kathasaritsagara echo)

IN-GHAZIPUR.detail: Skandagupta's own account of the tottering fortunes of his house, the Pushyamitra war and the Hun victory, set up at Bhitari in Ghazipur.
IN-GHAZIPUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 25-27

IN-GHAZIPUR.detail: Sher Shah Suri routs Humayun, driving the Mughals toward exile
IN-GHAZIPUR.outcome: Sur victory — Sher Shah routs Humayun on the Ganges

NP-KATHMANDU.text: Manadeva raises the Changu Narayan pillar
NP-KATHMANDU.detail: The earliest dated inscription of Nepal (Saka 386): the Licchavi king Manadeva records his father's death and his own campaigns east and west of the valley.
NP-KATHMANDU.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 83-84

NP-KATHMANDU.text: Amsuvarman dies — c. 621 (modern dating; HCIP gives 651).
NP-KATHMANDU.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 85

NP-KATHMANDU.detail: with the marriage of Bhrikuti and the Chinese embassies of 643, Srong-btsan-sgam-po's suzerainty is acknowledged in the valley; the Nepalese army marches for the Tibetans against Kanauj in 648.
NP-KATHMANDU.belligerents: Tibetan Empire (Srong-btsan-sgam-po) vs Licchavi dynasty of Nepal (Narendradeva)
NP-KATHMANDU.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 85-86, 137-138 (T'ang annals; Levi)

NP-KATHMANDU.text: Chinese envoys find Narendradeva on the throne of Nepal
NP-KATHMANDU.detail: The Licchavi restored with Tibetan help receives the Tang mission bound for Magadha; Nepal is now within the Tibetan orbit.
NP-KATHMANDU.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 85, 137

NP-KATHMANDU.text: Narendradeva of Nepal sends a mission to China
NP-KATHMANDU.detail: The Licchavi king's embassy reaches the Tang court; Nepal is described as a country of merchants and copper coinage.
NP-KATHMANDU.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 137; chronology p. 715
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 137

NP-KATHMANDU.detail: after failing in 1757 and 1764, Prithvi Narayan Shah’s Gorkhas take the hill town guarding Kathmandu in 1767, opening the Valley to conquest.
NP-KATHMANDU.belligerents: Nepal (Gorkha, Prithvi Narayan Shah) vs Malla (Kathmandu Valley)
NP-KATHMANDU.outcome: Nepal victory; Kirtipur surrenders and its defenders are mutilated in reprisal
NP-KATHMANDU.source: web-only; library silent on Nepal’s unification (HCIP IX p. 235 only notes 'the newly founded Gurkha kingdom of Nepal which extended from Sikkim to the borders of Kashmir'). Famous and uncontested; it matters because it opened the Kathmandu Valley.

NP-KATHMANDU.detail: Prithvi Narayan Shah enters Kathmandu during Indra Jatra (September 1768), then takes Patan and Bhaktapur (1769), ending Malla rule and making Kathmandu the Gorkha capital.
NP-KATHMANDU.belligerents: Nepal (Gorkha, Prithvi Narayan Shah) vs Malla (Kathmandu Valley)
NP-KATHMANDU.outcome: Nepal victory; the three Malla kingdoms fall and Nepal is unified under the Shah dynasty
NP-KATHMANDU.source: web-only; library silent (HCIP IX p. 235 notes only 'the newly founded Gurkha kingdom of Nepal'). Famous and uncontested (1768–69); it is the founding of the Nepal the atlas shows.

NP-KATHMANDU.text: Jang Bahadur Kunwar becomes Prime Minister of Nepal, founding the Rana ascendancy that turned Nepal into a firm British ally.
NP-KATHMANDU.source: HCIP IX p. 1025: 'The British relations with Nepal were still further improved when Jang Bahadur became the Prime Minister in 1846. He was by far the most remarkable Prime Minister of Nepal.' (The Kot massacre of September 1846 that brought him to power is web-only.)

NP-KATHMANDU.detail: King Tribhuvan returns from Delhi and the Delhi Compromise closes 104 years of hereditary Rana prime ministers
NP-KATHMANDU.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

NP-KATHMANDU.detail: the elected government of B. P. Koirala is dismissed, parties are banned and the partyless Panchayat system begins
NP-KATHMANDU.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

NP-KATHMANDU.detail: seven weeks of protest force King Birendra to lift the ban on parties and accept a constitutional monarchy
NP-KATHMANDU.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

NP-KATHMANDU.detail: Crown Prince Dipendra shoots King Birendra, Queen Aishwarya and seven others of the royal family at a family dinner, then himself; his uncle Gyanendra takes the throne
NP-KATHMANDU.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

NP-KATHMANDU.detail: the government is dismissed, the king assumes direct rule and cuts the country's telephone lines
NP-KATHMANDU.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

NP-KATHMANDU.detail: nineteen days of protest in April force King Gyanendra to restore parliament; in November the Comprehensive Peace Accord ends the civil war
NP-KATHMANDU.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

NP-KATHMANDU.detail: the Constituent Assembly abolishes the 240-year Shah monarchy at its first sitting
NP-KATHMANDU.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

IN-BHAVNAGAR.text: Bhatarka founds the Maitraka state of Valabhi
IN-BHAVNAGAR.detail: The Gupta senapati of Saurashtra makes himself master of the peninsula as the empire loosens; his descendants rule from Valabhi for three centuries.
IN-BHAVNAGAR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 61-62; chronology p. 709 (c. 465-75)

IN-BHAVNAGAR.detail: Maharaja Dronasimha of Valabhi, "anointed by the paramount sovereign in person", issues the first of the great series of Valabhi copper plates.
IN-BHAVNAGAR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 61; chronology p. 710
HCIP III ch. XX; date conventional

IN-BHAVNAGAR.detail: Dhruvasena II of Valabhi is defeated by Harsha and 'saved by the support of the Gurjara king Dadda II' of Broach; the war ends in a marriage — Harsha's daughter given to the Maitraka king.
IN-BHAVNAGAR.belligerents: Pushyabhuti (Harsha) vs Maitraka of Valabhi (Dhruvasena II) and Gurjaras of Nandipuri (Dadda II)
IN-BHAVNAGAR.outcome: Valabhi defeated but preserved; matrimonial alliance
IN-BHAVNAGAR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 104-105, 109-110 (Navsari grant of the Gurjaras; Hiuen Tsang)
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 147

IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.text: The Ajanta caves of the Vakataka age
IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.detail: Under Harishena of Vatsagulma and his minister Varahadeva the great painted viharas — caves XVI, XVII, I and II — are excavated: the Bodhisattva Padmapani, the Jatakas, the "Persian embassy" scene.
IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 184-186 (Ajanta cave XVI inscription); art chapter
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 186
Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.text: The Kailasa is cut at Ellora
IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.detail: Krishna I’s monolithic temple to Siva, carved from the top of the basalt down; the largest single rock-cut structure in the world.
IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.text: Krishna I dies — The Rashtrakuta who cut the Kailasa out of the rock at Ellora.
IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.text: Singhana II dies — The Yadava at Devagiri’s widest reach.
IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.text: Jnaneshwar is born — At Apegaon on the Godavari.
IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.detail: In 1296, Alauddin Khalji raided Devagiri, the capital of the Yadava kingdom in the Deccan region of India.

IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.text: Ramachandra dies — The last independent Yadava of Devagiri, a Khalji tributary since 1294.
IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.text: Eknath dies — At Paithan on the Godavari
IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.detail: The siege of Daulatabad in 1633 was a conflict between the Mughal Empire and the Ahmadnagar Sultanate, wherein the fort-city of Daulatabad was besieged by a Mughal force.
IN-AURANGABAD-MAH.belligerents: Mughal Empire vs Ahmadnagar Sultanate, Bijapur Sultanate

LK-MATALE.detail: the Mahavamsa's king Kasyapa I walls his father Dhatusena into a wall and seizes the throne; his brother Moggallana flees to India — the crime for which Kasyapa builds his fortress-palace at Sigiriya.
LK-MATALE.belligerents: Anuradhapura Kingdom: Kasyapa I vs Dhatusena and Moggallana
LK-MATALE.outcome: Kasyapa I usurps the throne; Sigiriya built
LK-MATALE.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 285-286

LK-MATALE.detail: Kasyapa builds his rock fortress: The patricide king of Ceylon raises palace, gardens and the Lion-gate on the rock of Sigiriya, with the painted "cloud maidens"; abandoned after his death in battle.
LK-MATALE.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 285-286

LK-MATALE.detail: Kasyapa I, coming down from Sigiriya to meet his brother's Indian-recruited army, is deserted by his own troops and cuts his throat on the field; Moggallana I restores the capital to Anuradhapura.
LK-MATALE.belligerents: Anuradhapura Kingdom (Moggallana I with Tamil mercenaries) vs Kasyapa I
LK-MATALE.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 286

LK-MATALE.text: Kasyapa I of Ceylon dies — Cut his own throat on the battlefield when his army deserted him.
LK-MATALE.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 286

LK-MATALE.detail: a peasant rising against new taxes, crushed within weeks under martial law. Puran Appu was executed on 8 August. The severity of the repression caused a parliamentary inquiry in London and the recall of the governor.
LK-MATALE.belligerents: Peasant rebels under Gongalegoda Banda and Puran Appu vs British Ceylon
LK-MATALE.outcome: Suppressed; the governor recalled after a parliamentary inquiry
LK-MATALE.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

IN-SAGAR.detail: Maharaja Matrivishnu's pillar at Eran, dated Gupta year 165, shows Budhagupta still sovereign in Malwa "between the Kalindi and the Narmada" — the last firm date of imperial Gupta rule in the west.
IN-SAGAR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 30-31

IN-SAGAR.detail: advancing from the Punjab, the Hun chief conquers 'a large part of Western India'; his boar-inscription at Eran shows Malwa in his first regnal year.
IN-SAGAR.outcome: Hun victory; Malwa, Rajasthan and the Doab under Hun rule
IN-SAGAR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 35 (Eran boar inscription, Toramana's year 1)

IN-SAGAR.detail: Bhanugupta 'the bravest man on the earth' fights 'a famous battle' with the Hun Toramana; his feudatory Goparaja falls and his wife mounts the pyre — the earliest dated sati record in India (Gupta year 191).
IN-SAGAR.outcome: Indecisive / Hun advantage — Eran remains in Hun hands
IN-SAGAR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 33-34 (Eran pillar of Goparaja, Gupta year 191 = 510)

IN-SAGAR.text: Goparaja dies — Killed at Eran fighting beside Bhanugupta
IN-SAGAR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 33

IN-LALITPUR.detail: The finest surviving Gupta structural temple, with its Anantasayana, Gajendramoksha and Nara-Narayana panels, c. 500. The Bhitargaon brick temple in Kanpur is of the same generation.
IN-LALITPUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) art chapter (ch. XVIII); date conventional

BD-COMILLA.detail: The Gunaighar plate of Maharaja Vainyagupta (Gupta year 188) shows a Gupta prince holding Samatata with the imperial titles — the seed of Bengal's separate kingdom.
BD-COMILLA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 33, 40; chronology p. 710

BD-COMILLA.text: Silabhadra is born — Born a prince of Samatata
BD-COMILLA.source: Hiuen Tsang (Beal); HCIP III ch. XX — date web-attested, verify

PK-SIALKOT.detail: the son of Toramana rules from Sakala over the Punjab, Kashmir and Malwa and is styled 'lord of the earth' — Cosmas calls the Hun chief 'the Lord of India'; his Gwalior inscription is of his 15th year.
PK-SIALKOT.belligerents: Alchon Huns (Mihirakula) vs the Gupta and regional kings
PK-SIALKOT.outcome: Hun supremacy in the north-west and Malwa, c. 515-528
PK-SIALKOT.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 35-37 (Gwalior inscription; Cosmas; Hiuen Tsang)
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 35

PK-SIALKOT.detail: Returning from his failed 1184 assault on Lahore, Muizz-ud-din Muhammad captured the fort of Sialkot and garrisoned it under Husain son of Kharmil; the Ghaznavid Khusrav Malik besieged it as soon as the Sultan left but was repulsed, sealing the fate of Lahore the next year.
PK-SIALKOT.belligerents: Ghurids vs Ghaznavids of Lahore (with Khokar tribesmen)
PK-SIALKOT.outcome: Sialkot taken and held against Khusrav Malik's counter-siege; Lahore fell in 1186

PK-SIALKOT.detail: Charat Singh's Sukerchakia Misl beat off a Durrani force under Jahan Khan at Sialkot — the first of two Sikh–Afghan actions at the town.
on 12 November 1763 Charat Singh, now joined by the Bhangi sardars, again defeated Jahan Khan's Durrani force at Sialkot — the second and larger action there.
PK-SIALKOT.belligerents: Sukerchakia Misl, Bhangi Misl vs Durrani Empire

PK-SIALKOT.detail: The Siege of Sodhra was a siege fought between the Sukerchakia Misl under Mahan Singh and the Bhangi Misl under Sahib Singh Bhangi of Gujrat.
the largest tank engagement since the Second World War, fought to a standstill in the Sialkot sector
PK-SIALKOT.outcome: Inconclusive — the Indian advance is halted short of Chawinda
PK-SIALKOT.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: The monk "third son of an Indian king, probably the Pallava king of Kanchi", received by Emperor Wu of Liang, brings the meditative school to China — Chan, and later Zen. Date and person semi-legendary.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 612, 616
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 258
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 260 (inferred)

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: Pulakesin II, having taken Vengi, drives south into Tondaimandalam; Mahendravarman I 'claims a victory at Pullalur' (Pallur, near Kanchi) but 'the Chalukya penetrated far into the heart of the Pallava kingdom'.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Pulakesin II) vs Pallava dynasty (Mahendravarman I)
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.outcome: Chalukya advance halted short of Kanchi; both sides claim the day
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 238, 259 (Aihole prasasti; Kasakudi plates); Sastri, A History of South India scan 134

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.text: Appar and Sambandar lead the Saiva revival
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: Tirunavukkarasar (Appar), who turned Mahendravarman I from Jainism, and the boy-saint Tirujnanasambandar, who reconverted the Pandya court, sing the Tevaram hymns through the Tamil country — the Bhakti movement in full voice.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 328; Sastri, A History of South India scan 134, 370
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 259

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: The pilgrim finds the Pallava capital "the birthplace of Dharmapala", with a hundred monasteries, and hears of Ceylon from the monks who fled its civil war.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 260
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 261

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: the Chalukya 'captured Kanchi and destroyed the family of Mahamalla'; by the Gadval plates of 674 his camp lay at Uragapura (Uraiyur) on the Kaveri — 'undertaken to efface the disgrace' of 642.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Vikramaditya I) vs Pallava dynasty (Mahendravarman II, Paramesvaravarman I)
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.outcome: Chalukya occupation of Kanchi; camp at Uraiyur 674
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 241-242, 261-262 (Gadval plates, 674) Re-dated from 668 to 670: the row names Paramesvaravarman I, who acceded in 670, and rests on the Gadval plates of 674; 668 put the capture before the king it names.
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 262

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.text: Rajasimha begins the Kailasanatha of Kanchi
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha (695-722) raises the first great structural temple of the Pallavas at Kanchi and the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 262, 281

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: the Chalukya emperor invaded the Pallava kingdom to efface his predecessors' disgrace, defeated his 'natural foe' and took Kanchi — but instead of sacking the city restored to its temples the valuables taken from them. Nandivarman II soon recovered his capital.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.outcome: Chalukya victory; Kanchi occupied and later recovered
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), p. 263; chronology p. 717 (c. 740)

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.text: Govinda III scatters the southern confederacy
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: taking advantage of Govinda's absence in the north, the Pallava, Pandya, Kerala and Ganga rulers formed a confederacy against him; he marched south with lightning speed and scattered them all before the end of 802, occupying Kanchi (c. 804) — a blow that so alarmed the king of Ceylon that he sent statues of himself and his minister in token of submission.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.belligerents: Rashtrakutas vs confederacy of Pallava, Pandya, Kerala and Ganga rulers
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 8; Kanchi invasion c. 804 at p. 151 and chronology p. 508

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: the Chola king attacked and slew the Pallava Aparajita, 'who was seated on the back of a tall elephant', earning the surname Kodandarama; the whole Pallava kingdom became Chola territory, bordering thereafter on the Rashtrakutas.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.outcome: Decisive Chola victory; Aparajita killed and Pallava rule extinguished (c. 893-897)
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 154; Sastri, A History of South India, block 144 of the archive.org text (897 for the completed annexation). Battle site unknown; placed in Tondaimandalam Date dispute: c. 893 (The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 152) vs 897 (Sastri: "the whole of the Pallava kingdom now became Chola territory... (897)"); the atlas follows 897 with the paint.

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: after Krishna III's death (967) the Cholas under Uttama and the young Rajaraja's predecessors pushed the Rashtrakutas out of the northern country they had held since Takkolam; by 973 the bulk of Tondaimandalam was Chola again.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 156: "The Rashtrakuta interregnum must have lasted for at least fifteen years, A.D. 953 to 968"; Sastri: "by [973] the bulk of Tondaimandalam had been recovered from the Rashtrakutas". Year approximate.

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.text: Ramanuja is born — By tradition at Sriperumbudur, in 1017.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: at the height of his power the Kalachuri Karna of Tripuri carried his arms the length of the peninsula, overrunning the Kanchi district then held by the Chola Rajadhiraja or Rajendradeva and claiming victories over the Nolamba-Pallavas, the Kongus of Salem and Coimbatore, the Muralas of the Malabar coast and the Pandyas of Madura — HCIP suggests these powers formed a confederacy under the Chola king against him. He also claimed a victory over Somesvara I of Kuntala. The whole southern adventure must have closed before 1048, the date of his Rewah inscription.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.belligerents: Kalachuris of Tripuri vs the Cholas and their southern allies
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.outcome: Kalachuri raid successful; Kanchi-vishaya overrun, but nothing annexed
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: HCIP V, printed p. 63: "He overran Kanchl-vishaya, modern Conjeeveram, Madras, which was then ruled by the Chola Rajadhiraja or Rajendradeva... His invasion of Southern India and the Deccan must have been completed before A.D. 1048, the date of the Rewah inscription, which mentions his fight with the people of those countries." (Note: coordinates for Kanchipuram; 1048 is the terminus ante quem, not a dated engagement.)

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: shortly before the battle of Koppam the Chalukya, with his general Pulikesin, invaded Tondaimandalam and took the old Pallava capital, from which the Chola governor fled — Bilhana's boast of the conquest is corroborated by an inscription of 1058.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 169; date approximate (shortly before Koppam, corroborating inscription AD 1058)

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: after nearly a decade of peace following his accession, the Chalukya emperor Vikramaditya VI marched against the Cholas and took Kanchi some time before 1085 — the deepest Chalukya thrust into the Tamil country since his father's day, and the opening move of the long contest for Vengi that he would not win until 1118.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.belligerents: Western Chalukyas of Kalyana vs the Cholas
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: HCIP V, printed p. 174: "After a long period of peace following his accession Vikramaditya VI marched against the Cholas and took Kahchl some time before A.D. 1085." (Note: 1085 is a terminus ante quem, not an attested date.)

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: The Battle of Uttaramallur was a battle fought during the reign of Venkatapati Raya.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.belligerents: Vijayanagar Empire Venkatagiri estate vs Nayaks of Vellore Chief of Uttiramerur
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

IN-CHENGALPUTTU.detail: Haidar Ali and Tipu intercept Colonel Baillie’s column at Perambakam, marching from Guntur to join Munro at Conjeeveram, "and annihilated" it on 10 September; the worst defeat the Company had yet suffered in India. Munro fell back on Madras. Hayavadana Rao III p. 516.
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.belligerents: Mysore (Haidar Ali, Tipu Sultan) vs East India Company (Baillie, Munro)
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.outcome: Mysore victory; Baillie’s force destroyed and its survivors taken to Srirangapatna
IN-CHENGALPUTTU.source: C. Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III pp. 333-337 (narrative of Perambakam, 10 Sept 1780) and p. 591 (block 516): 'intercepted by Haidar when on the point of junction at Perambakam, and annihilated (10th September)'

BD-DHAKA.text: Gopachandra founds an independent kingdom of Vanga
BD-DHAKA.detail: South and east Bengal "shook off the suzerainty of the Guptas" under Gopachandra, Dharmaditya and Samacharadeva, who "assumed the title Maharajadhiraja and issued gold coins like the Gupta emperors".
BD-DHAKA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 40-41, 77; chronology p. 711 (c. 525-75)

BD-DHAKA.text: Bangladesh Liberation War / Third India-Pakistan War
BD-DHAKA.outcome: Decisive Indian victory — Bangladesh liberated; 93,000 prisoners taken

BD-DHAKA.detail: the Pakistan Army moves against Dhaka on the night of 25 March to crush the Bengali movement; the killings begin the Liberation War
BD-DHAKA.belligerents: Pakistan Army against the people of East Pakistan
BD-DHAKA.outcome: Bangladesh declares independence the next day; nine months of war follow
BD-DHAKA.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

BD-DHAKA.text: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and most of his family are killed by army officers at his Dhanmondi home
BD-DHAKA.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

BD-DHAKA.detail: the army chief removes President Sattar and rules under martial law
BD-DHAKA.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

BD-DHAKA.text: The mass uprising forces General Ershad to resign after nine years
BD-DHAKA.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

BD-DHAKA.detail: student protests over job quotas grow into a national revolt; Sheikh Hasina flees to India on 5 August after fifteen years in power
BD-DHAKA.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

IN-SRINAGAR.text: Mihirakula seizes Kashmir and sacks Gandhara
IN-SRINAGAR.detail: the fugitive Hun 'stirred up a rebellion, killed the king and placed himself on the throne of Kashmir', then 'killed the king of Gandhara, exterminated the royal family, destroyed the stupas and sangharamas'.
IN-SRINAGAR.belligerents: Alchon Huns (Mihirakula) vs Kashmir; vs Gandhara
IN-SRINAGAR.outcome: Hun conquest of Kashmir and Gandhara; Mihirakula dies soon after
IN-SRINAGAR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 38; Kalhana, Rajatarangini I

IN-SRINAGAR.text: Mihirakula dies — Died in Kashmir "soon after" seizing it
IN-SRINAGAR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 38

IN-SRINAGAR.text: Durlabhavardhana founds the Karkota dynasty of Kashmir
IN-SRINAGAR.detail: The son-in-law of the last Gonanda king takes the throne; Hiuen Tsang will find the dynasty ruling "five other countries" from the valley.
IN-SRINAGAR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 132

IN-SRINAGAR.text: Hiuen Tsang at Kashmir and Taxila
IN-SRINAGAR.detail: The pilgrim spends two years (631-33) in Kashmir, where the Karkota king lends him twenty scribes, and finds Taxila a dependency of Kashmir and Gandhara desolate.
IN-SRINAGAR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 132-133

IN-SRINAGAR.text: Utpala war of succession in Kashmir
IN-SRINAGAR.detail: on Avantivarman's death in A.D. 883 civil war broke out among the descendants of Utpala; after a strenuous fight Sankaravarman put down the rival Yuvaraja Sukhavarman and other claimants and made himself absolute ruler of the country.
IN-SRINAGAR.belligerents: Sankaravarman's faction vs Sukhavarman and rival Utpala princes
IN-SRINAGAR.outcome: Sankaravarman victorious; sole ruler of Kashmir (r. 883-902)
IN-SRINAGAR.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 117

IN-SRINAGAR.text: Tantrins crush Sugandha's bid for power
IN-SRINAGAR.detail: the dowager queen Sugandha of Kashmir, backed by the Ekanga troops, marched on the capital in A.D. 914 to regain her sovereignty, but the Tantrin infantry — then the kingmakers of Kashmir — defeated the Ekangas and put Sugandha to death.
IN-SRINAGAR.belligerents: Tantrin infantry (for Partha) vs Sugandha and the Ekanga troops
IN-SRINAGAR.outcome: Tantrin victory; Sugandha executed, Kashmir left to Tantrin king-making
IN-SRINAGAR.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 119

IN-SRINAGAR.detail: the fugitive Kashmir king Chakravarman enlisted the Damara landholders, whose champion Samgrama inflicted a crushing defeat on the Tantrin infantry near Padmapura; Chakravarman re-entered Srinagar in triumph and the usurper Sambhuvardhana was executed.
IN-SRINAGAR.belligerents: Damaras (for Chakravarman) vs Tantrin infantry (for Sambhuvardhana)
IN-SRINAGAR.outcome: Damara victory; Tantrin power broken and Chakravarman restored (killed by robbers in 937)
IN-SRINAGAR.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 119. Date c. 935-936

IN-SRINAGAR.text: Didda dies — Queen of Kashmir for half a century, as regent and then in her own name.
IN-SRINAGAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SRINAGAR.detail: the two brothers of a collateral branch of the Lohara house, who had caught Harsha's eye by their bravery at the failed siege of Dugdhaghata, fled the capital in 1100 when the king took them for rivals to his son Bhoja. They returned almost at once with the Damaras, forced their way into Srinagar and burnt the royal palace. Harsha took refuge in a hut below the city, learned that Bhoja had been murdered, and was killed in an encounter with his enemies in 1101 — ending the first Lohara dynasty and putting Uchchala on the throne as founder of the second.
IN-SRINAGAR.belligerents: Uchchala and Sussala with the Damaras vs King Harsha of Kashmir
IN-SRINAGAR.outcome: Rebel victory; the palace burnt, and Harsha killed the following year — end of the first Lohara dynasty
IN-SRINAGAR.source: HCIP V, printed p. 99: "Uchchala and Sussala fled for their lives from the capital in A.D. 1100 as the king suspected them to be the rivals of his son Bhoja for the throne. Shortly afterwards the two brothers, with the help of the Damaras, forced their way into the capital and burnt the royal palace." (Note: Harsha's death and Uchchala's accession fall in 1101, just outside the century.)

IN-SRINAGAR.detail: The brothers Uchchala and Sussala, with Damara baron support, forced their way into Srinagar and burnt the royal palace; the temple-plundering king Harsha, his son Bhoja already murdered, was hunted down and killed, and Uchchala founded the second Lohara dynasty.
IN-SRINAGAR.belligerents: Uchchala and Sussala with the Damara barons vs King Harsha of Kashmir
IN-SRINAGAR.outcome: Harsha killed; Uchchala crowned, founding the second Lohara dynasty

IN-SRINAGAR.text: Murder of Uchchala and the Damara coup at Srinagar
IN-SRINAGAR.detail: Kashmir's king Uchchala was killed by his own city-prefect Chudda, whose brother Radda held the throne for a single night before being cut down by Gargachandra, a powerful Damara baron of Lohara. Gargachandra installed Uchchala's half-brother Salhana as a puppet and beat off Uchchala's brother Sussala, who had rushed from Lohara to seize the crown.
IN-SRINAGAR.belligerents: Kashmiri crown factions: Chudda and Radda vs the Damara baron Gargachandra vs Sussala of Lohara
IN-SRINAGAR.outcome: Gargachandra prevailed and made Salhana king; Sussala repulsed

IN-SRINAGAR.detail: after repeated attempts by Harsha's grandson to win back the Kashmiri throne, King Jayasimha finally trapped and killed him in 1130. It removed the one claimant with a hereditary case against the second Lohara line, and let Jayasimha turn to the far harder task of breaking the Damara barons who had made the last thirty years a bloodbath.
IN-SRINAGAR.belligerents: Jayasimha of Kashmir vs Bhikshachara and his Damara allies
IN-SRINAGAR.outcome: Bhikshachara killed; the rival claim to Kashmir extinguished

IN-SRINAGAR.text: Shah Mir takes the throne of Kashmir
IN-SRINAGAR.detail: The Swati adventurer deposes the queen Kota Rani and founds the Sultanate; the Lohara line and Hindu rule in the valley end.
IN-SRINAGAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SRINAGAR.text: Zain-ul-Abidin dies — The Budshah, fifty years king of Kashmir
IN-SRINAGAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SRINAGAR.detail: The Mughal conquest of Kashmir was an invasion of the Kashmir Sultanate by the Mughal Empire in 1585–1589.
IN-SRINAGAR.outcome: Mughal victory — the valley becomes a subah of the empire

IN-SRINAGAR.detail: Ahmad Shah sent an army guided by Ranjit Dev of Jammu against Sukhjivan, the diwan who had thrown off Durrani authority; after a first repulse the second expedition took him prisoner and annexed Kashmir again.
IN-SRINAGAR.belligerents: Durrani (Afghan) Empire, Jammu hill states vs Kashmir (Sukhjivan)
IN-SRINAGAR.outcome: Durrani victory; Sukhjivan captured, Kashmir re-annexed
IN-SRINAGAR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II pp. 488–489: 'Abdali set himself to recover Kashmir from Sukhjivan Ram Khatri ... A later expedition achieved complete success, Sukhjivan was defeated and taken prisoner, and Kashmir annexed to the Durrani empire.'

IN-SRINAGAR.detail: tribal lashkars and Pakistani forces enter Kashmir; the Maharaja accedes to India and Srinagar is held
IN-SRINAGAR.outcome: Inconclusive — UN ceasefire (1949) left India holding two-thirds of Kashmir
IN-SRINAGAR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars involving India

IN-MYSORE.detail: the Western Ganga Durvinita fights the Pallavas and the Kadambas for Kongu and the Punnata country — victories at Andari, Alattur, Porulare and Pelnagara are recorded, and his daughter married the Chalukya Pulakesin II.
IN-MYSORE.belligerents: Western Ganga dynasty (Durvinita) vs Pallava dynasty; vs Kadamba
IN-MYSORE.outcome: Ganga expansion into Kongu and the Tamil borderland
IN-MYSORE.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 269-270
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 269

IN-MYSORE.detail: punishing the allies of his deposed brother, Dhruva defeated the Ganga king Sripurusha, took the crown-prince Shivamara prisoner, and annexed the whole of Gangavadi, pushing the Rashtrakuta frontier to the Kaveri; the Pallava Dantivarman bought him off with an indemnity of elephants and Vengi sued for peace.
IN-MYSORE.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 4, 160. date approximate: shortly after Dhruva's accession in 780

IN-MYSORE.detail: the Western Ganga Nitimarga Ereyanga and other feudatories rose against Amoghavarsha I, whose famous general Bankeya campaigned successfully in Gangavadi before being recalled; the long Ganga war ended only with the marriage alliance of c. 860.
IN-MYSORE.belligerents: Rashtrakuta Empire vs Western Gangas and rebel feudatories
IN-MYSORE.outcome: Revolt largely suppressed; hostilities ended by the marriage of Amoghavarsha's daughter to the Ganga prince Butuga c. 860
IN-MYSORE.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 9-10; Sastri, A History of South India, block 143 of the archive.org text. Date approximate (c. 850-860)

IN-MYSORE.detail: The Hoysala Vishnuvardhana's general Gangaraja made a night attack on the army of the Chalukya emperor Vikramaditya VI, encamped at Kannegal under twelve samantas, and routed it — the high-water mark of the Hoysala bid for independence before Vikramaditya's counterstroke forced them back to vassalage.
IN-MYSORE.belligerents: Hoysalas of Dorasamudra vs Western Chalukya imperial army
IN-MYSORE.outcome: Hoysala victory; Chalukya suzerainty nevertheless reimposed by 1120
IN-MYSORE.source: HCIP V, p. 175 (Sravana Belgola inscription of 1118); battlefield location approximate

IN-MYSORE.detail: The Hoysala general Somanatha’s three-shrined temple, the most complete of its kind.
IN-MYSORE.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-MYSORE.text: Chikkadevaraja Wodeyar dies — Thirty-one years king of Mysore
IN-MYSORE.source: C. Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore I p. 500 (block 496): 'When the hand of Death was on him on November 16, 1704, in the sixtieth year of his age and the thirty-second year of his reign'

IN-MYSORE.belligerents: East India Company, Carnatic (Arcot Nawab) vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu), Hyderabad
IN-MYSORE.outcome: Mysore victory; Haidar appears before Madras and the Company accepts the Treaty of Madras (April 1769) on mutual restitution and a defensive alliance
IN-MYSORE.source: HCIP VIII p. 457-458: Haidar 'won the Nizam over and persuaded him to join an offensive alliance against the British ... The panick-stricken Madras Government was induced to sign a treaty on 4 April, 1769'. Rao III p. 141 is more guarded: the treaty 'gave away more than what it secured for Mysore'.

IN-MYSORE.detail: The siege of Bahadur Benda occurred when the forces of Mysore led by Tipu Sultan besieged Bahadur fort in 1787.
IN-MYSORE.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs Kingdom of Mysore

IN-MYSORE.detail: The Siege of Savendroog was conducted by British East India Company forces under the command of General Charles Cornwallis in December 1791, during the Third Anglo-Mysore War.
IN-MYSORE.belligerents: Sultanate of Mysore vs East India Company

IN-MYSORE.detail: the Bombay army under Stuart, advancing from the west coast, repulses Tipu's attack in the Coorg hills early in March 1799.
IN-MYSORE.belligerents: East India Company vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu)
IN-MYSORE.outcome: East India Company victory; Tipu repulsed
IN-MYSORE.source: HCIP VIII p. 466: 'Tipu was defeated by Stewart at Sedasere and by Harris at Malavally.' Hayavadana Rao III p. ~1069 (block 916, contemporary letter): 'the repulse he met at Sedaseer (about 20 days before)'.

IN-MYSORE.detail: by the Partition Treaty (22 June) Tipu's lands are shared out; the five-year-old Krishnaraja Wodeyar III is installed on 30 June with Purnaiya as Dewan, and the Subsidiary Treaty of 8 July lets the Company garrison Mysore.
IN-MYSORE.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III p. 1088: 'The Brahmans having fixed upon the 30th June as the most auspicious day for placing His Highness Sri Krishnaraja Wodeyar on the musnad of Mysore'; p. 1090 (block 934): 'Under the Subsidiary Treaty, concluded on 8th July 1799'. HCIP VIII p. 466: 'The Wodiyars ... were restored to a portion of the dominions'.

IN-MYSORE.detail: after the Nagar rising, Bentinck (7 September 1831) removes Krishnaraja Wodeyar III from power and puts the whole state under British Commissioners — an act he later admitted went beyond the 1799 treaty.
IN-MYSORE.source: HCIP IX p. 38: 'On September 7, 1831, Bentinck ... transferred the entire administration of the country into the hands of British officers'; p. 40: Bentinck 'could not help entertaining doubts, both as to the legality and the justice of the course that has been pursued.'

IN-BAGALKOT.text: Pulakesin I fortifies Badami and founds the Chalukya kingdom
IN-BAGALKOT.detail: The Chalukya makes the hill-fort of Vatapi his capital and performs the asvamedha — the dynasty that will rule the Deccan for two centuries steps out of Kadamba vassalage.
IN-BAGALKOT.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 231 (Badami cliff inscription, Saka 465 = 543)

IN-BAGALKOT.detail: the Chalukya makes 'the hill-fort of Vatapi' his capital in 543 and performs the asvamedha — the Kadamba feudatory becomes a sovereign, and Kadamba power ends under Harivarman (c. 547).
IN-BAGALKOT.outcome: Chalukya independence; Badami fortified; Kadamba dynasty ends
IN-BAGALKOT.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 231, 273 (Badami cliff inscription of 543)
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 231; chronology p. 711

IN-BAGALKOT.text: Mangalesa dedicates Cave III at Badami
IN-BAGALKOT.detail: The great Vishnu cave, "the earliest dated Hindu cave temple in India" (Saka 500), with its Varaha, Trivikrama and Narasimha reliefs — the Chalukya style is born.
IN-BAGALKOT.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 233-234 (Badami cave inscription of Mangalesa, Saka 500)

IN-BAGALKOT.text: Kirtivarman I dies — Leaving minor sons
IN-BAGALKOT.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 233; chronology p. 712

IN-BAGALKOT.detail: the Chalukya 'put to flight' the Kalachuri Buddharaja, son of Sankaragana, and 'appropriated the royal fortunes of the Katachchuris' — recorded in the Mahakuta pillar of 602.
IN-BAGALKOT.outcome: Chalukya victory; Kalachuri power south of the Narmada broken
IN-BAGALKOT.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 192, 196, 233 (Mahakuta pillar inscription, 602)

IN-BAGALKOT.text: Mangalesa dies — Killed in the civil war with Pulakesin II.
IN-BAGALKOT.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 234

IN-BAGALKOT.detail: After the civil war that killed his uncle Mangalesa, the greatest of the Badami Chalukyas begins the reign that will face Harsha, take Vengi and end at Vatapi.
IN-BAGALKOT.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 234; chronology p. 713 (610-11 to 642)

IN-BAGALKOT.detail: Mangalesa, trying to secure the throne for his own son, is defeated and killed by his nephew Pulakesin II, who 'saved his homeland from enemies' and took the crown in 610-11.
IN-BAGALKOT.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 234, 237 (Aihole prasasti; Hyderabad plates of 612)

IN-BAGALKOT.text: Pulakesin II and Khusrau II exchange embassies
IN-BAGALKOT.detail: Tabari records an embassy from "the king of India" to the Sasanian court in 625-26; tradition sees the Persian embassy in return painted on the walls of Ajanta cave I.
IN-BAGALKOT.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 240 (Tabari); chronology p. 713

IN-BAGALKOT.text: Battle of Manimangalam and the sack of Vatapi
IN-BAGALKOT.detail: Pulakesin's second Pallava war — Narasimhavarman I 'repeatedly defeated king Vallabha' at Pariyala, Manimangala and Suramara, and his general Siruttondar took Badami in 642 — Pulakesin II 'was defeated and probably killed'. Narasimhavarman styled himself Vatapikonda.
IN-BAGALKOT.belligerents: Pallava dynasty (Narasimhavarman I) vs Chalukya (Badami) (Pulakesin II)
IN-BAGALKOT.outcome: Decisive Pallava victory; Badami taken and burnt; thirteen years of Chalukya eclipse
IN-BAGALKOT.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 240-241, 260 (Kuram plates; Badami rock inscription of Narasimhavarman; Periyapuranam on Siruttondar)

IN-BAGALKOT.text: The Aihole prasasti of Pulakesin II
IN-BAGALKOT.detail: Ravikirti's Sanskrit eulogy on the Meguti Jain temple (Saka 556) records the Chalukya's conquests from the Konkan to Kanchi and his check of Harsha — and dates itself by the Mahabharata war.
IN-BAGALKOT.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 235-237

IN-BAGALKOT.text: Pulakesin II dies — "Defeated and probably killed" when Narasimhavarman I took Badami.
IN-BAGALKOT.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 240

IN-BAGALKOT.detail: thirteen years after the fall of Badami the son of Pulakesin II 'rehabilitated the fortunes of his dynasty', defeating the confederacy of three kings that had overrun the kingdom and recovering his ancestral lands.
IN-BAGALKOT.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Vikramaditya I) vs Pallava dynasty (Narasimhavarman I / Mahendravarman II) and their allies
IN-BAGALKOT.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 241, 261
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 245; chronology p. 716
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 245; chronology p. 716

IN-BAGALKOT.detail: the Rashtrakuta feudatory defeated Kirtivarman II and took Vatapi, ending two centuries of Badami Chalukya rule over the Deccan.
IN-BAGALKOT.belligerents: Rashtrakuta (Dantidurga) vs Chalukya of Badami (Kirtivarman II)
IN-BAGALKOT.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

IN-BAGALKOT.text: Krishna I extinguishes the Chalukya empire
IN-BAGALKOT.detail: Kirtivarman II, defeated but not destroyed by Dantidurga, retired to Karnataka and reorganised his forces for a further trial of strength; the new Rashtrakuta king Krishna I met the challenge so successfully that the Badami Chalukya empire was wiped out of existence by about 760.
IN-BAGALKOT.outcome: Rashtrakuta victory; end of the Badami Chalukya empire
IN-BAGALKOT.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 3. date approximate: Krishna I's accession by 758; Chalukya power finally extinguished by c. 760

IN-BAGALKOT.detail: The First Battle of Kudal-Sangamam was fought in 1062 by the forces of the Chola king Rajendra Chola II and the Western Chalukya king Someshvara I at Kudal-Sangamam.
IN-BAGALKOT.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)
Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-RAIGARH-MAH.detail: the great cave of Siva: The Mahesamurti and the Siva cave on the island of Gharapuri are cut in the sixth century, under the Kalachuris of Mahishmati or the Konkan Mauryas.
IN-RAIGARH-MAH.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) art chapter; attribution debated

IN-RAIGARH-MAH.detail: the Mauryas of the Konkan are attacked at their island capital 'Puri' (Elephanta or Rajpuri), 'invaded by Pulakesin's battleships and captured' — 'a hundred ships' in the Aihole verse.
IN-RAIGARH-MAH.belligerents: Chalukya (Badami) (Pulakesin II) vs Mauryas of Konkan
IN-RAIGARH-MAH.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 236 (Aihole prasasti)

IN-RAIGARH-MAH.detail: the Egyptian–Gujarati fleet defeats Portugal — avenged the next year at Diu
IN-RAIGARH-MAH.belligerents: Mamluk Egypt & Gujarat Sultanate vs Portugal
Gujarat Sultanate supported by Calicut, Mamluk Sultanate, Ottoman Empire vs Portuguese Empire / Portuguese India
IN-RAIGARH-MAH.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-RAIGARH-MAH.detail: Shivaji ambushes and captures Kartalab Khan's column in the ghats
Shivaji's invasions of Janjira were a series of military campaigns launched by the first Maratha ruler, Shivaji, against the Abyssinian rulers of the sea fortress of Janjira.
IN-RAIGARH-MAH.belligerents: Maratha Empire (Shivaji) vs Siddis of Janjira

IN-RAIGARH-MAH.text: Shivaji dies — At Raigad, aged fifty
IN-RAIGARH-MAH.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-RAIGARH-MAH.detail: The siege of Janjira was a military campaign undertaken by the Maratha Confederacy, commanded by Sambhaji, the second Maratha ruler, against the Siddis of Janjira in January 1682.
IN-RAIGARH-MAH.belligerents: Siddis of Janjira, Mughal Empire vs Maratha Confederacy, Rathores of Marwar

IN-BARA-BANKI.detail: the Haraha inscription of 554 has the Maukhari defeat 'the Andhras with their thousands of elephants, the Sulikas and the Gaudas' and take the imperial title; either he or his son also 'fought with the Hunas and defeated them'.
IN-BARA-BANKI.belligerents: Maukhari dynasty (Isanavarman) vs Vishnukundin Andhras, the Sulikas and the Gaudas
IN-BARA-BANKI.outcome: Maukhari ascendancy in Madhyadesa; Isanavarman crowned Maharajadhiraja
IN-BARA-BANKI.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 68-69 (Haraha inscription, Vikrama 611 = 554); p. 209 (the Vishnukundin Madhavavarman I as the Andhra)

IN-BARA-BANKI.detail: The Haraha inscription of Vikrama 611 proclaims the Maukhari Maharajadhiraja after his victories over the Andhras, Sulikas and Gaudas — a new imperial house at Kanauj.
IN-BARA-BANKI.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 68-69

IN-KARAIKAL.detail: the first Saiva saints: A sixth-century Saiva yogi, Tirumular, composes the Tirumantiram; the poetess of Karaikkal is remembered as the earliest of the sixty-three Nayanars — the Bhakti movement stirs in the Tamil south.
IN-KARAIKAL.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 328; Sastri, A History of South India ch. on religion

IN-UDAIPUR.text: Guhadatta founds the Guhila principality of Mewar
IN-UDAIPUR.detail: A chief "established a small principality in the western part of the old State of Udaipur" after the Gupta collapse — the ancestor of the Ranas of Mewar. Date traditional.
IN-UDAIPUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 157-159 (Atpur inscription of 977)

IN-UDAIPUR.text: Maharana Pratap dies — At Chavand, from a hunting injury
IN-UDAIPUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)
