IN-UDAIPUR.text: Jahangir-Rajput War / Mughal expedition of Mewar
IN-UDAIPUR.belligerents: Kingdom of Mewar vs Mughal Empire
IN-UDAIPUR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-UDAIPUR.detail: hired by the pretender Ratan Singh against Maharana Ari Singh II, Mahadji Sindhia (joined briefly by Tukoji Holkar) sat down before Udaipur in May 1769, then dropped the pretender and sold peace to the Rana for 64 lakhs.
IN-UDAIPUR.outcome: Scindia and Holkar victory; the Rana buys off the siege with an indemnity settled at 64 lakhs
IN-UDAIPUR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 519: 'Early in May 1769, Mahadji Sindhia marched from Ujjain to Udaipur in order to back the cause of Ratan Singh'; p. 520: 'it was reported from Mahadji's camp that the contribution from Udaipur had been settled at 64 lakhs.' Sarkar (p. 518) rejects Tod's story of a battle on the Sipra near Ujjain in January 1769.

IN-UDAIPUR.text: Krishnakumari of Mewar dies — the sixteen-year-old princess whose hand Jaipur and Jodhpur had fought over was given poison by decision of the Mewar nobles, under pressure from Amir Khan.
IN-UDAIPUR.source: Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages I p. 222: 'The nobles of Mewar held a conference and decided that disgrace to the royal family and the State could be avoided only by administering poison to Krishnakumari. The princess, then a girl of sixteen, took four cups of poison on 21 July, 1810.'

IN-GANJAM.detail: Gupta suzerainty still acknowledged in Orissa: King Prithivivigraha rules Kalinga "in the dominion of the Guptas" in Gupta year 250 — the last echo of the empire, half a century after Yasodharman claimed to have swept it away.
IN-GANJAM.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 42, 92

IN-GANJAM.detail: The Ganjam grant of Madhavaraja II of Kongoda acknowledges the Gauda king's suzerainty in Gupta year 300 — Sasanka's power then reached the Orissa coast; he is dead by the mid-620s.
IN-GANJAM.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 107; chronology p. 713

IN-GANJAM.detail: after Sasanka's death Harsha 'conquered Magadha' — styled king of Magadha in 641 — and carried his raids through West Bengal and Orissa 'up to Kongoda', subjugating the old dominions of the Gauda king.
IN-GANJAM.belligerents: Pushyabhuti (Harsha) vs the Gauda successors and Sailodbhavas of Kongoda
IN-GANJAM.outcome: Harsha holds Magadha, Odra and Kongoda; Bhaskaravarman takes Karnasuvarna
IN-GANJAM.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 107, 110 (Ma-twan-lin; Hiuen Tsang; the Ganjam grant of 619 as Sasanka's last date)

IN-KANNAUJ.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 70; chronology p. 711

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: on the news of Prabhakaravardhana's death 'the king of Malava' Devagupta kills the Maukhari Grahavarman at Kanauj and imprisons his queen Rajyasri; Rajyavardhana 'routed the Malava army with ridiculous ease'.
IN-KANNAUJ.belligerents: Later Gupta dynasty (Devagupta of Malava) vs Maukhari dynasty (Grahavarman); then Pushyabhuti (Rajyavardhana) vs Devagupta
IN-KANNAUJ.outcome: Grahavarman killed; Devagupta then routed by Rajyavardhana
IN-KANNAUJ.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 99-100, 121 (Harshacharita; Madhuban and Banskhera plates: "Devagupta and other kings defeated by Rajyavardhana")

IN-KANNAUJ.text: Devagupta of Malava dies — Routed by Rajyavardhana
IN-KANNAUJ.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 99, 121

IN-KANNAUJ.text: Grahavarman dies — The last Maukhari, killed by Devagupta of Malava.
IN-KANNAUJ.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 99

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: with 5,000 elephants, 2,000 horse and 50,000 foot Harsha 'waged incessant warfare, until in six years he had fought the five Indias' — the Gauda enemy driven from Kanauj, the Malava power broken, Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa won as ally.
IN-KANNAUJ.belligerents: Pushyabhuti (Harsha) vs Gauda (Sasanka), Malava (Devagupta) and others
IN-KANNAUJ.outcome: Harsha master of Madhyadesa; Kanauj becomes his capital
IN-KANNAUJ.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 100-108 (Hiuen Tsang; Bana)
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 99, 122

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: 'allured to confidence by false civilities on the part of the king of Gauda', the victorious Pushyabhuti is killed unarmed at Sasanka's table — the crime that brings Harsha to the throne and to his vow of vengeance.
IN-KANNAUJ.outcome: Rajyavardhana murdered; Harsha succeeds at Thanesar
IN-KANNAUJ.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 99, 122 (Bana; Hiuen Tsang; the Madhuban plate's "Gauda")

IN-KANNAUJ.text: Harsha exchanges embassies with the Tang court
IN-KANNAUJ.detail: Harsha's envoy reaches Chang-an and Tai-tsung sends Liang Huai-ching in return — the first of four Chinese missions to Kanauj in seven years.
IN-KANNAUJ.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 120; chronology p. 714

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: Twenty kings, three thousand monks and the Chinese pilgrim attend the great religious assembly in honour of Mahayana; a fire in the tower and an attempt on the king's life mar it.
IN-KANNAUJ.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 116-119

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: The last great emperor of the north dies without an heir; his minister Arjuna usurps the throne and "the history of Kanauj is wrapt in obscurity" for half a century.
IN-KANNAUJ.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 121, 124; HCIP IV p. xii
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 121

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: the usurper Arjuna of Tirabhukti, who seized Harsha's throne and plundered the Chinese embassy, is crushed by 1,200 Tibetan and 7,000 Nepalese troops — the capital 'captured after a siege of three days', Arjuna taken prisoner to China.
IN-KANNAUJ.belligerents: Kannauj (post-Harsha) (Arjuna / Arunasva) vs the Tang embassy of Wang Xuance with Tibetan Empire and Licchavi dynasty of Nepal troops
IN-KANNAUJ.outcome: Arjuna defeated and carried to China; 580 towns submit
IN-KANNAUJ.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 124-125 (T'ang annals)

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: the Karkota emperor of Kashmir, once his ally against the Tibetans, defeated the lord of Kannauj and made the Ganga plain acknowledge Kashmiri power for a generation.
IN-KANNAUJ.outcome: Kashmiri victory; Yashovarman reduced to tribute
IN-KANNAUJ.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: with Yashovarman gone and the Ayudhas holding Kanyakubja on sufferance, the Pratiharas from Avanti, the Palas from Bengal and the Rashtrakutas from the Deccan all turned on the imperial city. The contest ran for a century and a half; the engagements themselves are recorded year by year from 786.
IN-KANNAUJ.outcome: The contest opens; no single engagement
IN-KANNAUJ.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed pp. 22-28. This row FRAMES the contest and is not an engagement: the Wikipedia overview article was being carried as a single battle, pinned at Indore, with an outcome covering thirty years. The engagements are recorded individually from 786.

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: with the Rashtrakutas withdrawn to the Deccan and Vatsaraja's power broken, the Pala king convoked a great assembly at Kannauj to proclaim himself suzerain and to seat Chakrayudha on the throne in place of the defeated Indrayudha. The rulers of Bhoja, Matsya, Madra, Kuru, Yadu, Yavana, Avanti, Gandhara and Kira attended and gave their assent, the high-water mark of Pala paramountcy in northern India.
IN-KANNAUJ.outcome: Chakrayudha installed at Kannauj as a Pala nominee; Dharmapala acknowledged as paramount lord of northern India
IN-KANNAUJ.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 46: "His main object in convoking the great assembly was to proclaim himself as the suzerain and install Chakrayudha on the throne of Kanauj in place of Indrayudha whom he had defeated. The durbar was attended by a number of vassal chiefs among whom are mentioned the rulers of Bhoja, Matsya, Madra, Kuru, Yadu, Yavana, Avanti, Gandhara and Kira, who uttered acclamations of approval, 'bowing down respectfully with their diadems trembling.'" Same page: "we must hold that Dharmapala must have enjoyed, at least for some time, the unique position of a paramount lord in Northern India", and "These states were not annexed by Dharmapala, but their rulers acknowledged his suzerainty". Date approximate: HCIP gives no year, placing the durbar after Dhruva's return to the south of c. 790 (chronology, printed p. 508) and within Dharmapala's reign of c. 770-810 (printed p. 45). Not a battle: this is an assembly and an investiture, filed as Political. NOT IN WIKIPEDIA's Tripartite Struggle article, which mentions the imperial court only in passing under Dharmapala's conquest of Kannauj.

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: Nagabhata II took Kannauj from Chakrayudha, Dharmapala's protege, and moved the Pratihara capital there from Ujjayini - the central prize of the three-way war between Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas. No source gives a year for the seizure; the Buchkala record of 815 that gives Nagabhata II full imperial titles, and the date Schwartzberg gives for the transfer of the capital.
IN-KANNAUJ.belligerents: Gurjara-Pratihara (Nagabhata II) vs Chakrayudha, backed by the Pala Empire (Dharmapala)
IN-KANNAUJ.outcome: Pratihara victory; Kannauj becomes the imperial capital of northern India
IN-KANNAUJ.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers. Dated 816 here so that the map, the capital record and the milestone all give one year; the Buchkala record of 815 and Schwartzberg's "c. 815" are the evidence, and the year is approximate.

IN-KANNAUJ.text: Nagabhata II dies — The Pratihara who took Kannauj from the Palas.
IN-KANNAUJ.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-KANNAUJ.text: Mihira Bhoja dies — The Pratihara who held Kannauj against the Palas and the Rashtrakutas alike.
IN-KANNAUJ.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: Indra III stormed the Pratihara capital, the deepest southern thrust of the tripartite struggle; Mahipala I recovered the city only after the Rashtrakutas withdrew.
IN-KANNAUJ.belligerents: Rashtrakuta Empire (Indra III) vs Gurjara-Pratihara Empire (Mahipala I)
IN-KANNAUJ.outcome: Kannauj sacked; Pratihara prestige never fully recovered
IN-KANNAUJ.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: after the Rashtrakuta debacle of 916, the Pratihara Mahipala (Kshitipala) regained the imperial throne mainly through his powerful feudatories — a Chandella record says king Harsha 'placed Kshitipala on the throne', and the Guhilot chief Bhatta also fought for him.
IN-KANNAUJ.belligerents: Gurjara-Pratihara Empire with Chandela dynasty and Guhila feudatories vs remnants of the Rashtrakuta occupation
IN-KANNAUJ.outcome: Pratihara restoration at Kannauj (Mahipala attested ruling in A.D. 917)
IN-KANNAUJ.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 33, 36

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: The Ghaznavid invasion of Kannauj or the siege of Kannauj in 1018 was a military campaign conducted by Mahmud of Ghazni, the then ruler of the Ghaznavid Empire.
IN-KANNAUJ.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

IN-KANNAUJ.text: Ramapala's elephant army repulsed at Kanauj
IN-KANNAUJ.detail: having won back Varendra, the Pala king Ramapala tried to restore his family's old reach westward and sent an elephant corps against the Gahadavalas of Kanauj some time between 1100 and 1109. The young Gahadavala prince Govindachandra beat it back, fixing the Pala frontier and announcing the arrival of the man who would dominate the middle Ganga valley for fifty years.
IN-KANNAUJ.belligerents: Palas of Bengal vs Gahadavalas of Kanauj
IN-KANNAUJ.outcome: Gahadavala victory; Pala westward expansion checked
IN-KANNAUJ.source: HCIP V, p. 30

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: When Sultan Mas'ud III's officer Hajib Tughatigin crossed the Ganga and the Ghaznavid army took the Gahadavala king Madanachandra prisoner, prince Govindachandra defeated the Muslims and secured his father's release, announcing the Gahadavala revival at Kannauj.
IN-KANNAUJ.belligerents: Gahadavalas of Kannauj vs Ghaznavid army of Mas'ud III
IN-KANNAUJ.source: HCIP V, p. 95; undated in source — within Mas'ud III's reign (1099-1115), conventionally c. 1109

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: the Gahadavala king of Kanauj and Banaras, whose known dates are 1168 and 1169, beat back a Muslim invasion probably led by Khusrav Malik, the last Ghaznavid ruler of Lahore. It was the last time a Gahadavala turned back a Turkish army; twenty-five years later his son Jayachandra would die facing Muizz-ud-din at Chandawar.
IN-KANNAUJ.belligerents: Gahadavalas of Kanauj vs the Ghaznavids of Lahore
IN-KANNAUJ.source: HCIP V, p. 54

IN-KANNAUJ.detail: Sher Shah expels Humayun; the Sur Empire replaces the Mughals
IN-KANNAUJ.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-KURUKSHETRA.detail: The first Pushyabhuti to take the title Maharajadhiraja — "a lion to the Huna deer, a burning fever to the king of Sindhu, a troubler of the sleep of the Gurjara king" (Bana).
IN-KURUKSHETRA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 96-98; chronology p. 712

IN-KURUKSHETRA.text: Harshavardhana is born — Sixteen at his accession in 606 (Hiuen Tsang)
IN-KURUKSHETRA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 100-101

IN-KURUKSHETRA.text: Prabhakaravardhana dies — Died of fever at Thanesar
IN-KURUKSHETRA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 98-99

IN-KURUKSHETRA.text: Harsha ascends the throne of Thanesar
IN-KURUKSHETRA.detail: At sixteen, after the murders of his brother-in-law and brother, Harshavardhana takes the crown "without any hesitation" and vows vengeance on Gauda; the Harsha era begins.
IN-KURUKSHETRA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 100-102

IN-KURUKSHETRA.detail: marching before the Rajas of Hindustan could combine, Mahmud forced the river-line held by Rama, chief of Dera, then plundered the sacred city of Thanesar, breaking its idols and carrying the chief image to Ghazni for defilement.
IN-KURUKSHETRA.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs Rama of Dera and the Raja of Delhi's confederates
IN-KURUKSHETRA.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 10; HCIP dates it 1011 (often given as 1014)

IN-KURUKSHETRA.text: The Hindu confederacy recovers Hansi, Thanesar and Nagarkot
IN-KURUKSHETRA.detail: with Maudud pinned at Ghazni by the Saljuqs, a league of Indian chiefs under the Tomara raja of Delhi set out to end Muslim rule in the Punjab. They wrested Hansi, Thanesar and other places from Maudud's governors, took Nagarkot, and then marched on Lahore and invested it for seven months before a sortie by the desperate garrison scattered them. They kept Nagarkot, Hansi and the other conquests for years. HCIP names the Paramara Bhoja, the Kalachuri Karna and the Chahamana Anahilla as probable members of the confederacy — the high-water mark of Indian recovery between Mahmud and the Ghurids.
IN-KURUKSHETRA.belligerents: Confederacy of Indian chiefs under the Raja of Delhi vs the Ghaznavid governors of the Punjab
IN-KURUKSHETRA.outcome: Indian victory in the field — Hansi, Thanesar and Nagarkot recovered — but the siege of Lahore failed
IN-KURUKSHETRA.source: HCIP V, printed p. 94: "in A.D. 1043, some Indian chiefs formed a confederacy under the leadership of the Raja of Delhi to put an end to the Muslim rule in the Punjab. They wrested HansI, Thaneswar and other places from governors who were posted there by Maudud. After capturing Nagarkot they marched to Lahore and invested it for seven months." (Note: coordinates are for Thanesar/Kurukshetra, the middle of the recovered belt; Hansi 29.10N 75.96E, Nagarkot 32.10N 76.27E. Corroborated at HCIP V, printed p. 67, for Bhoja's share.)

IN-KURUKSHETRA.detail: Ghori defeats Prithviraj Chauhan and lays the foundation of Islamic rule in India
IN-KURUKSHETRA.belligerents: Ghurid Empire (Muizz-ud-din Muhammad) vs Chahamana (Chauhan) of Shakambhari (Prithviraja III) and the Rajput confederacy

IN-KURUKSHETRA.detail: Battle of Thanesar was fought on the eve of Solar eclipse holy bath fair on 9 April 1567, near Thanesar on the banks of the Saraswati Ghaggar River in the state of Haryana.
IN-KURUKSHETRA.belligerents: Mughal Empire vs Two rival groups of Sanyasis

IN-KURUKSHETRA.detail: The Battle of Thanesar (1710) was one among a series of battles fought between Nawab Firuz Khan Mewati and Governor Binod Singh.
IN-KURUKSHETRA.belligerents: Mughal Empire vs First Sikh State

IN-RAIPUR.text: Tivaradeva 'obtained mastery of the entire Kosala country'
IN-RAIPUR.detail: the Panduvamsi of Sripura conquers South Kosala and claims Utkala — the Sarabhapuriyas are displaced.
IN-RAIPUR.belligerents: Panduvamshi dynasty (Tivaradeva) vs Sharabhapuriya dynasty; Utkala
IN-RAIPUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 220 (Rajim and Baloda grants)

IN-RAIPUR.detail: the Lakshmana temple of the Panduvamsis: Queen Vasata's brick temple to Vishnu at Sripura, the Panduvamsi capital on the Mahanadi — the finest brick shrine of the age. Date approximate.
IN-RAIPUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 220-221 (Sirpur inscriptions of Vasata and Balarjuna)

IN-MADURAI.detail: the Pandya 'recovered the territory under the Kalabhra occupation' — the Velvikudi grant remembers the Kali king Kalabhran driven from the Pandya country.
IN-MADURAI.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 265-267 (Velvikudi grant)
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 267

IN-MADURAI.detail: Sena II of Ceylon, allied with the Pallavas and a Pandya pretender, sent an expedition into the Madurai kingdom which was a complete success — the capital was sacked, Srimara Srivallabha died of his wounds, and Varagunavarman II was enthroned by the Sinhalese commander-in-chief.
IN-MADURAI.belligerents: Sinhala kingdom (Sena II) and Pandya pretender vs Pandya kingdom of Srimara
IN-MADURAI.outcome: Madurai sacked; Srimara died of his wounds; Varagunavarman II installed (862)
IN-MADURAI.source: Sastri, A History of South India, block 142 of the archive.org text; The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 170 (Sena II, A.D. 844-79)

IN-MADURAI.detail: soon after his accession (907) the Chola king raided Madurai, winning the title Madhurantaka, and by his third regnal year assumed the title Maduraikonda ('captor of Madurai'), driving the Pandya Rajasimha II to seek Sinhalese aid.
IN-MADURAI.belligerents: Chola Empire (with Western Ganga, Kerala and Kodumbalur allies) vs Pandya kingdom
IN-MADURAI.outcome: Chola victory; Madurai taken and the Pandya king forced to seek Ceylonese help
IN-MADURAI.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 154 (title Maduraikonda by the third regnal year, i.e. c. 910)

IN-MADURAI.detail: the defeated Pandya Rajasimha II obtained the aid of the Ceylonese king Kassapa V, but about A.D. 915 Parantaka I beat the combined Pandya and Sinhalese army in a famous battle at Vellur, south-west of Madurai; a third campaign expelled Rajasimha about 920.
IN-MADURAI.belligerents: Chola Empire vs Pandya kingdom and Sinhalese expeditionary army
IN-MADURAI.outcome: Chola victory; Rajasimha II eventually expelled and Parantaka styled 'captor of Madurai and Ceylon'
IN-MADURAI.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 154, 170

IN-MADURAI.detail: following his Kerala victories Rajaraja I conquered Madurai and seized the Pandya king Amarabhujanga, then pressed into Kudamalai-nadu (Coorg) and took the stronghold of Udagai; the Pandya country was absorbed as Rajaraja-mandalam.
IN-MADURAI.outcome: Chola victory; Madurai taken, Amarabhujanga captured
IN-MADURAI.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 234; year approximate (early 990s)

IN-MADURAI.text: Pandyan Civil War and the sack of Madurai
IN-MADURAI.detail: about 1169 two claimants, Parakrama Pandya and Kulasekhara Pandya, went to war for Madurai. Kulasekhara, backed by the Cholas, besieged and took the city and killed his rival along with members of his family. The help Parakrama had begged from Parakramabahu I of Ceylon arrived too late — and turned a succession quarrel into a twenty-year international war.
IN-MADURAI.belligerents: Parakrama Pandya vs Kulasekhara Pandya, backed by the Cholas
IN-MADURAI.outcome: Kulasekhara took Madurai and killed Parakrama Pandya

IN-MADURAI.text: Lankapura's head nailed to the gates of Madurai
IN-MADURAI.detail: the Chola counter-stroke came under the general Pallavarayan. The Pallavarayanpettai inscription of Rajadhiraja II's eighth regnal year records that Lankapura was defeated and killed, his head fixed to the gate of Madurai, and Kulasekhara restored to the Pandya throne. The conversion of the Pandya country into a Ceylonese province was averted.
IN-MADURAI.belligerents: Cholas and Kulasekhara Pandya vs the Sinhalese army of Parakramabahu I
IN-MADURAI.outcome: Decisive Chola victory; Lankapura killed and Kulasekhara reinstated
IN-MADURAI.source: HCIP V, p. 265; Sastri, A History of South India, ch. on the later Cholas

IN-MADURAI.text: Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan I dies — The Pandya who took Kanchi and the Chola country
IN-MADURAI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-MADURAI.text: Malik Kafur's invasion of the Pandya kingdom
IN-MADURAI.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-MADURAI.text: Veera Ballala III dies — The last Hoysala, killed at Madurai by the sultan he had besieged
IN-MADURAI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-MADURAI.detail: Kumara Kampana, son of Bukka I of the Vijayanagara Empire, commanded a series of military campaigns that disestablished Muslim rule in southern India, annexing Madurai around 1370.
The Siege of Madurai was a conflict between the Vijayanagara Empire and the Madurai Nayaks. Venkatapati Raya marched against Virappa Nayaka.
IN-MADURAI.belligerents: Vijayanagar Empire Matli Chiefs vs Madurai Nayakas

IN-MADURAI.detail: The Mysore-Madurai Wars were a series of conflicts fought between the Kingdom of Mysore and the Madurai Nayakas, primarily in the 17th and early 18th centuries.
IN-MADURAI.belligerents: Madurai Nayakas supported by Vijayanagara, Maratha Kingdom, Bijapur, Thanjavur Marathas, Ikkeri Nayakas, Ramnad, Kalahasti vs Kingdom of Mysore
IN-MADURAI.outcome: Expulsion of Mysoreans from Madurai End of Mysore's expansion into Madurai

IN-MADURAI.text: Tirumala Nayaka rebuilds the Meenakshi temple
IN-MADURAI.detail: The Madurai Nayak raises the gopurams and the thousand-pillared hall that stand today, and the Thirumalai Nayakar Mahal beside them.
IN-MADURAI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-MADURAI.detail: The Mysore invasions of Samballi took place between 1641 and 1642 during the reign of Kanthirava Narasaraja I.
IN-MADURAI.belligerents: Madurai Nayakas, Chief of Samballi vs Flag of Kingdom of Mysore.png Kingdom of Mysore

IN-MADURAI.detail: The Battle of Madurai in 1656 was fought between the forces of Kingdom of Mysore and the Madurai Nayaks, with strong support from the Maravars.
IN-MADURAI.belligerents: Madurai Nayakas, Kingdom of Ramnad vs Flag of Kingdom of Mysore.png Kingdom of Mysore

IN-MADURAI.detail: the Arcot Nawab's son-in-law seizes Trichinopoly from Rani Minakshi, then Madurai and Dindigul; the queen takes her own life and the Madurai Nayak line ends.
IN-MADURAI.outcome: Carnatic victory; Chanda Sahib becomes master of the Nayak kingdom and Rani Minakshi commits suicide
IN-MADURAI.source: HCIP VIII (The Maratha Supremacy) p. 312-313: 'Chanda Sahib advanced to Trichinopoly a second time in 1736, captured Madura and Dindigul and became master of the Nayak kingdom, while Rani Minakshi committed suicide in despair.' (p. 336 n. 3: the chronicles give conflicting versions of the sequence.)

IN-MADURAI.detail: the Company's commandant of Madurai and Tinnevelly rebels against Nawab Muhammad Ali and is besieged in Madurai; he appeals in vain to Haidar and is hanged in 1764.
IN-MADURAI.belligerents: East India Company, Carnatic (Arcot Nawab) vs Muhammad Yusuf Khan (Madurai)
IN-MADURAI.outcome: East India Company victory; the revolt fails and Yusuf Khan is hanged (1764)
IN-MADURAI.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore II p. 518 (block 485): 'Muhammad Yusuf Khan, who commanded Madura in the English interests and had rebelled against them and been, in consequence, closely invested by them at Madura'; p. 248 n. (block 243): 'Yusuf Khan proved a rebel and was hanged in 1764' (OCR '1784'). Menon p. 234: 'The rebellion of Yusuf Khan failed as a result of the help rendered to the Nawab by the English.'

IN-JALOR.text: Brahmagupta is born — Thirty years old when he completed the Brahmasphutasiddhanta in Saka 550 (628), by his own statement.
IN-JALOR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 323

IN-JALOR.detail: At Bhillamala under the Chapa king Vyaghramukha, the thirty-year-old astronomer writes the treatise that first treats zero as a number and gives rules for negative quantities — carried to Baghdad a century later as the Sindhind.
IN-JALOR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 161, 323; chronology p. 713

IN-JALOR.detail: Kanhadadeva Chauhan falls after an epic defiance of Alauddin
IN-JALOR.belligerents: Delhi Sultanate vs Chauhans of Jalore

PK-SUKKUR.text: Chach seizes the throne of Sindh
PK-SUKKUR.detail: The Brahmin minister marries the widow of Rai Sahasi II and founds the dynasty that Muhammad ibn Qasim will destroy — 602 by the Chach-nama's own reckoning, which modern scholars place a generation later.
PK-SUKKUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 166 (Chach-nama; chronology uncertain)

PK-SUKKUR.text: Chach dies — After a forty-year reign by the Chach-nama
PK-SUKKUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 166

PK-SUKKUR.detail: Muhammad ibn Qasim defeated and killed Raja Dahir of Sindh; Aror, Multan and the lower Indus passed to the Umayyad caliphate — the Islamic world’s first province in India.
PK-SUKKUR.belligerents: Umayyad Caliphate (Muhammad ibn Qasim) vs Brahmin dynasty of Sindh (Raja Dahir)
PK-SUKKUR.outcome: Umayyad victory; Sindh becomes a Caliphal province
PK-SUKKUR.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

PK-SUKKUR.text: Raja Dahir dies — Killed at the battle on the Indus near Aror, fighting Muhammad ibn Qasim
PK-SUKKUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-VILUPPURAM.text: Mahendravarman I cuts the first Pallava rock temples
IN-VILUPPURAM.detail: The Mandagapattu cave records the "curious-minded" king's boast of a temple without brick, timber, metal or mortar — the beginning of Tamil stone architecture, continued at Tiruchirappalli and Mamallapuram.
IN-VILUPPURAM.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 259-260; Sastri, A History of South India scan 134

IN-VILUPPURAM.detail: The Battle of Gingee was a conflict between the forces of the Vijayanagara Empire and the army of Krishnappa Nayaka the ruler of Gingee.
IN-VILUPPURAM.belligerents: Vijayanagar Empire Venkatagiri estate vs Gingee Nayaks

IN-VILUPPURAM.detail: The siege of Jinji (1690–1698) was a protracted conflict between the Mughal Empire and the Maratha kingdom, wherein the triple-hill fortress of Jinji was besieged.

IN-VILUPPURAM.text: Fall of Gingee and death of Nasir Jang
IN-VILUPPURAM.detail: Bussy and d'Auteuil storm Gingee by night; in December the French advance into Nasir Jang's camp, the Nizam is shot dead by one of the Pathan Nawabs, and the captive Muzaffar Jang is raised to the throne — the height of Dupleix's power.
IN-VILUPPURAM.belligerents: French India, Muzaffar Jang vs Hyderabad (Nasir Jang)
IN-VILUPPURAM.outcome: French India victory; Nasir Jang killed and Muzaffar Jang made Subahdar (December 1750)
IN-VILUPPURAM.source: HCIP VIII p. 322: 'their assault and capture of the place in the course of a night attack greatly raised their fame ... Nasir Jang was shot dead through the heart by one of the Nawabs and Muzaffar Jang was released from prison and promptly elevated to the throne ... (December, 1750).'

IN-MURSHIDABAD.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 107

IN-MURSHIDABAD.detail: with Sasanka gone, the Kamarupa king occupies the Gauda capital — his Nidhanpur grant is issued 'from the camp of victory at Karnasuvarna' while Harsha reduces Magadha and Kongoda.
IN-MURSHIDABAD.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 91, 107 (Nidhanpur plates)

IN-MURSHIDABAD.detail: Rajendra Chola’s Ganga expedition — a Chola army marched up the east coast, defeated Mahipala I of the Palas in Bengal, and carried Ganga water south to consecrate the new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram — ‘the city of the Chola who took the Ganga’.
IN-MURSHIDABAD.belligerents: Chola Empire (Rajendra I) vs Pala Empire (Mahipala I), with the Somavamshis and lesser powers en route
IN-MURSHIDABAD.outcome: Chola victory; Ganga water carried to the new imperial capital
IN-MURSHIDABAD.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

IN-MURSHIDABAD.text: Murshid Quli Khan dies — First independent Nawab of Bengal, who moved the capital from Dacca to Murshidabad and remade the revenue system through contractors who became the zamindars.
IN-MURSHIDABAD.source: HCIP VIII p. 106: 'After the death of Murshid Quli Khan, on 30 June, 1727, without any male issue, his son-in-law Shuja-ud-din Muhammad Khan ... ascended the masnad of Bengal.' Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 44: 'When he died (30th June, 1727)'.

IN-MURSHIDABAD.text: Shuja-ud-din Muhammad Khan dies — Nawab of Bengal (1727–39), to whom Bihar was added
IN-MURSHIDABAD.source: Books disagree on the day: HCIP VIII p. 108: 'After the death of Shuja-ud-din on 30 March, 1739'; Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 44: 'On the death of Shuja (13th March, 1739)'.

IN-MURSHIDABAD.text: Alivardi Khan dies — Nawab of Bengal from 1740, who held off ten years of Maratha raids and the Afghan revolts, and left the masnad to his grandson Siraj-ud-daulah.
IN-MURSHIDABAD.source: Books disagree on the day: HCIP VIII p. 111: ''Ali Vardi died on 10 April, [1756] and was succeeded as the subahdar of Bengal by his favourite grandson and heir-designate Siraj-ud-daulah' (the scan reads '1750', evidently for 1756); HCIP VIII chronology p. 826: '1756, April 21 Death of Ali Vardi Khan, Subahdar of Bengal.'

IN-MURSHIDABAD.text: Siraj-ud-daulah dies — The last independent Nawab of Bengal, caught after Plassey and put to death at Murshidabad by Mir Ja‘far’s son Miran (July 1757).
IN-MURSHIDABAD.source: web-only; library silent on his death (HCIP VIII p. 339 says only that he 'lost his nerves and fled'). Famous and uncontested; the last independent Nawab of Bengal.

IN-MURSHIDABAD.text: Mir Qasim made Nawab of Bengal
IN-MURSHIDABAD.detail: by a treaty of 27 September 1760 the Calcutta Council makes Mir Qasim diwan and heir, in return for Burdwan, Midnapur and Chittagong; Mir Ja‘far, refusing, resigns and Mir Qasim is installed (October 1760).
IN-MURSHIDABAD.source: HCIP VIII p. 344: 'On 27 September a treaty was signed between Mir Qasim and the English by which the English agreed to appoint Mir Qasim to the post of Diwan and promised him the succession to Mir Ja‘far, while Mir Qasim agreed to cede to the English the districts of Burdwan, Midnapur and Chittagong ... Mir Ja‘far after some hesitation resigned his office altogether.' Sarkar II p. 542 dates the elevation 20 October 1760.

IN-MURSHIDABAD.text: Mir Ja‘far dies — The commander whose defection decided Plassey, twice made Nawab of Bengal by the Company (1757–60, 1763–65).
IN-MURSHIDABAD.source: HCIP VIII p. 350: 'Mir Ja‘far who was old and very ill died in February 1765.'

IN-MURSHIDABAD.detail: Failed rains in 1768-69 and the Company’s revenue demand together kill perhaps a third of the population of Bengal and Bihar - the figure of ten million is Hastings’s own.
IN-MURSHIDABAD.source: HCIP VIII p. 357: 'one of the worst tragedies of human history befell Bengal. This was the Bengal famine of 1770 in which nearly a third of the population is said to have been swept away. The absence of a government, properly speaking, and the action of self-seeking men in cornering grains, intensified the severity of the famine.' (Chronology p. 833: '1769-70 A terrible famine visits Bengal'.) The 'ten million' figure attributed to Hastings is web-only.

IN-KANCHEEPURAM.text: The rathas and reliefs of Mamallapuram
IN-KANCHEEPURAM.detail: Narasimhavarman I Mamalla gives his name to the port where the monolithic rathas, the Arjuna's Penance relief and the cave-temples are cut — the seaboard workshop of Pallava art.
IN-KANCHEEPURAM.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 260-261; art chapter

IN-KANCHEEPURAM.detail: The Battle of Chingleput was a short siege in early 1752, during the Second Carnatic War.
IN-KANCHEEPURAM.belligerents: British East India Company, Nawab of Arcot vs French East India Company

IN-THANE.detail: The first Arab raid on India — a naval expedition from Oman strikes Thana near Bombay under the Caliphate of 'Umar — repulsed, and the Caliph forbids further sea ventures; raids on Broach and Debal follow.
IN-THANE.belligerents: Rashidun Caliphate vs the Konkan (Mauryas / Chalukya sphere)
IN-THANE.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 167 (Baladhuri)

IN-THANE.detail: Between 1160 and 1162 the Chaulukya king despatched his minister Ambada with a large army against the Silahara Mallikarjuna of Konkan; assisted by the Paramara Dharavarsha and the Chahamana prince Somesvara (who claimed the kill), the Gujarat army slew Mallikarjuna and annexed his kingdom.
IN-THANE.belligerents: Chaulukyas of Gujarat with Paramara and Chahamana allies vs Silaharas of North Konkan
IN-THANE.outcome: Mallikarjuna killed; Konkan annexed to Gujarat

IN-THANE.detail: on 28 December 1774 a Bombay expedition seizes Thana on Salsette from the Marathas, without authority from Calcutta. It is the opening move of the first Anglo-Maratha war.
IN-THANE.belligerents: East India Company vs Maratha Empire
IN-THANE.outcome: East India Company victory; Thana and Salsette captured
IN-THANE.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 52: 'Thana was captured on 28th December ... according to which the capture of Thana was unauthorized.'

IN-MAYILADUTHURAI.text: Tirujnanasambandar is born — Born at Sirkali
IN-MAYILADUTHURAI.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 328; Sastri, A History of South India

IN-MAYILADUTHURAI.text: The Danish East India Company founds Tranquebar (Fort Dansborg) — its principal Indian colony until 1845

IN-MAYILADUTHURAI.detail: The siege of Dansborg or the siege of Fort Dansborg, was a siege of the newly finished Danish fort of Dansborg in Trangebar in 1624.
IN-MAYILADUTHURAI.belligerents: Danish India vs Thanjavur Nayak kingdom

IN-MAYILADUTHURAI.detail: The siege of Dansborg, or the siege of Fort Dansborg, was a short siege lasting from 20 to 30 December 1644, between general Tiagepule of Thanjavur and the Danish command.
The sieges of Tranquebar refer to the warfare between the Thanjavur Nayak kingdom and the Danish East India Company from 1655 to 1669.
The siege of Tranquebar was a siege of the Danish colony of Tranquebar by Shahuji I of the Thanjavur Maratha kingdom in 1699.
IN-MAYILADUTHURAI.belligerents: Danish India, English India vs Thanjavur Maratha

IN-MAYILADUTHURAI.detail: The Cattle War, also commonly referred to as the Perumal War or the Perumal Naik-War, was a colonial conflict between the Danish East India Company and the Thanjavur Marathas.
IN-MAYILADUTHURAI.belligerents: Danish India, French India vs Thanjavur

PK-KARACHI.detail: The Arabs reach Makran and Sindh — after Cadesia the Muslim armies enter Makran; a force sent against Debal (the port of Sindh) is 'defeated and their leader killed by the governor of Chach' according to the Chach-nama, though Arab historians record a victory.
PK-KARACHI.belligerents: Rashidun Caliphate vs Brahmin dynasty of Sindh (Chach)
PK-KARACHI.outcome: Arab repulse at Debal per the Chach-nama; Makran annexed
PK-KARACHI.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 166-169

PK-KARACHI.text: Pakistan adopts its first constitution and becomes an Islamic republic
PK-KARACHI.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

PK-KARACHI.detail: President Iskander Mirza abrogates the constitution and declares martial law under General Ayub Khan, who removes Mirza himself twenty days later
PK-KARACHI.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

IN-BHARUCH.text: Valabhi conquers the Gurjara kingdom of Nandipuri
IN-BHARUCH.detail: Dharasena IV Chakravartin of Valabhi issues grants from Broach in 648 — the Maitrakas briefly master the Gurjaras of Lata.
IN-BHARUCH.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 147; chronology p. 714

IN-BHARUCH.detail: Siladitya III of Valabhi issues grants from the Gurjara capital in 685 — the second Maitraka occupation of Lata.
IN-BHARUCH.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 149; chronology p. 716

IN-BHARUCH.text: Dhruva II repels the Pratihara invasion of Lata
IN-BHARUCH.detail: Mihira Bhoja, seeking to avenge Nagabhata II's defeat, invaded the Gujarat Rashtrakuta kingdom, but Dhruva II — reconciled with Amoghavarsha in 860 — held his own and confined the enemy to the other side of the Narmada, being secure on his throne again by 867.
IN-BHARUCH.belligerents: Rashtrakutas of Gujarat (Lata branch) vs Gurjara-Pratihara Empire
IN-BHARUCH.outcome: Pratihara invasion checked at the Narmada
IN-BHARUCH.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 10; Sastri, A History of South India, block 143 of the archive.org text. Date approximate (c. 860-867)

IN-BHARUCH.detail: continuing the same northern campaign, the Chalukya emperor sacked Lata, the coastal strip around Broach, and won a victory over the Gurjara king — the Chaulukya Kumarapala of Gujarat. It was a raid rather than a conquest, but it opened the long-running Deccan quarrel with Gujarat that Kumarapala, Bijjala and their successors would keep alive for forty years.
IN-BHARUCH.belligerents: Chalukyas of Kalyana vs the Chaulukyas of Gujarat

IN-NAWADA.text: Adityasena of Magadha performs the horse-sacrifice
IN-NAWADA.detail: The Later Gupta king assumes the imperial titles and celebrates the asvamedha; his Aphsad inscription rehearses his line back to Krishnagupta. "Magadha rose to a position of imperial greatness."
IN-NAWADA.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 126-127, 358 (Aphsad inscription)
HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 127

IN-TIRUNELVELI.detail: Arikesari Maravarman Parankusa 'won a great victory at Nelveli' (Tirunelveli), and 'extirpated the Paravas of the coast'; further victories over the Cheras are recorded in the Velvikudi grant.
IN-TIRUNELVELI.belligerents: Pandya dynasty (Arikesari Maravarman) vs the Cheras and the Paravas
IN-TIRUNELVELI.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 267 (Velvikudi and Larger Sinnamanur plates)

IN-JAIPUR.detail: The earliest dated Guhilot record: a chief of the Chatsu branch in eastern Rajasthan, Vikrama 741.
IN-JAIPUR.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) p. 160; chronology p. 716

IN-JAIPUR.detail: The Mughal Central Asia Campaign, also known as the Balkh Campaign, was a military campaign from 1645–1647 undertaken by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan against the Uzbek Khanate.
IN-JAIPUR.belligerents: Mughal Empire Kingdom of Jaipur Nurpur kingdom vs Khanate of Bukhara, Kazakh Khanate
IN-JAIPUR.outcome: Status quo ante bellum Plunder of southern Uzbek territories

IN-JAIPUR.detail: Jai Singh II’s observatory, the largest stone sundial in the world.
IN-JAIPUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-JAIPUR.detail: The Battle of Bagru was a military engagement fought between multiple Indian kingdoms in 1748 near the town of Bagru, Jaipur, India.
IN-JAIPUR.belligerents: Kingdom of Jaipur, Reinforced By, Kingdom of Bharatpur vs Forces of Madho Singh, Reinforced By, Holkar Clan
IN-JAIPUR.outcome: Madho Singh and allied victory; Ishvari Singh signs peace with the Marathas.

IN-JAIPUR.text: Ishwari Singh of Jaipur kills himself
IN-JAIPUR.detail: with Malhar Holkar's army a day's march away, Sawai Jai Singh's heir took poison on the night of 12 December 1750; the Marathas seated his brother Madho Singh, and on 10 January 1751 the citizens of Jaipur rose and massacred some 1,500 Maratha visitors.
IN-JAIPUR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 187: 'It was the 12th of December, 1750 ... At midnight he swallowed the poison and caused the cobra to sting him.' p. 189: 'Some fifteen hundred Marathas were slain and about a thousand wounded.' Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages I p. 252: 'Ishwari Singh ... escaped their rising pressure by committing suicide (December 1750). The Marathas occupied the city of Jaipur and placed Madho Singh on the gadi.'

IN-JAIPUR.detail: Sawai Pratap Singh’s screen of 953 windows for the women of the court.
IN-JAIPUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AMRAVATI.detail: The Rashtrakutas of Berar — Durgaraja, Govindaraja, Svamikaraja, Nannaraja Yuddhasura — hold Elichpur under the Chalukyas; the Multai grant of 709 is Nanna's. The kin, perhaps, of Dantidurga's line.
IN-AMRAVATI.source: HCIP III (Majumdar ed., The Classical Age) pp. 201-202; chronology p. 716

IN-AMRAVATI.detail: Daulat Rao Sindhia cedes everything between the Jamuna and the Ganges and north of Jaipur, Jodhpur and Gohad, with Broach and Ahmadnagar, and renounces control of the Mughal emperor.
IN-AMRAVATI.source: HCIP VIII p. 497: 'the treaty of Surji Anjangaon on 30 December, 1803. He recognised the treaty of Bassein and surrendered his territories between the Yamuna and the Ganga and all those situated to the north of Jaipur, Jodhpur and Gohad... and he renounced his control upon the Mughul emperor.'

IN-AMRAVATI.detail: by the treaty of 21 May 1853, the Nizam hands Berar, the Raichur doab and other districts to British management to pay for the Hyderabad Contingent.
IN-AMRAVATI.source: HCIP IX p. 86: 'A new treaty was concluded with the Nizam On May 21, 1853 ... the Nizam assigned the fertile districts of Berar, the cotton garden of Hindustan, the Raichur doab ... to the exclusive management of the British'; p. 647: 'the Nizam who was compelled to cede Berar by force and fraud in 1853'.

IN-ANANTNAG.detail: Lalitaditya builds the sun temple: The great Karkota temple of the sun on the Martand plateau above Anantnag, the largest of its age in Kashmir.
IN-ANANTNAG.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-MALDAH.detail: the king of Kanauj marched east, conquered West and East Bengal, and defeated and killed the lord of Gauda who also ruled Magadha — the exploit that gave Vakpati's poem Gaudavaho its name.
IN-MALDAH.outcome: Kanauj victory; the Gauda king slain
IN-MALDAH.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), pp. 127-128, 143. date approximate: conquest placed between A.D. 725 and 735

IN-MALDAH.detail: sent east by his father Somesvara I, the Chalukya prince Vikramaditya VI carried a Deccani army across northern India and defeated the Pala Vigrahapala III in Gauda shortly before 1068; on the same sweep he is credited with a successful expedition against Kamarupa. It is the deepest recorded penetration of Bengal by a southern power in the century and one more blow in the sequence that left Mahipala II's Pala kingdom open to the Kaivarta revolt.
IN-MALDAH.belligerents: Western Chalukyas of Kalyana vs the Palas of Bengal
IN-MALDAH.outcome: Chalukya victory; Vigrahapala III defeated in his own country
IN-MALDAH.source: HCIP V, printed p. 27: "Shortly before A.D. 1068 Vigrahapala had to suffer a defeat at the hands of the Chalukya Vikramaditya VI, who invaded Gauda on behalf of his father Somesvara I, king of the Deccan." (Note: HCIP gives only 'shortly before 1068'; coordinates are for the Gauda capital region near Malda. The Kamarupa expedition is at printed p. 43.)

IN-MALDAH.text: Ramapala dies — The Pala who won back Varendra from the Kaivartas
IN-MALDAH.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-MALDAH.detail: the Pala king Madanapala fought a severe battle near the Kalindi river in the Malda district against an invading army, almost certainly the Senas under Vijayasena. He drove the enemy back to the river, but the success was temporary — some time after the eighth year of his reign he had to surrender Varendra, the Pala homeland in north Bengal, and it never returned to his family.
IN-MALDAH.belligerents: Palas of Bengal vs the Senas of Radha
IN-MALDAH.outcome: Tactical Pala success, strategic defeat: Varendra lost soon after

IN-MALDAH.text: Vijayasena wrests Varendra from the Palas
IN-MALDAH.detail: About the middle of the twelfth century the Sena king overthrew Bhojavarman of Vikramapura, then invaded Varendri; despite a reverse near the Kalindi river he wrested North Bengal from the Pala Madanapala, making the Senas masters of Gauda, Vanga and Radha.
IN-MALDAH.belligerents: Senas of Bengal vs Palas (Madanapala) and Varmans of East Bengal
IN-MALDAH.outcome: Sena conquest of North and East Bengal; Pala rule reduced to a remnant in Bihar
IN-MALDAH.source: HCIP V, pp. 36-37; 'about the middle of the twelfth century', c. 1150s

IN-MALDAH.text: Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah dies — Founder of the independent sultanate of Bengal
IN-MALDAH.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-MALDAH.detail: Sikandar Shah’s mosque, the largest in the subcontinent when it was built.
IN-MALDAH.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-MALDAH.text: Alauddin Hussain Shah dies — The sultan of Bengal’s golden age
IN-MALDAH.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-KARGIL.detail: the Karkota emperor of Kashmir, in alliance with Yashovarman of Kanauj, beat back the Tibetans and the mountain tribes of the north-west frontier; his appeal of 733 for a Chinese alliance against Tibet won recognition but no troops, and he prevailed unaided.
IN-KARGIL.belligerents: Karkota dynasty of Kashmir (Lalitaditya) vs Tibetan Empire
IN-KARGIL.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), p. 133. date approximate: early in Lalitaditya's reign (acc. c. 724)

IN-KARGIL.detail: Indian armour is taken over an 11,500-foot pass for the first time in history, relieving Ladakh
IN-KARGIL.outcome: Indian victory — the road to Leh reopened
IN-KARGIL.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-KARGIL.detail: the six-week fight for the ridge overlooking the Srinagar-Leh highway turns the Kargil war
IN-KARGIL.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-KARGIL.detail: Indian forces evict intruders from the heights above the Srinagar-Leh highway
IN-KARGIL.outcome: Indian victory — all positions on the Indian side of the LoC recaptured
IN-KARGIL.source: Wikipedia: List of wars involving India

IN-JAMNAGAR.text: Arab invasion of the Saindhava kingdom
IN-JAMNAGAR.detail: in or before 739 the Arabs of Sindh invaded the realm of the Saindhavas of western Saurashtra, ruled from Bhutambilika (Ghumli) in a gorge of the Barda hills, during the reign of Pushyadeva.
IN-JAMNAGAR.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 99; chronology p. 506 (c. 739). date approximate: 'in or before A.D. 739'

IN-JAMNAGAR.text: Jam Rawal, driven out of Kutch, took the port of Nagnath from the Jethwas and founded Nawanagar in August 1540 — the state that became Jamnagar, and three centuries of enmity between the Jams and the Ranas of Porbandar.

IN-JAMNAGAR.detail: The Battle of Bhuchar Mori, also known as Battle of Dhrol, was fought between the army of Kathiawar led by Nawanagar State and the Mughal army at Bhuchar Mori plateau near Dhrol.
IN-JAMNAGAR.belligerents: Mughal Empire, Junagadh State vs Nawanagar State, Gujarat Sultanate, Muli State

IN-CHITTAURGARH.detail: the Guhila chief Bappa, who resisted the Arab raiders more successfully than his neighbours, took the fortress of Chitrakuta (Chittor) from the Mori (Maurya) king Manuraja, whose kingdom had been battered by the Arab incursions of 725-738.
IN-CHITTAURGARH.belligerents: Guhilas of Mewar vs Moris (Mauryas) of Chittor
IN-CHITTAURGARH.source: The Classical Age (HCIP III), p. 162: Maurya Dhavala still honoured in a Kota-region record of 738-39, so Bappa "can hardly" have taken Chitor before 738; Tod gives 728, Ojha 734 - the atlas paints c. 740 and records the dispute. Chittorgarh, Rajasthan - not Chittoor, Andhra.

IN-CHITTAURGARH.detail: Alauddin takes Mewar's citadel; the first jauhar of Chittor enters legend
IN-CHITTAURGARH.belligerents: Delhi Sultanate vs Guhilas of Mewar

IN-CHITTAURGARH.detail: Rana Kumbha’s nine-storey tower of victory over Mahmud Khalji of Malwa.
IN-CHITTAURGARH.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CHITTAURGARH.detail: The siege of Chittorgarh took place in 1535, when Sultan Bahadur Shah of Gujarat attacked Chittor Fort, after the death of Rana Sanga, with the aim of expanding his kingdom.
IN-CHITTAURGARH.belligerents: Gujarat Sultanate vs Kingdom of Mewar
Kingdom of Mewar vs Mughal Empire
IN-CHITTAURGARH.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-PORBANDAR.text: Arab fleet repulsed off the Barda hills
IN-PORBANDAR.detail: Hisham, governor of Sindh for Caliph al-Mansur, sent Amru bin Jamal with a fleet of barks against the Barada coast of Saurashtra; the Saindhavas, self-styled 'masters of the western sea', routed the invaders under the leadership of Krishnaraja.
IN-PORBANDAR.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 99; The Classical Age (HCIP III), chronology p. 718 (758). date approximate: Hisham appointed c. 756, expedition 758

IN-PORBANDAR.text: Second Arab naval expedition against Barada
IN-PORBANDAR.detail: about 776 the Arabs again sent a fleet against the Saindhava coast and captured a town (probably Ghumli), but were forced to withdraw — officially by an epidemic, in reality by the Saindhava king Agguka I, who 'rescued his country drowning in an ocean of naval force'; Caliph al-Mahdi thereupon gave up all designs on India.
IN-PORBANDAR.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 99-100; chronology p. 507 (c. 776)

IN-PORBANDAR.detail: Jam Barmaniyaji Jadeja stormed the Jethwa capital in the Barda hills, avenging his father Jam Unaji's defeat of 1309. Rana Bhanji Jethwa fled to Ranpur and Ghumli, capital of western Saurashtra since the Saindhavas, was never rebuilt.

IN-PORBANDAR.text: Rana Vikmatji Khimoji Jethwa took Porbandar from the Mughals and built its fort, with the fort of Madhavpur

IN-THIRUVANANTHAPURAM.detail: The Pandyas sack Vizhinjam — Jatila Parantaka stormed the Ay port below the hills of Thiruvananthapuram, opening a generation of Pandya pressure on the Ay country.
IN-THIRUVANANTHAPURAM.belligerents: Pandya dynasty (Jatila Parantaka) vs Ay kingdom
IN-THIRUVANANTHAPURAM.source: Added with the 700-799 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia and the research register.

IN-THIRUVANANTHAPURAM.detail: in the opening Chera war of Rajaraja I the Chola stormed and destroyed Vilinam (Vizhinjam) on the Kerala coast — recorded as falling before the naval seizure of Kandalur Salai — while Kollam (Quilon) was attacked separately. His adversary was the Chera Bhaskara Ravivarman (987-1036).
IN-THIRUVANANTHAPURAM.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 234; sequence (before Kandalur Salai) per source, exact year disputed

IN-THIRUVANANTHAPURAM.detail: on 3 January 1750 Marthanda Varma dedicates the enlarged kingdom of Travancore to Sri Padmanabha; thereafter its kings rule as the god's servants (Padmanabhadasas).
IN-THIRUVANANTHAPURAM.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 232-233: 'the dedication (Trippatidanam) of the newly expanded kingdom of Travancore to his tutelary deity, Sri Padmanabha ... The event took place on Wednesday, January 3, 1750'.

IN-THIRUVANANTHAPURAM.text: Marthanda Varma dies — the 'Maker of Modern Travancore', victor of Colachel, who annexed the neighbouring chiefdoms and dedicated the kingdom to Sri Padmanabha.
IN-THIRUVANANTHAPURAM.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 233: 'He is rightly regarded as the Maker of Modern Travancore ... Karthika Tirunal Rama Varma (1758-1798) ... succeeded Marthanda Varma on the throne'; p. 266: 'Marthanda Varma (1729-1758)'.

IN-THIRUVANANTHAPURAM.text: Karthika Tirunal Rama Varma, the Dharma Raja of Travancore, dies — forty years king, host to the refugees of the Mysore invasions, builder of the Nedumkotta and patron of Kathakali.
IN-THIRUVANANTHAPURAM.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 237: 'When the Raja passed away in 1798 after a long reign of 40 years he was already 74 years old.'

IN-THIRUVANANTHAPURAM.detail: a treaty negotiated by Velu Thampi makes Travancore a subsidiary ally paying Rs 8 lakhs a year and bound to take the Company's advice — the loss of its political freedom.
IN-THIRUVANANTHAPURAM.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 258: 'A fresh treaty of alliance and friendship was concluded between the English and Travancore in 1805. Under this treaty Travancore became a subsidiary ally ... The treaty of 1805 which was negotiated by Velu Tampi Dalawa resulted in the loss of the political freedom of Travancore.'

IN-BANGALORE-RURAL.detail: the Rashtrakuta emperor invaded the Western Ganga kingdom of Sripurusha, was encamped at Manne in 768, and effected a military occupation of the country, having earlier held the Ganga capital Manyapuram for a time.
IN-BANGALORE-RURAL.outcome: Rashtrakuta victory; military occupation of Gangavadi
IN-BANGALORE-RURAL.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 3, 160; chronology p. 507 (768)

IN-BANGALORE-RURAL.text: Tipu Sultan is born — At Devanahalli, Haidar Ali’s son.
IN-BANGALORE-RURAL.source: C. Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III p. 561-562 n. (block 492): 'Kirmani dates it November 19, 1749 ... Wilks in 1753 ... Kirkpatrick ... 1747, while the Haid. Nam. would refer it to 1752 ... Kirmani's date is adopted in this work as the more specific and reliable.' Conventional modern date 20 Nov 1750 (milestone M492); the row's 1751 has no book behind it.

IN-BANGALORE-RURAL.detail: Battle of Ooscota was a military engagement fought during the First Anglo-Mysore War, in which the Marathas intervened to aid the British.
IN-BANGALORE-RURAL.belligerents: Murari Rao of Gooty, East India Company vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu)
IN-BANGALORE-RURAL.outcome: Murari Rao victory — Haidar's night attack on Murari's camp at Hoskote (24 August 1768) beaten off, and Haidar withdraws his cavalry
IN-BANGALORE-RURAL.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III p. 77-78: 'On the night of the 24th, Haidar made a disposition for the attack of Murari's camp ... he did not think proper to renew the attack, and withdrew his cavalry. While Haidar's loss in this injudicious attempt was not inconsiderable'. (Wilks dates it 22 Aug, Robson 24 Aug.)

IN-DHARMAPURI.detail: Nedunjadaiyan (Varaguna I) conquered the Adigaimans of Tagadur (Dharmapuri) and brought the Kongu country under his control in spite of the aid they obtained from the Chera and Pallava rulers, making him master of the Tanjore, Tiruchirapalli, Salem and Coimbatore regions.
IN-DHARMAPURI.belligerents: Pandyas vs Adigaimans of Tagadur, with Chera and Pallava aid
IN-DHARMAPURI.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 158. date approximate: recorded in the Madras Museum plates of his 17th regnal year (c. 782)

IN-ETAWAH.text: Vatsaraja defeats the lord of Gauda
IN-ETAWAH.detail: the first encounter of the tripartite war, fought as the Pratihara and the Pala closed on Kannauj from opposite directions. Vatsaraja, aided by his Chahamana feudatory Durlabharaja of Sakambhari, won completely and carried away the Gauda king's umbrellas of state, but was beaten by the Rashtrakuta Dhruva before he could gather the spoils.
IN-ETAWAH.outcome: Pratihara victory; Dharmapala's state umbrellas taken, though the advantage was lost within a few years to the Rashtrakuta invasion
IN-ETAWAH.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), printed p. 45: "The first encounter took place between the Pratihara ruler Vatsaraja and Dharmapala, probably somewhere in the Gangetic Doab, in which the former gained a complete victory. He is said to have 'appropriated with ease the fortune of royalty of the Gauda' and 'carried away Gauda's umbrellas of state.'" Feudatory aid at printed p. 22: "Vatsaraja was aided in this expedition by his feudatory chiefs, one of whom, the Chahamana Durlabharaja of Sakambhari". Date approximate: HCIP gives no year, placing the encounter before Dhruva's northern expedition of c. 786-790. DISAGREEMENT ON THE RECORD: Wikipedia calls this an invasion of Bengal in which Durlabharaja I pursued and defeated Dharmapala in Gauda; HCIP IV, printed p. 23, holds that the claim that Durlabharaja "overran the whole of Bengal up to the confluence of the Ganga and the sea" comes from "a poetical work composed about four centuries after the event described" and is "difficult to take it as literally true", and that "it cannot be said definitely whether Vatsaraja actually invaded Bengal, or met and defeated the lord of Gauda somewhere in the Doab".

IN-ERNAKULAM.text: Adi Shankara is born — By tradition at Kalady on the Periyar, in 788.
IN-ERNAKULAM.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-ERNAKULAM.detail: The Battle of Cochin, sometimes referred as the second siege of Cochin, was a series of confrontations, between March and July 1504, fought on land and sea.
IN-ERNAKULAM.belligerents: Portuguese Empire Kingdom of Cochin vs Calicut
Zamorin with United Kingdom, English East India Company, Portuguese Empire / Portuguese India as listed vs Dutch Republic / Dutch East India Company
IN-ERNAKULAM.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-JHANSI.detail: entering the contest for Kanauj as a third claimant in c. 786, the Rashtrakuta emperor crossed the Narmada, occupied Malwa, and crushed Vatsaraja near Jhansi, driving him into the deserts of Rajputana; he then routed Dharmapala on the outskirts of the Doab, capturing the Pala king's white imperial umbrellas, before returning south c. 790 laden with booty.
IN-JHANSI.belligerents: Rashtrakuta Empire vs Gurjara-Pratihara Empire and Pala Empire
IN-JHANSI.outcome: Rashtrakuta victory over both Vatsaraja and Dharmapala
IN-JHANSI.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 5. date approximate: campaign c. 786-790 (midpoint given)

IN-JHANSI.detail: Raja Gangadhar Rao dies on 21 November 1853 after adopting a son; Dalhousie refuses to recognise the adoption and annexes Jhansi by lapse, setting aside Rani Lakshmibai.
IN-JHANSI.source: HCIP IX p. 65: '2. Jhansi. Gangadhar Rao, Raja of Jhansi, died on November 20, 1853. On November 19, he decided to adopt a son'; HCIP IX chronology p. 1187: '1854 Annexation of Jhansi.'

IN-JHANSI.detail: Hugh Rose invests Jhansi on 22 March, beats Tantia Tope's 22,000-man relief army on the Betwa on 1 April and storms the city on 3 April; Rani Lakshmibai escapes by night to Kalpi.
IN-JHANSI.belligerents: East India Company vs Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Tantia Tope's army
IN-JHANSI.outcome: East India Company victory; Tantia's relief force routed and Jhansi taken by assault
IN-JHANSI.source: HCIP IX p. 580-581: 'the city and the fort with his cavalry on 22 March'... 'defeated the host of Tantia who fled towards Kalpi (April 1, 1858). Two days later Rose took the city of Jhansi by assault... The Rani left the fort with a few attendants on the night of the 4th April' (the page's OCR is damaged)

IN-TUMKUR.text: Govinda III crushes the revolt of Stambha
IN-TUMKUR.detail: the accession of Govinda III in 793 was challenged by his elder brother Stambha, viceroy of Gangavadi, at the head of 'twelve kings' joined by the released Ganga prince Shivamara; Govinda quelled the rebellion, took his brother prisoner and magnanimously reinstated him, while Shivamara was returned to prison.
IN-TUMKUR.belligerents: Govinda III vs Stambha and twelve confederate kings
IN-TUMKUR.outcome: Govinda III's victory; undisputed overlord of the Deccan by c. 795
IN-TUMKUR.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 6, 160. date approximate: rebellion quelled A.D. 793-795

IN-THOOTHUKKUDI.detail: The Pandya monolith cut from the top of a granite hill and never finished — the vimana complete, the sanctum below it barely begun; eighth century.
IN-THOOTHUKKUDI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-THOOTHUKKUDI.detail: The Battle of Punnaikayal (1553) was a conflict between the Portuguese and a combined force of Ottomans, Kingdom of Calicut and Vijayanagara troops.
IN-THOOTHUKKUDI.belligerents: Vijayanagara Empire Madurai Nayakas Kingdom of Calicut, Ottoman Empire vs Portuguese Empire

IN-THOOTHUKKUDI.detail: Raghunatha Sethupathi suppressed the Ettayapuram polygar's rebellion on behalf of Tirumala Nayaka.
IN-THOOTHUKKUDI.belligerents: Madurai Nayaks and Kingdom of Ramnad vs the Polygar of Ettayapuram and rebel polygars
IN-THOOTHUKKUDI.outcome: Madurai–Ramnad victory; rebel confederation defeated, Ettayapuram polygar executed

IN-THOOTHUKKUDI.detail: the Company's attempt to end the palaiyakkarars' armed power in Tinnevelly, Madurai, Ramnad and Sivaganga provokes risings — Kattabomman of Panjalamkurichi (1799), then the Marudu brothers' league (1800–01) — ended by the disarming proclamation of 1 December 1801.
IN-THOOTHUKKUDI.belligerents: East India Company vs Tamil poligars (Panjalamkurichi, Sivaganga and allied palayams)
IN-THOOTHUKKUDI.outcome: East India Company victory; the poligars' military power suppressed and the southern districts disarmed
IN-THOOTHUKKUDI.source: HCIP VIII p. 628: 'The so-called Palegar War of 1799-1801 was marked by a recrudescence of anarchy and followed by their final suppression. Government, by a proclamation of 1 December, 1801, suppressed the use of all weapons of defence'. (Names of leaders: web-only; library silent.)

IN-THOOTHUKKUDI.text: Veerapandiya Kattabomman dies — the palaiyakkarar of Panjalamkurichi who defied the Company's tribute demands
IN-THOOTHUKKUDI.source: web-only; library silent — HCIP VIII p. 628 names only 'The so-called Palegar War of 1799-1801'. The hanging at Kayathar in October 1799 is uncontested and he is the best-known figure of the Tamil resistance.

IN-GULBARGA.text: Govinda III dies — The Rashtrakuta at the empire’s widest reach, from Kannauj to the Kaveri.
IN-GULBARGA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-GULBARGA.text: Amoghavarsha I dies — Sixty-four years on the Rashtrakuta throne
IN-GULBARGA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-GULBARGA.text: Krishna III dies — The last great Rashtrakuta
IN-GULBARGA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-GULBARGA.text: Battle of Kalighatta and the sack of Manyakheta
IN-GULBARGA.detail: Siyaka II threw off the Rashtrakuta yoke, defeated the aged emperor Khottiga at Kalighatta on the Narmada (his ally Kanka of Vagada dying in the fight), pursued him to Manyakheta and plundered the imperial capital in the spring of 972 — even the record-office copper plates were carried off. Khottiga died of a broken heart soon after, and the empire never recovered.
IN-GULBARGA.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 15, 96

IN-GULBARGA.detail: the feudatory of Tardavadi rose against Karka II, took Manyakheta, and founded the Western Chalukya empire of Kalyani.
IN-GULBARGA.belligerents: Western Chalukya (Tailapa II) vs Rashtrakuta Empire (Karka II)
IN-GULBARGA.outcome: Rashtrakuta empire ends; Kalyani Chalukya rule over the Deccan begins
IN-GULBARGA.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

IN-GULBARGA.text: Vakpati Munja dies — The Paramara captured and executed by Tailapa II of Kalyani after crossing the Godavari once too often.
IN-GULBARGA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-GULBARGA.text: Battle of Koluru on the Bhima
IN-GULBARGA.detail: driving into the Deccan immediately after Somesvara I's accession, the Chola Rajadhiraja I brushed aside the Chalukya feudatory Vichchaya at Pundi and the generals Nanni-Nolamba, Chamundaraja, Kalidasa, Kommayya and Villavaraja, and was finally met by Somesvara I in person at Koluru on the bank of the Bhima near Chitapur. The Cholas took heavy losses but forced Somesvara to withdraw, opening the road to Kalyana.
IN-GULBARGA.belligerents: Cholas vs the Western Chalukyas of Kalyana
IN-GULBARGA.outcome: Chola victory at heavy cost; Somesvara I forced to withdraw
IN-GULBARGA.source: HCIP V, printed p. 168: "The next resistance to the advance of the Cholas was given by Somesvara I at Koluru, on the bank of the Bhima, near Chitapur Railway Station, in the Shorapur District, Hyderabad Though the Cholas suffered a heavy loss on this occasion, they forced Somesvara I to withdraw." (Note: coordinates approximate, near Chitapur on the Bhima. HCIP dates the campaign to 1043-44.)

IN-GULBARGA.text: Alauddin Bahman Shah dies — Founder of the Bahmani sultanate at Gulbarga.
IN-GULBARGA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-GULBARGA.detail: The Bahmani mosque with a roofed courtyard, unique in India; Rafi of Qazvin its architect.
IN-GULBARGA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-GULBARGA.text: Firuz Shah Bahmani dies — The scholar-sultan
IN-GULBARGA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-GULBARGA.detail: The Siege of Gulbarga was a siege battle where Hussain Nizam Shah I of Ahmadnagar and Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah Wali of Golconda joined together to capture the fort of Gulbarga.
IN-GULBARGA.belligerents: Bijapur Sultanate vs Ahmednagar Sultanate, Golconda Sultanate

IN-MUNGER.detail: with Kannauj taken and Chakrayudha put down, Nagabhata II carried the war into the heart of the Pala dominions, where a pitched battle was fought, probably near Monghyr (Mudgagiri), against Dharmapala, ‘a mass of dark, dense cloud of mighty elephants, horses and chariots’; the Pratihara, aided by the feudatories Kakka, Vahukadhavala and Sankaragana, won a great victory. It was a field victory and not a conquest — no Pala district changed hands, and Magadha stayed Pala for another seventy years — but it secured the eastern flank of the city Nagabhata had just made his capital.
IN-MUNGER.outcome: Pratihara victory in the field; no territory taken, the Pala hold on Anga and Magadha unbroken
IN-MUNGER.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 25-26, 47-48; the Gwalior prashasti of Bhoja I, which names Chakrayudha first and the Gauda king after. Undated in the sources; the year is approximate, within 816-820. DISPUTED: Majumdar (HCIP) puts both the Kannauj conquest and this battle BEFORE Govinda III’s northern raid of c. 800; this atlas follows the later reading, because its own paint does - HCIP IV p. 26 has Dharmapala and Chakrayudha surrendering to Govinda III of their own accord in c. 800, so Chakrayudha still held Kannauj then, p. 25 has Nagabhata II defeating him "only in the early 9th century", and Schwartzberg has the Ayudhas "c. 815. Overthrown by Pratiharas". On that reading Dharmapala must still be reigning, which is A. M. Chowdhury (1967) 781-821 and B. P. Sinha (1977) 783-820 rather than Majumdar’s 770-810.
Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-MUNGER.text: Mahipala I dies — The Pala who recovered Bengal and Bihar after the Kamboja interlude
IN-MUNGER.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-MUNGER.text: Govindachandra takes the Pala country up to Monghyr
IN-MUNGER.detail: some time before 1146 the Gahadavala king of Kanauj and Banaras overran everything the Palas still held as far east as Monghyr on the Ganga, reducing Madanapala's kingdom to a rump. It was the deepest Gahadavala penetration into Bihar and left the Palas caught between Kanauj in the west and the rising Senas in the east.
IN-MUNGER.belligerents: Gahadavalas of Kanauj vs the Palas of Bengal and Bihar
IN-MUNGER.outcome: Gahadavala conquest of Pala Bihar up to Monghyr

IN-RUDRAPRAYAG.text: Adi Shankara dies — By tradition at Kedarnath, aged thirty-two
IN-RUDRAPRAYAG.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PRAKASAM.detail: Amoghavarsha I, after recovering his throne with the help of his Gujarat viceroy Karkka, destroyed a large host of the Eastern Chalukyas at Vingavalli near Stambhapuri (Kambham) and drove their army out of Rashtrakuta territory.
IN-PRAKASAM.belligerents: Rashtrakuta Empire vs Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi
IN-PRAKASAM.outcome: Decisive Rashtrakuta victory; Chalukya invasion rolled back and Vengi occupied
IN-PRAKASAM.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 9, 134; Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, block 142 of the archive.org text. Date disputed: HCIP implies c. 830 vs Vijayaditya II; Sastri places it against Vijayaditya III in the 850s

IN-NAGAUR.detail: the Daulatpura copper-plate of A.D. 843 shows Bhoja I reasserting Pratihara authority over Gurjaratra (central and eastern Rajputana), lost during Ramabhadra's inglorious reign, aided by loyal feudatories like the Guhilot Harsharaja who 'overcame the kings in the north'.
IN-NAGAUR.belligerents: Gurjara-Pratihara Empire vs rebellious Jodhpur Pratiharas and northern kings
IN-NAGAUR.outcome: Pratihara authority restored over Gurjaratra by A.D. 843
IN-NAGAUR.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 29-30 (Daulatpura plate, A.D. 843)

IN-NAGAUR.detail: The Battle of Nagaur was fought between the Rajputs of Mewar and the Nagaur Sultanate.
IN-NAGAUR.belligerents: Udaipur (Mewar) (Rana Kumbha) vs Khanzadas of Nagaur (Shams Khan and Mujahid Khan) with Gujarat Sultanate support

IN-NAGAUR.text: Mirabai is born — c. 1498 at Kudki near Merta, a Rathore princess.
IN-NAGAUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-NAGAUR.detail: Jayappa Sindhia, pursuing Bijay Singh of Marwar from Ajmer, beat the Rathors at Merta on 15 September 1754 and drove him into Nagaur, which he then besieged.
IN-NAGAUR.outcome: Maratha victory; Bijay Singh falls back to Nagaur and is besieged
IN-NAGAUR.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II p. 383: 'Jayappa immediately followed Bijay Sinh to Merta in August and in a stiff action inflicted a severe defeat on the Rathors on 15th September 1754. Thereupon Bijay Sinh fell back still further north to Nagore.'

IN-NAGAUR.text: Jayappa Sindhia is assassinated — the Sindhia chief besieging Bijay Singh in Nagaur was stabbed in his camp by men who came in with the Jodhpur envoys
IN-NAGAUR.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II p. 384: 'On the morning of Friday 25th July, 1755, the Jodhpur Vakil ... visited Jayappa's camp ... Suddenly two beggars ... ran at Jayappa ... and stabbed him, wounding him mortally, so that in an hour he died.' HCIP VIII chronology p. 826: '1755, July 25 Jayappa Sindia assassinated.'

IN-NAGAUR.detail: Sindhia's army under De Boigne defeats the Jodhpur army in Marwar. Bijay Singh of Jodhpur came to terms with Mahadji Sindhia the following January.
IN-NAGAUR.outcome: Scindia victory; De Boigne's brigades break the Rathor army; Jodhpur comes to terms, January 1791
IN-NAGAUR.source: The Maratha Supremacy (HCIP VIII), printed p. 838 (chronology). Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages I p. 256: 'the decisive blow which he struck against Jodhpur in the battle of Merta (September 1790) disturbed the balance of power in Hindustan.'

IN-TIRUVANNAMALAI.detail: The Battle of Tellaru was fought in 830 between the forces of the Pallava King Nandivarman III and the Pandyan King Srimara Srivallabha.
IN-TIRUVANNAMALAI.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07) Re-dated from 830 to 850. The row came from a Wikipedia category sweep that dates the battle to 830 while the same encyclopaedia dates its victor, Nandivarman III, to c. 846-869 - he was not yet king in 830. This atlas paints him from 847, and carries Srimara’s revenge at Kumbakonam in 859 and Nripatunga’s answer at Arisil in 861, so Tellaru belongs between the accession and 859.

IN-TIRUVANNAMALAI.detail: The Battle of Arnee occurred on 3 December 1751 during the Second Carnatic War.
IN-TIRUVANNAMALAI.belligerents: Great Britain, British East India Company, Maratha Empire vs Kingdom of France, Drapeau_du_régiment_de_la_Compagnie_des_Indes_en_1756.svg French East India Company, Nawab of Arcot (Chanda Sahib)

IN-TIRUVANNAMALAI.detail: the first action of the First Anglo-Mysore War (2 September 1767) — Colonel Smith meets the combined army of Haidar and Nizam Ali at the Changama pass.
IN-TIRUVANNAMALAI.belligerents: East India Company, Carnatic (Arcot Nawab) vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu), Hyderabad
IN-TIRUVANNAMALAI.outcome: Inconclusive — HCIP: Smith 'won a nominal victory ... It was on the whole a very indecisive affair'; the confederates got into the Karnatak regardless
IN-TIRUVANNAMALAI.source: HCIP VIII p. 458: 'In the first battle of the war, Colonel Smith won a nominal victory over Haidar Ali and Nizam Ali at Changama. It was on the whole a very indecisive affair.' Hayavadana Rao III synopsis (block 27) and index p. 47: 'the action at Changama, September 2, 1767'.

IN-TIRUVANNAMALAI.detail: on 26 September 1767 Smith defeats the Mysore–Hyderabad army at Trinomalee; soon after, Nizam Ali leaves the war and makes terms with the Company.
IN-TIRUVANNAMALAI.belligerents: East India Company, Carnatic (Arcot Nawab) vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu), Hyderabad
IN-TIRUVANNAMALAI.outcome: East India Company victory; Nizam Ali withdraws from the war
IN-TIRUVANNAMALAI.source: HCIP VIII p. 458: 'The next engagement was at Trinomali, where also the confederates were defeated. Thereupon Nizam Ali withdrew from the conflict.' Hayavadana Rao III synopsis (block 27): 'The action at Tiruvannamalai, September 26, 1767'.

IN-CHITTOOR.detail: the Nolamba Mahendra I, backed by the Western Gangas, sent his general Kaduvetti Muttarasa to invade Pulinadu, but the Banas and Vaidumbas attacked at Soremati about A.D. 878 and the Nolambas were repulsed.
IN-CHITTOOR.belligerents: Banas and Vaidumbas vs Nolambas and Western Gangas
IN-CHITTOOR.outcome: Bana-Vaidumba victory; the Nolamba invasion repulsed
IN-CHITTOOR.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 163, 511 (chronology: 'c. 878'). Locality in the Bana country (Chittoor-Punganur region) approximate

IN-CHITTOOR.detail: Matla Anantaraju breached Gurramkonda's defences and compelled the Golconda-backed Ravella chief to surrender.
IN-CHITTOOR.belligerents: Vijayanagara Empire and Matli chiefs vs Ravella Nayaks (backed by Golconda Sultanate)
IN-CHITTOOR.outcome: Vijayanagara victory; a bastion breached and the Ravella chief surrendered the fort

IN-CHITTOOR.detail: Raghuji Bhosle's Marathas, sent by Shahu to protect Tanjore, destroy the Arcot Nawab's army in the pass on 20 May 1740; Nawab Dost Ali and his son fall, and Arcot is taken.
IN-CHITTOOR.outcome: Maratha victory; Nawab Dost Ali and his son Hasan Ali killed, his Diwan captured, Arcot occupied
IN-CHITTOOR.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II p. 253 (block 205): 'Dost Ali, his son Hasan Ali and several prominent commanders lost their lives ... This happened on 20th May 1740.' HCIP VIII p. 313: 'the defeat and death of Dost Ali in the pass of Damalcheruvu'.

IN-CHITTOOR.text: Haidar Ali dies — In his camp at Narasingarayanpet near Chittoor, on 7 December 1782, of a cancer
IN-CHITTOOR.source: C. Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III p. 393-394 (block 357): 'Haidar breathed his last in his camp at Narasingarayanpet, near Chittoor, on the 7th of December 1782, at the age of sixty.' HCIP VIII p. 460: 'on 7 December, Haidar died'.

IN-CHITTOOR.detail: The Siege of Goorumconda was a series of conflicts fought at Goorumconda, a hill fort northeast of Bangalore, during the Third Anglo-Mysore War.
IN-CHITTOOR.belligerents: Kingdom of Mysore vs Hyderabad, British East India Company

IN-KHARGONE-WEST-NIMAR.detail: Bhoja I took the offensive against the Rashtrakutas, and a Pratihara record refers to the defeat of Krishna II, probably on the banks of the Narmada, and his retreat to the south of the river, after which Bhoja occupied Malwa and advanced towards Gujarat, taking Khetaka (Kaira).
IN-KHARGONE-WEST-NIMAR.outcome: Pratihara victory; Krishna II driven south of the Narmada. The Pratihara record also claims Malwa, but the map keeps Malwa Paramara under Rashtrakuta overlordship until 930
IN-KHARGONE-WEST-NIMAR.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 31. Date within c. 878-888 (early in Krishna II's reign); exact site on the Narmada uncertain. Note: HCIP credits the victory to Bhoja, against the older view of a Pratihara defeat DISAGREEMENT INSIDE ONE BOOK: HCIP IV p. 31 (Pratihara chapter) has Bhoja occupying Malwa after this victory; p. 95 (Paramara chapter) has the early Paramaras as Rashtrakuta vassals in Malava throughout and says Nagabhata II "could not reconquer Malava". The map follows p. 95 and gives the Pratiharas Malwa only in 930-946, so the outcome line here no longer states the occupation as fact.

IN-KHARGONE-WEST-NIMAR.text: Bajirao I dies — Of fever at Raverkhedi on the Narmada, 36 miles from Khargon, on campaign
IN-KHARGONE-WEST-NIMAR.source: HCIP VIII p. 97: 'While encamped at Raverkhedi 36 miles from Khargon he contracted fever on 23 April; after a short illness he passed away on Monday, 28 April, 1740 ... he is remembered to this day among the Marathas as the fighting Peshwa'.

IN-PULWAMA.text: Avantivarman of Kashmir dies — The Utpala king whose engineer Suyya drained the valley
IN-PULWAMA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

BD-JOYPURHAT.detail: the Pratihara emperor took Magadha from the Pala Narayanapala and pushed on into northern Bengal, where a pillar of his fifth regnal year stands in the Somapura monastery at Paharpur. How much ground he actually held beyond Bihar is disputed — Majumdar reads the pillar as occupation of part of Varendra, Schwartzberg keeps the whole region inside the Pala core.
BD-JOYPURHAT.outcome: Magadha lost to the Pratiharas; the extent of the Bengal push is disputed
BD-JOYPURHAT.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 33, 53, 57 n.45 Re-dated from 895 to 886 to agree with the map, which has taken Magadha from the Palas in 886 since the 800-1188 layer on HCIP IV p. 33 - "shortly after his accession he conquered Magadha", with records from his 2nd regnal year on. The Paharpur pillar of his 5th year (c. 890) dates the later push into north Bengal, not the conquest of Magadha.

PK-GUJRAT.detail: the Kashmir king invaded the Gurjara country of the Punjab (modern Gujrat) and forced its king Alakhana to surrender the Takka land east of the Chenab, while Prithivichandra of Trigarta acknowledged his supremacy and even the Pratihara Mahendrapala ceded territories in the Punjab.
