PK-GUJRAT.belligerents: Utpala dynasty of Kashmir (Sankaravarman) vs Gurjaras of the Punjab (Alakhana) and their allies
PK-GUJRAT.outcome: Kashmiri victory; Takka land ceded, Trigarta submitted, Pratihara territory in the Punjab ceded
PK-GUJRAT.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 33, 118. Date approximate (within Sankaravarman's reign, 883-902; campaign usually placed c. 885-890)

PK-GUJRAT.detail: Ahmad Khan Shahanchi Bashi, Shah Zaman's governor at Rohtas, surprised the Sikh chiefs near Gujrat on 29 April 1797 and drove them into the fort, but was shot dead from its walls; his army broke and was pursued to the Jhelum.
PK-GUJRAT.outcome: Sikh victory; the Durrani governor killed and some 3,000 Afghans slain or wounded
PK-GUJRAT.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs III pp. 85–86: 'In the hailstorm of balls and bullets Ahmad Khan was struck dead. The Durrani troops finding themselves leaderless sought safety in flight. They were hotly pursued by the Sikhs as far as the banks of the Jhelum ... nearly 3,000 Afghans were slain and wounded.'

PK-GUJRAT.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs East India Company
PK-GUJRAT.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

PK-GUJRAT.detail: the Khalsa army is destroyed; Punjab is annexed
PK-GUJRAT.belligerents: East India Company vs Sikh Empire
PK-GUJRAT.outcome: East India Company victory; the Sikh army routed and pursued fifteen miles (21 February 1849); general surrender on 12 March
PK-GUJRAT.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 286: 'a pitched battle was fought on February 21, 1849. The Sikh army was defeated and completely routed, and the British cavalry pursued them for fifteen miles. On March 12, 1849, there was a general surrender of the Sikhs.'

PK-SWABI.detail: the Kashmir king's military operation against Lalliya Shahi of Udabhanda, who had supported Alakhana against him, did not meet with success; Kalhana says Lalliya's glory outshone all the rulers of the north.
PK-SWABI.belligerents: Kashmir (Utpala dynasty) vs Hindu Shahi kingdom of Udabhanda
PK-SWABI.outcome: Kashmiri failure; the Shahi kingdom remained independent
PK-SWABI.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 112, 118. Date approximate (c. 885-895, during Sankaravarman's Punjab wars)

PK-SWABI.text: Prabhakara restores the Shahi throne at Udabhanda
PK-SWABI.detail: the Kashmiri minister Prabhakara led an expedition against the Shahi kingdom and secured the throne of Udabhanda for Lalliya Shahi's son Toramana-Kamaluka by defeating the usurper Samanta.
PK-SWABI.belligerents: Kashmir expeditionary force and Toramana-Kamaluka vs the usurper Samanta
PK-SWABI.outcome: Samanta defeated; Kamaluka installed as Hindu Shahi king
PK-SWABI.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 112, 118. Date approximate (c. 900-904, during Gopalavarman's short reign)

IN-WEST-GODAVARI.detail: after Vijayaditya III's death (892) the Rashtrakutas under Krishna II occupied Vengi, but Chalukya-Bhima I fought many battles to overthrow the foreign domination — at Niravadyapura his son killed a Rashtrakuta dandesa (general) — and, though Bhima was once taken prisoner, Chalukya rule was restored.
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.belligerents: Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi vs Rashtrakuta Empire
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.outcome: Chalukya independence restored under Bhima I, who thereafter ruled Vengi (at times as a nominal feudatory)
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), pp. 12, 136. Date approximate (c. 892-895)

IN-WEST-GODAVARI.text: Chola restoration of Saktivarman in Vengi
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.detail: Rajaraja I intervened in the Eastern Chalukya succession, ending the twenty-seven-year interregnum (973-999) by placing Saktivarman I on the Vengi throne, partly to forestall Satyasraya's scheme of uniting the two Chalukya houses against the Cholas. Vengi became a Chola protectorate and the cockpit of the century's wars.
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.belligerents: Cholas and Eastern Chalukya loyalists vs rivals backed by the Western Chalukyas
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 203, 234-235; accession dated 999

IN-WEST-GODAVARI.detail: in the early part of his reign the Kalachuri Yasahkarna of Tripuri, son of Karna, campaigned against Champaranya in north Bihar and then plundered the Andhra country of the Eastern Chalukya Vijayaditya VII. Coming on top of Kulottunga I's demand for the throne of Andhra, the raid destroyed Vijayaditya's remaining strength; he surrendered Vengi and took refuge with the Ganga Rajaraja I of Kalinganagara. The Chola sources add that the raid was 'without any appreciable results' for the Kalachuris themselves.
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.belligerents: Kalachuris of Tripuri vs the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.outcome: Kalachuri plundering raid; Vengi fatally weakened and lost to the Cholas three years later
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.source: HCIP V, printed p. 204: "The situation became worse for Vijayaditya when, shortly before A.D. 1073, the kingdom of Vehgi was plundered by the Kalachuri Yasahkarna of Tripurl." (Note: 1073 is a terminus ante quem. Coordinates for Vengi/Pedavegi. Corroborated at printed p. 243.)

IN-WEST-GODAVARI.detail: some time between 1091 and 1093 the Chalukya emperor and his general Govindarasa burnt Vengi and defeated the Velananti chief Gonka I, and Chalukya records claim that the Andhra country was wrested from Vira-Choda, son of Kulottunga I. The raid did not change who governed the province. Kulottunga's sons held the Vengi viceroyalty without a break — Vira-Choda to 1092, then his brother Vikrama Chola from 1092 to 1118 — which is why the map does not move here. Vikramaditya VI's object of separating the Eastern Chalukya and Chola crowns was achieved only at the end of his reign, when Vengi passed to him in 1118.
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.belligerents: Western Chalukyas of Kalyana vs the Cholas and the Velanandu chiefs
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.outcome: Chalukya victory in the field; Vengi burnt, but the Chola viceroyalty of the province continued unbroken
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.source: HCIP V, printed p. 174: "Some time between A.D. 1091 and 1093 he, along with his general Govindarasa, burnt Vengi, defeated the Velananti Gonka I, and wrested Andhra from Vira-Choda, son of Kulottunga Chola I. In the latter part of A.D. 1099 Kulottunga reconquered Vengi from the Chalukyas." — DISAGREEMENT ON THE RECORD: this paragraph of the Later Chalukyas chapter stands alone. Sastri, History of South India, block 167, gives an unbroken Chola viceroyalty — "Rajaraja Mummudi Chola (1076-8), Vira Choda (1078-84), Rajaraja Chodaganga (1084-9), Vira Choda again (1089-92), and lastly, Vikrama Chola (1092-1118)" — and block 168 holds that "up to 1115 the extent of the Chola empire remained undiminished under Kulottunga… extending at least up to the Godavari on the east coast." HCIP V's own Chola chapter, p. 244, places the separation of the two crowns in the last decade of Vikramaditya's reign, and its Eastern Deccan chapter, p. 217, gives Vira-Choda's viceroyalties as 1078-84 and 1088-92 with no interruption after; the volume's chronology table lists the 1099 reconquest but no 1091-93 conquest to reconquer from. The atlas follows the majority and treats 1091-93 as a raid — raids never repaint — so the territory changes hands in 1118, where the map already moves.

IN-WEST-GODAVARI.detail: In late 1099 Kulottunga Chola I wrested the Vengi country back from the Western Chalukyas, who had burnt Vengi and expelled his son Vira-Choda between 1091 and 1093, and held the Andhra province until 1117.
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.belligerents: Chola empire vs Western Chalukyas of Kalyani
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.outcome: Chola victory; Vengi held by the Cholas until 1117

IN-WEST-GODAVARI.detail: When Vikrama Chola left the Andhra viceroyalty for the Chola capital to secure his succession, the aged Vikramaditya VI annexed the Vengi country, at last severing the Eastern Chalukya and Chola realms — his greatest victory over Kulottunga I.
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.belligerents: Western Chalukyas of Kalyani vs Chola empire
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.outcome: Chalukya occupation of Vengi, held until Vikramaditya's death in 1126

IN-WEST-GODAVARI.detail: The skirmish of Narsapur Road took place on 14 December 1643 at the road off Narsapur in Golconda between two Danish ships and one Bengali ship.
IN-WEST-GODAVARI.belligerents: Danish India vs Mughal Empire Bengal Subah

PK-ABBOTTABAD.detail: returning from a punitive expedition through Uttarapatha, the Kashmir king was passing through Urasa (modern Hazara) when the inhabitants resisted the quartering of his army; in the affray an arrow shot from a hilltop pierced his neck and he died shortly after, his death concealed until the army reached the Kashmir border.
PK-ABBOTTABAD.belligerents: Utpala dynasty of Kashmir vs Urasa (Hazara hill kingdom)
PK-ABBOTTABAD.outcome: Sankaravarman mortally wounded (A.D. 902); Kashmir's expansion into the Punjab collapsed
PK-ABBOTTABAD.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 118

IN-VELLORE.detail: on the death of Aditya I, Krishna II invaded the Chola kingdom to secure the throne for his grandson Kannara, but was decisively defeated by Parantaka I at Vallala (modern Tiruvallam in North Arcot District).
IN-VELLORE.outcome: Decisive Chola victory; the Rashtrakuta bid to control the Chola succession failed
IN-VELLORE.source: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 12. Date approximate (between Parantaka's accession in 907 and Krishna II's death in 914)

IN-VELLORE.detail: The Siege of Vellore was a major Siege battle in which the Vijayanagara forces tried to bring Lingama Nayaka under control after he rebelled.
IN-VELLORE.belligerents: Vijayanagar Empire Nayaks of Kalahasti, Venkatagiri estate vs Nayaks of Vellore

IN-VELLORE.detail: The Battle of Vellore (1646) was a military conflict fought on 4 April 1646 between the armies of the Vijayanagara Empire and the Bijapur Sultanate near Vellore.
IN-VELLORE.belligerents: Vijayanagar Empire Kalahasti Nayaks vs Bijapur Sultanate

IN-VELLORE.detail: The siege of Vellore was an intermittent series of sieges and blockades conducted during the Second Anglo-Mysore War by forces of the Kingdom of Mysore.
IN-VELLORE.belligerents: British East India Company vs Kingdom of Mysore

IN-VELLORE.detail: sepoys of the Madras Army, provoked by orders against caste marks and beards and a new leather-cockaded turban, rise at Vellore, where Tipu's family lived, and kill many of the European garrison before the rising is crushed.
IN-VELLORE.belligerents: Madras sepoys at Vellore vs East India Company
IN-VELLORE.outcome: East India Company victory; the mutiny put down the same day (suppression: web-only; library silent)
IN-VELLORE.source: HCIP IX p. 428: 'the mutiny at Vellore in 1806. It was caused by what the sepoys regarded as an affront to their religion ... forbidding the men to wear the marks of caste upon their fore-heads, ordering them to shave off their beards'. HCIP IX p. 2: Bentinck 'recalled in 1807' over it.

IN-RANIPET.detail: The Battle of Takkolam (948–949) was a military engagement involving a contingent of troops led by Rajaditya, crown prince and eldest son of the Chola king Parantaka I (907–955).
IN-RANIPET.belligerents: Chola Empire, Cheras vs Rashtrakuta Empire, Western Ganga Dynasty
IN-RANIPET.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07) Date: The Age of Imperial Kanauj (HCIP IV), p. 155: "A decisive engagement took place at Takkolam in A.D. 949".

IN-RANIPET.detail: The siege of Arcot took place at Arcot, India, and involved forces of the British East India Company led by Robert Clive allied with Muhammad Ali Khan Wallajah.
IN-RANIPET.belligerents: East India Company, Carnatic (Arcot Nawab) vs French India, Chanda Sahib
IN-RANIPET.outcome: East India Company victory; Raza Sahib raises the 50-day siege on 24 November 1751
IN-RANIPET.source: HCIP VIII p. 324: 'The subsequent siege of Arcot by Raza Sahib, assisted by French troops lasted 50 days ... Murar Rao definitely went over to the side of the English. On the 24th of November the enemy raised the siege and retreated'.

IN-RANIPET.detail: Clive, back from Arcot, beats the French and Raza Sahib's force that had been ravaging the country round Madras.
IN-RANIPET.belligerents: East India Company, Carnatic (Arcot Nawab) vs French India, Chanda Sahib
IN-RANIPET.source: HCIP VIII p. 324: 'In February 1752, Clive won the victory of Kaveripauk.'

IN-RANIPET.detail: after destroying Baillie, Haidar renews the siege of the Nawab's capital on 19 September; Arcot capitulates in November and the Payanghat is overrun.
IN-RANIPET.belligerents: Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu) vs East India Company, Carnatic (Arcot Nawab)
IN-RANIPET.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III p. 300-301 chapter synopsis (block 278): 'Haidar's movements ; renews the siege of Arcot, September 19, 1780; capitulation of Arcot, November 28, 1780 ; reduction of the Karnatic-Payanghat' (the vol. synopsis at block 9 reads 'November 23').

IN-RANIPET.detail: Coote attacks Haidar's army posted in the Sholinghur pass on the Vellore road; after a heavy cannonade Haidar's army flees towards Kaveripak, and Vellore is relieved.
IN-RANIPET.belligerents: East India Company vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu)
IN-RANIPET.outcome: East India Company victory; 'Haidar's forces precipitately fled from the field'
IN-RANIPET.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III p. ~362 (block 331): 'by evening victory again declared for the English. Haidar's forces precipitately fled from the field of action towards Kaveripak' (Rao: 27 September 1781; HCIP VIII p. 459: 'Solingar (27 October)').

IN-RANIPET.detail: Coote fights Haidar on the field of Baillie's disaster and forces him to retire.
IN-RANIPET.belligerents: East India Company vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu)
IN-RANIPET.outcome: East India Company victory; Haidar's forces retreat from the field
IN-RANIPET.source: Hayavadana Rao III index p. 1306 (block 1142): 'takes part in the battles of Pallilore (Aug. 27) and Sholinghur (Sept. 27) forcing Haidar's forces to retreat from the field, 360-363'. HCIP VIII p. 459: 'Coote defeated Haidar on two other occasions in the second battle of Pollilore (27 September)'. Dates differ: Rao 27 Aug, HCIP 27 Sept 1781.

IN-CHHATARPUR.detail: Yashovarman’s Vaikuntha Vishnu temple, dedicated in 954, the first of the great Chandela temples; the Kandariya Mahadeva followed under Vidyadhara.
IN-CHHATARPUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-GADAG.detail: the newly enthroned Chalukya faced the Ganga usurper Panchaladeva, whose kingdom reached the Krishna; after the Chalukya rear fled, the day was saved by the feudatory Bhutigadeva, who defeated and killed Panchaladeva some time before 977. The victory secured Taila's supremacy up to northern Mysore.
IN-GADAG.belligerents: Western Chalukyas of Kalyana vs Gangas under Panchaladeva
IN-GADAG.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 161-162; date bracketed as before AD 977. Battle site not recorded; placed in the Gadag-Mulgund country

IN-GADAG.detail: The siege of Nargund took place in 1778 when troops from the Sultanate of Mysore attempted to capture the town of Nargund, a possession of the Maratha Confederacy.

IN-GADAG.belligerents: Maratha Empire, Hyderabad vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu)
IN-GADAG.outcome: Inconclusive — Tipu won the field (Adoni, Savanur, Bahadur Benda) but by the Gajendragad peace (March 1787) he paid arrears of tribute, ceded Badami and restored Adoni, Kittur and Nargund; Malet thought the treaty 'highly advantageous to Tipu'
IN-GADAG.source: HCIP VIII p. 461-462: 'The generally accepted opinion was that Tipu concluded a successful campaign by an inglorious peace. But Malet ... thought that the treaty was highly advantageous to Tipu.'

IN-GADAG.detail: The second siege of Nargund was a siege conducted by Tipu Sultan, the Sultan of Mysore, in Nargund in 1785.
IN-GADAG.belligerents: Maratha Confederacy vs Kingdom of Mysore

IN-DAKSHIN-DINAJPUR.detail: ascending a throne reduced to south Bihar in c. 988, the Pala king wrested back his 'paternal kingdom usurped by others' — north Bengal from the Kamboja chiefs and, within his first three regnal years, east Bengal as well, as attested by the Bangarh grant of his ninth year.
IN-DAKSHIN-DINAJPUR.belligerents: Palas vs Kamboja rulers of Gauda (and Chandras of East Bengal)
IN-DAKSHIN-DINAJPUR.outcome: Pala victory; North and East Bengal recovered
IN-DAKSHIN-DINAJPUR.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 24; date c. 988 onwards

IN-DAKSHIN-DINAJPUR.text: Bakhtiyar Khalji dies — Murdered at Devkot by his own officer Ali Mardan, after the disaster of the Tibet expedition.
IN-DAKSHIN-DINAJPUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-KHORDHA.detail: The "gem of Odishan architecture", with its torana; the Lingaraja was raised beside it a century later.
IN-KHORDHA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-KHORDHA.detail: The Somavamshi temple to Tribhuvanesvara, its deul fifty-five metres high; the peak of the Kalinga style.
IN-KHORDHA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

PK-PESHAWAR.detail: Mahmud of Ghazni with 15,000 picked cavalry routed the Shahi Jayapala's 12,000 horse, 30,000 foot and 300 elephants outside Peshawar before noon on 27-28 November 1001; Jayapala was captured with his sons and later ransomed. Thrice defeated by the Turks, the old king burnt himself on a pyre, and Anandapala succeeded him.
PK-PESHAWAR.outcome: Ghaznavid victory; Jayapala captured, later self-immolated
PK-PESHAWAR.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 6-7

PK-PESHAWAR.text: Jayapala dies — The Hindu Shahi, defeated by Mahmud at Peshawar, gave up the throne and burned himself on a pyre.
PK-PESHAWAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

PK-PESHAWAR.detail: Turning to the northern route after his disaster at Kasahrada, and invited by Chakradeo of Jammu against the Ghaznavid Khusrav Malik, Muizz-ud-din Muhammad invaded the Punjab and took Peshawar in 1178, opening his decade-long reduction of the last Ghaznavid kingdom.
PK-PESHAWAR.belligerents: Ghurids (allied with Chakradeo of Jammu) vs Ghaznavids of Lahore
PK-PESHAWAR.outcome: Peshawar annexed; the Ghurid vice closed on Lahore (Sialkot 1185, Lahore 1186)

PK-PESHAWAR.detail: The Battle of Khyber Pass was an engagement fought on 26 November 1738 between the Afsharid Iran of Nader Shah and the Mughal vassal state of Peshawar.

PK-PESHAWAR.outcome: Maratha victory — the high-water mark, held barely a year

PK-PESHAWAR.detail: The Battle of Balakot was the final battle fought between the Sikh forces under prince Sher Singh and mujahideen under Syed Ahmad Barelvi at Balakot on 6 May 1831.
The city of Peshawar was formally annexed on 6 May 1834 by the Sikh Empire.
PK-PESHAWAR.outcome: Sikh Empire victory; Sultan Muhammad Khan fled to Kabul and Peshawar came under direct Sikh rule, Hari Singh Nalwa governor (May 1834)
PK-PESHAWAR.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 174: 'Prince Nau Nihal Singh, Ventura and Court were sent from Lahore to Peshawar ... Sultan Muhammad Khan fled away to Kabul ... The Maharaja established his own administration at Peshawar in May, 1834, and appointed Hari Singh Nalwa its governor.'

PK-PESHAWAR.detail: The Standoff at the Khyber Pass (1834–1835) was a short conflict from May 1834 to May 1835 between the Sikh forces led by Maharaja Ranjit Singh and the Afghan forces.
PK-PESHAWAR.belligerents: Sikh Empire, Peshawar Sardars vs Emirate of Kabul

PK-PESHAWAR.detail: The Battle of Jamrud was fought between the forces of the Emirate of Afghanistan under Wazir Akbar Khan, and the Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh on 30 April 1837.
PK-PESHAWAR.belligerents: Emirate of Kabul (Barakzai) vs Sikh Empire
PK-PESHAWAR.outcome: Inconclusive — books disagree: the Afghans won the first day's fighting and killed Hari Singh Nalwa, but withdrew to Jalalabad without taking Jamrud or Peshawar
PK-PESHAWAR.source: Books disagree. HCIP IX p. 165: 'He sent an army under his two sons who defeated the Sikh army at Jamrud (A.D. 1837), but did not follow up their victory.' HCIP IX p. 245: 'The Afghans, after watching for five or six days, finally retired, without achieving any conspicuous success.' Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 181: 'the Afghans hurriedly retired to Jalalabad ... The two sides lost heavily, about 7,000 men'; p. 308: 'Hari Singh Nalwa was killed, but neither Jamrud fort nor Peshawar was taken.'

PK-PESHAWAR.text: Hari Singh Nalwa dies — Ranjit Singh's great frontier general, governor of Hazara and Peshawar, mortally wounded at Jamrud.
PK-PESHAWAR.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 180: 'Hari Singh Nalwa rallied his men and rode to the front. He was struck by two balls, one in the stomach and the other in the side ... Hari Singh then expired.' p. 153: 'Hari Singh Nalwa who was killed on 30 April, 1837, in the battle of Jamrud.'

PK-PESHAWAR.detail: The Army Public School attack — Tehrik-i-Taliban gunmen kill 149 people at a school in Peshawar, 132 of them children; the state answers with the National Action Plan and the Zarb-e-Azb offensive
PK-PESHAWAR.outcome: The deadliest terrorist attack in Pakistan's history
PK-PESHAWAR.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

PK-MULTAN.text: Capture of Bhatiya and siege of Multan
PK-MULTAN.detail: Mahmud's capture of Bhatiya and Multan — after a three-day battle Mahmud stormed the walled city of Bhatiya, whose ruler Baji Ray fled and stabbed himself (1004); in 1005-06 he crossed the Punjab against the Ismaili ruler Abu-l Fath Daud and reduced Multan, annexing the lower Indus route to Ghazni.
PK-MULTAN.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs Baji Ray of Bhatiya; Ismaili amirate of Multan
PK-MULTAN.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 7-8; chronology p. 868

PK-MULTAN.detail: Muhammad Bahlim, the Ghaznavid governor of the Punjab, fortified Nagaur and declared independence, plundering neighbouring Indian princes; Sultan Bahram Shah marched against the rebel and defeated him at Multan, Bahlim and his sons perishing in the flight.
PK-MULTAN.belligerents: Ghaznavid Sultan Bahram Shah vs the rebel governor Muhammad Bahlim
PK-MULTAN.outcome: Rebellion crushed; the Punjab restored to direct Ghaznavid rule under Salar Husain
PK-MULTAN.source: HCIP V, pp. 95-96; undated in source, conventionally c. 1128 (Bahram r. 1118-1152)

PK-MULTAN.text: Muizz-ud-din Muhammad takes Multan and Uch
PK-MULTAN.detail: Entering India by the Gomal pass, Shihab-ud-din (Muizz-ud-din) Muhammad of Ghur wrested Multan and Uch from their Qaramitah (Ismaili) chiefs in 1175 — the opening move of the Ghurid conquest of Hindustan.
PK-MULTAN.belligerents: Ghurids vs Qaramitah (Ismaili) chiefs of Multan and Uch
PK-MULTAN.outcome: Multan and Uch annexed to the Ghurid dominion; by 1182 the Sumra chief of lower Sindh also submitted

PK-MULTAN.detail: In November 1296, the Delhi Sultanate ruler Alauddin Khalji sent an expedition to conquer Multan.
The siege of Multan took place in 1398, it was led by Pir Muhammad and Timur.
The Battle of Multan, also known as the Battle of Daurana Langana, was fought in September 1749 by Kaura Mal's Mughal forces assisted by Jassa Singh Ahluwalia's Sikhs.
PK-MULTAN.belligerents: Kaura Mal's forces vs Shah Nawaz Khan's forces

PK-MULTAN.detail: The Battle of Shujabad took place in February 1780, during the Afghan–Sikh Wars.

Misr Diwan Chand's army took the city in February 1818 and stormed the fort on 20 June after a long siege; Nawab Muzaffar Khan and two of his sons fell in the breach, and Multan passed to the Sikh Empire.
PK-MULTAN.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Durrani (Afghan) Empire (Nawab Muzaffar Khan of Multan)
PK-MULTAN.outcome: Sikh Empire victory; Multan fort stormed, Muzaffar Khan killed, province annexed
PK-MULTAN.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 111: 'On 20 June, 1818, Sadhu Singh Akali, at the head of his Nihangs, rushed into one breach ... Nawab Muzaffar Khan standing in a breach with sword in hand fought hard along with his four sons in a heroic combat, and fell dead.' p. 110: 'The city of Multan fell in February, 1818.'

PK-MULTAN.detail: Mulraj's revolt ignites the Second Anglo-Sikh War
PK-MULTAN.belligerents: East India Company vs Multan (Diwan Mulraj) and Sikh rebels
PK-MULTAN.outcome: East India Company victory; the city carried by assault on 2 January 1849 and Mulraj surrendered on 22 January
PK-MULTAN.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy pp. 277–278 (murder of Agnew and Anderson at Multan, April 1848) and p. 286: 'the city was carried by assault on January 2, 1849, and Mulraj unconditionally surrendered on January 22.'

IN-BIJAPUR-KAR.detail: Battle of Donur was fought between the Cholas, during the reign of Raja Raja Chola I, and the Western Chalukya king Satyashraya at the town of Donur in Bijapur district.

IN-BIJAPUR-KAR.text: Basava is born — At Basavana Bagewadi
IN-BIJAPUR-KAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BIJAPUR-KAR.text: Yusuf Adil Shah dies — Founder of the Adil Shahi sultanate of Bijapur.
IN-BIJAPUR-KAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BIJAPUR-KAR.detail: Vijaynagar Invasion of Bijapur (1552) was a campaign initiated by Vijayanagar and the Ahmednagar Sultanate against the Bijapur Sultanate.
IN-BIJAPUR-KAR.belligerents: Vijayanagar Empire, Ahmednagar Sultanate vs Bijapur Sultanate

IN-BIJAPUR-KAR.text: Aliya Rama Raya dies — Captured and beheaded at Talikota
IN-BIJAPUR-KAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BIJAPUR-KAR.detail: the allied Deccan sultanates crush Vijayanagara, whose capital is sacked
Muhammad Adil Shah’s tomb, its dome the second largest unsupported in the world, with the whispering gallery.
IN-BIJAPUR-KAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BIJAPUR-KAR.detail: The Battle of Umrani was a 1673 Indian conflict between the Bijapur Sultanate and the Marathas west of Bijapur.

IN-BIJAPUR-KAR.outcome: Mughal victory — the city fell in 1686; the Adil Shahi ends
IN-BIJAPUR-KAR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-KANGRA.detail: pursuing the Hindu army broken on the plain of Chach, Mahmud besieged the hill fortress-temple of Bhimnagar (Kot Kangra), whose accumulated treasure of generations — gold, silver, pearls and coined wealth — surpassed 'the treasury of any king in India'; it surrendered and was stripped.
IN-KANGRA.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs Hindu Shahis and the Kangra temple-fort garrison
IN-KANGRA.outcome: Ghaznavid victory; fort and treasure taken
IN-KANGRA.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 9

IN-KANGRA.text: Gangeyadeva's expedition to the Kira country
IN-KANGRA.detail: in the same year that the Ghaznavid governor Ahmad Niyaltigin sacked his city of Banaras, the Kalachuri Gangeyadeva Vikramaditya of Tripuri struck back at the far end of the Ghaznavid frontier, leading a successful expedition into the Kira country — the Kangra valley — which was then under Muslim control. It is the first recorded counter-raid by an Indian power into Ghaznavid-held territory, and his son Karna repeated it a decade later.
IN-KANGRA.belligerents: Kalachuris of Tripuri vs the Ghaznavid occupation of the Kangra hills
IN-KANGRA.outcome: Kalachuri victory; the Kira country raided
IN-KANGRA.source: HCIP V, printed p. 61: "In A.D. 1034 Gangeyadeva had to bear the brunt of an attack of the Muslims. Ahmad Niyaltigin, governor of the Punjab under the Ghaznavids, plundered Banaras, and carried away immense riches. Gangeyadeva launched a successful expedition against the Kira country, modern Kangra valley in the Punjab, which was under the sway of the Muslims." (Note: coordinates are for Kangra/Nagarkot, the centre of the Kira country.)

IN-KANGRA.detail: the Ghaznavid restoration in the Punjab came under Sultan 'Abd-ur-Rashid, who appointed Nushtigin Hajib governor of the country east of the Indus. Nushtigin recaptured Nagarkot, which the Indian confederacy had held since 1043, closing the nine-year Hindu reoccupation of the Kangra hills. Nushtigin then went on to break the usurper Tughril at Ghazni and set Farrukhzad on the throne.
IN-KANGRA.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs the Indian holders of Nagarkot
IN-KANGRA.outcome: Ghaznavid victory; Nagarkot retaken after nine years
IN-KANGRA.source: HCIP V, printed p. 94: "NushtL gin captured Nagarkot, which had been in the possession of the Hindus since A.D. 1043." (Note: HCIP places 'Abd-ur-Rashid's accession in 1051 and his murder in 1052-53, so the recapture falls in 1051-52; coordinates for Kangra.)

IN-KANGRA.detail: The siege of Kangra Fort was a military expedition conducted by the forces of Delhi Sultanate led by Firuz Shah Tughlaq against the Raja Rup Chand, the ruler of Nagarkot.

IN-KANGRA.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-KANGRA.detail: called in by Raja Sansar Chand, Ranjit Singh surrounded Amar Singh Thapa's Gorkha army that had besieged Kangra fort for three years and cut off its supplies; the Gorkhas withdrew and the Sikhs took the fort on 24 August 1809, ending Nepali expansion west of the Sutlej.
IN-KANGRA.outcome: Sikh Empire victory; Gorkhas raise the siege and retire, Kangra fort passes to Ranjit Singh
IN-KANGRA.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V pp. 68–69: 'Ranjit Singh surrounded the Gorkha army which had besieged the fort. He cut off their supplies completely ... Amar Singh raised the siege ... The Maharaja expelled Sansar Chand's men, and took possession of the fort on 24 August, 1809.'

LK-POLONNARUWA.text: Rajendra completes the conquest of Lanka
LK-POLONNARUWA.detail: the Chola fleet captured Mahinda V, last king of Anuradhapura, who died in exile in India; the whole island passed under Chola administration.
LK-POLONNARUWA.belligerents: Chola Empire (Rajendra I) vs Anuradhapura Kingdom (Mahinda V)
LK-POLONNARUWA.outcome: Chola victory; Mahinda V captured, Anuradhapura kingdom extinguished
LK-POLONNARUWA.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

LK-POLONNARUWA.detail: after fifteen years of campaigning from Ruhuna, Vijayabahu took Polonnaruwa and ended seventy-five years of Chola rule in Lanka.
LK-POLONNARUWA.belligerents: Kingdom of Polonnaruwa (Vijayabahu I) vs Chola Empire
LK-POLONNARUWA.outcome: Sinhalese victory; the island reunified under Polonnaruwa
LK-POLONNARUWA.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

LK-POLONNARUWA.text: Vijayabahu I dies — Drove the Cholas from Ceylon and made Polonnaruwa his capital.
LK-POLONNARUWA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)
Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

LK-POLONNARUWA.text: Five days of murder at Polonnaruva
LK-POLONNARUWA.detail: Mahendra VI of the Kalinga clan killed King Vijayabahu II and seized the Ceylonese throne. Five days later Kirtinihsanka, better known as Nihsankamalla, himself Kalinga-born and Vijayabahu's Uparaja, killed Mahendra and took the crown. He ruled nine years, built temples and tanks, set up milestones along the highroads, and claimed victories over the Cholas and Pandyas.
LK-POLONNARUWA.belligerents: Rival Kalinga-descended claimants to the throne of Ceylon
LK-POLONNARUWA.outcome: Nihsankamalla seized the throne after killing the usurper Mahendra VI

LK-POLONNARUWA.detail: an invasion from the Kalinga coast with a largely south Indian mercenary army deposed and blinded the last king of Polonnaruwa. Magha held the north until about 1236, and the Sinhalese political centre moved permanently to the south-west - the end of the great irrigation civilisation of the dry zone.
LK-POLONNARUWA.belligerents: Magha of Kalinga vs the kingdom of Polonnaruwa
LK-POLONNARUWA.outcome: Polonnaruwa sacked; the dry-zone kingdom never recovered
LK-POLONNARUWA.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

IN-RAICHUR.detail: Rajendra I crushed the Chalukya Jayasimha II, 'who turned his back at Musangi and hid himself,' claiming the seven-and-a-half-lakh country of Irattapadi; yet Jayasimha soon recovered the Raichur Doab and re-established his line on the Tungabhadra, so the Chola conquest proved rhetorical.
IN-RAICHUR.outcome: Chola tactical victory; frontier restored to the Tungabhadra soon after
IN-RAICHUR.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 237-238

IN-RAICHUR.detail: massacre in the Krishna–Tungabhadra doab; Mudgal changes hands
IN-RAICHUR.outcome: Inconclusive — the doab stayed contested for two centuries
IN-RAICHUR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-RAICHUR.detail: The War of the Goldsmith's Daughter or the Bahmani–Vijayanagar War of 1406 was a significant conflict between the Bahmani Sultanate and the Vijayanagar Empire.
IN-RAICHUR.belligerents: Bahmani Sultanate, Reddi Kingdom, Velama chiefs vs Vijayanagar empire

IN-RAICHUR.detail: Deva Raya II holds the line at Mudgal
IN-RAICHUR.outcome: Inconclusive — status quo restored by treaty
IN-RAICHUR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-RAICHUR.detail: The Bahmani–Vijayanagar War of 1443 marked the seventh war between the Bahmani Sultanate and the Vijayanagara empire in peninsular India.
Krishnadevaraya defeats Bijapur at the height of Vijayanagara power
IN-RAICHUR.belligerents: Vijayanagara Empire vs Sultanate of Bijapur

IN-HARDOI.detail: after the Rahib, the Sultan marched on Bari, thirty miles east of Kanauj, where the Pratiharas had moved their capital when their old city was sacked. Trilochanapala, son of Rajyapala, fled before he arrived; the Muslims entered unopposed and levelled the town.
IN-HARDOI.outcome: Bari razed; the Pratiharas driven to the Prayaga country
IN-HARDOI.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 17: "Mahmud advanced towards Bari, where the Pratiharas had shifted their capital after the sack of Kanauj... The Muslims entered into the city without any opposition, and at the Sultan's command razed it to the ground."

IN-PUNCH.detail: after razing Bari and breaking Trilochanapala Shahi, Mahmud of Ghazni turned on Kashmir a second time and led an army against Lohkot, the hill fortress guarding the Pir Panjal approach to the valley, which had already defied him once; he besieged it fruitlessly for a month and then raised the siege and withdrew, leaving the Lohara kingdom of Kashmir the one north-western state Mahmud never subdued.
IN-PUNCH.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs the Loharas of Kashmir
IN-PUNCH.outcome: Ghaznavid failure; the siege raised after a month
IN-PUNCH.source: HCIP V, printed p. 18: "Shortly afterwards, in A.D. 1021, the Sultan led an army against Lohkot, in Kashmir, which he had failed to capture on a previous occasion. However, he did not fare better this time. After making a fruitless attempt for a month to take possession of it, he raised the siege." (Note: Lohkot/Loharkot is placed in the Pir Panjal above the Poonch valley; the coordinates are approximate.)

IN-PUNCH.detail: Driven from Srinagar in 1120 by Harsha's grandson Bhikshachara and the Damaras, King Sussala inflicted a crushing defeat on the pretender's army as it advanced on the Lohara fortress and swiftly recovered the throne of Kashmir.
IN-PUNCH.belligerents: Sussala of the second Lohara dynasty vs Bhikshachara and the Damara barons
IN-PUNCH.outcome: Bhikshachara's army destroyed; Sussala restored in Kashmir

IN-PUNCH.detail: Sussala's half-brother Lothana rose in the mountain principality of Lohara and destroyed the army Jayasimha sent against him — one of the worst reverses of the reign. Lothana's triumph was brief: later the same year his own supporters deposed him, and Jayasimha's half-brother Mallarjuna took the fort instead, leaving Kashmir's western gateway in hostile hands.
IN-PUNCH.belligerents: Jayasimha of Kashmir vs Lothana of Lohara
IN-PUNCH.outcome: Royal army destroyed; Lothana then deposed by his own partisans

IN-PUNCH.detail: a year after his army was wrecked in the same mountains, the Kashmiri king took the fortress of Lohara from his half-brother Mallarjuna. Holding Lohara mattered enormously: it commanded the Pir Panjal route into the valley and had been the launching point of every serious rebellion since 1101. Jayasimha followed up by deposing Vikramaditya of Vallapura and installing his own nominee Gulhana.
IN-PUNCH.outcome: Jayasimha took Lohara and reinstalled his authority in the hill principalities

IN-BANDA.detail: in 1021-22 Mahmud invested Gwalior, extracting tribute from the Kachchhapaghata Kirttiraja, then besieged Vidyadhara in Kalanjara; the long siege ended in a negotiated peace, 300 elephants and an exchange of compliments — the Turk's deepest thrust into Bundelkhand was halted at the Chandella walls.
IN-BANDA.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 18; chronology p. 869

IN-BANDA.text: Mahmud of Lahore's raid on Kannauj and Kalanjara
IN-BANDA.detail: after the deaths of Bhoja and Karna removed the two princes who had frightened the Ghaznavids out of Hindustan for half a century, Ibrahim's son Mahmud, governor of the Punjab, drove into the Doab some time between 1086 and 1090. He plundered Kannauj and Kalanjara and invaded Ujjain, took Agra by defeating its chief Jaipal, and found an ally in Kannauj named Chand Rai — HCIP identifies him with Chandradeva, the founder of Gahadavala power, who seized the throne of Kannauj from the Rashtrakuta Gopala in the disorder that followed Mahmud's departure. At Kalanjara the Chandella Kirttivarman fought Mahmud off successfully.
IN-BANDA.belligerents: Ghaznavids of Lahore vs the Rashtrakutas of Kannauj, the Chandellas and the Paramaras
IN-BANDA.outcome: Kannauj and Kalanjara plundered; Kirttivarman repulsed the attack on Kalanjara and Lakshmadeva the attack on Ujjain
IN-BANDA.source: HCIP V, printed p. 51: "Some time between A.D. 1086 and 1090 prince Mahmud, the governor of the Punjab, plundered Kanauj and Kalanjara and invaded Ujjain. On that occasion he found an ally in Kanauj named Chand Rai, who may be identified with Chandradeva." (Note: coordinates for Kalanjara; Kannauj 27.06N 79.92E. Kirttivarman's successful defence is at printed p. 58: 'Some time before A.D. 1090 Kirttivarman fought successfully with Mahmud, governor of the Punjab under the Ghaznavids, who invaded Kalanjara.' Mahmud's conquest of Agra and Kannauj is at printed pp. 94-95.)

IN-BANDA.detail: The Siege of Kalinjar was a important military campaign of the Ghurid Empire under the leadership of Qutb al-Din Aibak and Iltutmish against the Chandel Empire of Jejakabhukti.
IN-BANDA.belligerents: Ghurid Empire vs Chandel Empire of Jejakabhukti

IN-BANDA.text: Sher Shah Suri dies — Killed by a magazine explosion at the siege of Kalinjar
IN-BANDA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-GIR-SOMNATH.detail: The Sack of Somnath in 1026 was a military campaign orchestrated by Mahmud of Ghazni, the ruler of the Ghaznavid Empire, against the Chaulukya dynasty of Gujarat.
IN-GIR-SOMNATH.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs Chaulukya dynasty, Abhira dynasty

IN-MAHESANA.detail: Bhima I’s temple to Surya on the Pushpavati, with its stepped kund; Vikram Samvat 1083.
IN-MAHESANA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SUBARNAPUR.text: Chandihara Yayati recovers Kosala and Utkala
IN-SUBARNAPUR.detail: raised to the Somavamsi throne by the ministers after warring chiefs — and probably the Cholas, who had carried off king Indraratha from Yayatinagara — had overrun the realm, Yayati Mahasivagupta III (c. 1025-55) freed both Kosala and Utkala and claimed conquest of Trikalinga, uniting upland and coastal Orissa under one house.
IN-SUBARNAPUR.belligerents: Somavamsis of Kosala-Utkala vs occupying chiefs, Chola garrisons and encroaching Kalachuris
IN-SUBARNAPUR.outcome: Somavamsi victory; Kosala and Utkala reunited
IN-SUBARNAPUR.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 209-210; date c. 1025-30, reign c. 1025-55

IN-VARANASI.detail: the Kalachuri Gangeyadeva 'Vikramaditya' defeated Mahipala I, lord of Anga, and wrested the Banaras region from the Palas some time between 1026 and 1034 — the Muslim chronicler Baihaqi found the city in the possession of 'Gang' in 1034.
IN-VARANASI.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 25-26, 61; date bracketed 1026-1034

IN-VARANASI.detail: the Ghaznavid governor of the Punjab dashed across the Gangetic plain and plundered the markets of Banaras, then held by the Kalachuri Gangeyadeva, who bore the brunt of the attack — the first Muslim raid to reach the holy city.
IN-VARANASI.belligerents: Ghaznavid governorate of the Punjab vs Kalachuris of Tripuri
IN-VARANASI.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 25, 61; chronology p. 870

IN-VARANASI.text: Kabir is born — By tradition at Varanasi, in 1398
IN-VARANASI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-VARANASI.text: Tulsidas dies — At Varanasi, on the Assi ghat
IN-VARANASI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-VARANASI.text: Rani Lakshmibai is born — At Varanasi, as Manikarnika.
IN-VARANASI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SIROHI.detail: Vimala Shah, Bhima I’s minister, raises the first of the marble Jain temples of Mount Abu.
IN-SIROHI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SIROHI.text: Kumarapala deposes the Paramara of Mount Abu
IN-SIROHI.detail: fresh from beating the Chahamana Arnoraja, the Chaulukya king turned on Vikramasimha, the Paramara chief of Chandravati on Mount Abu, who had gone over to his enemies during the war. Kumarapala threw him into prison and installed his nephew Yasodhavala instead. Yasodhavala repaid the favour by killing Ballala of Ujjain in battle for his overlord.
IN-SIROHI.belligerents: Chaulukyas of Gujarat vs the Paramaras of Mount Abu
IN-SIROHI.outcome: Vikramasimha deposed and imprisoned; Yasodhavala installed as a loyal vassal

IN-SIROHI.detail: The Battle of Kasahrada, also known as Battle of Kayadara or Battle of Gadararaghatta, was fought in 1178 at modern Kasahrada in Sirohi district near Mount Abu.
IN-SIROHI.belligerents: Chaulukya dynasty, Feudal states, Paramaras of Chandravati Chauhans of Nadol Chahamanas of Jalor vs Ghurid Empire
IN-SIROHI.outcome: Chaulukyan victory Mularaja II defeated Mohmmad Ghori

IN-SIROHI.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-BAHRAICH.detail: Raja Suhaldev of Shravasti, with a league of chiefs from the tarai, destroys the army of Salar Masud - "Ghazi Miyan", the nephew of Mahmud of Ghazni - and ends the Ghaznavid push into Awadh. Known almost wholly from the Mirat-i-Masudi, a romance of c. 1620; the date (14 June 1034) is the romance’s.
IN-BAHRAICH.belligerents: Suhaldev of Shravasti and allied chiefs vs Salar Masud (Ghazi Miyan), Ghaznavid
IN-BAHRAICH.outcome: Ghaznavid army destroyed; Salar Masud killed and buried at Bahraich, where his dargah stands
IN-BAHRAICH.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-ARIYALUR.detail: Rajendra I builds his capital and its temple to mark the Ganga campaign; the vimana a little lower than his father’s at Thanjavur, on purpose.
IN-ARIYALUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-ARIYALUR.text: Rajendra I dies — Took the Ganga and sent a fleet to Srivijaya
IN-ARIYALUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-ARIYALUR.detail: in 1067-68 the Chalukya prince Vikramaditya (later Vikramaditya VI) carried the war into the Chola heartland, marching on the imperial capital Gangaikonda and plundering it — the boldest Chalukya counterstroke of the fifty years' war.
IN-ARIYALUR.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 171; chronology p. 871 (1067-1068)

IN-ARIYALUR.text: Kulottunga I dies — Fifty years on the Chola throne
IN-ARIYALUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-HISAR.detail: Mas'ud I's storming of Hansi — against the advice of counsellors who begged him to face the Saljuqs instead, Sultan Mas'ud I marched from Ghazni into the Punjab, encamped on the Jhelum near Dinarkotah, and invested the fort of Hansi in the Hissar district. After a strenuous fight Hansi fell; he then took Sonpat, defeating its governor Dipal Har, and extorted presents from the neighbouring Ram Rai before turning back. It was the deepest Ghaznavid penetration of the Haryana plain since Mahmud, and the effort that fatally weakened Mas'ud in the west.
IN-HISAR.belligerents: Ghaznavids vs the chiefs of Hansi and Sonpat
IN-HISAR.outcome: Ghaznavid victory; Hansi and Sonpat taken
IN-HISAR.source: HCIP V, printed p. 93: "Thence he went to Hansi, in the Hissar District, Punjab, and invested the fort. After a strenuous fight Hansi fell into his hands. He then marched to Sonpat and defeated its governor Dipal Har." (Note: coordinates are for Hansi; the campaign ran on to Sonipat, 28.99N 77.02E.)

IN-HISAR.detail: Prithviraja II of Sakambhari posted his maternal uncle, the Guhila chief Kilhana, at Asika (Hansi) to keep the Muslims of the Punjab in check. Kilhana burned the city of Panchapura, identified with Panchapattana on the Sutlej, and carried off its ruler as a prisoner — his adversary apparently being Khusrav Malik, the last Ghaznavid, who was then also fighting the Gahadavalas.
IN-HISAR.belligerents: Chahamanas of Sakambhari vs the Ghaznavids of Lahore
IN-HISAR.outcome: Chahamana victory; Panchapura burnt and its ruler captured

IN-HISAR.detail: The Battle of Hisar Firoza took place in Hisar, in the state of Haryana, India between Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur and Hamid Khan on 26 February 1526.

PK-LAHORE.detail: The Siege of Lahore (1043) was a military engagement during the decline of the Ghaznavid Empire.
PK-LAHORE.belligerents: Ghaznavid Empire vs Indian confederacy Tomaras of Delhi Kalachuris of Tripuri Paramara dynasty
PK-LAHORE.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

PK-LAHORE.text: Muizz-ud-din at the gates of Lahore
PK-LAHORE.detail: raiding India almost every year, the Ghurid sultan reached Lahore in 1181. Khusrav Malik, the last Ghaznavid, bought him off with a treaty and surrendered one of his sons as a hostage. It was the first of three descents on Lahore — 1181, 1184 and 1186 — by which the Ghurids strangled the Ghaznavid kingdom without a pitched battle.
PK-LAHORE.belligerents: Ghurids vs the Ghaznavids of Lahore
PK-LAHORE.outcome: Ghurid diplomatic victory; a Ghaznavid prince surrendered as hostage
PK-LAHORE.source: HCIP V, p. 97

PK-LAHORE.text: Qutb-ud-din Aibak dies — Fell from his horse at polo in Lahore
PK-LAHORE.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

PK-LAHORE.detail: In the winter of 1297, Kadar, a noyan of the Mongol Chagatai Khanate invaded the Delhi Sultanate ruled by Alauddin Khalji.
PK-LAHORE.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

PK-LAHORE.text: Shah Jahan is born — At Lahore, as Prince Khurram.
PK-LAHORE.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

PK-LAHORE.text: Guru Arjan dies — Tortured to death at Lahore on Jahangir’s order
PK-LAHORE.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

PK-LAHORE.text: Nur Jahan dies — At Lahore, eighteen years after Jahangir
PK-LAHORE.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

PK-LAHORE.detail: The Haidari Flag crusade or War of the Haidari Flag was a series of clashes in 1710 between Sikh forces and a coalition raised at Lahore during the Sikh rising in Punjab.
PK-LAHORE.belligerents: Sikhs vs Muslim crusaders of Lahore, Mughal provincial forces of Lahore, Hindu allies
PK-LAHORE.outcome: Sikh victory; crusading forces defeated and dispersed.
PK-LAHORE.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

PK-LAHORE.text: Bahadur Shah I dies — At Lahore on 27 February 1712, the last Mughal emperor who 'held the reins of administration fast in his hands'
PK-LAHORE.source: HCIP VIII p. 15-16: 'About the middle of January 1712 his health began to decline and he died on 27 February, 1712... With the death of Bahadur Shah disappeared even the last semblance of the glory and greatness of the Mughuls.'

PK-LAHORE.text: Zakariya Khan dies — Mughal governor of Lahore for two decades, the persecutor of the Sikhs whose death let them return to Amritsar in numbers.
PK-LAHORE.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs IV p. 73: 'Zakariya Khan died on 1st July, 1745. He was succeeded by weak-[lings]'; p. 27: 'On Zakariya Khan's death the Sikhs began visiting Amritsar in large numbers.'

PK-LAHORE.detail: The Battle of Lahore was fought between Afghan forces of the Durrani Empire under Ahmad Shah Durrani and Mughal forces under Shah Nawaz on 11 January 1748.
PK-LAHORE.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

PK-LAHORE.detail: The Battle of Lahore was battle which took place between the invading Ahmed Shah Abdali and Mir Mannu, the Mughal governor of Punjab in 1752.
PK-LAHORE.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

PK-LAHORE.detail: Ahmad Shah Abdali takes them from the Mughals
PK-LAHORE.outcome: Durrani victory — Punjab and Kashmir ceded
PK-LAHORE.source: Jadunath Sarkar

PK-LAHORE.text: Muin-ul-Mulk (Mir Mannu) dies — Mughal viceroy of the Punjab from 1748 who beat Abdali at Manupur and then held Lahore for him
PK-LAHORE.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs IV p. 17: 'He died on November 3, 1753. Then Panjab plunged into anarchy ... In three years from 1753 to 1756 nine changes took place in the office of the governor.'

PK-LAHORE.detail: The Battle of Qarawal was fought between the Sikhs under the command of Charat Singh against the Afghan forces led by Ahmad Shah Abdali and his Kalat ally Mir Nasir Khan I.
PK-LAHORE.belligerents: Durrani Empire, Khanate of Kalat vs Sukerchakia Misl
PK-LAHORE.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

PK-LAHORE.detail: as soon as Ahmad Shah turned home, the Bhangi chiefs Lahna Singh and Gujar Singh, with Sobha Singh, entered Lahore and divided the city between them; the chiefs then struck the Khalsa coin at Amritsar.
PK-LAHORE.belligerents: Sikh misls (Bhangi) vs Durrani (Afghan) Empire (Kabuli Mal, governor of Lahore)
PK-LAHORE.outcome: Sikh victory; Lahore held by the Sikh chiefs until Ranjit Singh
PK-LAHORE.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs IV p. 225: 'On the occasion of Baisakhi at Amritsar, both Lahna Singh and Gujar Singh planned the occupation of Lahore ... They occupied Lahore jointly.' Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II pp. 494–495 puts it in 1764, right after Abdali left: 'the three Sikh leaders Lehna Singh, Gujar Singh and Sobha Singh attacked Lahor. The masterless city capitulated ... the three chiefs divided the city between them.' Books differ on the year (Gupta 1765, Sarkar 1764).

PK-LAHORE.detail: the Durrani king re-entered the Punjab in the autumn of 1798 and sat at Lahore, but could not bring the Sikhs to battle or to submission, and retired from the Punjab in January 1799 — the last invasion of India from the north-west.
PK-LAHORE.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs III p. 97 ('The Shah enters India'): 'Shah Zaman left Kabul early in September, and reached Peshawar by the end of the month'; p. 117: '27. Shah Zaman retires from the Panjab. From the 1st to the 3rd January, 1799, the Shah held repeated conferences ...'. Preface: 'The last Muslim invasion of India took place in 1799.'

PK-LAHORE.detail: with Rani Sada Kaur's Kanhaiya troops, the Sukerchakia chief entered Lahore through the Lahori Gate on 6 July 1799 and received the fort from Chait Singh on 7 July — the foundation of the Sikh monarchy.
PK-LAHORE.belligerents: Sukerchakia Misl (Ranjit Singh), Kanhaiya Misl vs Sikh misls (Bhangi chiefs of Lahore)
PK-LAHORE.outcome: Sukerchakia victory; Lahore occupied, Chait Singh and Mohar Singh allowed to retire
PK-LAHORE.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 30: 'Occupation of the Fort, 7 July, 1799 ... Chait Singh opened negotiations through Sada Kaur. He was permitted to retire in peace'; pp. 35–36: 'Ranjit Singh's occupation of Lahore formed an important landmark in the history of the Panjab. This event marked the beginning of the downfall of the independent chiefs on the one hand, and the establishment of a monarchy on the other.'

PK-LAHORE.detail: the Company, Ranjit Singh and Shah Shuja agreed to restore Shah Shuja at Kabul, with Ranjit Singh to support him with money and material; the Army of the Indus then marched from Firozpur through Bahawalpur, Sindh and the Bolan — the Indian side of the First Anglo-Afghan War.
PK-LAHORE.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V pp. 304–305: 'In July, 1838, a Tripartite Treaty was made between Shah Shuja-ul-Mulk, Ranjit Singh and the British Government. Shah Shuja was to be placed on the throne at Kabul by the British army. Ranjit Singh was to support Shah Shuja with money and material. The British army marched from Firozpur via Bahawalpur, Shikarpur, Quetta, Kandhar and Ghazni to Kabul.' Also p. 288: 'Ranjit Singh did not like it because it was mainly aimed against him.'

PK-LAHORE.text: Ranjit Singh dies — At Lahore on 27 June 1839, after years of illness following a stroke in 1834
PK-LAHORE.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 534: '27 June, 1839. On Thursday morning, 27 June ... The soul flew out of his body through the eyes at 5 p.m.' HCIP IX p. 249: 'Ranjit Singh died on June 27, 1839, and was succeeded by Kharak Singh, his eldest son.'

PK-LAHORE.text: Kharak Singh dies — Ranjit Singh's eldest son and successor, dead after little more than a year on the throne.
PK-LAHORE.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 250: 'Kharak Singh died on 5 November, 1840.'

PK-LAHORE.text: Nau Nihal Singh dies — Ranjit Singh's grandson and the real power under Kharak Singh, killed by a falling gateway returning from his father's cremation, the same day
PK-LAHORE.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 250: 'Nao Nihal Singh duly performed the funeral rites of his father, but on his way back, while passing under a covered gateway, a portion of the structure fell down and caused his death. Although positive evidence was lacking, it was generally believed that Nao Nihal's death was due to a deliberate conspiracy on the part of the Rajas of Jammu.'

PK-LAHORE.text: Maharaja Sher Singh is murdered — with his son Pratap Singh and the minister Dhian Singh, by the Sandhanwalia sardars
PK-LAHORE.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 262: 'on September 15, 1843, Sher Singh, his son Pratap Singh, as well as the Prime Minister Dhian Singh were all murdered by the Sandhanwalia Sardars, Attar Singh and his nephew Ajit Singh.'

PK-LAHORE.detail: a British Resident at Lahore was given 'full authority to direct and control all matters in every department of the State' during Dalip Singh's minority, with a Council of Regency and a British garrison — the Punjab in all but name a protectorate.
PK-LAHORE.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 275: 'the Treaty of Bhyrowal was signed on the following day, December 16, 1846. This treaty provided that "a British officer ... shall be appointed by the Governor-General to remain at Lahore, which officer shall have full authority to direct and control all matters in every department of the State."'

PK-LAHORE.detail: ending the first Anglo-Sikh war, the Lahore state ceded the Jullundur Doab and everything south of the Sutlej, gave up the hill country between the Beas and the Indus in lieu of indemnity, cut its army and surrendered its war guns; Dalip Singh kept the throne.
PK-LAHORE.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 272: 'On March 9 a treaty was concluded at Lahore ... The British annexed the Jullundur Doab to their dominions ... they took possession of the entire hill country between the Beas and the Indus, to be alienated to Gulab Singh'; p. 49: 'The Sikh Government had to cede the Jalandar doab between the Beas and the Sutlej and all the territories lying to the south of the last-named river.'

PK-LAHORE.detail: after Gujrat and the Sikh army's surrender at Rawalpindi (12 March), Dalhousie's treaty of 29 March 1849 made Dalip Singh resign the sovereignty of the Punjab for a pension; the Sikh Empire ended.
PK-LAHORE.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 287: '... March 29, 1849, and ratified by the Governor-General on April 5. By this treaty Dalip Singh resigned the sovereignty of the Panjab and the British agreed to give him a pension between four and five lakhs of Rupees a year.' p. 286: 'On March 12, 1849, there was a general surrender of the Sikhs ... The Sikh army ceased to exist.'

PK-LAHORE.detail: 3 Jat fights into the outskirts of Lahore in one of the war's fiercest infantry actions
PK-LAHORE.outcome: Indian victory — Dograi captured on the Ichhogil canal
PK-LAHORE.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-YADADRI-BHONGIRI.detail: after pillaging Kalyana and burning its palace, Rajadhiraja I pressed on to Kollippakkai (Kolanupaka in Telangana), where Somesvara I made a stand with his son Vikramaditya, Vijayaditya of Vengi and the commanders Sangamaya, Gandappaya and Gangadhara. The resistance was stiff but the town fell; Gandappaya and Gangadhara died in the encounter and Somesvara fled. Rajadhiraja then overran the Deccan and went home to celebrate with a virabhisheka as Vijayarajendra.
IN-YADADRI-BHONGIRI.belligerents: Cholas vs the Western Chalukyas of Kalyana
IN-YADADRI-BHONGIRI.outcome: Chola victory; Kollippakkai stormed and two Chalukya commanders killed
IN-YADADRI-BHONGIRI.source: HCIP V, printed p. 168: "Somesvara, along with his son Vikramaditya, Vijayaditya of Vengi and his commanders Sangamaya, Gandappaya, Gangadhara and others, gave the Cholas here a stiff resistance, but Kollippakkai could not be defended. Gandappaya and Gangadhara lost their lives in the encounter and Somesvara I fled away like a coward." (Note: coordinates for Kolanupaka, Nalgonda district.)

IN-BIDAR.detail: Rajadhiraja's sack of Kalyana — invading immediately on Somesvara I's accession (1043-44), the Chola forced the Bhima crossing at Koluru, marched on the Chalukya capital Kalyana, pillaged the city and burnt the palace, celebrating a virabhisheka there with the title Vijayarajendra before storming on to Kollippakkai.
IN-BIDAR.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), pp. 167-168; chronology p. 870 (1043-44)

IN-BIDAR.text: Vikramaditya VI usurps the Chalukya throne
IN-BIDAR.detail: With the help of the Hoysala Ereyanga and a Pandya chief, Vikramaditya VI defeated and imprisoned his elder brother Somesvara II and seized the sovereignty of the Deccan, inaugurating the fifty-year golden age of the Kalyani Chalukyas.
IN-BIDAR.belligerents: Vikramaditya VI with Hoysala and Pandya allies vs Chalukya emperor Somesvara II
IN-BIDAR.outcome: Somesvara II captured and deposed; Vikramaditya VI enthroned at Kalyani
IN-BIDAR.source: HCIP V (Struggle for Empire), pp. 173-174; accession 1076 (one inscription suggests 1078)

IN-BIDAR.text: Vikramaditya VI dies — Fifty years at Kalyani
IN-BIDAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BIDAR.detail: Emboldened by Taila III's capture by the Kakatiyas, the Kalachuri feudatory Bijjala, aided by the Silahara Vijayaditya of Karahataka and the general Racha, seized the throne of the Deccan in 1156 and occupied Kalyani before 1160, beginning the twenty-five-year Kalachuri usurpation.
IN-BIDAR.belligerents: Kalachuris of Mangalavada and allied feudatories vs Western Chalukya empire
IN-BIDAR.outcome: Bijjala sovereign of the Deccan (nominal Chalukya sway acknowledged until Taila III's death in 1163)

IN-BIDAR.text: Bijjala dies — The Kalachuri usurper of Kalyani, assassinated
IN-BIDAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BIDAR.text: Somesvara IV restores the Chalukyas at Kalyana
IN-BIDAR.detail: Taila III's son, who had spent the Kalachuri usurpation in obscurity, ascended the throne in 1181-82 and with his general Brahma defeated the Kalachuri rulers Ahavamalla and Singhana within two or three years, recovering Kalyana and the ancestral kingdom. The restoration was real but brief: by 1189 the Yadava Bhillama had taken it all.
IN-BIDAR.belligerents: Chalukyas of Kalyana under Somesvara IV vs the Kalachuris
IN-BIDAR.outcome: Chalukya restoration; Kalyana and most of the Deccan recovered

IN-BIDAR.text: The Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan at Bidar
IN-BIDAR.detail: The Bahmani minister’s three-storey college, tiled in the Persian manner, with a library of three thousand books.
IN-BIDAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BIDAR.text: Mahmud Gawan dies — The Bahmani minister, executed on a forged letter
IN-BIDAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BIDAR.detail: The First Battle of Kalyani was a confrontation between the Vijayanagara Empire led by the regent Rama Raya and the combined forces of the Sultanates of Ahmadnagar and Golconda.
IN-BIDAR.belligerents: Vijayanagar Empire vs Deccan Sultanates Ahmednagar Sultanate Golconda Sultanate Bidar Sultanate

IN-BIDAR.detail: The Battle of Kalyani (1549) was a conflict fought between the allied forces of Vijayanagar and Ahmednagar against the sultanates of Bidar and Bijapur.
IN-BIDAR.belligerents: Vijayanagar Empire, Ahmednagar Sultanate vs Bijapur Sultanate, Bidar Sultanate

IN-BIDAR.detail: The siege of Bidar was a twenty-seven day siege of Bidar Fort mounted by the Mughal Empire against the Bijapur Sultanate.
IN-BIDAR.belligerents: Mughal Empire vs Adil Shahi dynasty

IN-BIDAR.detail: Salabat Jang's Diwan Ramdas, backed by Bussy, invades Maratha territory in 1751 and fails. In November 1752 the Nizam makes peace with Peshwa Balaji Rao at Bhalki and cedes western Berar.
IN-BIDAR.source: HCIP VIII p. 182: 'Ramdas was not successful and concluded a treaty at Shingwa ... Then Salabat Jang made peace with the Peshwa at Bhalki in November, 1752.' Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II p. 325: 'cemented by a formal exchange of visits ... on 24th November 1752. The main part of this treaty of Bhalki was the cession of the whole western half of Berar'.

IN-PALAKKAD.detail: The Battle of Koppam was fought between the Medieval Chola kings Rajadhiraja Chola I and Rajendra Chola II with the Chalukya king Someshvara I in 1054, or in 1052 according to Sen.

IN-MAHOBA.text: Karna's conquest of Bundelkhand and Gopala's counterstroke
IN-MAHOBA.detail: some time after 1051 the Kalachuri Karna defeated the Chandella Kirttivarman and occupied Jejakabhukti outright. The Chandella recovery was the work not of the king but of his vassal Gopala, who defeated Karna, drove him out and restored Kirttivarman to the throne; the minister Vatsaraja recovered the mandala and built the fort of Kirttigiri, identified with Deogarh in Jhansi. It is the clearest case in the century of a feudatory saving a dynasty.
IN-MAHOBA.belligerents: Kalachuris of Tripuri vs the Chandellas of Jejakabhukti
IN-MAHOBA.outcome: Kalachuri occupation, then reversed; Kirttivarman restored by his vassal Gopala
IN-MAHOBA.source: HCIP V, printed p. 63: "Some time after A.D. 1051 Karna captured Bundelkhand by defeating the Chandella Klrttivarman. Subsequently Gopala, a feudatory of the Chandellas, drove him out, and helped Klrttivarman in regaining his throne." (Note: HCIP gives only 'some time after 1051'; the year is approximate. Coordinates for Mahoba. Corroborated at printed p. 58.)

IN-MAHOBA.detail: Prithviraja III defeats Paramardi — In his 1182 digvijaya the Chahamana king invaded Jejakabhukti, captured Sirswa on the Pahuj, defeated the Chandella Paramardi and plundered Mahoba and Kalanjara — the war remembered in the Alha-Udal ballads of the Banafar heroes who died defending Mahoba; the Chandellas recovered their capital by 1183.
IN-MAHOBA.belligerents: Chahamanas of Ajmer vs Chandellas of Jejakabhukti
IN-MAHOBA.outcome: Chandella army routed; Mahoba and Kalanjara plundered, though Chandella rule was restored within a year
IN-MAHOBA.source: HCIP V, pp. 107-108 (Madanpur inscriptions of 1182); chronology p. 874

IN-MAHOBA.detail: The Battle of Jaitpur was fought between the Maratha Empire under Peshwa Baji Rao I, on behalf of Chhatrasal Bundela, the ruler of Bundelkhand; and the Mughal Empire.
IN-MAHOBA.belligerents: Panna, Maratha Empire vs Mughal Empire (Muhammad Khan Bangash)
IN-MAHOBA.outcome: Maratha victory; Baji Rao relieved Chhatrasal and defeated Muhammad Khan Bangash, receiving a jagir in Bundelkhand
IN-MAHOBA.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 817: '1729, March 22 Peshwa Baji Rao, on a request from Chhatrasal Bundela for help, defeats Muhammad Khan Bangash and obtains a Jagir in Bundlekhand (pp. 83, 139, 40).'

IN-KOLHAPUR.detail: on his third invasion of the Chalukya kingdom, accompanied by his brother Rajendra, Rajadhiraja I seized Kollapuram, burnt many Jain temples and defiled and damaged the Jain sanctuaries there. Somesvara I checked the Chola advance and pursued the retreating army south, and the two hosts met for the decisive trial at Koppam, where Rajadhiraja was killed on his elephant.
IN-KOLHAPUR.belligerents: Cholas vs the Western Chalukyas of Kalyana
IN-KOLHAPUR.outcome: Chola sack of Kolhapur; the Chalukyas then counter-attacked, leading to Koppam
IN-KOLHAPUR.source: HCIP V, printed p. 168: "In A.D. 1051-52 Rajadhiraja invaded the kingdom of Somesvara I for the third time, and was accompanied by his brother Rajendra on this occasion. He seized Kollapuram, burnt down many Jain temples, and defiled and damaged the Jain sanctuaries." (Note: HCIP dates the campaign 1051-52. Rajendra II later erected a victory pillar at Kolhapur, printed p. 241.)

IN-KOLHAPUR.detail: The Battle of Pavan Khind was a rearguard last stand that took place in September 1660, at a mountain pass in the vicinity of Vishalgad.
IN-KOLHAPUR.outcome: Bijapur held the field; the Maratha rearguard was destroyed but Shivaji's escape to Vishalgad was secured

IN-KOLHAPUR.detail: The siege of Panhala was led by Siddi Jauhar on behalf of the Bijapur Sultanate, dispatched by Ali Adil Shah II to reclaim the Panhala Fort, was a momentous undertaking.
The siege of Panhala was one of the important conflicts between Mughals and Marathas during the Deccan Wars between 1694 and 1696.
The Siege of Panhala in 1701 was a significant military expedition led by Mughal emperor Aurangzeb during his campaign against the Marathas.
Rajasbai, Rajaram's second wife, imprisons Tarabai and her son Shivaji II and puts her own son Sambhaji II on the throne. The Kolhapur line continues under Sambhaji II.
IN-KOLHAPUR.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II p. 23: 'During the monsoon of 1714 Rajasbai contrived to put Tarabai and her son Shivaji in confinement and place her own son Sambhaji in the Chhatrapati's seat.' HCIP VIII p. 54: 'About this time Tara Bai ... lost her power in Kolhapur and was thrown in confinement.'

IN-KOLHAPUR.detail: Shahu's forces rout the army of Sambhaji II of Kolhapur in March 1730. The Nizam had just been beaten, and Sambhaji had no ally left, so the defeat led to the Treaty of Warna.
IN-KOLHAPUR.outcome: Maratha victory; the Kolhapur army routed
IN-KOLHAPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 231: 'After the defeat of the Nizam, the Kolhapur prince was isolated; his army was routed at Shirole in March, 1730; after negotiations and a personal meeting of the two cousins, the treaty of Warna was concluded in April, 1731.'

IN-DHAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-DHAR.detail: In 1305, the Delhi Sultanate ruler Alauddin Khalji sent an army to capture the Paramara kingdom of Malwa in central India.
IN-DHAR.outcome: Delhi Sultanate victory End of Paramara Dynasty

IN-DHAR.detail: The Tughlaq governor at Dhar declares himself sultan as the Delhi sultanate breaks up after Timur; his son Hoshang moves the capital to Mandu.
IN-DHAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-DHAR.text: Hoshang Shah dies — Builder of Mandu
IN-DHAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-DHAR.text: Mahmud Khalji I dies — The Malwa sultan who fought Mewar, Gujarat and the Bahmanis for thirty-three years.
IN-DHAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-DHAR.detail: Chimaji Appa surprises Girdhar Bahadur, the Mughal governor of Malwa, at Amjhera on 29 November 1728. He destroys the Mughal army, and the Mughal administration of Malwa does not recover.
IN-DHAR.outcome: Maratha victory; Girdhar Bahadur and Daya Bahadur slain, Mughal army annihilated
IN-DHAR.source: HCIP VIII p. 81: 'surprised the Subahdar Girdhar Bahadur in his camp at the border town of Amjhera (November 29, 1728) ... the Mughul force was annihilated, its commanders Girdhar and his cousin Daya Bahadur ... were slain ... It was a complete victory for Chimnaji'; p. 145: 'The Mughul administrative control ... had been rapidly breaking up since the battle of Amjhera (November, 1728)'.

IN-DAVANAGERE.detail: between 1059 and 1061 Somesvara I, his son Vikramaditya and the general Valadeva invaded the Chola country but were met at Mudakaru on the Tunga by Rajendra II and prince Rajamahendra; the Chalukyas were defeated and fled, Valadeva dying in the engagement.
IN-DAVANAGERE.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 169; dated between AD 1059 and 1061

IN-PATAN.text: The Rani ki Vav at Patan
IN-PATAN.detail: Queen Udayamati’s stepwell in memory of Bhima I, seven storeys down, five hundred sculptures.
IN-PATAN.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PATAN.text: Bhima I dies — The Chaulukya who built the sun temple at Modhera and whose queen dug the Rani ki Vav.
IN-PATAN.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PATAN.text: Jayasimha Siddharaja dies — The Chaulukya at Gujarat’s height
IN-PATAN.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PATAN.text: Kumarapala dies — The Chaulukya who took the Jain vows under Hemachandra and banned animal slaughter in Gujarat.
IN-PATAN.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PATAN.text: Muzaffar Shah I makes Gujarat independent
IN-PATAN.detail: Zafar Khan, the Tughlaq governor, takes the title of sultan at Anhilwada; his grandson Ahmad Shah founds Ahmedabad four years later.
IN-PATAN.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BELLARY.detail: challenged by Somesvara I to a second trial at Kudal, the Chola waited a month at Kandai for an enemy who never came, then ravaged Rattapadi and planted a pillar of victory on the Tungabhadra before turning to Vengi — all his wars with Ahavamalla being fought before his fifth regnal year (1067).
IN-BELLARY.outcome: Chola victory by default; victory pillar erected
IN-BELLARY.source: The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 171; chronology p. 871 (1067)

IN-BELLARY.text: Harihara I dies — The first king of Vijayanagara.
IN-BELLARY.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BELLARY.text: Bukka I dies — The second king of Vijayanagara, who took the Madurai sultanate through his son Kumara Kampana.
IN-BELLARY.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BELLARY.detail: The siege of Vijayanagara or Bahmani–Vijayanagara war of 1423 was a military campaign by the Bahmani Sultanate in the Deccan Plateau, led by Ahmad Shah I Wali.
IN-BELLARY.belligerents: Bahmani Sultanate vs Vijayanagara Empire, Velama Chiefs

IN-BELLARY.text: Deva Raya II dies — Vijayanagara’s greatest king before Krishnadevaraya
IN-BELLARY.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BELLARY.detail: Krishnadevaraya raises the east tower of the old temple for his coronation; the Krishna and Vittala temples follow.
IN-BELLARY.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BELLARY.text: Krishnadevaraya dies — The poet-king of Vijayanagara
IN-BELLARY.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BELLARY.detail: the Mysore adventurer raids the Dharwar country and kills Dhondopant Gokhale near Kittur; hunted by Arthur Wellesley and the Patwardhans, he is killed fighting near Bellary on 10 September 1800.
IN-BELLARY.belligerents: East India Company, Maratha Empire vs Dhondia Wagh
IN-BELLARY.outcome: East India Company victory; Dhondia killed with six hundred followers
IN-BELLARY.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 362: 'he was compelled to stand an action at Bhanu near Bellary on 10th September 1800, when he was killed fighting along with six hundred followers.'

IN-KRISHNA.detail: The Battle of Vijayawada was fought in 1068 between the Chola army under Virarajendra Chola and the Western Chalukya army commanded by Vikramaditya VI.
IN-KRISHNA.outcome: Chola victory Coronation of Vijayaditya VII as Eastern Chalukya ruler

IN-KRISHNA.detail: The Bahmani–Vijayanagar War (1398) of 1398 marked the military conflicts between the Bahmani Sultanate under Tajuddin Firuz Shah and the Vijayanagar empire under Harihara II.
IN-KRISHNA.belligerents: Bahmani Sultanate, Velama chiefs of Telangana vs Vijayanagara Empire

IN-KRISHNA.detail: Krishnadevaraya seized the Gajapati fortress of Kondapalli, extending Vijayanagara control across the Krishna–Godavari doab.

IN-KRISHNA.text: The Dutch (1605) and English (1611) establish factories at Masulipatnam, chief port of Golconda

IN-VISAKHAPATNAM.detail: early in the reign of Anantavarman Chodaganga, Kulottunga I sent a great army into Kalinga under his general Karunakara Tondaiman. The Chola army took Visakhapattana and renamed it Kulottungasolapattanam; Anantavarman could not resist, and the whole of Kalinga up to the Orissa border fell to Karunakara — probably shortly after 1083, the date of a Mukhalingam inscription of Anantavarman's reign. It is the campaign that set up the two Kalinga wars of Kulottunga's later years.
IN-VISAKHAPATNAM.belligerents: Cholas vs the Eastern Gangas of Kalinganagara
IN-VISAKHAPATNAM.outcome: Chola victory; northern Kalinga overrun and Visakhapatnam renamed
IN-VISAKHAPATNAM.source: HCIP V, printed p. 205: "The Chola army took possession of Visakhapattana (Visakhapatnam) and changed its name to Kulottuhgasolapattanam. Anantavarman could not resist the advancing Chola army. The whole of Kalinga up to the border of Orissa fell into the hands of Karunakara, probably shortly after A.D. 1083" (Note: HCIP says 'probably shortly after A.D. 1083'; the year is approximate.)

IN-VISAKHAPATNAM.detail: Krishnadevaraya invaded Kalinga and forced the Gajapati emperor Prataparudra Deva to make peace, sealed by marrying his daughter.
IN-VISAKHAPATNAM.outcome: Vijayanagara victory; Prataparudra Deva sued for peace

BD-NAOGAON.detail: The Pala king, backed by fourteen feudatory chiefs led by his uncle Mathanadeva of Anga, crossed the Ganga into Varendri and defeated the Kaivarta king Bhima in a pitched battle, capturing him and later killing him with his kin — the war immortalised in Sandhyakara Nandi's Ramacharita.
BD-NAOGAON.belligerents: Palas and fourteen allied feudatory chiefs vs Kaivarta kingdom of Varendri
BD-NAOGAON.outcome: Decisive Pala victory; Bhima captured and executed, Varendra restored to the Palas, new capital Ramavati founded
BD-NAOGAON.source: HCIP V, pp. 29-30; battle undated in source — placed in the last quarter of the 11th century (Ramapala r. 1077-1120)

NP-RAUTAHAT.detail: the Karnata warrior established the dynasty of Mithila on 10 July 1097, the date preserved on the Simraungadh stone pillar — the polity this atlas carries as Tirhut.
NP-RAUTAHAT.outcome: Karnata (Tirhut) rule over Mithila and the eastern Terai, to 1324
NP-RAUTAHAT.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

IN-SOLAPUR.text: Vikramaditya VI marches on the rebel Silahara Bhoja
IN-SOLAPUR.detail: the Chalukya emperor of Kalyana took the field in person against Bhoja, the Silahara chief of Karahataka (Karad), who had thrown off his allegiance and attacked the neighbouring Sinda chiefs of Erambarage. The emperor encamped on the Bhimarathi river in 1100, but the punishment failed: Bhoja was still ruling as late as 1108, showing how loosely the great Chalukya empire held its border barons.
IN-SOLAPUR.belligerents: Chalukyas of Kalyana vs Silaharas of Karahataka
IN-SOLAPUR.outcome: Indecisive; Bhoja survived and was still ruling in 1108

IN-SOLAPUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SOLAPUR.detail: in October 1750 Peshwa Balaji Rao makes an agreement with the new Chhatrapati, Ramraja, at Sangola that fixes the powers of the ministers and sardars. In November Tarabai confines Ramraja, and from then on power at Satara rests with the Peshwa.
IN-SOLAPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 182: 'the Peshwa arrived at a settlement at Sangola in October, 1750 with Ram Raja ... On 24 November, 1750, Ram Raja was put in confinement by his grand-mother Tara Bai. He thus ceased to be an active or directive factor'; chronology p. 824.

IN-SOLAPUR.detail: General Smith overtakes the fleeing Peshwa's army at Ashti in February 1818. Bapu Gokhale is killed, Bajirao II flees, and the Raja of Satara and the Peshwa's treasure fall to the British.
IN-SOLAPUR.belligerents: East India Company vs Maratha Empire
IN-SOLAPUR.outcome: East India Company victory; Bapu Gokhale killed and the Raja of Satara taken
IN-SOLAPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 507: 'On 20 February, 1818, Bapu Gokhale was overtaken by General Smith at Ashta and killed in a hotly contested battle.' Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 493: 'At Ashta Bapu Gokhale was overtaken by General Smith and was killed in a stiff action on 19th February 1818 ... The Raja of Satara and his party ... fell into the British hands.' The two books differ by a day (19 or 20 February).

IN-HASSAN.detail: Vishnuvardhana’s temple to Vijayanarayana, begun after Talakad; the Hoysala style in soapstone.
IN-HASSAN.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-HASSAN.detail: The twin Siva temple of the Hoysala capital, built by the merchants of Dwarasamudra.
IN-HASSAN.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-HASSAN.text: Vishnuvardhana dies — The Hoysala who built Belur and Halebidu and took the Gangavadi from the Cholas.
IN-HASSAN.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-HASSAN.text: Veera Ballala II dies — The Hoysala who took the imperial title and held the Deccan between the Yadavas and the Cholas.
IN-HASSAN.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-HASSAN.detail: Malik Kafur plunders the Hoysala capital's fabled wealth
IN-HASSAN.outcome: Delhi victory — the southern capital stripped of its fabled wealth
IN-HASSAN.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-HASSAN.detail: Battle of Banavar was a land battle fought between the Maratha Empire and the Kingdom of Mysore in the year 1682.
IN-HASSAN.belligerents: Maratha Empire, Thanjavur Maratha Kingdom, Golconda Sultanate vs Kingdom of Mysore

IN-HAVERI.text: Vishnuvardhana's great raid on the Chalukya heartland
IN-HAVERI.detail: the Hoysala king led his army deep into his overlord's territory during the reign of Somesvara III, taking Banavasi, storming the hill-fort of Uchchangi and laying siege to Panungal (modern Hangal), held by the Kadamba chief Mallikarjuna. The Chalukya army eventually routed the Hoysalas, but the raid showed the empire could no longer control its own vassals.
IN-HAVERI.belligerents: Hoysalas of Dvarasamudra vs the Chalukyas of Kalyana and their Kadamba vassals
