IN-HAVERI.outcome: Hoysalas ultimately routed, but Chalukya prestige badly damaged

IN-HAVERI.detail: Peshwa Madhav Rao draws Haidar out of his chosen position and surrounds him; Haidar retreats to Anavatti, is beaten again in December, and must pay tribute and give up Savanur and Gooty lands.
IN-HAVERI.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu)
IN-HAVERI.outcome: Maratha victory; Haidar 'sustained a severe loss involving the flower of his army', then defeated again at Anavatti and forced to pay 28 lakhs
IN-HAVERI.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore II p. 497: 'Haidar was not only foiled in all his objects, but also sustained a severe loss involving the flower of his army.' HCIP VIII p. 455: 'Haidar Ali was defeated in an engagement at Ratehalli ... on 3 May, 1764 ... a treaty was concluded by which Haidar paid 28 lakhs as tribute'.

IN-HAVERI.detail: The Battle of Savanur occurred between the Kingdom of Mysore and Maratha Empire.
IN-HAVERI.belligerents: Kingdom of Mysore vs Maratha Empire

IN-KUPWARA.detail: the exiled Lothana built a formidable coalition against Jayasimha of Kashmir — the Damara chief Alamkarachakra of Karnaha, the king's own half-brother Vigraharaja, and Bhoja son of Salhana, encouraged by Viddasiha of the Darad country. Jayasimha penned them in the island fort of Sirahsila. Alamkarachakra bought peace by handing over Lothana and Vigraharaja; Bhoja escaped but later surrendered. HCIP V does not give the year precisely, placing it after 1132.
IN-KUPWARA.belligerents: Jayasimha of Kashmir vs Lothana's coalition of Damaras, princes and Darad allies
IN-KUPWARA.outcome: Coalition broken; Lothana and Vigraharaja surrendered to the king

IN-PALI.detail: the Chahamana principality of Nadol in southern Marwar changed hands twice in two years. Asaraja's son Katudeva occupied Nadol in 1143-44, but Rayapala, son of the previous ruler Ratnapala, won it back before 1145. The squabble left the house so weakened that by 1154 Kumarapala of Gujarat could hand Nadol to his own governor.
IN-PALI.belligerents: Rival branches of the Chahamanas of Nadol
IN-PALI.outcome: Katudeva held Nadol briefly; Rayapala recovered it before 1145

IN-PALI.detail: The Battle of Sammel, also known as the Battle of Giri-Sumel, took place in 1544.
IN-PALI.belligerents: Sur Empire vs Kingdom of Marwar

IN-PALI.detail: The Battle of Kharda also called the Battle of Khurla, took place in 1795 between the Nizam of Hyderabad and the Maratha Empire, in which the Nizam was defeated.
IN-PALI.outcome: Maratha victory; the Nizam, shut up without food or water in Kharda fort, sought a cease-fire (13 March) and by the treaty of 10 April 1795 ceded territory worth about 32 lakhs including Daulatabad and gave up his minister Azim-ul-Umara
IN-PALI.source: HCIP VIII p. 446: 'the final battle took place on 11 March, 1795 ... Sindia's forces forced back the Nizam's troops. The Nizam took shelter in the small fort of Kharda ... the Nizam realised the futility of resistance and requested for a cessation of hostilities'; p. 447: 'Territories yielding an annual revenue of about 32 lakhs ... including the fort of Daulatabad, were to be ceded to the Peshwa.'

IN-CUTTACK.text: Anantavarman Chodaganga dies — Seventy years on the Eastern Ganga throne
IN-CUTTACK.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CUTTACK.text: Kapilendra Deva dies — Founder of the Gajapati empire
IN-CUTTACK.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CUTTACK.text: Purushottama Deva dies — The Gajapati who took Kondavidu and Udayagiri from Vijayanagara.
IN-CUTTACK.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CUTTACK.text: Prataparudra Deva dies — The last great Gajapati
IN-CUTTACK.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CUTTACK.detail: The Siege of Barabati (1745) was a significant military engagement during the Maratha invasions of Bengal.
IN-CUTTACK.belligerents: Bengal Subah vs Maratha Empire Kingdom of Nagpur

IN-CUTTACK.detail: The Siege of Cuttack occurred in May 1749 during the Fifth Maratha invasion of Bengal, when Alivardi Khan, Nawab of Bengal, sought to reconquer Orissa.
IN-CUTTACK.belligerents: Bengal Subah vs Maratha Empire Kingdom of Nagpur
IN-CUTTACK.outcome: Bengal Subah victory; Barabati surrenders to Alivardi about the start of June 1749, but Mir Habib retakes Katak within a week of the Nawab’s leaving
IN-CUTTACK.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I pp. 96–97: 'He entered the city of Katak (c. 18 May), and fifteen days later received the surrender of Barabati. Thus, the reconquest of Orissa was complete ... Six or seven days after Alivardi had marched out of Katak, Mir Habib reappeared before that town ... Thus, Alivardi’s work was undone within a week.'

IN-CUTTACK.detail: by Alivardi’s treaty of May–June 1751, Mir Habib governs Orissa south of the Subarnarekha for Raghuji Bhonsle’s army and Bengal pays twelve lakhs a year as chauth; after Mir Habib’s murder (24 August 1752) the Bhonsles rule Orissa outright.
IN-CUTTACK.belligerents: Maratha Empire (Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur) vs Bengal (Nawab)
IN-CUTTACK.outcome: Maratha victory; Orissa’s revenue and then its government pass to Nagpur. HCIP VIII (chronology p. 824) calls it 'ceding Orissa'; Sarkar I p. 104 says 'It is a mistake to say that Alivardi ceded Orissa' — it was a revenue assignment turned into rule after 1752
IN-CUTTACK.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I pp. 101–104: 'Mir Habib would now become a servant of Alivardi and act as naib-nazim (deputy governor) of Orissa on his behalf ... It is a mistake to say that Alivardi ceded Orissa to the Marathas ... the weakness of Alivardi’s successors ... enabled the Marathas to turn their fiscal right over Orissa into full political sovereignty'; HCIP VIII p. 110 and chronology p. 824 ('ceding Orissa to the Marathas and agreeing to pay Rs. 12 lakhs as chauth').

IN-AJMER.detail: Avenging an insult to his queen, Jayasimha's daughter, Kumarapala led an aggressive expedition against the Chahamana Arnoraja, devastated the Sapadalaksha country around Ajmer and defeated him a second time, though he allowed him to keep his throne.
IN-AJMER.belligerents: Chaulukyas of Gujarat vs Chahamanas of Sakambhari
IN-AJMER.outcome: Sapadalaksha devastated; Arnoraja defeated but retained as ruler

IN-AJMER.detail: Early in his reign the young Chahamana king marched against his rebel cousin Nagarjuna, son of Vigraharaja IV, besieged and took the city of Gudapura from which Nagarjuna fled, and hung the severed heads of the rebels on the gates of Ajmer as a warning.
IN-AJMER.belligerents: Prithviraja III of Ajmer vs the rebel prince Nagarjuna
IN-AJMER.outcome: Revolt crushed; Gudapura taken, Nagarjuna's family captured
IN-AJMER.source: HCIP V, pp. 106-107; shortly after 1178, c. 1180; Gudapura unidentified (coordinates approximate, Ajmer region)

IN-AJMER.text: Prithviraj Chauhan dies — Captured after the second battle of Tarain and put to death
IN-AJMER.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AJMER.text: Dara Shukoh is born — At Ajmer, Shah Jahan’s eldest son and heir.
IN-AJMER.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AJMER.detail: Aurangzeb's final victory over Dara Shikoh near Ajmer
Battle of Bandanwara was fought between the Kingdom of Mewar and Mughals in 1711 CE at Bandanwara, near Khari river in Bhilwara district, Rajasthan, India.
IN-AJMER.belligerents: Kingdom of Mewar vs Mughal Empire

IN-AJMER.detail: The battle of Gangwana was a military engagement fought between the Kingdom of Marwar and a combined army of the Jaipur Kingdom and the Mughal Empire in 1741.
IN-AJMER.belligerents: Kingdom of Jaipur, Reinforced By, Mughal Empire vs Rathores of Bakht Singh

IN-AJMER.text: The Rajput states accept British protection
IN-AJMER.detail: in a run of treaties from November 1817 to December 1818 — Karauli, Kota, Jodhpur, Udaipur, Bundi, Bikaner, Kishangarh, Jaipur and others — the Rajput princes acknowledged the Company's supremacy and paid it the tribute once taken by Sindhia, Holkar and Amir Khan.
IN-AJMER.source: Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages III p. 39: 'Karoli—9th Nov. 1817; Kotah—26th Dec. 1817; Jodhpur—6th Jan. 1818; Udaipur—13th Jan. 1818; Bundi—10th Feb. 1818; Bikaner—9th Mar. 1818; Kishangarh—2nd April 1818 ...'. Bakshi I p. 225 (Udaipur): 'The treaty was signed in Delhi on 13 January, 1818 ... By Article 3 the Rana promised to act in subordinate co-operation with the British Government and acknowledge its supremacy'; p. 295 (Jaipur): 'a tardy and ungracious assent to a treaty on 2 April, 1818.' Coordinates: Ajmer, where the Company replaced Sindhia.

IN-CENTRAL.text: Vigraharaja IV conquers Delhi from the Tomaras
IN-CENTRAL.detail: The Chahamana Vigraharaja IV (Visaladeva) conquered Dhillika (Delhi) from the Tomaras and seized Hansi, fighting repeated battles with the Muslims in the Punjab; his Delhi Siwalik pillar inscriptions boast that he made Aryavarta once more the land of the Aryas.
IN-CENTRAL.belligerents: Chahamanas of Sakambhari vs Tomaras of Delhi (and Ghaznavid garrisons of the Punjab)
IN-CENTRAL.outcome: Delhi and Hansi annexed; Chahamana empire extended to the Siwalik hills
IN-CENTRAL.source: HCIP V, pp. 82-83; undated in source — within his known dates 1153-1163, c. 1152-64 (disputed) Date: Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, p. 63 gives 1151 explicitly; The Struggle for Empire (HCIP V), p. 82 bounds it 1153-63. The atlas follows Satish Chandra and records the dispute.
Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-CENTRAL.text: Iltutmish dies — The sultan who finished the Qutb Minar and named his daughter his heir.
IN-CENTRAL.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CENTRAL.text: Balban dies — The slave-sultan of the iron hand
IN-CENTRAL.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CENTRAL.detail: The Khalji invasion of Mithila took place between 1297–1298 as a military expedition led by the Delhi Sultanate against the Karnats of Mithila in present-day Northern Bihar.
IN-CENTRAL.belligerents: Delhi Sultanate vs Karnats of Mithila
IN-CENTRAL.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

IN-CENTRAL.detail: Alauddin Khalji, the ruler of the Delhi Sultanate in India, faced three rebellions in 1301 while engaged in the conquest of Ranthambore.
IN-CENTRAL.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

IN-CENTRAL.detail: a Chagatai army under Taraghai reached Delhi itself while two of the Sultanate's field armies were away; Alauddin Khalji held the city and the Mongols withdrew — the first of two Chagatai invasions three years apart.
IN-CENTRAL.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

IN-CENTRAL.text: Alauddin Khalji dies — Conqueror of Gujarat, Ranthambore, Chittor and the south
IN-CENTRAL.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CENTRAL.detail: The Tughlaq campaign in Bengal, launched in 1324 by Sultan Ghiyas-ud-din Tughluq, aimed to reassert Delhi’s authority over the independent principality of Bengal.
IN-CENTRAL.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

IN-CENTRAL.text: Firuz Shah Tughlaq dies — Thirty-seven years
IN-CENTRAL.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CENTRAL.detail: Timur annihilates the Tughlaq army and puts the capital to the sword
IN-CENTRAL.source: Curated sweep (Sarkar; Majumdar; Schwartzberg)
Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-CENTRAL.detail: Shah Jahan begins the citadel of Shahjahanabad; finished 1648, the Jama Masjid beside it in 1656.
IN-CENTRAL.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CENTRAL.text: Dara Shukoh dies — Executed at Delhi by Aurangzeb’s order after the war of succession
IN-CENTRAL.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CENTRAL.text: Guru Tegh Bahadur dies — Beheaded at Chandni Chowk, Delhi, on Aurangzeb’s order
IN-CENTRAL.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CENTRAL.detail: The poll tax on non-Muslims, abolished by Akbar in 1564, is restored; the Rajput and Maratha wars of his last decades followed.
IN-CENTRAL.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CENTRAL.text: Banda Singh Bahadur dies — Executed at Delhi with hundreds of his followers after the fall of Gurdas Nangal.
IN-CENTRAL.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs IV p. 6: 'He was taken prisoner along with Banda in December, 1715. Banda was executed on June 9, 1716.' HCIP VIII p. 18: 'The place was stormed and Banda was forced into submission, brought to Delhi where he was brutally put to death.'

IN-CENTRAL.detail: the Sayyid brothers seize the emperor in the Delhi palace (February 1719), imprison and torture him and have him strangled in April — the first Mughal sovereign killed at the behest of a noble; the puppets Rafi-ud-Darajat and Rafi-ud-Daulah follow.
IN-CENTRAL.source: HCIP VIII p. 19-20: 'He was overpowered, arrested, and consigned to prison... At last, executioners were sent and they strangled him to death in April 1719. This was the first instance of a sovereign of the Mughul dynasty losing his life at the behest of a noble.'

IN-CENTRAL.text: Saadat Khan dies — Founder of the Awadh nawabate, by his own hand at Delhi during Nadir Shah's occupation.
IN-CENTRAL.source: HCIP VIII p. 113: 'Sa‘adat Khan, an immigrant from Khorasan and originally known as Mir Muhammad Amin, was the founder of the kingdom of Awadh... But, for some undesirable transactions with Nadir, he committed suicide on 20 March, 1739.'

IN-CENTRAL.text: Muhammad Shah dies — At Delhi on 25 April 1748, weeks after his army's victory at Manupur
IN-CENTRAL.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 823: '1748, April 25 Death of Mughul emperor Muhammad Shah (pp. 38, 184).'

IN-CENTRAL.detail: on 2 June 1754 the new wazir Imad-ul-Mulk, backed by Malhar Holkar, brings Aziz-ud-din out of the princes' prison and crowns him Alamgir II, and has Ahmad Shah arrested (he was later blinded).
IN-CENTRAL.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 338: '§ 18. Fall of Emperor Ahmad Shah... they entered the Diwan-i-am, where this prince was seated on the throne... and he was proclaimed Padishah Alamgir II. The new Emperor immediately ordered his predecessor to be brought under arrest.'; HCIP VIII chronology p. 825: '1754, June 2 Imad-ul-Mulk, with the help of the Marathas, deposes Mughul emperor Ahmad Shah'

IN-CENTRAL.detail: fearing the emperor would become Abdali's tool, the wazir Imad-ul-Mulk has him lured to the Kotla of Firuz Shah and killed on 29 November 1759, and Intizam-ud-daulah strangled the next day; Prince Ali Gauhar, in Bihar, proclaims himself Shah Alam II.
IN-CENTRAL.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 213: '§ 8. Imad murders Alamgir II. and Intezam-ud-daulah... He got the harmless crowned puppet murdered on 29th November and his long powerless old rival Intizam-ud-daulah strangled the next day.'

IN-CENTRAL.detail: The Battle of Barari Ghat बुराडी घाट was a military engagement between the Durrani-Rohilla Afghans and the Maratha army in which the Maratha army was defeated.
IN-CENTRAL.belligerents: Durrani Empire, Kingdom of Rohilkhand vs Maratha Empire
IN-CENTRAL.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 222: '§ 12. Battle of Barari-ghat; Dattaji slain. Here Sabaji was surprised at his post on 9th January 1760. Najib crossed the river unperceived'; HCIP VIII chronology p. 828 dates it 10 January 1760

IN-CENTRAL.text: Dattaji Sindhia dies — Killed at Barari Ghat on the Jamuna fighting Najib's Rohillas and Abdali's Afghans, a year before Panipat.
IN-CENTRAL.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 222: '§ 12. Battle of Barari-ghat; Dattaji slain.'; HCIP VIII chronology p. 828: '1760, January 10 Dattaji Sindia is killed in the battle of Buradi Ghat against Ahmad Shah Abdali' (Sarkar dates the battle 9 January)

IN-CENTRAL.detail: to avenge his father, Jawahir Singh besieges Najib-ud-Daula in Delhi with Malhar Holkar's Marathas, Sikh bands and Naga mercenaries (November 1764 – February 1765); Holkar's double-dealing and his own captains' collusion force him to make peace.
IN-CENTRAL.belligerents: Bharatpur, Maratha Empire (Malhar Rao Holkar), Sikh misls vs Najib-ud-Daula (Rohilla)
IN-CENTRAL.outcome: Najib-ud-Daula victory; Delhi held despite famine, and Jawahir Singh made peace in February 1765
IN-CENTRAL.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 461: 'The first battle took place on 15th November'; p. 467: 'At last Jawahir realized that he had nothing to hope for from the faith of Malhar, the prestige of Imad, or the arms of the Sikhs and Nagas... Negotiations for peace were set on foot on 4th February'; HCIP VIII chronology p. 830: '1765, February Jawahir Singh Jat makes peace with Najib Khan Rohilla'
Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-CENTRAL.text: Ghulam Qadir blinds Shah Alam II
IN-CENTRAL.detail: the Rohilla Ghulam Qadir, with Ismail Beg, seizes Delhi (30 July 1788), deposes Shah Alam II for Bidar Bakht and, hunting the palace treasure, gouges out the old emperor's eyes on 10 October; princes and princesses die of starvation before Mahadji Sindhia retakes the city.
IN-CENTRAL.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire III p. 453: '§ 8. Shah Alam blinded... On 10th October, in a frenzy of vindictiveness and avarice, Ghulam Qadir had needles driven through the eyes of Shah Alam.'; HCIP VIII chronology p. 837-838: '1788, July 30 Ghulam Qadir and Ismail Beg jointly take possession of Delhi... 1788, August 1 Ghulam Qadir deposes Shah Alam II and installs Bidar Bakht' (HCIP dates the atrocities to August, Sarkar the blinding to 10 October)

IN-CENTRAL.text: Shah Alam II passes under British protection
IN-CENTRAL.detail: after the battle of Patparganj the blind emperor invites Lake into Delhi; Lake's audience on 16 September 1803 ends Maratha control of the Mughal throne.
IN-CENTRAL.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire IV p. 293-294: '§6 Shah Alam II comes under British protection, 16th September... “The descendant of the great Akbar and Aurangzib was found blind and aged, stripped of authority and reduced to poverty”'; HCIP VIII chronology p. 841: '1803, September 16 Shah Alam seeks British protection.'

IN-WARANGAL-U.text: Kakatiya Prola II captures Taila III
IN-WARANGAL-U.detail: When the Kakatiyas of Telingana revolted, the Chalukya emperor Taila III marched on Warangal with the Santara Jagaddeva but was taken prisoner by Prola II, who released him out of professed devotion — a humiliation that shattered Chalukya prestige and invited Bijjala's usurpation.
IN-WARANGAL-U.belligerents: Kakatiyas of Telingana vs Western Chalukya empire
IN-WARANGAL-U.outcome: Taila III captured and released; Chalukya authority fatally discredited
IN-WARANGAL-U.source: HCIP V, p. 179; undated in source — before 1156, c. 1153-57 (disputed)

IN-WARANGAL-U.detail: on succeeding Prola II the Kakatiya king faced a general revolt of his feudatories. He subdued Domma and Meda of the Pakhal country, stripped Malligideva of Polavasa, and burnt the city of Chododaya of Kondapalli, whose rival Bhima fled into the forest abandoning Vardhamanapura. By 1162 Telingana was under a single hand for the first time.
IN-WARANGAL-U.belligerents: Kakatiyas of Warangal vs their rebel feudatories
IN-WARANGAL-U.outcome: Kakatiya victory; the Telingana chiefs brought under one authority

IN-WARANGAL-U.text: The Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamkonda
IN-WARANGAL-U.detail: Rudradeva’s Kakatiya temple to Siva, Vishnu and Surya, dated 1163.
IN-WARANGAL-U.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-WARANGAL-U.text: Ganapati Deva dies — Sixty-three years on the Kakatiya throne
IN-WARANGAL-U.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-WARANGAL-U.text: Rudrama Devi dies — The Kakatiya queen, killed in battle against the Kayastha chief Ambadeva (Chandupatla inscription).
IN-WARANGAL-U.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-WARANGAL-U.detail: In late 1309, the Delhi Sultanate ruler Alauddin Khalji sent his general Malik Kafur on an expedition to the Kakatiya capital Warangal.
IN-WARANGAL-U.outcome: Stalemate, •Both parties agreed to a truce.

IN-WARANGAL-U.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-WARANGAL-U.detail: In 1318, the Delhi Sultanate ruler Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah sent an army to subjugate the Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra who had stopped making tribute payments to Delhi.

IN-WARANGAL-U.belligerents: Delhi Sultanate (Ulugh Khan, the later Muhammad bin Tughluq) vs Kakatiya dynasty (Prataparudra)

IN-JAISALMER.detail: the Bhati capital moved from thrice-sacked Lodhruva to a new fort on Trikuta hill, named for its founder.
IN-JAISALMER.outcome: Jaisalmer replaces Lodhruva as the Bhati seat; the state endures to 1947
IN-JAISALMER.source: Added with the 800-1188 layer; researched against Britannica, Banglapedia, Epigraphia Indica and regional gazetteers.

IN-JAISALMER.detail: 120 men and a handful of jeeps hold a Pakistani armoured brigade through the night until the Hunters arrive at dawn
IN-JAISALMER.outcome: Decisive Indian victory — the Pakistani thrust into Rajasthan destroyed
IN-JAISALMER.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-ANANTAPUR.detail: the Kalachuri usurper of Kalyana spent his early years as sovereign subduing the south of the Deccan. Encamped at Balligave in Banavasi before 1162, he destroyed Tagarate in the Shimoga country, defeated the Santara chief Jagaddeva of Pomburcha, and besieged and destroyed the great hill fort of Gutti in Anantapur. Only after this was his hold on the Chalukya inheritance secure.
IN-ANANTAPUR.belligerents: Kalachuris of Kalyana vs the Santaras of Pomburcha and the chiefs of the southern Deccan
IN-ANANTAPUR.outcome: Kalachuri victory; Tagarate and Gutti destroyed

IN-ANANTAPUR.detail: The Siege of Penukonda in 1590 was a conflict between the Vijayanagara Empire and the Golconda Sultanate.

IN-JABALPUR.text: Kalachuri Jayasimha of Chedi turns back a Turushka raid
IN-JABALPUR.detail: the Kalachuri king of Tripuri, who had already fought successfully against Kumarapala of Gujarat and against his namesake Bijjala of the Deccan, repulsed an attack by the Turushkas early in his reign. HCIP V identifies this as the same Muslim raid, led by Khusrav Malik of Lahore, that the Gahadavala Vijayachandra beat back, though whether the two kings acted together is unknown.
IN-JABALPUR.belligerents: Kalachuris of Tripuri vs a Ghaznavid raiding force

IN-JABALPUR.detail: Rani Durgavati, wounded, dies sword in hand against Asaf Khan's Mughal army
IN-JABALPUR.outcome: Mughal victory — Gondwana plundered of legendary treasure
IN-JABALPUR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-JABALPUR.detail: The Mughal conquest of Garha was launched by the Mughal Empire in 1564 under Asaf Khan I against the Garha Kingdom led by regent Rani Durgavati.

IN-JABALPUR.text: Rani Durgavati dies — Killed her own self at Narrai rather than be taken by Asaf Khan’s army
IN-JABALPUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-RAMANATHAPURAM.detail: Parakramabahu I sent an army under the generals Lankapura and Jagadvijaya across the strait into the Pandya country, with orders not to stop until Madurai was taken and given to a prince of Parakrama Pandya's house. They won a string of engagements against Kulasekhara's lieutenants and installed the dead king's son Vira Pandya at Madurai — the high-water mark of Ceylonese power on the mainland.
IN-RAMANATHAPURAM.belligerents: Ceylon under Parakramabahu I vs Kulasekhara Pandya and the Cholas
IN-RAMANATHAPURAM.outcome: Initial Sinhalese success; Vira Pandya installed at Madurai

IN-RAMANATHAPURAM.detail: The Battle of Paramakudi was a conflict between Kumara Krishnappa Nayak and the rebel Tumbicchi Nayaka, who had fortified himself at Paramakudi and begun plundering nearby areas.
IN-RAMANATHAPURAM.belligerents: Vijayanagar Empire Madurai Nayakas vs Polygar of Paramakudi

IN-GUNTUR.detail: The Battle of Palnadu took place sometime in the years 1178–1182 CE, between a Haihaya king called Nalagamaraju, who ruled the then Gurazala kingdom, and his step-brother.
IN-GUNTUR.belligerents: Haihaya chiefs of Palnadu - Nalagama of Gurajala with the Velanati Chodas vs Malideva of Macherla with Kakatiya dynasty (Rudradeva)

IN-GUNTUR.detail: Ganapati’s Coastal Andhra Campaign was a major campaign initiated by Kakatiya ruler Ganapati to expand the boundaries of Kakatiya dynasty into Coastal Andhra.
IN-GUNTUR.belligerents: Kakatiyas Kota Vamsa Natavadi Malyala Chiefs vs Velanati Chodas, Ayya Chiefs
IN-GUNTUR.outcome: Kakatiya victory, Ganapatideva conquered Velanadu region

IN-GUNTUR.detail: Krishnadevaraya took Kondavidu by a night assault on a weak point, capturing the fort and the Gajapati prince Virabhadra.
IN-GUNTUR.outcome: Vijayanagara victory; fort stormed, Gajapati prince Virabhadra captured

IN-GUNTUR.detail: The Battle of Betamcharla was a battle between the forces of Aliya Rama Raya and the army of Salakamraju Tirumala, led by Chintagunti Raghupati.
IN-GUNTUR.belligerents: Aliya Rama Raya's Faction vs Salakamraju Pedda Tirumala's Faction

IN-GUNTUR.detail: The Battle of Juturu was a significant battle between Aliya Rama Raya and the forces of Salakamraju Tirumala, commanded by his general, Salakaya.
IN-GUNTUR.belligerents: Aliya Rama Raya's Faction vs Salakamraju Pedda Tirumala's Faction

IN-GUNTUR.detail: The Battle of Komali was a conflict between the faction of Salakamraju Tirumala and the forces of Aliya Rama Raya, led by Pemmasani Erra Timmanayudu.
IN-GUNTUR.belligerents: Aliya Rama Raya's Faction vs Salakamraju Pedda Tirumala's Faction

IN-GUNTUR.detail: The Vijayanagar Civil War (1542–1543) was a conflict between Rama Raya and Salakamraju Tirumala, when Salakaraju Tirumala usurped the throne by assassinating Venkata I.
IN-GUNTUR.belligerents: Aliya Rama Raya's Faction vs Salakamraju Pedda Tirumala's Faction

IN-GUNTUR.detail: The Vijayanagara invasion of Golconda happened in the from 1562–1563 when Rama Raya wanted to control more land in the Deccan.
The Battle of Kodur was fought between rival chiefs of the Vijayanagara Empire led by Velugoti Kasturi Ranga Nayaka on one side and the Kondraju brothers on the other.
IN-GUNTUR.belligerents: Vijayanagar Empire Venkatagiri estate, Kalahasti Nayaks Sari Chiefs vs Vijayanagar Empire Chiefs of Siddavatam, Matli Chiefs

IN-GUNTUR.detail: Krishnamraju’s Rebellion was an uprising against the Vijayanagara Empire during the reign of Venkatapati Raya.
IN-GUNTUR.belligerents: Vijayanagar Empire Matli Chiefs, Pemmasani Nayaks Hande Nayaks vs Chiefs of Nandyala, Chiefs of Kurnool

IN-GUNTUR.detail: Tirupatiraju’s Rebellion was a rebellion against the Vijayanagara Empire. The rebellion began soon after the death of Sriranga Deva Raya, when Tirupatiraju tried to rule Siddavatam.
IN-GUNTUR.belligerents: Vijayanagara Empire vs Chiefs of Siddhavatam

IN-BARMER.text: Muizz-ud-din sacks Kiradu and takes Nadol
IN-BARMER.detail: on the desert march that ended in his defeat at Kasahrada, the Ghurid sultan reached Kiradu near Barmer in Marwar, plundered its temple of Somesvara, and then seized and plundered Nadol, capital of a collateral branch of the Chahamanas. News of Nadol's fall reached Ajmer, where the minister Kadambavasa persuaded the young Prithviraja III to let the invader exhaust himself against Gujarat first.
IN-BARMER.belligerents: Ghurids vs the Chahamanas of Nadol
IN-BARMER.outcome: Ghurid success; Kiradu plundered and Nadol occupied

IN-BARMER.detail: In 1308, the Delhi Sultanate ruler Alauddin Khalji captured the Siwana fort located in present-day Rajasthan, India.
IN-BARMER.belligerents: Paramaras of Siwana vs Delhi Sultanate

IN-REWARI.detail: some time before 1182 the young Chahamana king invaded the country of the Bhadanakas, probably the Rewari, Bhiwani and old Alwar tracts south-west of Delhi. Their chief met him with a powerful elephant force and was severely defeated. The campaign secured the approaches to the Delhi region before Prithviraja turned east against the Chandellas in his digvijaya of 1182.
IN-REWARI.belligerents: Chahamanas of Ajmer vs the Bhadanakas
IN-REWARI.outcome: Chahamana victory; the Bhadanaka country subdued

IN-MANDYA.detail: After Bhillama V's Seuna (Yadava) army overran the Hoysala kingdom as far as Seringapatam, Ballala II organised a fresh army and confronted the invaders at Ingalakupe (Ingalaguppe), inflicting in 1188-89 a severe defeat that drove the Yadavas out of the Hoysala country and opened Ballala's conquest of the Krishna frontier.
IN-MANDYA.belligerents: Hoysalas of Dorasamudra vs Seunas (Yadavas) of Bhillama V
IN-MANDYA.outcome: Decisive Hoysala victory; Bhillama withdrew north, losing the Banavasi-Belvola marches to Ballala II by 1192

IN-MANDYA.detail: The siege of Seringapatam in 1639 was a conflict between the Bijapur Sultanate's forces, led by Randaula Khan and the Mysorean army commanded by Kanthirava Narasaraja I.
IN-MANDYA.belligerents: Flag of the Bijapur Sultanate Bijapur Sultanate vs Flag of Kingdom of Mysore.png Kingdom of Mysore

IN-MANDYA.detail: The Maratha invasion of Srirangapatnam (1682) was a major invasion during Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar’s rule.
IN-MANDYA.belligerents: Flag of the Maratha Empire Maratha Kingdom vs Flag of Kingdom of Mysore.png Kingdom of Mysore

IN-MANDYA.detail: The Maratha–Mysore War (1682) was a conflict between the Maratha Empire and the Kingdom of Mysore in southern India, driven by their rivalry for regional dominance.
two campaigns (Nov 1725–May 1726 against Chitradurga, Nov 1726–Apr 1727 to Srirangapatna) carry Maratha tribute-collection into the far south; the Raja of Mysore buys the army off.
IN-MANDYA.outcome: Maratha victory; the Raja of Srirangapatna submits and pays a tribute of 21 lakhs
IN-MANDYA.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II p. 88 (block 73): 'the first from November, 1725 to May 1726 and the second from November 1726 to April 1727 ... named after Chitaldurg and ... Shrirangapattan'; p. 91-92 (block 75): 'The Raja of Shrirangapattan also offered his submission by paying a tribute of 21 lacs in cash.'

IN-MANDYA.detail: the Peshwa's army besieges Srirangapatna; Nanjaraj promises 32 lakhs, pays six and pledges fifteen taluks — the crisis that brings Haidar Ali to command of the field army.
IN-MANDYA.outcome: Maratha victory; Mysore promises 32 lakhs and hands over fifteen taluks as security
IN-MANDYA.source: HCIP VIII p. 453: 'The Marathas again invaded in 1757 and Nanjaraj agreed to pay them 32 lakhs, but could pay only six, and for the payment of the balance handed over fifteen taluks as security.'

IN-MANDYA.text: Haidar Ali becomes master of Mysore
IN-MANDYA.detail: after surviving Khande Rao's cannonade of 12 August 1760 and a Maratha blockade at Bangalore, Haidar besieges Srirangapatna; the king surrenders Khande Rao and Haidar rules as the Wodeyars' regent.
IN-MANDYA.source: HCIP VIII p. 454: 'On 12 August, 1760, a cannonade was opened from the ramparts of the fort of Seringapatam on Haidar's residence ... When Haidar besieged Seringapatam, the King made an abject surrender and handed over Khande Rao.' Menon p. 243 dates Haidar's ascent 'As soon as Haider Ali ascended the throne of Mysore (1761)'.

IN-MANDYA.detail: Trimbak Rao catches Haidar's retreating army in the hills eleven miles from Srirangapatna; an exploding tumbril sets off a panic and the Maratha horse cut the square to pieces. Haidar and Tipu barely escape.
IN-MANDYA.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu)
IN-MANDYA.outcome: Maratha victory; Haidar loses his artillery, stores and equipment, but Srirangapatna holds
IN-MANDYA.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III p. 187-188 (blocks 183-184): 'The action at Chinkurli ... March 6 ... The rest was a scene of unresisted slaughter at the hands of the enemy's Pindaris'. HCIP VIII p. 456: 'defeated Haidar completely in the battle of Chinkurli or Moti Talao on 5 March, 1771 ... Haidar lost his entire equipment'. Dates differ: Rao 6 March; HCIP p. 423/456 5 March, p. 213 7 March 1771.

IN-MANDYA.belligerents: Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu), French India vs East India Company, Carnatic (Arcot Nawab)
IN-MANDYA.outcome: Inconclusive — Treaty of Mangalore (11 March 1784): mutual restitution of conquests and prisoners, a peace Englishmen 'regarded ... as humiliating'

IN-MANDYA.detail: Cornwallis, marching on Srirangapatna, drives Tipu from his position on 15 May 1791 — but with his army starving he abandons the siege five days later and falls back on Bangalore.
IN-MANDYA.belligerents: East India Company vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu)
IN-MANDYA.outcome: East India Company victory; Tipu withdraws into Srirangapatna, but Cornwallis gives up the attack on 20 May
IN-MANDYA.source: HCIP VIII p. 464: 'In an action at Arikera Tipu could not maintain his ground and had to withdraw to Seringapatam.' Hayavadana Rao III p. 785-787 synopsis (block 683): 'Tipu opposes the English at Karighatta ... the English victory on the 15th ... Lord Cornwallis relinquishes the attempt against Seringapatam, May 20, 1791'.

IN-MANDYA.detail: The 1792 siege of Seringapatam was a battle and siege of the Mysorean capital city of Seringapatam (Srirangapatna) at the end of the Third Anglo-Mysore War.
IN-MANDYA.belligerents: East India Company, Hyderabad, Maratha Empire vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu)
IN-MANDYA.outcome: East India Company victory; after the Sultan's redoubt falls, Tipu offers terms and surrenders half his dominions
IN-MANDYA.source: HCIP VIII p. 464-465: 'When the most important of his redoubts, called the Sultan's redoubt, was taken by Cornwallis ... Tipu offered terms. Half of his territory he surrendered'.

IN-MANDYA.detail: Tipu cedes half his dominions to the Company, the Marathas and the Nizam — Malabar, Dindigul and Baramahal to the Company — frees Coorg and pays 3.3 crores (preliminaries 22 February, definitive treaty 18 March 1792).
IN-MANDYA.source: HCIP VIII p. 464-465: 'Half of his territory he surrendered, to be divided equally among the three allies ... The British got Baramahal, Dindigul, as also Malabar. Tipu had also to give independence to the Raja of Coorg'. Hayavadana Rao III p. 922 (block 795): 'the Definitive Treaty of Seringapatam (March 18, 1792)'.

IN-MANDYA.belligerents: East India Company, Hyderabad vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu)
IN-MANDYA.outcome: East India Company victory; Tipu killed at Srirangapatna on 4 May 1799 and his dynasty ended
IN-MANDYA.source: HCIP VIII p. 466: 'He had no allies to help him. The Nizam's army did not play much effectual part on the British side and the Peshwa's troops were not there to help the British.' Sardesai III p. 360: 'Wellesley resented the Peshwa's refusal to join in his war against Tipu Sultan'.

IN-MANDYA.detail: on 27 March 1799 Harris's main army, with the Nizam's contingent under Arthur Wellesley, beats Tipu's attempt to stop its march on Srirangapatna.
IN-MANDYA.belligerents: East India Company, Hyderabad vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu)
IN-MANDYA.outcome: East India Company victory; Tipu falls back on his capital
IN-MANDYA.source: HCIP VIII p. 466: 'Tipu was defeated by Stewart at Sedasere and by Harris at Malavally. He was driven to the defences of his capital'. Hayavadana Rao III index (block 1203): 'action at between the English and Tipu as described by Gen. Harris (March 27, 1799), 974-977'.

IN-MANDYA.belligerents: East India Company, Hyderabad vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu)
IN-MANDYA.outcome: East India Company victory; Srirangapatna stormed on 4 May 1799 and Tipu killed
IN-MANDYA.source: HCIP VIII p. 466: 'the siege was begun on 17 April and the assault was made on 4 May, 1799. Tipu fell fighting bravely.'

IN-MANDYA.text: Tipu Sultan dies — Killed at the water-gate of Srirangapatna on 4 May 1799 as the British stormed the breach. Hayavadana Rao III p. 881.
IN-MANDYA.source: C. Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III p. 1024 (block 881; running head '1024 HISTORY OF MYSORE'); HCIP VIII p. 466: 'Tipu fell fighting bravely.'

IN-KANNUR.detail: The Battle of Nettur was an engagement between the Chola Emperor Kulothunga Chola III and Vira Pandya, the claimant to the Pandya throne in 1188.
IN-KANNUR.belligerents: Chola Empire and Pandyan kingdom vs Pandyan troops loyal to Vira Pandya
IN-KANNUR.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07) (Note: no source in our library gives the site of Nettur; the coordinate is the Nettur near Thalassery and is approximate.)

IN-KANNUR.detail: The First Battle of Cannanore was a naval engagement between the Third Portuguese Armada under João da Nova and the naval forces of Calicut.
The Battle of Cannanore took place in 1506 off the harbour of Cannanore in India, between the Indian fleet of the Zamorin of Calicut and a Portuguese fleet.
IN-KANNUR.belligerents: Portuguese Empire vs Kingdom of Calicut

IN-KANNUR.detail: The siege of Tellicherry was a military embargo that happened in Thalassery.
IN-KANNUR.belligerents: East India Company, Kottayam vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu), Kolathunad, Kadathanad
IN-KANNUR.outcome: East India Company victory; relieved by Abington in 1781, Tellicherry holds, and Mahe is retaken on 9 January 1782
IN-KANNUR.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 246: 'the troops of Sirdar Khan laid siege to Tellicherry both from sea and land (October 1780). The siege lasted for 18 months ... Tellicherry was saved and Mahe was recaptured on 9th January 1782.'

IN-BATHINDA.belligerents: Ghurid Empire vs Chahamanas of Ajmer
IN-BATHINDA.outcome: Ghurid capture; later besieged by Rajputs
IN-BATHINDA.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-BATHINDA.detail: The Battle of Lahira, also known as the Battle of Gurusar or the Battle of Mehraj, was fought between the Mughal Empire and Sikhs assisted by the Kangra State in 1631 or 1634.
IN-BATHINDA.belligerents: Akal Sena (Sikhs), Kangra State vs Mughal Empire

IN-KARNAL.detail: Prithviraj Chauhan defeats Muhammad of Ghor, who retreats to Ghazni
IN-KARNAL.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-KARNAL.detail: Nadir Shah shatters the Mughal army and goes on to sack Delhi
IN-KARNAL.outcome: Afsharid victory; the Mughal army broken and Muhammad Shah made captive (24 February 1739)
IN-KARNAL.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 820: '1739, February 24 Emperor Muhammad Shah is made a captive by Nadir Shah (p. 92).'

IN-KARNAL.detail: Nadir Shah carries off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor
IN-KARNAL.outcome: Afsharid victory; general massacre of Delhi's people on 21 March, the Peacock Throne and the treasury carried off
IN-KARNAL.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 820: '1739, March 20 Nadir Shah, the Persian invader, enters Delhi with his army (pp. 33, 93)... 1739, March 21 ... Due to a rumour, a tumult breaks out and Nadir Shah orders a general massacre of Delhi population'

IN-KARNAL.detail: The Battle of Taraori in 1759 was a military engagement between the Durrani Empire and the Maratha Empire and the Mughals in the fields of Taraori.
IN-KARNAL.belligerents: Durrani Empire vs Maratha Empire, Mughal Empire

IN-KARNAL.detail: The Battle of Kunjpura was fought on 17 October 1760, and it was a significant engagement during the Maratha-Afghan Wars.
IN-KARNAL.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs Durrani Empire, Kingdom of Rohilkhand

IN-KARNAL.detail: The siege of Kunjpura was a 14-day siege in April to May 1772 by Sikh forces led by Sahib Singh against the Mughal coalition forces led by Mughal Ali Khan.

IN-BULANDSHAHR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-BULANDSHAHR.detail: Malhar Holkar's light horse fall on Emperor Ahmad Shah's camp in the Doab on the night of 25–26 May 1754; the emperor flees to Delhi leaving his mother and harem in Maratha hands, and within a week Imad-ul-Mulk deposes him.
IN-BULANDSHAHR.belligerents: Maratha Empire (Malhar Rao Holkar), with Imad-ul-Mulk vs Mughal Empire (Emperor Ahmad Shah)
IN-BULANDSHAHR.outcome: Maratha victory; the imperial camp dispersed in panic and the royal ladies captured
IN-BULANDSHAHR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 334: '§ 11. Malhar surprises imperial camp at Sikandrabad, 26 May 1754. But in the night between, spies brought the news that 20,000 Maratha light horse under Malhar had arrived within 24 miles of the camp.'; Sarkar II p. 437 dates Holkar's raid 25 May

IN-BULANDSHAHR.detail: The Battle of Sikandrabad was a military engagement between the Afghan Durranis and the Marathas near the city of Sikandrabad.
IN-BULANDSHAHR.belligerents: Durrani Empire, Kingdom of Rohilkhand vs Maratha Empire
IN-BULANDSHAHR.outcome: Durrani victory; Malhar Rao Holkar's army routed by Jahan Khan
IN-BULANDSHAHR.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 828: '1760, March 4 The Maratha army under the command of Malhar Rao Holkar is defeated by Ahmad Shah Abdali’s forces at Sikandrabad (pp. 192, 254).'; Sarkar II contents: 'Malhar Holkar routed by Jahan Khan, 228'

IN-ALIGARH.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-ALIGARH.text: Bahlul Lodi dies — At Jalali near Aligarh
IN-ALIGARH.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-ALIGARH.detail: The siege of Aligarh, also known as the Battle of Aligarh, was fought between the Maratha Confederacy and the British East India Company during the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
IN-ALIGARH.belligerents: East India Company vs Maratha Empire, Gwalior (Scindia)
IN-ALIGARH.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 841: '1803, September 4 The English army led by Lake defeats Sindia’s forces at Aligarh (pp. 266, 496).'; Sarkar IV contents: 'Lake routs Perron, 281—storms Aligarh fort, 283'

IN-FIROZABAD.detail: Ghori defeats Jaichandra of Kannauj, extending Ghurid power down the Ganga
IN-FIROZABAD.belligerents: Ghurid Empire vs Gahadavala dynasty / Rajputs
IN-FIROZABAD.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-FIROZABAD.text: Jayachandra dies — The Gahadavala of Kannauj, killed at Chandawar on the Yamuna fighting Muhammad of Ghor.
IN-FIROZABAD.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BHARATPUR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-BHARATPUR.belligerents: Mughal Empire vs Kingdom of Mewar
IN-BHARATPUR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-BHARATPUR.belligerents: Rajput Confederacy vs Mughal Empire and Afghans
IN-BHARATPUR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-BHARATPUR.detail: Babur breaks Rana Sanga's Rajput confederacy, securing the Mughal foothold
The Battle of Kumher was a conflict between the Kingdom of Bharatpur, led by Maharaja Suraj Mal, and the Mughal Empire, supported by its allies, including the Marathas.
IN-BHARATPUR.belligerents: Bharatpur vs Maratha Empire, Mughal Empire (Imad-ul-Mulk), Jaipur
IN-BHARATPUR.outcome: Bharatpur victory; Kumher held for four months (Jan.–May 1754), Khande Rao Holkar killed, the besiegers withdrew on the promise of a 30-lakh indemnity
IN-BHARATPUR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 324-325: 'Khande Rao having made covered lanes approached the walls... the fort opened fire and he was killed by a zamburak shot'; II p. 437: 'After four months (Jan.-May, 1754) the fort remained untaken, and the besiegers were glad to go away on receiving promise of an indemnity of 30 lakhs of Rupees.'

IN-BHARATPUR.text: Badan Singh dies — At Dig, the founder of the Bharatpur Jat state, long blind and a figurehead while Suraj Mal ruled for him.
IN-BHARATPUR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 433: 'Badan Singh died at Dig on [?]th June 1756; but for many years before it he was a quiescent figure, stationary at his capital... The policy of his State in war and diplomacy was shaped and its campaigns were led by' Suraj Mal (day of month illegible in the scan)

IN-BHARATPUR.detail: Najaf Khan starves the great Jat fortress of Dig; Ranjit Singh flees on the night of 29 April 1776, the fort and city are sacked, and the Jat state is reduced to Bharatpur and a few districts.
IN-BHARATPUR.belligerents: Mughal Empire (Mirza Najaf Khan) vs Bharatpur (Ranjit Singh)
IN-BHARATPUR.outcome: Mughal Empire victory; Dig taken after six weeks' blockade, the last defenders of the citadel killed
IN-BHARATPUR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire III p. 125: '§ 15. Fall of Dig. In six weeks famine completed its work in that crowded den. Finally, in the night of 29th April 1776, Ranjit Singh himself fled away with the remnant of his troops'; HCIP VIII p. 160 places the final submission at Bharatpur c. February 1778

IN-BHARATPUR.detail: The Battle of Chaksana was fought between the Mughal Empire and the Maratha Confederacy in 1788.
IN-BHARATPUR.belligerents: Maratha Empire, Gwalior (Scindia) vs Najib-ud-Daula (Rohilla) — Ghulam Qadir, with Ismail Beg's Mughal troops
IN-BHARATPUR.outcome: Rohilla–Mughal victory (Ghulam Qadir and Ismail Beg); the Maratha cavalry broke and De Boigne's battalions covered the withdrawal
IN-BHARATPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 261: 'At Chaksana, eight miles from Bharatpur, the two armies met (April 1788). The Maratha cavalry cracked before the furious onslaught of the Musalman chiefs, but the day was saved by De Boigne’s battalions; the Maratha army withdrew'; chronology p. 837: 'Sindia’s army is defeated at the battle of Chaksana by the Rohillas'

IN-BHARATPUR.detail: The Battle of Deeg, fought on 13 November 1804, took place outside Deeg, now in the Bharatpur district of Rajasthan, India.
IN-BHARATPUR.belligerents: East India Company vs Maratha Empire, Holkar (Indore State), Bharatpur
IN-BHARATPUR.outcome: East India Company victory; Holkar's infantry defeated outside Dig on 13 November and the fortress captured on 23 December 1804
IN-BHARATPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 498: 'The latter suffered a reverse at Dig on 13 November, 1804... Ranjit Singh assigned the fort of Dig to Holkar... Dig was captured on 23 December, 1804'

IN-BHARATPUR.detail: The siege of Bharatpur took place between 2 January and 22 February 1805 in the Indian Princely state of Bharatpur, during the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
IN-BHARATPUR.belligerents: Bharatpur, Maratha Empire, Holkar (Indore State) vs East India Company
IN-BHARATPUR.outcome: Bharatpur victory; Lake's assaults on the fort failed and the siege became a blockade, with 3,203 British casualties — though the Raja then sued for peace (April 1805), paying twenty lakhs and giving up Dig
IN-BHARATPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 498-499: 'The siege of Bharatpur by Lake began on 7 January, 1805. Three attempts to take the fort by assault having failed, Lake converted the siege into a blockade... The Raja of Bharatpur, despite his success, realised he could not stand up to the British and sued for peace... He paid twenty lakhs'; HCIP IX p. 30: 'The fort of Bharatpur, which had defied four attacks of Lord Lake in 1805'

IN-BHARATPUR.detail: to unseat the usurper Durjan Sal and erase the memory of Lake's failure, Combermere breaches the 'impregnable' Jat fortress with mines and storms it.
IN-BHARATPUR.belligerents: East India Company vs Bharatpur (Durjan Sal)
IN-BHARATPUR.outcome: East India Company victory; Bharatpur stormed, Durjan Sal deposed and the minor Balwant Singh installed
IN-BHARATPUR.source: HCIP IX (British Paramountcy) p. 30-31: 'The General reached Bharatpur on December 10, and after a breach was effected by bombardment from the artillery and by laying undergound mines, the fort of Bharatpur was taken by assault on December 18, 1825. The failure of Lord Lake in 1805 was thus avenged.'; HCIP IX chronology p. 1186 lists 'Fall of Bharatpur' under 1826. DATE CONFLICT: HCIP body says 18 Dec 1825; the storm is generally dated 18 January 1826 — year kept at 1826 per the chronology

IN-GWALIOR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-GWALIOR.detail: in the first Anglo-Maratha war, Captain Popham escalades and surprises Mahadji Sindhia's fortress of Gwalior on 3 August 1780 — an exploit Hastings called nearly equal to Plassey.
IN-GWALIOR.belligerents: East India Company vs Maratha Empire, Gwalior (Scindia)
IN-GWALIOR.outcome: East India Company victory; Gwalior fort taken by surprise
IN-GWALIOR.source: HCIP VIII p. 256: 'Col. Popham surprised the fort of Gwalior on 3 August, 1780 and Hastings called it the most gallant enterprise nearly equal in its advantage to the battle of Plassey.'

IN-GWALIOR.text: Maratha Conquest of Gwalior and Gohad
IN-GWALIOR.detail: The Maratha conquest of Gwalior and Gohad is the military conflict between Maratha Confederacy and Kingdom of Gohad.
IN-GWALIOR.belligerents: Maratha Empire, Gwalior (Scindia) vs Gohad (Jat Ranas)
IN-GWALIOR.outcome: Maratha victory; Mahadji Sindhia stormed Gwalior fort (31 July 1783) and seized Gohad and Rana Chhatra Singh (25–26 February 1784)
IN-GWALIOR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire III p. 273: 'he had crushed his persistent rival in North Malwa, Rana Chhatra Singh of Gohad, by storming Gwalior fort (31 July 1783) and seizing Gohad and the Rana’s person (25 Feb. 1784.)'; HCIP VIII p. 258: 'Gwalior fort was reoccupied on 31 July, 1783 and Gohad was reduced on 26 February, 1784'

IN-GWALIOR.detail: Gawilghur in western India was captured by British East India Company forces under the command of Sir Arthur Wellesley on 15 December 1803, during the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
IN-GWALIOR.outcome: East India Company victory; Gawilgarh stormed on 15 December 1803
IN-GWALIOR.source: HCIP VIII p. 496: 'Arthur and Stevenson captured Gawilgarh on December 15, 1803'; p. 248: the Treaty of Deogaon left the Raja 'the country ... south of the Narnalla and Gawilgarh hills'.

IN-GWALIOR.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs East India Company
IN-GWALIOR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-GWALIOR.detail: Cornwallis's peace with Daulat Rao Sindhia restores Gwalior fort and Gohad to him while he renounces all claims north of the Chambal.
IN-GWALIOR.source: HCIP VIII p. 499: 'Daulat Rao Sindia concluded the treaty of Mustafapur with the Company’s Government on 21 November, 1805. Gohad and the fort of Gwalior were restored to him. But he renounced his claims on the territories north of the Chambal.'

IN-GWALIOR.detail: Gwalior's army is defeated in a single afternoon
IN-GWALIOR.source: HCIP IX (British Paramountcy) p. 231-232: 'on 29 December, the British troops, under the Commander-in-Chief, Hugh Gough, came into clash with the Gwalior troops... they unexpectedly met with the enemy troops at Maharajpur... though the Maratha troops fought with courage, they were dislodged... The British army gained a complete victory but suffered heavy losses'

IN-GWALIOR.detail: on the same day as Maharajpur (29 December 1843), Grey's wing of the Gwalior expedition defeats a second Gwalior army at Punniar south-west of Gwalior.
IN-GWALIOR.outcome: East India Company victory; a large body of Gwalior troops defeated
IN-GWALIOR.source: HCIP IX p. 232: 'On the same day, another wing of the British army defeated a large body of Gwalior troops near Punniar... It seems to be certain, however, that the British army took the aggressive and attacked the Maratha force without any formal declaration of war on either side.'

IN-GWALIOR.detail: Rose takes Morar on 16 June; at Kotah-ki-Serai on 17 June Rani Lakshmibai, leading her troops in man's dress, is cut down; the rebels are driven from the city on 19 June and the fort stormed on 20 June, and Sindhia is restored.
IN-GWALIOR.belligerents: East India Company vs Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Tantia Tope, Rao Sahib, Gwalior Contingent rebels
IN-GWALIOR.outcome: East India Company victory; Gwalior city and fort retaken, the Rani of Jhansi killed, Tantia Tope escaped
IN-GWALIOR.source: HCIP IX p. 583-584: 'He left Kalpi on June 6... arrived on the 16th within five miles of the Morar cantonments... carried the cantonments by assault'; 'Thus died the Rani of Jhansi... Rose immediately attacked them, and after a short but sharp engagement, drove away the rebels and occupied the city. Next morning, June 20... Rose attacked the strong fortress and carried it by assault.'

IN-GWALIOR.text: Rani Lakshmibai dies — Killed in the fighting at Kotah-ki-Serai outside Gwalior, in uniform, on 17 June.
IN-GWALIOR.source: HCIP IX p. 584: '“Clad in the attire of a man and mounted on horseback, the Rani of Jhansi might have been seen animating her troops throughout the day... A hussar, close upon her track, ignorant of her sex and rank, cut her down.” According to another account the Rani was struck by a bullet.'

IN-GWALIOR.detail: the fugitives from Kalpi — Rao Sahib, Tantia Tope and the Rani of Jhansi — march on Gwalior; on 1 June 1858 Jayaji Rao Sindhia's army goes over to them, he flees to Agra, and Nana Sahib is proclaimed Peshwa in the fort.
IN-GWALIOR.belligerents: Rao Sahib, Tantia Tope, Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai) vs Gwalior (Scindia)
IN-GWALIOR.outcome: Tantia Tope and Rao Sahib victory; Sindhia's army deserted to the rebels and Gwalior with its treasury and arsenal was seized
IN-GWALIOR.source: HCIP IX p. 582-583: 'On June 1, Sindhia marched out with his army to oppose them... Sindhia’s infantry and cavalry, his bodyguards alone excepted, either joined the rebels... Sindhia turned and fled... He did not draw rein till he reached Agra... entered the fort of Gwalior, seized the treasury and the arsenal, and proclaimed Nana Sahib as Peshwa.'

IN-BUDAUN.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

BD-MUNSHIGANJ.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-MULUGU.detail: Recherla Rudra’s Kakatiya temple, built on sandbox foundations with floating bricks in its sikhara.
IN-MULUGU.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

PK-NOWSHERA.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

PK-NOWSHERA.detail: The Battle of Nowshera (1674) was a major confrontation between the Afghan tribal alliance under Khushal Khan Khattak and the forces of the Mughal Empire.
PK-NOWSHERA.belligerents: Afghans, Khattak, Afridi vs Mughals, Mughal Empire

PK-NOWSHERA.detail: Diwan Mohkam Chand, bringing supplies to the Sikh garrison of Attock, beat Wazir Fateh Khan's Afghans and Dost Muhammad's ghazis near Haidru on the Indus on 9 July 1813; the Afghans fled across the river and Attock stayed Sikh.
PK-NOWSHERA.outcome: Sikh Empire victory; Fateh Khan's army driven across the Indus, Attock held
PK-NOWSHERA.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V pp. 101–102: 'His Ghazis and cavalry fled helter skelter towards the river ... As this battle was fought near the village of Haidru, it is called the battle of Haidru. It took place on 9 July, 1813 ... Ranjit Singh celebrated this victory by illuminating the cities of Lahore and Amritsar.' (Gupta gives 9 July; the row's text had 13 July.)

PK-NOWSHERA.text: Akali Phula Singh dies — the Nihang leader who stormed Kasur and Multan for Ranjit Singh, killed at the battle of Nowshera.
PK-NOWSHERA.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 151: 'The Sikhs also suffered heavily. Their two notable commanders, Akali Phula Singh and General Balbhadra Singh Gorkha, with about 2,000 men lost their lives.'

PK-NOWSHERA.detail: The Battle of Nowshera, also called the Battle of Tihri, Battle of Naushahra, or Battle of Pir Sabaq, was fought in March 1823 near Nowshera by the forces of Ranjit Singh.
PK-NOWSHERA.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Peshawar Sardars (Barakzai), Azim Khan's Afghans and Yusafzai tribesmen
PK-NOWSHERA.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 151 ('The Battle of Tihri or Naushahra, 14 March, 1823'): 'Azim Khan was so much frightened that leaving his guns, tents and other equippage, fled to Peshawar and then to Kabul ... The Sikhs also suffered heavily. Their two notable commanders, Akali Phula Singh and General Balbhadra Singh Gorkha, with about 2,000 men lost their lives.'

PK-NOWSHERA.detail: The Battle of Akora Khattak was the first significant clash between the Mujahidin movement led by Syed Ahmad Barelvi and the Sikh Empire.
The Battle of Shaidu, also known as the Battle of Pirpai, was fought in March 1827 between the Sikh forces led by Hari Singh Nalwa and the Mujahideen troops.
The Battle of Ramkani was fought on 4 May 1835 by the Sikh forces led by Maharaja Ranjit Singh and Barakzai forces including Ghazis.
PK-NOWSHERA.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Barakzais, Assisted by Ghazis

IN-PERAMBALUR.detail: Kopperunjinga takes the emperor prisoner — the Kadava chief defeated Rajaraja III and held him captive at Sendamangalam until Hoysala Narasimha II marched to his rescue — a Chola emperor imprisoned by his own feudatory.
IN-PERAMBALUR.belligerents: Kadava chiefdom (Kopperunjinga) vs Chola Empire (Rajaraja III), relieved by the Hoysalas
IN-PERAMBALUR.outcome: Rajaraja III restored by Hoysala arms; Chola sovereignty visibly hollow
IN-PERAMBALUR.source: Cross-referenced against Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, and the Chola Empire literature (Aug 2026).

IN-UDUPI.text: Madhvacharya is born — At Pajaka near Udupi.
IN-UDUPI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-UDUPI.text: Madhvacharya dies — By tradition at Udupi
IN-UDUPI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-KAITHAL.text: Razia Sultan dies — Killed near Kaithal with her husband Altunia, fleeing the nobles who had deposed her.
IN-KAITHAL.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PURBA-MEDINIPUR.detail: The Battle of Katasin was fought in 1243 CE between Narasingha Deva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty and Tughral Tughan Khan, the governor of the Mamluk dynasty of Delhi, at Katasin.
IN-PURBA-MEDINIPUR.belligerents: Eastern Ganga dynasty vs Delhi Sultanate

IN-KANSHIRAM-NAGAR.text: Amir Khusrau is born — At Patiyali on the Ganga.
IN-KANSHIRAM-NAGAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-KANSHIRAM-NAGAR.detail: the wazir Safdar Jang's huge army, invading the Bangash country, is broken by Ahmad Khan Bangash's Afghans north of Etah; Safdar Jang is wounded and disgraced and the Afghans overrun Oudh and besiege Allahabad.
IN-KANSHIRAM-NAGAR.belligerents: Farrukhabad (Bangash) vs Mughal Empire, Awadh (wazir Safdar Jang), Bharatpur (Suraj Mal)
IN-KANSHIRAM-NAGAR.outcome: Farrukhabad (Bangash) victory; Safdar Jang's army routed after his wings had first beaten the Afridi division
IN-KANSHIRAM-NAGAR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 246-247: '§ 6. Safdar Jang defeated at Ram Chatauni. At three hours after sunrise, on the 18th of September 1750, the wazir’s army advanced upon the enemy'; HCIP VIII p. 113 and chronology p. 824: '1750, September 13 Safdar Jang is defeated by the Afghans at Ram Chatauni' (Sarkar himself gives 13 Sep. on p. 253 and 18 Sep. on p. 246)

IN-SRI-POTTI-SRIRAMULU-NELLORE.detail: The Battle of Mudugur was a mid-13th century conflict fought between the forces of the Pandyan Empire under Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan I and a coalition.
IN-SRI-POTTI-SRIRAMULU-NELLORE.belligerents: Pandyan Empire vs Kakatiya-led alliance, Seunas (Yadavas), Bana kingdom
IN-SRI-POTTI-SRIRAMULU-NELLORE.outcome: Pandyan victory The Pandyas captured Nellore and incorporated it into the Pandyan Empire

IN-SRI-POTTI-SRIRAMULU-NELLORE.detail: Krishnadevaraya's general Saluva Timma (Timmarusu) took the Gajapati hill-fort of Udayagiri after a long siege, opening the Kalinga war.
IN-SRI-POTTI-SRIRAMULU-NELLORE.outcome: Vijayanagara victory; the Udayagiri hill-fort was taken

IN-SRI-POTTI-SRIRAMULU-NELLORE.detail: The Siege of Udayagiri was a military conflict between the Vijayanagara Empire under Sriranga III and the Golconda Sultanate.

IN-KAPURTHALA.detail: The Battle of Beas River took place between the Chagatai Khanate and the Mamluk Sultanate of Delhi on 9 March 1285.
IN-KAPURTHALA.belligerents: Delhi Sultanate (Balban; Prince Muhammad, who fell) vs the Chagatai Mongols
IN-KAPURTHALA.outcome: Mamluk victory Mongol forces withdrew Balban’s son Muhammad Khan killed in Multan

IN-KAPURTHALA.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-KAPURTHALA.text: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia dies — commander of the Dal Khalsa from 1748, the foremost Sikh chief of the misl age.
IN-KAPURTHALA.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs IV p. 283: 'Jassa Singh Ahluwalia died in October, 1783.' p. 13: '[Kapur Singh] placed it [the Dal Khalsa] under the command of Jassa Singh Ahluwalia.' (Place not given; coordinates are his seat, Kapurthala.)

IN-KAPURTHALA.detail: pursued by Lake to the Beas, Yashwant Rao Holkar makes peace with the Company, renouncing his claims north of the Chambal and in Bundelkhand, ending the second Anglo-Maratha war.
IN-KAPURTHALA.source: HCIP VIII p. 499: 'Yashwant Rao was compelled to conclude the treaty of Rajpurghat with Lake on the banks of the Beas on 24 December, 1805.'; p. 149: 'Treaty of Rajghat (Dec. 24, 1805)'

IN-SAWAI-MADHOPUR.detail: The Capture of Jhain was a military expedition carried out by the Delhi Sultanate under Jalal-ud-din Khalji against the Kingdom of Ranthambore.
IN-SAWAI-MADHOPUR.belligerents: Delhi Sultanate vs Chauhans of Ranthambore

IN-SAWAI-MADHOPUR.text: Hammira Deva dies — The Chauhan of Ranthambore, killed when Alauddin took the fort after a year’s siege.
IN-SAWAI-MADHOPUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SAWAI-MADHOPUR.detail: Alauddin Khalji storms the great Chauhan fortress
IN-SAWAI-MADHOPUR.belligerents: Delhi Sultanate vs Chauhans of Ranthambore
Kingdom of Mewar vs Mughal Empire
IN-SAWAI-MADHOPUR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-KAUSHAMBI.text: Jalaluddin Khalji dies — Murdered at Kara on the Ganga by his nephew Alauddin, who took the throne.
IN-KAUSHAMBI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PUNE.text: Jnaneshwar takes samadhi — At Alandi, aged twenty-one
IN-PUNE.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PUNE.text: Shivaji is born — At Shivneri fort near Junnar.
IN-PUNE.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PUNE.text: Tukaram dies — At Dehu on the Indrayani, by tradition taken up bodily
IN-PUNE.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PUNE.detail: The Battle of Chakan in 1660 took place between Mughal forces led by Shaista Khan and Maratha forces commanded by Firangoji Narsala at Chakan in Maharashtra.
IN-PUNE.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

IN-PUNE.detail: The Battle of Purandar was fought between the Mughal Empire and the Marathas in 1665.
IN-PUNE.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

IN-PUNE.detail: The Battle of Sinhagad, also known as Battle of Kondhana, involved an attack by Marathas during the night of 4 February 1670 on the Mughal fort of Sinhagad.
IN-PUNE.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

IN-PUNE.detail: The first siege of the Shivneri Fort was a military engagement between the Mughal Army and the Maratha Army near Shivneri Fort; the Mughals were victorious.
IN-PUNE.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

IN-PUNE.detail: The Second Siege of Shivneri Fort was a military engagement between the Mughal Army and the Maratha Army in Shivneri Fort.
IN-PUNE.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

IN-PUNE.text: Sambhaji dies — Captured at Sangameshwar and executed at Tulapur by Aurangzeb after weeks of torture.
IN-PUNE.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PUNE.detail: The Battle of Torna was fought on between the Mughal Empire and the Maratha Kingdom.
IN-PUNE.source: Wikipedia (category sweep, 2026-07)

IN-PUNE.detail: The Battle of Khed took place on 12 October 1707, between Shahu I and the forces of Tarabai led by Dhanaji Jadhav.
IN-PUNE.belligerents: Forces of Shahu I vs Forces of Tarabai
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII p. 47: 'The old soldier refused to take arms against his legitimate sovereign and carried with him the major part of the army. The remnant was too small to make a stand against the combined forces and fled to Satara. (Battle of Khed, 12 October 1707).'

IN-PUNE.detail: Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath meets Kanhoji Angre at Valvan near Lonavla and wins him from Tarabai's side to Shahu's. Kanhoji keeps the fleet, his Konkan territory and the title of Sarkhel.
IN-PUNE.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II p. 26: 'they had a cordial meeting at Valvan, a suburb of Lonavla, early in January 1714.' HCIP VIII p. 54: 'On being confirmed in command of the fleet, his territory in Konkan and his title of Sarkhel, he agreed to renounce Shambhuji ... and maintain the cause of Shahu.'

IN-PUNE.text: Balaji Vishwanath dies — the first Peshwa, who won Shahu his throne and the Deccan chauth grants of 1719
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII p. 61: 'he retired to Saswad near Poona and died there on 2 April, 1720 ... Balaji Vishwanath has been truly called the second founder of the Maratha State.'

IN-PUNE.text: Chimaji Appa dies — Bajirao I's brother and general, the victor of Amjhera and of Bassein.
IN-PUNE.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II p. 192: 'Chimnaji Appa died at Poona on 17th December. This premature death was severely mourned by the whole nation.'

IN-PUNE.text: Madhavrao I born — the Peshwa who restored Maratha power after Panipat.
IN-PUNE.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II chronology p. 463: '1745, February 16 Madhavrao born.'

IN-PUNE.detail: after Panipat and Balaji Rao's death, his second son Madhavrao, aged sixteen, is made Peshwa, with his uncle Raghunathrao as regent and the real ruler.
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII p. 201: 'Madhav Rao, the second son of Balaji Baji Rao, was placed on the Peshwa's gadi in his seventeenth year; Raghunath became Regent and the de facto ruler of the State.'

IN-PUNE.text: Peshwa Balaji Bajirao (Nanasaheb) dies — five months after Panipat, where his son and his cousin were killed.
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII p. 197: 'Shortly after hearing the result of the battle of Panipat Balaji Rao Peshwa died on 23 June, 1761.'

IN-PUNE.detail: the Nizam invades after Panipat and ravages the country up to Toka. His army is routed at Uruli near Poona in January 1762, but the regent Raghunathrao grants him lenient terms.
IN-PUNE.outcome: Maratha victory; the Nizam's army suffered a clear defeat
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII p. 201: 'Skirmishes extending over several months were followed by a decisive battle in January, 1762, in which the Nizam's army suffered a clear defeat ... the Regent ... conciliated the defeated enemy by granting him very favourable terms.' Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II chronology pp. 463–464: 'Nizam Ali occupies Chas and comes to Uruli where he is routed.'

IN-PUNE.text: Madhavrao I dies — At Theur, of consumption, aged twenty-seven
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII p. 222: 'Madhav Rao died a premature death on 18 November, 1772.' (Theur and the cause of death remain web-only.)

IN-PUNE.text: Peshwa Narayanrao murdered — killed at Poona in a plot laid by his uncle Raghunathrao. The ministers then formed the Barbhai regency against Raghunathrao.
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII p. 256: 'Narayan Rao ... was murdered in August 1773. It was soon discovered that his uncle Raghunath and his wife were the prime movers behind the plot'; chronology p. 834: '1773, August 30'.

IN-PUNE.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs East India Company
IN-PUNE.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-PUNE.detail: Calcutta repudiates the Surat treaty and makes peace with the Poona regency in March 1776. Bombay does not honour it, and war resumes in 1778.
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 835: '1776, March Treaty of Purandhar to secure a general peace between the E.I. Company and the Marathas.' p. 286: the Supreme Government 'declared the treaty concluded with Raghoba (Raghunath Rao) invalid and the Maratha war as impolitic, dangerous, unauthorized and unjust'.

IN-PUNE.detail: The Battle of Wadgaon was fought between the Maratha Confederacy and the British East India Company near Vadgaon Maval village in Maharashtra.
IN-PUNE.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs East India Company
IN-PUNE.outcome: Maratha victory; the Bombay army advancing on Poona with Raghunathrao was surrounded near Wadgaon and signed the Convention of Wadgaon (16 January 1779), agreeing to surrender Raghunathrao and give up Salsette
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII p. 256: 'The English force ... was almost overwhelmed, and concluded on 16 January, 1779, the convention of Wadgaon, agreeing to the surrender of Raghunath Rao, evacuation of Salsette and other islands ... Mahadji Sindia was the architect of this debacle of English arms at Wadgaon.'

IN-PUNE.detail: Goddard marches on Poona by the Bor Ghat and is held at Khandala by Haripant Phadke, the Patwardhans and Tukoji Holkar. After three months of harassment he retreats to Bombay with heavy losses.
IN-PUNE.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs East India Company
IN-PUNE.outcome: Maratha victory; Goddard's army forced back to Bombay with about 3,000 killed and wounded
IN-PUNE.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 108: 'Constant skirmishing continued for three months, February to April, below the ghats, in which the Marathas inflicted several defeats and losses upon the enemy ... Goddard found himself isolated at Khandala ... went back to Bombay suffering severe losses ... three thousand men dead and wounded'.

IN-PUNE.text: Mahadji Scindia dies — At Wanowrie near Pune, of a fever
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 839: '1794, February 12 Death of Mahadji Sindia at Vanawadi (near Poona) (pp. 263, 407).'

IN-PUNE.text: Peshwa Sawai Madhavrao dies — from a fall from a palace window in Poona, seven months after Kharda.
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII p. 263: 'The Peshwa from whom he derived support, accidentally fell down from a palace window or committed suicide (27 October, 1795).'

IN-PUNE.detail: after Sawai Madhavrao's death, Raghunathrao's son is installed on 5 December 1796, aged twenty-one, by Nana Phadnavis with the consent of Scindia, Holkar, the Bhonsle and the Nizam.
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII p. 488: 'He was installed as the Peshwa at the age of twenty-one on December 5, 1796, by Nana Phadnis with the consent of the great feudatories of the State—Sindia, Holkar, Bhosle and the Nizam.'
HCIP VIII chronology p. 840: '1800, March 13 Death of Nana Phadnis'; p. 516 lists among the losses of the decade 'Nana Phadnis on 13 March, 1800'.

IN-PUNE.detail: The Battle of Pune took place on 25 October 1802 near Pune between the states of the Maratha Confederacy.
IN-PUNE.belligerents: Holkar (Indore State) vs Maratha Empire, Gwalior (Scindia)
IN-PUNE.outcome: Holkar victory; Yashwantrao defeated the Peshwa's and Scindia's armies at Hadapsar and Bajirao II fled Poona for the coast
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII p. 492: 'Yashwant's victory over Sindia's general Sadashiv Bhaskar in the plains of Hadapsar on 25 October, 1802 ... The Peshwa fled from Poona ... Yashwant Rao Holkar's triumph at Hadapsar drove the Peshwa into the arms of the English.'

IN-PUNE.detail: the Peshwa's attack on the Poona residency fails
IN-PUNE.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs East India Company
IN-PUNE.outcome: East India Company victory; Bapu Gokhale's attack on the small force at Kirkee failed with about 500 Maratha casualties to 86 British
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII pp. 505–506: 'Bapu Gokhale with 18,000 horse, 8,000 foot and 14 guns launched an unsuccessful attack on the small force led by Captain Burr ... In the battle of Kirkee, the British losses were 86 killed and wounded as against 500 of the Marathas.'

IN-PUNE.detail: ten days after Khadki, General Smith crosses the Mula-Mutha at Yerwada on 15 November 1817 and defeats Bapu Gokhale. Bajirao II abandons Poona for Purandar, and the British flag goes up over the Peshwa's palace.
IN-PUNE.belligerents: East India Company vs Maratha Empire
IN-PUNE.outcome: East India Company victory; Bapu Gokhale defeated and Poona abandoned by the Peshwa
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII p. 506: 'From Sirur General Smith arrived at Kirkee, defeated Bapu Gokhale at the battle of Yeravda on 15 November, 1817, and compelled the Peshwa to retreat to Purandhar.' Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 490: 'Smith on 15th November crossed the river at Yeravda'.

IN-PUNE.detail: on 13 June 1817 Elphinstone forces Bajirao II to hand over Trimbakji Dengle, formally dissolve the Maratha confederacy and give up his claims on Baroda.
IN-PUNE.source: HCIP VIII p. 503: 'The Peshwa was compelled by Elphinstone to sign the treaty of Poona on 13 June, 1817 ... The Peshwa recognised the dissolution in form and substance of the Maratha confederacy'.

IN-PUNE.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs East India Company
IN-PUNE.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-PUNE.detail: a small Company force holds off the Peshwa's army on the Bhima
IN-PUNE.belligerents: East India Company vs Maratha Empire
IN-PUNE.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 492: 'Staunton, taken by surprise, took cover in the village where a bitter fight raged throughout the day ... Towards evening they showed signs of exhaustion having lost about 175 men ... Bajirao, however, suddenly resumed his flight, having been apprized of General Smith's approach on his track. Staunton returned to Sirur with his wounded.'

PK-JAMSHORO.detail: In 1298–99, a Mongol army invaded the Sindh region of the Delhi Sultanate, and occupied the fort of Sivistan in present-day Pakistan.
PK-JAMSHORO.belligerents: Mongols, possibly Neguderi fugitives vs Delhi Sultanate, Soomra dynasty

IN-GANDHINAGAR.detail: Alauddin Khalji's conquest of Gujarat, also known as the Muslim conquest of Gujarat, began in 1299 when the Delhi Sultanate ruler Alauddin Khalji sent an army.
IN-GANDHINAGAR.outcome: Delhi Sultanate victory Fall of Vaghelas

IN-GANDHINAGAR.detail: In 1520 Rana Sanga, the Rana of Mewar, led Rajput armies of Kingdom of Mewar and its vassal states to invade the Gujarat Sultanate.
IN-GANDHINAGAR.belligerents: Kingdom of Mewar vs Gujarat Sultanate

IN-NORTH-DEL.detail: Alauddin Khalji turns back the Mongol army at the gates of Delhi
The Battle of Narela (1452) was a decisive battle fought during the Lodi–Sharqi War near Narela, north of Delhi.
The Battle of Narela took place on 16 January 1757, at Narela, on the outskirts of Delhi, between the Maratha Army led by Antaji Mankeshwar and an army of Ahmad Shah Abdali.

IN-JYOTIBA-PHULE-NAGAR.detail: Malik Nayak crushes the Mongol invasion of Hindustan

PK-KHANEWAL.detail: Duwa sent a fresh Chagatai expedition under Kopek to answer the reverse of 1305; it was met and broken up in the Punjab river country by Malik Kafur and Malik Tughluq — a separate invasion from that of 1303.
PK-KHANEWAL.outcome: Delhi victory; Mongol forces expelled from India.

PK-KHANEWAL.detail: The Battle of the Ravi Ford took place on 12 December 1762 between Afghans and Sikhs on the Ravi River.

PK-OKARA.detail: The Battle of Saraswati was fought between two factions of the Delhi Sultanate in 1320, on the Delhi-Dipalpur route, at a place called Saraswati.
PK-OKARA.belligerents: Malik Tughluq's forces Khokhars vs Khusrau Khan's forces

PK-OKARA.detail: The Battle of Basarke, also known as Battle of Basarke and Hujra Shah, was fought on 23 October 1736 between the Sikh forces led by Nawab Kapur Singh and the Mughal forces.
PK-OKARA.outcome: Sikh victory; the Buddha Dal defeated at Basarke.

IN-SOUTH-EAST.detail: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq raises the third city of Delhi, thirteen gates and sloping walls, on the ridge; abandoned within fifteen years.
IN-SOUTH-EAST.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SOUTH-EAST.text: Amir Khusrau dies — Poet, musician, "parrot of India"
IN-SOUTH-EAST.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SOUTH-EAST.text: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq dies — Killed when a pavilion built for his welcome at Afghanpur collapsed
IN-SOUTH-EAST.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SOUTH-EAST.text: Nizamuddin Auliya dies — The Chishti saint of Delhi
IN-SOUTH-EAST.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SOUTH-EAST.belligerents: Hem Chandra Vikramaditya vs Mughal Empire
IN-SOUTH-EAST.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-SOUTH-EAST.detail: Haji Begum’s tomb for her husband, the first garden-tomb in India and the model for the Taj.
IN-SOUTH-EAST.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SOUTH-EAST.detail: Peshwa Baji Rao I appears before the Mughal capital on 29 March 1737; when the defenders sally out, his commander Satvoji Jadhav lures them from their guns and routs them, and the Peshwa withdraws as suddenly as he came.
IN-SOUTH-EAST.outcome: Maratha victory; the Mughal sally near Delhi routed, the Turani party discredited at court
IN-SOUTH-EAST.source: HCIP VIII p. 89: 'the defenders sallied out to attack the Peshwa’s troops. The Peshwa’s commander, Satvoji Jadhav, lured the Mughul force beyond the protection of its artillery and then enveloping it, completely routed it.'; chronology p. 819: '1737, March 30 Peshwa’s commander, Satvoji Jadhav, routs the Mughul army near Delhi'

IN-SOUTH-EAST.detail: the dismissed wazir Safdar Jang, with Suraj Mal's Jats, besieges the capital from March to November against Emperor Ahmad Shah, Imad-ul-Mulk and Najib Khan; his grand assault fails and he withdraws to Awadh.
IN-SOUTH-EAST.belligerents: Mughal Empire (Ahmad Shah, Imad-ul-Mulk, Najib Khan's Rohillas, Maratha contingent) vs Awadh (Safdar Jang), Bharatpur (Suraj Mal)
IN-SOUTH-EAST.outcome: Mughal Empire victory; Safdar Jang's attacks repulsed and he lost the wazirship and retired to Awadh, though Sarkar notes the imperialists 'gained no decisive victory'
IN-SOUTH-EAST.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 310-311: '§ 19. Grand battle of 29 September... He then took horse, charged and routed the Jats... But though the imperialists repulsed every attack of Safdar Jang and steadily pushed him further away from the capital, they gained no decisive victory.'; HCIP VIII p. 113-114: 'a civil war between the emperor and Safdar Jang from March 1753 and ultimately he departed for Awadh in November 1753'

IN-HOSHANGABAD.text: Prataparudra II dies — The last Kakatiya, taken at Warangal by Ulugh Khan
IN-HOSHANGABAD.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-KOPPAL.text: Fall of Kampili to the Delhi Sultanate
IN-KOPPAL.outcome: Delhi victory — the kingdom annexed; its embers light an empire

IN-KOPPAL.detail: The Siege of Koppal was conducted during the Third Anglo-Mysore War by forces of the Nizam of Hyderabad under the command of Mahabat Jung.
IN-KOPPAL.belligerents: Kingdom of Mysore vs Hyderabad, British East India Company

IN-NEEMUCH.belligerents: Udaipur (Mewar) (Hammir Singh) vs Delhi Sultanate (Muhammad bin Tughluq)
IN-NEEMUCH.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

PK-THATTA.text: Muhammad bin Tughlaq dies — At Thatta, chasing rebels in Sindh
PK-THATTA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BANGALORE.detail: The Bahmani–Vijayanagar War of 1375–1378 between the Bahmani Sultanate and the Vijayanagara Empire began under the reign of Vijayanagara ruler Bukka Raya I.
Krishnadevaraya's Bahmani expedition or Krishnadevaraya's Deccan expedition was a pivotal event in the history of the Bahmani Sultanate and the Vijayanagara Empire.
