IN-BANGALORE.belligerents: Vijayanagara Empire vs Bahmani Sultanate Sultanate of Bijapur Bidar Sultanate Golconda Sultanate Ahmadnagar Sultanate

IN-BANGALORE.detail: The Vijayanagar Invasion of Bijapur was a coordinated campaign by a coalition of Ahmadnagar, Golkonda, and Vijayanagara, aimed at weakening the Bijapur Sultanate in the year 1543.
The Ahmednagar invasion of Bidar led by Burhan Nizam Shah I was a campaign aimed at expanding his influence in the Deccan.
IN-BANGALORE.belligerents: Deccan Sultanates Ahmednagar Sultanate Golconda Sultanate Berar Sultanate vs Deccan Sultanates Bijapur Sultanate Bidar Sultanate

IN-BANGALORE.detail: Saif Ain-ul-Mulk's Rebellion was a rebellion against the sultan of Bijapur Ibrahim Adil Shah I by Saif Ain-ul-Mulk after he was wrongly blamed by Ibrahim Adil Shah.
The Siege of Bangalore was a siege of the town and fortifications of Bangalore during the Third Anglo-Mysore War by forces of the British East India Company.
IN-BANGALORE.belligerents: East India Company, Kingdom of Great Britain vs Kingdom of Mysore

IN-BUXAR.belligerents: Jaunpur Sultanate vs Ujjainiyas of Bhojpur
IN-BUXAR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-BUXAR.detail: the Company beats Mir Qasim, Awadh and the Mughal emperor together, winning the Diwani of Bengal
IN-BUXAR.belligerents: East India Company vs Mughal Empire, Awadh & Mir Qasim of Bengal
IN-BUXAR.outcome: East India Company victory; Shuja-ud-daulah’s 'crushing defeat' leaves Awadh and Shah Alam at the Company’s mercy — Mir Qasim, already stripped by Shuja, took no real part
IN-BUXAR.source: HCIP VIII p. 115: 'The two armies met at Buxar on 22 October, 1764. It resulted in Shuja-ud-daulah’s crushing defeat ... It confirmed British supremacy over Bengal and Bihar'; p. 349: 'Before the battle Mir Qasim had been imprisoned and deprived of his possessions by Shuja-ud-daulah.' Books disagree on the date: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 545: 'crushing defeat at Buxar (23 October 1764)'.

LK-COLOMBO.detail: Zheng He carries off Vira Alakesvara — the Ming admiral's fleet took the last king of the Gampola line, ruling from Kotte, captive to China, the only occasion on which a Chinese expedition removed a South Asian ruler. The Ming released and enthroned Parakramabahu VI, whose Kingdom of Kotte dates from 1412.
LK-COLOMBO.belligerents: Ming Chinese fleet under Zheng He vs Gampola (Vira Alakesvara, ruling from Kotte)
LK-COLOMBO.outcome: Chinese victory; the ruler taken to Nanjing, Parakramabahu VI enthroned
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-COLOMBO.belligerents: Sitawaka, Kandy, Raigama, Jaffna, Calicut, Tanjore, Vanni chieftains, Dutch East India Company from 1638 vs Portuguese Empire, Portuguese India, Portuguese Ceylon, Lascarins, Kotte
LK-COLOMBO.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

LK-COLOMBO.detail: the Portuguese field army was destroyed by Sitawaka, the high-water mark of that kingdom and the heaviest Portuguese defeat of the century on the island.
LK-COLOMBO.belligerents: Sitawaka vs the Portuguese and Kotte
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-COLOMBO.detail: after seven months of blockade and severe famine the Portuguese garrison surrendered in May 1656. The Dutch then shut their Kandyan allies out of the city, and the alliance broke.
LK-COLOMBO.belligerents: Dutch East India Company vs the Portuguese garrison of Colombo
LK-COLOMBO.outcome: Portuguese surrender; the Dutch keep the city for themselves
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-COLOMBO.detail: The British take Dutch Ceylon — Trincomalee, Batticaloa, Jaffna, Mullaitivu and Mannar fell through the autumn, and Colombo surrendered on 15 February 1796.
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-COLOMBO.detail: The Japanese carrier strike on Colombo — Japanese carrier aircraft struck the harbour on 5 April and sank the cruisers Dorsetshire and Cornwall the same day. On 9 April they struck Trincomalee and sank the carrier Hermes off Batticaloa. The Eastern Fleet withdrew to East Africa - the heaviest attack ever made on the island.
LK-COLOMBO.belligerents: Imperial Japanese Navy vs the Royal Navy and RAF
LK-COLOMBO.outcome: Japanese tactical victory; the Eastern Fleet withdraws from Ceylon
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-COLOMBO.text: Ceylon becomes an independent dominion under D. S. Senanayake
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

LK-COLOMBO.text: The Sinhala Only Act makes Sinhala the sole official language
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

LK-COLOMBO.text: The anti-Tamil riots of May and June
LK-COLOMBO.detail: some 300 killed and 12,000 displaced under a state of emergency
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

LK-COLOMBO.text: Prime Minister S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike is shot at his Colombo home by a Buddhist monk and dies the next day
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

LK-COLOMBO.text: Sirimavo Bandaranaike becomes the world's first woman prime minister
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

LK-COLOMBO.text: Ceylon becomes the Republic of Sri Lanka, cutting the last ties to the Crown
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

LK-COLOMBO.detail: after an LTTE ambush killed thirteen soldiers at Thirunelveli on 23 July, organised mobs attacked Tamil civilians in Colombo, Kandy and elsewhere for a week, using electoral rolls to find homes and businesses. Fifty-three Tamil detainees were killed inside Welikada prison on 25 and 27 July. About 150,000 people were displaced and mass Tamil emigration began. No one has ever been convicted for any of it. This was not a battle, and it is where the civil war starts.
LK-COLOMBO.belligerents: Organised mobs, with documented state facilitation, against Tamil civilians
LK-COLOMBO.outcome: The pogrom that began the twenty-six-year civil war
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-COLOMBO.detail: fought as reciprocal assassination rather than as battles, and answered by state-linked death squads. Over ten thousand bodies were recovered and the claims of enforced disappearance run far higher. The JVP leadership was captured and killed in November 1989.
LK-COLOMBO.belligerents: Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna vs the government of Sri Lanka and state-linked death squads
LK-COLOMBO.outcome: The JVP destroyed; tens of thousands dead or disappeared on both sides
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-COLOMBO.text: President Ranasinghe Premadasa is killed by an LTTE suicide bomber at the May Day rally in Colombo
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

LK-COLOMBO.detail: signed on 22 February and monitored by a Nordic mission. It held in form for six years. The LTTE left the talks in 2003 and split in 2004 when its eastern commander defected to the government side, taking the East with him.
LK-COLOMBO.belligerents: Government of Sri Lanka and the LTTE, brokered by Norway
LK-COLOMBO.outcome: Four years of formal truce; the LTTE splits in 2004
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-COLOMBO.detail: suicide attacks on three churches and three hotels in Colombo, Negombo and Batticaloa kill 269
LK-COLOMBO.belligerents: National Thowheeth Jama'ath against worshippers and hotel guests
LK-COLOMBO.outcome: The deadliest attack since the war; a state of emergency
LK-COLOMBO.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

IN-WANAPARTHY.detail: Deva Raya I routs Firuz Shah Bahmani, breaking Bahmani momentum
IN-WANAPARTHY.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-JHALAWAR.detail: The Siege of Gagron (1423) was a military campaign by Sultan Hoshang Shah of Malwa Sultanate against the fort of Gagron, a key stronghold of the Khichi Chauhans.
IN-JHALAWAR.belligerents: Malwa Sultanate, Kherla kingdom vs Khichi Chauhan Rajputs

IN-JHALAWAR.detail: The Siege of Gagron in 1444 was a military campaign led by Mahmud Khalji of the Malwa Sultanate against the Khichi Chauhan Rajputs.
IN-JHALAWAR.belligerents: Malwa Sultanate vs Khichi Chauhan Rajputs, Kingdom of Mewar

IN-JHALAWAR.detail: The Battle of Gagron was fought in 1519 between Mahmud Khalji II of Malwa and the Kingdom of Mewar's Rana Sanga.
IN-JHALAWAR.belligerents: Kingdom of Mewar Kingdom of Jaipur Tomaras of Gwalior Rathores of Merta vs Malwa Sultanate, Gujarat Sultanate
IN-JHALAWAR.outcome: Mahmud Khalji II taken as prisoner for six months.

IN-AHMADABAD.detail: Ahmad Shah I’s congregational mosque, 260 pillars, in the city he had founded thirteen years before.
IN-AHMADABAD.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)
Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AHMADABAD.detail: Raghunathrao and Damaji Gaekwad besiege Ahmedabad, capital of Gujarat's Muslim rulers for three centuries, and Jawan Mard Khan Babi surrenders it on 20 March 1753.
IN-AHMADABAD.outcome: Maratha victory; Jawan Mard Khan Babi surrendered the city and retired to Radhanpur
IN-AHMADABAD.source: HCIP VIII p. 284: 'The capital of Musalman kings for over three centuries was stoutly defended by Jawan Mard Khan Babi. After a long investment Babi surrendered the capital city on 20 March and retired to his jagir at Radhanpur.' Chronology p. 825 dates it 1753, March 20.

IN-AHMADABAD.detail: General Goddard and Fateh Singh Gaekwad, allied by the treaty of Kandila, take Ahmedabad by assault on 15 February 1780 and hand it to the Gaekwad.
IN-AHMADABAD.belligerents: East India Company, Fateh Singh Gaekwad vs Maratha Empire
IN-AHMADABAD.outcome: East India Company victory; Ahmedabad taken by assault
IN-AHMADABAD.source: HCIP VIII p. 286: 'the allies marched on Ahmadabad and took it by assault on 15 February, 1780, whereupon it was delivered to Fateh Singh.' Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire III p. 222: 'Goddard captured Ahmadabad on 15th Feb. 1780'.

IN-RAJGARH.belligerents: Kingdom of Mewar and Kingdom of Marwar vs Malwa Sultanate, Gujarat Sultanate, Nagaur Sultanate
IN-RAJGARH.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-MADHUBANI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

LK-JAFFNA.text: Kotte conquest of the Jaffna kingdom
LK-JAFFNA.detail: Parakramabahu VI's adopted son Prince Sapumal takes Jaffna (1450) after breaking the Vanni chiefs, and rules it as viceroy of Kotte until 1467.
LK-JAFFNA.belligerents: Kingdom of Kotte vs Jaffna Kingdom, Vanni chieftaincies (until 1450)
LK-JAFFNA.outcome: Kotte victory; Jaffna under Prince Sapumal as viceroy, 1450-1467

LK-JAFFNA.detail: Kanakasooriya Cinkaiariyan returns from Madurai with mercenaries and retakes the Jaffna kingdom from Kotte in the year Parakramabahu VI dies; Sapumal leaves for the Kotte succession.
LK-JAFFNA.belligerents: Jaffna Kingdom (Kanakasooriya Cinkaiariyan) vs Kingdom of Kotte
LK-JAFFNA.outcome: Jaffna victory; the kingdom independent again until the Portuguese (1619)
LK-JAFFNA.source: Wikipedia, Jaffna Kingdom; Kotte conquest of the Jaffna kingdom (web; flagged for promotion)

LK-JAFFNA.detail: The Battle of Vannarpannai was a battle fought in 1619 between the forces of Cankili II, the last ruler of the Jaffna Kingdom, and the Portuguese under Phillippe de Oliveira.
LK-JAFFNA.belligerents: Nandi flag Jaffna Kingdom, Thanjavur Nayaks vs Portuguese Empire

LK-JAFFNA.text: Portuguese conquest of the Jaffna kingdom
LK-JAFFNA.detail: Cankili II was taken to Goa and executed. The last independent Tamil kingdom on the island came to an end.
LK-JAFFNA.belligerents: Portuguese under Filipe de Oliveira vs Cankili II of Jaffna
LK-JAFFNA.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-JAFFNA.text: The burning of the Jaffna Public Library
LK-JAFFNA.detail: police and paramilitaries destroy 97,000 volumes, one of the finest Tamil collections in Asia
LK-JAFFNA.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

LK-JAFFNA.detail: the Indian Peace Keeping Force fights the LTTE it came to disarm
LK-JAFFNA.source: Wikipedia: List of wars involving India

LK-JAFFNA.detail: the Indian Peace Keeping Force arrived under the Indo-Lanka Accord to disarm the LTTE and ended up fighting it for three years. India took Jaffna at heavy cost, lost some twelve hundred dead and withdrew in March 1990 without disarming anyone; the LTTE walked back into Jaffna behind it. Independent Tamil human-rights monitors documented the killing of some sixty to seventy patients and staff at Jaffna Teaching Hospital in October 1987; India has never acknowledged it or held an inquiry.
LK-JAFFNA.belligerents: Indian Peace Keeping Force vs the LTTE
LK-JAFFNA.outcome: India withdraws; the LTTE returns to Jaffna stronger
LK-JAFFNA.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-JAFFNA.detail: the army recovered LTTE-held ground in the Jaffna peninsula for the first time, and was stopped not by the Tigers but by India, which turned back a relief flotilla and then airdropped supplies into the peninsula under fighter escort on 4 June.
LK-JAFFNA.belligerents: Sri Lanka Army and Air Force vs the LTTE
LK-JAFFNA.outcome: Vadamarachchi taken; the offensive halted under Indian pressure
LK-JAFFNA.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-JAFFNA.text: Operation Riviresa and the fall of Jaffna
LK-JAFFNA.detail: the army took Jaffna city in early December and held it for the rest of the war. Between a third and half a million civilians left the peninsula in an exodus the LTTE ordered.
LK-JAFFNA.belligerents: Sri Lanka Army vs the LTTE
LK-JAFFNA.outcome: Jaffna taken and held; mass civilian displacement
LK-JAFFNA.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

IN-NAGAON.text: Sankaradeva is born — At Bordowa in Nagaon.
IN-NAGAON.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-NAGAON.detail: a Burmese army wins at Khagarjan (Nowgong), drives out Purandar Singha and Ruchinath and restores Chandrakanta Singha as a Burmese client.
IN-NAGAON.belligerents: Konbaung (Burmese) Empire vs Ahom Kingdom (Purandar Singha, Ruchinath)
IN-NAGAON.outcome: Konbaung victory; Chandrakanta reinstated, Purandar and Ruchinath flee to Bengal
IN-NAGAON.source: HCIP IX p. 129: 'A Burmese army successfully invaded Assam in 1819, and reinstated Chandrakanta on the throne. Both Ruchinath and his protege fled to Bengal.' Acharyya, History of Medieval Assam p. 27: 'the victory of the Burmese army at Khagarjan (Nowgong) in 1819.'

IN-LUCKNOW.detail: The Lodi–Sharqi War (1452–1500) were a series of prolonged conflicts between the Lodi dynasty of Delhi and the Sharqi dynasty of Jaunpur in northern India.
Asaf-ud-Daula’s famine-relief work, the vaulted hall unsupported by beams, with the labyrinth above it.
IN-LUCKNOW.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-LUCKNOW.detail: under pressure from Wellesley, Nawab-Wazir Saadat Ali Khan signs a new subsidiary treaty in November 1801 ceding Rohilkhand, Gorakhpur and the lower Ganga–Jamuna Doab — about half his kingdom — to the Company.
IN-LUCKNOW.source: HCIP VIII p. 524: 'The unfortunate Nawab had to yield, “a passive, helpless and reluctant obedience”. In November 1801 a new subsidiary treaty was signed by which he ceded what are now known as Gorakhpur and Rohilkhand divisions, besides the lower portion of the Ganga-Jamuna Doab.'

IN-LUCKNOW.detail: Wajid Ali Shah refuses to sign away his kingdom, taking off his turban and placing it in Outram's hands; the Company proclaims Oudh British territory (February 1856) and exiles the king to Calcutta.
IN-LUCKNOW.source: HCIP IX p. 308-309: 'On 4 February, 1856, the Resident had an interview with “His Majesty” Wajid Ali... Outram could not, by any means, persuade him to sign the treaty... Thereupon a proclamation... was issued, “declaring the province of Oude to be thenceforth, for ever, a component part of the British Indian Empire.”'

IN-LUCKNOW.detail: Awadh's rebels besiege the British garrison from 30 June 1857; Havelock and Outram fight their way in on 25 September but are themselves shut up, and Colin Campbell breaks through on 17 November and evacuates the Residency, leaving the city to the rebels until March 1858.
IN-LUCKNOW.belligerents: East India Company vs Awadh (Begum Hazrat Mahal's government), rebel sepoys
IN-LUCKNOW.outcome: East India Company victory; the Residency held and its garrison relieved and withdrawn, though the city stayed in rebel hands
IN-LUCKNOW.source: HCIP IX p. 568-570: 'the tiny besieged garrison at the Residency were heroically defending themselves against enormous odds since June 30... joined the garrison at Lakhnau on the evening of the 25th... he joined the besieged in the Residency on November 17... The Residency was vacated, and Outram took his position at Alambagh outside the city.'

IN-LUCKNOW.detail: Campbell's army, joined by Jang Bahadur's Gurkhas, fights its way through the fortified city street by street from 3 March and holds all of Lucknow by 21 March, though some sixty thousand rebels escape into the Awadh countryside.
IN-LUCKNOW.belligerents: East India Company, Nepal vs Awadh (Begum Hazrat Mahal's government), rebel sepoys
IN-LUCKNOW.outcome: East India Company victory; Lucknow retaken, but the rebel army was allowed to disperse unpursued
IN-LUCKNOW.source: HCIP IX p. 571: 'On March 3 and 4, the advanced section of the British army reached the outskirts of the city, and though the sepoys fought with stubborn courage... the British gained possession of the whole city by 21 March. The Gurkha troops under Jang Bahadur had joined the British army on 11 March, and took part in the assault on Lakhnau.'

IN-NEW-DELHI.detail: The Siege of Delhi (1452) was a military campaign during the Lodi–Sharqi War in which Sultan Mahmud Shah Sharqi of the Jaunpur Sultanate besieged the city of Delhi.

IN-NEW-DELHI.text: Humayun dies — Fell down the stairs of his library at the Purana Qila, six months after regaining Delhi.
IN-NEW-DELHI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-NEW-DELHI.detail: Bajirao I raids to the gates of Delhi. On 30 March his commander Satvoji Jadhav draws the Mughal force away from its guns and routes it, and the Peshwa then withdraws.
IN-NEW-DELHI.outcome: Maratha victory; the Mughal sortie routed outside Delhi
IN-NEW-DELHI.source: HCIP VIII p. 89: 'The Peshwa's commander, Satvoji Jadhav, lured the Mughul force beyond the protection of its artillery and then enveloping it, completely routed it'; chronology p. 819: '1737, March 30 Peshwa's commander, Satvoji Jadhav, routs the Mughul army near Delhi.'

IN-NEW-DELHI.detail: The Battle of Delhi in 1757, also referred to as the Second Battle of Delhi, was fought on 11 August 1757 by the Maratha Confederacy under the command of Raghunath Rao.
IN-NEW-DELHI.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs Rohilkhand (Rohillas) — Najib Khan
IN-NEW-DELHI.outcome: Maratha victory; Raghunath Rao forced Najib to evacuate Delhi, Najib making peace on 9 September
IN-NEW-DELHI.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 827: '1757, August 11 Raghunath Rao, the Maratha general, attacks Delhi and captures it (p. 188)... 1757, September 9 Najib Khan Rohilla makes peace with the Marathas (p. 188).'; Sarkar II contents: 'Raghunath attacks Delhi, 146—Najib evacuates Delhi, 151'

IN-NEW-DELHI.detail: The Capture of Delhi, fought in 1760, pitted the forces of the Maratha Empire against those of the Durrani Empire led by Yakub Ali Khan.
IN-NEW-DELHI.belligerents: Maratha Empire, Bharatpur State vs Durrani Empire
IN-NEW-DELHI.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 828: '1760, August 2 Sadashiv Rao Bhau, the commandant of the Marathas, captures Delhi (p. 193)'; Sarkar II p. 252: '§ 7. The Bhau captures Delhi.'

IN-NEW-DELHI.detail: Sikh attacks on Delhi were a number of attacks and raids carried out by the Sikhs on the Mughal capital of Delhi in the second half of the 18th century.
IN-NEW-DELHI.belligerents: Sikh Confederacy, Rohillas (from 1787), Co-belligirents vs Mughal Empire, Rohillas (until 1787), Maratha Confederacy (1784-1788)
IN-NEW-DELHI.outcome: Sikh victory; plunder of Mughal, Rohilla and Rajput territories.

IN-NEW-DELHI.detail: In 1771, the forces of the Maratha Empire led by Mahadaji Shinde captured Delhi from the Rohillas and installed the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II on the throne of Delhi.
IN-NEW-DELHI.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 833: '1771, February 10 Mahadji Sindia captures Delhi and requests Shah Alam to return to his capital (pp. 221, 255, 367).'; Sarkar III contents: 'Delhi captured by Marathas 1771, 29'

IN-NEW-DELHI.detail: when Shah Alam II defies them over Zabita Khan, the Marathas under Visaji Krishna and Tukoji Holkar defeat the imperial army of Najaf Khan and Madec below the Old Fort of Delhi (17 December 1772); the emperor submits, makes Zabita Mir Bakhshi and grants them Kora and Allahabad.
IN-NEW-DELHI.outcome: Maratha victory; the imperialists shut up in Delhi and the emperor forced to accept Maratha terms
IN-NEW-DELHI.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire III p. 69: '§15. Battle of Purana Qila... the decisive engagement came off on Friday the 17th of December... superior generalship, even more than superior numbers, decided the issue against him'; p. 73: 'But it was decisive.'; HCIP VIII chronology p. 834: '1772, December The Marathas (Holkar and Visaji Krishna) compel Shah Alam II to confer the office of Mir Bakshi on Zabita Khan'

IN-NEW-DELHI.text: Mir Qasim dies — The able Nawab of Bengal (1760–63) who tried to rule free of the Company, lost at Buxar and died a wanderer near Delhi.
IN-NEW-DELHI.source: HCIP VIII p. 349: 'he was allowed to escape from the battle-field, led a wandering life for some years till he met with his end near Delhi in 1777. Thus ended the last efforts of a Bengal prince to maintain his independence of English control.'

IN-NEW-DELHI.text: Mirza Najaf Khan dies — Regent of the empire and victor of Barsana and Dig
IN-NEW-DELHI.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire III p. 227: 'after lingering in bed for months the regent passed away on 6th April. With him departed the last hope of the Mughals in India.'; HCIP VIII p. 257: 'Mirza Najaf Khan, the emperor’s Regent, died on 6 April, 1782'

IN-NEW-DELHI.detail: The Capture of Delhi took place in 1788 between the forces of Ghulam Qadir Rohilla supported by Mirza Ismail Beg, and the Marathas under Mahadji Shinde on behalf of Shah Alam II.
IN-NEW-DELHI.belligerents: Maratha Empire, Gwalior (Scindia) vs Najib-ud-Daula (Rohilla) — Ghulam Qadir, with Ismail Beg
IN-NEW-DELHI.outcome: Maratha victory; Mahadji Sindhia occupied Delhi on 2 October 1788 and restored Shah Alam II on 16 October; Ghulam Qadir fled and was captured on 31 December
IN-NEW-DELHI.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 838: '1788, October 2 Mahadji Sindia occupies Delhi (p. 399). 1788, October 16 Shah Alam II is reinstated on the Delhi throne by the Marathas (p. 399). 1788, December 31 Ghulam Qadir captured'

IN-NEW-DELHI.detail: The siege of Delhi was a decisive conflict of the Indian Rebellion of 1857.
IN-NEW-DELHI.belligerents: East India Company vs Mughal Empire (Bahadur Shah II), rebel sepoys
IN-NEW-DELHI.outcome: East India Company victory; Delhi stormed 14–20 September 1857, Nicholson mortally wounded, Bahadur Shah surrendered to Hodson on 21 September and his sons were shot
IN-NEW-DELHI.source: HCIP IX p. 567: 'the British force made a full-scale attack on Delhi on September 14. The Kashmir Gate was forced... On September 20, the British troops took the Lahore Gate and the Jumma Masjid, and finally the gates of the Red Fort were blown in... Bahadur Shah surrendered to Hodson on the sole condition that his life should be spared.'

IN-NEW-DELHI.detail: Lutyens’ Viceroy’s House and Baker’s Secretariats, twenty years in the building; the India Gate finished the same year.
IN-NEW-DELHI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-NEW-DELHI.detail: Stafford Cripps offers dominion status after the war in return for support in it; Congress and the League both refuse - "a post-dated cheque on a crashing bank" - and Quit India follows in August.
IN-NEW-DELHI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-NADIA.detail: Clive defeats Siraj-ud-Daulah through betrayal, seizing Bengal for the Company
IN-NADIA.belligerents: East India Company vs Bengal (Nawab), with French gunners
IN-NADIA.outcome: East India Company victory; Siraj-ud-daulah, deserted by Mir Ja‘far’s divisions and recalling his attacking troops, flees — militarily 'an insignificant engagement', politically a revolution that made Mir Ja‘far Nawab and gave the Company the 24 Parganas
IN-NADIA.source: HCIP VIII p. 339: 'On 23 June, 1757, took place one of the decisive events in world history. Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah ... found himself deserted in the field of battle by the general under whom was ranged the major part of his forces ... From the military point of view the battle of Plassey was an insignificant engagement. The English gathered an undeserved victory on account of the Nawab’s order of recall to his attacking troops ... After Plassey, the 24 Parganas were added to their Zamindari.'

IN-JODHPUR.text: Rao Jodha dies — Founder of Jodhpur and the Mehrangarh fort.

IN-JODHPUR.text: Rao Maldeo dies — The Rathore who made Marwar the strongest Rajput state before Akbar.

IN-JODHPUR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-KOZHIKODE.belligerents: Kingdom of Calicut, Venice, Mamluks vs Portugal
IN-KOZHIKODE.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-KOZHIKODE.detail: The naval Battle of Calicut was a military encounter between the 16 ships of the 4th Portuguese Armada and a fleet led by two Arabic corsairs.
IN-KOZHIKODE.belligerents: Portuguese Empire vs Kozhikode, Arab privateers
Zamorin of Calicut vs Portuguese Empire / Portuguese India
IN-KOZHIKODE.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-KOZHIKODE.detail: The siege of Calicut occurred in 1526, when the Zamorin, the local Indian ruler, captured the fort of Calicut from the Portuguese.
The siege of Chale or siege of Chaliyam took place in 1571 as a part of the war of the league of the Indies between the Zamorin of Calicut and the Portuguese Empire.

IN-KOZHIKODE.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs Portuguese Empire / Portuguese India
IN-KOZHIKODE.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-KOZHIKODE.detail: The Mysore invasion of Calicut was the result of the Calicut's attack on Palghat in 1756–1757.
IN-KOZHIKODE.outcome: Mysore victory; the Zamorin restores his Palghat conquests and pays an indemnity of 12 lakhs
IN-KOZHIKODE.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 243: 'The prompt and effective action taken by the combined forces of Mysore and Palghat put the Calicut forces to flight. The Zamorin was also forced to restore his Palghat conquests and to pay a war indemnity of 12 lakhs of rupees to Mysore.'

IN-KOZHIKODE.detail: Mysore's army, joined by the Ali Raja of Cannanore, overruns Kolathunad, Kottayam and Kadathanad and enters Calicut; the Zamorin, unable to pay a crore of mohurs, blows up his palace and dies in it.
IN-KOZHIKODE.belligerents: Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu), Arakkal vs Calicut (Zamorin), Kolathunad
IN-KOZHIKODE.outcome: Mysore victory; Calicut occupied and the Zamorin dies by self-immolation
IN-KOZHIKODE.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 244: 'The Mysorean army thereupon entered Calicut. The Zamorin sent the members of his family to Ponnani, blew up his palace and committed self-immolation.' Kareem, Kerala under Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan p. 32: 'He set his palace on fire and was burnt to death'.

IN-KOZHIKODE.detail: The Mysorean invasion of Malabar (1766–1792) was the military invasion of the Malabar region of Kerala, including the territories of the Zamorin of Calicut.
IN-KOZHIKODE.belligerents: Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu), Arakkal vs Calicut (Zamorin), Kolathunad, Cochin, Travancore, East India Company
IN-KOZHIKODE.outcome: East India Company victory; Mysore's quarter-century in Kerala ends with Malabar ceded to the Company in 1792
IN-KOZHIKODE.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 248: 'By the treaties of Seringapatam ... Tipu formally ceded Malabar to the British ... Thus the Mysorean attempts for about a quarter of a century to establish hegemony over Kerala ultimately ended only in the establishment of British supremacy.'

IN-KURNOOL.text: Yusuf Adil Shah's Invasion of Vijayanagara
IN-KURNOOL.detail: Yusuf Adil Shah's invasion of Vijayanagara (1505) was a conflict between the Vijayanagara Empire and the Bijapur Sultanate.
The Battle of Adoni was a battle between the Vijayanagara forces led by Venkatadri and the Bijapur army under the command of Asad Khan.
The siege of Adavani was a siege battle between Rama Raya's forces, led by Cina Timma Nayaka, and Salakamraju Tirumala's army under the command of Sanjar Khan.
IN-KURNOOL.belligerents: Aliya Rama Raya's Faction vs Salakamraju Pedda Tirumala's Faction

IN-KURNOOL.detail: The Siege of Adoni was a military conflict when Rama Raya’s brothers, Timraj and Govindraj, took control of Adoni and nearby areas while Rama Raya was away.
IN-KURNOOL.belligerents: Vijayanagara Empire, Golconda Sultanate vs Rebels

IN-KURNOOL.detail: The siege of Adoni was a military conflict that occurred between the forces of Tipu Sultan of the Kingdom of Mysore and the Maratha Confederacy.
IN-KURNOOL.belligerents: Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu) vs Hyderabad, Maratha Empire
IN-KURNOOL.outcome: Mysore victory; the confederates relieve Adoni but then evacuate it, and it falls to Tipu
IN-KURNOOL.source: HCIP VIII p. 461: 'Tipu could not carry the place by assault and had to raise the siege as the confederates marched to its relief. But as no arrangements had been made for a prolonged campaign ... the confederates evacuated the place which fell into the hands of Tipu.'

IN-RATNAGIRI.belligerents: Bijapur Sultanate vs Portuguese Empire / Portuguese India
IN-RATNAGIRI.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-DIU.detail: The Battle of Diu was a naval battle fought on 3 February 1509 in the Arabian Sea, in the port of Diu, India, between the Portuguese Empire and a joint fleet.
IN-DIU.belligerents: Portuguese Empire vs Mamluk Sultanate, Gujarat Sultanate, Kingdom of Calicut

IN-NORTH-GOA.belligerents: Bijapur Sultanate vs Portuguese Empire / Portuguese Goa
IN-NORTH-GOA.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-NORTH-GOA.detail: The Portuguese–Adil Shahi War (1555–1557) was conflict between the Portuguese Empire and the Bijapur Sultanate under Ibrahim Adil Shah I.
IN-NORTH-GOA.outcome: Peace Treaty End of Abdullah's rebellion

IN-NORTH-GOA.detail: The Vijayanagara invasion of Goa (1558) was a campaign initiated by Rama Raya against the Portuguese after years of growing tensions between the two powers.
IN-NORTH-GOA.belligerents: Vijayanagara Empire Keladi Nayakas vs Portuguese Empire
IN-NORTH-GOA.outcome: Vijayanagara Victory End of Portuguese attacks on Vijayanagara Empire

IN-NORTH-GOA.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-NORTH-GOA.detail: The siege of Ponda took place during the summer of 1675 in the region around Ponda, Goa.

IN-NORTH-GOA.belligerents: Kingdom of Mysore, Maratha Empire, Kolhapur State, Sawantwadi State vs Portuguese Empire / Portuguese India with support from Soonda and Sawantwadi as listed
IN-NORTH-GOA.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-NORTH-GOA.detail: The siege of Alorna in 1746 was a military engagement that took place in India, fought by Portuguese forces under the command of the Viceroy of India, Dom Pedro Miguel de Almeida.
IN-NORTH-GOA.belligerents: Portuguese Empire vs Maratha Empire Sawantwadi State

IN-NORTH-GOA.detail: The Battle of Tiracol was a military engagement fought by Portuguese forces under the command of the Viceroy of India Dom Pedro Miguel de Almeida Portugal e Vasconcelos.

IN-NORTH-GOA.detail: Indian forces end 451 years of the Estado da Índia in 36 hours

BD-CHITTAGONG.detail: Jai Singh’s envoy Haridas Gossain agrees with Verelst at Chittagong (14 September 1762) on an offensive and defensive alliance against Burma — Manipur’s first treaty with the Company; the relief column turned back sick.
BD-CHITTAGONG.source: HCIP IX p. 1027: 'The terms of the alliance were settled on 14th September, 1762. This was the first formal agreement between the Government of Manipur and the British Government of India ... The British contingent, however, suffered from rain and disease and had to return without achieving any success.'

IN-AGRA.detail: c. 1598, the third volume of the Akbarnama - the administration, the revenue of every province, the army, the mint, the court - the fullest statistical account of any state before modern times.
IN-AGRA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AGRA.text: Akbar dies — At Agra, after fifty years
IN-AGRA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AGRA.detail: Shah Jahan’s tomb for Mumtaz Mahal on the Yamuna; twenty-two years, twenty thousand workers.
IN-AGRA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AGRA.text: Shah Jahan dies — A prisoner in Agra Fort for eight years, within sight of the Taj.
IN-AGRA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-AGRA.detail: Bahadur Shah I wins the succession after Aurangzeb's death
IN-AGRA.belligerents: Bahadur Shah I vs Muhammad Azam Shah
IN-AGRA.source: HCIP VIII (The Maratha Supremacy) chronology p. 813: '1707, June 18 Prince M‘uazzam defeats and kills Prince A‘zam at the battle of Jajau near Samugarh (pp. 11, 78).'

IN-AGRA.detail: The Mughal war of succession (1707–1709) or the Mughal Civil War was a period of political disorder and armed conflict over succession in the Mughal Empire.
IN-AGRA.belligerents: Bahadur Shah I vs Azam Shah

IN-AGRA.detail: Farrukhsiyar, backed by the Sayyid brothers of Barha, defeats his uncle the emperor Jahandar Shah near Agra and takes the Mughal throne; Jahandar is betrayed by Asad Khan and put to death with Zulfiqar Khan.
IN-AGRA.belligerents: Farrukhsiyar and the Sayyid brothers vs Jahandar Shah and Zulfiqar Khan
IN-AGRA.outcome: Farrukhsiyar victory; Jahandar Shah fled to Delhi, was betrayed and killed, and the Sayyid brothers became the power behind the throne
IN-AGRA.source: HCIP VIII (The Maratha Supremacy) p. 17: 'Near Agra he confronted the hastily assembled hosts of his uncle. Treachery in his camp, combined with improper disposition of his forces; brought defeat upon the head of Jahandar Shah, who, with his mistress, fled to Delhi in a bullock cart.'; chronology p. 814: '1713, January Farrukh-siyar ascends the Mughul throne'

IN-AGRA.detail: The Battle of Fatehpur Sikri occurred near Fatehpur Sikri on 26 September 1721 between Mughal forces and those of the Jats.

after Panipat the Jat raja besieges the old Mughal capital and its garrison opens the gates on 12 June 1761; its artillery and treasure are carried off to Bharatpur and Dig, and the Jat kingdom reaches its greatest extent.
IN-AGRA.belligerents: Bharatpur vs Mughal Empire (garrison of Agra fort)
IN-AGRA.outcome: Bharatpur victory; the qiladar surrendered Agra fort for a lakh of rupees and five villages
IN-AGRA.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 443-444: '§ 10. Suraj Mal captures Agra fort, June 1761... the qiladar opened the gates on 12th June 1761, on being promised one lakh of Rupees in cash and five villages.'

IN-AGRA.text: Jawahir Singh dies — Assassinated, the son of Suraj Mal who besieged Delhi and fought Jaipur at Maonda
IN-AGRA.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 832: '1768, July Jawahir Singh Jat is assassinated (p. 219).'; Sarkar III p. 2: 'When Jawahir Singh’s tempestuous career ended in an appropriately violent death (June 1768)' (month differs)

IN-AGRA.detail: Rana Khan's Maratha–Jat army, with De Boigne's and Lesteneau's battalions, destroys Ismail Beg's army at Bagh Dehra outside Agra on 18 June 1788, after Ghulam Qadir has left him to defend his own Doab lands; Agra fort is relieved.
IN-AGRA.belligerents: Maratha Empire, Gwalior (Scindia), Bharatpur vs Mughal Empire (Ismail Beg)
IN-AGRA.outcome: Maratha victory; Ismail Beg's army 'ceased to exist as an instrument of war', he swam the Jamuna wounded
IN-AGRA.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire III p. 423-425: 'In the fateful morning of the 17th of June'... 'Ismail Beg’s defeat was complete and irretrievable. His army ceased to exist as an instrument of war.'; HCIP VIII p. 261: 'Sindia’s forces once more took the field and this time destroyed Ismail Beg’s army on the plains of Agra (18 June, 1788)'; chronology p. 837 gives 17/18 June

IN-AGRA.detail: Lake storms Sindhia's seven battalions outside Agra on 10 October and the fort, Sindhia's northern capital with its arsenal and 22 lakhs of treasure, surrenders on 18 October.
IN-AGRA.belligerents: East India Company vs Maratha Empire, Gwalior (Scindia)
IN-AGRA.outcome: East India Company victory; Agra fort surrendered on 18 October with all its stores
IN-AGRA.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire IV p. 294-295: '§7 The fall of Agra, 18th October... the fort was surrendered to the English on the 18th and all the immense wealth and armament within it fell into the victors’ hands' (OCR of the scan is damaged; the section heading is clear); HCIP VIII chronology p. 842: '1803, October 18 The English capture Agra (p. 496)'

IN-SANT-KABIR-NAGAR.text: Kabir dies — By tradition at Maghar, in 1518
IN-SANT-KABIR-NAGAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-KOTA.belligerents: Kingdom of Mewar vs Delhi Sultanate
IN-KOTA.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-KOTA.detail: The Battle of Mukandwara Pass, also known as the Battle of Mokandra Pass or Monson's Retreat, was fought from 8 to 10 July 1804 by forces of the Indore Maharaja.
IN-KOTA.belligerents: Maratha Empire Indore State vs British Empire, East India Company Kota State

IN-KOTA.text: Zalim Singh of Kota dies — the regent who ruled Kota for half a century in the Maharao's name and kept it out of Maratha hands.
IN-KOTA.source: Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages I p. 340: 'Zalim Singh died in 1824. Madho Singh succeeded him "with the full power exercised by his father".' p. 338: 'But for the able management of Zalim Singh, Kotah would have long since fallen an easy prey to Sindhia and Holkar.'

IN-PANIPAT.detail: Babur's guns destroy Ibrahim Lodi, ending the Delhi Sultanate and founding the Mughal Empire

IN-PANIPAT.text: Ibrahim Lodi dies — Killed at Panipat
IN-PANIPAT.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PANIPAT.text: Hemu dies — Wounded at the second battle of Panipat and beheaded in Akbar’s camp
IN-PANIPAT.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-PANIPAT.detail: Akbar defeats Hemu to re-establish Mughal suzerainty in India

IN-PANIPAT.text: Sadashivrao Bhau dies — Commander of the Maratha army, killed at the third battle of Panipat with the Peshwa’s heir Vishwasrao.
IN-PANIPAT.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 343: 'The wounded lion turned at bay and struck three or four of his assailants with his spear before he was killed and his head cut off and carried away by his slayers. Thus perished Sadashiv Rao Bhau'; p. 341: '§ 20. Death of Vishwas Rao'

IN-PANIPAT.detail: Ahmad Shah Abdali defeats the Marathas, who suffer a crippling blow
IN-PANIPAT.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs Durrani (Afghan) Empire, Rohilkhand (Rohillas), Awadh
IN-PANIPAT.outcome: Durrani victory; the Maratha army destroyed, Vishwas Rao and Sadashivrao Bhau killed, Holkar and Sindhia contingents fled
IN-PANIPAT.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 828: '1761, January 14 Ahmad Shah Abdali, defeats the Maratha army at the third battle of Panipat (pp. 44, 125, 132, 137, 146, 194-97).'; Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 274: '§16. How Shuja-ud-daulah was won over to Abdali’s side'; II contents: 'death of Vishwas Rao, 341—Bhau’s last charge and death, 342'

IN-PANIPAT.detail: The Raid of Panipat (1770) was a raid on 4 January 1770 by the Sikh forces led by Jassa Singh Ahluwalia against the Mughal forces led by Zabita Khan.
IN-PANIPAT.belligerents: Dal Khalsa vs Kingdom of Rohilkhand, Mughal Empire

IN-SAMBHAL.detail: The siege of Sambhal of 1526 by the Mughal Empire resulted in the fall and capture of Sambhal.
IN-SAMBHAL.belligerents: Mughal Empire vs Western Afghan Confederates

IN-CHANDIGARH.detail: The Mughal–Rajput wars were a series of battles between various Rajput Kingdoms and Dynasties with the Mughal Empire.
IN-CHANDIGARH.belligerents: Mughal Empire vs Rajput Kingdoms and Dynasties

IN-JALAUN.text: Rana Sanga dies — At Kalpi, a year after Khanwa
IN-JALAUN.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-JALAUN.detail: Rose defeats the Rani of Jhansi and Tantia Tope at Kunch, then at Golauli before Kalpi on 22 May 1858, and enters the deserted fortress next day.
IN-JALAUN.belligerents: East India Company vs Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Rao Sahib, Nawab of Banda, Tantia Tope's army
IN-JALAUN.outcome: East India Company victory; the rebels defeated at Golauli and Kalpi abandoned
IN-JALAUN.source: HCIP IX p. 581-582: 'On the way, he was met by the Rani and Tantia at a town called Koonch... they were severely defeated by Rose... On May 22, Rose was attacked by the rebels, but they were completely defeated. Next day when the British advanced through the ravines to Kalpi, they found that the enemy had fled'

IN-ASHOKNAGAR.detail: Babur storms the fortress held by Medini Rai
IN-ASHOKNAGAR.belligerents: Mughal Empire (Babur) vs Medini Rai of Chanderi, the Rajput chief of Malwa

IN-BALLIA.detail: Babur defeats the Afghan lords of Bengal and Bihar, completing his conquests
IN-BALLIA.belligerents: Mughal Empire vs Sultanate of Bengal

IN-CHITRAKOOT.text: Tulsidas is born — By tradition at Rajapur on the Yamuna, in 1532.
IN-CHITRAKOOT.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-DIMAPUR.detail: the Kachari capital falls; the court flees to Maibang
IN-DIMAPUR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

PK-NAROWAL.text: Guru Nanak dies — At Kartarpur on the Ravi, the town he founded
PK-NAROWAL.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

PK-NAROWAL.detail: The Conquest of Rasulnagar, also known as the Siege of Rasulnagar, was led by Maha Singh of the Sukerchakia Misl, with support from Jai Singh of the Kanhaiya Misl.
PK-NAROWAL.belligerents: Sukerchakia Misl, Kanhaiya Misl vs Chattha tribe

PK-UMERKOT.text: Akbar is born — At Umerkot in the Thar, where Humayun had taken refuge with the Rana.
PK-UMERKOT.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-JOGULAMBA.detail: The Battle of the Tungabhadra River marked the last battle of a series of conflicts in the Vijayanagar Civil War (1542-1543) between Salakamraju Tirumala and Rama Raya.
IN-JOGULAMBA.belligerents: Aliya Rama Raya's Faction vs Salakamraju dodda Tirumala's Faction

IN-AHMADNAGAR.detail: The siege of Ahmadnagar was a conflict between the Vijayanagara Empire led by Rama Raya and the Ahmadnagar Sultanate commanded by Burhan Nizam Shah I.
the first Vijayanagara-led siege of Hussain Nizam Shah I's capital, closed by a negotiated peace.
the second siege of the city in four years, this time raised in Ahmednagar's favour, with Murtaza Nizam Shah I in the defence and Ali Adil Shah I among the besiegers.
The Raid of Ahmednagar took place in 1657, when the Marathas led by Shivaji penetrated as far as Ahmednagar in hopes of asseting Bijapur Sultan, the raid, however, was repulsed.

IN-AHMADNAGAR.text: Raghunathrao dies — the ex-Peshwa (Raghoba), whose bid for the Peshwaship brought on the first Anglo-Maratha war.
IN-AHMADNAGAR.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 127: 'Raghunathrao returned to Kacheshvar in the vicinity of Kopargaum and there expired on 11 December 1783 at the age of 48.'

IN-AHMADNAGAR.detail: The siege of Ahmednagar was the first battle of the Second Anglo-Maratha War fought between the Maratha Confederacy and the British East India Company.
IN-AHMADNAGAR.belligerents: British Empire, East India Company vs Maratha Empire

IN-RANGAREDDY.text: Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk dies — Founder of the Qutb Shahi sultanate of Golconda, murdered at ninety by his son Jamsheed.
IN-RANGAREDDY.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-RANGAREDDY.detail: The Battle of Bhatvadi was fought in 1624, near modern Bhatodi Pargaon village in Maharashtra, India.
IN-RANGAREDDY.belligerents: Ahmadnagar Sultanate vs Bijapur Sultanate, Mughal Empire, Golconda Sultanate

IN-RANGAREDDY.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-DEVBHUMI-DWARKA.text: Mirabai dies — c. 1547 at Dwarka, by tradition merging into the image of Krishna
IN-DEVBHUMI-DWARKA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-OSMANABAD.detail: The siege of Paranda was a confrontation between the forces of Bijapur and the allied armies of Vijayanagar and Ahmadnagar led by Burhan Nizam Shah I.
IN-OSMANABAD.belligerents: Vijayanagar Empire, Ahmednagar Sultanate vs Bijapur Sultanate

IN-OSMANABAD.detail: The siege of Parenda (1634) was a 17th-century military conflict between the Mughal Empire and the Sultanate of Bijapur over Paranda Fort.
IN-OSMANABAD.belligerents: Mughal Empire vs Bijapur Sultanate, Ahmadnagar Sultanate

IN-LUDHIANA.detail: The Battle of Machhiwarra was fought between Mughal Empire and Suri Empire in 1555.
The siege of Sirhind was fought between the Mughal Empire and Sikh forces in 1710.
IN-LUDHIANA.belligerents: First Sikh State vs Mughal Empire

IN-LUDHIANA.detail: Harry Smith's "battle without a mistake" on the Sutlej
IN-LUDHIANA.belligerents: East India Company vs Sikh Empire

IN-LUDHIANA.detail: The battle of Baddowal was an engagement between the Sikh Khalsa Army and British forces which occurred on 21 January 1846 during the First Anglo-Sikh War.
IN-LUDHIANA.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs East India Company
IN-LUDHIANA.outcome: Sikh Empire victory; Harry Smith surprised on the march to Ludhiana, with heavy losses and his baggage and hospital stores captured
IN-LUDHIANA.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 271: 'Sir Harry Smith, while proceeding to relieve Ludhiana, was surprised at Baddowal (January 21, 1846). His losses in men were very heavy, and even his baggage and hospital stores were captured by the Sikhs. He was saved by the timely arrival of a British detachment.'

IN-FATEHGARH-SAHIB.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-FATEHGARH-SAHIB.detail: The Battle of Manupur took place on 11 March 1748 between the forces of the rising Durrani Empire led by Afghan Emperor Ahmad Shah Durrani and the armies of the Mughal Empire.
IN-FATEHGARH-SAHIB.belligerents: Durrani Empire vs Mughal Empire, Kingdom of Jaipur, Malerkotla State

IN-FATEHGARH-SAHIB.outcome: Maratha victory — Delhi and Sirhind taken
IN-FATEHGARH-SAHIB.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-FATEHGARH-SAHIB.detail: The Battle of Harnaulgarh was fought between the Durrani Empire and the Sikh Misls of Dal Khalsa in 1762.

IN-FATEHGARH-SAHIB.belligerents: Sikh misls vs Durrani (Afghan) Empire (Zain Khan, faujdar of Sarhind)
IN-FATEHGARH-SAHIB.outcome: Sikh victory; Zain Khan defeated and slain, Sarhind sacked
IN-FATEHGARH-SAHIB.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 492: 'then attacked Sarhind in a body 40,000 strong (December 1763.) ... The faujdar of Sarhind, at the head of a small impoverished army, came out of the city and was defeated and slain, with the loss of his baggage and armament. The Sikhs, flushed with victory, entered Sarhind, and "looted and totally devastated it".' Sarkar dates the attack December 1763; the decisive fight is usually put in January 1764.

IN-KATHUA.detail: The siege of Mankot (1557) was a major confrontation between the Sur Empire and the Mughal Empire led by a young Akbar.
The Battle of Basoli was fought between the Mughal Empire and the Sikhs.
IN-KATHUA.belligerents: Khalsa (Sikhs) vs Mughal Empire, Kahlur State, Guler State

IN-INDORE.detail: The Mughal conquest of Malwa was a military campaign launched by the Mughal Empire in 1560 during the reign of Akbar against the Sultanate of Malwa.
IN-INDORE.belligerents: Mughal Empire vs Malwa Sultanate, Khandesh Sultanate, Berar Sultanate

IN-INDORE.detail: Aurangzeb defeats Jaswant Singh in the war of succession
three months after Yashwantrao Holkar took Ujjain, Daulatrao Scindia's army under Sarje Rao Ghatge defeats him at Indore on 14 October 1801 and scatters his forces.
IN-INDORE.outcome: Scindia victory; Yashwantrao Holkar defeated and his forces scattered
IN-INDORE.source: HCIP VIII p. 491: 'Yashwant Rao, however, suffered a defeat at the hands of Sarza Rao Ghatge on 14 October, 1801'; chronology p. 841: '1801, October 14 Daulat Rao Sindia attacks Indore and scatters the forces of Holkar'.

IN-INDORE.detail: the last Peshwa surrenders to Malcolm on 3 June 1818. The Peshwaship ends, and he is pensioned off to Bithur.
IN-INDORE.source: HCIP VIII p. 507: 'He surrendered to Malcolm at Mhow near Indore on 3 June, 1818. The Peshwa lost his title ... The Governor-General ... guaranteed the Peshwa a pension of eight lakhs of rupees per annum.' (Place given as Mhow in HCIP; other accounts say Dholkot near Asirgarh.)

IN-SIVASAGAR.detail: Nara Narayan and general Chilarai sack the Ahom capital Garhgaon
IN-SIVASAGAR.outcome: Koch victory — Garhgaon sacked; tribute follows
IN-SIVASAGAR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-SIVASAGAR.detail: The Battle of Dhai Ali was fought between Captain Welsh of the East India Company and the Moamorias led by Bharath Singha, reinforced by a contingent of troops sent to his aid.
IN-SIVASAGAR.belligerents: East India Company, Ahom Dynasty vs Moamorias

IN-SAHIBGANJ.detail: Daud Khan Karrani is executed; Bengal becomes a Mughal subah

IN-SAHIBGANJ.text: The Company’s war with Mir Qasim
IN-SAHIBGANJ.detail: after Ellis seizes Patna (June 1763) the Company restores Mir Ja‘far and routs Mir Qasim’s Western-trained army at Katwa, Gheria and Udaynala, takes Monghyr and storms Patna; Mir Qasim, after murdering Gurgin Khan, the Seths and his English prisoners, flees to Awadh.
IN-SAHIBGANJ.belligerents: East India Company vs Bengal (Nawab) — Mir Qasim
IN-SAHIBGANJ.outcome: East India Company victory; Mir Qasim deposed and driven into Awadh, Mir Ja‘far restored
IN-SAHIBGANJ.source: HCIP VIII p. 349: 'The Nawab’s army was routed at Katwa, at Murshidabad and at Udaynalla and the English then laid siege to Monghyr ... he caused Gurgin Khan, his Armenian Commander-in-Chief, the Seths and then his English prisoners, to be murdered in succession, and when the English army carried Patna by storm, Mir Qasim escaped into Awadh.'

IN-SAHIBGANJ.detail: Sido and Kanhu Murmu raise the Santhals at Bhognadih on 30 June against the zamindars, moneylenders and the Company; ten thousand march on Calcutta. Put down by 1856 with martial law and the deaths of some fifteen thousand; the Santhal Parganas were made a separate district after it.
IN-SAHIBGANJ.belligerents: Santhals (Sido and Kanhu Murmu) vs East India Company and the zamindars
IN-SAHIBGANJ.outcome: East India Company victory; after routing Major Burrough’s column and holding the Bhagalpur–Rajmahal country, the Santals, over 30,000 in arms in August 1855, fought on until their leaders were taken in February 1856
IN-SAHIBGANJ.source: HCIP IX pp. 456–458: 'Under the leadership of two brothers, Sidhu and Kanhu ... ten thousand Santals met in June 1855, and declared their intention ‘to take possession of the country and set up a Government of their own’ ... A British force under Major Burrough was defeated ... Even in August, the number of insurgents exceeded 30,000 men in arms. They ... were openly at war with the British till February, 1856, when their leaders were arrested.' The 15,000 dead and the creation of the Santal Parganas are web-only.

IN-DAMAN.belligerents: Mughal Empire vs Portuguese Empire / Portuguese India
IN-DAMAN.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-DAMAN.belligerents: Mughal Empire vs Portuguese Empire / Portuguese India
IN-DAMAN.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-SHUPIYAN.detail: The Battle of Hastivanj was fought between armies of Mughal Empire under Qasim Khan and Kashmir Sultanate under Shams Chak.
The Battle of Shopian took place on 3 July 1819 between an expeditionary force from the Sikh Empire and Jabbar Khan, the governor of the Kashmir Valley province.
IN-SHUPIYAN.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Durrani (Afghan) Empire (Jabbar Khan, governor of Kashmir)
IN-SHUPIYAN.outcome: Sikh Empire victory; Jabbar Khan routed twice and fled to Kabul; the Sikh army entered Srinagar on 15 July 1819 and Kashmir was annexed
IN-SHUPIYAN.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V pp. 129–130: 'The Sikh army reached Shupian on 5 July, 1819. In a sharp engagement lasting for a few hours the Afghans were repulsed ... In a fierce fight Jabbar Khan was again defeated ... The Sikh Army entered Srinagar on 15 July, 1819.' (Gupta: 5 July; the row's text has 3 July.)

PK-BUNER.detail: The Battle of the Malandari Pass was fought on 16 February 1586 in what is now the Buner District in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province.
PK-BUNER.belligerents: Afghan people Yousafzai tribe Jadoon tribe vs Mughal Empire

PK-BUNER.detail: The Battle of Panjtar was fought in November 1836 as part of the Afghan–Sikh Wars.

IN-KADAPA-YSR.detail: Vijayanagara forces routed a Golconda relief army on the Pennar during the campaign to recover Gandikota.
IN-KADAPA-YSR.belligerents: Vijayanagara Empire (with Venkatagiri and vassals) vs Golconda Sultanate
IN-KADAPA-YSR.outcome: Vijayanagara victory; Golconda army routed, Krishna River accepted as frontier

IN-KADAPA-YSR.detail: Vijayanagara forces captured Gandikota after defeating Golconda relief armies and a three-month siege.
IN-KADAPA-YSR.belligerents: Vijayanagara Empire (with Venkatagiri and Matli allies) vs Golconda Sultanate
IN-KADAPA-YSR.outcome: Vijayanagara victory; Gandikota captured after a siege of nearly three months

IN-AMRITSAR.detail: Guru Arjan lays the foundation of the temple in the pool at Amritsar — Mian Mir of Lahore, by tradition, laying the stone; the Adi Granth was installed there in 1604.
IN-AMRITSAR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)
Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-AMRITSAR.detail: The siege of Amritsar was a siege that took place in March 1748.
The Siege of Ram Rauni was a siege of the Sikh fort of Ram Rauni at Amritsar in 1748 by Mughal forces under Mir Mannu.
IN-AMRITSAR.belligerents: Mughal Empire, Subah of Lahore vs Sikh Confederacy
IN-AMRITSAR.outcome: Sikh victory; the Sikhs granted one-fourth of the revenue of Pargana Patti.

IN-AMRITSAR.detail: at the Baisakhi gathering at Amritsar on 29 March 1748 Nawab Kapur Singh organised the Sikh bands into a single army, the Dal Khalsa, under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia — the start of the misl confederacy.
IN-AMRITSAR.source: Hari Ram Gupta, History of the Sikhs IV p. 13: 'On March 29, 1748, the day of Baisakhi, all the members of the Khalsa brotherhood had gathered at Amritsar ... He named this organisation the Dal Khalsa. He placed it under the command of Jassa Singh Ahluwalia.' Also p. 17: 'The misls as members of the Dal Khalsa were organised on March 29, 1748.'

IN-AMRITSAR.text: Nawab Kapur Singh dies — leader of the Sikhs through the persecutions and founder of the Dal Khalsa in 1748.
IN-AMRITSAR.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs IV p. 76: 'He died in October, 1753. His tomb stands near the temple of Baba [Atal] ...' and '[he] was the founder of the Dal Khalsa in 1748.'

IN-AMRITSAR.detail: The Battle of Pipli Sahib, also known as Battle of Amritsar, was fought by the Sikh Misls and the Durrani Empire.
during Shah Zaman's occupation of Lahore the Sikhs, some fifty thousand strong, fought the Durrani army at Amritsar on 12 January 1797 and drove it back to the gates of Lahore.
IN-AMRITSAR.outcome: Sikh victory; the Durrani army gave way and was pursued to Lahore; Shah Zaman soon withdrew to Afghanistan
IN-AMRITSAR.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs III p. 76 ('Shah Zaman defeated at Amritsar'): 'It commenced at 8 o'clock in the morning on the 12th January ... Both the armies thus continued for nearly four hours, when the Durrani army gave way. They "were pursued by the Scikhs to the very entrance of Lahore."'

IN-AMRITSAR.detail: Ranjit Singh and the Company fix the Sutlej as the boundary between them; the cis-Sutlej Sikh states pass under British protection, and the Punjab is his to the north of it.
IN-AMRITSAR.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 240: 'the Treaty was signed at Amritsar on 25 April, 1809'; p. 241, Article 1: 'the British Government will have no concern with the territories and subjects of the Raja to northward of the river Sutlej.'

IN-AMRITSAR.detail: the Company made over Kashmir and the hill country to Gulab Singh of Jammu as an independent Maharaja, for cash — the founding charter of the Dogra state of Jammu and Kashmir.
IN-AMRITSAR.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 273: 'Gulab Singh got his promised reward of sovereignty over Kashmir and Jammu on payment of fifty lakhs in cash ... A treaty was concluded on March 16, 1846, recognizing Maharaja Gulab Singh independent sovereign of Kashmir.'

IN-AMRITSAR.detail: troops fire on an unarmed gathering at Amritsar
fought over Kashmir; UN ceasefire and the Tashkent Declaration restored the status quo
IN-AMRITSAR.outcome: Inconclusive — status quo ante restored at Tashkent; both sides claimed victory

IN-HYDRABAD.detail: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah’s four-minaret gateway at the centre of his new city of Hyderabad.
IN-HYDRABAD.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-HYDRABAD.text: Nizam Ali takes power in Hyderabad
IN-HYDRABAD.detail: he deposes his brother Salabat Jang (a chronology dates this July 1761), confines him on 7 July 1762 and has him killed in September 1763.
IN-HYDRABAD.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II p. 337: 'Salabat Jang could not hold his own against Nizam Ali, who first put him into confinement on 7th July 1762, and later put him to death on 16th September 1763.' Sardesai II chronology p. 463 dates 'Nizam Ali deposes Salabat Jang' to 1761, July 6. HCIP VIII p. 122: 'Nizam Ali rose to power about 1760'.

IN-HYDRABAD.detail: on 1 September 1798 Wellesley binds Nizam Ali to a subsidiary alliance, and a British force replaces the Nizam's French-officered corps.
IN-HYDRABAD.source: HCIP VIII p. 449: 'Immediately on his arrival Wellesley bound the Nizam with the subsidiary alliance on 1 September, 1798, and substituted his French force with that of the British.'

IN-HYDRABAD.text: Nizam Ali Khan (Asaf Jah II) dies — ruler of Hyderabad since the 1760s, who lost at Rakshasbhuvan and Kharda and accepted the subsidiary alliance of 1798.
IN-HYDRABAD.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 352: 'During the seven years of Nizam Ali's illness (he died on 6th August 1803)'.

IN-HYDRABAD.detail: a five-day police action integrates Hyderabad, the largest princely state
IN-HYDRABAD.outcome: Indian victory — the Nizam accedes to India
IN-HYDRABAD.source: Wikipedia: List of wars involving India

LK-KANDY.detail: a Portuguese army marched on Kandy to install a puppet queen and was annihilated in the retreat through the Dumbara defiles. Its commander died in captivity, and Konappu Bandara took the throne as Vimaladharmasuriya I. Kandy stayed independent for another two centuries.
LK-KANDY.belligerents: Portuguese under Pedro Lopes de Sousa vs the kingdom of Kandy under Konappu Bandara
LK-KANDY.outcome: Kandyan victory; the Portuguese army destroyed
LK-KANDY.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-KANDY.detail: the last Portuguese offensive into the interior ended with their field army annihilated as it withdrew from Kandy. By one account thirty-three men survived.
LK-KANDY.belligerents: Kandy under Rajasinha II vs the Portuguese under Diogo de Melo de Castro
LK-KANDY.outcome: Kandyan victory; the Portuguese never marched inland again
LK-KANDY.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-KANDY.detail: the Company reached and burned Kandy but could not hold it. The Treaty of Batticaloa in 1766 gave the Dutch the entire coastline and left the kingdom landlocked.
LK-KANDY.belligerents: Kandy under Kirti Sri Rajasinha vs the Dutch East India Company
LK-KANDY.outcome: Kandy keeps its independence and loses its coast
LK-KANDY.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-KANDY.detail: a British force occupied a deserted Kandy in February, was destroyed by disease and guerrilla attrition, and the garrison that surrendered on 24 June was massacred, the sick killed in the hospital afterwards. No pitched battle was fought. The received British account of the massacre is now under scholarly revision in Sri Lanka.
LK-KANDY.belligerents: Britain under Hay Macdowall vs the kingdom of Kandy
LK-KANDY.outcome: British defeat; Kandy independent for another twelve years
LK-KANDY.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-KANDY.text: Second Kandyan War and the fall of Kandy
LK-KANDY.detail: the Kandyan chiefs turned against Sri Vikrama Rajasinha and the British occupied the capital with little fighting. The Kandyan Convention of 2 March ceded the kingdom to the Crown - the end of some two thousand years of indigenous monarchy on the island, and the first time one power held all of it.
LK-KANDY.belligerents: Britain vs the kingdom of Kandy
LK-KANDY.outcome: Kandy annexed; the whole island under British rule
LK-KANDY.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-KANDY.detail: The hundred days of martial law — communal rioting between Sinhalese and Muslim communities was answered with shoot-on-sight martial law that killed far more than the riots had. The repression, and the execution of Henry Pedris, turned a generation of the Ceylonese elite towards the independence movement.
LK-KANDY.belligerents: Sinhalese rioters and Muslim communities; then the British military and the population
LK-KANDY.outcome: Riots suppressed; the governor recalled; a catalyst for the independence movement
LK-KANDY.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

BD-BARISAL.detail: The Mughal Conquest of Bakla was a military campaign by the Mughal Empire against the Chandradwip Kingdom, which covered much of the present-day Barisal Division of Bangladesh.

BD-JESSORE.detail: The Mughal conquest of Jessore in 1611–1612 was a military campaign by the Mughal Empire against the rebellious Zamindar of Jessore, Pratapaditya.
BD-JESSORE.belligerents: Mughal Empire Kingdom of Jaipur vs Zamindars of Jessore

BD-JESSORE.detail: an armoured action inside East Pakistan a fortnight before the formal war opens
BD-JESSORE.outcome: Indian victory — Pakistani armour destroyed at Garibpur
BD-JESSORE.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-DOHAD.text: Aurangzeb is born — At Dahod in Gujarat.
IN-DOHAD.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-WEST-TRIPURA.detail: The Mughal campaign of Tripura (1618) was a military expedition launched by the Mughal Empire under Ibrahim Khan Fath-i-Jang, the Subahdar of Bengal.

IN-RAJOURI.text: Jahangir dies — On the road down from Kashmir, near Rajauri
IN-RAJOURI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-THE-DANGS.detail: Shah Jahan I, also called Shah Jahan the Magnificent, was the fifth Mughal Emperor from 1628 until his deposition in 1658.
IN-THE-DANGS.belligerents: Mughal Empire (Shah Jahan; Aurangzeb as viceroy of the Deccan) vs Baglana (the Rathod rajas of Mulher)

LK-MONARAGALA.detail: a Portuguese army under the Captain-General was destroyed in Uva when most of its Sinhalese lascarin troops changed sides in the middle of the battle. Constantino de Sa de Noronha was killed.
LK-MONARAGALA.belligerents: Kandy under Senarat and Rajasinha II vs the Portuguese
LK-MONARAGALA.outcome: Kandyan victory; the Portuguese field army destroyed
LK-MONARAGALA.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-MONARAGALA.detail: a Marxist youth movement attacked some seventy police stations at once on 5 April and briefly held parts of the south. It was crushed within three weeks with foreign help, and about sixteen thousand people were detained. The reprisals killed far more than the rising did.
LK-MONARAGALA.belligerents: Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna vs the government of Ceylon
LK-MONARAGALA.outcome: Insurrection crushed; mass detention and reprisal killings
LK-MONARAGALA.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

IN-BURHANPUR.text: Mumtaz Mahal dies — In childbirth at Burhanpur
IN-BURHANPUR.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BURHANPUR.detail: The sacking of Burhanpur refers to the looting of the wealthy city of Burhanpur in Madhya Pradesh by the Maratha ruler Sambhaji.
The Battle of Balapur marked a civil conflict among Mughal leaders, triggered by the uprising of the Sayyid Brothers.
IN-BURHANPUR.belligerents: Mughal Empire, (under Nizam) vs Sayyid Brothers, Maratha Confederacy, Kingdom of Rohilkhand

IN-BURHANPUR.text: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I dies — At Burhanpur, aged seventy-seven
IN-BURHANPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 122: 'Nizam-ul-Mulk died on 21 May, 1748, at the age of seventy-seven.' (The book does not name the place; Burhanpur remains web-only.)

IN-BURHANPUR.detail: General Doveton and Malcolm take Asirgarh from Scindia's commandant Yashwant Rao Lad, who had sheltered the fugitive Appa Saheb. This is the last fortress action of the war.
IN-BURHANPUR.belligerents: East India Company vs Gwalior (Scindia) garrison
IN-BURHANPUR.outcome: East India Company victory; Asirgarh taken on 8 April 1819
IN-BURHANPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 506: 'On 8 April, 1819, General Doveton, with the help of Sir John Malcolm, wrested Asirgarh from its commandant Yashwant Rao Lad.'

IN-JALANDHAR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-NIWARI.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-KAMRUP.detail: The Battle of Sualkuchi was a crucial conflict in the Ahom-Mughal wars of 1636, marking the resumption of hostilities after a 21-year hiatus.

IN-KAMRUP.belligerents: Ahom Kingdom (Gadadhar Singha) vs Mughal Empire (Mansur Khan, faujdar of Guwahati)

IN-RUPNAGAR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-RUPNAGAR.belligerents: The Sikhs of Guru Gobind Singh vs Bilaspur (Kahlur) and the Hill Rajas (Himachal)
IN-RUPNAGAR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-RUPNAGAR.detail: The Battle of Anandpur was fought at Anandpur, between the armies of the Sikh Guru Gobind Singh and the Mughal forces aided by the Nawab of Bahawalpur state.
IN-RUPNAGAR.belligerents: Khalsa (Sikhs) vs Mughal Empire, Rajas of the Sivalik Hills

IN-RUPNAGAR.detail: The First battle of Chamkaur was fought in 1702 between the Sikhs and the Mughals.
IN-RUPNAGAR.belligerents: Khalsa (Sikhs) vs Mughal Empire, Bilaspur State
IN-RUPNAGAR.outcome: Sikh victory, Mughal General Sayyad Beg defects to the Sikhs.

IN-RUPNAGAR.detail: The Battle of Chamkaur, also known as Battle of Chamkaur Sahib or the Second battle of Chamkaur, was fought by the Khalsa, led by Guru Gobind Singh.
IN-RUPNAGAR.belligerents: Mughal Empire, Alliance of Hill States and Jammu State (c. 850–1812) vs Khalsa (Sikhs)
IN-RUPNAGAR.outcome: Mughal and Hindu Hill Chief victory

IN-RUPNAGAR.detail: The Battle of Sarsa was fought on 21 December 1704 between the Khalsa and the Mughal Empire.
IN-RUPNAGAR.belligerents: Khalsa (Sikhs) vs Mughal Empire Alliance of Hill Rajas, led by Kahlur

IN-RUPNAGAR.detail: The First Battle of Anandpur in 1704 was fought between the Mughal Empire and the Sikhs.
The second siege of Anandpur, also known as the second battle of Anandpur (1704), was a siege at Anandpur, between Sikhs and the Mughal governors dispatched by Aurangzeb.
IN-RUPNAGAR.belligerents: Khalsa (Sikhs) vs Mughal Empire, Alliance of 22 Hill Rajas

IN-RUPNAGAR.detail: The Battle of Anandpur was fought in 1812 by the Sikh forces led by Sodhi Surjan Singh and the Rajput forces of Kahlur led by Raja Mahan Chand.

LK-BATTICALOA.text: The Westerwolt treaty and the fall of Batticaloa
LK-BATTICALOA.detail: Rajasinha II allied with the Dutch East India Company against the Portuguese, and the first Portuguese fort fell in May. The alliance would cost Kandy its coastline.
LK-BATTICALOA.belligerents: Kandy and the Dutch East India Company vs the Portuguese
LK-BATTICALOA.outcome: Batticaloa taken; the Dutch conquest of the littoral begins
LK-BATTICALOA.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-BATTICALOA.detail: The clearing of the East — the last major LTTE stronghold in the Eastern Province fell in July after thirteen years. The army then turned north with its whole weight.
LK-BATTICALOA.belligerents: Sri Lanka Army vs the LTTE
LK-BATTICALOA.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-TRINCOMALEE.detail: The Dutch take Trincomalee, the great harbour of the east coast, from the Portuguese
LK-TRINCOMALEE.belligerents: Dutch East India Company vs the Portuguese
LK-TRINCOMALEE.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-TRINCOMALEE.detail: the LTTE closed the sluice gates of an irrigation channel in July, cutting water to some fifteen thousand farming families, and the army went in to reopen them. The ceasefire was never formally revoked at this point, but this is where it ended and the final war began.
LK-TRINCOMALEE.belligerents: Sri Lanka Army and Air Force vs the LTTE
LK-TRINCOMALEE.outcome: Gates reopened; the ceasefire collapses in practice
LK-TRINCOMALEE.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

IN-NORTH-TWENTY-FOUR-PARGANAS.detail: The Danish rescue mission to Pipli refers to a rescue mission by the Danish East India Company to rescue then recently imprisoned Danes from Mughal imprisonment.

IN-NORTH-TWENTY-FOUR-PARGANAS.text: Mangal Pandey dies — Hanged at Barrackpore on 8 April
IN-NORTH-TWENTY-FOUR-PARGANAS.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-GARHWAL.detail: Queen-regent Karnavati's hillmen destroy Najabat Khan's expedition
IN-GARHWAL.outcome: Garhwal victory — the "nose-cutting queen" enters legend
IN-GARHWAL.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-BALESHWAR.belligerents: Mughal Empire Bengal Subah vs Danish India Gowa

IN-BALESHWAR.detail: Mirza Mumin's assault and subsequent destruction of the Danish factory at Pipli in Bengal by Mughal forces occurred in late 1641.
IN-BALESHWAR.belligerents: Mughal Empire Bengal Subah vs Danish India

IN-BALESHWAR.detail: The Expulsion of Danes from Balasore was a violent expulsion and ousting of the Danish East India Company from the Mughal harbour and trading hub of Balasore in 1643 or 1644.
The Battle of Balasore was an engagement between Bengali and English ships against Danish ships at Balasore.
Alivardi Khan routs Rustam Jang’s son-in-law Baqar Ali on the plain four miles north of Balasore on 3 March 1741 and takes Orissa from Sarfaraz’s kinsmen.
IN-BALESHWAR.belligerents: Bengal (Nawab) — Alivardi Khan vs Rustam Jang (Murshid Quli II), deputy governor of Orissa
IN-BALESHWAR.outcome: Alivardi Khan victory; Rustam Jang flees by sea to Masulipatam and Alivardi occupies Katak
IN-BALESHWAR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 45: 'on 3rd March, 1741, a battle was precipitated by Rustam’s impetuous son-in-law, Baqar Ali, who ... attacked Alivardi on the plain of Fulwari (four miles north of Balesar town), but was routed after a severe fight.' HCIP VIII p. 109: Rustam Jang 'was ultimately overpowered and fled to the Deccan.'

IN-THIRUVALLUR.detail: The Battle of Pulicat (1644) was a military conflict fought between the forces of the Vijayanagara Empire and the Golconda Sultanate near Pulicat on the Coromandel Coast.
IN-THIRUVALLUR.belligerents: Vijayanagara Empire, Dutch Republic vs Golconda Sultanate

IN-SATARA.detail: Shivaji's conquest of Jawali was a military engagement fought between the Maratha rebels, led by Shivaji and the Mores under the command of Chandra Rao More, in the year 1656.
IN-SATARA.belligerents: Maratha Empire (Shivaji) vs the Mores of Javali (Jaoli State)

IN-SATARA.detail: Shivaji slays Afzal Khan and announces Maratha power to the Deccan
IN-SATARA.belligerents: Maratha Empire (Shivaji) vs Bijapur (Adil Shahi) (Afzal Khan)

IN-SATARA.detail: The Battle of Satara was fought between the Mughal Empire and Maratha Kingdom between December 1699 and 21 April 1700.
after Khed, Shahu took Satara from Tarabai's garrison and ascended the Maratha throne in January 1708; Tarabai withdrew to Panhala and Rangna, and the Maratha state split into two lines.
IN-SATARA.source: HCIP VIII (The Maratha Supremacy) p. 47: 'It was on a Saturday in January 1708, that the victorious entry was made'; p. 48: 'After a week's time Shahu ascended the Gadi in ceremony and appointed his new ministers.' Chronology p. 813: '1708, January  Raja Shahu ascends the Maratha throne at Satara.'

IN-SATARA.detail: Shahu gives the robes of office at Masur to Balaji Vishwanath's twenty-year-old son on 17 April 1720, over the objections of older ministers.
IN-SATARA.source: HCIP VIII p. 63: 'Baji Rao, the eldest son of Balaji Vishwanath, who was about twenty years old, succeeded him in the Peshwaship on 17 April, 1720 ... conferred the robes of the Peshwaship on Baji Rao at Masur.'

IN-SATARA.detail: Shahu appoints Bajirao I's nineteen-year-old son on 25 June 1740.
IN-SATARA.source: HCIP VIII p. 170: 'He succeeded Baji Rao I on 25 June, 1740. He was only nineteen at the time'.

IN-SATARA.text: Nana Phadnavis born — minister of the Peshwas, who led the Barbhai regency and ran the Maratha state for a quarter-century.
IN-SATARA.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 358: 'born on 12th February 1742 he was only 58 years and one month in age'.

IN-SATARA.text: Chhatrapati Shahu dies — the Maratha king whose forty-year reign saw the Peshwas carry Maratha power into Hindustan
IN-SATARA.source: HCIP VIII p. 181: 'Shahu died on 15 December, 1749 ... Ram Raja being weak and incompetent and being a puppet in the hands of Tara Bai, the power of the State gradually fell into the hands of the Peshwa.'

IN-SATARA.text: Battle of the Venna (Damaji Gaekwad's revolt)
IN-SATARA.detail: answering Tarabai's call, Damaji Gaekwad marches on Satara. On 15 March 1751 the Peshwa's troops defeat him on the Venna and trap his force. On 30 April the Peshwa plunders his camp and imprisons him, and Damaji later gives up half of Gujarat.
IN-SATARA.belligerents: Maratha Empire (Peshwa Balaji Rao) vs Damaji Gaekwad and Tarabai's party
IN-SATARA.outcome: Peshwa victory; Damaji Gaekwad defeated, confined and made to cede half his Gujarat holdings
IN-SATARA.source: HCIP VIII p. 283: 'The Peshwa's forces challenged the Gaikwar on the Venya river near Satara, defeated him and trapped his force in Satara on 15 March, 1751 ... the Peshwa plundered his camp on 30 April and confined Damaji Gaikwar'. (An earlier action at Bahadurpura in Khandesh, 18 Feb 1751, went Damaji's way: 'Brushing aside the Peshwa's troops'.)

IN-SATARA.text: Tarabai dies — Rajaram's queen, who led the Maratha war against Aurangzeb and later opposed Shahu and the Peshwas.
IN-SATARA.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II p. 122: 'the aged Tarabai, Chhatrapati Rajaram's wife also died ten years later on December 9, 1761.'

IN-SATARA.detail: the British set up Chhatrapati Pratap Singh, rescued at Ashti, as ruler of a small state around Satara. The treaty of 1819 formalises it.
IN-SATARA.source: HCIP VIII p. 507: 'Chhatrapati Pratap Singh was set up as a ruler of a small principality "as a sop to Maratha sentiment"'; HCIP IX (British Paramountcy) p. 151: 'The treaty of 1819, by which the principality of Satara was created'.

IN-SATARA.text: The Third Anglo-Maratha War ends Maratha power

IN-SATARA.detail: the Raja refuses to sign an admission of treason, is dethroned on 5 September 1839 and exiled to Banaras. His brother Appa Sahib replaces him.
IN-SATARA.source: HCIP IX (British Paramountcy) p. 157: 'the Raja refused to sign the memorandum. He was dethroned on September 5, 1839, and deported to Banaras, where he died in A.D. 1847.' p. 24 calls the charges 'allegations, which appear to be unfounded to a very large extent'.

IN-SATARA.text: Satara annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse
IN-SATARA.detail: Raja Appa Sahib dies on 5 April 1848 with only an adopted son. Dalhousie's council, upheld by the Court of Directors, sets the adoption aside and annexes the state.
IN-SATARA.source: HCIP IX p. 68: 'when Appa Sahib, the Raja of Satara, died on April 5, 1848'; p. 65: 'He had no male issue, but adopted a son without the previous consent of the British Government ... Satara was accordingly annexed and the claim of adopted son set aside.' (The annexation took effect in 1848–49 after the reference to London.)

IN-FATEHPUR.detail: Aurangzeb defeats Shah Shuja, who flees to Arakan

after Buxar, Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh and his Maratha ally Malhar Holkar are finally defeated by the Company's army under Fletcher (3 May 1765); Awadh falls under British control and Shah Alam II takes refuge with the English at Allahabad.
IN-FATEHPUR.belligerents: East India Company vs Awadh, Maratha Empire (Malhar Rao Holkar)
IN-FATEHPUR.outcome: East India Company victory; Shuja-ud-Daula's last army dispersed and Awadh occupied
IN-FATEHPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 115: 'After running from one place to another he was finally defeated at the battle of Kora on 3 May 1765... Awadh fell completely under British control.'; chronology p. 830: 'The allies of exile Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-daulah and Malhar Rao Holkar are finally defeated at Kora by the English army under Sir Robert Fletcher'

IN-MORIGAON.detail: The Battle of Kaliabor, also known as Battle of Kaliabar, was a riverine naval battle fought by the Mughal Empire, under the command of its general Mir Jumla II.

IN-SURAT.text: William Hawkins reaches Surat aboard the Hector
IN-SURAT.detail: William Hawkins · England (East India Company) · Surat
