The Battle of Surat, also known as the Sack of Surat, was a land battle that took place on 5 January 1664 and ended on 13 January 1664, near the city of Surat.
IN-SURAT.outcome: Maratha victory The Maratha sacks the city for five or six days

IN-SURAT.text: François Caron arrives at Surat for the Compagnie des Indes

IN-SURAT.detail: on 6 March 1775 Raghunathrao buys Bombay's military help to regain the Peshwaship. He promises to cede Bassein, Salsette and other islands, and parts of Gujarat. The treaty sets off the first Anglo-Maratha war.
IN-SURAT.source: HCIP VIII p. 286: 'At Surat Raghunath Rao concluded a treaty with the English on 6 March, 1775 ... and to cede in perpetuity Bassein with its dependencies, Salsette and other islands, the districts of Jambusar, Olpad and part of Ankalesar.'

BD-FENI.detail: Mughal conquest of Chittagong refers to the conquest of Chittagong in 1666.
BD-FENI.belligerents: Mughal India Bengal Subah Kingdom of Portugal vs Kingdom of Mrauk U

IN-ERODE.detail: The Battle of Erode, fought in 1667, was a conflict involving the Confederacy Army of the Vijayanagar Empire, the Madurai Nayakas, the Bijapur Sultanate and the Nayaks of Kalahasti.
IN-ERODE.belligerents: Vijayanagar Empire, Bijapur Sultanate, Madurai Nayakas vs Flag of Kingdom of Mysore.png Kingdom of Mysore

IN-HUGLI.detail: The Attack in Hooghly was a Danish attack on two Bengali ships during the Dano-Mughal War in 1671.
The siege of Dannemarksnagore took place in 1707 at the Danish colony of Dannemarksnagore in Bengal, between the Danes and the Mughal subahdar of Bengal, Azim-ush-Shan.
IN-HUGLI.belligerents: Mughal Empire Bengal Subah vs Danish India

IN-HUGLI.detail: The raid on Dannemarksnagore took place in 1713 at the Danish colony of Dannemarksnagore in Bengal, between the Danes and a local Mughal zamindar.
IN-HUGLI.belligerents: Mughal Empire Bengal Subah vs Danish India

IN-HUGLI.detail: Clive and Admiral Watson take the French settlement on the Hooghly on 23 March 1757, three months before Plassey, removing the French from Bengal.
IN-HUGLI.belligerents: East India Company vs French India
IN-HUGLI.outcome: East India Company victory; Fort d’Orléans surrenders and Chandernagore is taken
IN-HUGLI.source: web-only; library silent (HCIP VIII and Sarkar do not narrate it). Famous and uncontested (23 March 1757); it matters because it removed the French from Bengal before Plassey.

IN-HUGLI.detail: a Dutch expedition from Batavia, encouraged by Mir Ja‘far, is beaten by Clive’s forces on the Hooghly, ending any Dutch challenge in Bengal.
IN-HUGLI.belligerents: East India Company vs Dutch India
IN-HUGLI.outcome: East India Company victory; 'the Dutch were badly defeated and humbled'
IN-HUGLI.source: HCIP VIII pp. 341–342: 'An expedition was despatched from Batavia, but delayed so long ... that Clive got sufficient time for preparations ... with the result that the Dutch were badly defeated and humbled (December 1759).' (Web accounts date the land battle at Biderra to 25 November 1759.)

IN-HUGLI.text: Ram Mohan Roy is born — At Radhanagar in Hooghly
IN-HUGLI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-HUGLI.text: Ramakrishna is born — At Kamarpukur in Hooghly.
IN-HUGLI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

PK-KHYBER.detail: The Battle of Ali Masjid, also known as Battle of Landi Kotal and Battle of Khyber, was fought on 30 April 1672 by the Mughal Empire led by Muhammad Amin.
PK-KHYBER.belligerents: Afridi tribe, Mohmand tribe, Shinwari tribe vs Mughal Empire

PK-KHYBER.detail: The Battle of Langarkot (1674) was a military engagement fought in 1674 by the combined Khattak and Yusufzai tribes under the leadership of Khushal Khan Khattak.
PK-KHYBER.belligerents: Khattak tribe, Yousafzai tribe vs Mughal Empire Gujjars

PK-KHYBER.detail: The Battle of Mangal was fought between the Sikh forces led by Hari Singh Nalwa and the Jadoon, led by Muhammad Khan
PK-KHYBER.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Jadoon, Tareen, Awan

PK-KHYBER.detail: after waiting two months at Peshawar, General Pollock marched through the Khyber in early April 1842, with Sikh help in carrying the pass, and relieved Jalalabad on 16 April.
PK-KHYBER.belligerents: East India Company, Sikh Empire vs Emirate of Kabul (Afridi and Afghan forces)
PK-KHYBER.outcome: East India Company victory; the pass carried and Jalalabad relieved
PK-KHYBER.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 196: 'It was not till the beginning of April that he could commence his march through the Khyber Pass towards Jalalabad, and relieve that garrison on April 16.' p. 249: 'when they again proceeded to Kabul, under General Pollock ... the Sikh army offered valuable aid in carrying the Khyber Pass.'

PK-KHYBER.detail: Brigadier Wild, trying to force the Khyber to relieve Jalalabad, was beaten at the mouth of the pass on 19 January 1842; he fell back on Jamrud and Ali Masjid fell to the Afghans.
PK-KHYBER.belligerents: Emirate of Kabul (Afridi and Afghan forces) vs East India Company
PK-KHYBER.outcome: Afghan victory; Wild falls back on Jamrud, Ali Masjid lost
PK-KHYBER.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 196: 'Wild advanced to the Pass, but was decisively defeated on January 19, at the entrance of the Pass, as his sepoys had no heart in the fight. He fell back on Jamrud, and Ali Masjid fell into the hands of the Afghans.'

IN-NASHIK.detail: the Marathas beat a Mughal field army in open battle for the first time
The Sieges of Ramsej were a series of military confrontations between the Maratha Kingdom headed by Sambhaji and the Mughal Empire led by Aurangzeb.
Baji Rao I outmanoeuvres the Nizam — a masterclass of mobile warfare
IN-NASHIK.outcome: Maratha victory; the Nizam, cut off from food and water near Palkhed on 25 February 1728, sued for terms and by the treaty of Mungi-Shevgaon (6 March 1728) recognised Shahu as Chhatrapati with the chauth and sardeshmukhi of the six subahs
IN-NASHIK.source: HCIP VIII p. 69: 'The Nizam found himself challenged for action in a waterless tract near Palkhed on 25 February. Starved of food and water, the Nizam's army would not fight ... a treaty was concluded at Mungi-Paithan in pargana Shevgaon on 6 March, 1728. The main articles were the recognition of Raja Shahu as Chhatrapati'.

IN-NASHIK.detail: Madhavrao I defeats his uncle Raghunathrao and Govindrao Gaekwad's contingent at Dhodap on 10 June 1768. Raghunathrao is captured and held in the Shaniwar Wada.
IN-NASHIK.belligerents: Maratha Empire (Peshwa Madhavrao I) vs Raghunathrao's faction and Govindrao Gaekwad
IN-NASHIK.outcome: Peshwa Madhavrao I victory; Raghunathrao taken captive, Govindrao Gaekwad taken prisoner
IN-NASHIK.source: HCIP VIII p. 204: 'battle was fought and won by the Peshwa on June 10, 1768. The fort was captured. Raghunath was taken to Poona and confined in the Shaniwar Wada'; p. 284: 'At the battle of Dhodap in 1768, a Gaikwar contingent under Damaji's son Govind Rao, fought against the Peshwa and was defeated.'

IN-HAORA.belligerents: Mughal Empire vs East India Company
IN-HAORA.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-HAORA.text: Swami Vivekananda dies — At Belur Math, aged thirty-nine.
IN-HAORA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SIRMAUR.detail: The Battle of Bhangani was fought between Guru Gobind Singh's army and Bhim Chand (Kahlur) of Bilaspur on 18 September 1686 or 1688, at Bhangani near Paonta Sahib.
IN-SIRMAUR.belligerents: Akal Sena (Sikhs) Pir Budhu Shah's disciples Udasis vs Alliance of 16 Hill States, including, Kahlur

IN-MUMBAI.detail: The Battle of Wai was fought in December of 1687 as a part of the Mughal–Maratha Wars.
The Battle of Alegaon was fought between Nizam Ali Khan of Hyderabad and Raghunathrao of the Maratha Empire against Madhavrao I of the Maratha Confederacy.
IN-MUMBAI.belligerents: Maratha Empire (Peshwa Madhavrao I) vs Raghunathrao's faction, Hyderabad, Janoji Bhonsle
IN-MUMBAI.outcome: Hyderabad and Raghunathrao victory; the young Peshwa, beaten in two battles in November 1762, submitted to his uncle and was confined, and Raghunathrao ceded Daulatabad, Shivneri, Asirgarh and Ahmadnagar to Nizam Ali
IN-MUMBAI.source: HCIP VIII p. 202: 'Raghunath ... received active assistance from Nizam Ali and Janoji Bhosle. In November, 1762, the Peshwa's army was defeated in two battles ... He surrendered to Nizam Ali several districts including the forts of Daulatabad, Shivneri, Asirgarh and Ahmadnagar.' Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II chronology p. 463: 'Madhavrao being defeated at Alegaon submits to Raghunathrao and is confined.'

IN-MUMBAI.detail: On 16 April the first train in India runs the thirty-four kilometres from Bori Bunder to Thane, three engines and fourteen carriages, four hundred passengers.
IN-MUMBAI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-MUMBAI.text: Bal Gangadhar Tilak dies — At Bombay
IN-MUMBAI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-MUMBAI.detail: The arch on the Bombay waterfront for the visit of 1911, finished thirteen years later; the last British troops left through it in 1948.
IN-MUMBAI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-HAMIRPUR-HIM.belligerents: Bilaspur State and allied hill/Mughal forces as listed vs Akal Sena (Sikhs) and allied forces as listed
IN-HAMIRPUR-HIM.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-PALGHAR.detail: The Mughal–Portuguese War of 1692–1693 was a brief conflict between the Mughal Empire and Portuguese India, launched by the Mughal general Matabar Khan against the Portuguese.
Chimaji Appa storms the Portuguese northern capital for the Marathas
IN-PALGHAR.belligerents: Maratha Empire vs Portuguese Empire / Portuguese India
IN-PALGHAR.source: HCIP VIII p. 96: 'Bassein capitulated on 5 May, 1739 ... The fall of Bassein marked the end of Portuguese rule in north Konkan ... The Marathas acquired besides Bassein, eight cities, twenty fortresses and the island of Salsette.' Chronology p. 819 dates the Maratha seizure of Thana and Salsette, the opening of the campaign, to March 1737.

IN-PALGHAR.detail: Goddard besieges Bassein from November 1780, and Visaji Pant surrenders it in December. The Maratha relief commander, Ramchandra Ganesh, is killed the same day.
IN-PALGHAR.belligerents: East India Company vs Maratha Empire
IN-PALGHAR.outcome: East India Company victory; Bassein surrendered
IN-PALGHAR.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III p. 107: 'the garrison was so hard-pressed that Visaji Pant surrendered Bassein to Goddard on 12 December. It was a severe blow to Maratha pride'. Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire III p. 222 gives 'Goddard took Bassein on 11th December'. The two books differ by a day.

IN-PALGHAR.detail: Peshwa Bajirao II, driven from Poona by Holkar, accepts a subsidiary alliance with the Company at Bassein; Scindia and Bhonsle refuse it, and the second Anglo-Maratha war begins.
IN-PALGHAR.source: HCIP VIII p. 492: 'the treaty of Bassein which was "constructed after the latest and most approved model of subsidiary alliances". It was signed before the commencement of the New Year and ratified by the Governor-General on March 18, 1803. By this treaty, the Peshwa agreed to receive from the Company on a permanent basis no less than 6,000 regular native infantry'.

IN-CHITRADURGA.detail: The Battle of Dodderi was a three-day battle of the Deccan wars between the Maratha forces led by Santaji Ghorpad and the Mughal army, with support from the Nayak of Chitradurga.
IN-CHITRADURGA.belligerents: Maratha Empire, Nayakas of Chitradurga vs Mughal Empire

IN-CHITRADURGA.detail: The siege of Basavapatan was a military engagement between the Mughal Army and the Maratha troops led by Santaji Ghorpade, the Marathas were defeated and Basavapatan was relieved.

Haidar's second siege of the Nayaka fortress (1778–79) ends when the Jarimale chiefs and the fort's Muslim corps go over to him; the Palegar Madakari (Medekere) Nayaka is taken and the state annexed (the Obavva story belongs to this siege).
IN-CHITRADURGA.belligerents: Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu) vs Chitradurga (Nayaka)
IN-CHITRADURGA.outcome: Mysore victory; the fort capitulates in March 1779 and Chitradurga is annexed
IN-CHITRADURGA.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III p. 259-260 (blocks 243-244): 'the fort, overwhelmed by the superior numbers of the Mysore military, capitulated at last in March 1779'.

IN-YADGIR.detail: During the final siege of Wagingera, the Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb sent for Zulfiqar Khan Nusrat Jung, who arrived on March 27, and the next day attacked Lal Tikri Hillock.

IN-MUKTSAR.detail: The Battle of Sri Muktsar Sahib (Muktsar) or Battle of Khidrāne Dee Dhāb took place on 29 December 1705, (29 Poh) following the siege of Anandpur Sahib.

IN-BILASPUR-CHH.detail: Mughal Prince Bidar Bakht launched an expedition in March 1706 against the Maratha incursions into Gujarat led by Dhanaji Jadhav.

IN-NANDED.text: Guru Gobind Singh dies — At Nanded on the Godavari, of a wound from an Afghan assassin
IN-NANDED.source: HCIP VIII, The Maratha Supremacy p. 126: 'After the assassination of Guru Govind Singh in 1708, the Sikhs got a leader in Banda, his chosen disciple.' Gupta, History of the Sikhs IV p. 5 places him at Nander in September 1708.

IN-NANDED.detail: Madhavrao I, with the Nizam as his ally, plunders Nagpur and Berar. On 23 March 1769 Janoji Bhonsle submits, gives up territory worth 8 lakhs and agrees to serve as a loyal vassal.
IN-NANDED.source: HCIP VIII p. 204: 'The Peshwa plundered Nagpur, captured several forts and ravaged Berar. Peace was concluded at Kanakapur (at the confluence of the Manjra and the Godavari) on 23 March, 1769. Janoji Bhosle surrendered territories worth 8 lakhs and agreed to perform the duties of a loyal vassal.'

IN-PATIALA.detail: The Battle of Samana was fought between the Khalsa under the leadership of Banda Singh Bahadur and the Mughal Government of Samana in 1709.
IN-PATIALA.belligerents: Khalsa Peasants Dahiyas of Khanda vs Mughal Empire
IN-PATIALA.outcome: Sikh victory, Establishment of the First Sikh State

IN-PATIALA.detail: The siege of Patiala was a 7-day siege fought between the Sikh forces led by Raja Amar Singh and Mughal forces led by Abdul Ahad Khan.
The Battle of Mardanpur was fought between the Sikh forces of Patiala state led by Bibi Sahib Kaur and the Maratha forces led by Lakshmi Rao.

IN-SONIPAT.detail: The Battle of Sonipat was fought between Sikhs and the Mughal Empire in 1709.
IN-SONIPAT.belligerents: Khalsa (Sikhs) Dahiya Jat Chaudharies of Kharkhoda vs Mughal Empire

IN-SAHARANPUR.text: Banda Singh's Invasion of Yamuna-Ganga Doab
IN-SAHARANPUR.detail: Banda Singh's Invasion of Yamuna-Ganga Doab was a 1710 expedition by Banda Singh Bahadur and the Khalsa into the tract between the Yamuna and the Ganga.

IN-SAHIBZADA-AJIT-SINGH-NAGAR.detail: The Battle of Chappar Chiri, also called Battle of Sirhind, was fought between Mughal Empire and the Sikhs on 12 May 1710 at Chappar Chiri, located 20 kilometers from Sirhind.
IN-SAHIBZADA-AJIT-SINGH-NAGAR.belligerents: First Sikh State Jats vs Mughal Empire

IN-SHAHID-BHAGAT-SINGH-NAGAR.detail: The Battle of Rahon was fought between Sikhs and the Mughal Empire on 11 October 1710.
IN-SHAHID-BHAGAT-SINGH-NAGAR.belligerents: First Sikh State vs Mughal Empire

IN-YAMUNANAGAR.detail: The Battle of Sadhaura was fought between Sikhs and the Mughal, Sayyid, and Shaykh forces in Sadhaura in 1710.
IN-YAMUNANAGAR.belligerents: First Sikh State Peasants vs Mughal Empire Sayyids Shaykhs

IN-YAMUNANAGAR.detail: The First Battle of Lohgarh was fought between the Sikhs, and the Mughal Empire in 1710.
IN-YAMUNANAGAR.belligerents: Khalsa vs Mughal Empire Rohillas Balochs Jats Bundelkhand
IN-YAMUNANAGAR.outcome: Mughal victory; the Mughals capture Lohgarh after a long siege.

IN-YAMUNANAGAR.detail: The Second Siege of Lohgarh, also known as the Second Siege of Lohgarh and Saudhara, was fought in 1713 by Sikh forces led by Banda Singh Bahadur and Mughal forces.
IN-YAMUNANAGAR.outcome: Saudhara: Mughal victory; Saudhara captured by the Mughals.

IN-JAMMU.detail: The Battle of Jammu was fought between the Sikhs under the command of Banda Singh Bahadur against the Mughal forces near the hills of Jammu on 22 January 1712.
IN-JAMMU.belligerents: First Sikh State vs Mughal Empire, Hindu rulers of the Deva dynasty of Jammu

IN-JAMMU.text: Jammu is given to Gulab Singh
IN-JAMMU.detail: the Dogra principality, conquered for Ranjit Singh in 1809, was assigned to Gulab Singh for a tribute of four lakhs a year — the beginning of Dogra rule in Jammu.
IN-JAMMU.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 65: 'In 1809 Bhawani Das conquered Jammu, and it became a part of Ranjit Singh's kingdom. Jamadar Khushhal Singh was its first governor. In 1818, Jammu was assigned to Gulab Singh for an annual tribute of Rs. 4 lakhs.'

IN-GURDASPUR.belligerents: First Sikh State vs Mughal Empire
IN-GURDASPUR.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs IV p. 6: '[Baj Singh] was taken prisoner along with Banda in December, 1715.' HCIP VIII p. 18: 'Banda ... was compelled to evacuate Lohgarh and retreat to Gurdaspur ... The place was stormed and Banda was forced into submission.'

IN-GURDASPUR.detail: after Sikhs killed Jaspat Rae of Eminabad, his brother Lakhpat Rae, chief minister at Lahore, with Governor Yahiya Khan hunted down and massacred large numbers of Sikhs; Kapur Singh led the survivors into Malwa.
IN-GURDASPUR.belligerents: Mughal Empire (Lahore: Yahiya Khan, Lakhpat Rae) vs Khalsa (Sikhs)
IN-GURDASPUR.outcome: Mughal victory; the Sikh bands massacred and dispersed, survivors withdraw into Malwa
IN-GURDASPUR.source: Hari Ram Gupta, History of the Sikhs IV p. 74: 'Lakhpat Rae vowed vengeance. With the approval of Yahiya Khan, he persecuted the Sikhs and massacred large numbers of them. The Sikhs called it Chhota Ghallughara or a small carnage. Kapur Singh led the survivors into Malwa.' (Place: the Kahnuwan marshes of Gurdaspur is tradition, not in the book; coordinates approximate.)

IN-GURDASPUR.detail: The Battle of Pathankot, also known as the Battle of Dinanagar, took place in 1775 near Awankha in pargana Dina Nagar.
IN-GURDASPUR.belligerents: Kanhaiya Misl, Sukerchakia Misl, Ahluwalia Misl vs Bhangi Misl, Ramgarhia Misl, Dogra Flag of Jammu and Kashmir Jammu
IN-GURDASPUR.outcome: Near collapse of the Bhangi Misl

IN-GURDASPUR.detail: The Battle of Achal, also known as the Battle of Randpura, was fought in Achal, near Batala, in 1785 by the Sukerchakia Misl, Ramgarhia Misl and Sansar Chand.
IN-GURDASPUR.belligerents: Sukerchakia Misl, Ramgarhia Misl, Kangra State vs Kanhaiya Misl

IN-BARWANI.detail: The Battle of Pilsud was fought between Sawai Jai Singh and the Marathas under Kanhoji Bhonsle and Khanderao Dabhade.
IN-BARWANI.belligerents: Kingdom of Jaipur, Bundelkhand, Bundi, Raghogarh vs Maratha Confederacy Afghan chieftains

IN-PALWAL.detail: after the murder of Sayyid Husain Ali, Emperor Muhammad Shah's army meets Sayyid Abdullah Khan's forces fifty miles south of Delhi (13–14 November 1720); Abdullah is crushed and captured, ending the Sayyid ascendancy.
IN-PALWAL.belligerents: Muhammad Shah (Mughal Empire) vs Sayyid Abdullah Khan
IN-PALWAL.outcome: Muhammad Shah victory; Sayyid Abdullah Khan defeated and taken prisoner, poisoned two years later
IN-PALWAL.source: HCIP VIII p. 23: 'the imperial army reached Hasanpur, fifty miles south of Delhi on 14 November, 1720... But ‘Abdullah suffered a crushing defeat at the battle of Hasanpur. He was taken prisoner'; chronology p. 815 dates the battle 13 November 1720

IN-BHOPAL.detail: The Battle of Ratanpur or Battle of Pandhar or Battle of Husainpur or Battle of Khandwa in June 1720 A.D.
IN-BHOPAL.belligerents: Mughal Empire Deccan Subah vs Mughal Empire Sayyid Brothers

IN-BHOPAL.detail: Bajirao I's Marathas surround and starve the Nizam-ul-Mulk's Mughal army outside Bhopal (December 1737 – January 1738); by the Treaty of Bhopal that follows, the Mughals cede Malwa to the Marathas.
IN-BHOPAL.outcome: Maratha victory — the Nizam concedes Malwa
IN-BHOPAL.source: HCIP VIII p. 91: 'the Nizam begged for terms on 7 January, 1738, at Duraha Sarai, and signed a convention promising the Peshwa: (i) the subahdari of the province of Malwa ... (iv) promise of 50 lakhs of rupees to meet his war expenses. The victory of Bhopal marks the zenith of the Peshwa's triumphant career.'

IN-IMPHAL-EAST.detail: Manipur’s greatest king throws off Burmese overlordship and leads repeated raids into the Burmese plains (1725, 1735, 1738, 1739, 1749).
IN-IMPHAL-EAST.outcome: Manipur victory; 'several successful expeditions into Burma' — reversed after his death, when from 1755 Burma dominated Manipur
IN-IMPHAL-EAST.source: HCIP IX p. 1027: 'Gharib Niwaz, the most powerful ruler of Manipur, led several successful expeditions into Burma in 1725, 1735, 1738, 1739 and in 1749. Due to disunity among the successors of Gharib Niwaz, however, Manipur lost her independence.'

IN-IMPHAL-EAST.detail: when Marjit Singh, Burma’s vassal since 1812, shows independence and skips Bagyidaw’s coronation, a Burmese army occupies Manipur; Marjit flees to Cachar and the seven-year devastation of Manipur begins.
IN-IMPHAL-EAST.outcome: Konbaung victory; Marjit expelled and Manipur occupied until 1825
IN-IMPHAL-EAST.source: HCIP IX p. 1027: 'In 1812 Marjit occupied the throne of Manipur as a vassal of Burma. But in 1818-1819, when he showed signs of independence, a Burmese army occupied Manipur. Marjit fled from Manipur.' HCIP IX p. 129: 'the expulsion of the king of Manipur who had failed to attend the coronation ceremony of Bagyidaw.'

IN-IMPHAL-EAST.detail: with Company sanction and his own Manipur Levy, the exiled prince drives the Burmese out of Manipur and takes the capital.
IN-IMPHAL-EAST.outcome: Manipur victory; Burmese driven out and Gambhir Singh’s title recognised at Yandabo
IN-IMPHAL-EAST.source: HCIP IX p. 103: 'Gambhir Singh, who had joined the British camp with his troops, was permitted to conquer it on his own account. He did so and occupied the capital.' HCIP IX p. 1028: 'The Burmese forces were driven out of Manipur.' (Year from the course of the war: the book narrates it after the 1824 rains; web accounts give June 1825.)

IN-IMPHAL-EAST.text: Gambhir Singh dies — The Manipuri prince who drove the Burmese out of Manipur in the first Burmese war and ruled it as an ally of the Company.
IN-IMPHAL-EAST.source: HCIP IX p. 1029: 'Gambhir Singh died in 1834, leaving a son, Chandrakirti, only two years old.'

IN-IMPHAL-EAST.detail: Manipur's brief resistance ends in annexation
the Japanese Fifteenth Army and the INA drive into Manipur and are broken in four months of siege
IN-IMPHAL-EAST.belligerents: British Raj & Allies vs Japan & Indian National Army
IN-IMPHAL-EAST.outcome: Allied victory — the Japanese offensive collapses with catastrophic losses
IN-IMPHAL-EAST.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-VADODARA.detail: The Battle of Dabhoi was fought on 28 April 1731, and it was a major confrontation between the Trimbak Rao Dabhade and Baji Rao I due to political interference of the Peshwas.
IN-VADODARA.belligerents: Trimbakrao's Maratha faction vs Bajirao's Maratha faction
IN-VADODARA.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 818: '1731, April 1 Armies led by Trimbak Rao Dabhade Senapati and the Peshwa clash against each other at Dabhoi and the army led by the Senapati is defeated and he is slain'. HCIP gives 1 April; the row's text, following Wikipedia, gives 28 April 1731.

IN-VADODARA.detail: Damaji Gaekwad gives the Peshwa half of Gujarat, pays arrears and tribute, and becomes the Peshwa's subordinate tributary.
IN-VADODARA.source: HCIP VIII p. 283: 'From this date, the Gaikwar became a subordinate tributary of the Peshwa ... The partition of Gujarat took place in 1752.' Chronology p. 824: '1752, March Gujarat partitioned between the Peshwa and Damaji Gaikwar.'

IN-VADODARA.text: Damaji Gaekwad dies — the ablest of the Gaekwads, who expelled the Mughal nawabs and brought nearly all of Gujarat under Maratha rule.
IN-VADODARA.source: HCIP VIII p. 284: 'Damaji died on 18 August, 1768 ... By far he was the ablest of the Gaikwar family. He brought practically the whole of Gujarat, including Kathiawar under his rule'.

IN-VADODARA.detail: by the convention of Cambay (March 1802) and the treaty of 6 June 1802, Anandrao Gaekwad accepts a British subsidiary force of 2,000 sepoys and cedes Dholka, Nadiad, Vijapur and Kadi to pay for it.
IN-VADODARA.source: HCIP VIII p. 290: 'entered into a convention with him at Cambay in March, 1802 by which Raoji agreed to receive a subsidiary force of two thousand sepoys ... He had already (6 June 1802) entered into a subsidiary alliance with the East India Company'.

IN-PANNA.text: Chhatrasal Bundela dies — At Panna, aged eighty-two
IN-PANNA.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 817: '1731, December 14 Death of Chhatrasal Bundela at Panna at the age of 82 (p. 140).'

IN-SANGLI.detail: Shahu and Sambhaji II divide the Maratha kingdom on 13 April 1731. The land from the Warna south to the Tungabhadra goes to Kolhapur, which becomes a separate principality.
IN-SANGLI.source: HCIP VIII p. 71: 'the treaty of Warna was concluded on 13 April, 1731. The territory held by Shambhuji was recognised as his State'; p. 232: 'Kolhapur remained an integral part of the Maratha empire until the treaty of Warna (in 1731) formed it into an independent principality.'

IN-KHEDA.text: Pilaji Gaekwad dies — founder of the Gaekwad house of Baroda, murdered at Dakor on the orders of Abhay Singh, the Mughal governor of Gujarat.
IN-KHEDA.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II p. 131: 'Abhay Sinh managed to encompass Pilaji's murder by treacherous means at Dakor on 14th April 1732.' HCIP VIII p. 280: 'Songarh henceforth became the cradle of the Gaikwar house.'

IN-KANNIYAKUMARI.belligerents: Travancore vs Dutch Empire / Dutch East India Company
IN-KANNIYAKUMARI.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-KANNIYAKUMARI.detail: Travancore under Marthanda Varma routs the Dutch VOC — a rare decisive Indian defeat of a European power
IN-KANNIYAKUMARI.belligerents: Kingdom of Travancore vs Dutch East India Company (VOC)
IN-KANNIYAKUMARI.outcome: Travancore victory; many Dutchmen captured, D'Lannoy among them
IN-KANNIYAKUMARI.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 229: 'In the famous battle fought at Colachel (10th August 1741) the forces of Marthanda Varma won a resounding victory over the Dutch ... A disaster of the first magnitude for the Dutch'

IN-BARDDHAMAN.detail: The Battle of Katwa was a decisive engagement fought on 27 September 1742 between the forces of Nawab Alivardi Khan of Bengal and the Maratha general Bhaskar Pandit.
IN-BARDDHAMAN.belligerents: Bengal Subah vs Maratha Empire Kingdom of Nagpur
IN-BARDDHAMAN.outcome: Bengal Subah victory; Alivardi bridges the Ajay by night and surprises Bhaskar’s camp at Katwa — the Marathas flee leaving tents and baggage, and are driven beyond the Chilka lake by December 1742
IN-BARDDHAMAN.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 58: 'The surprise was complete. The Marathas fled without waiting to ascertain the strength of the attacking force ... the Nawab’s victory was complete, the Marathas had to leave all their tents, equipment and property behind.' HCIP VIII chronology p. 821: '1742, September 27 Ali Vardi Khan raids the Maratha camp under the command of Bhaskar Ram'.

IN-KOLKATA.detail: The First Maratha invasion of Bengal occurred in 1742, led by Bhaskar Pandit under the command of Raghuji Bhonsle, the Maratha ruler of Nagpur.
IN-KOLKATA.belligerents: Bengal Subah vs Maratha Empire Kingdom of Nagpur

IN-KOLKATA.detail: Alivardi Khan invites Bhaskar Pandit to a peace interview near Berhampore on 31 March 1744 and has him and twenty-one Maratha generals cut down, ending the third Maratha incursion.
IN-KOLKATA.belligerents: Bengal Subah vs Maratha Empire Kingdom of Nagpur
IN-KOLKATA.outcome: Bengal Subah victory; won by treachery — Bhaskar and his generals killed at the interview and their army routed, after which Bengal had fifteen months’ peace
IN-KOLKATA.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 66: 'an auspicious day (the second day of the Bengali new-year, 31 March, 1744) was fixed for the interview. The place selected for the meeting was the plain of Mankara ... the Nawab ... cried out, “Kill these wretched misbelievers.”'; p. 67: 'The three eastern provinces enjoyed peace and happiness for fifteen months after the death of Bhaskar.'

IN-KOLKATA.text: The fall of Calcutta and the 'Black Hole'
IN-KOLKATA.detail: Siraj-ud-daula storms the Kasimbazar factory (4 June) and takes Fort William (20 June 1756). Holwell said 123 prisoners died overnight in the fort’s guardroom; HCIP rejects the story as untrue. Plassey followed within the year.
IN-KOLKATA.source: HCIP VIII p. 112: 'On 4 June, 1756, the factory of the English at Kasimbazar was stormed by the Nawab’s soldiers, and starting for Calcutta on 5 June, the Nawab captured Calcutta on 20 June ... But Holwell’s story of the ‘Black Hole’ has been proved by modern researches to be untrue.' Holwell’s figure of 123 is from Holwell’s narrative (web); books disagree.

IN-KOLKATA.detail: after Clive and Watson retake Calcutta, Siraj-ud-daulah restores the Company’s trade rights and factories, promises compensation and lets it fortify Calcutta and coin sicca rupees (9 February 1757).
IN-KOLKATA.source: HCIP VIII p. 112: 'Adverse circumstances now forced Siraj-ud-daulah to conclude the treaty of ‘Alinagar on 9 February, 1757, by which trade rights and factories of the English East India Company were restored to them ... the English were granted permission by him to fortify Calcutta and to coin sicca rupees.'

IN-KOLKATA.detail: on the Panchen Lama’s intercession Hastings makes peace with the Deb Raja; Bhutan’s tribute for Falakata passes to the Company and Bhutanese caravans may trade duty-free to Rangpur.
IN-KOLKATA.source: HCIP IX p. 1020: 'As a result of his intercession a treaty was made between the Government of India and Bhutan on 25th April, 1774. The tribute of five Tangan horses, which had been paid by Bhutan to the Cooch Behar Raja for the province of Falakata, was transferred to the East India Company.'

IN-KOLKATA.text: Maharaja Nandakumar is hanged at Calcutta — The former diwan who accused Warren Hastings of taking bribes was tried for forgery by the new Supreme Court and executed.
IN-KOLKATA.source: HCIP VIII p. 374: 'Nandkumar was tried by the Supreme Court, and a jury entirely consisting of Eurasian inhabitants of Calcutta under English law which was of doubtful application at the time in India, and was sentenced to death on the charge.' HCIP VIII chronology p. 835: '1775, May Nandkumar executed on forgery charges' (the hanging is usually dated 5 August 1775).

IN-KOLKATA.detail: Cornwallis fixes the land revenue of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa for ever and makes the zamindars its proprietors; the cultivators become their tenants.
IN-KOLKATA.source: HCIP VIII p. 479: 'Special attention must be devoted to Cornwallis’ Permanent Settlement of Bengal land revenue ... Cornwallis, faced with a country in ruins, decided on Permanent Settlement making the zamindars or rent collectors permanent land-owners. The settlement secured for the Company a fixed amount of revenue.' HCIP IX p. 374 gives the date: 'the Permanent Settlement of 1793'.

IN-KOLKATA.text: Ramakrishna dies — At Cossipore, of cancer of the throat
IN-KOLKATA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-KOLKATA.detail: Curzon’s marble monument on the Maidan, twenty years in the building.
IN-KOLKATA.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-CHENNAI.belligerents: French India vs East India Company, Carnatic (Arcot Nawab)
IN-CHENNAI.outcome: Inconclusive — Aix-la-Chapelle brought a 'mutual exchange of prisoners and places'; Madras was restored to the English in August 1749
IN-CHENNAI.source: HCIP VIII p. 317-319, 321: 'There was mutual exchange of prisoners and places taken in the war. The English got back Madras'.

IN-CHENNAI.detail: a small French force scatters the Nawab of Arcot's army, exposing Indian armies to European tactics
IN-CHENNAI.outcome: French India victory; Mahfuz Khan's army broken by Paradis's small force
IN-CHENNAI.source: HCIP VIII p. 318-319: 'He sent a strong force under his eldest son Mahfuz Khan to wrest Madras from the unfaithful French ... The French fire was too hot and quick for the Muhammadans.'

IN-CHENNAI.detail: La Bourdonnais bombards Fort St George, which surrenders on 21 September 1746; Dupleix then refuses the ransom and holds the town until the peace.
IN-CHENNAI.belligerents: French India vs East India Company
IN-CHENNAI.outcome: French India victory; Fort St George surrenders on 21 September 1746
IN-CHENNAI.source: HCIP VIII p. 318: 'The French erected batteries, and after a short bombardment received the surrender of the Fort from the English (September 21).'

IN-CHENNAI.belligerents: France/French East India Company, Mughal Empire, Mysore, Nawab of Arcot (Chanda Sahib), Hyderabad (Muzaffar Jang) vs Great Britain/British East India Company, Maratha Empire, Nawab of Arcot (Wallajah), Hyderabad (Nasir Jung)
IN-CHENNAI.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-CHENNAI.text: Seven Years' War / Third Carnatic War
IN-CHENNAI.belligerents: France and allies including French East India Company; Mughal Empire from 1757 vs Great Britain and allies including British East India Company; Portugal from 1761
IN-CHENNAI.outcome: Status quo ante in Europe; colonial transfers
IN-CHENNAI.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-CHENNAI.detail: Lally occupies the Black Town and bombards Fort St George for ten weeks from 12 December, but raises the siege when Pocock's fleet appears in February 1759.
IN-CHENNAI.belligerents: French India vs East India Company
IN-CHENNAI.outcome: East India Company victory; Lally precipitately raises the siege
IN-CHENNAI.source: HCIP VIII p. 334: 'Lally began the long-pending siege of Madras (December 12) ... When the English fleet under Admiral Pocock was sighted off the coast, Lally precipitately raised the siege and moved to Arcot'.

IN-CHENNAI.text: Muhammad Ali Khan Wallajah dies — the Company's Nawab of Arcot since the Carnatic wars, whose debts to Company servants drew the Company ever deeper into the Carnatic.
IN-CHENNAI.source: HCIP VIII p. 484: 'Muhammad Ali died in October, 1795 and Umdat-ul-Umara succeeded him.'

IN-CHENNAI.detail: Wellesley declares the Nawab a public enemy on Tipu's papers; on Umdat-ul-Umara's death (15 July 1801) his nephew Azim-ud-daula accepts the title and a pension, and the Company takes over the whole civil and military government.
IN-CHENNAI.source: HCIP VIII p. 526: 'Umdat-ul-Umara died on 15 July, 1801 ... the offer was made to a nephew of the deceased Nawab, Azim-ud-daulah. He accepted ... and the whole civil and military administration was taken over by the British.'

IN-CHENNAI.text: The Carnatic and Tanjore titles extinguished
IN-CHENNAI.detail: when Nawab Muhammad Ghaus dies childless (17 October) and Raja Shivaji of Tanjore dies leaving only daughters (29 October 1855), Dalhousie abolishes the nawabship and declares the Tanjore Raj extinct.
IN-CHENNAI.source: HCIP IX p. 81: 'On October 17, 1855, Muhammad Ghaus, the Nawab of the Carnatic, died without leaving any issue ... It was, however, decided that the title of Nawab should be abolished.' p. 82: 'On 29 October, 1855, died Shivaji, the Raja of Tanjore ... The Council of Madras ... decided that the Tanjore Raj was extinct'.

IN-CHENNAI.detail: Two failed monsoons across the Deccan and the south, and grain exported through it; some five million dead in British territory and more in the states, while Lytton held the Delhi Durbar.
IN-CHENNAI.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-BHAGALPUR.detail: Battle of Bhagalpur in 1745 was a military conflict between Marathas under Raghuji I of Nagpur and Nawab Alivardi Khan in the Bihar province of Bengal Subah.
IN-BHAGALPUR.belligerents: Bengal Subah vs Maratha Empire Nagpur State

IN-ALAPPUZHA.detail: after the Treaty of Mannar (1742) is broken, Ramayyan Dalawa takes the Kayamkulam fort and palace; the Raja flees and his kingdom is absorbed, completing Marthanda Varma's hold on the old Quilon lands.
IN-ALAPPUZHA.outcome: Travancore victory; Kayamkulam annexed and its Raja flees
IN-ALAPPUZHA.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 230: 'The Raja thereafter fled from his kingdom. The Travancore army captured the Kayamkulam fort and palace ... Immediately after the annexation of Kayamkulam (1746)'.

IN-ALAPPUZHA.detail: ratifying the accord of 1748, the Dutch renounce interference in Kerala's quarrels, abandon their other princely allies and agree to live at peace with Travancore.
IN-ALAPPUZHA.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 230: 'by the treaty of 1748, ratified later by the treaty of Mavelikkara (1753), the Dutch had undertaken to follow a strict policy of non-involvement in native disputes ... The treaty was a tremendous gain to Marthanda Varma'.

IN-ALAPPUZHA.detail: the northern confederacy under Cochin, backing the dispossessed Rajas of Ambalapuzha, Tekkumkur and Vadakkumkur, is routed by Travancore; the Cochin commander Idikkela Menon is executed and Cochin sues for peace.
IN-ALAPPUZHA.outcome: Travancore victory; the Cochin army routed, its commander executed, Karappuram conquered
IN-ALAPPUZHA.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 231: 'In a decisive battle that ensued the Cochin forces were routed and put to flight ... Idikkela Menon, the Commander of the Cochin forces, was captured and executed ... The Cochin Raja sued for peace.' (Menon's text gives both 'end of 1756' and '3rd January 1754'; p. 240 dates the battle 1754.)

IN-TONK.detail: The Battle of Rajamahal was a military engagement fought in 1747 in Jaipur, India.
IN-TONK.belligerents: Kingdom of Jaipur vs Kingdom of Mewar, Supporters of Madho Singh, Holkar State

IN-TONK.detail: The Battle of Kakkor was fought by the Maratha Holkar principality of Indore, led by the veteran Gangadhar Tatya, who was sent into battle by Malhar Rao Holkar.

Lakhwa Dada's army — Pohlmann's brigade of De Boigne's corps, Dudrenec's Holkar brigade and a Kota battalion — broke Sawai Pratap Singh's Jaipur army and its Rathor cavalry from Jodhpur on 16 April 1800, despite a Rathor charge that rode down Dudrenec's brigade.
IN-TONK.belligerents: Gwalior (Scindia), Holkar (Indore State) contingent vs Jaipur, Jodhpur (Marwar)
IN-TONK.outcome: Scindia victory; Jaipur's guns, camp and baggage lost; Pratap Singh pays 25 lakhs for peace
IN-TONK.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire IV p. 159: 'Lakhwa struck a decisive blow at the Rajput army. Battle of Malpura, 16 April 1800.' Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages I p. 257: 'A decisive battle fought at Malpura in April 1800 ... 74 out of 80 pieces of cannon brought into the field were lost, together with the entire camp, baggage and warlike stores ... He made peace on payment of 25 lakhs (May 1800).'

IN-BAREILLY.text: Ali Muhammad Khan Rohilla dies — Founder of Rohilla power in Katehr (Rohilkhand), months after re-establishing himself there against Mughal rule.
IN-BAREILLY.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 823: '1748, February All Muhammad Rohilla... returns to Rohilkhand with his followers and re-establishes himself in March/April 1748, overthrowing Mughul rule... 1748, September 15 Death of Ali Muhammad Rohilla (p. 136)'

IN-BAREILLY.detail: Campbell's converging columns reach Rohilkhand's rebel capital; Khan Bahadur Khan's army, with its charges of Ghazis, is beaten on 5 May and Bareilly occupied next day, though Khan Bahadur escapes to fight on.
IN-BAREILLY.belligerents: East India Company vs Rohilkhand rebels (Khan Bahadur Khan)
IN-BAREILLY.outcome: East India Company victory; Bareilly occupied on 6 May, Khan Bahadur Khan escaped with most of his army
IN-BAREILLY.source: HCIP IX p. 572-573: 'Sir Colin reached the city on May 4... A fierce battle took place the next day, but though he was defeated, his men gave a good account of themselves... After six hours’ severe fighting the British gained a complete victory and occupied Bareilly the next day (May 6). Khan Bahadur Khan effected his escape'

IN-PUDUCHERRY.detail: Admiral Boscawen's fleet and army attack the French capital before the rains, but Dupleix's new works hold and the English withdraw with heavy loss.
IN-PUDUCHERRY.belligerents: East India Company vs French India
IN-PUDUCHERRY.outcome: French India victory; the English siege is withdrawn and Dupleix's reputation 'stood greatly enhanced'
IN-PUDUCHERRY.source: HCIP VIII p. 319: 'the English attack could make no impression and had to be withdrawn with considerable loss through sickness and lack of caution. Dupleix's reputation stood greatly enhanced after this set-back for the English.'

IN-PUDUCHERRY.detail: Dupleix's successor and the Madras Governor agree that both Companies renounce Indian offices and stop fighting for their Nawabs; the truce is never ratified and the Seven Years' War overtakes it.
IN-PUDUCHERRY.source: HCIP VIII p. 329: 'The provisional treaty of January 1755 between himself and the English Governor declared that both the Companies should renounce all Indian governments and dignities and not interfere in the disputes of the Indian powers'.

IN-PUDUCHERRY.detail: the British take France's capital in India; the Compagnie's power is broken
IN-PUDUCHERRY.belligerents: East India Company vs French India
IN-PUDUCHERRY.outcome: East India Company victory; Lally surrenders unconditionally (January 1761) and the fortifications are razed
IN-PUDUCHERRY.source: HCIP VIII p. 335: 'After more than four months of desperate resistance, Lally ... surrendered unconditionally (January 1761). The English ruthlessly demolished all the fortifications of the city.'

IN-PUDUCHERRY.detail: on news of the Anglo-French war, Munro besieges the French capital from 8 August; it falls on 18 October, and the Company moves on Mahe — the step that drives Haidar into the Second Mysore War.
IN-PUDUCHERRY.belligerents: East India Company vs French India
IN-PUDUCHERRY.outcome: East India Company victory; Pondicherry surrenders in October 1778
IN-PUDUCHERRY.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III p. ~309 (block 285): 'Pondicherry, held by the French, was besieged by the English (8th August to 18th October 1778). On the fall of Pondicherry in October'.

IN-TIRUPATHUR.detail: French-backed Chanda Sahib wins the Carnatic succession
IN-TIRUPATHUR.belligerents: French India, Chanda Sahib, Muzaffar Jang vs Carnatic (Arcot Nawab)
IN-TIRUPATHUR.outcome: French India victory; Nawab Anwar-ud-din defeated and slain, Chanda Sahib installed at Arcot (August 1749)
IN-TIRUPATHUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 321: 'At Ambur, 50 miles to the west of Arcot, Anwar-ud-din was defeated and slain ... Chanda Sahib was formally installed as the Nawab of the Karnatak by Muzaffar Jang.'

IN-TIRUPATHUR.detail: The siege of Ambur was conducted by a combined force of Mysorean and Hyderabadi troops under the command of Hyder Ali against the town of Ambur in southern India.
IN-TIRUPATHUR.belligerents: East India Company, Carnatic (Arcot Nawab) vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu), Hyderabad
IN-TIRUPATHUR.outcome: East India Company victory; Calvert's garrison holds until Smith's relief on 7 December 1767
IN-TIRUPATHUR.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III p. ~62-63 (blocks 79-80): 'the frequent sallies that Captain Calvert, with his 500 sepoys ... made from the fort, prevented him from attempting to take it by storm ... the British colours still flying on the morning of the 7th of December'.

IN-FARRUKHABAD.text: Siege of Fatehgarh and the rout of the Rohillas
IN-FARRUKHABAD.detail: Safdar Jang brings in Jayappa Sindhia and Malhar Holkar; on 18 April 1751 the Marathas crush Sadullah Khan's Rohilla relief army across the Ganges, Ahmad Bangash abandons Fatehgarh, and the Marathas loot the Bangash country.
IN-FARRUKHABAD.belligerents: Maratha Empire, Awadh (Safdar Jang), Bharatpur vs Farrukhabad (Bangash), Rohilkhand (Rohillas)
IN-FARRUKHABAD.outcome: Maratha victory; over ten thousand Afghans slain or wounded, Fatehgarh occupied on 19 April, the Bangash and Rohilla chiefs driven to the foothills
IN-FARRUKHABAD.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 255-256: 'After a great battle defeat fell in the end on the Afghans. Sadullah and Mahmud fled away with their bare lives... over ten thousand of their men were slain or wounded... In the morning (19th April), the Marathas occupied Fatehgarh'; HCIP VIII chronology p. 824: 'The combined armies of Mughuls and the Marathas inflict severe defeats on the Rohillas'

IN-FARRUKHABAD.detail: The Battle of Farrukhabad, also called the Battle of Fatehgarh, was an engagement during the Second Anglo-Maratha War fought by forces of the East India Company.
IN-FARRUKHABAD.belligerents: Maratha Empire, Holkar (Indore State) vs East India Company
IN-FARRUKHABAD.outcome: East India Company victory; Yashwant Rao Holkar routed by Lake's cavalry at Farrukhabad on 17 November 1804
IN-FARRUKHABAD.source: HCIP VIII p. 498: 'Holkar himself was routed by Lake at Farrukhabad on 17 November, 1804, and was compelled to turn to Ranjit Singh, the Raja of Bharatpur, for supplies of money and arms.'

IN-DARBHANGA.detail: The Battle of Kandarpi Ghat occurred between the Nawab of Bengal and Raj Darbhanga in October 1753.

IN-FAIZABAD.text: Safdar Jang dies — Nawab of Awadh and former Mughal wazir, beaten at Ram Chatauni and in the Delhi civil war
IN-FAIZABAD.source: HCIP VIII p. 114: 'Safdar Jang died in October 1754 and his son Shuja-ud-daulah became subahdar of Awadh.'

IN-FAIZABAD.text: Shuja-ud-Daula dies — Nawab-Wazir of Awadh, Abdali's ally at Panipat and the Company's enemy at Buxar
IN-FAIZABAD.source: HCIP VIII p. 119: 'Shuja-ud-daulah died on 26 January, 1775, and was succeeded by his eldest son Asaf-ud-daulah. Awadh, for all practical purposes, became a dependency of the East India Company.'

IN-KATIHAR.detail: Siraj-ud-daulah marches on Purnea and kills his cousin and rival Shaukat Jang, whom Mir Ja‘far had egged on to claim the masnad.
IN-KATIHAR.belligerents: Bengal (Nawab) — Siraj-ud-daulah vs Shaukat Jang, Nawab of Purnea
IN-KATIHAR.outcome: Siraj-ud-daulah victory; Shaukat Jang killed on 16 October 1756
IN-KATIHAR.source: HCIP VIII p. 112: 'By marching from Calcutta towards Purnea, on 24 September, 1756, Siraj-ud-daulah defeated and killed him in a battle at Manihari on 16 October, 1756.' (also chronology p. 826)

IN-SINDHUDURG.detail: The Battle of Vijaydurg was fought between Tulaji Angre, the Admiral of the Maratha Navy, and the combined forces of the British East India Company and the Maratha Empire.
IN-SINDHUDURG.belligerents: East India Company, Maratha Empire (Peshwa) vs Tulaji Angre (Kolaba Angres)
IN-SINDHUDURG.outcome: East India Company and Maratha victory; Tulaji Angre surrendered to the Peshwa's commander on 12 February 1756 and the English occupied Vijaydurg, restoring it to the Peshwa in October for Bankot
IN-SINDHUDURG.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 826: '1756, February 12 Tulaji Angria surrenders to the Maratha commander when attacked by the joint forces of the Marathas and the English'; p. 306: 'Vijayadurg was restored to the Peshwa on 12 October, 1756. In lieu of it, the English obtained Bankot'; p. 183: 'he destroyed the naval power of Tulaji Angria with the help of the British.'

IN-VIZIANAGARAM.detail: The Battle of Bobbili, comprising the attack on the fort of Bobbili on 24 January 1757, was a significant event in the princely state of Vizianagaram.
IN-VIZIANAGARAM.outcome: French India victory; Bussy storms Bobbili and puts the defenders to the sword
IN-VIZIANAGARAM.source: HCIP VIII p. 332: 'except at Bobbili where, at the instigation of the crafty Vijayarama Raju of Vijayanagaram, he put to the sword all the brave defenders.'

IN-MATHURA.text: Battle of Chaumuha and the sack of Mathura
IN-MATHURA.detail: sent by Ahmad Shah Abdali to put the Jat country 'to the edge of the sword', Jahan Khan and Najib break Jawahir Singh's stand at Chaumuha eight miles north of Mathura (28 February 1757) and massacre the pilgrims of Mathura, Vrindavan and Gokul.
IN-MATHURA.outcome: Durrani victory; after nine hours' fighting the Jat army broke and Mathura was sacked
IN-MATHURA.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 117-118: 'Outside the village of Chaumuha, eight miles north of Mathura, Jawahir Singh barred the invader’s path with less than 10,000 men and offered a desperate resistance (28th February.) From sunrise the battle raged for nine hours... and the broken remnant of the Jat army took the road to their homes.'

IN-MATHURA.detail: hired by Ranjit Singh in the Jat succession war, the Marathas under Ramchandra Ganesh and Mahadji Sindhia defeat the Bharatpur raja Nawal Singh near Sonkh (6 April 1770) — the first blow in the decline of Jat power.
IN-MATHURA.belligerents: Maratha Empire, Ranjit Singh (Jat claimant) vs Bharatpur (Nawal Singh)
IN-MATHURA.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 833: '1770, April 6 The Marathas defeat Nawal Singh, Jat ruler, near Sonkh (p. 220)'; Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire III contents: 'Marathas hired by Ranjit, 8—Nawal S. defeated at Sonkh, 9'

IN-MATHURA.detail: Mirza Najaf Khan's new-model imperial army, the first in Upper India to face European-trained sepoys on both sides, destroys the Jat army of Nawal Singh and Sombre between Sahar and Barsana (30 October 1773); Kotban falls and Agra is recovered for the emperor.
IN-MATHURA.belligerents: Mughal Empire (Mirza Najaf Khan) vs Bharatpur (Nawal Singh, Sombre's battalions)
IN-MATHURA.outcome: Mughal Empire victory; decisive defeat of the Jat army, Nawal Singh fled
IN-MATHURA.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire III p. 98-101: '§6. Battle before Barsana; Jat disaster. Fall of Kotban. After skirmishes for ten days, the decisive battle was fought on 30th October, midway between Sahar and Barsana'; p. 101 running head 'Decisive defeat of Jat army'

IN-MATHURA.text: Ghulam Qadir dies — The Rohilla who blinded Shah Alam II, captured by Mahadji Sindhia's men, blinded in his turn and put to death near Mathura.
IN-MATHURA.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 838: '1788, December 31 Ghulam Qadir captured (p. 262)... 1789, March 3 Ghulam Qadir put to death (p. 399).'; Sarkar IV p. 9: '3rd March the Ruhela’s eyes were dug out and sent in a casket to Shah Alam'

IN-HOSHIARPUR.detail: The Battle of Mahilpur was fought between the combined forces of Adina Beg Khan and Sikh Misls and the Durrani Empire in December 1757.
IN-HOSHIARPUR.belligerents: Sikh Misls, Adina Beg vs Durrani Empire

IN-HOSHIARPUR.text: Adina Beg Khan dies — the survivor who played Mughals, Afghans, Sikhs and Marathas against each other and ended as Maratha-backed governor of the Punjab
IN-HOSHIARPUR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 77: 'Adina Beg Khan enjoyed his highest glory for five months only. On 13 October 1758 he died after a prolonged illness ... Immediately afterwards, confusion broke out in the Panjab.' (Place of death not given in the book; coordinates approximate, Hoshiarpur district.)

IN-BULDANA.detail: the Peshwa's army under Dattaji Scindia besieges Ramchandra Jadhav in Sindkhed. After four days of fighting (12–16 December 1757), Nizam Ali's attempt to break the siege fails, and on 17 December he asks for terms. Peace is made at Sakharkherda.
IN-BULDANA.outcome: Maratha victory; Nizam Ali acknowledged defeat and sued for terms
IN-BULDANA.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II p. 334: 'A fierce battle was fought continuously for four days at the gate of Sindkhed ... Victory remained with the Marathas ... On 17th December Nizam Ali acknowledging defeat sent Vithal Sundar to the Maratha camp begging for terms.' HCIP VIII p. 182: 'A peace was made at Sakharkharda'.

PK-ATTOCK.belligerents: Maratha Empire and Sikh Confederacy vs Durrani Empire and Rohilkhand
PK-ATTOCK.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

PK-ATTOCK.detail: The Battle of Hasan Abdal took place on June 7, 1813, between the Sikhs led by Bhayya Ram Singh and Afghans led by Fateh Khan Barakzai at Hasan Abdal.
PK-ATTOCK.outcome: Durrani victory; Bhayya Ram Singh's 500 men put to flight and Attock besieged
PK-ATTOCK.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V pp. 99–100: 'Wazir Fatah Khan attacked Hasan Abdal on 7 June, 1813 with 2,000 Afghans. Ram Singh had only 500 horse and foot. About 50 men were killed on both sides. Ram Singh and his men took to flight.'

IN-BIJNOR.detail: Dattaji Sindhia besieges Najib Khan's entrenched camp on the Ganges from September to December 1759; Najib holds out until Abdali's return to the Punjab forces the Marathas to raise the siege.
IN-BIJNOR.belligerents: Maratha Empire (Dattaji Sindhia) vs Rohilkhand (Rohillas) — Najib Khan
IN-BIJNOR.outcome: Rohilla victory; the Maratha siege failed and Dattaji raised it on 8 December
IN-BIJNOR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 207: '§ 5. Dattaji’s siege of Shukartal; fighting.'; p. 216: 'There was nothing left for Dattaji now but to raise his futile siege (8th December.)'

IN-VAISHALI.detail: on his second invasion of Bihar the new emperor Shah Alam II beats Raja Ram Narayan, the Nawab’s deputy, four miles east of Fatuha on 9 February 1760.
IN-VAISHALI.belligerents: Mughal Empire (Shah Alam II, Kamgar Khan) vs Bengal (Nawab) — Ram Narayan, with East India Company sepoys
IN-VAISHALI.outcome: Mughal victory; Ram Narayan defeated and wounded, three of his commanders go over, four companies of Company sepoys cut off with Captain Cochrane
IN-VAISHALI.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II pp. 539–540: 'Ram Narayan ... had issued from Patna and given battle to the imperialists at Masumpur on 9th February; but three of his divisional commanders treacherously went over to the enemy ... Ram Narayan had to retreat to his fort defeated and wounded. Four companies of English sepoys were cut off with all their three European officers, including Captain Cochrane.'

IN-MEERUT.detail: The Battle of Meerut was a military skirmish initiated by Emperor Ahmed Shah Durrani in an attempt to capture Govind Pant Bundela, who had taken refuge in Meerut.

Bapuji Sindhia, Sindhia's amil of Saharanpur, attacks a Rohilla raiding force near Sardhana and, after a very long action, totally defeats and disperses it; the Rohilla leader Umar Khan and his son are killed and a standard taken. The Resident judged it unlikely the Rohillas would again 'raise commotion in the Doab'.
IN-MEERUT.belligerents: Gwalior (Scindia) — Bapuji Sindhia, amil of Saharanpur — vs Rohilla raiders under Umar Khan
IN-MEERUT.outcome: Sindhia victory; Umar Khan and his son killed; Rohilla incursions into the upper Doab end
IN-MEERUT.source: William Palmer, Resident with Sindhia, to Sir John Shore, Governor-General, from Lakhwa Dada's camp, 24 October 1796 — letter no. 40 in Jadunath Sarkar (ed.), Daulat Rao Sindhia and North Indian Affairs (Poona Residency Correspondence). Facsimile supplied by the Scindia Research Centre, Gwalior, September 2026. A Resident's dispatch six days after the action; the amil's own report is its source.

IN-MEERUT.detail: the great revolt across north and central India
IN-MEERUT.belligerents: Mughal Empire, Oudh, forces of Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, Nana Sahib, various rajas/nawabs/zamindars/taluqdars/chieftains vs East India Company, United Kingdom, Nepal, allied princely/chiefly forces

IN-MEERUT.text: The Meerut rising and the seizure of Delhi
IN-MEERUT.detail: on 10 May 1857 the 3rd Cavalry and two infantry regiments at Meerut free their imprisoned comrades and kill their officers; next morning they reach Delhi, and on 12 May Bahadur Shah II places himself at their head as Emperor of Hindustan.
IN-MEERUT.source: HCIP IX p. 473: 'On May 10, Sunday, at about sunset... several hundreds of them galloped to the jail and released not only their comrades but also its other inmates'; p. 505: 'On reaching Delhi on the morning of May 11, they went straight to the Red Fort... Bahadur Shah placed himself at the head of the sepoys and assumed the title of the Emperor of Hindusthan.'

IN-LATUR.detail: Sadashivrao Bhau routs the Nizam's army near Udgir on 3 February 1760. By the treaty of 11 February, the Nizam cedes territory worth sixty lakhs together with Burhanpur and Asirgarh, Daulatabad, Ahmadnagar and Bijapur.
IN-LATUR.outcome: Maratha victory; the Nizam ceded 60 lakhs of territory and four fortress-capitals
IN-LATUR.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas II p. 337: 'On 3rd February a stiff action was fought in which the Asaf Jahi forces were so completely routed that Nizam Ali sent ambassadors seeking terms. He agreed to surrender to the Peshwa territory worth sixty lacs'. HCIP VIII p. 183: 'The Nizam's forces were completely defeated ... Final victory was gained on 3 February, 1760.'

PK-GUJRANWALA.detail: The Battle of Gujranwala was fought between the Durrani Empire and the Sikh Confederacy in September 1761.

PK-GUJRANWALA.text: Ranjit Singh is born — son of Mahan Singh, chief of the Sukerchakia misl
PK-GUJRANWALA.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 6: '2nd Maghar fell on 13 December, 1780, which is the correct date of Ranjit Singh's birth'; pp. 6–7: 'It is generally believed that Ranjit Singh was born in his father's home at Gujranwala. This assertion is against facts ... Atar Singh Bhadauria ... says that "Ranjit Singh was born in Pind Badrukhan".'

PK-GUJRANWALA.detail: Sikh cavalry checks Gough on the Chenab
PK-GUJRANWALA.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs East India Company
PK-GUJRANWALA.outcome: Sikh Empire victory; Gough's attack on the Sikh detachments at Nawala near Ramnagar was beaten off with heavy British loss (22 November 1848)
PK-GUJRANWALA.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 285: 'a few small scattered groups were on the left bank, at Nawala near Ramnagar. Lord Gough sent troops to drive these Sikhs, but the British suffered defeat with a heavy loss of life (November 22).'

IN-BARAN.detail: Malhar Rao Holkar, with the Sindhia family contingent and Zalim Singh's Kota troops, destroyed Madho Singh's Jaipur army between Mangrol and Bhatwara on 29 November 1761, ending the anti-Maratha coalition that Panipat had encouraged in Rajputana.
IN-BARAN.outcome: Maratha victory; the Jaipur army destroyed and its camp and guns taken. (Tod's Rajput tradition credits the Kota contingent at 'Butwarro'; Sarkar rejects it.)
IN-BARAN.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 507: 'Next day the battle raged from the morning and ended near sunset in the total destruction of the Jaipur army.' p. 508: 'The victory was decisive; it at once destroyed all chance of forming an anti-Maratha coalition, and restored Maratha prestige.' Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages I p. 253: 'in November 1761 a large Jaipur army was defeated by Malhar Rao Holkar in the battle of Mangrol.'

IN-BARAN.detail: Maharao Kishore Singh of Kota, trying to recover real power from the regent Zalim Singh, was defeated in October 1821 by a British force sent to support the regent under the 1817–18 treaty; his brother Prithvi Singh was killed.
IN-BARAN.belligerents: East India Company, Kota (regent Zalim Singh) vs Kota (Maharao Kishore Singh)
IN-BARAN.outcome: East India Company victory; Kishore Singh retreats to Mewar and later submits
IN-BARAN.source: Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages I p. 338: 'Kishore Singh returned from Brindaban to Kotah at the head of a force; but he was defeated (October 1821) by a British force which had been sent to co-operate with the Regent. Prithvi Singh was killed.' (The book does not name the field; Mangrol is the usual name.)

IN-SANGRUR.detail: Ahmad Shah, marching by forced stages from Lahore, caught the Sikh army near Kup, six miles north of Maler Kotla, on 5 February 1762 and pursued it all day; some ten thousand Sikhs were killed.
IN-SANGRUR.belligerents: Durrani (Afghan) Empire, Maler Kotla vs Sikh misls
IN-SANGRUR.outcome: Durrani victory; the Great Massacre (Vadda Ghallughara) of the Sikhs
IN-SANGRUR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II pp. 485–486: 'Early in the forenoon of 5th February, Zain Khan's vanguard ... fell in with the Sikhs near the village of Kup (6 miles north of Maler Kotla) ... In the course of this running fight, some ten thousand Sikhs were slain and the day is still remembered by them as that of the Ghallu-ghara or great scrimmage.'

IN-JALNA.detail: the Nizam and Janoji Bhonsle had sacked Poona in May 1763. Madhavrao I wins Janoji over, then defeats Nizam Ali's army under Vithal Sundar on the Godavari on 10 August 1763. Peace follows on 25 September.
IN-JALNA.outcome: Maratha victory; the Nizam's army under Vithal Sundar defeated and peace made in September 1763
IN-JALNA.source: HCIP VIII p. 202: 'In May, 1763, Nizam Ali plundered Poona ... On August 10, 1763, a portion of Nizam Ali's army under the command of Vithal Sundar was defeated by the Peshwa in the battle of Rakshasbhuvan. Peace was concluded on September 25, 1763'; p. 244: 'defeated the Nizam signally at Rakshasbhuvan in August, 1763'; p. 284 (Damaji's horse 'materially contributed to the final victory').

IN-JALNA.detail: Wellesley's outnumbered force narrowly beats Scindia's Marathas — his 'finest battle'
IN-JALNA.belligerents: East India Company vs Gwalior (Scindia), Nagpur (Bhonsle)
IN-JALNA.outcome: East India Company victory; the combined army of Scindia and Bhonsle was beaten, but at a cost of 663 European and 1,778 Indian casualties
IN-JALNA.source: HCIP VIII p. 495: 'On 23 September, 1803, in the hotly contested battle of Assaye ... the combined army of Sindia and Bhosle led by Gopal Rao Bhau and Vithal Pant Bakhshi was soundly beaten by Arthur Wellesley ... achieved at an enormous cost of men (663 Europeans and 1,778 Indian killed or wounded).'

IN-THRISSUR.detail: The Battle of Thrissur took place at Thrissur in 1763 between the forces of the Kingdom of Travancore and the Zamorin of Calicut.
IN-THRISSUR.outcome: Travancore victory; the Zamorin's forces are driven out of Cochin, and the Zamorin sues for peace and pays Rs 1,50,000
IN-THRISSUR.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 234: 'The Zamorin's forces were driven out of Cochin territory. The Zamorin himself sued for peace ... In 1763 the Zamorin himself paid a visit to the Travancore Raja ... to pay Rs. 1,50,000 as indemnity'.

IN-THRISSUR.text: Tipu's attack on the Travancore Lines
IN-THRISSUR.detail: Tipu's first assault on the Nedumkotta on 29 December 1789 is thrown back; on 15 April 1790 he breaks through, takes Cranganore, Ayakotta, Alangad and Parur and reaches Alwaye, but withdraws when the Company declares war — the cause of the Third Mysore War.
IN-THRISSUR.belligerents: Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu) vs Travancore
IN-THRISSUR.outcome: Mysore victory; the Lines are breached in April 1790 after the December 1789 repulse, but Tipu withdraws from Kerala
IN-THRISSUR.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 248: 'Tipu attacked the Travancore Lines on the 29th December 1789 ... On the 15th April 1790 the Travancore Lines were breached and Travancore troops were put to flight.' HCIP VIII p. 463: 'Tipu's first attack on Travancore lines failed ... His next attack came in April, 1790.'

IN-THRISSUR.text: Sakthan Thampuran dies — Rama Varma of Cochin (ruling in fact from 1769, crowned 1790), who broke the Nair nobility and centralised the state.
IN-THRISSUR.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 241: 'Saktan Tampuran (1790-1805) ... he was in full charge of the administration of the State from 1769 onwards'.

IN-GHAZIABAD.detail: Suraj Mal, marching on Delhi against its Rohilla regent Najib-ud-Daula, is ambushed while crossing a ravine by the Hindan near Ghaziabad on 25 December 1763 and killed; his army withdraws in the night.
IN-GHAZIABAD.outcome: Najib-ud-Daula victory; Suraj Mal shot and cut down by Rohilla musketeers in ambush, the Jat army retreated
IN-GHAZIABAD.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 451: 'It was the 25th of December... in crossing a nala left behind by the river, he fell into an Afghan ambuscade and was shot down with most of his companions by the Ruhela musketeers lying concealed among the jhau bushes.'; HCIP VIII chronology p. 829: '1763, December 25 Death of Suraj Mal Jat in a contest with Najib-ud-daulah on the bank of the Hindaun'

IN-GHAZIABAD.text: Suraj Mal dies — Killed in a Rohilla ambush by the Hindan, aged fifty-five, 'at the height of his greatness'
IN-GHAZIABAD.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 453: 'Thus perished Suraj Mal at the height of his greatness at the age of fifty-five.'

BD-RANGPUR.detail: armed bands of Hindu sannyasis and Muslim fakirs (Majnu Shah, Bhawani Pathak) raid Company factories and revenue posts across north Bengal and Bihar for a generation, until Hastings and his successors put them down.
BD-RANGPUR.belligerents: Sannyasis and Fakirs (Majnu Shah, Bhawani Pathak) vs East India Company
BD-RANGPUR.outcome: East India Company victory; the bands suppressed by c. 1800
BD-RANGPUR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire I p. 104: the Marathas 'showed the way for the organised looting of Bengal and Bihar to the up-country robber bands calling themselves sannyasis and faqirs, whom it required the genius of a Warren Hastings to suppress.' Dates 1763–1800 and leaders web-only; library silent on the details.

PK-BAHAWALPUR.detail: The Battle of Chenab was fought in early 1764 between the forces of the Durrani Empire, led by Ahmad Shah Durrani, and the combined armies of several Sikh Misls.
The Battle of Multan was an indecisive engagement fought in December 1766 by the forces of the Bhangi Misl, led by Jhanda Singh Bhangi and Ganda Singh Bhangi.
PK-BAHAWALPUR.outcome: Inconclusive territorial division agreed by treaty

PK-BAHAWALPUR.text: General Zia-ul-Haq's C-130 crashes minutes after take-off from Bahawalpur, killing him, the American ambassador and the army's senior command
PK-BAHAWALPUR.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

IN-DHAULPUR.detail: Jawahir Singh's Jats, with Sikh allies, defeat Raghunath Rao's Maratha army on the Chambal (13–14 March 1766) and occupy Dholpur.
IN-DHAULPUR.belligerents: Bharatpur, Sikh misls vs Maratha Empire
IN-DHAULPUR.outcome: Bharatpur victory; the Maratha army defeated and Dholpur occupied, several Maratha commanders captured
IN-DHAULPUR.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 831: '1766, March 13/14 The combined Jat-Sikh army under the leadership of Jawahir Singh defeats the Maratha army at the battle of Dholpur and occupy Dholpur (p. 217)'; p. 831: 'Jawahir Singh Jat concludes peace with Raghunath Rao by surrendering Maratha commanders captured in March, 1766'

IN-BHIND.text: Malhar Rao Holkar dies — At Alampur near the Chambal, founder of the house of Holkar and for thirty years the Maratha power in Hindustan.
IN-BHIND.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 831: '1766, May 20 Death of Malhar Rao Holkar at Alampur (pp. 146, 217, 255, 269).'

IN-SIKAR.detail: The Battle of Maonda and Mandholi was fought between the Rajput rulers of Jaipur and the Jat rulers of Bharatpur in 1767 in Rajasthan.
IN-SIKAR.outcome: Jaipur victory; the Jat army fled at the first shock and abandoned its artillery and baggage, though Sombre's and Madec's battalions saved Jawahir Singh — who claimed a 'most Pyrrhic victory'
IN-SIKAR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 478-479: 'the Jaipur horse... at last threw themselves sword in hand on the Jat army, which fled away at the first shock... Jawahir had saved himself and the men of his army and claimed the victory; but it was a most Pyrrhic victory... Madho Singh followed up his success'. BOOKS DISAGREE: HCIP VIII chronology p. 832: '1767, December 14 Jawahir Singh wins a pyrrhic victory over Jaipur troops in the battle of Maonda'

IN-SIKAR.detail: Mahadji Sindhia's brigades under Benoît de Boigne break the Rajput confederacy of Jaipur and Jodhpur, with the Mughal contingent of Ismail Beg, on the plain at Patan. It is the victory that reverses the indecision of Lalsot three years earlier and opens Rajputana to Maratha tribute.
IN-SIKAR.belligerents: Gwalior (Scindia) vs Jaipur, Jodhpur (Marwar), Ismail Beg's Mughal troops
IN-SIKAR.outcome: Scindia victory; the Rajput confederacy broken (20 June 1790)
IN-SIKAR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire IV ch. 38. Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages I p. 256: 'Ismail Beg and Bijay Singh of Jodhpur had assisted Pratap Singh of Jaipur in the battle of Tunga. These three allies again joined their forces and challenged Sindhia, but De Boigne's battalions crushed them in the battle of Patan (20 June, 1790).'

IN-SIKAR.detail: The Battle of Fatehpur was fought in March 1799, in present-day Sikar district of India, between the Maratha Kingdom of Gwalior and the Rajput Kingdom of Jaipur.
IN-SIKAR.belligerents: Gwalior (Scindia) — Vaman Rao with George Thomas — vs Jaipur
IN-SIKAR.outcome: Scindia victory; George Thomas's corps routs the Jaipur army; the Rajputs lose over 2,000, Thomas 300
IN-SIKAR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire IV pp. 229–230 ('§10 Battle of Fathpur, February 1798'): 'The rout of the enemy was complete ... On that long and bloody day, the Rajput casualties exceeded 2,000, while Thomas lost 300 men.' Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages I p. 257: 'In 1799 the Marathas, assisted by George Thomas ... invaded Jaipur territory and defeated the Rajputs in the battle of Fatehpur.' Both books give the victory to the Maratha side; they differ on the year (Sarkar February 1798, Bakshi 1799).

PK-RAWALPINDI.detail: The Sikh conquest of Rawalpindi (1767) was the occupation of Rawalpindi by forces of Gujjar Singh Bhangi during the winter of 1767.
PK-RAWALPINDI.belligerents: Bhangi Misl vs Gakhars, Awans, Janjuas

PK-RAWALPINDI.text: Liaquat Ali Khan, the first prime minister, is shot dead at a public meeting in Company Bagh, Rawalpindi
PK-RAWALPINDI.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

PK-RAWALPINDI.detail: Ayub Khan resigns after months of protest and hands power to the army chief, General Yahya Khan
PK-RAWALPINDI.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

PK-RAWALPINDI.text: Operation Fair Play, the third coup
PK-RAWALPINDI.detail: General Zia-ul-Haq overthrows Zulfikar Ali Bhutto after the disputed election; martial law lasts eight years
PK-RAWALPINDI.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

PK-RAWALPINDI.text: Zulfikar Ali Bhutto is hanged in Rawalpindi Central Jail after a murder conviction his supporters called judicial
PK-RAWALPINDI.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

PK-RAWALPINDI.text: Benazir Bhutto is assassinated leaving a rally at Liaquat Bagh, Rawalpindi, the park where Liaquat Ali Khan was shot in 1951
PK-RAWALPINDI.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

IN-HAPUR.text: Najib-ud-Daula dies — Near Hapur on 31 October 1770
IN-HAPUR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire II p. 415: 'He had only reached the district of Hapur, when death overtook him on 31 October... Thus ended the career of the most powerful personality in India during these ten years.'

IN-ALIPURDUAR.text: The Company expels the Bhutanese from Cooch Behar
IN-ALIPURDUAR.detail: after Bhutan carries off the Cooch Behar raja (1772), a small Company force drives the Bhutanese out and takes the fort of Buxa; Cooch Behar accepts Company protection.
IN-ALIPURDUAR.belligerents: East India Company and Cooch Behar vs Bhutan (Deb Raja)
IN-ALIPURDUAR.outcome: East India Company victory; Bhutanese driven from Cooch Behar and Buxa taken
IN-ALIPURDUAR.source: HCIP IX p. 1020: 'In 1772, the Bhutanese invaded Cooch Behar and carried off the Raja ... The Cooch Behar ruling family solicited British aid. A small British force drove the Bhutanese out of Cooch Behar and captured the fort of Buxa.' (The 1773 date of the fighting is from its sequence; the book gives only 1772 for the invasion.)

IN-ALIPURDUAR.detail: Bhutan cedes the eighteen Duars and the Dewangiri hills to British India for a subsidy rising to Rs 50,000 a year, and submits disputes with Cooch Behar and Sikkim to Indian arbitration.
IN-ALIPURDUAR.source: HCIP IX p. 1024: 'a treaty was made on 11th November, 1865. The Government of India agreed, in return for the Duars, to pay to the Bhutan Government an annual sum of Rs. 25,000 in the first year ... and Rs. 50,000 on every succeeding year ... The 18 Duars was ceded to the Government of India.' The name Sinchula is web-only; the book gives only the date.

IN-SHAHJAHANPUR.text: Hafiz Rahmat Khan dies — Regent of the Rohillas, killed fighting at Miranpur Katra as Awadh and the Company conquered Rohilkhand.
IN-SHAHJAHANPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 118: 'The decisive battle was fought at Miranpur Katra six days later. Hafiz Rahmat Khan was killed fighting bravely.'

IN-SHAHJAHANPUR.text: Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah dies — The Faizabad maulavi who led the siege of the Lucknow Residency and styled himself King of Hindustan, shot at the gate of Powain and beheaded for the Company's reward.
IN-SHAHJAHANPUR.source: HCIP IX p. 573: 'On June 5, the Maulavi went to Powain... the Raja’s followers fired a volley and shot the Maulavi dead... Thus ended the career of one of the greatest patriots and leaders of the revolution of 1857'

IN-ANAND.detail: on 17 February 1775 the Barbhai regency's army under Haripant Phadke routs the ex-Peshwa Raghunathrao and Govindrao Gaekwad near Wasad on the Mahi. Raghunathrao flees to Surat and the English.
IN-ANAND.belligerents: Maratha Empire (Barbhai regency) vs Raghunathrao's faction and Govindrao Gaekwad
IN-ANAND.outcome: Maratha Empire victory; Raghunathrao's army utterly routed, his artillery and standard taken
IN-ANAND.source: Sardesai, New History of the Marathas III pp. 49–50: 'Haripant waited till the 17th February, when a severe action was fought in which the stars rewarded Haripant with victory. R'rao's army was utterly routed'; note: 'This battle is variously known after the several villages of the region, Napar, Anand-mogri and Adas'. HCIP VIII p. 286: 'defeated at Anand Mogri near Aras on 17 February, 1775'. (A second action on nearly the same field, 18/28 May 1775, Sardesai III p. 51 calls 'not decisive for either party'; that is the one usually called 'Arras'.)

IN-GURGAON.detail: The Battle of Pachgaon was fought on 26 January 1775 for accession to the throne of the Nagpur Kingdom in central India.
IN-GURGAON.outcome: Mudhoji Bhonsle victory; Sabaji Bhonsle killed
IN-GURGAON.source: HCIP VIII chronology p. 835: '1775, January 26 The battle of Panchgaon fought between Mudhoji Bhosle and Sabaji Bhosle in which Sabaji is killed.'

NP-NUWAKOT.text: Prithvi Narayan Shah dies — The Gorkha king who conquered the Kathmandu Valley (1768–69) and founded unified Nepal
NP-NUWAKOT.source: web-only; library silent on Prithvi Narayan Shah. Famous and uncontested; the founder of the Nepal state the atlas shows.

NP-NUWAKOT.text: The Nepal–Tibet war and the Chinese invasion of Nepal
NP-NUWAKOT.detail: after Gorkha raids into Tibet, a Qing army drives the Gurkhas back and advances to within a few miles of Kathmandu, forcing a peace; China tightens its grip on Tibet and closes the passes to India.
NP-NUWAKOT.belligerents: Qing China and Tibet vs Nepal
NP-NUWAKOT.outcome: Qing victory; Nepal accepts peace and quinquennial tribute to Peking
NP-NUWAKOT.source: HCIP IX p. 1059: 'in 1791-1792 when war broke out between Nepal and Tibet, leading to the intervention of China. A Chinese army supported the Tibetans in driving back the Gurkhas from Tibet and advancing within a few miles of the capital of Nepal.' HCIP IX p. 1021: 'in 1792, when the Gurkhas of Nepal invaded Tibet and a Chinese army drove them out ... they closed all the passes of Tibet to natives of India.'

IN-DHARWAD.detail: The Battle of Saunshi was fought between the Kingdom of Mysore and the Maratha Empire in 1777.
IN-DHARWAD.belligerents: Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu) vs Maratha Empire
IN-DHARWAD.outcome: Mysore victory; Haidar's general Muhammad Ali routs the Marathas at Saunshi
IN-DHARWAD.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III p. 247-248: 'came up with the Mahrattas at Saunsi (ten miles north of Savanur) and found them drawn up to offer him battle'; index: 'opposes and puts to rout the Mahrattas at Saunsi (Nov. 1776), 247-248'. The row's 1777 comes from Wikipedia.

IN-DHARWAD.detail: The Siege of Darwar was a 29 week siege of the fort at Dharwad in 1790 and 1791, then near the frontier, between the Kingdom of Mysore and the Maratha Empire.
IN-DHARWAD.belligerents: Maratha Empire, East India Company vs Kingdom of Mysore

IN-SHIVPURI.detail: after being surprised at Kolaras in March, Mahadji Sindhia harries Camac's and Muir's column and defeats it near Sipri (Shivpuri) on 1 July 1781, leading to the truce of October 1781 and the Treaty of Salbai.
IN-SHIVPURI.belligerents: Maratha Empire, Gwalior (Scindia) vs East India Company
IN-SHIVPURI.outcome: Maratha victory; the Company force defeated near Sipri, truce on 'no gain, no loss' terms in October
IN-SHIVPURI.source: HCIP VIII p. 257: 'Sindia improved his position by constantly harassing the enemy’s flanks and inflicting a defeat on 1 July, near Sipri. On 13 October, 1781 a temporary truce was effected between Mahadji Sindia and Col. Muir on terms of no gain, no loss to either party.'

IN-SHIVPURI.text: Tantia Tope dies — Hanged at Shivpuri after his betrayal by Man Singh of Narwar
IN-SHIVPURI.source: HCIP IX p. 585: 'Man Singh not only surrendered, but led a few sepoys of the British detachment to the hiding place of Tantia Topi... carried him to the British camp at Sipri. He was tried by a court martial on April 15, 1859, and was hanged on the 18th'

IN-CUDDALORE.detail: on 1 July 1781 Eyre Coote turns Haidar's entrenched position on the coast and routs his army — the Company's first great recovery after Pollilur.
IN-CUDDALORE.belligerents: East India Company vs Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu)
IN-CUDDALORE.outcome: East India Company victory; 'Haidar's defeat was thus complete'
IN-CUDDALORE.source: Hayavadana Rao, History of Mysore III p. 356: 'in a quarter of an hour his whole army was dispersed ... Haidar's defeat was thus complete'. HCIP VIII p. 459: 'It was a great tactical victory for the British, but it had no important strategic effects.'

IN-CUDDALORE.detail: The siege of Cuddalore was a siege attempt by British troops against a combined French and Mysorean garrison at the fortress of Cuddalore in the Second Anglo-Mysore War.
IN-CUDDALORE.belligerents: Kingdom of Great Britain British East India Company Hanover vs Sultanate of Mysore, Kingdom of France

IN-NAGAPATTINAM.detail: The siege of Negapatam was the first major offensive military action on the Indian subcontinent following the arrival of news that war had been declared.
IN-NAGAPATTINAM.belligerents: Kingdom of Great Britain vs Dutch Republic, 22x Sultanate of Mysore

IN-MORENA.detail: Mahadji Scindia mediates the peace that ends the first Anglo-Maratha war; the Company keeps Salsette, gives back everything else, and gets twenty years of peace with Poona.
