IN-MORENA.source: HCIP VIII p. 257: 'The temporary truce of 1781 was spelt out in a formal treaty of seventeen articles at Salbai on 17 May, 1782... Mahadji Sindia agreed to be “the mutual guarantee of both parties”... The English surrendered Raghunath Rao... and all the territories occupied by them except Salsette and two other islands near Bombay.'

IN-DAKSHINA-KANNADA.detail: The siege of Mangalore was conducted during the Second Anglo-Mysore War by Tipu Sultan and forces of the Kingdom of Mysore against a British East India Company garrison.
IN-DAKSHINA-KANNADA.belligerents: Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu) vs East India Company
IN-DAKSHINA-KANNADA.outcome: Mysore victory; Campbell's garrison capitulates on 30 January 1784 and is shipped to Tellicherry
IN-DAKSHINA-KANNADA.source: HCIP VIII p. 460: 'Tipu besieged Mangalore and the siege lasted from 20 May, 1783 to 30 January, 1784. Campbell, who defended the place capitulated on condition that the English garrison should be transported to Tellicherry.'

IN-DAKSHINA-KANNADA.detail: after Mangalore's garrison capitulates, Macartney's Madras Government makes peace with Tipu on 11 March 1784 on mutual restitution of conquests and prisoners — a treaty Englishmen regarded as humiliating.
IN-DAKSHINA-KANNADA.source: HCIP VIII p. 460: 'There was to be a mutual restitution of conquests. The prisoners were to be restored. The Treaty was signed on 11 March, 1784.' p. 461: 'the Treaty of Mangalore and the treaty itself were regarded by Englishmen as humiliating'.

PK-HYDERABAD.text: The Talpurs supplant the Kalhoras in Sindh
PK-HYDERABAD.detail: the Baluchi Talpur family ousted the Kalhora rulers and divided Sindh among branches at Hyderabad, Khairpur and Mirpur, nominally under the Durrani crown.
PK-HYDERABAD.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 202: 'At the end of the eighteenth century Sindh, nominally a part of the Durani kingdom in Afghanistan, was ruled by a Baluchi tribe called Talpuris who had ousted the Kaloras in 1783.'

PK-HYDERABAD.text: The Amirs of Sindh accept a subsidiary force
PK-HYDERABAD.detail: to open the road for the Army of the Indus, Khairpur became a protected state (treaty ratified 10 January 1839); Sir John Keane marched on Hyderabad, Karachi was seized, and the Hyderabad Amirs signed away Karachi on 3 February and took a subsidiary force on 11 March 1839.
PK-HYDERABAD.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 207: 'A treaty was concluded with the Khairpur State on December 24, 1838, and ratified by the Governor-General on January 10, 1839, by which it became a protected State'; p. 208: 'the recalcitrant Amirs who signed a treaty on February 3, 1839, surrendering Karachi (fort and town), and another on March 11, 1839, agreeing to receive a subsidiary force, not exceeding 5,000 men, and pay three lakhs yearly.'

PK-HYDERABAD.detail: Napier beats Sher Muhammad of Mirpur, the last Talpur Amir still in the field, six miles from Hyderabad on 24 March 1843; Mirpur and Umarkot fall and Sindh is annexed.
PK-HYDERABAD.belligerents: East India Company vs Sindh (Talpur Amirs)
PK-HYDERABAD.outcome: East India Company victory; Mirpur taken 27 March, Umarkot soon after; Sindh annexed (notification of 5 March 1843)
PK-HYDERABAD.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 214: 'Napier marched against him and defeated him at Dabo, six miles from Hyderabad, on March 24, 1843 ... Mirpur was taken on March 27, and Amarkot fell shortly after ... Already, on March 5, the annexation of Sindh had been virtually proclaimed by a notification.'

PK-HYDERABAD.detail: Napier defeats the Talpur Amirs and conquers Sindh
PK-HYDERABAD.belligerents: East India Company vs Sindh (Talpur Amirs)
PK-HYDERABAD.outcome: East India Company victory; about 6,000 Baluchis and 275 British killed; six Amirs surrender and Hyderabad is occupied on 20 February
PK-HYDERABAD.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 214: 'He marched with his army of 2,800 and defeated the enemy after a severely contested battle on February 17, 1843 ... The casualties were 275 British and 6,000 Baluchis. Six of the Amirs now surrendered as prisoners of war and Hyderabad was occupied on the 20th.'

IN-DAUSA.detail: The Battle of Tunga was a battle fought by the Rajput kingdoms of Jaipur and Jodhpur against the Marathas under Mahadji Scindia over the collection of taxes.
IN-DAUSA.belligerents: Gwalior (Scindia) vs Jaipur, Jodhpur (Marwar), Ismail Beg's Mughal troops
IN-DAUSA.outcome: Inconclusive — the battle at Tunga (28 July 1787) 'had no decisive result' (Sarkar III p. 380), but the emperor's Hindustani battalions deserted Mahadji Sindhia and he retreated to Dig: 'almost a second Panipat' for him (HCIP VIII p. 260), a strategic success for Jaipur and Jodhpur
IN-DAUSA.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire III p. 380: 'Thus the battle of Tunga,—miscalled that of Lalsot,—"though sanguinary, had no decisive result."' p. 387: '§11. The retreat from Lalsot, 1-9 Aug. 1787.' Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages I p. 256: 'fought an indecisive pitched battle at Tunga (also called Lalsot) in July 1787. The Rajputs claimed it as a great victory ... Within a few days he retreated from the Jaipur territory.' HCIP VIII p. 260: 'The battle of Lalsot against Rajput combination turned out to be almost a second Panipat on account of the desertion of the emperor's Hindustani battalions ... He himself retreated to the protection of the Jat Raja's fortress of Dig.'

IN-WEST-SIK.detail: the Gorkhas invade Sikkim in 1791 and by 1793 hold all its territory south and west of the Tista.
IN-WEST-SIK.outcome: Nepal victory; Sikkim west of the Tista annexed until restored by the Company in 1817
IN-WEST-SIK.source: HCIP IX p. 1065: 'the only important event after that seems to be a Nepalese invasion in 1791. Two years later, during the Sino-Napalese war, the Nepalese firmly established themselves in the Sikkim territory, lying to the south and west of the river Tista.'

IN-WEST-SIK.detail: Campbell’s levy, occupying Sikkim west of the Rangit to force the return of kidnapped subjects, is attacked by Sikkimese and Tibetan Bhutias on 27 November 1860 and flees to Darjeeling.
IN-WEST-SIK.belligerents: Kingdom of Sikkim (Namgyal) vs British Raj
IN-WEST-SIK.outcome: Sikkim victory; Campbell’s Sebundy Sappers routed, a havildar and nineteen sepoys captured with all arms and ammunition
IN-WEST-SIK.source: HCIP IX pp. 1068–1069: 'established his outpost at Ringchingpong. They were attacked on November 27 by a mixed force of Tibetan and Sikkim Bhutias under the direction of the Diwan and forced to retreat ... one Havildar and nineteen sepoys were captured by the Sikkim army, and all the arms and ammunition of Campbell’s force fell into their hands.'

IN-COIMBATORE.detail: The Siege of Coimbatore was a siege conducted by forces of the Kingdom of Mysore against a garrison of British East India Company and Travancorean troops.
IN-COIMBATORE.belligerents: Mysore Sultanate (Hyder Ali & Tipu) vs East India Company, Travancore
IN-COIMBATORE.outcome: Mysore victory; Tipu recaptures Coimbatore after Cornwallis's retreat
IN-COIMBATORE.source: HCIP VIII p. 464: 'His siege train having been destroyed, Cornwallis ... fell back to Bangalore. Tipu recaptured Coimbatore.'

IN-CHIKKABALLAPURA.detail: The Siege of Nundydroog was conducted by British Indian forces under the command of General Charles Cornwallis in October 1791, during the Third Anglo-Mysore War.
IN-CHIKKABALLAPURA.belligerents: Kingdom of Mysore vs East India Company

IN-BUNDI.detail: De Boigne's brigades and Sindhia's cavalry routed Tukoji Holkar's army (with Dudrenec's battalions) at the Lakheri pass on 1 June 1793, settling the Sindhia–Holkar rivalry in Rajputana in Sindhia's favour.
IN-BUNDI.outcome: Scindia victory; Holkar 'knocked out of the Rajput ring', Jaipur passes under Sindhia's control
IN-BUNDI.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire IV p. 50: 'by the middle of 1793, Holkar had been knocked out of the Rajput ring, in consequence of Sindhia's victory at Lakheri (1st June) and the Jaipur State came under Sindhia's control.' Battle narrative pp. 93–94. Bakshi, Rajasthan through the Ages I p. 256: 'The Sindhia-Holkar rivalry reached its climax in the battle of Lakheri (June 1793). Holkar's defeat decided the political issue in favour of Sindhia.'

IN-WAYANAD.detail: Kerala Varma Pazhassi Raja of Kottayam, passed over when the Company leased Kottayam to his uncle, stops the revenue and wages guerrilla war from Wynad; on 18 March 1797 Major Cameron's column is cut to pieces in the Periya pass and the Company treats.
IN-WAYANAD.belligerents: Pazhassi Raja (Kottayam) vs East India Company
IN-WAYANAD.outcome: Pazhassi victory; the Kurumbranad lease is cancelled and the Raja accepts a pension of Rs 8,000
IN-WAYANAD.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 261: 'On March 18, 1797, a contingent of 1,100 men under Major Cameron was ambushed and cut to pieces ... truce with the Pazhassi Raja became a matter of political expediency ... The agreement with the Kurumbranad Raja was cancelled'.

IN-WAYANAD.detail: when the Company claims Wynad under the 1799 partition, Pazhassi Raja's Nairs, Kurichiyas and Mappilas fight a guerrilla war (Panamaram fort taken in 1802) until Baber's Kolkars corner the Raja, who is shot dead on 30 November 1805.
IN-WAYANAD.belligerents: East India Company vs Pazhassi Raja (Kottayam)
IN-WAYANAD.outcome: East India Company victory; the Raja killed and the resistance collapses
IN-WAYANAD.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 261: 'In 1800 the Raja again rose in revolt ... The immediate cause ... was the British move to take possession of Wynad'; p. 263: 'On the 30th November 1805 the Raja was shot dead ... The death of the Pazhassi Raja symbolised the collapse of the resistance movement.'

IN-WAYANAD.text: Pazhassi Raja dies — Kerala Varma of the Kottayam house, who fought the Company from the Wynad forests for twelve years
IN-WAYANAD.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 263: 'On the 30th November 1805 the Raja was shot dead.'

IN-JORHAT.text: Gaurinath Singha dies — The Ahom king of the Moamaria rebellion, restored by Captain Welsh’s expedition
IN-JORHAT.source: HCIP IX p. 127: 'After the death of king Gaurinath Singh in A.D. 1795, the Bura Gohain, Purnananda, murdered his rival, the Bar Barua, and placed on the throne his own nominee Kamaleswar Singh'; its note 2 (p. 144): 'Bhuyan, p. 429; Banerjee gives the date as 1794.' Acharyya p. 131 lists his reign as ending 1794.

IN-JORHAT.detail: at the invitation of the fugitive Bar Phukan Badan Chandra, Bodawpaya’s army defeats the Assamese and occupies the Ahom capital Jorhat.
IN-JORHAT.outcome: Konbaung victory; Jorhat occupied, Badan Chandra installed in power under Chandrakanta Singha
IN-JORHAT.source: HCIP IX p. 128: 'Badan succeeded in inducing Bodawpaya, the powerful king of Burma, to send an expedition to Assam (A. D. 1817). The Assamese troops were severely defeated by the Burmese army which occupied Jorhat, the capital of Assam.'

IN-JORHAT.detail: Purandar Singha, installed by the Company as ruler of Upper Assam on 2 March 1833 and reduced to a jagirdar that June, is deposed in October 1838 and Upper Assam annexed.
IN-JORHAT.source: HCIP IX pp. 134–135: 'a treaty was concluded on March 2, 1833, at Gauhati by which Purandar Singh became the ruler of Upper Assam ... So Purandar Singh was formally dethroned or discharged from his Jagir in October 1838, and retired on a pension of Rs. 1,000 a month.'

IN-JORHAT.text: Maniram Dewan is hanged — The Assamese noble and tea pioneer executed at Jorhat for plotting a rising in Assam in 1857.
IN-JORHAT.source: Acharyya, History of Medieval Assam p. 27: the chronicle 'continues his account up to the execution of Mani Ram Dewan in 1858.' (Place, Jorhat, and the 1857 plot are web-only.)

IN-BELGAUM.detail: the Raja of Kolhapur, leading his army in person, defeats the Peshwa's general Parashuram Bhau Patwardhan near Pattankudi on 16 September 1799. Parashuram Bhau is mortally wounded.
IN-BELGAUM.outcome: Kolhapur victory; Parashuram Bhau Patwardhan totally defeated and mortally wounded
IN-BELGAUM.source: HCIP VIII p. 238: 'near the village of Pattankudi he encountered the Kolhapur forces headed by the Raja himself when he suffered a total defeat and was mortally wounded (16 September, 1799).'

IN-BELGAUM.text: Kittur Chennamma dies — In prison at Bailhongal, five years after her rising against the Company.
IN-BELGAUM.source: Wikipedia (web-only; to be promoted to a book citation)

IN-SIVAGANGA.text: The Marudu brothers (Periya and Chinna Marudu) die — the Sivaganga leaders of the 1800–01 poligar league and its Tiruchirappalli proclamation
IN-SIVAGANGA.source: web-only; library silent — HCIP VIII p. 628 records only the Palegar War of 1799-1801 and its end in the proclamation of 1 December 1801. The execution is uncontested and they are the war's central figures.

IN-AKOLA.detail: The Battle of Argaon took place on 29 November 1803, between the British under the command of Major-General Arthur Wellesley and the forces of the Bhonsles of Berar.
IN-AKOLA.belligerents: East India Company vs Nagpur (Bhonsle), Gwalior (Scindia)
IN-AKOLA.outcome: East India Company victory; the Bhonsle's army decisively defeated
IN-AKOLA.source: HCIP VIII p. 496: 'Wellesley's and Stevenson's combined army decisively defeated Bhosle at Argaon on 29 November, 1803. Bhosle's troops behaved with conspicuous gallantry.'

IN-EAST-DEL.detail: The Battle of Delhi or Battle of Patparganj took place on 11 September 1803 during the Second Anglo-Maratha War, and involved British East India Company troops of the Bombay Army.
IN-EAST-DEL.belligerents: East India Company vs Maratha Empire, Gwalior (Scindia)
IN-EAST-DEL.outcome: East India Company victory; Bourquien's corps of Perron's army broken at Patparganj and driven into the Jamuna, and Shah Alam II passed under British protection
IN-EAST-DEL.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire IV p. 292-293: 'It was a splendid victory; it completed the work begun at Aligarh by destroying Perron’s entire field army'; HCIP VIII chronology p. 841: '1803, September 11 The English army defeats Sindian forces at the battle of Delhi (pp. 266, 496).'

IN-ALWAR.detail: The Battle of Laswari took place on 1 November 1803 near Laswari village, Alwar.
IN-ALWAR.belligerents: East India Company vs Maratha Empire, Gwalior (Scindia)
IN-ALWAR.outcome: East India Company victory; 'the annihilation of the whole of the regular forces in Sindhia’s service', at a cost of 822 British casualties
IN-ALWAR.source: Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire IV p. 306: 'The battle of Laswari ended in “the annihilation of the whole of the regular forces in Sindhia’s service commanded by French officers,” as Lake justly claimed after his victory... On the British side 822 men were “killed and wounded”'; HCIP VIII chronology p. 842

IN-DEHRADUN.detail: Pradyumna Shah of Garhwal falls fighting the Gorkha invasion
IN-DEHRADUN.outcome: Nepal victory; Pradyumna Shah falls and Garhwal stays under Gorkha rule until 1815
IN-DEHRADUN.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-DEHRADUN.detail: the Company invades the Gorkha empire on a front from the Sutlej to the Kosi; checked at Nalapani and Jaithak, it wins in Kumaon and at Malaun (1815) and at Makwanpur (1816), and the Treaty of Sugauli ends the war.
IN-DEHRADUN.belligerents: East India Company, Garhwal Kingdom, Patiala State, Kingdom of Sikkim vs Nepal
IN-DEHRADUN.outcome: East India Company victory; by the Treaty of Sugauli (ratified 4 March 1816) Nepal cedes Garhwal and Kumaon west of the Kali and much of the Terai
IN-DEHRADUN.source: HCIP VIII pp. 531–532: 'The treaty of Sagauli signed in March 1816 made some modification in the terms concerning the cession of the Tarai ... this cession of Garhwal and Kumaon to the west of the Kali river drove a wedge of British territory between Sikh dominion on the one side and Gurkha dominion on the other.' HCIP IX p. 1025: 'the Anglo-Gurkha War which broke out in 1814 and was ended by the Treaty of Segowli on 4 March, 1816.'

IN-DEHRADUN.detail: the Gurkhas' epic stand at Kalanga opens the Anglo-Nepal War
IN-DEHRADUN.outcome: East India Company victory at heavy cost; Gillespie killed in an impatient first assault, and after bombardment Balbhadra’s garrison broke out and escaped
IN-DEHRADUN.source: HCIP VIII p. 531 (OCR partly garbled): 'The Gurkha commander, Balbhadra Singh, was a very intrepid soldier. Gillespie attempted an impatient assault, was killed ... bombardment was resorted to. The Gurkha commandant [evacuated] the place with the remnants of his garrison, escaping.'

PK-KASUR.detail: The battle of Kasur took place on 10 February 1807 between the Sikh Empire and the Afghan-appointed governor of Kasur, and was a part of the Afghan–Sikh Wars.
PK-KASUR.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs Kasur (Pathan chiefs Qutb-ud-din Khan and Nizam-ud-din's heirs)
PK-KASUR.outcome: Sikh Empire victory; Kasur fort stormed and the principality annexed, March 1807
PK-KASUR.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 72: 'The battle was fought on 10 February, 1807. The Afghans were forced to take shelter in the fort ... Phula Singh and his Nihangs made a sudden dash into a breach ... Qutb-ud-din was captured. Kasur was annexed in March, 1807.'

IN-KOLLAM.text: Revolt of Velu Thampi and Paliath Achan
IN-KOLLAM.detail: the chief ministers of Travancore and Cochin storm the Resident's house at Cochin (18 December 1808), attack Cochin, and Velu Thampi calls the people to arms in the Kundara Proclamation (11 January 1809); defeated at Quilon and deserted by his Raja, he kills himself.
IN-KOLLAM.belligerents: Travancore, Cochin vs East India Company
IN-KOLLAM.outcome: East India Company victory; Velu Thampi dies, Paliath Achan is deported, and Cochin becomes a subsidiary ally (6 May 1809)
IN-KOLLAM.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 264: 'On the midnight of December 18, 1808, the Resident's house at Cochin was stormed ... proclamation dated ... (January 11, 1809)'; p. 265: 'By a treaty concluded on 6th May 1809 Cochin became a subsidiary ally of the British'.

IN-PATHANAMTHITTA.text: Velu Thampi Dalawa dies — the Travancore minister who led the 1808–09 rising against the Company
IN-PATHANAMTHITTA.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 265: 'Here, he was overpowered by the Raja's men but before they could capture him alive, the Dalawa committed suicide.'

IN-BARAMULA.detail: The Battle of Baramulla was an engagement fought in 1814 during Ranjit Singh's expedition toward Kashmir.
IN-BARAMULA.outcome: Sikh victory The Sikh detachment later withdrew safely under negotiated terms

IN-BARAMULA.detail: Indian strikes on terrorist infrastructure across the border after the Pahalgam attack; ceasefire after four days of exchanges
IN-BARAMULA.outcome: Indian victory — stated objectives against terror infrastructure achieved
IN-BARAMULA.source: Wikipedia: List of wars involving India

IN-SOLAN.detail: Ochterlony, taking Ramgarh and the other Gurkha forts of the Sutlej hills one by one, forces Amar Singh Thapa to surrender Malaun (May 1815), ending Nepali rule west of the Kali.
IN-SOLAN.outcome: East India Company victory; Amar Singh Thapa surrenders Malaun and the Gorkha posts from the Sutlej to the Kali
IN-SOLAN.source: HCIP VIII p. 531: 'Ochterlony in the extreme west, however, succeeded in getting better of Amar Singh Thapa, the most celebrated of the Gurkha commanders. He succeeded in capturing two of the most important Gurkha forts' ... and 'compelled the Gurkha [commander Amar Singh] Thapa to surrender the strong fort of Malaun' (OCR partly garbled).

IN-ALMORA.detail: Gardner’s irregulars and Nicolls’s regulars push the Gorkhas back on Almora (April 1815) and force the surrender of Kumaon, although Hearsey’s column on the Kali is beaten and he is captured.
IN-ALMORA.outcome: East India Company victory; Nepal surrenders the whole of Kumaon with its forts
IN-ALMORA.source: HCIP VIII p. 531 (OCR partly garbled): 'Gardner succeeded in pushing the [Gurkh]as up to Almora. But Hearsey advancing up the Kali river [was defeated] by the Gurkhas and taken prisoner ... [the Gurkhas] had to surrender the whole district of Kumaon with all the forts.'

NP-MAKAWANPUR.detail: when the Darbar balks at ratifying the treaty, Ochterlony marches on Kathmandu and defeats the Gorkhas at Makwanpur, twenty miles from the capital (February 1816).
NP-MAKAWANPUR.outcome: East India Company victory; with the capital open to assault the Nepalese Darbar ratifies the Treaty of Sagauli
NP-MAKAWANPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 532: 'He came up with his enemy at Makwanpur, about 20 miles from Khatmandu and succeeded in defeating them. The rapid success of Ochterlony’s operations and the consciousness that the capital now lay open to assault, induced the Nepalese Darbar to ratify the treaty.'

IN-PURBA-CHAMPARAN.detail: signed 2 December 1815 and ratified by Nepal on 4 March 1816 after Makwanpur, it ends the Anglo-Nepal war — Nepal cedes Garhwal and Kumaon west of the Kali and much of the Terai (part restored in 1816), accepts a British Resident at Kathmandu and gives up Sikkim.
IN-PURBA-CHAMPARAN.source: HCIP IX p. 1025: 'the Anglo-Gurkha War which broke out in 1814 and was ended by the Treaty of Segowli on 4 March, 1816.' HCIP VIII p. 532: 'The treaty of Sagauli signed in March 1816 made some modification in the terms concerning the cession of the Tarai ... this cession of Garhwal and Kumaon to the west of the Kali river drove a wedge of British territory between Sikh dominion on the one side and Gurkha dominion on the other.' The first signature (2 December 1815) is web-only; the library dates only the March 1816 ratification.

IN-UTTAR-DINAJPUR.detail: the Company restores to the Raja of Sikkim the lands the Gorkhas had taken west of the Tista, and Sikkim becomes a Company protectorate (February 1817).
IN-UTTAR-DINAJPUR.source: HCIP VIII p. 532: 'A portion of the Tarai was given to the Raja of Sikkim. The Raja of Sikkim also signed a protective treaty in February 1817.' HCIP IX p. 1066: 'by a treaty concluded in 1817, restored to the Raja of Sikkim the territory that had been wrested from him by the Nepalese.'

LK-BADULLA.detail: The Uva-Wellassa rising — the Kandyan chiefs rose against the British and were put down by a scorched-earth campaign. Crops, cattle, granaries and irrigation tanks were destroyed and Uva was left depopulated for generations. Keppetipola Disawe was executed in November 1818 and the guarantees of the Kandyan Convention were revoked.
LK-BADULLA.belligerents: Kandyan chiefs and the Uva-Wellassa peasantry vs British Ceylon
LK-BADULLA.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

PK-BHAKKAR.detail: The Siege of Mankera, also known as the Fall of Mankera, was a military conflict from 7 December 1821 to 1 January 1822, fought by the Sikh forces led by Ranjit Singh.
PK-BHAKKAR.belligerents: Sikh Empire, Assisted by, Tiwanas of Mitha Tiwana vs Mankera State

BD-COX-S-BAZAR.detail: Maha Bandula, advancing from Arakan, overwhelms the Company’s detachment at Ramu in Chittagong district on 17 May 1824 — the Company’s worst defeat of the first Burmese war.
BD-COX-S-BAZAR.belligerents: Konbaung (Burmese) Empire vs East India Company
BD-COX-S-BAZAR.outcome: Konbaung victory; the British retreat 'turned out to be a veritable rout', the captain and most officers killed, and troops pulled back from Sylhet to cover Chittagong
BD-COX-S-BAZAR.source: HCIP IX p. 102: 'On May 17, 1824, Maha Bandula attacked this post ... the British detachment had to retreat; and the retreat turned out to be a veritable rout ... the Captain and the rest were all killed.'

IN-CACHAR.belligerents: East India Company and Manipur (Gambhir Singh) vs Konbaung (Burmese) Empire
IN-CACHAR.outcome: East India Company victory; by the Treaty of Yandabo (24 February 1826) Ava renounces Assam, Cachar and Jaintia, recognises Gambhir Singh in Manipur, cedes Arakan and Tenasserim and pays one crore — at a cost of some 15,000 Company dead, mostly of disease
IN-CACHAR.source: HCIP IX pp. 101–110: 'The British Government issued a formal declaration of war on February 24, 1824' (p. 101); 'The treaty was signed at Yandabo on February 24, 1826' (p. 107); '40,000 men passed through the cadres, 15,000 died, and the war cost £5,000,000' (p. 110).

IN-CACHAR.detail: after Raja Govinda Chandra is assassinated (24 April 1830) — a murder the Company traced to Gambhir Singh of Manipur — the Company refuses every claimant and annexes the Kachari kingdom of the plains.
IN-CACHAR.source: HCIP IX pp. 136–137: 'Govinda Chandra was assassinated on April 24, 1830 ... Having thus disposed of all the claims the British Government annexed Cachar.' Year 1832 (proclamation of 14 August 1832) is web-only; the book gives no year.

IN-WEST-KHASI-HILLS.text: The Khasi rising of U Tirot Singh
IN-WEST-KHASI-HILLS.detail: the Khasi chiefs, resenting the Company’s road through their hills, massacre the post at Nongkhlaw on 5 May 1829 and fight a four-year guerrilla war from the hills.
IN-WEST-KHASI-HILLS.belligerents: Khasi States (U Tirot Singh of Nongkhlaw, Bar Manik) vs East India Company
IN-WEST-KHASI-HILLS.outcome: East India Company victory; Tirot Singh surrenders in January 1833 on promise of his life
IN-WEST-KHASI-HILLS.source: HCIP IX pp. 453: 'On 5 May, 1829, a strong party of Khasis, aided by the Garos, raided Nunklow and massacred the European and Bengali inmates ... The long and harassing warfare with the Khasis continued for four years ... Tirut Singh surrendered in January, 1833, on condition that his life should be spared.'

IN-RANCHI.detail: the Mundas of Chota Nagpur, joined by the Hos, rise against revenue-farmers from outside and the new Bengal regulations; the revolt spreads over Ranchi, Hazaribagh, Palamau and Manbhum and about a thousand settlers are killed.
IN-RANCHI.belligerents: Kols (Mundas and Hos) of Chota Nagpur vs East India Company
IN-RANCHI.outcome: East India Company victory; suppressed in March 1832 after extensive operations — Buddho Bhagat died defending his village with 150 followers
IN-RANCHI.source: HCIP IX p. 455: 'when the Mundas of Chota Nagpur broke out into revolt in 1831, the Hos joined them ... After extensive military operations the insurrection was suppressed in March, 1832 ... one, Buddho Bhagat, rather than surrender, perished with his whole family and 150 followers in defending his village.'

IN-PURBI-SINGHBHUM.detail: a disappointed claimant to Barabhum kills the diwan, sacks Barabazar and, with Chuar and Bhumij levies, drives the government force back to Bankura in June 1832.
IN-PURBI-SINGHBHUM.belligerents: Bhumij and Chuars (Ganganarayan) vs East India Company
IN-PURBI-SINGHBHUM.outcome: East India Company victory; troops scour the country late in 1832 and Ganganarayan’s death ends the rising
IN-PURBI-SINGHBHUM.source: HCIP IX pp. 455–456: 'in the first week of June, 1832, government force had to retire to Bankura leaving Barabhum to the possession of the rebel chief. Ganganarayan assumed the title of raja ... the death of Ganganarayan, shortly after, put an end to the insurrection.'

IN-KODAGU.detail: after a quarrel over fugitives and a detained envoy, four Company columns invade Coorg; Madikeri falls on 6 April 1834, Coorg is annexed five days later and Chikka Virarajendra goes into exile.
IN-KODAGU.belligerents: East India Company vs Kingdom of Coorg
IN-KODAGU.outcome: East India Company victory; Coorg annexed (April 1834)
IN-KODAGU.source: HCIP IX p. 43: 'On April 6, the British force entered the capital of Coorg, Madikeri or Mercara, and five days later Coorg was annexed to the British dominions by a formal Proclamation. The Raja, Viraraja the Younger, surrendered with his family on April 23.'

IN-LEH-LADAKH.detail: Zorawar Singh, Gulab Singh's governor of Kishtwar, marched through the Suru valley, beat the Ladakhis and forced the Gyalpo to pay a war indemnity and tribute; a Dogra fort was built outside Leh.
IN-LEH-LADAKH.outcome: Dogra victory; the Gyalpo pays Rs 50,000 and an annual tribute of Rs 20,000, Ladakh annexed to Jammu
IN-LEH-LADAKH.source: Gupta, History of the Sikhs V p. 195: 'Zorawar Singh at the head of troops marched from Kishtwar ... The advance guard under Mehta Basti Ram fought against the Ladakhis ... Eventually Gyalpo agreed to pay Rs. 50,000 as the cost of war and an annual tribute of Rs. 20,000. A fort was built outside the city of Leh.'

IN-LEH-LADAKH.detail: The Dogra–Tibetan war, also called the Sino–Sikh war, was fought from May 1841 to August 1842 by the Dogra-led Kingdom of Jammu, a federal subject of the Sikh Empire.
IN-LEH-LADAKH.belligerents: Qing dynasty Tibet vs Sikh Empire Dogra dynasty
IN-LEH-LADAKH.outcome: Inconclusive — status quo ante; Ladakh confirmed under the Dogras by the Treaty of Chushul

IN-LEH-LADAKH.detail: The Battle of Chushul was one of the major engagements of the Dogra–Tibetan war fought between the Dogra dynasty against the Tibetans under the Qing dynasty.
IN-LEH-LADAKH.belligerents: Sikh Empire Dogra dynasty vs Qing dynasty Tibet
IN-LEH-LADAKH.outcome: Tibetan attack on Ladakh repulsed by Rajputs Dogra dynasty annexes Ladakh

IN-LEH-LADAKH.detail: 114 men of 13 Kumaon hold the Chushul approach to the last round; Major Shaitan Singh is awarded the Param Vir Chakra
IN-LEH-LADAKH.outcome: Chinese advance on Chushul halted at ruinous cost — 114 of 120 defenders killed
IN-LEH-LADAKH.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

BD-SYLHET.detail: on the pretext of human sacrifices at Gobha, the Company confiscates Raja Rajendra Singh’s plains (proclamation of 15 March 1835); he gives up the hills, and the Court of Directors condemns the act but does not reverse it.
BD-SYLHET.source: HCIP IX p. 139: 'On March 15, 1835, Jaintia Pargana was formally annexed to the British dominion by a formal proclamation, and Gobha was annexed a few weeks later. Rajendra Singh thereupon voluntarily gave up the hilly tracts of his dominion.'

IN-DARJILING.detail: the Raja of Sikkim is induced to grant the Darjeeling tract to the Company unconditionally by a Deed of Grant (February 1835).
IN-DARJILING.source: HCIP IX p. 1066: 'This was effected about a decade later in February, 1835, when the Raja of Sikkim was induced to cede unconditionally the Darjeeling tract under a Deed of Grant.'

IN-DARJILING.detail: after Campbell and Hooker are seized in Sikkim (November 1849), Dalhousie annexes the Morang (Terai) and the Darjeeling hills west of the Tista — about 1,670 square miles — and stops the Raja’s allowance.
IN-DARJILING.source: HCIP IX p. 1068: 'Lord Dalhousie took very strong measures against the Raja and annexed the hill tracts of Darjeeling west of the Tista and the Murung (Terai) district. The Raja’s allowance was also stopped.' HCIP IX p. 90: 'an outlying tract of Sikkim, about 1670 sq. miles in area, was added to British India'; p. 47: 'partly by a military expedition in 1850.'

IN-MALAPPURAM.detail: twenty-two violent outbreaks in Ernad and Valluvanad against Hindu landlords and the Company's order; in 1855 the Malabar District Magistrate H. V. Conolly is murdered at Calicut.
IN-MALAPPURAM.source: Sreedhara Menon, Survey of Kerala History p. 280: 'Twenty-two such riots were reported from different parts of Malabar, particularly the Ernad and Valluvanad taluks, during the period 1836-1856'; p. 281: 'in 1855 H.V. Connolly, the District Magistrate of Malabar, was murdered by four Mappila convicts in his bungalow at Calicut.'

IN-TINSUKIA.detail: when Bar Senapati’s heirs refuse a tribute and the separation of Moran, the Company annexes the Moamaria (Matak) chiefdom to Lakhimpur district in November 1839.
IN-TINSUKIA.source: HCIP IX p. 142: 'This was strenuously opposed not only by Maju Gohain but all the other brothers ... So the British Government annexed Matak to the Lakhimpur district in November, 1839.'

IN-TINSUKIA.detail: the Khamtis surprise the Company’s post at Sadiya, destroy its garrison and kill Political Agent Major White; the Singphos rise alongside them.
IN-TINSUKIA.belligerents: Khamtis (and Singphos) vs East India Company
IN-TINSUKIA.outcome: East India Company victory; order restored with the Matak chief’s help, the Khamtis withdraw to the Mishmi hills and the last surrender in December 1843
IN-TINSUKIA.source: HCIP IX p. 141: 'They suddenly attacked Sadiya, destroyed the British regiment stationed there, and burnt the barracks. Major White himself was killed in action. With the help of the Matak Chief, order was restored ... The rising was not however put down till December 1843.' (p. 454 dates the Singpho rising 1839 and calls White 'Col.')

PK-KALAT.detail: The storming of Kalat — a British column takes the Khanate capital; Mehrab Khan dies defending it
PK-KALAT.outcome: Company victory — a puppet khan installed
PK-KALAT.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-FIROZPUR.detail: The Battle of Ferozeshah was fought on 21 December and 22 December 1845 between the British East India Company and the Sikh Empire, at the village of Ferozeshah in Punjab.
IN-FIROZPUR.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs East India Company

IN-FIROZPUR.detail: the first clash of the First Anglo-Sikh War
IN-FIROZPUR.belligerents: East India Company vs Sikh Empire
IN-FIROZPUR.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 49: 'the four successive battles of Mudki (December 18, 1845), Firozshah (December 21-22), Aliwal (January 28, 1846) and Sobraon (February 10, 1846)'; p. 270: 'After the battle had begun, Lal Singh, according to plan, deserted the army ... the Sikh force was repulsed.'

IN-FIROZPUR.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs East India Company and Patiala
IN-FIROZPUR.source: Wikipedia: List of wars in the Indian subcontinent

IN-TARN-TARAN.detail: The Battle of Sobraon was fought on 10 February 1846, between the forces of the East India Company and the Sikh Khalsa Army.
IN-TARN-TARAN.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs British Empire, East India Company

IN-TARN-TARAN.detail: Pakistan's 1 Armoured Division is destroyed in the sugarcane fields near Khem Karan — the 'graveyard of Patton tanks'
IN-TARN-TARAN.outcome: Decisive Indian victory — around 97 Pakistani tanks lost or captured
IN-TARN-TARAN.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-KANDHAMAL.detail: the Khonds of Gumsur and the Khondmals, fearing for their lands, rise against the Company’s campaign against Meriah sacrifice and hold out in the hills for three years under Chakra Bisayi.
IN-KANDHAMAL.belligerents: Khonds (Chakra Bisayi) vs East India Company
IN-KANDHAMAL.outcome: East India Company victory; suppressed in 1848 and the exiled Khond chief recalled, though Chakra Bisayi fought on to 1855
IN-KANDHAMAL.source: HCIP IX p. 456: 'made the Khonds to break into an open rebellion in 1846 ... the Khonds, undaunted by defeat, held out in the depths of their highland lairs. When, in 1848, the rebellion was suppressed, the exiled Khond Chief was recalled and placed at the head of Khonds.'

PK-MANDI-BAHAUDDIN.detail: the Sikhs maul the Company army in one of its hardest-fought battles
PK-MANDI-BAHAUDDIN.belligerents: Sikh Empire vs East India Company
PK-MANDI-BAHAUDDIN.outcome: Inconclusive — the British lost 2,446 men and the colours of three regiments; some count it a British victory, others a defeat, many a drawn battle
PK-MANDI-BAHAUDDIN.source: HCIP IX, British Paramountcy p. 285: 'When night fell the British had lost 2,446 men and the colours of three regiments ... The result of the battle of Chilianwala has been estimated in various ways. Some regard it as a victory of the British; others, including many Englishmen, look upon it as a defeat; while many describe it as a drawn battle.'

IN-KANPUR-NAGAR.text: Bajirao II dies — the last Peshwa, at Bithur after thirty-three years on a British pension.
IN-KANPUR-NAGAR.source: HCIP VIII p. 507: 'Baji Rao II was allowed to live at Bithur, 12 miles north-west of Kanpur, for more than thirty years in splendid isolation till his death on 14 January, 1851.'

IN-KANPUR-NAGAR.detail: Tantia Tope's Gwalior Contingent defeats Windham and takes Kanpur city (27–28 November), but Campbell, hurrying back from Lucknow, routs him on 6 December — the last battle for Kanpur.
IN-KANPUR-NAGAR.belligerents: East India Company vs Tantia Tope's army (Gwalior Contingent rebels, Nana Sahib's forces)
IN-KANPUR-NAGAR.outcome: East India Company victory; Tantia Tope routed and driven back on Kalpi, after first beating Windham
IN-KANPUR-NAGAR.source: HCIP IX p. 568: 'Though Tantia was defeated on the Pandu-nadi on 26 November, he attacked Kanpur the next day, and after a strenuous fight for two days repulsed the British troops... Sir Collin Campbell... hastened back to Kanpur and won a complete victory over Tantia’s troops on 6 December. That was the last battle fought for Kanpur.'

IN-KANPUR-NAGAR.detail: The siege of Cawnpore was a key episode in the Indian Rebellion of 1857.
IN-KANPUR-NAGAR.belligerents: East India Company vs Nana Sahib's forces, Rebel Company soldiers

IN-DIMA-HASAO.detail: Tularam’s hill kingdom, left to him in 1834 and kept by his sons after his death in 1851, is annexed when Nakulram attacks a Naga village without Company consent.
IN-DIMA-HASAO.source: HCIP IX p. 138: 'The act of Nakulram was a violation of article 7 of the treaty whereby he had agreed not to make war without the consent of the British. Accordingly, the country was formally annexed to the British dominions in 1854.'

IN-BHOJPUR.detail: The siege of Arrah took place during the Indian Mutiny.
IN-BHOJPUR.belligerents: East India Company, United Kingdom vs Jagdishpur estate, Mutinying Sepoys
IN-BHOJPUR.outcome: East India Company victory; Boyle’s house held out from 27 July, Dunbar’s relief column was cut up on 29 July, and Vincent Eyre relieved Arrah on 3 August 1857 and sacked Jagdishpur
IN-BHOJPUR.source: HCIP IX p. 551: 'On July 27 the Danapur mutineers reached Arrah ... attacked Boyle’s house, under the leadership of Kunwar Singh ... On the 29th a detachment under Captain Dunbar ... was attacked at night ... and forced to retreat with heavy loss ... Arrah was relieved, on August 3, by Vincent Eyre.'

IN-BHOJPUR.detail: back in his home village after his Azamgarh campaign, the aged Kunwar Singh routs Le Grand’s column from Arrah on 23 April 1858 — his last victory, three days before his death.
IN-BHOJPUR.belligerents: Jagdishpur (Kunwar Singh, Amar Singh) vs East India Company
IN-BHOJPUR.outcome: Jagdishpur victory; two-thirds of the British force, including Le Grand, killed and the rest flee to Arrah
IN-BHOJPUR.source: HCIP IX p. 579: 'Next day Kunwar was attacked by a detachment of British troops from Arrah led by Le Grand ... the British were forced to retreat and the retreat was soon converted to a rout. It was a veritable disaster. Two-thirds of the British force, including the commander, were killed ... this was the last great victory of the old veteran.'

IN-BHOJPUR.text: Kunwar Singh dies — At Jagdishpur, days after routing Le Grand’s column there, of the wound (his right wrist amputated) taken as he crossed the Ganga
IN-BHOJPUR.source: HCIP IX p. 579: 'But this was the last great victory of the old veteran. Three days later Kunwar Singh died at his own house at Jagdishpur. He had been hit by a cannon ball and his right wrist was amputated ... Evidently this brought about the end on 9 May, 1858.' The page gives both 'three days later' (i.e. c. 26 April) and 9 May 1858.

NP-BANKE.text: The Naya Muluk restored to Nepal
NP-BANKE.detail: for Jang Bahadur’s help in 1857–58 the Government of India returns a large part of the western Terai ceded at Sugauli (Banke, Bardiya, Kailali, Kanchanpur).
NP-BANKE.source: HCIP IX p. 1026: 'As a reward for his services the Government of India restored to Nepal a large part of the former Gurkha possessions in the Terai, which had been ceded to the British in 1816.' Year 1860 (treaty of 1 November 1860) is web-only; the book gives no year.

IN-NORTH-SIK.detail: Gawler’s column reaches the Sikkim capital almost unopposed and on 28 March 1861 the heir Sidkyong Namgyal signs a treaty that fines Sikkim, expels the Diwan, bans slave-dealing and opens the road to Tibet — 'practically reduced to vassalage'.
IN-NORTH-SIK.source: HCIP IX p. 1069: 'On 28 March, 1861, a new treaty was concluded with the heir apparent, Sidkyong Nam Gyal ... all former treaties were abrogated ... which meant that Sikkim was practically reduced to vassalage. The Raja was fined Rs. 7,000.'

PK-CHITRAL.detail: a besieged garrison is relieved across the high passes
PK-CHITRAL.belligerents: British Raj vs Chitrali & Jandoli forces

PK-HANGU.detail: twenty-one Sikh soldiers' last stand against thousands
PK-HANGU.belligerents: British Raj (36th Sikhs) vs Afridi & Orakzai tribes

PK-MALAKAND.detail: the frontier rising breaks against the Malakand garrison
PK-MALAKAND.belligerents: British Raj vs Pashtun tribal rising

IN-KOHIMA.detail: the 'Stalingrad of the East' — the Japanese advance is halted on the tennis court of the Deputy Commissioner's bungalow
IN-KOHIMA.outcome: Allied victory — the turning point of the Burma campaign
IN-KOHIMA.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-GILGIT.detail: In November 1947, the paramilitary force of Gilgit Scouts stationed at Gilgit rebelled against the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, soon after it acceded to the Indian Union.
IN-GILGIT.belligerents: India & Jammu and Kashmir State Forces vs Gilgit Scouts & Pakistan
IN-GILGIT.outcome: Pakistani victory — Gilgit-Baltistan passes out of the Maharaja's control

IN-BADGAM.detail: Major Somnath Sharma's company holds the approach to Srinagar aerodrome and wins the first Param Vir Chakra
IN-BADGAM.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-GANDERBAL.detail: the raiders' advance on Srinagar is broken on the city's outskirts
IN-GANDERBAL.outcome: Decisive Indian victory — the tribal lashkars are routed and Baramulla retaken
IN-GANDERBAL.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-SKARDU.detail: The siege of Skardu was a prolonged military blockade carried out by the pro-Pakistani forces of Ibex Force, Chitral Scouts and Chitral State Bodyguards.
IN-SKARDU.belligerents: India, Jammu and Kashmir State Forces vs Pakistan, Chitral Scouts

IN-TAWANG.detail: the opening Chinese assault overruns 7 Infantry Brigade below Thagla ridge
IN-TAWANG.outcome: Chinese victory — the brigade is destroyed and Tawang falls
IN-TAWANG.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-ANJAW.detail: the easternmost battle of the war, held for three weeks against repeated assaults
IN-ANJAW.outcome: Chinese victory after prolonged Indian resistance
IN-ANJAW.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-AJK.detail: Indian infantry take the pass astride the infiltration route into Kashmir
IN-AJK.outcome: Indian victory — the pass captured (returned at Tashkent)
IN-AJK.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-EAST-SIK.text: Nathu La and Cho La clashes
IN-EAST-SIK.detail: Indian troops hold the Sikkim passes in the sharpest fighting since 1962
IN-EAST-SIK.outcome: Indian victory — Chinese forces pushed back from the passes
IN-EAST-SIK.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-SAMBA.detail: the decisive armoured battle of the western front; Second Lieutenant Arun Khetarpal is awarded a posthumous Param Vir Chakra
IN-SAMBA.outcome: Decisive Indian victory — the Shakargarh bulge secured
IN-SAMBA.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

BD-DINAJPUR.detail: the bitterest fighting of the eastern campaign, contested for a fortnight
BD-DINAJPUR.outcome: Indian victory after heavy casualties on both sides
BD-DINAJPUR.source: Wikipedia: List of battles involving India

IN-GHANCHE.detail: India occupies the Siachen Glacier, the highest battlefield on earth
IN-GHANCHE.outcome: Indian victory — Siachen and the Saltoro ridge secured
IN-GHANCHE.source: Wikipedia: List of wars involving India

LK-KILINOCHCHI.detail: the LTTE besieged the base commanding the isthmus into the Jaffna peninsula and a seaborne relief force broke through after a month. The largest set-piece battle of the war to that point, and a government victory.
LK-KILINOCHCHI.belligerents: LTTE vs the Sri Lanka Army
LK-KILINOCHCHI.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-KILINOCHCHI.detail: The fall of Elephant Pass — an LTTE offensive rolled back everything the army had gained in the Vanni and took the isthmus in April, reaching the outskirts of Jaffna before it was halted. The high-water mark of the Tigers as a conventional force.
LK-KILINOCHCHI.belligerents: LTTE vs the Sri Lanka Army
LK-KILINOCHCHI.outcome: LTTE victory; the army loses the Vanni and the isthmus
LK-KILINOCHCHI.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-MULLAITIVU.detail: the LTTE overran the army base in four days and killed more than a thousand soldiers, one of the worst defeats the army suffered. Six months earlier a suicide bombing at the Central Bank in Colombo had killed about a hundred civilians and injured fourteen hundred.
LK-MULLAITIVU.belligerents: LTTE vs the Sri Lanka Army
LK-MULLAITIVU.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

LK-MULLAITIVU.text: Battle of Mullivaikkal and the end of the war
LK-MULLAITIVU.detail: the last months were fought in a strip of coast a few kilometres across holding something over 300,000 civilians. Successive government-declared no-fire zones were shelled and hospitals inside them struck more than two dozen times; the LTTE held the population as a buffer and shot people who tried to leave. Fighting ended on 18 May and Prabhakaran was found dead the next day. The LTTE was destroyed and the war was over after twenty-six years. Civilian deaths in this phase are disputed and no independent forensic accounting has ever been allowed: a contemporaneous UN field tally counted 7,721 killed to 13 May, the UN Secretary-General's Panel of Experts held in 2011 that a figure as high as 40,000 could not be ruled out, and the state has never published a count of its own. The Panel found credible allegations of war crimes against both sides; none has been adjudicated.
LK-MULLAITIVU.belligerents: Sri Lanka Armed Forces vs the LTTE, with over 300,000 civilians inside the pocket
LK-MULLAITIVU.outcome: The LTTE destroyed and the civil war ended; the civilian death toll disputed
LK-MULLAITIVU.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

NP-ROLPA.detail: The Maoist insurgency begins — the CPN (Maoist) attacks police posts in Rolpa, Rukum and Sindhuli on 13 February, opening a ten-year "People's War" that kills some 17,000
NP-ROLPA.belligerents: Government of Nepal vs Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist)
NP-ROLPA.outcome: Comprehensive Peace Accord, November 2006; the Maoists enter parliament
NP-ROLPA.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

LK-VAVUNIYA.detail: an eighteen-month attempt to force a land corridor up the A9 to Kilinochchi, the longest and costliest operation of the war. It was abandoned in December 1998 without reaching its objective.
LK-VAVUNIYA.belligerents: Sri Lanka Army vs the LTTE
LK-VAVUNIYA.outcome: Government failure; the corridor never opened
LK-VAVUNIYA.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

PK-ISLAMABAD-CAPITAL-TERRITORY.detail: General Pervez Musharraf's army takes Islamabad after Nawaz Sharif tries to dismiss him while his flight is in the air
PK-ISLAMABAD-CAPITAL-TERRITORY.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

PK-ISLAMABAD-CAPITAL-TERRITORY.detail: after a week-long stand-off the army storms the Red Mosque in the capital; over a hundred die, and the Pakistani Taliban's war on the state begins
PK-ISLAMABAD-CAPITAL-TERRITORY.belligerents: Pakistan Army vs the Lal Masjid militants
PK-ISLAMABAD-CAPITAL-TERRITORY.outcome: The mosque is taken; a wave of suicide bombings follows
PK-ISLAMABAD-CAPITAL-TERRITORY.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

PK-ISLAMABAD-CAPITAL-TERRITORY.text: Imran Khan becomes the first prime minister removed by a vote of no confidence
PK-ISLAMABAD-CAPITAL-TERRITORY.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)

LK-GAMPAHA.detail: The raid on Katunayake — LTTE commandos destroyed half the air force combat fleet and several airliners on the ground beside the international airport. The insurance and tourism consequences pushed both sides towards the ceasefire.
LK-GAMPAHA.belligerents: LTTE Black Tigers vs the Sri Lanka Air Force
LK-GAMPAHA.outcome: Half the combat fleet destroyed; a direct pressure toward the 2002 ceasefire
LK-GAMPAHA.source: BharatRajya research pass, Sri Lanka (see scripts/add_srilanka_battles.py)

NP-GORKHA.text: The Gorkha earthquake of 25 April kills nearly 9,000
NP-GORKHA.source: BharatRajya research pass, the neighbours after 1947 (Wikipedia)
